tt03/robbertvanginkel_hamming74.summary: This project implements a Hamming(7,4) encoder and decoder for error correction. It has a mode pin to select between encoding (0) and decoding (1), with 4-bit input and 7-bit output in encode mode, and 7-bit input with 4-bit data plus error flag in decode mode. The design is purely combinational and can be tested using the provided Python test script. It is a compact hardware implementation of a classic error-correcting code.
tt03/robbertvanginkel_hamming74.review_notes: The input pins and operation only describe encode/decode modes, not discrete encoder/decoder circuits, so those type tags were removed.

tt03/rolfmobile99_alu_fsm_top.summary: This design is a 4-bit ALU inspired by the Supercon.6 badge, implemented as a finite state machine with combinational logic in Verilog. It takes two 4-bit data inputs and a control signal, and produces a 4-bit result along with a carry-out. The design is tested using cocotb, a Python-based verification framework. No external hardware is required.
tt03/rolfmobile99_alu_fsm_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'art' tag; added 'education' for the badge/teaching context.

tt03/rotary_encoder.summary: This design reads an incremental rotary encoder and displays the resulting count on a seven-segment display. It samples the encoder pins every clock cycle, detects rising edges on pin A, and increments or decrements a 4-bit counter based on the state of pin B, with a debounce period of 125 clock cycles. The design requires an external rotary encoder connected to pins A and B. After reset, turning the encoder updates the displayed count.

tt03/s4ga.summary: This design implements a single fracturable 5-input lookup table (LUT) that can be configured via serial SRAM or FLASH frames. It receives 92-bit LUT configuration frames serially, four bits per cycle, and evaluates the LUT every 23 clock cycles. The last 283 LUT output values are stored on-chip to serve as inputs for subsequent LUTs, and the design includes two FPGA input pins and seven output pins plus a debug pin. Testing is described as tricky, and external serial memory is required for configuration.

tt03/secretFile.summary: This project is titled 'Secret File' and provides no meaningful documentation; the one-line description says 'Nothing to see here' and the how-it-works section states 'Leving it alone works'. The design has a clock input and eight output bits, but no explanation of their function. The test instructions say 'Don't test me' and the external hardware requirement is a shredder, indicating a humorous or intentionally undocumented design. There is insufficient information to determine what the design actually does.
tt03/secretFile.review_notes: Removed security tag as unsupported; the project is intentionally undocumented rather than security-focused.

tt03/seven_segment_seconds.summary: This project is a 7-segment seconds counter that counts up to 10, one second at a time. It uses registers to divide the clock and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display. A slower square wave is output on output 7. After reset, the counter should increase by one every second.
tt03/seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the actual 7-segment counter design.

tt03/shadow1229_player.summary: This project plays the song 'Bad Apple' through a piezo speaker connected across two output pins using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and plays it back when a 12 kHz clock is provided and a reset pulse is applied. The design requires an external piezo speaker connected between io_out[0] and io_out[1]. It is notable for being a simple music player based on a previous Tiny Tapeout project.
tt03/shadow1229_player.review_notes: Removed demoscene and sound-generator; added music, audio, buzzer, pwm, verilog which are directly supported.

tt03/shan1293_2bitalu.summary: This design is a 2-bit ALU that performs 16 different operations on two 2-bit inputs, A and B, selected by a 4-bit opcode. The result is an 8-bit output. To use it, provide the A and B inputs, set the opcode for the desired operation, and observe the result on ALU_out. No external hardware is required.
tt03/shan1293_2bitalu.review_notes: Removed unsupported instruction-decoder and logic-gate tags; added combinational.

tt03/stevenmburns_toplevel.summary: This project is a 16-bit greatest common divisor unit based on Knuth's binary GCD algorithm, written in Chisel. Operands are loaded and results are read back through a scan chain using the ld, u_bit, and v_bit pins, with a done signal indicating completion. The design is verified with ChiselTest unit tests run through sbt, and it requires no external hardware. Its notable feature is the use of scan chains for I/O, which conserves pins on the Tiny Tapeout tile.

tt03/swalense_top.summary: This module is a configurable 8-bit counter driven by a two-channel Gray code signal, intended to interface with incremental rotary encoders. It provides parallel and UART serial counter outputs, a direction signal, and a PWM output whose duty cycle tracks the counter value, and it supports optional debouncing, wrapping, and an X1/X2/X4 gearbox for acceleration. Configuration is loaded over SPI as a 32-bit word that sets initial and maximum values, gearbox timing, and other options. External hardware needed is a Gray code source, possibly with filtering or Schmitt triggers for mechanical encoders, and the UART output runs at the clock rate.

tt03/thezoq2_yafpga.summary: This project is titled YaFPGA and describes itself as yet another FPGA, implemented in the Spade language. The pin list shows four general inputs, four general outputs, and a config data and config clock pair, suggesting a small configurable logic fabric. However, both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are marked TODO, so the documentation is essentially absent. No behavior, configuration format, or test procedure can be confirmed from the provided text.
tt03/thezoq2_yafpga.review_notes: Removed lookup-table tag as it is not supported by the source documentation.

tt03/tholin_avalonsemi_5401.summary: This is a 4-bit microprocessor with a 4-bit ALU, accumulator, 8-bit memory address register, and 12-bit destination register, supporting 16 instructions including arithmetic, logic, load/store, and branches. It can address 4096 bytes of program memory and 254 words of data memory, with six words of on-chip RAM and two general-purpose input ports. Testing is done manually with a debounced push button as clock and DIP switches to key in instructions, following a documented sequence that produces known output patterns. External hardware at minimum includes program memory and glue logic, as shown in the example system diagram.
tt03/tholin_avalonsemi_5401.review_notes: Removed register-file because the source describes an accumulator and address/destination registers, not a register file.

tt03/tholin_avalonsemi_tbb1143.summary: This is a programmable sound generator with two square-wave voices, one sawtooth voice, and one noise channel, and it can also serve as a general-purpose frequency generator. Tone generation divides a ring-oscillator-derived internal clock by a programmable divisor, producing a 6-bit digital sample that can be converted to analog with a resistor chain. Programming is done through a 4-bit data bus with address and write strobe pins, and a documented register sequence produces a roughly 440 Hz tone. External hardware includes a DAC or resistor network and a microcontroller or microprocessor to program the device.

tt03/thunderbird_taillight_ctrl.summary: This design is a taillight controller for a 1965 Ford Thunderbird, implemented as a Moore state machine in Verilog. It takes left, right, and hazard inputs and drives six outputs labeled r1-r3 and l1-l3 for the rear lamps. After reset the state machine enters an idle mode, and the documentation gives no further test procedure or external hardware requirements. The design is notable mainly for reproducing a classic automotive sequential turn-signal behavior.

tt03/tiny_bnn.summary: This project implements a tiny binarized neural network with eight output neurons in Verilog. Inputs are shared between parameter loading and data input depending on the setup pin, and the eight outputs are either neuron results or a parameter value. The documentation consists only of pin names and a TODO for both the operation and test sections, so the internal architecture and weight-loading scheme cannot be determined. The design is incomplete and lacks sufficient documentation to describe its full functionality.

tt03/tiny_fft.summary: This design computes a small FFT, taking four 4-bit signed real inputs and producing four 6-bit complex outputs. Data is written using a write-enable signal and read back from the data output pins, with an rd_idx_zero output indicating the read index. The documentation is brief and does not specify the transform length, scaling, or ordering beyond the input and output widths. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design is intended as a compact DSP building block.
tt03/tiny_fft.review_notes: Removed fixed-point tag since the source only describes signed integers, not a fixed-point format.

tt03/tiny_kinda_pic.summary: This project implements a small microcontroller with a subset of the PIC mid-range instruction set, including six general-purpose registers and 16 program words, but no special function registers, carry, or call/stack support. Programs are shifted in serially through prog_data with prog_strobe, using a 28-bit word per instruction, after which the device runs standalone. Four general-purpose inputs and eight general-purpose outputs are provided, with GPR 6 and GPR 7 mapped to GPI and GPO. External hardware is needed only at startup to shift in the program, such as another microcontroller or USB GPIO interface.

tt03/tinysat.summary: This project implements a tiny SAT solver that uses a counter to iterate over all possible assignments to a simple SAT problem. It has inputs for clock, reset, run, load, and 4-bit data, and outputs for 4-bit assignment, solution found, and done signals. The author plans to test it with an RP2040 using the same tests as in test.py. The documentation is present but does not describe a cellular automaton or 7-segment display.
tt03/tinysat.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the SAT solver description.

tt03/tomkeddie_top_tto.summary: This design drives an HD44780-compatible character LCD to display a clock, using a 4-bit LCD interface with data pins D4-D7 plus enable and register-select lines. Hour and minute set inputs allow the time to be adjusted, and the design runs from the Tiny Tapeout clock. The documentation consists only of links to an external GitHub README, so the internal implementation and exact test procedure are not described in the provided text. External hardware required is an HD44780 LCD module.
tt03/tomkeddie_top_tto.review_notes: Removed timer; added rtc and text to reflect the clock function and character LCD text output.

tt03/tomkeddie_top_tto_a.summary: This project drives half of a P10 16x16 LED display module and initially displays the string TT03. It provides a 600 baud UART input to paint pixels, erase pixels, clear the display, and change the displayed color. Functionality is limited by resource availability and clock rate, with single color at once, no double buffer, and low refresh rate causing some flicker. A mode pin allows for two different clocking patterns, and external hardware includes an LED panel and a level converter to 5V logic.
tt03/tomkeddie_top_tto_a.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the LED panel driver documentation.

tt03/top_tt03.summary: This project is a ring-oscillator-based temperature sensor implemented in Verilog. It uses counters to count ring-oscillator cycles within a clock period and sends the result over UART. The design includes internal and external clock inputs, oscillator selection and enable signals, and a reset. It is intended to characterize the temperature versus frequency relationship.
tt03/top_tt03.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated ALU/adder; corrected to the documented ring-oscillator temperature sensor.

tt03/tt2_tholin_diceroll.summary: This design emulates a six-sided die by generating a pseudo-random number from 1 to 6 using a linear-feedback shift register. When the ROLL input is pulsed, the 7-segment display rapidly cycles through numbers before settling on a final value, and the decimal point lights up to indicate completion. It requires an external 7-segment display, such as the one on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, and is controlled by a clock and reset signal. The project is notable for its simple, self-contained implementation of a familiar game element on a single tile.

tt03/tt2_tholin_multiplexed_counter.summary: This design implements a timer that measures up to 99 minutes and 59 seconds by multiplexing four seven-segment displays. The documentation is essentially empty, with both the 'How it works' and 'How to test' sections marked as TODO. It requires four seven-segment displays plus 74-series logic chips to build the selection circuitry, but no further usage details are provided. Because of the missing documentation, little can be said about its internal operation or testing procedure.
tt03/tt2_tholin_multiplexed_counter.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc and removed redundant display tag; summary already accurate.

tt03/tt2_tholin_multiplier.summary: This design is a purely combinational 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit numbers on its input pins and produces an 8-bit product on its output pins. It is implemented using AND gates and several adders, without any sequential logic. To use it, a user would apply the two operands via switches or other sources and read the binary result on LEDs. The project is a straightforward arithmetic building block and requires external hardware such as DIP switches and LEDs for input and output.
tt03/tt2_tholin_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source describes only a multiplier.

tt03/tt2_tholin_namebadge.summary: This design echoes a predefined text message to a 20x4 character LCD. It contains a ROM holding the text and logic to perform the initialization sequence and cursor positioning, operating from an external clock since it lacks an internal divider. The design requires a 20x4 character LCD connected according to the pinout, and optionally LEDs on two output pins. It is notable as a simple demonstration of driving a character display from a Tiny Tapeout tile.

tt03/tucanae47_gray_ctr6.summary: This design implements a 6-bit Gray code counter in the Amaranth HDL. It outputs a sequence where only one bit changes between successive counts, which can help reduce switching noise in certain applications. The counter is controlled by external clock and reset signals and requires no additional hardware. The project serves as a simple educational example of Gray code and Amaranth-based design.

tt03/udxs_sqrt_top.summary: This design computes the square root of a 7-bit integer in 4.2 fixed-point format, rounding down to the nearest quarter. It uses Newton's method and produces a result after three clock cycles. The inputs are the 7-bit value and a clock, and the output is a 6-bit fixed-point number. Optionally, a binary-to-BCD converter can be added to display the result, but no other external hardware is required.
tt03/udxs_sqrt_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu tag; summary is otherwise accurate.

tt03/user_module_339501025136214612.summary: This project is a straight-through test that connects the eight inputs directly to the eight outputs. It is implemented in Wokwi and uses DIP switches for inputs and a 7-segment display for outputs. Setting any DIP switch high lights the corresponding LED segment on the display. The design demonstrates basic input-to-output wiring.
tt03/user_module_339501025136214612.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm and industrial tags; added 7-segment, led, and template tags.

tt03/user_module_340318610245288530.summary: This design implements a 1-bit ALU from Tanenbaum's book, supporting AND, NOT, OR, and ADD operations selected by two mode inputs. It includes enable and invert controls for the inputs and a carry-in for addition, and the output is shown on a 7-segment display with the carry-out on the decimal point. The design is intended for educational use and can be chained to create wider ALUs. No external hardware is needed beyond the on-board display.

tt03/user_module_340805072482992722.summary: This project counts up from 0 to 9, incrementing once per second. It uses a 4-bit counter to sequence and combinational logic to drive a 7-segment display. The clock is set to 1 Hz for testing. The design is implemented in Wokwi.
tt03/user_module_340805072482992722.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the 7-segment counter documentation.

tt03/user_module_341164910646919762.summary: This design combines two independent circuits: a Fibonacci sequence calculator using 56-bit integers and a Gold code generator for CCSDS X-band PN Delta-DOR. The Fibonacci terms are displayed one hex character at a time on the 7-segment display, with the decimal point marking the least significant bit. The Gold code generator uses LFSRs and allows parallel loading of 6 bits to select different sequences; the display dot shows either the Fibonacci output or the Gold code output based on an input select. The design is tested manually by driving the clock and setting the appropriate inputs; no external hardware is required.
tt03/user_module_341164910646919762.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and esoteric tags; added communication and adder.

tt03/user_module_341178154799333971.summary: This is a pseudo-random number generator based on a 16-bit Fibonacci linear-feedback shift register. It produces one new random bit per clock cycle, with the last 8 bits available on the output pins, and supports loading a custom seed value via the data_in pin when load_en is high. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by manually clocking the circuit and observing the output on a hex display. No external hardware is needed.

tt03/user_module_341178481588044372.summary: This design implements an LED chaser on a 7-segment display. A shift register is used to sequentially light up segments, with the input controlled by a push button. When the button is pressed, the illuminated segment shifts, creating a chasing effect. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires no external hardware.
tt03/user_module_341178481588044372.review_notes: Removed led (segments are 7-segment, not discrete LEDs) and added button for the push-button input.

tt03/user_module_341277789473735250.summary: This chip performs conversions and comparisons between binary-encoded ternary and unary-encoded ternary, with both machine-readable and human-readable outputs. It supports four operation modes selected by opcodes, and outputs results either on a 7-segment display or as binary signals. The design is implemented using mixed radix circuit synthesis (MRCS) and Wokwi, and it can be tested by setting the mode and input pins to verify the conversion or comparison. No external hardware is required.
tt03/user_module_341277789473735250.review_notes: Removed encoder and decoder tags; the source describes ternary conversion/comparison, not encoding or decoding circuits.

tt03/user_module_341279123277087315.summary: This design is a counter that displays its count on a 7-segment display or allows manual entry of a number in binary. It includes a clock divider to slow down the counting speed, and the counter can be enabled or disabled. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by enabling the counter and clock divider to observe counting, or by disabling the counter and setting the inputs to display a specific number. No external hardware is needed.

tt03/user_module_341353928049295956.summary: This design is a clock divider implemented using a series of flip-flops. The documentation is minimal, with only the title and a brief description, and no testing instructions are provided. It is implemented in Wokwi and uses a 7-segment display for output, but the exact functionality and usage are not described. No external hardware is mentioned.
tt03/user_module_341353928049295956.review_notes: Removed flip-flop and sequential-logic because the source does not document the internal implementation beyond the one-line description.

tt03/user_module_341423712597181012.summary: This chip is a scalable synchronous 4-bit tri-directional loadable counter that can count up, down, or pause, and supports loading a new count value. It is intended to be usable as a program counter, for example to set the next address for a jump instruction. The design is implemented using mixed radix circuit synthesis (MRCS) and Wokwi, and it can be tested by resetting the state, setting the direction and count enable, and clocking the circuit. No external hardware is needed.

tt03/user_module_341432030163108435.summary: This design replicates the functionality of TI's 74xx1G97 and 74xx1G98 configurable logic gates, along with a 74xx1G79 D flip-flop. It includes two configurable gates and one D flip-flop, each with complementary outputs. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by referring to the TI datasheets for the original parts. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout setup.
tt03/user_module_341432030163108435.review_notes: Removed combinational because the design contains a flip-flop; added retro for the 74xx logic family replication.

tt03/user_module_341438392303616596.summary: This design implements a 4-digit electronic padlock that checks a sequence of button presses against a stored code. Each button press is detected by a rising edge detector and the resulting binary code is stored in a shift register, which is continuously compared to a reference value. The design outputs signals indicating button press detection and code validity. It requires external push buttons with debounce circuitry and a clock source.

tt03/user_module_341490465660469844.summary: This design drives a 7-segment LED display to alternate between the text 'NIC' and 'JAC'. It uses a prescaler with selectable tap points to divide the clock, which then feeds a ripple counter and a chain of multiplexers to control each segment. The decimal point blinks based on the highest counter bit. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires external switches for prescaler selection and a 7-segment display.

tt03/user_module_341516949939814994.summary: This design is a 40-bit shift register that compares the shifted value against a hardcoded 40-bit number and drives its output high only on a match. It is used by shifting bits in via the data and clock inputs, with each rising clock edge advancing the register. Testing with the known number requires only a DIP switch for data, a button for clock, and an LED on the output; without the number, reverse engineering or side-channel attacks are suggested. The project is notable as a hardware puzzle challenge rather than a functional block, and its documentation is sufficient to describe the intended use.

tt03/user_module_341541108650607187.summary: This design implements a finite state machine that counts from 0 to 3, with the count advanced by a button press when the first input is enabled. The count is displayed on a seven-segment display, and other inputs have various logic to play with. It is a copy of the author's earlier Tiny Tapeout submission, meant to run on a Steam Deck. Testing requires enabling the first input, turning off all others, and pressing the button to progress the FSM.
tt03/user_module_341541108650607187.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; no source evidence that it is intended for teaching.

tt03/user_module_341546888233747026.summary: This design is a four-bit adder that takes two four-bit binary numbers and produces their sum on a seven-segment display, with the carry shown on the decimal point. It uses four full adders feeding a binary-to-seven-segment decoder, and is tested by setting the two numbers on DIP switches. Display of sums greater than nine is noted as questionable, and no external hardware is needed. The project is a straightforward arithmetic and display demonstration.
tt03/user_module_341546888233747026.review_notes: Removed alu because the source describes only an adder and decoder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

tt03/user_module_341557831870186068.summary: This design is a 4-word by 4-bit read/write RAM with separate data and address inputs and a write enable signal. Data is written to the addressed location when write enable is asserted, and the stored word is presented on the read data outputs. It is tested by setting the data and address lines, cycling write enable, and then reading the value on the read data outputs. No external hardware is required, and the design serves as a basic memory block.
tt03/user_module_341557831870186068.review_notes: Removed sram and register-file; the source describes a plain 4x4 read/write RAM, covered by memory.

tt03/user_module_341571228858843732.summary: This design implements a small R-2R digital-to-analog converter by adding a resistor ladder to the outputs of D flip-flops. It is tested by attaching an external R-2R ladder and a non-inverting op-amp to the output to observe the analog voltage. The design requires external resistors and an op-amp, and the documentation notes that an AND gate was removed and a pin is used as a passthrough. The project is a simple mixed-signal experiment.
tt03/user_module_341571228858843732.review_notes: Removed opamp tag because the amp is external test equipment, not part of the design; added mixed-signal and flip-flop based on source.

tt03/user_module_341589685194195540.summary: This design implements the Chi function of the Xoodoo permutation protected with threshold implementation using two shares. It is tested by setting the last four inputs, and the outputs are connected to a seven-segment display. The design is a cryptographic building block aimed at side-channel resistance, and no external hardware is mentioned. The documentation is very brief and does not provide detailed test procedures or expected results.

tt03/user_module_341608574336631379.summary: This design implements the Chi function of the Xoodoo permutation protected with threshold implementation using three shares. It is tested by setting all inputs, and the outputs drive a seven-segment display. The design is a cryptographic building block intended for side-channel resistance, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and lacks detailed test instructions or expected behavior.

tt03/user_module_341609034095264340.summary: This design displays a BCD counter on a seven-segment display, with the segment logic simplified using sum-of-products equations. It can run automatically with the clock switch on and all toggle switches in zero position, or individual BCD bits can be toggled with the clock off. The design includes a decimal point toggle. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board and display.
tt03/user_module_341609034095264340.review_notes: Removed education (no teaching intent stated) and dropped the unsupported educational-purpose sentence.

tt03/user_module_341613097060926036.summary: This design implements a finite state machine that cycles through the letters A, d, and i on a seven-segment display when a button is pushed. It is tested by connecting a push button and a seven-segment display, then pressing the button to advance the sequence. The design is a simple test FSM that requires only minimal external hardware. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand its operation.
tt03/user_module_341613097060926036.review_notes: Removed counter tag because the FSM cycles letters rather than counting; left education tag as the description 'Test FSM' is consistent with educational intent.

tt03/user_module_341614346808328788.summary: This design implements the wolf, goat and cabbage river crossing puzzle as a combinational logic block. Four input pins represent the positions of the farmer, wolf, goat and cabbage, and the outputs drive the segments of a 7-segment display to indicate a win, a loss, or which river bank has an unattended situation. The game is played interactively by setting the input switches and observing the 7-segment display. The design is built with Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes.
tt03/user_module_341614346808328788.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm and logic-gate tags and added combinational to match the truth-table implementation.

tt03/user_module_341614374571475540.summary: This design implements the Chi function of the Xoodoo permutation protected at first order by DOM masking. It is a cryptographic building block aimed at side-channel resistance. The design is built with Wokwi and takes a clock and reset input while driving the seven segment outputs. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the internal state encoding or test procedure beyond setting the inputs.
tt03/user_module_341614374571475540.review_notes: Removed unsupported hash and 7-segment tags; added cipher and insufficient-doc.

tt03/user_module_341620484740219475.summary: This design is an 8x8 bit serial programmable, addressable and playable memory. It uses a shift register to store data and can drive an LED matrix to display the stored pattern. The design is built with Wokwi and includes a UART interface for programming. It is intended for educational purposes.

tt03/user_module_341628725785264722.summary: This design contains free-running oscillators built from combinational loops with dividers, intended to compare simulation against silicon and to provide a true random number source. It is a process and simulation-verification experiment rather than a functional application. The design includes a ring oscillator, a true random number generator, and a clock divider. It is built with Wokwi.

tt03/user_module_341631511790879314.summary: This design is a low-speed UART transmitter with limited character set loading, using a 13-bit shift register built from D flip-flops. It accepts a 300 Hz input clock and 5-bit character data, and outputs UART serial signals in multiple polarities and gating options. The shift register cycles the word with start and stop bits until a new word is loaded or the output is disabled. Testing involves loading a character and attaching a UART receiver or oscilloscope to the output.
tt03/user_module_341631511790879314.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the UART transmitter description.

tt03/user_module_341631644820570706.summary: This design cycles through the characters of the string LAB11 on a 7-segment display, one character per clock cycle. It is built with Wokwi and uses gates and flip-flops to change the state of the LED segments to form the next character. The design takes a clock and reset input and drives the seven segment outputs. It is intended as a simple educational demonstration, and the documentation notes that characters are most readable at the lowest clock speed.
tt03/user_module_341631644820570706.review_notes: Removed unsupported button and logic-gate tags; added counter and sequential-logic.

tt03/user_module_341678527574180436.summary: This design makes an L on a seven-segment display when buttons 1 and 2 are pressed. It is implemented as just an AND gate. The documentation is minimal but clearly describes the intended behavior. The design uses two button inputs and seven segment outputs.
tt03/user_module_341678527574180436.review_notes: Corrected tags to match the simple AND-gate seven-segment design.

tt03/user_module_342981109408072274.summary: This design is a shift register that generates different LED patterns based on selectable feedback inputs. Inputs control feedback conditions, direction, and a clock divider to create patterns such as every other LED, every third LED, every fourth LED, or a single scanning light. The outputs drive eight LEDs. The design is built with Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes.
tt03/user_module_342981109408072274.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented shift-register LED pattern generator.

tt03/user_module_346553315158393428.summary: This design implements the core of a paper-tape pseudorandom bit sequence generator electrically, computing (C ? A : B) ^ D from five input bits. It is built with Wokwi and uses a multiplexer and XOR logic rather than the original optomechanical tape mechanism. The design is purely combinational, with no clock or sequential storage elements. Testing consists of applying the 32 possible input patterns and verifying the documented output sequence.
tt03/user_module_346553315158393428.review_notes: Removed unsupported flip-flop and education tags; added multiplexer, prng and combinational based on the described (C ? A : B) ^ D function.

tt03/user_module_346916357828248146.summary: This design uses two configurable gates to drive SR and D flip-flops, enabling a variety of complex flip-flop functions. It is built with the Wokwi simulator. When SEL and INV are low, the 0 inputs directly drive the flip-flops, and A-0 can be connected to the clock for use with the D flip-flop. The outputs include multiplexer and XOR results as well as the flip-flop Q and Q# signals.
tt03/user_module_346916357828248146.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added flip-flop/multiplexer/logic-gate/combinational tags.

tt03/user_module_347140425276981843.summary: This design implements a single-character UART transmitter using a 17-bit shift register built from D flip-flops and multiplexers. It transmits a user-selected ASCII character from 0x40 to 0x5F, including capital letters, at a 300 Hz clock rate. The design is tested by connecting an Arduino's serial RX pin to the output and configuring the Arduino serial monitor to 300 baud, then toggling switches to load and transmit the character. External hardware includes an Arduino and a computer with a serial monitor. The design is notable for its use of discrete flip-flops and multiplexers to implement the shift register, and it is a Wokwi-based project.
tt03/user_module_347140425276981843.review_notes: Removed generic communication tag; kept uart, shift-register, 7-segment, wokwi and ascii tags supported by the source.

tt03/user_module_347144898258928211.summary: This design implements a UART transmitter capable of sending a string of multiple ASCII characters using five 21-bit shift registers. It operates at a 300 Hz clock and is controlled via switches for load, transmit, and output enable. Testing involves connecting an Arduino's serial RX pin to the output and setting the Arduino serial monitor to 300 baud, then toggling switches to transmit the string. External hardware includes an Arduino and a computer with a serial monitor.
tt03/user_module_347144898258928211.review_notes: Removed 7-segment tag as the display outputs are simulation-only debug indicators, not a design feature.

tt03/user_module_347417602591556180.summary: This design implements a customizable digital padlock that can be set to a user-defined code using switches. The code is entered via a push button, and the seven-segment display shows 'L' for locked and 'U' for unlocked. The design is tested by setting the code with switches, toggling the set switch, and then entering the code to unlock. No external hardware is required beyond the PCB's switches and display.

tt03/user_module_347497504164545108.summary: This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through characters. It operates at a 1 Hz clock and includes a reset input to restart the counter. Testing is done by simply powering the design and observing the display, with an optional reset toggle. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for its use of a counter and lookup logic to display a fixed message, and it is implemented in Wokwi.

tt03/user_module_347592305412145748.summary: This design simulates a 4-spin Ising chain in an external field using the Metropolis-Hastings Monte Carlo algorithm. It uses a 32-bit LFSR to generate random numbers for spin flip acceptance and can be chained with other instances to form longer chains. The design is tested by enabling neighbour inputs and observing the evolution to a ground state. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for being a self-contained physics simulation on a tiny tapeout chip, implemented in Wokwi.

tt03/user_module_347594509754827347.summary: This design implements a LUTRAM with a 4-bit address and 8-bit output, preloaded with a binary-to-7-segment decoder for digits 0-9. The memory content can be updated via clock and data pins, and a reset reverts to default data. Testing involves providing clock, data, reset, and address signals to display the corresponding digit. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for its use of a lookup table as memory and its limitation to 0-9 due to size constraints, implemented in Wokwi.

tt03/user_module_347619669052490324.summary: This design is a UART template that can be connected to an Arduino. It includes a clock and reset input and outputs to a 7-segment display. Testing is done by hooking it up to an Arduino. External hardware includes an Arduino.
tt03/user_module_347619669052490324.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc tag as the documentation, while minimal, adequately describes the design's purpose and interface.

tt03/user_module_347688030570545747.summary: This design encodes binary-coded decimal (BCD) inputs in the range 0-9 to 7-segment display control signals. It was fully generated using a lookup table generator from a truth table, and invalid BCD inputs result in a blank display. Testing is done by setting the input switches and observing the displayed digit. External hardware includes input switches and a 7-segment display on the PCB. The design is notable for being automatically generated from a truth table, implemented in Wokwi.

tt03/user_module_347690870424732244.summary: This design implements a state machine to control German traffic lights at an intersection with main and side streets, including pedestrian signals. It operates at a 1 Hz clock and generates a blinking yellow light for the side street in the reset state. Testing requires providing a clock, connecting LEDs, and generating a reset signal; an additional inverter is needed for pedestrian red signals. External hardware includes LEDs and an inverter.
tt03/user_module_347690870424732244.review_notes: Removed industrial (not an industrial control application) and kept led, which is supported by the LED outputs and test instructions.

tt03/user_module_347787021138264660.summary: This design reads inputs from external photodiodes, sums the binary values, and displays the total on a 7-segment display. It includes a clock and reset input, and can be tested using dip switches instead of photodiodes, with a switch to select step or continuous sampling mode. External hardware includes a breadboard, resistors, and photodiodes. The design is notable for interfacing with analog sensors to display light intensity, implemented in Wokwi.
tt03/user_module_347787021138264660.review_notes: Removed photodiode because it is external hardware; added instrumentation and dip-switch based on the documentation.

tt03/user_module_347894637149553236.summary: This design implements a 4-bit 2-stage FIR filter that multiplies input samples by tap coefficients and sums the results. Coefficients are loaded serially by setting values and pulsing the load signal twice per tap, and the filter runs by changing the input each clock cycle. Select pins allow debugging by routing internal signals such as multiplier outputs or stored tap values to the output pins. The FIR output discards the least significant bit due to output pin limitations, and external hardware such as an Arduino or FPGA is needed to drive inputs and read results.

tt03/user_module_348121131386929746.summary: This project generates a rotating dash animation on a six-segment display, driven by an external clock. It can run continuously or be stepped manually using a mode switch and a step button, with a low-active reset. The design is intended for the default PCB and uses DIP switches for control. Documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.
tt03/user_module_348121131386929746.review_notes: Removed counter, clock-divider, and button tags because the design is a display animation and the buttons are external hardware.

tt03/user_module_348195845106041428.summary: This design detects phase shifts between two square waves, using a reference clock and a feedback clock as inputs. The outputs are an up signal and an inverted down signal that indicate the phase difference. If the feedback clock leads the reference clock, the up signal shows the phase difference; if it lags, the down signal shows the difference. External hardware consists of signal generators for the square wave inputs.
tt03/user_module_348195845106041428.review_notes: Replaced unrelated audio/display tags with phase-detector and PLL tags and rewrote the summary to match the source.

tt03/user_module_348242239268323922.summary: This design produces siren-like tones and light patterns reminiscent of 1970s effects, using a chain of D flip-flops to divide the clock into various frequencies. Higher frequencies generate tones for audio output, while lower frequencies control the patterns on a seven-segment display and modulate the tones. A pattern select input chooses between two groups of patterns. External hardware such as a speaker with a series resistor or an audio amplifier is required for sound output.

tt03/user_module_348255968419643987.summary: This project is a tiny synthesizer that generates a C scale by modulating the clock frequency based on input pins corresponding to notes C through B. It outputs square waves at four octave-related pitches. The documentation is incomplete, with the author noting they will add more details later, and the external hardware needed to make sound is not fully determined. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires a clock input.

tt03/user_module_348260124451668562.summary: This design generates and checks PRBS15 sequences using an LFSR. It can be enabled to generate the sequence and, when in check mode, compares the output to detect errors. Testing requires a logic analyzer and jumper leads to monitor the error and checked signals. The design is a straightforward implementation of a pseudo-random bit sequence generator and checker.
tt03/user_module_348260124451668562.review_notes: Removed prng because PRBS is not a general PRNG; added sequence-detector for the checker function.

tt03/user_module_348381622440034899.summary: This project displays an animation of a segmented worm traveling along a pseudo-random path on a seven-segment LED display. It includes controls for disabling auto-reset, manual reset, and a turbo mode that bypasses a clock divider. The number of worm segments can be set to two or three. The design is a simple animation demo and requires only the default PCB for use.
tt03/user_module_348381622440034899.review_notes: Removed prng because the source only mentions a pseudo-random path, not a PRNG circuit; added maze based on the title and described behavior.

tt03/user_module_348540666182107731.summary: This design is a test circuit for various flip-flop types, including D, C, S, R, NAND-based, and Muller configurations. Inputs are provided to select and control the flip-flops, and outputs drive a seven-segment display to show their states. The documentation states it is 'nothing special - just testing' and suggests changing inputs to observe outputs. A logic analyzer is listed as external hardware for debugging.
tt03/user_module_348540666182107731.review_notes: Added incomplete because the documentation is very thin and the design is only described as testing.

tt03/user_module_348787952842703444.summary: This design computes the dot product of two 2-element vectors, each element being a 2-bit integer. The inputs are packed into the 8 input pins, and the result is displayed on a seven-segment display. The documentation provides a test example: setting input to 11011010 yields an output of 00001000. The design is a simple arithmetic unit implemented in Wokwi.
tt03/user_module_348787952842703444.review_notes: Removed dsp and generic display; added adder and combinational to match the arithmetic-only design.

tt03/user_module_349011320806310484.summary: This design implements a single cell of Conway's Game of Life, calculating whether the cell survives or dies based on the number of neighbours and its current state. It uses five inputs to represent up to nine neighbours in two stages, with a half-select signal to switch between stages. The output is shown on a seven-segment display, and an inverted clock is provided. External hardware is needed to supply the neighbour states and reroute the current state.
tt03/user_module_349011320806310484.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm and redundant display; added combinational for the decision logic.

tt03/user_module_349047610915422802.summary: This design implements a minimal neuron-like influence field calculation with open neurons, taking a clock and reset as inputs and driving a 7-segment display. It is intended to be tested by clocking in a reference vector with some inversions, presenting the device under test, and reading the output. The documentation is very thin and does not explain the neuron model, the vector width, or how the influence field is computed. No external hardware beyond the 7-segment display is described.
tt03/user_module_349047610915422802.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added insufficient-doc plus led output tag.

tt03/user_module_349228308755382868.summary: This project implements a state machine whose transition table is stored in an external SPI flash device, with inputs and current state shifted out to look up the next state and outputs. It uses a clock, reset, data in, and four general inputs, and drives chip select, data out, and five general outputs. Testing requires connecting a SPI flash device that supports the 0x03 read command with 24-bit addressing and is preloaded with state machine values. The documentation gives no details on the state encoding or flash contents.
tt03/user_module_349228308755382868.review_notes: External SPI flash is a lookup component; memory and communication tags overstate on-chip features and SPI is not used as a protocol endpoint.

tt03/user_module_349255310782759507.summary: This design is a binary coded ternary test block that takes eight inputs labeled C+, C-, N+, N-, O+, O-, P+, and P- and drives a 7-segment display plus a dot output. It is described as a ternary selector, and testing consists of setting the inputs and reading the outputs. The documentation is extremely sparse and does not explain the ternary encoding, the meaning of the input pairs, or what the display shows. No external hardware is mentioned beyond the 7-segment display.
tt03/user_module_349255310782759507.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source gives no indication of a teaching purpose.

tt03/user_module_349546262775726676.summary: This design is a BCD to 7-segment decoder that accepts four binary-coded decimal inputs, a decimal dot passthrough, and an output invert control, and drives seven segment lines plus a dot output. It is tested by connecting the segment outputs to a 7-segment display and configuring the inputs as weights 1, 2, 4, and 8 so the input value appears on the display. The only external hardware needed is a 7-segment display. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the function, and the design is a straightforward decoder.
tt03/user_module_349546262775726676.review_notes: Removed education (not stated) and redundant display tag; summary last sentence adjusted to drop the unsupported educational claim.

tt03/user_module_349729432862196307.summary: This project implements a (7, 1/2) convolutional encoder following the CCSDS 131.0-B-4 standard. The encoder is a half-rate code with constraint length seven, generating two output bits for every input bit. It is implemented in Wokwi and uses a 7-segment display to show the encoded output. Testing involves writing a 6-bit input and shifting to observe the encoded symbols.
tt03/user_module_349729432862196307.review_notes: Removed incorrect counter tag; added encoder and error-correction tags; summary corrected to describe the convolutional encoder.

tt03/user_module_349790606404354643.summary: This design is an 8-bit shift register with an optional latch and hex decode that displays alternating high and low nibbles on a 7-segment display. It provides controls for display clock, shift in, shift clock, latch, cycle display, nibble selection, latch usage, and MSB/LSB order, and outputs the seven segments plus a high/low nibble indicator. Testing involves clocking in 8 bits, optionally latching them, and observing the alternating nibbles, with switches and a 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is clear about the control signals and behavior, making it a useful shift-register demonstration.
tt03/user_module_349790606404354643.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added decoder for the hex-to-7-segment decode function.

tt03/user_module_349813388252021330.summary: This design is a basic 4:2 compressor that takes four main input bits plus a carry-in and produces two compressed outputs and a carry-out. It is intended for use in compressing partial products inside multipliers. Testing is done by following the standard 4:2 compressor truth table with the four inputs and carry-in and observing the two outputs and carry-out. The documentation is short but sufficient to describe the function, and no external hardware is required.
tt03/user_module_349813388252021330.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp, adder, and education tags; added combinational as the design is purely combinational.

tt03/user_module_349833797657690706.summary: This project implements two banks of CRC-16/XModem and even parity calculators based on Ben Eater's error detection videos, each with shift data, shift clock, active-low reset, and active-low read controls. The read-back mode disables the feedback XOR so the calculated CRC and parity can be shifted out for inspection. Testing is done by connecting a Pico as shown in Wokwi, sending a string, and comparing the read-back CRC and parity values. The design can also be driven by switches or any microcontroller, and the documentation explains the control scheme clearly.

tt03/user_module_349886696875098706.summary: This design scrolls the text 'ctag' across a 7-segment display using a 4-state machine built from two flip-flops. It is controlled by a clock and reset input, and the outputs directly drive the seven segment lines. The design is intended for the Wokwi simulator, where the clock can be set to a button to step through the states. It is a minimal demonstration of a scrolling marquee on a 7-segment display.
tt03/user_module_349886696875098706.review_notes: Removed counter (not a counter) and redundant display; added flip-flop and text tags.

tt03/user_module_349901899339661908.summary: This design implements a two-player scoreboard that displays an 8-bit score as a two-digit hexadecimal value on a 7-segment display. It uses two counters to track the scores, which can be updated and selected for display via input pins. The design is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. It is a test run from CNS Lab, demonstrating a simple scoreboard application.

tt03/user_module_349934460979905106.summary: This design implements a PS/2 keyboard interface that accepts hexadecimal scan codes via input pins and transmits the corresponding key press and release signals to a computer. It uses a parallel-to-serial converter to send data according to the PS/2 protocol. The design requires a 3.3V to 5V logic level converter for proper operation. The documentation notes that it most likely does not work, indicating a potential limitation.
tt03/user_module_349934460979905106.review_notes: Removed uart tag because the interface is PS/2, not UART.

tt03/user_module_349952820323025491.summary: This design implements a single FFT butterfly unit with 2-bit resolution, processing two complex inputs to produce two complex outputs. It is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. The design can be tested by changing the input values. It is a low-resolution demonstration of a fundamental DSP operation.
tt03/user_module_349952820323025491.review_notes: Removed alu because an FFT butterfly is not an ALU; added incomplete due to very thin documentation.

tt03/user_module_349953952950780498.summary: This design is a test run from CNS Lab, labeled as the second design. It takes a clock and reset input and drives a 7-segment display, but the documentation does not specify its exact function beyond applying inputs and observing outputs. It is intended for the Wokwi simulator and requires no external hardware. The lack of detailed documentation makes it difficult to determine its purpose or behavior.
tt03/user_module_349953952950780498.review_notes: Removed generic display tag because the documented output is specifically a 7-segment display.

tt03/user_module_354091612057990145.summary: This project implements a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit numbers and adds them. The first number is input on bits 0-3 and the second on bits 4-7. The result is output on bits 0-3 with a carry output on bit 4. The design uses simple logic gates and is implemented in Wokwi.
tt03/user_module_354091612057990145.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the documented 4-bit adder.

tt03/user_module_357106633951414273.summary: This project sets a railway signal based on track information. It takes inputs such as track free status, pre-signal, allow shunting, and shorter braking distance. The outputs control various signal lamps including green, orange, red, yellow, and white indicators. The design simply switches lamps on and off based on the input toggles.
tt03/user_module_357106633951414273.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented railway signal controller.

tt03/user_module_357752736742764545.summary: This project implements a very simple 7-segment cellular automaton using about 200 basic logic gates. At each clock cycle, each of the seven segments is set alive or dead based on whether it had exactly one living neighbor when alive or exactly two living neighbors when dead, where touching segments are neighbors. Seven flip-flops hold the state, combinatorial logic computes the next state, and the state is latched on a clock edge; support logic allows manual loading, clock division, and run mode. It is tested on the standard Tiny Tapeout PCB using DIP switches for control and the seven-segment display for output, with additional puzzles suggested for the reader.
tt03/user_module_357752736742764545.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a neural-network encoder; corrected to the documented cellular automaton with puzzle aspect.

tt03/user_module_357897381919942657.summary: This project implements a small 4x4-bit memory using D flip-flops, where four data inputs are stored at an address selected by two address bits when write enable is asserted. The stored data is continuously output on four pins corresponding to the selected address. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and requires external clock, reset, write enable, address, and data switches, with outputs readable via LEDs. The design is a basic educational memory block with no silicon test results reported.
tt03/user_module_357897381919942657.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; added flip-flop to match the documented D flip-flop storage.

tt03/user_module_357917324056483841.summary: This design uses three AND gates to drive a 7-segment display so that pressing the first four input buttons displays the letter 'M'. The outputs correspond to the seven segments plus a dot, and the inputs are four buttons. It is built for the Wokwi simulator and demonstrates simple combinational logic. No silicon test results are provided.
tt03/user_module_357917324056483841.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added combinational and button tags supported by the source.

tt03/user_module_358370685977079809.summary: This project combines four sub-designs—a shift register, a hexadecimal seven-segment encoder, a 1-bit ALU, and a 3-bit adder—selectable via two project-select pins. The remaining six inputs are used for data and control depending on the selected mode, and outputs drive a 7-segment display or provide results. It is built for the Wokwi simulator and serves as a multi-purpose educational tool. No silicon test results are reported.
tt03/user_module_358370685977079809.review_notes: Encoder tag incorrectly describes the seven-segment display decoder as a generic encoder; counter tag added for the shift register.

tt03/user_module_358970514554149889.summary: This design stores a single decimal digit (0–9) and displays it on a 7-segment display. It has clock and reset inputs and outputs for the seven segments and dot. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.
tt03/user_module_358970514554149889.review_notes: Summary already accurate; no tag changes needed.

tt03/user_module_359353377078748161.summary: This project implements a 4-bit S-box for the SKINNY cipher algorithm. It takes four input bits and produces four output bits according to the S-box mapping. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

tt03/user_module_359357227471086593.summary: This project implements a stateful combination lock that requires three correct codes in sequence to unlock. A two-bit state machine tracks progress, and any wrong code resets to the initial state. The lock status is output on a single pin, and inputs include reset, enter, and five code-digit pins. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and is described as an experiment or puzzle; no silicon test results are provided.

tt03/user_module_359360834113498113.summary: This project implements Ascon's 5-bit S-box, a cryptographic substitution box used in the Ascon cipher. It takes five input bits and produces five output bits according to the S-box definition. The documentation references external papers for details but provides no local explanation. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

tt03/user_module_359372419264319489.summary: This project implements an 8-bit S-box for the SKINNY cipher algorithm. It takes eight input bits and produces eight output bits according to the S-box mapping. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it. It is implemented in Wokwi and lacks any silicon test results.

tt03/user_module_359387860730498049.summary: This project implements a binary door lock that takes an 8-bit input and opens only when a specific combination is entered. With 8 bits, there are 256 possible combinations, and only one sets the output high. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and can be tested there. No silicon test results are provided.

tt03/user_module_360014965627378689.summary: This project implements a whac-a-mole style game called 'Catch the fish', using a 6-bit Fibonacci LFSR and a simple timer to generate pseudo-random outputs. Players press one of three buttons when the corresponding feedback output is high to score, with a reward feedback provided. It requires a clock and three buttons, and outputs feedback signals. It is designed for the Wokwi simulator and is a game; no silicon test results are reported.

tt03/user_module_360295047631610881.summary: This project implements an 8-byte RAM using shift registers. It stores data bits and provides 8 parallel outputs. The design is written in Wokwi and uses a clock and address inputs to control data storage. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it stores stuff, and lacks detailed testing instructions.
tt03/user_module_360295047631610881.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the documentation is very thin and testing instructions are missing.

tt03/user_module_360745091952588801.summary: This is a 4-bit ALU that supports eight operations and includes a built-in 4-bit accumulator register. It performs operations such as load, negate, shift right, subtract, AND, XOR, OR, and add, with the result stored in the accumulator. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested using a push-button, debouncer, DIP-switch, and LEDs, as described in the documentation. The ALU outputs the accumulator value and a carry flag, and it can be reset by setting all inputs to zero.
tt03/user_module_360745091952588801.review_notes: Removed the incorrect instruction-decoder tag and added sequential-logic because the accumulator is clocked.

tt03/user_module_361684719151591425.summary: This project converts a 4-bit binary number to either decimal or hexadecimal and displays the result on a 7-segment display. The user selects the conversion mode via dedicated input pins (Dec or Hex) and inputs the binary number through four pins. The design is implemented in Wokwi and outputs the seven segment control signals plus a dot. The documentation explains the basic operation and testing but does not provide detailed implementation details.
tt03/user_module_361684719151591425.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd tag and added display output tag.

tt03/user_module_361728533238569985.summary: This project consists of eight inverters that invert every input line. It is also used to fill empty design spaces on the chip. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by setting input switches and observing the corresponding LEDs. The documentation is very brief and does not provide additional context or applications.
tt03/user_module_361728533238569985.review_notes: Removed incomplete because the design is a complete inverter test; kept logic-gate and wokwi.

tt03/user_module_361728681519813633.summary: This project creates a random walk animation on a 7-segment display, where the active segment moves randomly. It uses a finite state machine with 14 flip-flops and a linear feedback shift register to generate randomness. A clock divider, controlled by DIP switches, slows the walk to a visible speed, and an optional flashing dot can be enabled. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is self-initializing, requiring no reset signal.
tt03/user_module_361728681519813633.review_notes: Added led tag because the 7-segment display is an LED output device.

tt03/user_module_362208154278843393.summary: This project divides the input clock frequency by 2 raised to the power of a 4-bit binary number entered via input pins. It outputs the divided clock on a single pin. The design is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by entering a binary number and probing the output. The documentation is very brief and lacks detailed implementation or testing information.
tt03/user_module_362208154278843393.review_notes: Removed divider because it denotes arithmetic division, not clock frequency division.

tt03/user_module_362249236392794113.summary: This project implements a 3-bit parallel adder-subtractor that can add or subtract two 3-bit binary numbers. It uses a carry-in input to select between addition and subtraction (via two's complement). The result is displayed on a 7-segment display, with outputs mapped to segments. The design is implemented in Wokwi and includes a clock and reset, though their role is not fully explained in the documentation.
tt03/user_module_362249236392794113.review_notes: Removed weakly supported 7-segment tag and added display and combinational tags.

tt03/user_module_362336485347742721.summary: This project is a 3-bit down counter that counts through the sequence 7, 3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 4, 0. It uses three flip-flops and count signals to trigger each flip-flop in sequence. The counter value is displayed on a 7-segment display, and a DIP switch is used to provide count signals. The design is implemented in Wokwi and includes a reset input.
tt03/user_module_362336485347742721.review_notes: Removed asynchronous tag as the design uses a clock and flip-flops; added dip-switch and sequential-logic.

tt03/user_module_362371515213982721.summary: This project converts Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) input to decimal digits for display on a 7-segment display. It uses a decoder circuit to drive the appropriate segments based on the BCD value. The design is implemented in Wokwi and outputs the segment control signals. The documentation describes the basic operation but does not provide detailed testing instructions or pin mappings.

tt03/user_module_362379207695863809.summary: This project implements a 3-bit binary multiplier that computes the product of two 3-bit numbers, producing a 6-bit result. It uses full adders to sum partial products and outputs the result to a 7-segment display. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is purely combinational. The documentation explains the multiplication algorithm but lacks detailed pin mappings and testing procedures.
tt03/user_module_362379207695863809.review_notes: Removed 7-segment tag because the pin list does not support a 7-segment display interface.

tt03/user_module_362441918332875777.summary: This design subtracts two 4-bit binary numbers using 2's complement subtraction, implemented with four full adders built from XOR and AND gates. The two 4-bit operands are applied to the eight input pins, and the 8-bit result drives the segments of a seven-segment display. Testing is done by entering two 4-bit binary numbers on the inputs and observing the displayed difference. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the output encoding or how negative results are shown.
tt03/user_module_362441918332875777.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; no other changes.

tt03/user_module_362592986761938945.summary: This project implements a full adder using two 4:1 multiplexers instead of conventional gates, with the sum and carry outputs driving a seven-segment display. Three inputs A, B and Cin are provided on input pins, and the design is clocked at 1 Hz. Testing involves setting the clock and applying two 3-bit binary numbers, then reading the sum and carry on the display. The documentation is somewhat inconsistent about the number of inputs and the role of the clock.
tt03/user_module_362592986761938945.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the source describes a full adder, not an ALU.

tt03/user_module_362633503928580097.summary: This design uses two input bits to sequentially display the letters H, O, L and A on a seven-segment display. The four combinations 00, 01, 10 and 11 select which letter is shown. The project is described in Spanish and appears to be a simple demonstration or test chip. The documentation is very thin and does not explain the internal logic or the exact mapping of inputs to letters.
tt03/user_module_362633503928580097.review_notes: Removed education as unsupported; added text and insufficient-doc for the letter display and thin documentation.

tt03/user_module_362675777226104833.summary: This is a four-state Moore finite state machine intended for a microrobot that detects water contamination, with two sensor inputs and two motor enable outputs. The state transitions are defined by a truth table, and the current state is stored in D flip-flops. The design requires external hardware including a 3-electrode sensor and motors. The documentation is clear and includes a complete truth table.
tt03/user_module_362675777226104833.review_notes: Removed unsupported 7-segment tag; the documentation does not describe a seven-segment display.

tt03/user_module_362788954641333249.summary: This design monitors a water tank level using two inputs and drives four LEDs to indicate Full, Half1, Half2 and Empty states, plus a motor control output. It uses D flip-flops for synchronization and state storage, and the motor starts when the tank is empty and stops when full. Testing involves a clock and two inputs, with five outputs connected to LEDs and a motor indicator. The documentation is somewhat unclear about the exact input encoding and the role of the clock.
tt03/user_module_362788954641333249.review_notes: Removed sensor-interface and 7-segment tags because the source describes generic level inputs and LED outputs, not a sensor interface or seven-segment display.

tt03/user_module_362833471952037889.summary: This project implements a 5-to-1 multiplexer that selects one of five inputs based on three select lines and displays the selected input on a seven-segment display. The select lines are labeled S1, S2 and S3, with S3 also connected to the clock pin. Testing involves applying different select combinations such as 000 for I1, 100 for I2, 001 for I3, 101 for I4 and 111 for I5. The documentation is brief and the select encoding is not fully consistent with a standard 5-to-1 mux.
tt03/user_module_362833471952037889.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not indicate an educational purpose; added multiplexer, 7-segment and wokwi.

tt03/user_module_362867354023533569.summary: This is a two-minute toothbrush timer that divides a 10 kHz clock to produce 30-second increments, with each increment indicated by a segment on the seven-segment display. Each of the four increments can be gated by an enable switch so the user must acknowledge completion before moving on, and at the end all middle segments flash. A pause input freezes the timer, and a reset input restarts it. The documentation is detailed and includes testing instructions, though it notes that the first increment may be shorter than 30 seconds after a hard reset.

tt03/user_module_362886316051042305.summary: This design implements a 3-bit wide, 4-position register file using multiplexers for address decoding and data storage. It provides separate write and read addresses, a write enable, and outputs for the read data plus internal state and an inverted write enable. Testing involves setting the data bits and write address with write enable toggled to store a value, then setting the read address to retrieve it. The documentation is concise but sufficient to understand the basic operation.
tt03/user_module_362886316051042305.review_notes: Removed generic 'memory' tag; register-file is the accurate canonical tag.

tt03/user_module_362911430638568449.summary: This is a customized UART string transmitter that sends the fixed string "EDM!" using five 21-bit shift registers, with a 300 Hz clock and a 300 baud rate. It is a copy of a previous Tiny Tapeout design and requires an external MCU or UART-to-USB adapter connected to the TX output pin. Testing involves setting the clock, load and output enable switches appropriately and receiving the string on a serial terminal. The documentation is brief but includes clear testing steps and acknowledges the design's origin.

tt03/user_module_nickoe.summary: This design implements an LED chaser effect using the LiteX LED core demo, with the duty cycle controlled by input pins io_in[7:2]. It is generated from LiteX/Migen and synthesizes to Verilog, and it does not include a CPU. The design can be tested by connecting LEDs to the eight outputs or probing the signals with an oscilloscope to observe a moving train of pulses. It serves as a small demonstration of synthesizing Verilog from LiteX.
tt03/user_module_nickoe.review_notes: Removed led-matrix because outputs are discrete LED lines; added wokwi per facts, though the design itself is a LiteX/Verilog demo.

tt03/user_module_skylersaleh.summary: This design flashes the letters 'H-E-L-L-O' on a 7-segment display by using a configurable clock divider and a character generator ROM. It includes a debug mode that allows direct indexing of the character ROM and sourcing the slow clock from input pins. The design requires no external hardware beyond a 7-segment display. It is notable for its built-in test harness and configurable flashing behavior.
tt03/user_module_skylersaleh.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added text tag for the letter rendering.

tt03/vaishnavachath_rotary_toplevel.summary: This design implements a counter that increments or decrements based on rotary encoder input and displays the count on a 7-segment display. It includes a test mode that emulates encoder signals using the clock and an inverted clock. The design requires an external rotary encoder for normal operation. It is a straightforward application of a rotary encoder interface with a display.

tt03/wokwi_tt03_simon_top.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors, each associated with a tone. The sequence is shown on four LEDs and played through a speaker, and the user responds using four buttons. The game supports four clock speeds selected by two inputs, and it plays level-up and game-over sounds. It requires external hardware including four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, and optionally a speaker or buzzer.

tt03/wormy_top.summary: Wormy is a simple snake-like game where a worm grows by eating and must avoid colliding with itself. It is played using four buttons that are debounced and synchronized to prevent metastability. The game state is displayed on a 4x4 grid of LEDs driven by a multiplexing scheme using eight outputs. The design is educational, explaining concepts such as multiplexing and button filtering, and is tested by observing a moving and growing pixel after reset.
tt03/wormy_top.review_notes: Removed snake-game and education; added led-matrix, multiplexer, debouncer, synchronizer, and verilog tags.

tt03/wren6991_whisk_tt2_io_wrapper.summary: Whisk is a 16-bit serial RISC CPU that executes instructions from up to 64 kilobytes of external SPI SRAM. It uses a single SPI interface for instruction fetch, loads, and stores, and internally operates in a fully serial manner to match the SPI memory throughput. An optional IO port interface provides up to 16 outputs and 8 inputs using shift registers. The design requires a host board with SPI SRAM and a host interface for loading programs, and it is notable for its compact serial architecture.
tt03/wren6991_whisk_tt2_io_wrapper.review_notes: Removed gpio: the IO port is a serial shift-register interface, not general purpose digital IO.

tt03/xor_shift32_evango.summary: This design implements the XorShift32 algorithm to generate a 32-bit random number, which is truncated to 3 bits and displayed on a 7-segment display. It reads a 6-bit seed value from input pins while reset is asserted, and generates a new number every 1000 clock cycles after reset is deasserted. The design requires no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display. It is a compact hardware implementation of a pseudo-random number generator.

tt03/xor_shift32_quantamhd.summary: This design implements the XorShift32 algorithm to generate a 32-bit random number, which is truncated to 3 bits and displayed on a 7-segment display. It reads a 6-bit seed value from input pins while reset is asserted, and generates a new number every 1000 clock cycles after reset is deasserted. The design requires no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display. It is a compact hardware implementation of a pseudo-random number generator.

tt03/xyz_peppergray_Potato1_top.summary: Potato-1 is the control logic for a Brainfuck CPU, decoding the eight Brainfuck instructions plus HALT and NOP into register increment/decrement and memory read/write control signals. It reads instruction, zero flag and IO wait inputs on each rising clock edge and updates its output pins on the falling edge, pausing on Put/Get until IO wait is released. Using it requires external hardware: three bidirectional counters for program counter, data pointer and value, a ROM for instructions, a RAM for data, and TTL gates for write control. The design is deliberately minimal and slow, and the documentation notes it is only the control portion of a CPU rather than a complete processor.
tt03/xyz_peppergray_Potato1_top.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not describe a teaching or learning purpose.

tt03/yannickreiss_dot_op.summary: This design is a 3-bit dot operation calculator that performs multiplication or division based on an opcode input. It takes two 3-bit operands and outputs the product or quotient and remainder on six output pins. The design requires external switches and LEDs for input and output. The documentation is minimal, providing only basic operation and testing instructions.
tt03/yannickreiss_dot_op.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and corrected summary to avoid claiming educational intent.

tt03/yubex_egg_timer.summary: tiny egg timer is a configurable countdown timer implemented as a three-state finite state machine (Idle, Waiting, Alarm) with counters for clock cycles, seconds and minutes. The user sets a wait time in minutes on five input pins and asserts start; a 7-segment display shows the countdown with the decimal point toggling each second, and an 'A' is displayed when the time expires. The alarm is stopped by deasserting the start switch, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the intended operation and test procedure.
tt03/yubex_egg_timer.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-divider tag; summary is accurate.

tt03/yubex_tiny_logic_analyzer.summary: This is a tiny logic analyzer that samples a single digital input and displays its current state and edge events on a 7-segment display. It uses a shift register to detect rising and falling edges, and counters to extend the display duration for visibility. The design requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board, and can be tested using a dip switch as the data input. It is intended as a simple debugging tool for observing signal transitions.

tt03/yupferris_bitslam.summary: bitslam is a programmable sound chip with two LFSR-based voices and a mixer, controlled through a register write interface using an address/data selector pin. Each voice has a clock divider for pitch and a 4-bit tap mask selecting LFSR feedback taps, while the mixer register sets per-voice volume from silent to full. It is intended to be driven by an external host such as a microcontroller, and a 4-bit DAC connected to the four digital outputs is required to produce analog audio. The design is notable for its compact LFSR tone generation and the documentation credits a fix for an interconnect bug.
tt03/yupferris_bitslam.review_notes: Removed register-file as the source describes a small control register interface, not a general register file; added sound-generator as the canonical type.

tt03/zl_uart.summary: This project implements a UART interface that allows reading and writing internal registers via a simple two-byte protocol.
