It includes a signature, an internal register, an LED register, and input status readback. The design is tested by sending specific command bytes and observing responses, with initial LED display showing three horizontal segments. It requires a UART host for communication and provides a basic register access mechanism.

tt03/zoechip.summary: This design spells out the name 'zoe' and the age '4' on a seven-segment display, driven by four input pins labeled Z, O, E and F. The documentation is extremely thin, stating only that it 'spells leters' and that testing involves shifting a one-hot value, so the exact encoding and sequencing are not described. No external hardware is mentioned beyond the seven-segment display itself. Because the description is so sparse, the tags and summary are largely inferred from the title and pin names.
tt03/zoechip.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register and education tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt03/zymason_tinytop.summary: This SystemVerilog design stores up to twelve seven-segment digit patterns in registers and can read them back sequentially at a variable rate controlled by a clock divider. In write mode the segment inputs are multiplexed to set the first four segments and then the remaining three, with the select pin advancing to the next digit; in read mode the stored digits cycle on the outputs with a period from about 82 ms to 2.6 s. The user is responsible for tracking how many digits have been set. No external hardware is required.
tt03/zymason_tinytop.review_notes: Removed fsm (no state machine described) and corrected the summary, which invented a warning about stale data not present in the source.

tt03p5/tt_um_MichaelBell_hovalaag.summary: This is a hardware implementation of the HOVALAAG VLIW processor, originally from a programming game. It uses 32-bit instructions and 12-bit I/O, with data transferred over 5 clocks per processor clock. The design can be programmed using an external assembler and tested by loading programs and observing outputs. It is notable for being a faithful recreation of a game CPU in hardware.
tt03p5/tt_um_MichaelBell_hovalaag.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added retro for the game-derived processor.

tt03p5/tt_um_Reloj_top.summary: This design is a wall clock with an alarm feature, using an 8-digit 7-segment display multiplexed via time-division. It includes three buttons for setting the time and alarm. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a brief description and no detailed testing instructions. It requires external hardware such as a 7-segment display and buttons.
tt03p5/tt_um_Reloj_top.review_notes: Replaced clock-generator/counter with rtc and button to match the actual wall-clock design.

tt03p5/tt_um_TrainLED2_top.summary: This design is a fully digital RGB LED driver that accepts WS2812 protocol data and controls three LEDs with 8-bit PWM per channel. It includes a dithering scheme for flicker-free dimming at low clock rates and can forward additional data to another driver. The design requires external LEDs connected to the outputs and a microcontroller to generate the slowed-down WS2812 input. It is notable for its robust clocked implementation and testbench.

tt03p5/tt_um_algofoogle_solo_squash.summary: Solo Squash is a single-player Pong-like game that outputs a 640x480 VGA signal and simple tones. The player controls a paddle to keep a ball bouncing within a playfield, with no score. The design includes a leading zero counter experiment that outputs on the bidirectional pins. It requires external VGA connections with resistors, buttons, and an optional speaker.
tt03p5/tt_um_algofoogle_solo_squash.review_notes: Leading-zero counter was mislabeled as a priority encoder; corrected to counter.

tt03p5/tt_um_apu_pulse.summary: This project is an attempt to recreate the NES APU pulse oscillator using XLS. It implements a base oscillator with adjustable period and duty cycle, and outputs multiple octave-shifted signals. The design requires external hardware such as an ADC, potentiometers, and a speaker for testing. It is notable for using XLS for hardware generation and targeting audio synthesis.
tt03p5/tt_um_apu_pulse.review_notes: Removed verilog tag because the design is written in XLS, not Verilog.

tt03p5/tt_um_as1802.summary: AS1802 is an implementation of the CDP1802 microprocessor architecture with a Q-SPI memory interface. It supports external ROM and RAM chips for program and data storage, and includes general-purpose I/O. The design is tested by connecting a W25Q-series ROM preloaded with a program that blinks the Q output. It is notable for being a CPU with external memory support.
tt03p5/tt_um_as1802.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart tag; added retro and qspi tags supported by the source.

tt03p5/tt_um_cam.summary: This module implements a 16x7 content-addressable memory (CAM) that is addressed by its contents rather than explicit addresses. It uses behavioral Verilog to infer comparators and registers, and supports writing with automatic replacement of the oldest entry. The design is tested using a cocotb testbench and requires no external hardware. It is notable for being a simple, purely behavioral CAM implementation.

tt03p5/tt_um_gatecat_fpga_top.summary: This project is a small FPGA test design featuring a 2:1 multiplexer and configuration logic. The documentation is incomplete, with 'TODO' placeholders for how it works, how to test, and external hardware. The pin names suggest it involves configuration frame signals and selection inputs. Due to the lack of documentation, the exact functionality and usage cannot be determined.

tt03p5/tt_um_greycode_top.summary: This design selects one of six ring oscillators or the system clock and divides the chosen frequency by 10 and 100. It outputs a 5-bit Gray-coded decimal value representing the divided count. The design is intended as a test structure for characterizing ring oscillators on the ASIC. It requires no external hardware beyond the clock and provides a way to observe oscillator behavior through the divided outputs.
tt03p5/tt_um_greycode_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter/oscillator tags and added verilog, which is stated in the source.

tt03p5/tt_um_htfab_totp.summary: This project implements a TOTP authenticator that generates 6 to 8 digit codes for two-factor authentication, compatible with common apps like Google Authenticator. It accepts a shared secret and timestamp via a serial input and displays the generated code on a 7-segment display. Debug outputs are available on the bidirectional pins for inspecting internal SHA1 and HMAC operations. The design is documented only by its pin names and a TODO placeholder, so detailed operation and testing procedures are not provided.
tt03p5/tt_um_htfab_totp.review_notes: Removed uart tag because the serial input is custom, not a UART interface; added insufficient-doc due to TODO documentation.

tt03p5/tt_um_kiwih_tt_top.summary: QTCore-A1 is an accumulator-based 8-bit microprocessor with a Von Neumann architecture, designed for Tiny Tapeout 3.5. It includes a control unit, program counter, instruction register, accumulator, and 19 bytes of memory, all accessible via a scan chain. The processor is programmed and controlled through an external microcontroller's SPI interface, using the SPI clock to drive both the scan chain and the processor. Notably, all functional Verilog was generated by GPT-4 through conversation, with human-written testbenches used for validation.
tt03p5/tt_um_kiwih_tt_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added fsm, scan-chain and spi tags supported by the source.

tt03p5/tt_um_loopback.summary: This is a simple loopback test module that mirrors input 0 to outputs 0 through 6, and outputs the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7 on output 7. It is used to verify signal integrity and timing by toggling input 0 and measuring the delay until the corresponding outputs change. The design requires no external hardware beyond the input signals. It serves as a basic infrastructure test for the Tiny Tapeout 3.5 shuttle.
tt03p5/tt_um_loopback.review_notes: Removed gpio because the design is a loopback test; added factory-test and combinational.

tt03p5/tt_um_millerresearch_top.summary: SPINet is a network-on-chip designed to connect microcontroller clusters via SPI. It provides SPI interfaces for up to four nodes, with handshake signals for data flow control. The design is documented with a reference to an external video for background, but the on-chip documentation is minimal. Testing instructions are not provided, so users must infer operation from pin names and the external reference.
tt03p5/tt_um_millerresearch_top.review_notes: Removed soc as the design is a network-on-chip, not a system-on-chip; added insufficient-doc due to very thin documentation.

tt03p5/tt_um_moyes0_top_module.summary: The M0 is a 16-bit bit-serial microprocessor based on the SUBLEQ architecture, requiring external SPI RAM and ROM for operation. It includes a transmit UART for serial output and interoperates with Oleg Mazonka's HSQ C-compiler for SUBLEQ. The design can be tested without RAM/ROM by observing SPI clock patterns and UART output, or with external memory for full program execution. Notable for fitting a capable processor into a very small area, though it operates slowly due to its bit-serial nature.

tt03p5/tt_um_power_test.summary: This is a power test module that replicates the standard Tiny Tapeout test design but includes a PMOS transistor to control power to the module. The PMOS requires an external active-low enable signal. The design passes input signals directly to outputs, allowing verification that outputs toggle when power is enabled. It is used to evaluate the power switching FET on the TT03p5 shuttle.
tt03p5/tt_um_power_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported application and interface tags; kept test and power-gating tags.

tt03p5/tt_um_psychogenic_neptuneproporti.summary: This project is a guitar tuner that measures the frequency of input pulses and displays the result on a 7-segment display. It uses clock dividers and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display, and outputs a slower square wave on output 7. The design is documented with a TODO placeholder, so detailed operation and testing are not fully described. It requires an external signal representing the frequency to be measured.
tt03p5/tt_um_psychogenic_neptuneproporti.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added incomplete due to TODO in description.

tt03p5/tt_um_ringosc_cnt_pfet.summary: This design is a ring oscillator with a 64-bit counter that counts oscillations, gated by a PFET for power switching tests. The counter value can be shifted out via inputs, and the counter can be reset or stopped. It is used to evaluate the power switching FET on the TT03p5 shuttle. The design requires no external hardware beyond control signals.
tt03p5/tt_um_ringosc_cnt_pfet.review_notes: Summary was already four sentences; no factual changes needed.

tt03p5/tt_um_ternaryPC_radixconvert.summary: This design implements a 4-trit balanced ternary program counter with up, down, and hold counting modes, as well as jump/load capability. It also includes a 3-trit asynchronous balanced ternary radix converter that converts to signed binary and back. The design is written in MRCS and tests the capabilities of the MRCS Verilog generator and Tiny Tapeout's bidirectional pins. It is verified on an FPGA with a provided testbench, and the ASIC version is functionally similar.
tt03p5/tt_um_ternaryPC_radixconvert.review_notes: Removed cpu because this is a program counter and converter, and added fpga and mixed-signal based on the source.

tt03p5/tt_um_test.summary: This design is a test module that either outputs a counter to its 8 outputs and bidirectional pins or mirrors its 8 inputs to the outputs, depending on the state of input 0. It is used by setting input 0 high and observing that the outputs toggle. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself. This is a simple factory test pattern with minimal documentation.
tt03p5/tt_um_test.review_notes: Pins are generic test signals, not a seven-segment display; counter behavior is only one test mode, so factory-test is the appropriate type.

tt03p5/tt_um_thorkn_vgaclock.summary: This design generates a 5-pin VGA signal from a 25 MHz clock, displaying a clock with three bars whose heights represent hours, minutes, and seconds. It is tested on an FPGA and requires a VGA screen connected to the pins. The Verilog is generated from a SpinalHDL project and manually adapted to the TT03p5 requirements. The design uses only one digital pin per color channel, limiting color depth.
tt03p5/tt_um_thorkn_vgaclock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator as the design is a clock display, not a clock signal generator; added rtc and spinalhdl.

tt03p5/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This circuit drives a 16x16 P10 LED panel, initially displaying the string 'TT03P5'. It accepts a 1.2 Mbaud UART input to paint pixels, erase pixels, clear the display, and change the displayed color, but resource limitations restrict it to a single color at a time and no double buffering. A mode pin allows selection between two clocking patterns to accommodate different panel wiring. External hardware includes an LED panel and a level converter to 5V logic.

tt03p5/tt_um_urish_dffram.summary: This design implements a 128-byte DFFRAM module with address, write enable, and data input/output pins. The documentation consists only of 'TODO' placeholders, so the exact functionality and usage are not described. The pin names indicate a memory interface with 7 address bits, a write enable, 8 data inputs, and 8 data outputs. No test or usage information is provided.
tt03p5/tt_um_urish_dffram.review_notes: Removed register-file tag as unsupported; memory and insufficient-doc retained.

tt03p5/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This design implements the 'Simon Says' memory game, where the user repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors, each associated with a tone played on a speaker. It requires four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, and optionally a speaker or buzzer; the game is reset and then started by pressing any button. The design needs a 50 kHz clock input and has been tested in the Wokwi online simulator. It is a simple educational game with clear documentation.
tt03p5/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed wokwi and education tags because the implementation is Verilog and no educational intent is stated.

tt03p5/tt_um_urish_sram_poc.summary: This design is a proof-of-concept SRAM controller for 128 bytes of memory, with pins for address, write enable, and data input/output, including a bank select signal that multiplexes some bidirectional pins. The documentation is entirely 'TODO', so the detailed operation and usage are not described. The pin names suggest a banked memory interface with 9 address bits and 8 data bits. No test or implementation details are provided.

tt03p5/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This design shows the time on a VGA screen using a 31.5 MHz clock, with pins for hsync, vsync, and 6-bit color output (two bits per RGB channel). It uses a pre-generated font loaded into registers and 'races the beam' to generate the display. External hardware includes an R2R DAC to convert the digital color outputs to analog VGA signals and a VGA monitor. The design supports adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds via input pins.
tt03p5/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (misleading; it is a time display) and added rtc.

tt03p5/tt_um_wokwi_347144898258928211.summary: This Wokwi project outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display, using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through the characters. The counter increments with a 1 Hz clock and resets after 11, determining which character is displayed. Test inputs include a reset counter, clock disable, and four test logic pins, but the testing procedure is not explained in the documentation. The truth table for the design is provided in an external spreadsheet.

tt03p5/tt_um_wokwi_347417602591556180.summary: This Wokwi project outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display, using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through the characters. The counter increments with a 1 Hz clock and resets after 11, determining which character is displayed. Test inputs include a reset counter, clock disable, and four test logic pins, but the testing procedure is not explained in the documentation. The truth table for the design is provided in an external spreadsheet.

tt03p5/tt_um_wokwi_347497504164545108.summary: This Wokwi project outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display, using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through the characters. The counter increments with a 1 Hz clock and resets after 11, determining which character is displayed. Test inputs include a reset counter, clock disable, and four test logic pins, but the testing procedure is not explained in the documentation. The truth table for the design is provided in an external spreadsheet.

tt03p5/tt_um_wokwi_366318576852367361.summary: This design is an asynchronous ternary selector, with pins named for ternary inputs and outputs, including error flags and test controls. The documentation is minimal, with only placeholder text for how it works and how to test. The pin names suggest a ternary logic function, but the exact operation and usage are not described. It is likely a process or logic experiment.
tt03p5/tt_um_wokwi_366318576852367361.review_notes: Removed esoteric as unsupported; added combinational based on the selector pin structure.

tt04/tt_um_4_LUT_Baungarten.summary: This design, named LFMPDM (Lightning Fast Matrix Programmable Design Module), implements 8 four-input look-up tables (LUTs) that can be configured via input pins. The documentation contains only placeholder text for how it works and how to test, so the detailed operation is not described. The pin names indicate an address/data bus for loading configuration, a data input, and a single output. It appears to be a small programmable logic block but lacks sufficient documentation.

tt04/tt_um_ALU_NicolasOrcasitas.summary: This project is an 8-bit ALU that implements eight operations. The outputs drive the segments of a 7-segment display, with the eight uo pins mapped to segments a through g and the decimal point. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the specific operations, input mapping and test procedure are not described. It is a small 1x1 tile design written in Verilog, but little else can be confirmed from the provided material.

tt04/tt_um_BounceFSM_RSX92.summary: This design is a finite state machine that checks a hard-coded password entered by the user. Four input pins carry the data nibble, one pin is a send strobe and one is a clock enable, while the eight outputs present an acknowledge byte. The documentation states that the password is 3044238, which is the only test instruction given. It is a small 1x1 Verilog project, and no external hardware beyond the input switches and output observation is described.
tt04/tt_um_BounceFSM_RSX92.review_notes: Removed security tag as unsupported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_CPU.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit CPU based on 8bitworkshop. Eight input pins form the data input bus, eight bidirectional pins carry a write strobe and a seven-bit address, and eight output pins provide the data output bus. The documentation is limited to a one-line description and a note that testing is a brief explanation, so the instruction set and memory interface are not detailed. It is a 1x1 Verilog tile with no further test or hardware information provided.
tt04/tt_um_CPU.review_notes: Removed memory tag because the design is a CPU, not a memory block.

tt04/tt_um_FSM.summary: This design is a finite state machine that controls the direction of a micro-robot based on front, left and right sensors. Motor direction is driven by four outputs intended for an H-bridge, and an 8-bit PWM resolution value is loaded from the bidirectional pins while reset is active, with the PWM signal appearing on an output pin. The documentation notes that the pinout matches the TT Audio template and that testing involves changing inputs to observe state and motor direction changes. It is a 1x1 Verilog design aimed at simple micro-robot navigation experiments.

tt04/tt_um_FreqMeter_Juan_Garcial.summary: This project is a frequency meter that measures an input signal and displays the result. A single input pin receives the signal to be measured, and three output pins drive a multiplexed 7-segment display through segment, digit-select and segment-select lines. The documentation is placeholder text, so the measurement method, range and test procedure are not described. It is a 1x1 Verilog design whose capabilities can only be inferred from the title and pin names.
tt04/tt_um_FreqMeter_Juan_Garcial.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the documentation is placeholder text.

tt04/tt_um_LEOGLM_hamming_code_top.summary: This project implements a (11,7) Hamming code encoder and decoder that communicate over a UART protocol. The encoder adds four parity bits to parallel data and the UART transmitter serialises it, while the receiver converts serial data back to parallel and the decoder corrects up to one bit error before outputting the original message. A mode pin switches between encoder and decoder functions, and the shared input/output ports are used for both. Testing involves feeding parallel data to the encoder and checking the serial coded output, or feeding serial coded data with at most one bit error to the decoder.

tt04/tt_um_MichaelBell_nanoV.summary: This is a minimal RV32E bit-serial processor that uses an external SPI RAM for both instructions and data, with the SPI RAM and UART connected to the bidirectional pins. It has no caches and runs at roughly clock speed divided by 32, with registers x3 and x4 hardcoded for cheap access to RAM and peripherals, and no support for ebreak or interrupts. The eight inputs and eight outputs are general-purpose GPIO, and the outputs can also drive a 7-segment display; the UART runs at clock speed divided by 128 with simple status bits and no FIFOs. Silicon testing by the author confirmed the design works, and programs can be built with the nanoV-sdk and tested against an SPI RAM or an RP2040-based emulator.

tt04/tt_um_MultiPatternLEDSequencer_RSYO.summary: This project is a multi-pattern LED sequencer that drives eight LEDs with thirty-one selectable patterns plus a demo mode that cycles through all of them. Pattern selection is set by five input pins, and two further pins choose between 1 Hz, 2 Hz, 5 Hz and 50 Hz clock rates derived from the 10 MHz input by an internal divider. Patterns are generated using counters, feedback loops and an LFSR for pseudo-random sequences, and the design is split into a PLL/divider module and the main MPLS module. Testing is done through Icarus Verilog testbenches, with a full-pattern simulation and a longer PLL simulation that can produce very large VCD files.
tt04/tt_um_MultiPatternLEDSequencer_RSYO.review_notes: Removed clock-divider; it is a secondary support block and the design is primarily a LED pattern sequencer.

tt04/tt_um_RELOG_10M_Juan_Garcial.summary: This project is a clock that displays the time on a multiplexed 7-segment display. Input pins select display type, format, programming mode and time adjustment, while outputs provide an AM/PM indicator plus segment, digit-select and segment-select lines. The documentation is placeholder text, so the timekeeping source, programming procedure and test method are not described. It is a 1x1 Verilog design whose functionality is inferred mainly from the title and pin names.
tt04/tt_um_RELOG_10M_Juan_Garcial.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (wrong type) and added counter and insufficient-doc to match the timekeeping design and placeholder documentation.

tt04/tt_um_RS_Vfreq.summary: This design is a clock frequency divider that generates several divided clock signals from a user-selected modulo value. Eight input pins set the modulo M, and the bidirectional pins output clocks divided by 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 along with the raw modulo M pulse, while the eight outputs drive a 7-segment display. Internally a counter counts to M-1 and its terminal signal clocks a 7-bit counter whose stages provide the divided outputs. Testing only requires setting the modulo value on the dedicated input switches.
tt04/tt_um_RS_Vfreq.review_notes: Removed signal-generator; added clock-divider, counter and 7-segment tags supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_USM_temp_sens_hyst.summary: This design implements a temperature sensor using a ring oscillator whose frequency varies with temperature, counted over a clock period and averaged over four samples. The averaged value is output via UART and the standard I/O pins, and a hysteresis module provides a temperature warning output. The ring oscillator starts after reset and enable are set, and a UART command initiates the measurement. The design is notable for its use of a ring oscillator for temperature sensing.
tt04/tt_um_USM_temp_sens_hyst.review_notes: Removed unsupported sensor-interface and timer tags; removed unsupported low-power claim from summary.

tt04/tt_um_adder_NestorMatajira.summary: This design adds two 4-bit numbers. It consists of four adders: one half adder and three full adders. The first number is set on pins 0 to 3 and the second number on pins 4 to 7. The result is output on five output pins.
tt04/tt_um_adder_NestorMatajira.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the 4-bit adder documentation.

tt04/tt_um_adriannovosel_top.summary: This design is an early work-in-progress implementation of a low-power sensor interface for a multichannel acoustic emission detector. It contains four 12-bit pulse counters with overflow detection, an mm:ss real-time clock, and a parallel-in serial-out readout register controlled by a state machine. The counters accumulate pulses on four input channels and are read out serially after each RTC overflow or channel overflow. It is intended for low-power wake-up sensor interfaces, acoustic event detection, non-destructive testing, and particle counting.
tt04/tt_um_adriannovosel_top.review_notes: Corrected the summary, which wrongly claimed sparse documentation, and added counter/rtc/uart/fsm/instrumentation tags.

tt04/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray-casting game demo implemented in Verilog. It renders a realtime 3D-like view of a hard-coded 16x16 map with textures and flat-colored floor/ceiling, inspired by Wolf3D. A host controller sets the point of view via SPI, and SPI2 sets ceiling/floor colors. It outputs 640x480 VGA at about 60 Hz from a 25 MHz clock and has a partial silicon test report.
tt04/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated edge detector; corrected to the documented VGA ray caster.

tt04/tt_um_alu.summary: This design is a 4-bit ALU that can perform addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and bitwise AND. The A and B inputs are the data for the ALU, and the S input selects the operation. The result is output on eight output pins. External hardware includes buttons or DIP switches.
tt04/tt_um_alu.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the 4-bit ALU documentation.

tt04/tt_um_alu4_alonso59.summary: This project is titled '4-bits 1-channel PWM and ALU 4 bits' and is described as a 4-bit, 1-channel PWM module. The documentation states only that ui_in[7:0] is used as input and uo_out should be read to get the output. No details are provided about the ALU or PWM behavior.
tt04/tt_um_alu4_alonso59.review_notes: Replaced unsupported random/analog tags with ALU and insufficient-doc.

tt04/tt_um_ashleyjr_delay_line.summary: This design is a simple tapped delay line with instrumentation. The continually changing data races through a chain of inverters and is sampled at different stages to become a digital signal. An edge detection circuit finds the rising edge, which is converted into a binary value, and a bank of flops samples eight sequential rising edge values. The UART is the only interface to the design, with commands for shift in, shift out, full sample, and scope.
tt04/tt_um_ashleyjr_delay_line.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the delay line instrumentation documentation.

tt04/tt_um_biased_trng.summary: This design is a variable duty-cycle true random number generator based on seven 7-stage ring oscillators. The oscillators are enabled by an 'ena' signal and their outputs are combined at a common node. An inverter-bias system using a vDAC selects a voltage from the first four input pins. The resulting signal passes through two D flip-flops and an AND gate to produce the final random output.
tt04/tt_um_biased_trng.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the TRNG/ring-oscillator design.

tt04/tt_um_bulls_and_cows.summary: This design implements the Bulls and Cows game where users try to discover a secret pattern of four 3-bit numbers. The user inputs four 3-bit numbers and the design outputs bulls and cows indications on a seven segment display. Bulls indicate correct numbers in the correct position, while cows indicate correct numbers in the wrong position. The goal is to achieve four bulls indications.
tt04/tt_um_bulls_and_cows.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the source; corrected to reflect the Bulls and Cows game.

tt04/tt_um_ccollatz_SergioOliveros.summary: This design computes the Collatz orbit of an 8-bit input number. It outputs the number of iterations required to reach 1 and a status bit indicating whether the calculation is in progress or complete. Once the process is finished, the circuit keeps the iteration count indefinitely so that it can be checked. Testing requires a clock signal, an 8-bit input number, and the active-low rst_n signal to start the iterations.
tt04/tt_um_ccollatz_SergioOliveros.review_notes: Replaced unsupported tags with fsm, sequential-logic, and verilog, and rewrote the summary to match the Collatz design.

tt04/tt_um_chip_SP_Soy_de_Zacapa.summary: This design outputs ASCII-encoded text sequences character by character, selecting between two texts using a 2-bit input. One text is the beginning of a traditional Guatemalan song, and the other lists the project participants' names. An internal counter increments each clock cycle until a limit is reached, then resets to repeat the sequence. Testing requires an external microcontroller to read the 8 output pins synchronously and forward the characters over UART to a computer terminal; the author tested it with a TIVA C and an FPGA.
tt04/tt_um_chip_SP_Soy_de_Zacapa.review_notes: Removed uart and education tags not supported by the design itself.

tt04/tt_um_chip_SP_measure_delay.summary: This project attempts to build a cascaded NOT-gate ring oscillator for delay measurements, but the synthesizer does not support combinatorial feedback and collapsed the cascaded inverters into buffers, so the original ring oscillator goal was not achieved. The two enable inputs control signal propagation through the gate chain to three output taps representing different gate stages. A square wave can be applied to the inputs and an oscilloscope used to measure stage delays for comparison with theoretical calculations. The design is presented as an educational experiment about synthesis limitations rather than a working oscillator.
tt04/tt_um_chip_SP_measure_delay.review_notes: Removed unsupported combinational and delay-line tags; added incomplete because the stated ring oscillator goal was not achieved.

tt04/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This is an 8-bit wide, 128-byte ROM containing information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, with the shuttle name in 7-segment encoding and a null-terminated ASCII chip descriptor of key-value lines. The address is set on the eight input pins and the data is read from the eight output pins. The first bytes can be read by toggling the first four DIP switches and observing the on-board 7-segment display. The author's silicon test report states that the entire ROM was read back correctly.
tt04/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed 7-segment because the design only stores 7-segment-encoded data rather than driving a seven-segment display.

tt04/tt_um_chiplet_jtag.summary: This design implements JTAG test logic with four test data registers: an 8-bit boundary scan register between the fixed input and output pins, plus blink_in, blink_out and blink_dir registers for the two bidirectional pins. The JTAG TCK, TMS, TDI, TRSTn and TDO signals are routed through user IO, and the default clock and reset are left unconnected because JTAG supplies its own. It is controlled by resetting the core, shifting an instruction into the IR to select a TDR, then shifting data bits into that register. Testing requires a JTAG debug adapter, and the cocotb simulation includes helper routines for driving the JTAG state machine.
tt04/tt_um_chiplet_jtag.review_notes: Removed fsm and bist tags that are not supported as primary design characteristics.

tt04/tt_um_ciro.summary: The project is titled "Later" and its one-line description, how-it-works and how-to-test sections all consist only of the word "Later". No functional description, pin names or test procedure are provided, so it is impossible to determine what the design does. The only concrete information is that it is a 1x1 Verilog tile with a 10 MHz clock. This appears to be an unfinished placeholder project with essentially no documentation.
tt04/tt_um_ciro.review_notes: Removed template tag as source is a placeholder, not a template.

tt04/tt_um_control.summary: This project is described in Spanish as a counter from 0 to 16 with load capability, implemented in Verilog. The pin names indicate a clock, reset, an initialisation or load input, an enable input, and outputs for a 7-segment display including segments b through g and the dot. However, the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are still the unfilled template text, so the exact counting behaviour, load mechanism and display encoding cannot be confirmed. The design is likely a simple counter driving a 7-segment display, but the documentation is too thin to describe it in detail.
tt04/tt_um_control.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and redundant display tags, added insufficient-doc, and removed the unsupported educational claim from the summary.

tt04/tt_um_currymottled.summary: This is a configurable PID control block intended to be configured over I2C, with six bidirectional GPIO pins used for error and control signals and two pins used as SDA and SCL. It also drives a 7-segment display through eight output pins. The description notes it was meant to be a final project but was undercut, and the how-to-test section refers to I2C files for the register addresses and an I2C test file for an example. The documentation does not specify the PID parameters, fixed-point format or control loop details.
tt04/tt_um_currymottled.review_notes: Added controller as the central function and removed insufficient-doc because the design purpose and pinout are described; the sparse configuration details are already reflected in the summary.

tt04/tt_um_dandy_dance.summary: This is a serial vector graphics adapter that receives primitive drawing instructions over a UART at 921600 baud and drives X and Y outputs for an XY vector display. It has sixteen instruction registers that can be programmed and updated live over serial, with a state machine executing primitives such as lines and squares, and a safe/unsafe mode toggle plus a clock divider input for slow DAC drive speeds. The 8-bit X and Y outputs can be converted to analog with an R2R ladder or similar DAC arrangement, and the author tested it with a Teensy 4.1. External hardware needed includes two DACs, a vector graphics display such as an oscilloscope in XY mode, and a fast UART source.
tt04/tt_um_dandy_dance.review_notes: Removed vga, dac, and r2r-dac tags as the design does not implement these interfaces; added graphics, uart, fsm, demoscene, and verilog tags supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_darkfsegura_collatz.summary: This component computes the Collatz sequence for an 8-bit input number, using a four-register datapath and ALU that emulates basic assembler instructions driven by a simple state machine. Data is presented on the 8-bit input bus and the reset signal is activated to latch the input and begin the series calculation, with results appearing on the 8-bit output bus. The sequence is computed at close to the clock rate, so intermediate values are not visible without probing individual digital channels on an oscilloscope. The design is synchronous and includes a reset input, but the documentation gives no further detail on the instruction set or timing.
tt04/tt_um_darkfsegura_collatz.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file, pipeline, sequencer, and esoteric tags.

tt04/tt_um_db_PWM.summary: This design generates a PWM signal by comparing a selected duty-cycle bus against a counter, with the counter maximum resolution set by three bidirectional bit-selector pins. Higher resolution requires more counter bits and therefore produces a lower PWM frequency, and a D flip-flop on the comparator output synchronises the signal and reduces glitches when values change mid-run. The duty value is applied to the eight input pins and the PWM appears on the first output pin, with the maximum bits set on the bidirectional pins. Testing involves setting the duty bus and maximum bits, then pressing reset for the PWM to operate as configured.
tt04/tt_um_db_PWM.review_notes: Changed 'restart' to 'reset' to match the actual reset function of the design.

tt04/tt_um_dcb277_ALU.summary: This project is a programmable counter and clock divider that drives a 7-segment display. It divides the 10 MHz clock to generate a 1 Hz counter by default, and displays the lower 8 bits of the counter on the 7-segment display while outputting them on the bidirectional pins. The inputs can override the default compare value to change the counting speed. The documentation focuses on the counter aspect and does not describe any arithmetic operations.
tt04/tt_um_dcb277_ALU.review_notes: Removed alu because no arithmetic is documented, and corrected the summary to match the source.

tt04/tt_um_devinatkin_arduino_vga.summary: This project aims to create a VGA output driver for Arduino, generating a 640x480 60Hz signal. It currently outputs a random noise pattern and can be configured via SPI to display a solid colour or other patterns. The design is in an early stage, with features like character memory not yet fully implemented due to utilization constraints. It requires a VGA connector and an external microcontroller for control, and has been simulated but not yet fully tested on hardware.
tt04/tt_um_devinatkin_arduino_vga.review_notes: Removed 'incomplete' as the design is functional with a partial silicon report; added 'silicon-tested' to match the reported silicon status.

tt04/tt_um_divider_urielcho.summary: This project is a clock divider that outputs multiple divided clock signals. The documentation is essentially empty, with placeholder text for how it works and how to test. It likely divides the input clock by powers of two, but the exact implementation and usage are not described. The design appears to be a simple experiment or test.
tt04/tt_um_divider_urielcho.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the source only supports clock division, not clock generation.

tt04/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv4.summary: This project implements a 4-bit combinational multiplier and divider unit that supports both signed and unsigned operations. The multiplier uses a ripple carry array, while the divider uses a restoring array algorithm. It has error indicators for division overflow and divide-by-zero. The design was created in Logisim and exported to Verilog, and silicon tests confirm it works.

tt04/tt_um_dlmiles_tt04_poc_usbdev.summary: This is a USB FullSpeed/LowSpeed device controller implemented in SpinalHDL, designed to be controlled by a CPU over a Wishbone bus. It includes a TT2WB Wishbone bridge to fit the limited Tiny Tapeout I/O. The design supports up to 4 endpoints with 52 bytes of buffer, which may be insufficient for some USB classes. It requires external USB connector hardware and an FPGA or RP2040 for testing and demonstration.
tt04/tt_um_dlmiles_tt04_poc_usbdev.review_notes: Removed fpga tag because the design targets ASIC, not FPGA; added cocotb, asic, and clock-domain-crossing based on explicit documentation.

tt04/tt_um_eldritch_pwm_peripheral.summary: This project is an open-source PWM peripheral with advanced features such as deadband generation and counter synchronization, aimed at power electronics applications. It contains three counters, each with two comparators and two deadband generators, configurable via a register file. The peripheral is controlled through a simple parallel interface, and can be tested with a microcontroller or manually using switches. The PWM outputs are observed on the output pins; the summary's 'external hardware required' wording is softened because the documentation documents the pins and testing method.
tt04/tt_um_eldritch_pwm_peripheral.review_notes: Removed unsupported motor-control and softened the external-hardware claim.

tt04/tt_um_f_hal_fft.summary: This project implements a 4-point, 8-point, and 16-point FFT calculator using the radix-2 Cooley-Tukey algorithm with 4-bit fixed-point precision. It features a simple user interface with buttons for mode selection and data entry, and displays results on a 7-segment display. The design is intended for low-complexity circuits and includes bit-reversal ordering and a single butterfly unit. It requires external buttons and a way to input and read 8-bit data.
tt04/tt_um_f_hal_fft.review_notes: Removed calculator and education tags; added button tag for the mode/enter controls.

tt04/tt_um_fabian.summary: This project, titled 'Later', has no documentation beyond a title and placeholder text. It appears to drive a 7-segment display but its functionality is entirely unspecified. The design is likely incomplete or a placeholder. There is not enough information to determine what it does or how to use it.
tt04/tt_um_fabian.review_notes: Replaced template with placeholder because the source contains only placeholder documentation.

tt04/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module for Tiny Tapeout 04. When input 0 is high, it outputs a counter on the output and bidirectional pins; otherwise it mirrors the inputs to the outputs. It is used to verify the chip's functionality. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected.

tt04/tt_um_fifo_stevej.summary: This project implements an 8-bit FIFO with a depth of 16, featuring First-Word Fall-Through read operation. It includes status flags such as empty, full, underflow, overflow, almost_empty, and almost_full. The FIFO allows communication between two parties with a limited channel, and can be tested by writing and reading items while checking status bits. Unit tests are available for further verification.
tt04/tt_um_fifo_stevej.review_notes: Summary was already four sentences; no factual changes needed.

tt04/tt_um_fing_synchronizer_hga.summary: This design implements and compares three different clock domain crossing synchronizers: a two flip-flop synchronizer, a recirculation mux synchronizer, and a toggle synchronizer. The user can select which synchronizer output to observe using a 3-bit selector input, and the design includes an enable control block to run each synchronizer once. External hardware is not required beyond clock and data sources to drive the inputs. The project is notable for being an educational testbed to study metastability mitigation techniques in multi-clock designs.

tt04/tt_um_fir_top.summary: This design implements a 4-tap FIR filter with user-configurable coefficients, or default coefficients set to 1. It takes an input signal x[n] and produces output y[n] by multiplying the last four input samples with the coefficients and summing the results. The coefficients can be assigned via switches when the enable signal is high, and a reset sets past values to zero and coefficients to ones. External hardware includes a microcontroller to send the x[n] values, and the design is notable for being a simple digital filter implementation.
tt04/tt_um_fir_top.review_notes: Removed shift-register tag as it is not a primary documented feature.

tt04/tt_um_fm_transmitter.summary: This design is an FM transmitter that takes an audio signal via I2S and modulates it onto a higher carrier frequency using a numerically controlled oscillator with a piecewise linear approximation of a sine wave. It outputs a 4-bit digital signal intended for an external R-2R ladder DAC to generate the analog FM signal. The design is not intended for real on-air use and requires external filtering to comply with regulations. It is notable for its resource-efficient approximation of sine generation and its ability to produce FM signals in the broadcast band despite a lower sampling frequency.
tt04/tt_um_fm_transmitter.review_notes: Removed unsupported music and spi tags; added rf and r2r-dac based on the FM broadcast output and external R-2R DAC.

tt04/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit consisting of an 8x8 grid of identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop, and a buffer, with each tile individually rotatable and mirrorable via configuration. Configuration and state are managed through a scan chain, and a loop breaker mechanism helps debug combinational loops. The design supports loading and dumping state, single-stepping, and free running, and it has been tested on silicon with a provided test suite. It is notable for being a port of a larger FPGA design to TinyTapeout with significant area optimization.
tt04/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag because the design occupies only one tile.

tt04/tt_um_i2c.summary: This project implements an I2C slave with address 0x04, as indicated by the title and pin names. It provides 6-bit data paths to and from a master, along with control signals, but the documentation is essentially empty, so its exact functionality and usage cannot be determined. External hardware would likely include an I2C master to communicate with the device. The project is notable only for its sparse documentation and minimal description.
tt04/tt_um_i2c.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc; added register-file based on the 6-bit data path pins.

tt04/tt_um_ja_TrafficLight.summary: This is a traffic light controller implemented as a finite state machine that, when started, cycles through red, green, and yellow lights with durations of 30, 20, and 3 seconds respectively, using a clock frequency divider for timing. The design requires three external LEDs to display the lights, though they are optional. It was created for the LatinPractice Bootcamp at the University of Illinois Springfield (UIS). The project is notable for its educational context and simple, practical application.

tt04/tt_um_jayraj4021_SAP1_cpu.summary: This design is an implementation of the SAP-1 (Simple As Possible) CPU from the book 'Digital Computer Electronics' by Malvino and Brown. It executes a fixed program hard-coded in a 16x8 ROM, implementing instructions like LDA, ADD, SUB, and OUT, with the results appearing on an 8-bit output. It requires an external clock and reset signal, and the output can be observed via LEDs. The project is notable for being an educational CPU implementation that adapts the book's shared-bus architecture to CMOS-friendly design.

tt04/tt_um_jk2102.summary: This design is a controller for a Pulsed Plasma Thruster (PPT) that generates a configurable number of pulses with adjustable frequency and pulse width, controllable via an I2C slave interface. It can also run with default settings using an override input, producing a pulse train at 0.25 Hz with 16 pulses. The design outputs pulse train status and a divided clock, and displays pulses on a 7-segment display. It is verified in simulation and prototyped on an FPGA.
tt04/tt_um_jk2102.review_notes: Removed unsupported physics and industrial tags; added signal-generator, clock-divider, 7-segment, i2c, and verilog based on source evidence.

tt04/tt_um_kpwebb_adder.summary: This design is a simple 8-bit adder built using RustHDL, which adds two 8-bit inputs (ui_in and uio_in) and outputs the sum on uo_out. It requires only a clock and reset signal to function, and no external hardware is needed beyond the connections. The design is notable for being implemented in RustHDL, showcasing an alternative hardware description language. It is a straightforward arithmetic building block with minimal complexity.
tt04/tt_um_kpwebb_adder.review_notes: Summary was already four sentences; no factual changes needed.

tt04/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.summary: This design implements a Karplus-Strong string synthesis algorithm to generate plucked string sounds, with a register map configurable via SPI and audio output via I2S. It also includes two PRBS noise generators for adding noise to the string model. The design requires an external I2S DAC or codec to output the synthesized audio. It is notable for being a digital music synthesizer implementation based on published papers and for its use of a 2x2 tile area.
tt04/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.review_notes: Removed unsupported 7-segment tag; added sound-generator for the plucked-string synthesis.

tt04/tt_um_led_multiplexer_display.summary: This design stores four characters in internal memory and displays them on a 16x4 LED matrix. It accepts four data bits and two position bits to load a hexadecimal character when the load signal is high, and otherwise cycles through the display columns using an internal character map. The design requires an external 16x4 LED matrix connected to the column and line outputs, and it must be reset before use. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation and interface.
tt04/tt_um_led_multiplexer_display.review_notes: Removed counter tag: column scanning is not a counting circuit.

tt04/tt_um_loopback.summary: This is a loopback test module that mirrors input 0 to outputs 0 through 6, and computes the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7 on output 7. It is intended for testing signal integrity and timing by toggling input 0 and measuring the delay until output 0 changes. The design has no external hardware requirements beyond the chip's pins. The documentation is minimal but clearly describes the function and test procedure.

tt04/tt_um_losaias.summary: This design implements an arithmetic logic unit that performs addition, multiplication, XOR, or shift-left on two 8-bit operands. Operands are entered via a 4x4 matrix keyboard, decoded and stored in a register bank, and the operation is selected by two input pins. The result is output on an 8-bit port, and the design includes a two-bit counter for keyboard scanning. The documentation describes the data flow and test procedure, but the pin names are somewhat cryptic and the design requires an external keyboard.

tt04/tt_um_machinaut_systolic.summary: This design is a 2x2 systolic array tile for matrix multiplication, capable of streaming accumulation of a 2xN by Nx2 matrix product. It supports FP8 input formats and FP16 accumulators, with a pipelined multiply-accumulate operation and modes for passthrough, multiply-accumulate, and read-write of accumulators. The design is intended to be tiled in a grid, with data moving along rows and columns via 4-bit data and 1-bit control wires per direction. The documentation is extensive, including timing diagrams and example usage, but the design has not been tested in a full systolic array and safe clock speeds are unknown.

tt04/tt_um_marno_factorize.summary: This design takes an 8-bit input and computes its factors, displaying them one by one on a seven-segment display with a one-second interval. It also indicates prime factors up to 19 on the bidirectional pins and uses the dot on the display to indicate primality. The design uses a modulo computation trick with hardcoded values and includes a clock divider to generate the one-second delay. Silicon testing confirmed it works, and the author notes it was a learning experience in hardware design.
tt04/tt_um_marno_factorize.review_notes: Removed calculator tag; added silicon-tested and counter to match the source and silicon report.

tt04/tt_um_mgyenik_bfcpu.summary: This design is a hardware CPU for the brainfuck esolang with extensions for compressing consecutive operations. It uses an external asynchronous bus to access program and data memory, as well as I/O, since the memory does not fit on the chip. The bus protocol multiplexes address and data, and the CPU requires an external bus device, such as an RP2040, to operate. The documentation is detailed but the design is complex and requires careful integration with external hardware.
tt04/tt_um_mgyenik_bfcpu.review_notes: Removed gpio and memory tags that misdescribe the custom external bus and off-chip memory.

tt04/tt_um_mjbella_led_matrix_driver.summary: This design uses a counter and combinational logic to drive a seven-segment display with the counter value. It also outputs the lower 8 bits of the counter on bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the input pins to program a 24-bit compare value, with a default of one second per increment at 10 MHz. The documentation is brief but describes the operation and test procedure.
tt04/tt_um_mjbella_led_matrix_driver.review_notes: Removed 'led-matrix' and 'driver' as the source describes a seven-segment counter, not an LED matrix driver.

tt04/tt_um_mod_u_cnt_BCD.summary: This design is an up-down counter that counts from 0 to 15 with options for enable, synchronous clear, and parallel load. It uses a clock divider to generate a 1 Hz counting rate from a 10 MHz input and decodes the count to BCD for display on a seven-segment display. The counter direction is controlled by an up input, and the load value is taken from four input pins. The documentation clearly explains the operation and test procedure.
tt04/tt_um_mod_u_cnt_BCD.review_notes: Removed redundant generic display and added the specific canonical tags for BCD, clock division, up-down counting, comparator, and clock generation that are explicitly supported.

tt04/tt_um_morningjava_top.summary: ChipTune is an 8-bit programmable sound generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It features two rectangular pulse generators, a triangle wave generator, and a noise generator, each controlled by four 8-bit registers. Configuration data is received via a UART interface at 9600 baud, and the audio output is pulse-width modulated. The design requires an external analog PWM filter and audio driver for testing, and it can be interfaced with a computer COM port.
tt04/tt_um_morningjava_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported signal-generator tag and added chiptune/retro tags supported by the vintage PSG description.

tt04/tt_um_noritsuna_8bitcounter_AI.summary: This is a simple 8-bit counter that was generated automatically by an Edge AI environment. It has no inputs and outputs the counter value on 8 pins. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it was generated by LLaMa2 and providing a link to the Edge Circuit Designer project. The design serves as a demonstration of AI-generated hardware.
tt04/tt_um_noritsuna_8bitcounter_AI.review_notes: Removed 'machine-learning' and 'education' as the source describes an AI-generated counter, not ML hardware or an educational design.

tt04/tt_um_onehot.summary: This project implements a 3-bit one-hot decoder in Verilog. It takes three input bits and produces eight output bits, with exactly one output asserted for each valid input combination. The documentation is essentially a template with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. No external hardware or testing details are provided.
tt04/tt_um_onehot.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added insufficient-doc for the placeholder documentation.

tt04/tt_um_phansel_laplace_lut.summary: This project is a read-only memory that stores ASCII encodings of LaTeX code for typesetting Laplace transforms of common functions. It is controlled by an address input and a start signal, and it outputs the function and its transform character by character on two separate 8-bit output buses. The design uses two address spaces: one for the character data and one for pointers to each transform's start and length. It was verified on silicon and correctly recalled 43 Laplace transforms after a proper reset.
tt04/tt_um_phansel_laplace_lut.review_notes: Removed dsp and education tags; added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt04/tt_um_pong_neopixel.summary: This project implements a two-player Pong game in Verilog. It uses an 8x8 NeoPixel LED matrix as the display and six push buttons for control: two for each player's paddle movement, one to start the game, and one for reset. The game ends when the ball hits the left or right side of the matrix. External hardware includes the NeoPixel matrix and six push buttons with pull-up resistors.
tt04/tt_um_pong_neopixel.review_notes: Removed gpio because the pins are dedicated game controls and NeoPixel output, and added button, led-matrix, and retro tags supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_priority_decoder_Juan_Garcial.summary: This project is described as a 7-segment clock, but the documentation is a placeholder with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The pin names suggest a serial data input and a data output with a valid signal, but the functionality is unclear. No external hardware or testing details are provided. The design is likely incomplete or undocumented.
tt04/tt_um_priority_decoder_Juan_Garcial.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/counter and added insufficient-doc and incomplete.

tt04/tt_um_pwl_RaulprTech.summary: This project is a module named reciprocal, but the documentation is a placeholder with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The pin names indicate a single input and a single output, suggesting a combinational function. The author's tags mention inverse and piecewise-linear, but no further details are given. No external hardware or testing details are provided.
tt04/tt_um_pwl_RaulprTech.review_notes: Removed unsupported signal-generator and alu tags; added lookup-table based on the pwl author tag.

tt04/tt_um_pwm.summary: This project is a simple PWM generator with a variable duty cycle controlled by two buttons. It includes debounce logic for the buttons and uses a 4-bit counter to generate the PWM signal. The duty cycle can be increased or decreased by pressing the respective buttons. External hardware includes two push buttons with pull-down resistors and an oscilloscope to observe the PWM output.

tt04/tt_um_quardinlyttle_top.summary: This project is a 2-bit ALU with a 4-bit opcode that supports 16 operations including logical, arithmetic, shift, and comparison functions. It also includes a running sum mode that continuously adds the input to the output every second. The outputs are provided on an 8-bit bus and a 7-segment display interface. Testing can be done by connecting the outputs to LEDs or a BCD converter to observe the results.
tt04/tt_um_quardinlyttle_top.review_notes: Removed instruction-decoder and education, and added logic-gate, subtractor, multiplier, comparator, shift-register, and counter tags supported by the documented operations.

tt04/tt_um_rebot449_lingret_ALU_Top.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit ALU with six instructions selected by the three least significant bits of an instruction input. The operations include logical OR, NAND, NOR, AND, addition, and subtraction. The design is based on the Overture architecture from the game Turing Complete. Testing involves applying instructions and data inputs and verifying the 8-bit result output.

tt04/tt_um_rejunity_telluride2023_neuron.summary: This project is a standalone test for a binarized Leaky Integrate and Fire (LIF) neuron, part of a larger experimental design from the Telluride Neuromorphic Workshop 2023. It supports eight binary inputs and binarized weights, accumulating them on an internal membrane that decays exponentially each clock cycle. When the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, the neuron emits a spike and the membrane is decreased. The only output is a binary spike signal. Testing involves holding reset to assign weights, then observing spikes after reset is released.

tt04/tt_um_rgb_mixer.summary: This project uses three rotary encoders to control three PWM generators, intended for mixing RGB LED colors. Each encoder is debounced and adjusts the duty cycle of its corresponding PWM output. The design provides three PWM outputs on the first three output pins. External hardware includes three digital rotary encoders and an RGB LED or other PWM-driven device.
tt04/tt_um_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed led and rgb-led tags because the design only outputs PWM signals and does not directly drive LEDs.

tt04/tt_um_riceshelley_tinyFPGA.summary: Grain-Flex-FPGA is a small field-programmable gate array with one configurable logic block (CLB) containing four 4-input look-up tables, each with an optional output flip-flop. The CLB has four inputs and four outputs that can be routed to any of eight IO buffers, and each LUT input can be connected to any CLB input or any LUT output. The device is programmed through a scan chain using dedicated clock, reset, enable, and data-in pins, with data-out on a single pin. The SpinalHDL project includes examples for generating bitstreams, but no silicon test results are provided, and the documentation notes that VTR support is still forthcoming.

tt04/tt_um_robojan_pong_top.summary: This project implements a two-player Pong game in Verilog, outputting a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. Each player controls a paddle with three buttons (left, right, action), and the game ends when one player runs out of lives. The design uses a VGA timing module and painter modules to generate graphics and detect collisions, with the ball bouncing at different angles depending on where it hits the paddle. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC built from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.
tt04/tt_um_robojan_pong_top.review_notes: R2R DAC is external hardware, not part of the design; added silicon-tested tag based on working silicon report.

tt04/tt_um_robojan_top.summary: Tiny Breakout is a single-player Breakout game in Verilog that outputs a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. The game is controlled by three buttons (left, right, action) and includes an SPI interface for reading the game state and writing commands to modify it. The design uses a VGA timing module, painter modules for graphics, and a shift register to store the 13x16 block grid efficiently. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC made from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.
tt04/tt_um_robojan_top.review_notes: Removed r2r-dac (external hardware only) and added silicon-tested and speaker.

tt04/tt_um_rodrigomunoz1_rotempsensor_to.summary: This design implements a temperature sensor using four ring oscillators whose frequencies vary with temperature. It counts the oscillator cycles over a fixed period of the system clock, accumulates the counts based on a selectable sum factor, and transmits the 3-byte sum over UART when a start code is received. The oscillator counter divided by two is also output on the bidirectional pins and upper output pins. The project is based on a previous Tiny Tapeout design and requires an external clock and UART connection for testing; no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_rodrigomunoz1_rotempsensor_to.review_notes: Removed temperature-sensor and sensor-interface tags because the design only exposes oscillator counts and does not implement a sensor interface.

tt04/tt_um_rs_write_decodifier_fjrn_cinv.summary: This project is a 12-bit write decodifier for a reservation station, likely part of a CPU design. It takes a 12-bit input on the ui and uio pins and produces a 12-bit output on the uo and uio pins, selecting the appropriate reservation station based on the input. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it works by selecting the corresponding RS needed and that testing involves manipulating input switches to observe outputs. No external hardware or silicon test results are mentioned.
tt04/tt_um_rs_write_decodifier_fjrn_cinv.review_notes: Removed cpu because the design is a decodifier block, not a processor core.

tt04/tt_um_sahrdayalfsr.summary: This project is titled as a 4-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) random number generator with configurable feedback polynomials based on a mod input, resetting to an initial state when reset is asserted. The documentation, however, describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal converter for a 7-segment display, with a 24-bit compare register that defaults to 10,000,000 for a 1-second interval at 10 MHz, and inputs that can override bits 11-18 of the compare value. The bottom 8 bits of the counter are output on the bidirectional pins, and the 7-segment segments are driven on the outputs. The mismatch between the title and the description suggests the documentation may be incorrect or incomplete; no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_sahrdayalfsr.review_notes: Title and documentation contradict each other, so a second opinion is needed on the actual design function.

tt04/tt_um_santacrc_tamagotchi.summary: This project implements a simple Tamagotchi virtual pet game in Verilog that communicates over a serial UART interface. The user connects rx and tx to a serial terminal, and the game starts automatically; the pet has stats for food, sleep, happiness, hygiene, and social, which must be maintained by pressing keys (E, S, P, B, T, W) to feed, sleep, play, clean, talk, or wake up. If the pet dies, the reset button restarts the game. The design requires a 27 MHz clock and a serial terminal; no silicon test results are provided.

tt04/tt_um_santiago.summary: This project implements a CDMA transmitter and receiver in Verilog for academic study of spread-spectrum effects and pseudonoise sequences. It uses two 5-bit LFSRs to generate Gold codes, which are used to spread a transmitted signal and to despread a received signal, with a seed input to initialize the LFSRs. The design includes a testbench that simulates transmission and reception, and an LED indicates a valid seed. External hardware includes an operational amplifier for adding noise to simulate a channel, a testboard, and an LED; no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_santiago.review_notes: Removed prng and opamp tags; op-amp is external channel-simulation hardware, and LFSRs generate Gold codes rather than general PRNG output.

tt04/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This project is a 7-segment display counter that increments once per second, counting up to 10. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for the display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter also output on the bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the input pins to override bits 11-18 of a 24-bit compare register; with all inputs zero, the compare is 10,000,000, giving a 1-second interval at 10 MHz. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and a 7-segment display; no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd tag and added canonical tags for the documented 7-segment display, clock divider, counter, timer, and Verilog implementation.

tt04/tt_um_shift.summary: This project is a serializer implemented as a shift register, with a clock, reset, and 6-bit parallel data input, and a single serial output Q plus an end-of-sequence output eos. The documentation is essentially empty, containing only placeholder text for how it works and how to test. No external hardware or silicon test results are mentioned. The functionality is inferred from the pin names and title.

tt04/tt_um_silva.summary: The project is titled "Later" and its one-line description, how-it-works and how-to-test sections all consist only of the word "Later". No functional description, pin names or test procedure are provided, so it is impossible to determine what the design does. The only concrete information is that it is a 1x1 Verilog tile with a 10 MHz clock. This appears to be an unfinished placeholder project with essentially no documentation.
tt04/tt_um_silva.review_notes: Removed template tag as source is a placeholder, not a template.

tt04/tt_um_simple_processor_pablopabota.summary: This design implements an I2C slave port that can read and write the instruction memory of a RISC-V processor. It exposes four registers: one to set the memory address, one to read the current value, one to write a new value, and one unused register. The I2C interface uses external SDA and SCL pins, with an additional reset and chip-select input, and provides open-drain control for SDA. Testing requires an external I2C master to issue the documented read and write transactions.
tt04/tt_um_simple_processor_pablopabota.review_notes: Removed register-file: the four I2C registers are a control interface, not a register-file storage block.

tt04/tt_um_simplepiano.summary: This design is a digital piano that generates twelve independent musical notes across eight octaves and can also play two predefined songs stored in RTTTL format. It uses a 1 MHz clock to produce square-wave audio output and drives an LED bar as a visualizer. The design requires external hardware: twelve momentary switches for the keys, four toggle switches for mode and octave selection, an LED bar, and a speaker with an amplifier. It is notable for its musical application and the inclusion of demo songs, but it has no silicon test report.
tt04/tt_um_simplepiano.review_notes: Removed unsupported lookup-table tag; added button and led for the documented switches and LED bar.

tt04/tt_um_sorter.summary: This design sorts four 2-bit input values using odd-even sorting logic and outputs the sorted values. The four input values are provided on ui_in[7:0], and the sorted results appear on uo_out[7:0]. The sorting operation passes through four internal pipeline registers, so an external clock is required. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description and test instructions, with no silicon test results.
tt04/tt_um_sorter.review_notes: Removed 7-segment tag: the segment labels are pinout metadata, not the design's function.

tt04/tt_um_ternaryPC_radixconvert.summary: This design implements a 4-trit balanced ternary program counter with up, down, and hold counting modes, as well as jump/load capability. It also includes a 3-trit asynchronous balanced ternary radix converter that converts to signed binary and back. The design is written in MRCS and tests the capabilities of the MRCS Verilog generator and Tiny Tapeout's bidirectional pins. It is verified on an FPGA with a provided testbench, and the ASIC version is functionally similar.
tt04/tt_um_ternaryPC_radixconvert.review_notes: Removed cpu because this is a program counter and converter, and added fpga and mixed-signal based on the source.

tt04/tt_um_thezoq2_tmng.summary: This design is a time-multiplexed NAND gate, described as the furthest point in the time/space tradeoff. It uses a 10 MHz clock and provides outputs for a 7-segment display and a second counter. The documentation is essentially empty, with 'TODO' for both how it works and how to test, so the exact functionality cannot be determined. A silicon test report indicates the chip is working, but no further details are given.
tt04/tt_um_thezoq2_tmng.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplexer tag, added logic-gate and silicon-tested based on title and working silicon report.

tt04/tt_um_thorkn_pwmaudio.summary: This design generates audio using PWM output, as indicated by its title and pin names. It has two PWM audio outputs, labeled low and high. The documentation is a template with placeholder text, so no details about the synthesis method, testing, or external hardware are available. It is implemented in Wokwi, but no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_thorkn_pwmaudio.review_notes: Summary already accurate; no tag changes needed.

tt04/tt_um_tiny_processor.summary: This design is an 8-bit processor that communicates with an external device via SPI and can animate a 7-segment display. It requires an external driver, such as an FPGA, to load program and data memory and to start execution. The processor supports displaying register contents or animations on the 7-segment display, with switches to control the display mode. The documentation is detailed, including test instructions, but no silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_tiny_processor.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; 7-segment was already present in the proposed tags.

tt04/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This circuit drives a 16x16 P10 LED panel, initially displaying the string 'TT03P5'. It accepts a 1.2 Mbaud UART input to paint pixels, erase pixels, clear the display, and change the displayed color, but resource limitations restrict it to a single color at a time and no double buffering. A mode pin allows selection between two clocking patterns to accommodate different panel wiring. External hardware includes an LED panel and a level converter to 5V logic.

tt04/tt_um_top.summary: This design implements a pseudo-random number generator using two LFSRs (8-bit and 16-bit) and a 16-to-8 multiplexer. It produces 8-bit pseudo-random numbers that are displayed on two 7-segment displays. The design requires a 50 MHz clock, an enable signal, and an active-low reset. Testing involves connecting the clock and control signals and observing the random numbers on the displays. No silicon test results are provided.

tt04/tt_um_uninorte.summary: This design classifies images of numbers from 0 to 7 using the 16 most significant pixels of an 8x8 image as input features. The classification result is displayed on a 7-segment display. The design uses 16 input pins for the features and outputs to the seven segments plus a dot. Testing involves setting the feature inputs according to the pixel pattern of the desired number. No silicon test results are provided.
tt04/tt_um_uninorte.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; corrected summary to remove unsupported 10 MHz clock claim and align with source.

tt04/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This design implements the Simon Says memory game, where the player must repeat a growing sequence of colors. The sequence is shown via four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone played through a speaker, and the score is displayed on a two-digit 7-segment display. The game requires external hardware: four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, a speaker or buzzer, and optionally a two-digit 7-segment display. A silicon test report notes a minor bug where pressing a button immediately after failing skips the game over sound, which was fixed in a later version.
tt04/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Added wokwi and scoreboard tags; the summary is otherwise supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB to Serial bridge using the USB CDC protocol, allowing a computer to communicate with the chip as a virtual serial port. It uses a 48 MHz clock and connects to USB D+ and D- pins, requiring a 1.5k ohm pull-up resistor on D+ for device detection. Data received from the USB host appears on the rx output pins, and data can be transmitted by setting the tx input pins and asserting tx_valid. A silicon test report confirms both RX and TX work as expected, and the design is based on an open-source USB serial core.

tt04/tt_um_vc_cpu.summary: This project is a 16-bit RISC-V CPU implemented in Verilog with a 16-bit address and data interface exposed on the chip pins. It includes an assembler and a memory image, allowing programs to be assembled and executed. The CPU reads instructions and data from an external memory via the address and data pins, with a write strobe and address latch controls, and also provides an interrupt input. The documentation refers to a README for more details, but the provided text is limited, so the exact instruction set and testing procedure are not fully described here.
tt04/tt_um_vc_cpu.review_notes: Removed memory, interrupt-controller and asic tags that are not supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This design shows the time on a VGA screen using a 31.5 MHz clock, with pins for hsync, vsync, and 6-bit color output (two bits per RGB channel). It uses a pre-generated font loaded into registers and 'races the beam' to generate the display. External hardware includes an R2R DAC to convert the digital color outputs to analog VGA signals and a VGA monitor. The design supports adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds via input pins.
tt04/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (misleading; it is a time display) and added rtc.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347140425276981843.summary: This Wokwi design transmits a fixed string of ASCII characters, specifically 'tiny tapeout', over a UART serial interface. It supports uppercase ASCII characters from 0x40 to 0x5F and uses switches to control load/transmit and output enable, with a seven-segment display showing segment outputs. Testing is performed in the Wokwi simulator by setting the baud rate to 300 and toggling the switches; garbage characters may appear on initialization. The design is notable for being a simple UART transmitter that operates at a very low clock frequency of 1 Hz.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347140425276981843.review_notes: Removed shift-register tag because the documentation does not describe a shift register.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347144898258928211.summary: This Wokwi project is a customizable UART transmitter that sends multiple ASCII characters by storing each character in a column of flip-flops. Characters are set by tying multiplexer inputs to VCC or GND, and more characters can be added by copying and pasting columns. Testing involves setting the baud rate and Wokwi clock to 300, toggling the load/transmit and output-enable switches, and observing the serial output in the Wokwi Arduino serial monitor. The documentation notes that garbage characters may appear at initialization, and the 'How it works' section is marked TODO:FIXME, indicating incomplete documentation.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347144898258928211.review_notes: Removed reconfigurable (build-time customization only) and 7-segment (pin naming only, no display function described); shift-register was already correctly tagged.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347417602591556180.summary: This Wokwi design implements a simple padlock or safe code lock that displays status on a seven-segment display. The user sets a code using switches, locks and unlocks with another switch, and enters the code with a push button.
