The design includes a reset switch and an LED to indicate locked status; testing involves simulating the switch and button sequences in Wokwi. It is a basic educational example of a code-based lock with minimal documentation beyond the controls description.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347417602591556180.review_notes: Removed fsm tag because no state machine is documented.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_347497504164545108.summary: This Wokwi project outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display, using a modulo-11 counter to sequence through the characters. The counter increments with a 1 Hz clock and resets after 11, determining which character is displayed. Test inputs include a reset counter, clock disable, and four test logic pins, but the testing procedure is not explained in the documentation. The truth table for the design is provided in an external spreadsheet.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_369864099838656513.summary: This Wokwi project implements a 4x4 memory using 16 flip-flops, with switches to select lines and set bits, and a read/write control. The outputs show the stored values on a seven-segment display and additional inverted bits. Testing is done by setting switches to store data and observing the display, and the design includes a truth table for operation. The documentation is adapted from an SRAM cell structure, but it is a simple educational memory test rather than a full SRAM.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_369864099838656513.review_notes: Removed sram tag because the design is flip-flop based and the documentation states it is not a full SRAM.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_370011087462055937.summary: This Wokwi design implements an 8-bit 4-input sorting network that orders four input numbers from highest to lowest. It uses compare-swap circuits built from full adders and multiplexers, with a carry signal selecting the multiplexer output. Testing involves applying a reset, entering four 8-bit inputs over 8 clock cycles, then enabling the load signal for 8 cycles to see the sorted outputs. The design is a compact combinatorial circuit for sorting four values, but external hardware such as switches and displays would be needed to use it interactively.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_370533670565165057.summary: This Wokwi design is a multi-channel pulse counter with serial output, counting pulses on four input channels within a time interval measured by an RTC. It includes four 12-bit counters, overflow detection, and a state machine that periodically reads out the RTC time and counter values serially. Testing involves applying short pulses to the input channels and clocking out the serial data when overflow is signaled; the design is an early work-in-progress for a low-power sensor interface for acoustic emission detection. It is intended for applications such as sensor interfaces and non-destructive testing, and the documentation notes it is a work in progress.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_370533670565165057.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart tag and added canonical tags for the documented shift register, counters, RTC, FSM, sensor interface, Wokwi implementation, and incomplete status.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_371604537887211521.summary: This digital cipher and interlock system implements a hardware-based safety chain that requires a specific 8-bit input pattern to unlock an output. It uses combinational logic to verify that all subsystems are in the correct state, mimicking a standalone safety relay. The design provides feedback signals from internal gates and can be used as a puzzle demo or as an interlock for machinery. No external hardware is required, and testing involves applying the correct input pattern to activate the output.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_372184284115580929.summary: This design drives a 7-segment display to show the string 'ykM_1St_CHIP' character by character. It can operate in two modes: a default mode where it cycles through characters based on the clock, and a manual mode where individual characters are selected via BCD inputs. The design requires an external 7-segment LCD for output. Testing involves observing the character sequence or manually selecting characters as described in the documentation.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_372347167704674305.summary: This project implements the digital backend of a successive approximation register (SAR) analog-to-digital converter, supporting both I2C and parallel bus interfaces. It controls an external capacitor bank and comparator to perform analog-to-digital conversion with selectable 6-bit or 11-bit precision. The design requires external analog components such as an op-amp, precise capacitors, resistors, and MOSFETs. Notable limitations include an undetermined maximum clock speed and the need for external analog frontend circuitry.

The random bits are output on three pins, and additional outputs drive segments of a 7-segment display. The design is a simple digital building block for random number generation. Testing instructions are not provided, but the LFSR can be verified by observing the sequence of bits on the outputs.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374292646686728193.summary: This design is an 8-bit ripple-carry adder that adds two bytes and outputs the sum. It is built from one half adder and seven full adders connected in a ripple-carry configuration. The design requires external input devices (such as switches) to set the two input bytes and output devices (such as LEDs) to display the result. Testing involves applying input values and observing the sum on the outputs.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374494377414857729.summary: This controller automatically switches the polarity of DC-type model railway turntables to prevent short circuits when rotating along powered tracks. It uses a binary counter and full-bridge control signals to reverse polarity, with error detection if a trigger remains active too long. The design requires external hardware including XOR gates, a full-bridge driver, MOSFETs, and an RC network for the oscillator. Testing involves verifying the counter sequence, polarity switching, and error handling as described in the documentation.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374494377414857729.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and disables on error, and added motor-control, counter, oscillator, and industrial tags supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374515580784897025.summary: This project implements a hardware lock using a shift register made from flip-flops. The correct 11-bit sequence must be entered serially to activate an output, and a 7-segment display is provided for output. The design requires the user to input bits one at a time with clock pulses. Testing involves entering the correct sequence (10100100010) and verifying that the output turns on.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374515580784897025.review_notes: Removed security because the source describes a simple lock rather than a security-focused design, and added shift-register, flip-flop, sequence-detector, 7-segment, display, and wokwi tags supported by the source.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374636462642973697.summary: This project implements a 4-bit adder with carry that displays the result on a 7-segment display. The two input numbers are set using switches, with the first number on switches 4 to 1 and the second on switches 8 to 5. The display can only show results up to 15 in decimal, so larger sums cause an overflow. The documentation is minimal and does not explain how the circuit works or how to test it.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374636462642973697.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not indicate an educational purpose; added adder, 7-segment and wokwi.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374778387606763521.summary: This design is a PWM generator intended to regulate the power or speed of a device, specifically a servomotor. It requires an external clock of 12.5 kHz to produce a 50 Hz output, and the duty cycle is set by an 8-bit input value between 0 and 255. The documentation describes the internal logic as using OR gates to compare the input number and form a binary time value, with LEDs on the outputs to monitor the counting. The project is implemented in Wokwi and the documentation is partly unclear about the exact operation.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374778387606763521.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design takes an external clock rather than generating one.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374815911155542017.summary: This project implements a 3-to-8 demultiplexer using NAND and NOT gates, mimicking the behavior of a 74LS138 decoder. It has three address inputs and three independent inputs that influence the NAND gates to produce one active-low output among eight, with the remaining outputs high. The circuit is tested using a 6-position DIP switch, and the documentation provides a detailed truth table for selecting each output. The design is built in Wokwi.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374815911155542017.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; no other changes.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374903567624066049.summary: This circuit performs both addition and subtraction of two 3-bit numbers, with optional carry and borrow inputs. The sum result is provided on four output pins (including carry), and the subtraction result on another four pins (including borrow). The inputs are arranged with the first number on IN0-IN2, the second on IN4-IN6, and the carry and borrow on IN3 and IN7 respectively. The project is a small educational design for the VLSI initiative, implemented in Wokwi.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374909346558831617.summary: This project is a custom edge detection circuit built using flip-flops. It is designed to detect rising and falling edges of a signal. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how the circuit works or how to test it. The only information available is the title and the author's tag 'testing'.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374962052813090817.summary: This design displays four different patterns on a 7-segment display: a figure 8, the letters CHS, the word CUSHIng, and the word roboticS. The pins map the eight outputs to the seven segments and the dot of the display. The documentation is very thin, only listing the patterns and leaving the testing method as a placeholder. It is implemented in Wokwi.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374962052813090817.review_notes: Removed pattern-generator as the source shows static display patterns, not a test pattern generator; added insufficient-doc for the placeholder testing section.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374967675785369601.summary: This project is a 4-bit full adder that adds two binary numbers using logic gates. The result is displayed on a 7-segment display. The inputs are set using switches, each assigned a binary weight such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, and the sum is shown on the display. The documentation is minimal, with only a brief description of the operation and testing.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374967675785369601.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and corrected summary claim that LEDs indicate the sum; the pins are 7-segment segments.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374968111036708865.summary: This project is a BCD to 7-segment decoder that converts a 4-bit binary input into a decimal digit displayed on a 7-segment display. It uses a logic function to map the binary number to the appropriate segments. The circuit is tested by entering a binary number on the inputs. The documentation is very brief and does not provide details on the logic implementation.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374968111036708865.review_notes: Removed education because no teaching intent is stated; added verilog based on the Wokwi implementation.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374969806854695937.summary: This design is a state machine for an impulse counter, intended as a debugging submittal for a bachelor's thesis project. It is not a standalone circuit but provides insight into the working principle of the larger design. The state machine cycles through address values every 12 clocks and controls a shift/load pin, with additional outputs for debugging. Testing involves resetting, pulsing the overflow pin, and then clocking the circuit to observe the address sequence.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374974793636964353.summary: This circuit is a BCD to 7-segment display decoder that shows characters to form words. It uses logic gates to create a function that displays two different words, selected by a control input. The user enters a binary number on inputs 0 to 3, with input 3 as the least significant bit, and the corresponding character is displayed; the word is chosen via input 7. The documentation is in Spanish and provides a basic explanation.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_374974793636964353.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and decoder tags; added text tag for character display.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375042398768251905.summary: This is a 4-bit mini ALU that performs XOR, OR, AND, and addition on two 4-bit inputs, with the operation selected by two bidirectional pins. The result is presented on four output pins, plus a carry output for addition. It is intended for educational use, allowing users to test all operations by setting the inputs and selector pins. The design is implemented in Wokwi and has no silicon test results.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375042398768251905.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and logic-gate tags; added alu, adder, and calculator tags.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375061599421794305.summary: The project is titled 'Logic Circuit 1' and described as a 'Logic Circuit Timing Test. Serial 1'. It has eight outputs intended to drive the segments of a 7-segment display, but the documentation does not explain the internal logic or how the timing test is performed. The 'How it works' and 'How to test' sections contain only placeholder text, so the design's functionality cannot be determined from the provided information. No external hardware requirements or silicon results are mentioned.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375163050120587265.summary: This design is a binary to 7-segment decoder that takes a 4-bit input and drives the seven segments of a display to show the corresponding decimal digit from 0 to 9. It is a combinational circuit with no clock, and testing involves applying input values from 0000 to 1001 and observing the displayed digits. The project is implemented in Wokwi and is suitable for educational purposes. No external hardware beyond the 7-segment display is required.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375165100039571457.summary: This project implements a simple artificial neuron with two 2-bit inputs and two 2-bit weight inputs. It uses a linear comparator as the activation function, producing a 1-bit output that indicates whether the neuron is activated. The design is a demonstration of inference in a neural network, and testing involves setting input and weight values and observing the output. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375165100039571457.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added neural-network, perceptron, and comparator tags.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375174630101280769.summary: This is a 4-bit adder that adds two 4-bit inputs and produces a 5-bit output, including the final carry. It is built from full-adder cells and is a purely combinational circuit. Testing is straightforward: apply the operand values to the eight input pins and observe the sum on the five output pins. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is suitable for educational use.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375174630101280769.review_notes: Removed alu because the design is only a 4-bit adder, and added combinational based on the explicit documentation.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375176944142127105.summary: This design displays the text 'UCHILE-FCFM-' on a 7-segment display by using a ripple counter built from D flip-flops. The counter can be clocked to cycle through the characters, or disabled to allow manual input of a counter value via four input pins. The logic was optimized using the Quine-McCluskey algorithm. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for educational purposes.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375217288209912833.summary: This project is a randomizer game that generates a random number between 0 and 3, lights up the corresponding LED, and then checks if the user presses the correct button. It uses a 4-bit counter for randomization, a decoder to drive the LEDs, and a comparator to determine if the pressed button matches the lit LED. The design includes a state maintainer to hold the result until reset. It requires external buttons and LEDs, and is implemented in Wokwi.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375217288209912833.review_notes: Removed fsm because no finite state machine is described, and added counter and decoder which are explicitly used.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375227079413963777.summary: This project, called 'Fastest Finger', determines which of up to eight buttons was pressed first and lights the corresponding LED. The outputs can also drive a 7-segment display. The design is a simple circuit that sets the output high for the first button pressed. Testing involves connecting buttons to the inputs and observing which output goes high. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended as a game.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375227079413963777.review_notes: Removed priority-encoder tag as the source does not describe a priority encoder; corrected summary to remove unsupported latching claim.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375245713375900673.summary: This project simulates a traffic light system for a two-way intersection with a pedestrian crosswalk. It uses the chip's internal clock and low-level reset to cycle through states, controlling two sets of traffic lights and pedestrian signals. The design is based on logical combinations to determine each state, and testing involves observing the sequence of lights. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires external LEDs for the lights.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375245713375900673.review_notes: Removed industrial, timer, and led tags not supported by the source; added fsm as the design is a state-based controller.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375246321309880321.summary: This project implements a 6-bit locker that stores a password and compares it with subsequent attempts. It uses D flip-flops for password and attempt registers, and XOR gates for comparison. The lock outputs a signal indicating whether the entered combination matches the stored password. It requires external step and reset buttons, as well as switches for password entry, and is implemented in Wokwi.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375246321309880321.review_notes: Removed register-file and fsm as they are not supported; added security which is already present but ensure it's kept.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375248885704300545.summary: This design is a basic logic tester that validates the operation of individual logic gates (AND, NAND, OR, NOR, NOT, XOR) and flip-flops (D, RS, JK). It provides common inputs for the gates and selection pins to choose which flip-flop to test, with outputs indicating the logic states. The design is intended for educational purposes, allowing users to verify truth tables by observing the outputs. It is implemented in Wokwi and requires no external hardware beyond the chip's pins.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375248885704300545.review_notes: Removed instrumentation tag as the design is educational, not measurement-focused.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375288605206694913.summary: This design animates a seven-segment display with a six-frame LED chaser pattern, using a configurable bank of clock dividers to slow the animation to human-visible speeds for any input clock frequency. It can also be used as a frequency counter. The chip requires an external clock source and a seven-segment display connected to its outputs, with optional DIP switches to select clock division factors. The design is notable for its wide range of supported clock frequencies and its robustness to noisy startup frames.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375300958229329921.summary: This design implements a 'Fastest Finger' game that determines which of eight buttons was pressed first. It uses a 3-bit counter and a 3-to-8 decoder to latch the first button press and illuminate the corresponding LED. The design requires external buttons connected to the inputs and LEDs (or a seven-segment display) connected to the outputs. It is a simple, clocked game suitable for educational or entertainment purposes.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375300958229329921.review_notes: Removed counter tag as it is a component, not the main type; summary is supported.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375310871188385793.summary: This design is an 8-bit digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that receives data via a QSPI-like interface and outputs an analog voltage using an external R-2R network. It also breaks out bidirectional pins for external testing of delays and electrical characteristics. To use the DAC, the user must remove the on-board seven-segment display and connect an external R-2R network. The design is intended as an experiment and includes a simple serial protocol for setting the DAC value.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375310871188385793.review_notes: Removed analog: the R-2R network is external hardware, the submitted design is digital.

tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375326293008530433.summary: This design implements simple triple modular redundancy (TMR) voters with an error injection option. It includes one single D flip-flop, three TMR-protected D flip-flops, and one TMR flip-flop that allows error injection. The design is tested by setting inputs, triggering the clock, and observing outputs to verify correct voting behavior. It is a minimal experiment for studying TMR concepts and requires no external hardware.
tt04/tt_um_wokwi_375326293008530433.review_notes: Removed error-correction because TMR voting is redundancy/fault tolerance, not coding-based error correction.

tt04/tt_um_yeokm1_pwm_audio.summary: This design takes 8-bit audio over a parallel port interface and generates an analog audio signal using PWM and a first-order sigma-delta modulator, similar to a Covox Speech Thing. It requires a 0.1uF capacitor to ground on the audio output pins for proper operation. The design has been tested in silicon and works as expected, providing a fixed-function sound card without the need for microcontroller firmware. It is notable for its simplicity and successful implementation in hardware.
tt04/tt_um_yeokm1_pwm_audio.review_notes: sigma-delta is not a canonical tag; replaced with modulator and added speaker for the audio output.

tt04/tt_um_zeptobars.summary: This design implements free-running oscillators to compare simulation with reality and includes a true random number generator (TRNG). It uses combinational loops with dividers to produce output frequencies below 50kHz, and the TRNG output is available on one pin. The design is tested by selecting an oscillator via input pins and measuring the frequency on the output pins, while observing random numbers on another pin. It is a process experiment and requires no external hardware.

tt05/tt_um_4_bit_pipeline_multiplier.summary: This design is a 4-bit pipelined Booth multiplier intended for learning purposes. It has been tested in silicon and verified to work correctly for all input pairs, with pipelining functioning as expected. The design achieved clock speeds of 146MHz at 1.8V and 154MHz at 1.9V core voltage. It is a simple educational project with no external hardware requirements.
tt05/tt_um_4_bit_pipeline_multiplier.review_notes: Removed 'alu' since the design is a multiplier, not an ALU.

tt05/tt_um_7segx4_clock_abhishek_top.summary: This design is a multi-mode clock with a four-digit seven-segment display. It uses registers to divide the clock and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter available on bidirectional outputs. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the inputs to program a 24-bit compare register, allowing the counter to increment at different rates. It requires an external seven-segment display and a 10MHz clock source.
tt05/tt_um_7segx4_clock_abhishek_top.review_notes: Removed 'clock-generator' because the design divides rather than generates a clock.

tt05/tt_um_BNNNeuron.summary: This design implements a single neuron in a binarized neural network (BNN), performing binary multiplication with XNOR, accumulation, and sign activation. It simulates the behavior of a neuron by accumulating XNOR results and applying a sign function to output +1 or -1. The design is tested by resetting the circuit and providing constant inputs and weights with an enable signal to begin the XNOR multiplication. It is a demonstration of BNN concepts and requires no external hardware.
tt05/tt_um_BNNNeuron.review_notes: Added perceptron tag as the design is a single-neuron classifier; summary unchanged.

tt05/tt_um_EventFilter.summary: The design implements a debouncer for event-based camera data, filtering out spurious events caused by noise. It accepts an 8-bit tuple (x, y, p, t) via input pins and outputs the tuple only if the data remains stable for 5 clock cycles. The polarity bit is used to indicate high or low events, and the design can be tested by setting switches to simulate event tuples. The project is notable for addressing thermal noise in event cameras, but the documentation is minimal and lacks details on testing and implementation.
tt05/tt_um_EventFilter.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; summary is supported by the source.

tt05/tt_um_Fiona_CMU.summary: This project implements a stream cipher using an 8-byte linear shift register to encrypt and decrypt messages. It accepts 8-bit data on input pins and uses bidirectional pins for control signals such as increment, encrypt, and view mode. The encrypted or decrypted message can be viewed by selecting an index, and the design supports toggling between encryption and viewing without resetting. Notable limitations include the need to reset after 16 bytes to avoid losing encrypted data, and the documentation provides clear testing steps.
tt05/tt_um_Fiona_CMU.review_notes: Removed lfsr because the source describes a linear shift register without feedback, and added shift-register and systemverilog.

tt05/tt_um_GrayCounter_ariz207.summary: The design is a 4-bit synchronous Gray code counter that increments on a clock input and outputs the Gray code value on four LED pins. It is intended to demonstrate binary values changing in Gray code sequence, and can be tested by connecting a clock source and LEDs. The documentation is very brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing instructions. There is no additional detail on implementation or features.

tt05/tt_um_LSNN.summary: This project implements a spiking LSTM network based on a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron with an adaptive threshold. It accepts a current input and outputs spikes, with the threshold increasing when spikes occur and decaying otherwise. The design is tested by applying different current levels and observing the spiking behavior and threshold adaptation. The documentation is somewhat sparse, lacking details on the LSTM integration and external hardware requirements.
tt05/tt_um_LSNN.review_notes: Removed neural-network tag as the design is a single neuron, not a network.

tt05/tt_um_Leaky_Integrate_Fire_nfjesifb.summary: This project uses a 24-bit counter and a programmable compare register to generate a periodic event, with the counter value shown on a 7-segment display. The lower 8 bits of the counter are also available on the bidirectional pins. With all inputs low the compare is set to 10,000,000, so the counter increments once per second at a 10 MHz clock, and setting the inputs programs bits 11 to 18 of the compare value to change the rate. The design can be tested by observing the counter increment every second and experimenting with the input pins to change the counting speed.
tt05/tt_um_Leaky_Integrate_Fire_nfjesifb.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network and clock-divider tags not supported by the documented counter/comparator behavior; summary rewritten to match the source.

tt05/tt_um_MichaelBell_spi_peri.summary: The design implements an SPI peripheral with an 8-byte RAM, 324-byte ROM, and a random source, supporting standard and quad SPI read/write commands. It is intended to be used as a ROM for an RP2040, allowing it to boot from the ROM, and also provides debug access via switches and a 7-segment display. Silicon testing showed that the SPI RAM works and the RP2040 boots from the ROM, but writes to the RAM were not functioning and the random source distribution is non-uniform. The project requires a custom RP2040 board and a PIO-based SPI master for full testing.

tt05/tt_um_SNN.summary: This project implements a basic spiking neural network that takes spiking patterns from three input neurons and produces spikes from two output neurons based on predefined weights. It is intended for studying spike generation and can be tested by feeding different input spike patterns and observing the output spikes. The documentation is minimal, with many pins marked as unspecified and no details on the network architecture or testing methodology. The design appears to be a simple feedforward network with limited configurability.
tt05/tt_um_SNN.review_notes: Removed generic neural-network tag; spiking-neural-network and neuromorphic are sufficient.

tt05/tt_um_adaptive_lif.summary: This project implements an adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire neuron with configurable adaptive threshold and decay rate. It accepts an 8-bit current input and outputs the membrane potential and spike output, with control pins to enable adaptive features. Silicon testing confirmed that the neuron fires in response to different current levels, though the spike output appeared as digital pulses rather than narrow spikes. The design aims to enhance spike sparsity while preserving input features, and the documentation includes simulation and test results.
tt05/tt_um_adaptive_lif.review_notes: Removed overly broad neural-network tag and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt05/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_spi_rom.summary: This project reads data from an SPI flash ROM and displays it on a VGA monitor, supporting two resolutions and two line modes for buffered and direct display. It includes a loopback test and requires external hardware such as an SPI flash chip and a VGA DAC. Silicon testing showed that it displayed graphics on the screen, but the SPI ROM functionality was not fully tested. The documentation is detailed but notes that some aspects are still to be confirmed.
tt05/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_spi_rom.review_notes: Removed driver because the design is a display/readout experiment, and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt05/tt_um_alu_chip.summary: This project is a simple 4-bit ALU that performs operations such as addition, subtraction, AND, OR, and comparisons, and outputs the result in BCD on a 7-segment display. It accepts two 4-bit inputs and a 4-bit operation code, and provides the result on both the 7-segment display and bidirectional pins. The documentation is very brief, with only a one-line description and no detailed testing instructions. The design is straightforward and lacks advanced features.

tt05/tt_um_asinghani_tinyscanchain_tt05.summary: This is a test design for tinyscanchain, a scan-chain implementation written in under 80 lines of Python, built on top of the seven-segment-seconds counter design. After reset the counter increments once per second from a 1 kHz clock, and the scan chain allows inspection of the internal state of the design. The seven-segment outputs drive a display, while the scan-chain input, enable and output pins provide the debug interface. It is intended as a demonstration and test vehicle for the tinyscanchain tool rather than a standalone application.

tt05/tt_um_async_proc_paulschulz.summary: This circuit is an early investigation into an asynchronous parallel processor, where each processing node waits for valid data, computes a result from four 4-bit inputs, signals its neighbours, and then makes the result available. Inputs are loaded into buffers via dedicated load pins, and the result is displayed on seven-segment outputs with a data-ready dot. The design is explicitly described as a work in progress that does not do very much yet, with future plans for programmable nodes, a multi-node array, and a clockless version. Testing consists of resetting, loading input values, and observing the outputs.
tt05/tt_um_async_proc_paulschulz.review_notes: Removed accelerator and education (unsupported) and added incomplete and cpu based on the source description.

tt05/tt_um_blink.summary: This design instantiates eight inverters whose inputs and outputs are exposed on the input and bidirectional pins, together with a counter whose upper bits are driven to the outputs. The documentation is very thin, describing it only as a blink and suggesting checking reset, enable and counter function. It appears to be a simple test structure for observing inverter behaviour and counter operation on silicon. No external hardware is described beyond observing the pins.
tt05/tt_um_blink.review_notes: Removed timer and logic-gate; added characterization and insufficient-doc given the thin documentation.

tt05/tt_um_btflv_8bit_fp_adder.summary: This design adds two 8-bit floating point numbers, each with a 1-bit sign, 4-bit exponent and 3-bit mantissa, taking one operand from the input pins and the other from the bidirectional pins. The result, including rounding and infinity handling, appears on the output pins every clock cycle. A silicon test report notes that the adder works well for most values but produces incorrect results for some small values, and a linked script tests all possible input combinations. It is a compact arithmetic building block rather than a complete calculator.
tt05/tt_um_btflv_8bit_fp_adder.review_notes: Removed alu because the block is a dedicated adder; added silicon-tested because fabrication reports exist, even though the report is partial.

tt05/tt_um_carlosgs99_cro_udg.summary: This project implements a 50 MHz chronometer that displays minutes, seconds and hundredths of a second across six seven-segment displays. A start button initialises or pauses the counter, and a reset button restarts it from zero. It requires six common-cathode seven-segment displays plus push buttons for the start and reset inputs, with the cathodes driven by the unidirectional outputs and the anodes by the bidirectional pins. The design is a straightforward digital clock application with no reported silicon test results.
tt05/tt_um_carlosgs99_cro_udg.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design counts clock cycles rather than generating a clock.

tt05/tt_um_cejmu.summary: This is a fully combinational 4-bit ALU containing a ripple-carry adder, a carry-lookahead adder, a matrix multiplier, a Wallace-tree multiplier, a comparator and a barrel-shifter, selected by a 3-bit opcode on the bidirectional pins. The two 4-bit operands come from the input pins, and the 8-bit result appears on the outputs, with the barrel-shifter using b[1:0] for shift width and b[2] for direction. No clock is required, and a silicon test report confirms the adder was verified on the bringup stream. It is a compact educational ALU demonstrating several arithmetic architectures in one tile.
tt05/tt_um_cejmu.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not describe a teaching or learning purpose.

tt05/tt_um_chatgpt_snn_mtomlin5.summary: This design implements six programmable digital leaky integrate-and-fire neurons arranged in two layers of three, with 8-bit weights programmable over an SPI interface. Input spikes drive the first layer, whose outputs feed the second layer through nine programmable weights, and the second layer's spikes appear on the output pins as one-clock-cycle pulses. After reset the user programs thresholds, leak rates, refractory periods and weights over SPI, then applies input spikes and observes output spikes synchronously. The design is notable for having been generated with ChatGPT and for requiring an external FPGA for testing.
tt05/tt_um_chatgpt_snn_mtomlin5.review_notes: Removed machine-learning (not an ML accelerator) and added neuromorphic, which the LIF spiking network clearly supports.

tt05/tt_um_chip_inventor_music__6_bit_co.summary: This project combines two diagrams created with the Chip Inventor block-based design platform: a piano tune that drives a buzzer from a button, and a 6-bit counter. The counter's binary value can be observed on four LEDs connected in pull-up mode, and the buzzer plays a note when triggered. The documentation is brief and does not describe the internal implementation in detail. It serves mainly as a demonstration of the Chip Inventor design tool.

tt05/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design is an 8-bit wide, 128-byte ROM containing information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash in 7-segment encoding and an ASCII chip descriptor string. The contents are read by setting the 8-bit address on the input pins and observing the data on the output pins, with the first bytes viewable on an on-board seven-segment display. The ROM is automatically generated by the tt-support-tools during GDS build. It is a utility design for chip identification rather than a computational block.

tt05/tt_um_clkdiv.summary: This design uses a set of registers to divide the input clock by a 16-bit value supplied on the input and bidirectional pins, with the divided clock appearing on one output. The remaining seven outputs provide a simple random number generator output. The documentation is sparse, giving only a brief description and suggesting experimentation with different division inputs. It appears to be a basic clock-divider and PRNG test block with no reported silicon results.

tt05/tt_um_czlucius_alu.summary: This project implements a 4-bit arithmetic logic unit with 13 selectable operations, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, bitwise logic, shifts, and modulo. The two 4-bit operands are provided on the eight input pins, while three bidirectional pins select the operation and the eight output pins present the 8-bit result. The design is intended for educational use and requires external digital logic such as buttons or sensors to provide inputs and observe outputs. The documentation is clear but contains a contradictory testing note about a counter, which appears to be a copy-paste error.
tt05/tt_um_czlucius_alu.review_notes: Removed combinational tag because the source does not establish purely combinational behavior and the test note implies a counter.

tt05/tt_um_devinatkin_stopwatch.summary: This design implements a stopwatch with start, stop, soft reset, and increment/decrement controls, displaying minutes and seconds on a multiplexed 7-segment display. It was originally developed and verified on a Basys 3 FPGA board and later ported to Tiny Tapeout. The design requires external hardware: a common-anode 7-segment display and several buttons and switches for control. Silicon testing by the author confirmed full functionality with a breadboarded display, though the provided test report is truncated.
tt05/tt_um_devinatkin_stopwatch.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added silicon-tested to match the working silicon report.

tt05/tt_um_diadatp_spigot_e.summary: This project implements a bounded spigot algorithm to compute 31 digits of Euler's number (e) in BCD format. The digits are output on the bidirectional and output pins, requiring external BCD-to-7-segment decoders (such as 7447) to display them. The design uses a ring of gated shift registers for storage and shares calculation hardware across iterations to fit within a single tile. It is notable for its low memory footprint and the use of SpinalHDL, but it only produces a fixed number of digits and requires a slow clock (below 500 Hz) to observe the output.
tt05/tt_um_diadatp_spigot_e.review_notes: Removed 7-segment because the chip only outputs BCD digits; the seven-segment display and decoder are external.

tt05/tt_um_digital_clock_sellicott.summary: This project is a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format on six 7-segment displays. Because of limited output pins, the time data is shifted out serially to external 74xx596 shift registers that drive the displays. The time can be set using the hours_set and minutes_set inputs, with fast and slow increment modes, and pressing both set inputs clears the seconds. Silicon testing by the author using a logic analyzer confirmed correct operation of the serial output.
tt05/tt_um_digital_clock_sellicott.review_notes: Removed unsupported rtc/education tags; added counter and silicon-tested based on source and test report.

tt05/tt_um_dinogame.summary: This project implements an endless-runner game similar to the Chrome Dino game, rendered on a VGA monitor. The game uses four input buttons for jump, halt, debug, and mode control, and outputs VGA signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works well and is playable, though some testers noted occasional screen tearing at higher speeds. The documentation is minimal, consisting mainly of a brief description and pinout, but the test reports provide evidence of functionality.
tt05/tt_um_dinogame.review_notes: Removed redundant video tag; added button and retro tags supported by the pin names and game description.

tt05/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.summary: This design is an I2C peripheral that implements an 8-bit ALU to perform pattern testing and accumulate results, functioning as a bit error rate tester (BERT). It connects to an I2C controller (such as an RP2040) via the bidirectional pins and can be configured for different clocking modes and bus types through input pins. The design outputs results on a 7-segment display and includes power-on-reset configuration options. The documentation is somewhat technical and notes that further updates are planned, but it provides sufficient detail for operation.
tt05/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.review_notes: Removed unsupported error-correction tag; summary is accurate.

tt05/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module designed to verify the Tiny Tapeout chip infrastructure. When the select pin is high, it outputs an 8-bit counter on both the output and bidirectional pins; when low, it mirrors the bidirectional inputs to the outputs. Silicon results show correct counting up to 154 MHz with 4 mA drive and 202 MHz with 8 mA drive. It is a simple, high-speed utility block with no external hardware requirements beyond basic connectivity.
tt05/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed scan-chain tag not supported by the documentation.

tt05/tt_um_flappy_vga_cutout1.summary: This project is a clone of the Flappy Bird game, rendered on a 640x480 VGA display with a single button input for flapping. The game state is updated each frame, and the score is output in binary on the bidirectional pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a debounced active-low button, and a VGA adapter compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works and is playable, though several testers found it challenging.

tt05/tt_um_freq_hcohensa.summary: This design encodes input data into frequency variations and then decodes it back to the original data, using a phase-locked loop (PLL) for clock generation. It interfaces with switches for input and 7-segment displays for output, and includes a second counter whose lower bits are available on bidirectional pins. The documentation describes the general operation but lacks specific implementation details and test results, making it difficult to assess its practical use. It appears to be an experimental design for frequency-based encoding and decoding.
tt05/tt_um_freq_hcohensa.review_notes: Removed unsupported timer tag; added 7-segment tag supported by pin mapping.

tt05/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an input signal by counting transitions over a configurable period and displays the result on a 7-segment display. It includes a debug mode that outputs internal signals on the bidirectional pins and allows the user to load a new count period via an input. The frequency is computed by repeatedly subtracting ten from the count and displaying the tens and units digits. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and external hardware such as a signal source and a 7-segment display.
tt05/tt_um_frequency_counter.review_notes: Removed timer as unsupported; added instrumentation and debouncer.

tt05/tt_um_gchenfc_seven_segment_gerry.summary: This design displays names on a 7-segment display, showing one letter per second by default. The top three input bits select which name is shown, while the lower five bits configure the clock divider speed, allowing a manual push-button to step the display. The bottom eight bits of the internal counter are output on the bidirectional pins. It is based on the 7-segment counter template project and is intended for simple visual demonstrations.
tt05/tt_um_gchenfc_seven_segment_gerry.review_notes: Removed template because the project is a complete name-display design, not a starter template.

tt05/tt_um_gfg_development_tros.summary: This design implements three different ring oscillators with varying temperature dependence: a basic NAND-based oscillator, a capacitively loaded NAND oscillator, and a tri-state inverter oscillator with sub-threshold enable. Each oscillator drives a counter that can be latched and transferred via a Manchester-encoded serial data stream, and divided versions of each oscillator clock are also output. The design is intended for characterization and testing of oscillator behavior. Silicon tests confirmed that at least one oscillator output works, though full testing is incomplete.

tt05/tt_um_gharenthi_top.summary: This project is a single leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron with post-synaptic spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) learning. The documentation is essentially absent, with placeholder text for both the operation and testing sections. The pin names suggest a 7-segment display output and a counter, but the actual functionality cannot be determined from the provided information. No external hardware requirements or notable features are described.
tt05/tt_um_gharenthi_top.review_notes: Added 7-segment tag because the output pins are explicitly named as seven-segment segments.

tt05/tt_um_hadirkhan10_lif_neuron.summary: This design implements a configurable leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that mimics biological neuron behavior. It uses a state machine to configure parameters such as beta (decay rate) and threshold, then integrates an input current to produce a membrane potential and spike output. The neuron is controlled via input pins for configuration and current injection, with outputs for membrane potential and spike. It is intended for experimentation with neuron parameters and behavior.

tt05/tt_um_haozhezhu_top.summary: This design is a 4-bit wide memory that can operate as either a FIFO or LIFO, selected by a mode pin. It can store up to 30 entries, with full, empty, output valid, and overflow flags. A 7-segment display shows the number of stored entries up to nine, and disables with an overflow flag if more than nine entries are stored. The design is tested by loading and reading data, and it preserves stored data when switching modes.

tt05/tt_um_hh.summary: This design implements a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model in silicon, which produces action potentials in response to input current injection. An 8-bit input current is applied, interpreted as a 16-bit fixed-point value in uA/cm^2, and the membrane potential is output on both dedicated and bidirectional pins. The neuron fires periodically when the current exceeds a threshold of approximately 12 (in the 8-bit representation). It is intended for exploring neuron dynamics and spiking behavior.
tt05/tt_um_hh.review_notes: Removed 'spiking-neural-network' since the source describes a single neuron model rather than an SNN hardware block.

tt05/tt_um_himanshu5_prog_chipTop.summary: This project contains two compute units that perform ALU operations based on input instructions, with the final output being the XOR of their outputs. The design is controlled by reset and enable signals, and it was tested on EDA Playground with a testbench. The only output pins are for a 7-segment display, suggesting the result is shown visually. The documentation is brief and does not specify the exact ALU operations or instruction format.
tt05/tt_um_himanshu5_prog_chipTop.review_notes: Tags were already correct; no changes needed.

tt05/tt_um_hls_lfi.summary: This design implements a simple leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that integrates an input current and produces a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold. It has inputs for clock, current, and reset, and outputs the next membrane potential and a spike signal. The documentation notes that a current input of 100 after 20 cycles should produce a spike. The design is minimal and intended for basic testing of neuron behavior.
tt05/tt_um_hls_lfi.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'timer' tag; the source describes only LIF neuron behavior.

tt05/tt_um_hodgkin_huxley.summary: This project is titled Hodgkin-Huxley Chip Design, but the documentation describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter driving a 7-segment display, with no mention of neuron behavior. The inputs set a 24-bit compare value that controls counting speed, and the bottom 8 bits of the counter are output on bidirectional pins. With all inputs zero the compare is 10,000,000, giving one increment per second at 10 MHz. The documentation does not match the title, so the actual neuron implementation is unclear.
tt05/tt_um_hodgkin_huxley.review_notes: Title and documentation contradict each other; needs a second opinion on which is authoritative.

tt05/tt_um_htfab_cell_tester.summary: This project includes a sky130-compatible standard cell generator written in Python using gdstk, four example cells (mux2i, maj3, dlrtp, dfrtp), and a TinyTapeout test chip that compares foundry cells against custom-generated ones. The test chip uses an instrumentation framework with a ring oscillator, clock divider, and shift registers to perform both direct and advanced tests at speed. Silicon tests confirmed basic functionality in direct output mode, but the author cautions against using the custom cells in serious designs due to limited testing.

tt05/tt_um_if.summary: This design implements an integrate-and-fire neuron in silicon, where an 8-bit input current is injected and accumulated into a membrane potential. When the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, the neuron emits a spike. The membrane potential is exposed on the 8-bit output and the spike on a bidirectional pin, allowing observation with switches and probes. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the basic operation and testing.

tt05/tt_um_ja1tye_sound_generator.summary: This is a four-channel wavetable and PSG-style sound generator with an I2S output and an SPI control interface. It supports eight selectable waveforms, 16-bit frequency control, 8-bit volume in PSG mode, and a 32-entry 4-bit wavetable, with a sampling rate of about 48.8 kHz from a 50 MHz clock. The design is controlled over SPI mode 0 with 24-bit transactions, and the I2S output is 16-bit mono. It requires an external I2S DAC such as a PCM5102A to produce audible sound.
tt05/tt_um_ja1tye_sound_generator.review_notes: Removed music tag; sound generator is not a music composition design.

tt05/tt_um_jaylennee_wta_pwm.summary: This design generates eight 12-bit PWM signals with a common trigger and can also accept eight external PWM inputs, selecting between internal and external sources via SPI configuration. A time-domain winner-take-all circuit detects the falling edges of the PWM signals to find the smallest duration and the k-smallest durations, latching the corresponding addresses. The design includes a time-to-digital converter that digitizes PWM durations, and results are read out over SPI. It requires external SPI control and optional external PWM sources.
tt05/tt_um_jaylennee_wta_pwm.review_notes: Removed neuromorphic tag as the source does not describe neuromorphic processing; added comparator for the winner-take-all selection.

tt05/tt_um_jeffdi_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This design counts down from 9 to 0 at one-second intervals and displays the current digit on a 7-segment display. The counting speed can be changed by driving the input pins with a compare value, which sets the clock divider; with all inputs low the compare is 10,000,000 for a 10 MHz clock. The lower 8 bits of the counter are also available on the bidirectional pins. It is a simple timer/display demonstration with no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display.
tt05/tt_um_jeffdi_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed redundant verilog tag; summary unchanged.

tt05/tt_um_jkprz.summary: This project implements a basic leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Verilog. An input current is injected via switches, added to a decaying membrane potential, and a spike is triggered when the potential exceeds a threshold. The membrane potential is exposed on the output pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin. The documentation is minimal and does not detail the STDP mechanism or testing beyond observing firing rate changes with input current.
tt05/tt_um_jkprz.review_notes: Summary corrected to remove the unsupported STDP claim; tags unchanged.

tt05/tt_um_jleugeri_ticktocktokens.summary: This design implements a processor that uses Tick Tock Tokens, where each token is represented by a start and end event, to perform event-based computation inspired by Time Petri Nets. It accepts a 4-bit instruction and 8-bit data on the inputs, and outputs data with token start/stop flags and a good/bad token flag. The documentation is thin and admits that the test script and explanation may be incomplete. An Arduino is suggested to generate the I/O signals for testing.
tt05/tt_um_jleugeri_ticktocktokens.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; summary unchanged as it is supported.

tt05/tt_um_jmadden173_delta_modulation.summary: This design implements delta modulation spike encoding for spiking neural networks, mimicking the snnTorch implementation. It generates a spike when the difference between the current and previous 4-bit data inputs exceeds a configurable threshold, with an option to emit negative spikes. The previous data register can be read and forced for debugging, and the design can be tested with an ADC or by manually changing the data input and observing spikes on an oscilloscope. All numerical inputs and outputs are unsigned 4-bit integers.

tt05/tt_um_joerdsonsilva_top.summary: This multimode modem performs digital modulation and demodulation using amplitude-shift keying, frequency-shift keying, and phase-shift keying schemes. A 2-bit select input chooses the modulation type, and the modulated signal appears on a 7-bit output while the demodulated bit appears on a separate output. Silicon testing by a tester showed that ASK and FSK worked as documented, but PSK demodulation was stuck high and the output was a plain sine wave. An oscilloscope or signal analyzer is required to observe the analog-like outputs.

tt05/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is an RV32IMA RISC-V SoC capable of booting and running uLinux, with UART, SPI, and LED interfaces. It requires flashing a bootloader, device tree, and Linux image onto an external NOR flash, and a 22 pF capacitor on the NOR flash clock line was needed for reliable operation. Silicon tests by the author and testers confirmed successful Linux boot at around 30.5 MHz. The design includes a divider register for configuring the CLINT and UART.
tt05/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag to reflect the provided working silicon reports.

tt05/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.summary: This design implements Karplus-Strong plucked-string synthesis based on published papers, with a register map accessed via SPI and audio samples output through an I2S transmitter. It includes pseudo-random binary sequence generators for noise and a 7-segment display output, and operates with a 256 kHz clock to produce a 16 kHz sample rate. The design is configured through SPI mode 0, CPHA=1, and the synthesized samples are sent continuously over I2S. It requires an external I2S DAC to hear the sound.
tt05/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.review_notes: Removed 'lfsr' tag because the source specifies PRBS generators, not LFSR.

tt05/tt_um_kskyou.summary: This design computes continued fraction convergents of the square root of a 14-bit natural number entered via switches. Pressing one button advances to the next convergent pair P and Q, and another button cycles through the 16-bit P and Q values on the 8 status LEDs in four bytes. It is intended to be used alongside a phone calculator or paper to find fundamental solutions to Pell's equation x^2 - Dy^2 = 1. The design fits in roughly 1000 cells by avoiding comparisons and floor operations except on the first step, and it outputs binary rather than 7-segment values due to area constraints.
tt05/tt_um_kskyou.review_notes: Removed divider and alu because the source describes a continued fraction calculator, not a divider or ALU circuit.

tt05/tt_um_lif.summary: This project implements a current-based leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit slice of input current on the switches, integrates it into a membrane potential that leaks over time, and emits a spike when the potential crosses a threshold. The membrane potential is shown on the 8 output pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin, with a 7-segment display mentioned for spike detection in the test description. The documentation is thin and the test instructions refer to hardware not fully described in the pin list, so external setup details are unclear.
tt05/tt_um_lif.review_notes: Added spiking-neural-network tag to match the LIF neuron implementation.

tt05/tt_um_lif_n.summary: This design implements a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in 130 nm CMOS using Verilog. An input current is added to a membrane potential that decays by a factor beta, and a spike is triggered when the potential exceeds a threshold. The membrane potential is output on eight pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin. Testing involves resetting the circuit, varying the input current, and observing that higher current produces a higher spike rate; no external hardware beyond input switches and observation is described.

tt05/tt_um_loopback.summary: This is a simple loopback test module where input 0 is mirrored to outputs 0 through 6, and output 7 is the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7. It is used to measure signal delay by toggling input 0 and timing the response on output 0. Silicon tests measured a 20 ns falling-edge delay and 24 ns rising-edge delay, and the design was shown to work up to 90 MHz during bringup, with degraded behavior past 100 MHz. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
tt05/tt_um_loopback.review_notes: Removed gpio because the pins implement a fixed loopback/AND test structure, and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon test report.

tt05/tt_um_loopback_ericsmi.summary: This project is a loopback tile with input skew measurement, described as counting up to 10 one second at a time. It has an 8-bit compare input, an 8-bit second counter on bidirectional pins, and 7-segment display outputs. The documentation is essentially empty, with 'Need to write this' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections, so the exact function cannot be determined from the provided text. External hardware mentioned is programmable delay lines on the inputs.
tt05/tt_um_loopback_ericsmi.review_notes: Removed timer and instrumentation; added insufficient-doc because the documentation is empty.

tt05/tt_um_mabhari_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This is a two-digit seconds timer that counts from 00 to 99, with the target value loaded from 8 input switches as two BCD digits. A Load signal latches the target, and a Start signal begins counting at one second per tick from a 10 MHz clock. When the count reaches the target, the Time_Out output goes high, and the current ones or tens digit is displayed on a 7-segment display depending on a select input. Testing involves resetting, activating Load and Start, and observing the count and timeout.
tt05/tt_um_mabhari_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Tags and summary are fully supported by the source; no changes needed.

tt05/tt_um_manjushettar.summary: This project emulates a two-layer neural network of integrate-and-fire neurons in Verilog. The first layer accepts two 16-bit stimulus inputs, and its spikes feed into a second layer whose two neurons produce the final spiking outputs. Testing involves applying different input stimuli and observing the spiking states of the output layer. The design uses a reset signal to clear neuron states, and the one-line description mentions counting up to 10 one second at a time.
tt05/tt_um_manjushettar.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the summary's last sentence was adjusted to avoid asserting a class project not stated in the source.

tt05/tt_um_matrix_multiplier.summary: This module multiplies two 2x2 matrices where each element is an unsigned 2-bit number, with inputs provided on 8-bit wires and outputs on uo_out and uio_out. It performs error checking to ensure each element is in the range [0,2], outputting zero if any element is out of range. The design includes a Verilog testbench and a cocotb Python test script that verify the multiplication against expected results. Testing can also be done on an FPGA or in simulation with waveform viewing.
tt05/tt_um_matrix_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu and error-correction because the design is a matrix multiplier with range checking, not an ALU or error-correction block.

tt05/tt_um_matt_divider_test.summary: This analog test project implements a resistive voltage divider using three resistors connected between power and ground, with output taps on three pins. It is tested by enabling the block and checking that only the highest tap output is high. Silicon results show the divider worked, and a large capacitor increased the falling-edge delay from 20 ns to 31 ns and the rising-edge delay from 24 ns to 51 ns. The design is a simple analog test structure with no digital logic.
tt05/tt_um_matt_divider_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported factory-test and transistor-level tags; added silicon-tested.

tt05/tt_um_mattngaw_fp8.summary: This design is an 8-bit floating-point adder following the FP8 E5M2 standard. It combinationally computes the sum of two 8-bit floating-point numbers provided on the input and bidirectional pins, with the result appearing on the output pins. Testing is done by holding two 8-bit inputs and reading the sum from the outputs. No external hardware is required beyond the chip's pins.
tt05/tt_um_mattngaw_fp8.review_notes: Removed alu, which is not supported by the source's floating-point adder description.

tt05/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs the sound wave on uio_out[1:0]. A 100kHz clock is provided on the clk pin, and a brief reset on rst_n starts playback. A piezo speaker connected across uio_out[1:0] is required for audible output.

tt05/tt_um_mihailocode_neural_network.summary: This design implements a neural network on chip. The network calculates an output based on user-provided input and predefined weight parameters of the neural network. Drive inputs to [7:0] ui_in, and the result of the computation can be observed on [7:0] uo_out. The design is built out of perceptrons according to the author's description.
tt05/tt_um_mihailocode_neural_network.review_notes: Added perceptron tag from the one-line description and removed accelerator, which was not supported by the source.

tt05/tt_um_mingkaic1_stack_machine.summary: This design is an 8-bit stack machine written in SystemVerilog. It is documented with only a one-line description and has no detailed instruction set documentation. A single bidirectional pin is described as carrying data. The design can be tested in hardware or with simulation.
tt05/tt_um_mingkaic1_stack_machine.review_notes: Documentation is very thin; added insufficient-doc tag.

tt05/tt_um_minipit_stevej.summary: This design includes timer, interrupt-controller, counter, and clock-divider functionality. It is a timer and counter design with interrupt support. The documentation does not provide silicon test results.

tt05/tt_um_morningjava_top.summary: This design is an 8-bit Programmable Sound Generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It takes input from a serial UART interface and outputs PWM audio. An analog PWM filter and audio driver are needed for the test rig. It generates square, triangle, and noise sound channels.
tt05/tt_um_morningjava_top.review_notes: Added uart, chiptune and retro tags supported by the source; summary expanded to four supported sentences.

tt05/tt_um_multiplexed_clock.summary: This design is a multiplexed digital clock that counts hours in 24-hour format and minutes, with dots indicating 15/30/45/60 seconds. It drives a 4-digit 7-segment display via multiplexing, using uo_out for segments and uio_out[3:0] for digit selection. Two pull-up button inputs increase hours or minutes, and inputs configure anode/cathode and output negation. It has been partially tested on silicon.
tt05/tt_um_multiplexed_clock.review_notes: Removed inaccurate clock-generator/rtc tags; added display and silicon-tested (partial status).

tt05/tt_um_muncherkin_lioncage.summary: This design is a counter with FSM and sensor interface. It drives a 7-segment display and includes an up-down counter. The documentation explains the state machine logic but does not include silicon test results.

tt05/tt_um_mv_mult_alrdelcr.summary: This design multiplies an input vector by a matrix. The first input switch initializes a matrix multiplication between the current vector and the matrix, and the second bit sets matrix values line by line. A counter increases by one every second with a 10 MHz input clock, and outputs drive a seven-segment display. The documentation notes there is no current functionality to know which row of the matrix is set.
tt05/tt_um_mv_mult_alrdelcr.review_notes: Removed unsupported machine-learning and accelerator tags; added counter, 7-segment, display, verilog and incomplete, and corrected summary to match the matrix-vector multiplication description.

tt05/tt_um_mvm.summary: This design divides a 10MHz clock and increments a counter once per second when the internal compare value is set to 10,000,000. The bottom eight bits of the counter are exposed on the bidirectional outputs. Combinational logic converts the binary counter value to decimal for a seven-segment display. The compare value can be partially programmed through the input pins to change the counting speed.
tt05/tt_um_mvm.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the timer/counter and seven-segment display design.

tt05/tt_um_mvm_.summary: This design is a matrix-vector multiplication accelerator that takes a 3x3 weight matrix in Compressed Sparse Row format and a 3-bit spike train. It loads the sparse matrix and spike train into internal registers using handshake flags. An algorithm computes the resultant vector of the matrix-vector multiplication. The output vector is transmitted on the output line with a flag bit that flips for each new value.
tt05/tt_um_mvm_.review_notes: Removed incorrect music/interface tags and added accelerator, verilog, and pipeline tags.

tt05/tt_um_myuart.summary: This design implements a small UART transmitter that repeatedly sends a fixed string (the author's name) at 115200 baud with one start bit, eight data bits, one parity bit and one stop bit. It also generates a sinus signal on the remaining seven output pins. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and no inputs; testing only needs a UART receiver connected to uo_out[0]. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the behavior and pin usage.

tt05/tt_um_nickjhay_processor.summary: This project implements a 1-bit 8x8 matrix multiply using a systolic array, with eight data input pins and eight output pins for the result. A bidirectional pin selects between OR and XOR accumulation, and another bidirectional pin outputs a greeting. The documentation consists only of placeholder text ('Explain how your project works' and 'Explain how to test your project'), so the exact interface and operation cannot be verified beyond the pin names and title. The design is notable for targeting matrix multiplication in a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
tt05/tt_um_nickjhay_processor.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; added incomplete and insufficient-doc due to placeholder documentation.

tt05/tt_um_njzhu_uart.summary: This SystemVerilog design implements a UART transceiver with both transmit and receive functions at 9600 baud, using oversampling to sample the middle of each bit period. The receiver waits for a start bit, samples eight data bits and a stop bit, and asserts a data-ready signal; the transmitter sends a byte with correct timing when a data-ready input is set. The eight output pins double as 7-segment display segments and as the UART transmit data output, while bidirectional pins carry received data and a finished-read flag. Testing requires setting the data bits and data-ready input and observing the transmitted sequence on the tx output.
tt05/tt_um_njzhu_uart.review_notes: Added rs232 as the canonical serial-interface tag for the UART link; no incorrect tags were present.

tt05/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommythor.summary: This design is a 12-hour clock rendered on a 640x480 VGA display using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, where three triangle hands indicate the time and twelve dots aid readability. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 31.5 MHz clock, reset, and hour and minute advance buttons. Silicon test reports confirm it works out of the box with a Tiny VGA Pmod, with testers noting the hands move correctly and the time can be set by holding the buttons. The design is notable for its triangle-based rendering approach and includes a Rust software model for reference.
tt05/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommythor.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design only consumes an external clock; added silicon-tested and button based on the test reports and pinout.

tt05/tt_um_perceptron.summary: This design is described as a hardcoded perceptron, but the documentation actually describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter that increments once per second with a 10 MHz clock. The eight output pins carry the perceptron output, while the inputs can be used to program a 24-bit compare register to change the counting speed. The documentation is inconsistent with the title, and the perceptron behavior is not explained. Testing involves observing the counter increment and changing the input bits to alter the rate.
tt05/tt_um_perceptron.review_notes: Title and documentation contradict each other; escalated for a second opinion while removing the unsupported perceptron tag.

tt05/tt_um_perceptron_connorguzi.summary: This project implements a perceptron and a basic binary neural network that take a 7-bit input representing the number of curves and edges of a digit and output the expected number. The eight output pins drive a 7-segment display plus a dot, and the bidirectional pins expose a second counter. The documentation is largely copied from a counter project and does not explain the neural network operation or how to test it meaningfully. The design appears to be a class project, but the documentation is insufficient to verify its intended behavior.
tt05/tt_um_perceptron_connorguzi.review_notes: Removed counter tag tied to copied demo text; added machine-learning and insufficient-doc.

tt05/tt_um_perceptron_neuromeme.summary: This design implements a perceptron that reads two 8-bit inputs and computes a weighted sum with fixed 8-bit weights, classifying the result as 1 if it exceeds a threshold of 11111110 and 0 otherwise. The documentation explains the math with examples, such as any input with two or more 1s being classified as 1, and credits a UCSC professor. It is intended as a simple 9+10 adder or perceptron demonstration, and testing involves applying inputs and observing the 8-bit output. The design is notable for being an educational neuromorphic example with clear documentation.
tt05/tt_um_perceptron_neuromeme.review_notes: Removed unsupported neural-network, mac-unit, and education tags; kept perceptron and verilog.

tt05/tt_um_prg.summary: This design implements a Boolean function based pseudo random number generator using finite field arithmetic, with linear mappings, GF(2^4) multipliers, an inverter, and a square scaler. It takes five input bytes as seeds and produces three output shares, using masking with fresh randomness to prevent leakage. The documentation provides a detailed mathematical description of the three phases and a worked example, and testing involves loading input shares, toggling the enable signal, and reading the output ready flag and shares. The design is notable for its cryptographic masking approach and is implemented in a 1x2 tile configuration.
tt05/tt_um_prg.review_notes: Removed the unsupported cipher tag; the design is a masked PRNG, not an encryption cipher, and the rest of the tags and summary are consistent with the source.

tt05/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.summary: This project implements a bytebeat formula in hardware using the XLS toolkit, generating 8-bit PCM samples from four 4-bit parameters according to the formula ((t*a)&(t>>b))|((t*c)&(t>>d)). It requires an 8-bit PCM DAC and rotary encoders to tweak the parameter pins, and the design can be modified by editing the formula and regenerating the Verilog. A silicon test report from the author confirms it worked as expected after configuring the bidirectional mode correctly. The design is notable for being generated from a high-level synthesis tool and for bringing algorithmic music synthesis to Tiny Tapeout.
tt05/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.review_notes: Removed verilog because the source language is XLS; added dac and silicon-tested based on the documented external DAC and working silicon report.

tt05/tt_um_psychogenic_neptuneproportion.summary: This design is a guitar tuner that counts rising edges of an input pulse over a fixed sampling period and compares the count to frequencies of interest for standard guitar tuning, covering notes from about 80 to 400 Hz. It supports multiple clock configurations via three input bits and can drive either a dual or single 7-segment display, with the dot indicating an exact match in single mode. The raw pulse count is output on the bidirectional pins, and testing requires feeding a variable frequency signal and observing the closest note on the display. A silicon test report confirms it works, showing the closest note for a variable frequency input.

tt05/tt_um_psychogenic_shaman.summary: This design implements a SHA-256 hasher that generates a digest for data of arbitrary length. Data is fed in 64-byte blocks through an 8-bit input port, with control signals for starting, clocking data, and reading the 32-byte result. It requires an external microcontroller to provide data and read results, and supports a parallel mode for interleaving input and processing. The implementation is naive and unoptimized, with estimated throughput of about 6 MB/s at 50 MHz, and a silicon test report indicates it worked in one test run but not a second.
tt05/tt_um_psychogenic_shaman.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'pipeline'; added 'silicon-tested' to match the working silicon report.

tt05/tt_um_rebel2_balanced_ternary_ALU.summary: This is a 2-trit balanced ternary ALU that is part of the REBEL-2 balanced ternary logic CPU. It supports operations such as MIN, MAX, ADD, SUB, MUL, CMP, and SHFT, which can be performed trit-wise or word-wise. The design is generated and verified using the Mixed Radix Circuit Synthesizer (MRCS), and while automated tests exist for MRCS, a Verilog testbench and FPGA constraint file are still work in progress. The documentation is limited and the project appears to be a work in progress.
tt05/tt_um_rebel2_balanced_ternary_ALU.review_notes: Removed cpu tag: the project is an ALU component, not a processor core; 'ternary' is not in the canonical vocabulary.

tt05/tt_um_reflex_game.summary: This project is titled Reflex Game and is intended to be a reflex-based game using a 7-segment display. However, the documentation states that it does not work and suggests making a testbench. There is no description of how the game operates or how it is tested. The design is essentially undocumented and non-functional.

tt05/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square wave tone generators, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with 10 shapes. It is controlled via an 8-bit multiplexed data/address bus and produces audio through either an 8-bit digital output for an external DAC or a PWM output for analog filtering. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to hear the audio. Silicon test reports indicate it works well, with users successfully playing chiptunes and using the 128 divider mode.
tt05/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Removed dac (external only) and added silicon-tested and retro.

tt05/tt_um_rejunity_rule110.summary: This design implements a cellular automaton based on Rule 110, executing over 200 cells in parallel every clock cycle. It includes a parallel read/write bus for accessing and modifying cell states in 8-cell blocks, with control pins for halt and write enable. The automaton can be used for exploring complex behavior, pseudo-random number generation, and data compression, and is known to be Turing complete. The design is well-documented with timing diagrams and examples, and no external hardware is required beyond a clock and control signals.

tt05/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square wave tone generators and one noise generator with white and periodic noise. It is programmed via an 8-bit data bus and provides both digital 8-bit audio output and PWM output for analog audio. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to produce sound. The design is well-documented, includes a test suite, and aims for hardware preservation and education.

tt05/tt_um_rejunity_snn.summary: This project implements a 3-layer spiking neural network with on-chip weights. It has an 8-bit input bus, control signals for execution and synchronization, and outputs from the last layer's neurons. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is a 3-layer spiking neural net with on-chip weights and that testing begins after reset. There is insufficient information to describe its operation, external hardware requirements, or notable features.
tt05/tt_um_rejunity_snn.review_notes: Removed machine-learning because no learning or inference application is documented, and added insufficient-doc to reflect the very thin documentation.
