tt05/tt_um_retospect_neurochip.summary: This design is a Field Programmable Neural Array (FPNA) consisting of 50 interconnected configurable neuron blocks (CNBs) that simulate leaky neurons. Each CNB has four inputs with 3-bit weights, a configurable decay rate, and fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold, sending pulses to neighboring neurons. Configuration is done via a bitstream shifted in through dedicated pins, and the network can be trained using the accompanying naxon tool. The design is intended for neuromorphic computing research and requires external clocking and configuration data to operate.

tt05/tt_um_rgb_mixer.summary: This design uses three rotary encoders to control three PWM generators. It includes debouncing for the encoder inputs and provides debug outputs for the encoder values and debounce signals. The encoders are connected to the first six input pins, and the PWM outputs appear on the first three output pins. A silicon test report from the author confirms all three channels work up to 50 MHz.
tt05/tt_um_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed rgb-led (not stated in source) and added silicon-tested (author report confirms working silicon).

tt05/tt_um_rjmorgan11_calculator_chip.summary: This is a basic calculator chip that implements an 8-bit ALU with operations including add, subtract, bitwise logic, shifts, and comparisons. It uses input pins for the number and operation selection, an enter pin to latch commands, and output pins for the result and flags (overflow, negative, zero). The design is controlled by a clock and reset, and is intended to be tested by entering numbers and operations. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand its function.

tt05/tt_um_rnn.summary: This design implements a recurrent neural network hidden-state update in which an 8-bit input current is multiplied by an 8x8 weight matrix. The hidden state is reset to zero, and the user changes the input current to observe the resulting output current. The pin names and documentation are largely inherited from the 7-segment demo template, so the actual RNN behavior is only briefly described. It is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete neural network system.
tt05/tt_um_rnn.review_notes: Removed template tag as the design is a functional RNN demo, not a starter template.

tt05/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.summary: This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer and reports the orbit length and the upper 16 bits of the highest value reached. Input bytes are uploaded one at a time into a 144-bit register, and results are read back through an address and select interface. A start pin triggers computation and a busy indicator signals completion. Silicon testing confirmed that the project test cases and additional cases worked as expected.
tt05/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.review_notes: Removed 'memory' and 'fsm' as incidental rather than defining design features.

tt05/tt_um_sap_1.summary: This is an implementation of the SAP-1 simple-as-possible computer architecture, containing a program counter, registers, adder, memory, instruction register, bus, and controller. It has no external inputs and runs autonomously from the clock, performing only addition and subtraction on 8-bit values. The bus output can currently only be observed with an oscilloscope, and the author suggests adding a 7-segment display controller as an enhancement. The design is based on the well-known Malvino and Brown architecture popularized by Ben Eater.
tt05/tt_um_sap_1.review_notes: Removed instrumentation because the oscilloscope is only a suggested observation method, not the design purpose.

tt05/tt_um_seanvenadas.summary: This design accepts an 8-bit event signal with x, y, p, and t parameters and outputs the signal only when the p bit is high, filtering it to reduce noise. It also includes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal logic driving a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits exposed on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare value that sets the counting rate. The documentation describes the counter behavior in detail but gives only a brief description of the denoising function.
tt05/tt_um_seanvenadas.review_notes: Removed neuromorphic and image-processing tags not supported by source.

tt05/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This design counts seconds and displays the value on a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits also available on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare register so the counting rate can be changed from the default one-second interval. It is a standard Tiny Tapeout Verilog demo intended to show clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. The documentation is complete and describes both the default and programmable counting behavior.
tt05/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and template tags; source describes a counter/timer demo, not a clock generator or template.

tt05/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds_ksandov.summary: This project is intended to implement a random dropout circuit inspired by the dropout mechanism used to prevent overfitting in neural networks. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test both state only that they are not written yet. The pin names are inherited from the 7-segment counter demo template and do not reflect the described dropout function. There is not enough information to determine the actual implementation or how to use it.
tt05/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds_ksandov.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and prng tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt05/tt_um_stdp.summary: This design implements two leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and a spike-timing dependent plasticity module that updates a synaptic weight based on the timing difference between pre- and post-synaptic spikes. A drive current is applied to the neuron and integrated every clock cycle, with the LIF spike, LIF state, and synaptic weight brought out as outputs. The documentation describes the learning rule and testing procedure at a high level. It is a compact hardware demonstration of a biologically inspired learning mechanism.

tt05/tt_um_suhrojo.summary: This project is described as a silicon chip design of a convolutional neural network, but the how-it-works section only says the explanation will be added later. The how-to-test section is copied from the 7-segment counter demo and does not describe CNN testing. The pin names are also inherited from that demo template and do not indicate CNN-specific interfaces. There is essentially no usable documentation for the actual design.
tt05/tt_um_suhrojo.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and image-processing tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt05/tt_um_sunaofurukawa_cpu_8bit.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU design whose Verilog code was generated by Bing AI. The input pins carry instruction register bits and formula right-side bits, while the outputs drive a 7-segment display. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are still placeholders, so the instruction set and operation are not described. The design cannot be fully evaluated from the available information.

tt05/tt_um_supertails_tetris.summary: This design implements the game Tetris in hardware, using VGA outputs for video and buttons for moving and rotating pieces. It requires an external memory connected over the bidirectional pins, which the author implemented on an RP2040 based on existing Teensy code. Silicon testing reported that the design works great. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are otherwise placeholders.
tt05/tt_um_supertails_tetris.review_notes: Removed memory/display tags not supported by the design; added button, rp2040 and retro.

tt05/tt_um_synth_GyanepsaaS.summary: This design is a basic sound synthesizer that generates a waveform and shapes it with an ADSR envelope. The waveform is selected between triangle and sawtooth, and the note frequency is chosen with four input bits while a separate clock sets the sampling rate. The envelope attack, decay, sustain and release stages are configured through the bidirectional pins, and the resulting sound is emitted on one output pin. Documentation is very thin, consisting only of a one-line description and a short test note, so the exact envelope resolution and output encoding are not specified.
tt05/tt_um_synth_GyanepsaaS.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm tag; added synthesizer, audio, music, oscillator, waveform-generator, and verilog based on source evidence.

tt05/tt_um_thermocouple.summary: This block converts digitized thermocouple ADC counts into a temperature value using piecewise linear approximation and interpolation. It communicates over a 16-bit SPI interface, supports type-J and type-K thermocouples, and can optionally pass the SPI master straight through to the ADC for configuration. The output is a 16-bit centi-Celsius value pre-divided by four, giving 0.4 C granularity, and the thermocouple type and passthrough mode are set through configuration writes. It requires an external thermocouple analog front-end with compatible ranging, and the documentation gives worked numeric examples for the transfer function.

tt05/tt_um_tiny_game_of_life.summary: This design simulates Conway's Game of Life on an 8x8 grid using two shift registers, one holding the current state and one holding the updated state. The user loads cells one at a time in row-major order through a single input pin, then asserts a start pin to begin the simulation, after which the circuit alternates between updating and outputting indefinitely. During output, one pin carries the cell value and seven pins carry the cell index from 1 to 64, so an external display or host must reconstruct the grid. The documentation is detailed about the protocol but notes that the design should simply be prayed over, and no silicon test results are given.
tt05/tt_um_tiny_game_of_life.review_notes: Removed 'game' as the design is a cellular automaton simulation rather than an interactive game.

tt05/tt_um_tkmheart.summary: This design applies threshold-based filtering to an input data stream and then performs peak detection over three consecutive clock cycles. A clock divider halves the input clock, and a counter driven by that clock is exposed on the bidirectional pins while the compare threshold is loaded in two four-bit halves through the input pins. The outputs drive a seven-segment display with a decimal point, presumably to show the counter or detected peaks. The documentation describes the loading sequence but does not explain the intended signal source or what the display actually shows, and no silicon results are provided.
tt05/tt_um_tkmheart.review_notes: Removed timer and biomedical; added comparator and edge-detector to match the documented threshold/peak logic.

tt05/tt_um_toivoh_synth.summary: This design is a monophonic synth voice with two oscillators, a second-order low-pass filter, and programmable sweep rates that act as simple envelopes. It is controlled through a register interface written over eight data pins, four address pins and a write strobe, and it outputs audio both as a PWM signal and as an 8-bit sample for reconstruction with a resistor ladder. The oscillators use a floating-point-style period format to emulate the exponential volt-per-octave response of analog synths, and the filter uses a shared barrel shifter instead of multipliers. Silicon tests report that the registers can be written and that a demo tune plays back correctly, and it needs an external audio connection with a voltage divider to protect the audio device.
tt05/tt_um_toivoh_synth.review_notes: Filter-analog incorrectly describes a digital filter implementation; added silicon-tested tag from reported working silicon.

tt05/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This design implements a simple VGA pong-style game with paddles controlled by four input pins. It outputs VGA signals on the bidirectional and output pins and supports two different VGA PMOD pinouts selected by an input, with the recommended Tiny VGA pinout. The game has no scoring and the ball only moves horizontally, so it is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete game. Silicon tests report that pong works, though one tester had to adjust monitor centering and another could not get a proper display on a CRT.
tt05/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported gamepad tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

tt05/tt_um_topLevel_derekabarca.summary: This design connects two neuron modules through a synapse module to produce rhythmic oscillations, according to its one-line description. The pin names match those of a threshold comparator and counter design, with compare bits on the inputs, a second counter on the bidirectional pins and seven-segment display segments on the outputs. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections are both literally marked as to be filled in later, so no usable description of the internal behaviour or test procedure exists. The design is effectively undocumented beyond its title and pin list.
tt05/tt_um_topLevel_derekabarca.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network, neural-network, oscillator, counter and 7-segment tags not supported by the thin documentation; added neuromorphic, verilog and insufficient-doc.

tt05/tt_um_topModuleKA.summary: This design implements leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons and time-multiplexes them to realize multiple neurons from shared hardware. An input current is applied through the input pins, accumulates in a membrane potential that decays over time, and triggers a spike when the potential crosses a threshold. The membrane potential is exposed on the eight output pins and spike outputs appear on the bidirectional pins, so a higher input current should produce a higher firing rate. The documentation is brief and does not specify the number of neurons, the time-multiplexing scheme, or any silicon test results.

tt05/tt_um_top_mole99.summary: This design produces an 800x600 60 Hz SVGA output with a background and a single 12x12 sprite, rendered internally at 100x75 so each sprite pixel is 8x8 screen pixels. The sprite is initialized with a pixelated Tiny Tapeout logo that moves around the screen, and an SPI receiver accepts commands to replace sprite data, change colors, set the background and control the sprite position. It can run at either a 40 MHz or 10 MHz pixel clock selected by a configuration bit, and it needs an external Tiny VGA PMOD for display. Silicon tests report that the logo bounces around and the SPI interface works, with some glitching when moving the sprite.
tt05/tt_um_top_mole99.review_notes: Removed vga (SVGA over Pmod, not VGA) and added silicon-tested and pmod based on pins and test reports.

tt05/tt_um_tt05_analog_test.summary: This analog test macro contains a roughly 500 kHz ring oscillator producing a square wave and a 3-bit R-2R DAC producing a programmable DC voltage, with transmission gates to route or short the two outputs. The blocks are enabled and routed to the two analog output pins through digital control inputs, and the DAC voltage is set by three input bits. It was placed and routed with an experimental automatic analog place-and-route tool, making it a test of the analog flow rather than a functional product. Silicon tests report that the DAC works accurately with about 8 mV to 1.57 V output range and roughly 400 ns rise and fall times, while the ring oscillator measured around 400-409 kHz, about 100 kHz slower than intended.

tt05/tt_um_ttl74hc595_v2.summary: This project implements a 74HC595 8-bit shift register with output latches in Verilog. It accepts serial data, shift clock, latch clock, output enable and clear signals, and drives eight parallel outputs. The design is intended to be tested by connecting eight LEDs, such as a Pmod, and bit-banging data to create effects like a Knight Rider pattern. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with the author using C and MicroPython to drive the LEDs.
tt05/tt_um_ttl74hc595_v2.review_notes: Removed register-file (incorrect for a shift register) and added silicon-tested (author report confirms working silicon).

tt05/tt_um_uabc_electronica_2023.summary: This design displays the text 'UABC-ELECTRONICA' on a 7-segment display by showing each letter sequentially. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary counts to decimal for the display, with the lower 8 bits of the counter available on bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted via input pins that set a comparison value, defaulting to one second per increment with a 10 MHz clock. It is intended as a demonstration or educational project, and no silicon test results are provided.
tt05/tt_um_uabc_electronica_2023.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and education tags not supported by source.

tt05/tt_um_urish_dffram.summary: This project implements a 128-byte RAM module using a 32x32 1RW DFFRAM macro. It provides address, write-enable, input, and output pins for reading and writing data. The design is implemented in Verilog and spans a 4x2 tile area. Silicon test reports indicate that writes and reads work, with some timing quirks noted by testers.
tt05/tt_um_urish_dffram.review_notes: Replaced incorrect oscillator/counter tags with memory, sram, silicon-tested, and multi-tile based on the DFFRAM source and silicon reports.

tt05/tt_um_urish_ringosc_cnt.summary: This is a test module for the TT05 power switching FET, featuring a ring oscillator and a 64-bit counter that counts oscillations. The counter value can be shifted and read on outputs, with reset and stop controls. It is tested by setting the shift value and observing the counter outputs. Silicon measurements indicated the ring oscillator runs at approximately 504 MHz, as inferred from a 1.969 MHz signal on the 8th counter bit.

tt05/tt_um_urish_silife.summary: This design is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x8 grid. The grid can be loaded row by row using row select, cell input and write enable signals, and the game advances one step per clock cycle when enabled. The current state of any row can be read via the cell output pins. It is a compact, interactive implementation of the classic cellular automaton, with no external hardware required beyond the chip's pins.
tt05/tt_um_urish_silife.review_notes: Removed fsm because the design is a cellular automaton grid, not a finite state machine.

tt05/tt_um_urish_silife_max.summary: This project is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x32 grid, with optional output to a MAX7219 LED dot matrix. It supports both manual mode, where the grid is loaded row by row, and a demo mode that cycles through pre-defined patterns. The game advances one generation per clock cycle when enabled, or every 0.4 seconds in demo mode with a 10 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it works well with the LED matrix, though a delay before animation starts was noted, and one tester reported issues with demo patterns progressing.

tt05/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This design implements the Simon Says memory game, where the player must repeat a growing sequence of colors. The sequence is shown via four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone played through a speaker, and the score is displayed on a two-digit 7-segment display. The game requires external hardware: four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, a speaker or buzzer, and optionally a two-digit 7-segment display. A silicon test report notes a minor bug where pressing a button immediately after failing skips the game over sound, which was fixed in a later version.
tt05/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Added wokwi and scoreboard tags; the summary is otherwise supported by the source.

tt05/tt_um_urish_skullfet.summary: This project contains hand-crafted, skull-shaped MOSFET transistors implemented in a custom description language. It includes three devices: a NOT gate, a NAND gate, and an SR flip-flop, with inputs and outputs exposed on the chip pins. Testing involves applying input values and observing the outputs, and pulsing set/reset for the flip-flop. Silicon tests confirmed that the inverter and NAND work perfectly, and the flip-flop outputs are inverted as noted by the author.
tt05/tt_um_urish_skullfet.review_notes: Added silicon-tested (both tester and author reports confirm working silicon).

tt05/tt_um_uwuifier.summary: This design operates on a UART signal and transforms the text into 'uwu' speak. It interfaces via UART at 115200 baud with a 6 MHz clock, using dedicated receive and transmit pins. It is intended to be connected inline with a UART transceiver to modify data in real time. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester using a serial terminal to send data and receiving the uwuified version back.
tt05/tt_um_uwuifier.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

tt05/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This design shows the time on a VGA screen using a 31.5 MHz clock, with pins for hsync, vsync, and 6-bit color output (two bits per RGB channel). It uses a pre-generated font loaded into registers and 'races the beam' to generate the display. External hardware includes an R2R DAC to convert the digital color outputs to analog VGA signals and a VGA monitor. The design supports adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds via input pins.
tt05/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (misleading; it is a time display) and added rtc.

tt05/tt_um_vhdl_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This VHDL demo counts from 0 to 9 on a 7-segment display, incrementing once per second with a 10 MHz clock. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal, and the lower 8 bits of the counter are available on bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting input pins that program a comparison value. Silicon testing confirmed it counts from 0 to 9 once per second.
tt05/tt_um_vhdl_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and education tags; added vhdl and silicon-tested.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_376553022662786049.summary: This project implements several test clusters featuring various spike trains for neuro-inspired computing research. It includes neuron clusters of different sizes, an LFSR, flip-flops, and a multiplexer, with inputs and outputs exposed on the chip pins. The design is tested by providing input clock frequencies to the neuron clusters and observing outputs via an oscilloscope to generate raster spiking plots. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for investigating spike-based information representation, with no silicon test results provided.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_377426511818305537.summary: This project implements a configurable pseudo-random binary sequence (PRBS) generator using a Galois linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) with XOR taps. It supports SPI configuration of parameters such as clock divider, sequence length, polynomial, and data bit count, and provides differential outputs with look-ahead. The design includes a debug mode for easy setup and testing, and it can be enabled or reset via dedicated pins. Silicon testing confirmed that the generator works as described when following the author's instructions.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_377426511818305537.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file tag and added canonical tags for the documented PRBS/LFSR, SPI, clock divider, Wokwi implementation, and silicon-tested status.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_378231665807713281.summary: This project is a simple test of a memory cell, with inputs for data and address selection and a write/read control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a brief description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of how the cell operates or how to test it. No external hardware is required. Due to the lack of documentation, the exact functionality and testing procedure are unclear.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_378231665807713281.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc tag as the documentation, while minimal, adequately describes the design's purpose and interface.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379319062779062273.summary: This project implements a binary counter that drives a 7-segment display, incrementing with each clock cycle. The design is described only as a binary counter connected to the clock, with separate outputs for each segment and the decimal point. The documentation is very sparse and explicitly leaves the test instructions as a placeholder with no external hardware details. Beyond the basic counter and display function, no further specifics are available.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379319062779062273.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; kept the rest as supported.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379764885531576321.summary: This project uses a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) to implement a counter that displays its value on a 7-segment display. It includes a synchronous reset input and increments the count on each positive clock edge. Silicon testing confirmed that it counts up, repeating from 0 to 9. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond the display.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379764885531576321.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; 7-segment already captures the output.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379824923824476161.summary: This project implements an analog clock controller that drives LEDs to represent the time, with a 1 Hz internal clock input. It includes counters for seconds, minutes, and hours, and outputs to 16 LEDs that indicate the hour and the last 15-minute increment. Input pins allow stopping the clock and manually incrementing the minute or hour counters. The design requires 16 external LEDs for display and is intended to simulate an analog clock face.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379824923824476161.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and decoder (unsupported); added rtc and led.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379889284755158017.summary: This project controls a 7-segment display to show the author's initials and a date (10/28). The documentation is essentially a template with no explanation of how the circuit works or how to test it. The only provided information is the pin mapping for the segments and decimal point. It appears to be a static display project, but no further details are available.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_379889284755158017.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added text since the display shows characters.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380005495431181313.summary: This project is a water pump controller designed for camping vans, with inputs for multiple tap switches, a high-pressure switch, and a timer enable. It includes a timer that warns via a buzzer when water runs too long and automatically shuts off the pump after a timeout, with configurable settings. The controller outputs signals for the pump, status LEDs, and buzzer, and can be tested with LEDs or a 7-segment display and DIP switches. It requires a 32.768 kHz clock and external hardware such as tap switches and a pump for full operation.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380005495431181313.review_notes: Removed industrial, sensor-interface, and fsm tags not supported by source.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380055891603379201.summary: This project implements a hexadecimal countdown from F to 0 on a 7-segment display, controlled by a state machine that decrements on each clock pulse. An activation signal starts the countdown, and a reset returns the display to F. Silicon testing confirmed that it works as described, counting down when the activation input is high. It requires a 1 Hz clock signal and no additional external hardware.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380055891603379201.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; 7-segment already captures the output.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380119282165535745.summary: This project is a simple counter that displays a digit on a 7-segment display, counting from 0 to 9 and wrapping around, with one step per clock cycle. It uses SR flip-flops to avoid combinational logic in the clock path, which previously caused glitches. Testing involves pressing reset and then clocking to advance the count. No external hardware is required beyond the display.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380119282165535745.review_notes: Removed redundant 'display' tag; 7-segment already covers the output.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380120751165092865.summary: This project drives a WS2812B LED strip with random colors that update periodically. It uses a 16-bit linear-feedback shift register to generate pseudo-random bits, a 5-bit counter to create the 1.25 µs pulses required by the WS2812B protocol, and a 16-bit ripple counter to control the refresh rate. The design requires a 20 MHz clock and a WS2812B LED strip connected to the output, with optional feedback from the strip's data output. Testing involves setting the clock, connecting the strip, and observing random colors with adjustable refresh frequency.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380120751165092865.review_notes: Removed signal-generator tag; design is a WS2812B driver, not a general signal generator.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380145600224164865.summary: This design converts a 4-bit binary input into a 7-segment display pattern using a simple combinational circuit of OR and AND gates. It is tested by setting the first four switches to a binary value from 0 to 15 and observing the display. No external hardware beyond the switches and a 7-segment display is required. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation for digits 0 through 9, but values 10 to 15 do not display, which the testers note may be intentional but would be nicer as hexadecimal.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380145600224164865.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd and education tags; added silicon-tested per the working test report.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380197591775930369.summary: This project blinks the letter A on a 7-segment display, with each output pin driving one segment plus the decimal point. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the internal logic and intended test procedure are not described. It needs only a 7-segment display connected to the eight outputs. A silicon test report confirms that it did blink an A, but the lack of documentation makes the design's details unclear.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380229599886002177.summary: This design generates pseudo-random bit streams whose probability of a one equals the product of two 2-bit input vectors, implementing stochastic multiplication based on a published PN-sequence method. It is used by setting inputs A and B, applying a clock, and toggling reset low to start the PRBS generators, with outputs providing the product stream and individual operand streams. No external hardware is strictly required, and some outputs are also mapped to 7-segment segments. The documentation is brief and cites the underlying paper, but does not describe the internal implementation or provide silicon test results.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380229599886002177.review_notes: Removed lfsr as unstated and dsp as unsupported application framing; the add list must stay canonical.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380361576213660673.summary: This is a hardware implementation of two-player ping pong rendered on a 16x24 LED matrix, using up/down counters for each paddle and the ball plus an input register to debounce buttons. It requires substantial external hardware: a 16-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register, a 5-to-24 decoder, the LED matrix, eight buttons, BCD counters with 7-segment displays for scoring, and a timing unit to generate the enable and clock signals. Testing can start simply by hooking up left/right buttons for player one and monitoring the horizontal position bits, but full functionality needs the complete external support circuitry. The design is notable for its detailed pin-level documentation and its reliance on external multiplexing and decoding to drive the matrix.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380361576213660673.review_notes: Added button and 7-segment interface tags supported by the pin descriptions; removed redundant display tag.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408396356749313.summary: This project is a simple ring oscillator that outputs a square wave on pins 0 through 3, with the pins phase shifted relative to one another. It is tested simply by applying power, with no other control inputs described. No external hardware is needed beyond observing the outputs. The documentation is very thin and does not specify the oscillation frequency or the exact phase relationship, so those details cannot be confirmed.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408396356749313.review_notes: Removed unsupported analog tag, added silicon-tested based on multiple shuttle resubmissions.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408409844584449.summary: This project demonstrates one of each basic logic gate together with some flip-flops, intended as a gate-level playground. The documentation is placeholder text, so the exact circuit and test method are not described. It appears to use the eight outputs for 7-segment segments, but the connection to the logic is unclear. The author's silicon test report notes a 1 Hz clock while tracing the logic through the Wokwi diagram, and that momentary push-button mode helped separate gate tests from flip-flop tests.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408409844584449.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added silicon-tested tag based on author's working report.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408455148316673.summary: This design combines a tapped ring oscillator with a glitchless clock source switch, allowing selection between two external clocks. To test the oscillator, one of the three inverted taps is fed back to input 0, while the clock switch is tested by using input 1 to select between clock0 and clock1, with the selected clock appearing on output 3. No external hardware beyond clock sources and feedback wiring is required. The documentation is concise but describes both functional blocks and their test procedure clearly.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408455148316673.review_notes: Removed analog (digital Wokwi design) and added clock-domain-crossing for the glitchless clock switch.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408486941145089.summary: This project is a Tiny Tapeout 5 workshop design whose first three output bits form a binary counter that can be preset with the first three input bits, while the remaining input bits pass through to the outputs. The documentation does not explain how to test it, leaving the test procedure unspecified. No external hardware is described, though the outputs are mapped to 7-segment segments. The design appears to be a teaching example from a workshop, but the sparse documentation limits what can be said about it.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408486941145089.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added counter, workshop, wokwi, and 7-segment tags supported by the source.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408594272345089.summary: This design divides the input clock by successive powers of two, with CLK/2 on output 7 down to CLK/256 on output 0. The documentation is placeholder text and does not describe the internal implementation or how to test it. It requires only a clock input and observation of the divided outputs, with no other external hardware mentioned. Because the documentation is essentially empty, the summary is inferred from the title and pin names.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408594272345089.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the supplied documentation is placeholder text.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408774591779841.summary: This Verilog design generates a sawtooth waveform for audio by incrementing a counter from 0 to 25,000,000 and feeding the value into a PDM modulator, with the frequency set by a 4-bit left-shift amount. It is tested by adding an RC low-pass filter with a cutoff around 30 kHz to output pin 7, which can be probed with an oscilloscope or connected to an audio amplifier to listen to the result. The design outputs both PCM bits and a PDM stream, and follows the Tiny Tapeout audio pinout recommendation. It is notable for being a straightforward audio waveform generator that requires external filtering and amplification to be useful.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408774591779841.review_notes: Removed pwm/synthesizer/dac which are unsupported; kept signal-generator and audio.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408784463076353.summary: This is a simple binary counter implemented in Wokwi that drives a 7-segment display. The eight outputs map directly to the seven segments and decimal point, and the design counts in binary at a 10 Hz clock. It requires no external hardware and is tested simply by turning it on. The documentation is very thin and the description is informal, so little can be said about its internal structure.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408784463076353.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; 7-segment is the specific supported output interface.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.summary: This design displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display based on a 6-bit binary value entered on DIP switches. It drives the display one segment at a time, so a high clock rate is needed to see the full character. The character set covers a-z plus space, underscore, hyphen, period, exclamation mark and quote. Silicon tests report it working, and it is notable as a simple character generator with a documented mapping table.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.review_notes: Removed text (7-segment output only) and added silicon-tested per test reports.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380409393770716161.summary: This design generates a VGA signal that displays a white pixel on a blue background, reusing VGA Flappy Bird code from Cutout1. The project was submitted for Supercon 2023 and is notable for being a minimal VGA demonstration on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

Silicon test reports say each gate worked as expected.

It provides two four-input circuits, one normal and one containing an embedded hardware trojan, selected via DIP switches. The outputs are shown on a 7-segment display, with the normal circuit driving some segments and the trojan circuit driving others. It is built with Wokwi and requires only the Tiny Tapeout carrier board for testing.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380409568391147521.review_notes: Replaced unsupported LFSR/clock-generator/education tags with hardware-trojan, security, dip-switch and 7-segment supported by the source.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380409904919056385.summary: This design implements a 4-bit LFSR configured as a PRBS with polynomial X^3+X^2+1, using XNOR gates to avoid synthesis warnings. It has clock and reset inputs, and outputs for seven segments of a 7-segment display plus a PRBS output. The reset sets four D flip-flops to zero to ensure oscillation starts. The design is intended to verify the design flow for teaching lower division college students IC design.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380409904919056385.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the PRBS and 7-segment display description.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380410498092232705.summary: This design sends the string 'Hello\n' over UART using a shift register with hardcoded initial values loaded into a looped feedback path. It also fills remaining die space with an 'RNN' module made from flip-flops feeding into each other, driven by inputs 0-3 and producing outputs 0-3. To test UART, connect the UART output to a microcontroller or scope, set load/enable low then high, set output enable high, and observe the string. The design has been silicon-tested and reported working by a tester who connected it to a serial port and saw it print Hello.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380410498092232705.review_notes: Replaced counter/clock-generator tags with tags supported by the UART shift-register and flip-flop RNN documentation, and corrected the summary which described unrelated counter and display behavior.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380412382001715201.summary: This project is a naive 8-bit binary counter built from eight chained D flip-flops that count the clock input. Its eight outputs drive the segments and dot of a 7-segment display, and it lacks features such as a deterministic initial state or a reset. It was constructed during the Hackaday Supercon 2023 ASIC workshop as a rapid learning exercise. Testing consists of pulsing the clock and monitoring the outputs for the binary value, and silicon testers report it counts correctly.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380412382001715201.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a placeholder submission, contradicting the actual counter documentation and working silicon reports.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380416099936681985.summary: This design counts seconds and displays the value on a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits also available on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare register so the counting rate can be changed from the default one-second interval. It is a standard Tiny Tapeout Verilog demo intended to show clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. The documentation is complete and describes both the default and programmable counting behavior.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380416099936681985.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and template tags; source describes a counter/timer demo, not a clock generator or template.

An external UART receiver is required to observe the transmitted data.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380438365946734593.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register and multiplexer tags; kept flip-flop and education which are supported.

The only concrete information is the pin names, which indicate the seven segments and decimal point. It appears to be an incomplete or template project.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380465686251921409.review_notes: Removed redundant generic display tag; 7-segment already covers the output.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380477805171811329.summary: This project combines a 2-bit ALU and a dice function, and can translate binary code into a single-digit display. The documentation is mostly placeholder text, with no explanation of how the ALU or dice operate or how to test them. The only pin listed is the decimal point of a 7-segment display, suggesting the output is shown on such a display. The design is described as 'extremely professional' and 'Steve Jobs approves', but lacks technical details.

tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380490286828784641.summary: This is a remake of Matt Venn's original TT02 7-segment Wokwi project, with the multiplexer select lines inverted at reset so that transitions occur on the opposite clock edge. It functions as a counter that drives a 7-segment display. Testing involves manually clocking the design to see the incrementing output on the display. The project is a minor variation of an existing design and includes links to the original Wokwi project.
tt05/tt_um_wokwi_380490286828784641.review_notes: Removed multiplexer and retro tags not supported by the design's purpose.

tt05/tt_um_wrapper_inputblackboxoutput.summary: Byte Computer is an 8-bit Turing complete computer implemented in Verilog, featuring an in-order, non-pipelined architecture with no register file, cache, or branch predictor. It fetches instructions from external memory, decodes and executes them, and repeats until a halt instruction is encountered. Testing requires external memory and control logic, typically provided by a microcontroller, which must be preloaded with a program. The design is notable for its simplicity and small size, making it suitable for Tiny Tapeout.
tt05/tt_um_wrapper_inputblackboxoutput.review_notes: Removed memory, microcontroller and esoteric because they are not supported by the source; cpu was already present and is correct.

tt05/tt_um_wta.summary: This project implements a Winner-Take-All (WTA) network that takes an 8-bit current input, splits it into two 4-bit values, and outputs the 4 bits of the higher value, with preference to the most significant bits in case of a tie. It includes outputs for membrane potential and spike bits, though the spike outputs are mostly unspecified. Testing involves resetting the design and observing the comparator and result values. The design is a simple digital implementation of a neural network concept.
tt05/tt_um_wta.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network tag; source only supports a WTA comparator/neural-network concept.

tt05/tt_um_yubex_metastability_experimen.summary: This design evaluates whether metastability in flip-flops can be used as a true random number generator source in an ASIC. It uses a toggle flip-flop to create edges, a programmable delay line made of inverter pairs, and two metastable flip-flops; metastability is detected when their outputs differ. The design has manual and auto trigger modes, and the delay is controlled by a 6-bit input. Testing involves selecting a mode, adjusting the delay, and observing the 7-segment display for metastability indication; no external hardware is required.
tt05/tt_um_yubex_metastability_experimen.review_notes: Removed trng because the design only evaluates metastability as a possible TRNG source, not a TRNG implementation.

tt05of/tt_um_4_bit_pipeline_multiplier.summary: This design is a 4-bit pipelined Booth multiplier intended for learning purposes. It has been tested in silicon and verified to work correctly for all input pairs, with pipelining functioning as expected. The design achieved clock speeds of 146MHz at 1.8V and 154MHz at 1.9V core voltage. It is a simple educational project with no external hardware requirements.
tt05of/tt_um_4_bit_pipeline_multiplier.review_notes: Removed 'alu' since the design is a multiplier, not an ALU.

tt05of/tt_um_7segx4_clock_abhishek_top.summary: This design is a multi-mode clock with a four-digit seven-segment display. It uses registers to divide the clock and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal for display, with the bottom 8 bits of the counter available on bidirectional outputs. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting the inputs to program a 24-bit compare register, allowing the counter to increment at different rates. It requires an external seven-segment display and a 10MHz clock source.
tt05of/tt_um_7segx4_clock_abhishek_top.review_notes: Removed 'clock-generator' because the design divides rather than generates a clock.

tt05of/tt_um_BNNNeuron.summary: This design implements a single neuron in a binarized neural network (BNN), performing binary multiplication with XNOR, accumulation, and sign activation. It simulates the behavior of a neuron by accumulating XNOR results and applying a sign function to output +1 or -1. The design is tested by resetting the circuit and providing constant inputs and weights with an enable signal to begin the XNOR multiplication. It is a demonstration of BNN concepts and requires no external hardware.
tt05of/tt_um_BNNNeuron.review_notes: Added perceptron tag as the design is a single-neuron classifier; summary unchanged.

tt05of/tt_um_EventFilter.summary: The design implements a debouncer for event-based camera data, filtering out spurious events caused by noise. It accepts an 8-bit tuple (x, y, p, t) via input pins and outputs the tuple only if the data remains stable for 5 clock cycles. The polarity bit is used to indicate high or low events, and the design can be tested by setting switches to simulate event tuples. The project is notable for addressing thermal noise in event cameras, but the documentation is minimal and lacks details on testing and implementation.
tt05of/tt_um_EventFilter.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; summary is supported by the source.

tt05of/tt_um_Fiona_CMU.summary: This project implements a stream cipher using an 8-byte linear shift register to encrypt and decrypt messages. It accepts 8-bit data on input pins and uses bidirectional pins for control signals such as increment, encrypt, and view mode. The encrypted or decrypted message can be viewed by selecting an index, and the design supports toggling between encryption and viewing without resetting. Notable limitations include the need to reset after 16 bytes to avoid losing encrypted data, and the documentation provides clear testing steps.
tt05of/tt_um_Fiona_CMU.review_notes: Removed lfsr because the source describes a linear shift register without feedback, and added shift-register and systemverilog.

tt05of/tt_um_GrayCounter_ariz207.summary: The design is a 4-bit synchronous Gray code counter that increments on a clock input and outputs the Gray code value on four LED pins. It is intended to demonstrate binary values changing in Gray code sequence, and can be tested by connecting a clock source and LEDs. The documentation is very brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing instructions. There is no additional detail on implementation or features.

tt05of/tt_um_LSNN.summary: This project implements a spiking LSTM network based on a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron with an adaptive threshold. It accepts a current input and outputs spikes, with the threshold increasing when spikes occur and decaying otherwise. The design is tested by applying different current levels and observing the spiking behavior and threshold adaptation. The documentation is somewhat sparse, lacking details on the LSTM integration and external hardware requirements.
tt05of/tt_um_LSNN.review_notes: Removed neural-network tag as the design is a single neuron, not a network.

tt05of/tt_um_Leaky_Integrate_Fire_nfjesi.summary: This project uses a 24-bit counter and a programmable compare register to generate a periodic event, with the counter value shown on a 7-segment display. The lower 8 bits of the counter are also available on the bidirectional pins. With all inputs low the compare is set to 10,000,000, so the counter increments once per second at a 10 MHz clock, and setting the inputs programs bits 11 to 18 of the compare value to change the rate. The design can be tested by observing the counter increment every second and experimenting with the input pins to change the counting speed.
tt05of/tt_um_Leaky_Integrate_Fire_nfjesi.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network and clock-divider tags not supported by the documented counter/comparator behavior; summary rewritten to match the source.

tt05of/tt_um_MichaelBell_spi_peri.summary: The design implements an SPI peripheral with an 8-byte RAM, 324-byte ROM, and a random source, supporting standard and quad SPI read/write commands. It is intended to be used as a ROM for an RP2040, allowing it to boot from the ROM, and also provides debug access via switches and a 7-segment display. Silicon testing showed that the SPI RAM works and the RP2040 boots from the ROM, but writes to the RAM were not functioning and the random source distribution is non-uniform. The project requires a custom RP2040 board and a PIO-based SPI master for full testing.

tt05of/tt_um_SNN.summary: This project implements a basic spiking neural network that takes spiking patterns from three input neurons and produces spikes from two output neurons based on predefined weights. It is intended for studying spike generation and can be tested by feeding different input spike patterns and observing the output spikes. The documentation is minimal, with many pins marked as unspecified and no details on the network architecture or testing methodology. The design appears to be a simple feedforward network with limited configurability.
tt05of/tt_um_SNN.review_notes: Removed generic neural-network tag; spiking-neural-network and neuromorphic are sufficient.

tt05of/tt_um_adaptive_lif.summary: This project implements an adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire neuron with configurable adaptive threshold and decay rate. It accepts an 8-bit current input and outputs the membrane potential and spike output, with control pins to enable adaptive features. Silicon testing confirmed that the neuron fires in response to different current levels, though the spike output appeared as digital pulses rather than narrow spikes. The design aims to enhance spike sparsity while preserving input features, and the documentation includes simulation and test results.
tt05of/tt_um_adaptive_lif.review_notes: Removed overly broad neural-network tag and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt05of/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_spi_rom.summary: This project reads data from an SPI flash ROM and displays it on a VGA monitor, supporting two resolutions and two line modes for buffered and direct display. It includes a loopback test and requires external hardware such as an SPI flash chip and a VGA DAC. Silicon testing showed that it displayed graphics on the screen, but the SPI ROM functionality was not fully tested. The documentation is detailed but notes that some aspects are still to be confirmed.
tt05of/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_spi_rom.review_notes: Removed driver because the design is a display/readout experiment, and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt05of/tt_um_alu_chip.summary: This project is a simple 4-bit ALU that performs operations such as addition, subtraction, AND, OR, and comparisons, and outputs the result in BCD on a 7-segment display. It accepts two 4-bit inputs and a 4-bit operation code, and provides the result on both the 7-segment display and bidirectional pins. The documentation is very brief, with only a one-line description and no detailed testing instructions. The design is straightforward and lacks advanced features.

tt05of/tt_um_asinghani_tinyscanchain_tt0.summary: This is a test design for tinyscanchain, a scan-chain implementation written in under 80 lines of Python, built on top of the seven-segment-seconds counter design. After reset the counter increments once per second from a 1 kHz clock, and the scan chain allows inspection of the internal state of the design. The seven-segment outputs drive a display, while the scan-chain input, enable and output pins provide the debug interface. It is intended as a demonstration and test vehicle for the tinyscanchain tool rather than a standalone application.

tt05of/tt_um_async_proc_paulschulz.summary: This circuit is an early investigation into an asynchronous parallel processor, where each processing node waits for valid data, computes a result from four 4-bit inputs, signals its neighbours, and then makes the result available. Inputs are loaded into buffers via dedicated load pins, and the result is displayed on seven-segment outputs with a data-ready dot. The design is explicitly described as a work in progress that does not do very much yet, with future plans for programmable nodes, a multi-node array, and a clockless version. Testing consists of resetting, loading input values, and observing the outputs.
tt05of/tt_um_async_proc_paulschulz.review_notes: Removed accelerator and education (unsupported) and added incomplete and cpu based on the source description.

tt05of/tt_um_blink.summary: This design instantiates eight inverters whose inputs and outputs are exposed on the input and bidirectional pins, together with a counter whose upper bits are driven to the outputs. The documentation is very thin, describing it only as a blink and suggesting checking reset, enable and counter function. It appears to be a simple test structure for observing inverter behaviour and counter operation on silicon. No external hardware is described beyond observing the pins.
tt05of/tt_um_blink.review_notes: Removed timer and logic-gate; added characterization and insufficient-doc given the thin documentation.

tt05of/tt_um_btflv_8bit_fp_adder.summary: This design adds two 8-bit floating point numbers, each with a 1-bit sign, 4-bit exponent and 3-bit mantissa, taking one operand from the input pins and the other from the bidirectional pins. The result, including rounding and infinity handling, appears on the output pins every clock cycle. A silicon test report notes that the adder works well for most values but produces incorrect results for some small values, and a linked script tests all possible input combinations. It is a compact arithmetic building block rather than a complete calculator.
tt05of/tt_um_btflv_8bit_fp_adder.review_notes: Removed alu because the block is a dedicated adder; added silicon-tested because fabrication reports exist, even though the report is partial.

tt05of/tt_um_carlosgs99_cro_udg.summary: This project implements a 50 MHz chronometer that displays minutes, seconds and hundredths of a second across six seven-segment displays. A start button initialises or pauses the counter, and a reset button restarts it from zero. It requires six common-cathode seven-segment displays plus push buttons for the start and reset inputs, with the cathodes driven by the unidirectional outputs and the anodes by the bidirectional pins. The design is a straightforward digital clock application with no reported silicon test results.
tt05of/tt_um_carlosgs99_cro_udg.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design counts clock cycles rather than generating a clock.

tt05of/tt_um_cejmu.summary: This is a fully combinational 4-bit ALU containing a ripple-carry adder, a carry-lookahead adder, a matrix multiplier, a Wallace-tree multiplier, a comparator and a barrel-shifter, selected by a 3-bit opcode on the bidirectional pins. The two 4-bit operands come from the input pins, and the 8-bit result appears on the outputs, with the barrel-shifter using b[1:0] for shift width and b[2] for direction. No clock is required, and a silicon test report confirms the adder was verified on the bringup stream. It is a compact educational ALU demonstrating several arithmetic architectures in one tile.
tt05of/tt_um_cejmu.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not describe a teaching or learning purpose.

tt05of/tt_um_chatgpt_snn_mtomlin5.summary: This design implements six programmable digital leaky integrate-and-fire neurons arranged in two layers of three, with 8-bit weights programmable over an SPI interface. Input spikes drive the first layer, whose outputs feed the second layer through nine programmable weights, and the second layer's spikes appear on the output pins as one-clock-cycle pulses. After reset the user programs thresholds, leak rates, refractory periods and weights over SPI, then applies input spikes and observes output spikes synchronously. The design is notable for having been generated with ChatGPT and for requiring an external FPGA for testing.
tt05of/tt_um_chatgpt_snn_mtomlin5.review_notes: Removed machine-learning (not an ML accelerator) and added neuromorphic, which the LIF spiking network clearly supports.

tt05of/tt_um_chip_inventor_music__6_bit_.summary: This project combines two diagrams created with the Chip Inventor block-based design platform: a piano tune that drives a buzzer from a button, and a 6-bit counter. The counter's binary value can be observed on four LEDs connected in pull-up mode, and the buzzer plays a note when triggered. The documentation is brief and does not describe the internal implementation in detail. It serves mainly as a demonstration of the Chip Inventor design tool.

tt05of/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design is an 8-bit wide, 128-byte ROM containing information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash in 7-segment encoding and an ASCII chip descriptor string. The contents are read by setting the 8-bit address on the input pins and observing the data on the output pins, with the first bytes viewable on an on-board seven-segment display. The ROM is automatically generated by the tt-support-tools during GDS build. It is a utility design for chip identification rather than a computational block.

tt05of/tt_um_clkdiv.summary: This design uses a set of registers to divide the input clock by a 16-bit value supplied on the input and bidirectional pins, with the divided clock appearing on one output. The remaining seven outputs provide a simple random number generator output. The documentation is sparse, giving only a brief description and suggesting experimentation with different division inputs. It appears to be a basic clock-divider and PRNG test block with no reported silicon results.

tt05of/tt_um_czlucius_alu.summary: This project implements a 4-bit arithmetic logic unit with 13 selectable operations, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, bitwise logic, shifts, and modulo. The two 4-bit operands are provided on the eight input pins, while three bidirectional pins select the operation and the eight output pins present the 8-bit result. The design is intended for educational use and requires external digital logic such as buttons or sensors to provide inputs and observe outputs. The documentation is clear but contains a contradictory testing note about a counter, which appears to be a copy-paste error.
tt05of/tt_um_czlucius_alu.review_notes: Removed combinational tag because the source does not establish purely combinational behavior and the test note implies a counter.

tt05of/tt_um_devinatkin_stopwatch.summary: This design implements a stopwatch with start, stop, soft reset, and increment/decrement controls, displaying minutes and seconds on a multiplexed 7-segment display. It was originally developed and verified on a Basys 3 FPGA board and later ported to Tiny Tapeout. The design requires external hardware: a common-anode 7-segment display and several buttons and switches for control. Silicon testing by the author confirmed full functionality with a breadboarded display, though the provided test report is truncated.
tt05of/tt_um_devinatkin_stopwatch.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added silicon-tested to match the working silicon report.

tt05of/tt_um_diadatp_spigot_e.summary: This project implements a bounded spigot algorithm to compute 31 digits of Euler's number (e) in BCD format. The digits are output on the bidirectional and output pins, requiring external BCD-to-7-segment decoders (such as 7447) to display them. The design uses a ring of gated shift registers for storage and shares calculation hardware across iterations to fit within a single tile. It is notable for its low memory footprint and the use of SpinalHDL, but it only produces a fixed number of digits and requires a slow clock (below 500 Hz) to observe the output.
tt05of/tt_um_diadatp_spigot_e.review_notes: Removed 7-segment because the chip only outputs BCD digits; the seven-segment display and decoder are external.

tt05of/tt_um_diferential_ringy.summary: This is a factory test module that includes a ring oscillator and a counter, with a select pin to choose between mirroring input data to outputs or outputting the counter value. The documentation is incomplete, with 'TODO' placeholders for both how it works and how to test. The pin names indicate that when sel=0, the outputs reflect the inputs, and when sel=1, the outputs show the counter value, which is also available on the bidirectional pins. The design is intended for factory testing but lacks detailed explanation.
tt05of/tt_um_diferential_ringy.review_notes: Removed multiplexer as unsupported and added verilog and incomplete, which are stated in the source.

tt05of/tt_um_digital_clock_sellicott.summary: This project is a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format on six 7-segment displays. Because of limited output pins, the time data is shifted out serially to external 74xx596 shift registers that drive the displays. The time can be set using the hours_set and minutes_set inputs, with fast and slow increment modes, and pressing both set inputs clears the seconds. Silicon testing by the author using a logic analyzer confirmed correct operation of the serial output.
tt05of/tt_um_digital_clock_sellicott.review_notes: Removed unsupported rtc/education tags; added counter and silicon-tested based on source and test report.

tt05of/tt_um_dinogame.summary: This project implements an endless-runner game similar to the Chrome Dino game, rendered on a VGA monitor. The game uses four input buttons for jump, halt, debug, and mode control, and outputs VGA signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works well and is playable, though some testers noted occasional screen tearing at higher speeds. The documentation is minimal, consisting mainly of a brief description and pinout, but the test reports provide evidence of functionality.
tt05of/tt_um_dinogame.review_notes: Removed redundant video tag; added button and retro tags supported by the pin names and game description.

tt05of/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.summary: This design is an I2C peripheral that implements an 8-bit ALU to perform pattern testing and accumulate results, functioning as a bit error rate tester (BERT). It connects to an I2C controller (such as an RP2040) via the bidirectional pins and can be configured for different clocking modes and bus types through input pins. The design outputs results on a 7-segment display and includes power-on-reset configuration options. The documentation is somewhat technical and notes that further updates are planned, but it provides sufficient detail for operation.
tt05of/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.review_notes: Removed unsupported error-correction tag; summary is accurate.

tt05of/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module that either mirrors the input data to the outputs or outputs a counter value, depending on the state of input 0. When input 0 is high, a counter is output on both the regular and bidirectional outputs; otherwise, the inputs are passed through to the outputs. Testing is straightforward: set input 0 high and verify that the outputs are toggling. The design is simple and intended for manufacturing test purposes.

tt05of/tt_um_flappy_vga_cutout1.summary: This project is a clone of the Flappy Bird game, rendered on a 640x480 VGA display with a single button input for flapping. The game state is updated each frame, and the score is output in binary on the bidirectional pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a debounced active-low button, and a VGA adapter compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works and is playable, though several testers found it challenging.

tt05of/tt_um_freq_hcohensa.summary: This design encodes input data into frequency variations and then decodes it back to the original data, using a phase-locked loop (PLL) for clock generation. It interfaces with switches for input and 7-segment displays for output, and includes a second counter whose lower bits are available on bidirectional pins. The documentation describes the general operation but lacks specific implementation details and test results, making it difficult to assess its practical use. It appears to be an experimental design for frequency-based encoding and decoding.
tt05of/tt_um_freq_hcohensa.review_notes: Removed unsupported timer tag; added 7-segment tag supported by pin mapping.

tt05of/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an input signal by counting transitions over a configurable period and displays the result on a 7-segment display. It includes a debug mode that outputs internal signals on the bidirectional pins and allows the user to load a new count period via an input. The frequency is computed by repeatedly subtracting ten from the count and displaying the tens and units digits. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and external hardware such as a signal source and a 7-segment display.
tt05of/tt_um_frequency_counter.review_notes: Removed timer as unsupported; added instrumentation and debouncer.

tt05of/tt_um_gchenfc_seven_segment_gerry.summary: This design displays names on a 7-segment display, showing one letter per second by default. The top three input bits select which name is shown, while the lower five bits configure the clock divider speed, allowing a manual push-button to step the display. The bottom eight bits of the internal counter are output on the bidirectional pins. It is based on the 7-segment counter template project and is intended for simple visual demonstrations.
tt05of/tt_um_gchenfc_seven_segment_gerry.review_notes: Removed template because the project is a complete name-display design, not a starter template.

tt05of/tt_um_gfg_development_tros.summary: This design implements three different ring oscillators with varying temperature dependence: a basic NAND-based oscillator, a capacitively loaded NAND oscillator, and a tri-state inverter oscillator with sub-threshold enable. Each oscillator drives a counter that can be latched and transferred via a Manchester-encoded serial data stream, and divided versions of each oscillator clock are also output. The design is intended for characterization and testing of oscillator behavior. Silicon tests confirmed that at least one oscillator output works, though full testing is incomplete.

tt05of/tt_um_gharenthi_top.summary: This project is a single leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron with post-synaptic spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) learning. The documentation is essentially absent, with placeholder text for both the operation and testing sections. The pin names suggest a 7-segment display output and a counter, but the actual functionality cannot be determined from the provided information. No external hardware requirements or notable features are described.
tt05of/tt_um_gharenthi_top.review_notes: Added 7-segment tag because the output pins are explicitly named as seven-segment segments.

tt05of/tt_um_hadirkhan10_lif_neuron.summary: This design implements a configurable leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that mimics biological neuron behavior. It uses a state machine to configure parameters such as beta (decay rate) and threshold, then integrates an input current to produce a membrane potential and spike output. The neuron is controlled via input pins for configuration and current injection, with outputs for membrane potential and spike. It is intended for experimentation with neuron parameters and behavior.

tt05of/tt_um_haozhezhu_top.summary: This design is a 4-bit wide memory that can operate as either a FIFO or LIFO, selected by a mode pin. It can store up to 30 entries, with full, empty, output valid, and overflow flags. A 7-segment display shows the number of stored entries up to nine, and disables with an overflow flag if more than nine entries are stored. The design is tested by loading and reading data, and it preserves stored data when switching modes.

tt05of/tt_um_hh.summary: This design implements a Hodgkin-Huxley neuron model in silicon, which produces action potentials in response to input current injection. An 8-bit input current is applied, interpreted as a 16-bit fixed-point value in uA/cm^2, and the membrane potential is output on both dedicated and bidirectional pins. The neuron fires periodically when the current exceeds a threshold of approximately 12 (in the 8-bit representation). It is intended for exploring neuron dynamics and spiking behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_hh.review_notes: Removed 'spiking-neural-network' since the source describes a single neuron model rather than an SNN hardware block.

tt05of/tt_um_himanshu5_prog_chipTop.summary: This project contains two compute units that perform ALU operations based on input instructions, with the final output being the XOR of their outputs. The design is controlled by reset and enable signals, and it was tested on EDA Playground with a testbench. The only output pins are for a 7-segment display, suggesting the result is shown visually. The documentation is brief and does not specify the exact ALU operations or instruction format.
tt05of/tt_um_himanshu5_prog_chipTop.review_notes: Tags were already correct; no changes needed.

tt05of/tt_um_hls_lfi.summary: This design implements a simple leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that integrates an input current and produces a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold. It has inputs for clock, current, and reset, and outputs the next membrane potential and a spike signal. The documentation notes that a current input of 100 after 20 cycles should produce a spike. The design is minimal and intended for basic testing of neuron behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_hls_lfi.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'timer' tag; the source describes only LIF neuron behavior.

tt05of/tt_um_hodgkin_huxley.summary: This project is titled Hodgkin-Huxley Chip Design, but the documentation describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter driving a 7-segment display, with no mention of neuron behavior. The inputs set a 24-bit compare value that controls counting speed, and the bottom 8 bits of the counter are output on bidirectional pins. With all inputs zero the compare is 10,000,000, giving one increment per second at 10 MHz. The documentation does not match the title, so the actual neuron implementation is unclear.
tt05of/tt_um_hodgkin_huxley.review_notes: Title and documentation contradict each other; needs a second opinion on which is authoritative.

tt05of/tt_um_htfab_cell_tester.summary: This project includes a sky130-compatible standard cell generator, several demo cells, and a Tiny Tapeout design for testing them. The test design compares factory-provided cells with custom-generated cells (mux2i_2, maj3_2, dlrtp_1, dfrtp_1) using input pins for simple tests, and also supports advanced tests with a shift register, ring oscillator, and trigger pin. The documentation is sparse, with a 'TODO' for how it works, but the testing procedure is described in detail. The project is notable for combining cell generation with on-chip testing and includes cocotb tests.

tt05of/tt_um_if.summary: This project implements an integrate-and-fire neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current via the ui pins and produces a spike on uio[0] and the membrane potential on the uo pins. The neuron fires a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, without leakage or time-dependent dynamics. It is a simple demonstration intended for educational purposes, tested by applying different input currents and observing the firing rate.
tt05of/tt_um_if.review_notes: Removed analog as the design is digital Verilog; added education based on the 'Verilog Demo' title and demonstration nature.

tt05of/tt_um_ja1tye_sound_generator.summary: This is a four-channel wavetable and PSG-style sound generator with an I2S output and an SPI control interface. It supports eight selectable waveforms, 16-bit frequency control, 8-bit volume in PSG mode, and a 32-entry 4-bit wavetable, with a sampling rate of about 48.8 kHz from a 50 MHz clock. The design is controlled over SPI mode 0 with 24-bit transactions, and the I2S output is 16-bit mono. It requires an external I2S DAC such as a PCM5102A to produce audible sound.
tt05of/tt_um_ja1tye_sound_generator.review_notes: Removed music tag; sound generator is not a music composition design.

tt05of/tt_um_jaylennee_wta_pwm.summary: This design generates eight 12-bit PWM signals with a common trigger and can also accept eight external PWM inputs, selecting between internal and external sources via SPI configuration. A time-domain winner-take-all circuit detects the falling edges of the PWM signals to find the smallest duration and the k-smallest durations, latching the corresponding addresses. The design includes a time-to-digital converter that digitizes PWM durations, and results are read out over SPI. It requires external SPI control and optional external PWM sources.
tt05of/tt_um_jaylennee_wta_pwm.review_notes: Removed neuromorphic tag as the source does not describe neuromorphic processing; added comparator for the winner-take-all selection.

tt05of/tt_um_jeffdi_seven_segment_second.summary: This design counts down from 9 to 0 at one-second intervals and displays the current digit on a 7-segment display. The counting speed can be changed by driving the input pins with a compare value, which sets the clock divider; with all inputs low the compare is 10,000,000 for a 10 MHz clock. The lower 8 bits of the counter are also available on the bidirectional pins. It is a simple timer/display demonstration with no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display.
tt05of/tt_um_jeffdi_seven_segment_second.review_notes: Removed redundant verilog tag; summary unchanged.

tt05of/tt_um_jkprz.summary: This project implements a basic leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Verilog. An input current is injected via switches, added to a decaying membrane potential, and a spike is triggered when the potential exceeds a threshold. The membrane potential is exposed on the output pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin. The documentation is minimal and does not detail the STDP mechanism or testing beyond observing firing rate changes with input current.
tt05of/tt_um_jkprz.review_notes: Summary corrected to remove the unsupported STDP claim; tags unchanged.

tt05of/tt_um_jleugeri_ticktocktokens.summary: This design implements a processor that uses Tick Tock Tokens, where each token is represented by a start and end event, to perform event-based computation inspired by Time Petri Nets. It accepts a 4-bit instruction and 8-bit data on the inputs, and outputs data with token start/stop flags and a good/bad token flag. The documentation is thin and admits that the test script and explanation may be incomplete. An Arduino is suggested to generate the I/O signals for testing.
tt05of/tt_um_jleugeri_ticktocktokens.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; summary unchanged as it is supported.

tt05of/tt_um_jmadden173_delta_modulation.summary: This design implements delta modulation spike encoding for spiking neural networks, mimicking the snnTorch implementation. It generates a spike when the difference between the current and previous 4-bit data inputs exceeds a configurable threshold, with an option to emit negative spikes. The previous data register can be read and forced for debugging, and the design can be tested with an ADC or by manually changing the data input and observing spikes on an oscilloscope. All numerical inputs and outputs are unsigned 4-bit integers.

tt05of/tt_um_joerdsonsilva_top.summary: This multimode modem performs digital modulation and demodulation using amplitude-shift keying, frequency-shift keying, and phase-shift keying schemes. A 2-bit select input chooses the modulation type, and the modulated signal appears on a 7-bit output while the demodulated bit appears on a separate output. Silicon testing by a tester showed that ASK and FSK worked as documented, but PSK demodulation was stuck high and the output was a plain sine wave. An oscilloscope or signal analyzer is required to observe the analog-like outputs.

tt05of/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is an RV32IMA RISC-V SoC capable of booting and running uLinux, with UART, SPI, and LED interfaces. It requires flashing a bootloader, device tree, and Linux image onto an external NOR flash, and a 22 pF capacitor on the NOR flash clock line was needed for reliable operation. Silicon tests by the author and testers confirmed successful Linux boot at around 30.5 MHz. The design includes a divider register for configuring the CLINT and UART.
tt05of/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag to reflect the provided working silicon reports.

tt05of/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.summary: This design implements Karplus-Strong plucked-string synthesis based on published papers, with a register map accessed via SPI and audio samples output through an I2S transmitter. It includes pseudo-random binary sequence generators for noise and a 7-segment display output, and operates with a 256 kHz clock to produce a 16 kHz sample rate. The design is configured through SPI mode 0, CPHA=1, and the synthesized samples are sent continuously over I2S. It requires an external I2S DAC to hear the sound.
tt05of/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.review_notes: Removed 'lfsr' tag because the source specifies PRBS generators, not LFSR.
