tt05of/tt_um_kskyou.summary: This design computes continued fraction convergents of the square root of a 14-bit natural number entered via switches. Pressing one button advances to the next convergent pair P and Q, and another button cycles through the 16-bit P and Q values on the 8 status LEDs in four bytes. It is intended to be used alongside a phone calculator or paper to find fundamental solutions to Pell's equation x^2 - Dy^2 = 1. The design fits in roughly 1000 cells by avoiding comparisons and floor operations except on the first step, and it outputs binary rather than 7-segment values due to area constraints.
tt05of/tt_um_kskyou.review_notes: Removed divider and alu because the source describes a continued fraction calculator, not a divider or ALU circuit.

tt05of/tt_um_lif.summary: This project implements a current-based leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit slice of input current on the switches, integrates it into a membrane potential that leaks over time, and emits a spike when the potential crosses a threshold. The membrane potential is shown on the 8 output pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin, with a 7-segment display mentioned for spike detection in the test description. The documentation is thin and the test instructions refer to hardware not fully described in the pin list, so external setup details are unclear.
tt05of/tt_um_lif.review_notes: Added spiking-neural-network tag to match the LIF neuron implementation.

tt05of/tt_um_lif_n.summary: This design implements a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in 130 nm CMOS using Verilog. An input current is added to a membrane potential that decays by a factor beta, and a spike is triggered when the potential exceeds a threshold. The membrane potential is output on eight pins and the spike on a bidirectional pin. Testing involves resetting the circuit, varying the input current, and observing that higher current produces a higher spike rate; no external hardware beyond input switches and observation is described.

tt05of/tt_um_loopback.summary: This is a simple loopback test module where input 0 is mirrored to outputs 0 through 6, and output 7 is the logical AND of inputs 4 through 7. It is used to measure signal delay by toggling input 0 and timing the response on output 0. Silicon tests measured a 20 ns falling-edge delay and 24 ns rising-edge delay, and the design was shown to work up to 90 MHz during bringup, with degraded behavior past 100 MHz. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
tt05of/tt_um_loopback.review_notes: Removed gpio because the pins implement a fixed loopback/AND test structure, and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon test report.

tt05of/tt_um_loopback_ericsmi.summary: This project is a loopback tile with input skew measurement, described as counting up to 10 one second at a time. It has an 8-bit compare input, an 8-bit second counter on bidirectional pins, and 7-segment display outputs. The documentation is essentially empty, with 'Need to write this' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections, so the exact function cannot be determined from the provided text. External hardware mentioned is programmable delay lines on the inputs.
tt05of/tt_um_loopback_ericsmi.review_notes: Removed timer and instrumentation; added insufficient-doc because the documentation is empty.

tt05of/tt_um_mabhari_seven_segment_secon.summary: This is a two-digit seconds timer that counts from 00 to 99, with the target value loaded from 8 input switches as two BCD digits. A Load signal latches the target, and a Start signal begins counting at one second per tick from a 10 MHz clock. When the count reaches the target, the Time_Out output goes high, and the current ones or tens digit is displayed on a 7-segment display depending on a select input. Testing involves resetting, activating Load and Start, and observing the count and timeout.
tt05of/tt_um_mabhari_seven_segment_secon.review_notes: Tags and summary are fully supported by the source; no changes needed.

tt05of/tt_um_manjushettar.summary: This project emulates a two-layer neural network of integrate-and-fire neurons in Verilog. The first layer accepts two 16-bit stimulus inputs, and its spikes feed into a second layer whose two neurons produce the final spiking outputs. Testing involves applying different input stimuli and observing the spiking states of the output layer. The design uses a reset signal to clear neuron states, and the one-line description mentions counting up to 10 one second at a time.
tt05of/tt_um_manjushettar.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the summary's last sentence was adjusted to avoid asserting a class project not stated in the source.

tt05of/tt_um_matrix_multiplier.summary: This module multiplies two 2x2 matrices where each element is an unsigned 2-bit number, with inputs provided on 8-bit wires and outputs on uo_out and uio_out. It performs error checking to ensure each element is in the range [0,2], outputting zero if any element is out of range. The design includes a Verilog testbench and a cocotb Python test script that verify the multiplication against expected results. Testing can also be done on an FPGA or in simulation with waveform viewing.
tt05of/tt_um_matrix_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu and error-correction because the design is a matrix multiplier with range checking, not an ALU or error-correction block.

tt05of/tt_um_matt_divider_test.summary: This analog test project implements a resistive voltage divider using three resistors connected between power and ground, with output taps on three pins. It is tested by enabling the block and checking that only the highest tap output is high. Silicon results show the divider worked, and a large capacitor increased the falling-edge delay from 20 ns to 31 ns and the rising-edge delay from 24 ns to 51 ns. The design is a simple analog test structure with no digital logic.
tt05of/tt_um_matt_divider_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported factory-test and transistor-level tags; added silicon-tested.

tt05of/tt_um_mattngaw_fp8.summary: This design is an 8-bit floating-point adder following the FP8 E5M2 standard. It combinationally computes the sum of two 8-bit floating-point numbers provided on the input and bidirectional pins, with the result appearing on the output pins. Testing is done by holding two 8-bit inputs and reading the sum from the outputs. No external hardware is required beyond the chip's pins.
tt05of/tt_um_mattngaw_fp8.review_notes: Removed alu, which is not supported by the source's floating-point adder description.

tt05of/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario Bros. theme tune on a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs a differential sound wave on uo[0] and uo[1]. The design requires an external piezo speaker connected across those pins, and is tested by providing a 100 kHz clock and pulsing the reset pin. The project demonstrates a simple method for generating music from a hardware description language.
tt05of/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.review_notes: buzzer replaced with speaker since the source specifies a piezo speaker; added sound-generator for the ringtone playback.

tt05of/tt_um_mihailocode_neural_network.summary: This design implements a neural network on chip. The network calculates an output based on user-provided input and predefined weight parameters of the neural network. Drive inputs to [7:0] ui_in, and the result of the computation can be observed on [7:0] uo_out. The design is built out of perceptrons according to the author's description.
tt05of/tt_um_mihailocode_neural_network.review_notes: Added perceptron tag from the one-line description and removed accelerator, which was not supported by the source.

tt05of/tt_um_mingkaic1_stack_machine.summary: This design is an 8-bit stack machine written in SystemVerilog. It is documented with only a one-line description and has no detailed instruction set documentation. A single bidirectional pin is described as carrying data. The design can be tested in hardware or with simulation.
tt05of/tt_um_mingkaic1_stack_machine.review_notes: Documentation is very thin; added insufficient-doc tag.

tt05of/tt_um_minipit_stevej.summary: This design includes timer, interrupt-controller, counter, and clock-divider functionality. It is a timer and counter design with interrupt support. The documentation does not provide silicon test results.

tt05of/tt_um_morningjava_top.summary: This design is an 8-bit Programmable Sound Generator that replicates the audio processing unit of vintage video games. It takes input from a serial UART interface and outputs PWM audio. An analog PWM filter and audio driver are needed for the test rig. It generates square, triangle, and noise sound channels.
tt05of/tt_um_morningjava_top.review_notes: Added uart, chiptune and retro tags supported by the source; summary expanded to four supported sentences.

tt05of/tt_um_multiplexed_clock.summary: This design is a multiplexed digital clock that counts hours in 24-hour format and minutes, with dots indicating 15/30/45/60 seconds. It drives a 4-digit 7-segment display via multiplexing, using uo_out for segments and uio_out[3:0] for digit selection. Two pull-up button inputs increase hours or minutes, and inputs configure anode/cathode and output negation. It has been partially tested on silicon.
tt05of/tt_um_multiplexed_clock.review_notes: Removed inaccurate clock-generator/rtc tags; added display and silicon-tested (partial status).

tt05of/tt_um_muncherkin_lioncage.summary: This design is a counter with FSM and sensor interface. It drives a 7-segment display and includes an up-down counter. The documentation explains the state machine logic but does not include silicon test results.

tt05of/tt_um_mv_mult_alrdelcr.summary: This design multiplies an input vector by a matrix. The first input switch initializes a matrix multiplication between the current vector and the matrix, and the second bit sets matrix values line by line. A counter increases by one every second with a 10 MHz input clock, and outputs drive a seven-segment display. The documentation notes there is no current functionality to know which row of the matrix is set.
tt05of/tt_um_mv_mult_alrdelcr.review_notes: Removed unsupported machine-learning and accelerator tags; added counter, 7-segment, display, verilog and incomplete, and corrected summary to match the matrix-vector multiplication description.

tt05of/tt_um_mvm.summary: This design divides a 10MHz clock and increments a counter once per second when the internal compare value is set to 10,000,000. The bottom eight bits of the counter are exposed on the bidirectional outputs. Combinational logic converts the binary counter value to decimal for a seven-segment display. The compare value can be partially programmed through the input pins to change the counting speed.
tt05of/tt_um_mvm.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the timer/counter and seven-segment display design.

tt05of/tt_um_mvm_.summary: This design is a matrix-vector multiplication accelerator that takes a 3x3 weight matrix in Compressed Sparse Row format and a 3-bit spike train. It loads the sparse matrix and spike train into internal registers using handshake flags. An algorithm computes the resultant vector of the matrix-vector multiplication. The output vector is transmitted on the output line with a flag bit that flips for each new value.
tt05of/tt_um_mvm_.review_notes: Removed incorrect music/interface tags and added accelerator, verilog, and pipeline tags.

tt05of/tt_um_myuart.summary: This design implements a small UART transmitter that repeatedly sends a fixed string (the author's name) at 115200 baud with one start bit, eight data bits, one parity bit and one stop bit. It also generates a sinus signal on the remaining seven output pins. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and no inputs; testing only needs a UART receiver connected to uo_out[0]. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the behavior and pin usage.

tt05of/tt_um_nickjhay_processor.summary: This project implements a 1-bit 8x8 matrix multiply using a systolic array, with eight data input pins and eight output pins for the result. A bidirectional pin selects between OR and XOR accumulation, and another bidirectional pin outputs a greeting. The documentation consists only of placeholder text ('Explain how your project works' and 'Explain how to test your project'), so the exact interface and operation cannot be verified beyond the pin names and title. The design is notable for targeting matrix multiplication in a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
tt05of/tt_um_nickjhay_processor.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; added incomplete and insufficient-doc due to placeholder documentation.

tt05of/tt_um_njzhu_uart.summary: This SystemVerilog design implements a UART transceiver with both transmit and receive functions at 9600 baud, using oversampling to sample the middle of each bit period. The receiver waits for a start bit, samples eight data bits and a stop bit, and asserts a data-ready signal; the transmitter sends a byte with correct timing when a data-ready input is set. The eight output pins double as 7-segment display segments and as the UART transmit data output, while bidirectional pins carry received data and a finished-read flag. Testing requires setting the data bits and data-ready input and observing the transmitted sequence on the tx output.
tt05of/tt_um_njzhu_uart.review_notes: Added rs232 as the canonical serial-interface tag for the UART link; no incorrect tags were present.

tt05of/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommyth.summary: This design displays a 12-hour analog clock rendered with triangles using a race-the-beam technique on a 640x480 VGA output. It requires an external Tiny VGA interface and a 31.5 MHz clock, and accepts buttons to advance the hour and minute hands. The triangle coordinates are stored in a table and the rendering equations are recalculated during the vertical blanking interval by a small state machine. Debug pins allow inspection of internal variables, and a software model in Rust is provided for understanding.
tt05of/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommyth.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and game tags as they are not supported; added vga, video, graphics, and retro tags based on pins and description.

tt05of/tt_um_openframe_mask_rev.summary: This project displays the Caravel mask revision on a 7-segment display and outputs the lower 8 bits on bidirectional pins. It uses the ui pins as an index to cycle through the mask revision number in hexadecimal, LSB-first. The design is intended for identification purposes, requiring no external hardware beyond the display. It is a simple utility block for the Openframe/Caravel platform.
tt05of/tt_um_openframe_mask_rev.review_notes: Removed factory-test tag; added verilog tag supported by the language fact.

tt05of/tt_um_perceptron.summary: This design is described as a hardcoded perceptron, but the documentation actually describes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal counter that increments once per second with a 10 MHz clock. The eight output pins carry the perceptron output, while the inputs can be used to program a 24-bit compare register to change the counting speed. The documentation is inconsistent with the title, and the perceptron behavior is not explained. Testing involves observing the counter increment and changing the input bits to alter the rate.
tt05of/tt_um_perceptron.review_notes: Title and documentation contradict each other; escalated for a second opinion while removing the unsupported perceptron tag.

tt05of/tt_um_perceptron_connorguzi.summary: This project implements a perceptron and a basic binary neural network that take a 7-bit input representing the number of curves and edges of a digit and output the expected number. The eight output pins drive a 7-segment display plus a dot, and the bidirectional pins expose a second counter. The documentation is largely copied from a counter project and does not explain the neural network operation or how to test it meaningfully. The design appears to be a class project, but the documentation is insufficient to verify its intended behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_perceptron_connorguzi.review_notes: Removed counter tag tied to copied demo text; added machine-learning and insufficient-doc.

tt05of/tt_um_perceptron_neuromeme.summary: This design implements a perceptron that reads two 8-bit inputs and computes a weighted sum with fixed 8-bit weights, classifying the result as 1 if it exceeds a threshold of 11111110 and 0 otherwise. The documentation explains the math with examples, such as any input with two or more 1s being classified as 1, and credits a UCSC professor. It is intended as a simple 9+10 adder or perceptron demonstration, and testing involves applying inputs and observing the 8-bit output. The design is notable for being an educational neuromorphic example with clear documentation.
tt05of/tt_um_perceptron_neuromeme.review_notes: Removed unsupported neural-network, mac-unit, and education tags; kept perceptron and verilog.

tt05of/tt_um_prg.summary: This design implements a Boolean function based pseudo random number generator using finite field arithmetic, with linear mappings, GF(2^4) multipliers, an inverter, and a square scaler. It takes five input bytes as seeds and produces three output shares, using masking with fresh randomness to prevent leakage. The documentation provides a detailed mathematical description of the three phases and a worked example, and testing involves loading input shares, toggling the enable signal, and reading the output ready flag and shares. The design is notable for its cryptographic masking approach and is implemented in a 1x2 tile configuration.
tt05of/tt_um_prg.review_notes: Removed the unsupported cipher tag; the design is a masked PRNG, not an encryption cipher, and the rest of the tags and summary are consistent with the source.

tt05of/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.summary: This project implements a bytebeat formula in hardware using the XLS toolkit, generating 8-bit PCM samples from four 4-bit parameters according to the formula ((t*a)&(t>>b))|((t*c)&(t>>d)). It requires an 8-bit PCM DAC and rotary encoders to tweak the parameter pins, and the design can be modified by editing the formula and regenerating the Verilog. A silicon test report from the author confirms it worked as expected after configuring the bidirectional mode correctly. The design is notable for being generated from a high-level synthesis tool and for bringing algorithmic music synthesis to Tiny Tapeout.
tt05of/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.review_notes: Removed verilog because the source language is XLS; added dac and silicon-tested based on the documented external DAC and working silicon report.

tt05of/tt_um_psychogenic_neptuneproporti.summary: This design is a guitar tuner that counts rising edges of an input pulse over a fixed sampling period and compares the count to frequencies of interest for standard guitar tuning, covering notes from about 80 to 400 Hz. It supports multiple clock configurations via three input bits and can drive either a dual or single 7-segment display, with the dot indicating an exact match in single mode. The raw pulse count is output on the bidirectional pins, and testing requires feeding a variable frequency signal and observing the closest note on the display. A silicon test report confirms it works, showing the closest note for a variable frequency input.

tt05of/tt_um_psychogenic_shaman.summary: This design implements a SHA-256 hasher that generates a digest for data of arbitrary length. Data is fed in 64-byte blocks through an 8-bit input port, with control signals for starting, clocking data, and reading the 32-byte result. It requires an external microcontroller to provide data and read results, and supports a parallel mode for interleaving input and processing. The implementation is naive and unoptimized, with estimated throughput of about 6 MB/s at 50 MHz, and a silicon test report indicates it worked in one test run but not a second.
tt05of/tt_um_psychogenic_shaman.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'pipeline'; added 'silicon-tested' to match the working silicon report.

tt05of/tt_um_rebel2_balanced_ternary_ALU.summary: This is a 2-trit balanced ternary ALU that is part of the REBEL-2 balanced ternary logic CPU. It supports operations such as MIN, MAX, ADD, SUB, MUL, CMP, and SHFT, which can be performed trit-wise or word-wise. The design is generated and verified using the Mixed Radix Circuit Synthesizer (MRCS), and while automated tests exist for MRCS, a Verilog testbench and FPGA constraint file are still work in progress. The documentation is limited and the project appears to be a work in progress.
tt05of/tt_um_rebel2_balanced_ternary_ALU.review_notes: Removed cpu tag: the project is an ALU component, not a processor core; 'ternary' is not in the canonical vocabulary.

tt05of/tt_um_reflex_game.summary: This project is titled Reflex Game and is intended to be a reflex-based game using a 7-segment display. However, the documentation states that it does not work and suggests making a testbench. There is no description of how the game operates or how it is tested. The design is essentially undocumented and non-functional.

tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a classic 3-voice chip used in 8-bit computers and consoles. It features three square wave tone generators, a noise generator, and an envelope generator, and is controlled via a multiplexed data/address bus. It provides both PWM and digital 8-bit audio outputs, and requires external hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker to be heard. The design is well-documented with a test suite and aims for hardware preservation and education.

tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_rule110.summary: This design implements a parallel cellular automaton based on Rule 110, capable of running over 200 cells in parallel each clock cycle. It provides a read/write bus to inspect and modify cell states, with addresses for blocks of 8 cells. The automaton can be halted and resumed, and is intended for exploring complex behavior, pseudo-random number generation, and computation. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout interface.
tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_rule110.review_notes: Removed prng and esoteric as they are not primary functions; added cellular-automaton and memory based on the design's features.

tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This project is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, a classic chip used in many 8-bit systems. It includes three square wave tone generators and a noise generator with programmable attenuation, and is controlled via an 8-bit data bus. It outputs both PWM and digital audio, and requires external hardware such as a DAC or low-pass filter and speaker for playback. The design is parameterized to match various SN76489 family variants and includes a comprehensive test suite.
tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.review_notes: Removed pwm tag as it is not the primary output; added music, sound-generator, audio, chiptune, lfsr, and verilog tags supported by the source.

tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_snn.summary: This design implements a 3-layer spiking neural network with on-chip weights. It accepts an 8-bit input bus and control signals for execution and synchronization, and outputs the states of 8 neurons from the last layer. The documentation is minimal, with only a brief description and a truncated test instruction. It likely requires a host to provide inputs and control signals for operation.
tt05of/tt_um_rejunity_snn.review_notes: Removed machine-learning because no learning or inference application is documented, and added insufficient-doc to reflect the very thin documentation.

tt05of/tt_um_retospect_neurochip.summary: This design is a Field Programmable Neural Array (FPNA) consisting of 50 interconnected configurable neuron blocks (CNBs) that simulate leaky neurons. Each CNB has four inputs with 3-bit weights, a configurable decay rate, and fires when its membrane potential reaches a threshold, sending pulses to neighboring neurons. Configuration is done via a bitstream shifted in through dedicated pins, and the network can be trained using the accompanying naxon tool. The design is intended for neuromorphic computing research and requires external clocking and configuration data to operate.

tt05of/tt_um_rgb_mixer.summary: This design uses three rotary encoders to control three PWM generators. It includes debouncing for the encoder inputs and provides debug outputs for the encoder values and debounce signals. The encoders are connected to the first six input pins, and the PWM outputs appear on the first three output pins. A silicon test report from the author confirms all three channels work up to 50 MHz.
tt05of/tt_um_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed rgb-led (not stated in source) and added silicon-tested (author report confirms working silicon).

tt05of/tt_um_rjmorgan11_calculator_chip.summary: This is a basic calculator chip that implements an 8-bit ALU with operations including add, subtract, bitwise logic, shifts, and comparisons. It uses input pins for the number and operation selection, an enter pin to latch commands, and output pins for the result and flags (overflow, negative, zero). The design is controlled by a clock and reset, and is intended to be tested by entering numbers and operations. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand its function.

tt05of/tt_um_rnn.summary: This design implements a recurrent neural network hidden-state update in which an 8-bit input current is multiplied by an 8x8 weight matrix. The hidden state is reset to zero, and the user changes the input current to observe the resulting output current. The pin names and documentation are largely inherited from the 7-segment demo template, so the actual RNN behavior is only briefly described. It is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete neural network system.
tt05of/tt_um_rnn.review_notes: Removed template tag as the design is a functional RNN demo, not a starter template.

tt05of/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.summary: This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer and reports the orbit length and the upper 16 bits of the highest value reached. Input bytes are uploaded one at a time into a 144-bit register, and results are read back through an address and select interface. A start pin triggers computation and a busy indicator signals completion. Silicon testing confirmed that the project test cases and additional cases worked as expected.
tt05of/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.review_notes: Removed 'memory' and 'fsm' as incidental rather than defining design features.

tt05of/tt_um_sap_1.summary: This is an implementation of the SAP-1 simple-as-possible computer architecture, containing a program counter, registers, adder, memory, instruction register, bus, and controller. It has no external inputs and runs autonomously from the clock, performing only addition and subtraction on 8-bit values. The bus output can currently only be observed with an oscilloscope, and the author suggests adding a 7-segment display controller as an enhancement. The design is based on the well-known Malvino and Brown architecture popularized by Ben Eater.
tt05of/tt_um_sap_1.review_notes: Removed instrumentation because the oscilloscope is only a suggested observation method, not the design purpose.

tt05of/tt_um_seanvenadas.summary: This design accepts an 8-bit event signal with x, y, p, and t parameters and outputs the signal only when the p bit is high, filtering it to reduce noise. It also includes a clock divider and binary-to-decimal logic driving a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits exposed on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare value that sets the counting rate. The documentation describes the counter behavior in detail but gives only a brief description of the denoising function.
tt05of/tt_um_seanvenadas.review_notes: Removed neuromorphic and image-processing tags not supported by source.

tt05of/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This design counts seconds and displays the value on a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits also available on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare register so the counting rate can be changed from the default one-second interval. It is a standard Tiny Tapeout Verilog demo intended to show clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. The documentation is complete and describes both the default and programmable counting behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and template tags; source describes a counter/timer demo, not a clock generator or template.

tt05of/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds_ksand.summary: This project is intended to implement a random dropout circuit inspired by the dropout mechanism used to prevent overfitting in neural networks. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test both state only that they are not written yet. The pin names are inherited from the 7-segment counter demo template and do not reflect the described dropout function. There is not enough information to determine the actual implementation or how to use it.
tt05of/tt_um_seven_segment_seconds_ksand.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and prng tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt05of/tt_um_stdp.summary: This design implements two leaky integrate-and-fire neurons and a spike-timing dependent plasticity module that updates a synaptic weight based on the timing difference between pre- and post-synaptic spikes. A drive current is applied to the neuron and integrated every clock cycle, with the LIF spike, LIF state, and synaptic weight brought out as outputs. The documentation describes the learning rule and testing procedure at a high level. It is a compact hardware demonstration of a biologically inspired learning mechanism.

tt05of/tt_um_suhrojo.summary: This project is described as a silicon chip design of a convolutional neural network, but the how-it-works section only says the explanation will be added later. The how-to-test section is copied from the 7-segment counter demo and does not describe CNN testing. The pin names are also inherited from that demo template and do not indicate CNN-specific interfaces. There is essentially no usable documentation for the actual design.
tt05of/tt_um_suhrojo.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and image-processing tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt05of/tt_um_sunaofurukawa_cpu_8bit.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU design whose Verilog code was generated by Bing AI. The input pins carry instruction register bits and formula right-side bits, while the outputs drive a 7-segment display. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are still placeholders, so the instruction set and operation are not described. The design cannot be fully evaluated from the available information.

tt05of/tt_um_supertails_tetris.summary: This design implements the game Tetris in hardware, using VGA outputs for video and buttons for moving and rotating pieces. It requires an external memory connected over the bidirectional pins, which the author implemented on an RP2040 based on existing Teensy code. Silicon testing reported that the design works great. The documentation sections for how it works and how to test are otherwise placeholders.
tt05of/tt_um_supertails_tetris.review_notes: Removed memory/display tags not supported by the design; added button, rp2040 and retro.

tt05of/tt_um_synth_GyanepsaaS.summary: This design is a basic sound synthesizer that generates a waveform and shapes it with an ADSR envelope. The waveform is selected between triangle and sawtooth, and the note frequency is chosen with four input bits while a separate clock sets the sampling rate. The envelope attack, decay, sustain and release stages are configured through the bidirectional pins, and the resulting sound is emitted on one output pin. Documentation is very thin, consisting only of a one-line description and a short test note, so the exact envelope resolution and output encoding are not specified.
tt05of/tt_um_synth_GyanepsaaS.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm tag; added synthesizer, audio, music, oscillator, waveform-generator, and verilog based on source evidence.

tt05of/tt_um_thermocouple.summary: This block converts digitized thermocouple ADC counts into a temperature value using piecewise linear approximation and interpolation. It communicates over a 16-bit SPI interface, supports type-J and type-K thermocouples, and can optionally pass the SPI master straight through to the ADC for configuration. The output is a 16-bit centi-Celsius value pre-divided by four, giving 0.4 C granularity, and the thermocouple type and passthrough mode are set through configuration writes. It requires an external thermocouple analog front-end with compatible ranging, and the documentation gives worked numeric examples for the transfer function.

tt05of/tt_um_tiny_game_of_life.summary: This design simulates Conway's Game of Life on an 8x8 grid using two shift registers, one holding the current state and one holding the updated state. The user loads cells one at a time in row-major order through a single input pin, then asserts a start pin to begin the simulation, after which the circuit alternates between updating and outputting indefinitely. During output, one pin carries the cell value and seven pins carry the cell index from 1 to 64, so an external display or host must reconstruct the grid. The documentation is detailed about the protocol but notes that the design should simply be prayed over, and no silicon test results are given.
tt05of/tt_um_tiny_game_of_life.review_notes: Removed 'game' as the design is a cellular automaton simulation rather than an interactive game.

tt05of/tt_um_tkmheart.summary: This design applies threshold-based filtering to an input data stream and then performs peak detection over three consecutive clock cycles. A clock divider halves the input clock, and a counter driven by that clock is exposed on the bidirectional pins while the compare threshold is loaded in two four-bit halves through the input pins. The outputs drive a seven-segment display with a decimal point, presumably to show the counter or detected peaks. The documentation describes the loading sequence but does not explain the intended signal source or what the display actually shows, and no silicon results are provided.
tt05of/tt_um_tkmheart.review_notes: Removed timer and biomedical; added comparator and edge-detector to match the documented threshold/peak logic.

tt05of/tt_um_toivoh_synth.summary: This project implements an analog emulation monosynth with two oscillators and a second-order filter. It is controlled by writing to configuration registers via an 8-bit data bus and a 4-bit address bus, and provides both PWM and 8-bit digital audio outputs. The PWM output requires external filtering, and caution is advised when connecting to audio equipment. The documentation is incomplete, with register descriptions and oscillator/filter details marked as TODO.
tt05of/tt_um_toivoh_synth.review_notes: Removed dac because the 8-bit output is a digital sample bus for an external resistor ladder, not an on-chip DAC.

tt05of/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This design implements a simple VGA pong-style game with paddles controlled by four input pins. It outputs VGA signals on the bidirectional and output pins and supports two different VGA PMOD pinouts selected by an input, with the recommended Tiny VGA pinout. The game has no scoring and the ball only moves horizontally, so it is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete game. Silicon tests report that pong works, though one tester had to adjust monitor centering and another could not get a proper display on a CRT.
tt05of/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported gamepad tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

tt05of/tt_um_topLevel_derekabarca.summary: This design connects two neuron modules through a synapse module to produce rhythmic oscillations, according to its one-line description. The pin names match those of a threshold comparator and counter design, with compare bits on the inputs, a second counter on the bidirectional pins and seven-segment display segments on the outputs. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections are both literally marked as to be filled in later, so no usable description of the internal behaviour or test procedure exists. The design is effectively undocumented beyond its title and pin list.
tt05of/tt_um_topLevel_derekabarca.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network, neural-network, oscillator, counter and 7-segment tags not supported by the thin documentation; added neuromorphic, verilog and insufficient-doc.

tt05of/tt_um_topModuleKA.summary: This design implements leaky-integrate-and-fire neurons and time-multiplexes them to realize multiple neurons from shared hardware. An input current is applied through the input pins, accumulates in a membrane potential that decays over time, and triggers a spike when the potential crosses a threshold. The membrane potential is exposed on the eight output pins and spike outputs appear on the bidirectional pins, so a higher input current should produce a higher firing rate. The documentation is brief and does not specify the number of neurons, the time-multiplexing scheme, or any silicon test results.

tt05of/tt_um_top_mole99.summary: This design produces an 800x600 60 Hz SVGA output with a background and a single 12x12 sprite, rendered internally at 100x75 so each sprite pixel is 8x8 screen pixels. The sprite is initialized with a pixelated Tiny Tapeout logo that moves around the screen, and an SPI receiver accepts commands to replace sprite data, change colors, set the background and control the sprite position. It can run at either a 40 MHz or 10 MHz pixel clock selected by a configuration bit, and it needs an external Tiny VGA PMOD for display. Silicon tests report that the logo bounces around and the SPI interface works, with some glitching when moving the sprite.
tt05of/tt_um_top_mole99.review_notes: Removed vga (SVGA over Pmod, not VGA) and added silicon-tested and pmod based on pins and test reports.

tt05of/tt_um_tt05_analog_test.summary: This analog test macro contains a roughly 500 kHz ring oscillator producing a square wave and a 3-bit R-2R DAC producing a programmable DC voltage, with transmission gates to route or short the two outputs. The blocks are enabled and routed to the two analog output pins through digital control inputs, and the DAC voltage is set by three input bits. It was placed and routed with an experimental automatic analog place-and-route tool, making it a test of the analog flow rather than a functional product. Silicon tests report that the DAC works accurately with about 8 mV to 1.57 V output range and roughly 400 ns rise and fall times, while the ring oscillator measured around 400-409 kHz, about 100 kHz slower than intended.

tt05of/tt_um_ttl74hc595_v2.summary: This project implements a 74HC595 8-bit shift register with output latches in Verilog. It accepts serial data, shift clock, latch clock, output enable and clear signals, and drives eight parallel outputs. The design is intended to be tested by connecting eight LEDs, such as a Pmod, and bit-banging data to create effects like a Knight Rider pattern. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with the author using C and MicroPython to drive the LEDs.
tt05of/tt_um_ttl74hc595_v2.review_notes: Removed register-file (incorrect for a shift register) and added silicon-tested (author report confirms working silicon).

tt05of/tt_um_uabc_electronica_2023.summary: This design displays the text 'UABC-ELECTRONICA' on a 7-segment display by showing each letter sequentially. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary counts to decimal for the display, with the lower 8 bits of the counter available on bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted via input pins that set a comparison value, defaulting to one second per increment with a 10 MHz clock. It is intended as a demonstration or educational project, and no silicon test results are provided.
tt05of/tt_um_uabc_electronica_2023.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and education tags not supported by source.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_dffram.summary: This project implements a 128-byte RAM module using a 32x32 1RW DFFRAM macro. It provides address, write-enable, input, and output pins for reading and writing data. The design is implemented in Verilog and spans a 4x2 tile area. Silicon test reports indicate that writes and reads work, with some timing quirks noted by testers.
tt05of/tt_um_urish_dffram.review_notes: Replaced incorrect oscillator/counter tags with memory, sram, silicon-tested, and multi-tile based on the DFFRAM source and silicon reports.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_ringosc_cnt.summary: This is a test module for the TT05 power switching FET, featuring a ring oscillator and a 64-bit counter that counts oscillations. The counter value can be shifted and read on outputs, with reset and stop controls. It is tested by setting the shift value and observing the counter outputs. Silicon measurements indicated the ring oscillator runs at approximately 504 MHz, as inferred from a 1.969 MHz signal on the 8th counter bit.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_silife.summary: This design is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x8 grid. The grid can be loaded row by row using row select, cell input and write enable signals, and the game advances one step per clock cycle when enabled. The current state of any row can be read via the cell output pins. It is a compact, interactive implementation of the classic cellular automaton, with no external hardware required beyond the chip's pins.
tt05of/tt_um_urish_silife.review_notes: Removed fsm because the design is a cellular automaton grid, not a finite state machine.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_silife_max.summary: This project is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x32 grid, with optional output to a MAX7219 LED dot matrix. It supports both manual mode, where the grid is loaded row by row, and a demo mode that cycles through pre-defined patterns. The game advances one generation per clock cycle when enabled, or every 0.4 seconds in demo mode with a 10 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it works well with the LED matrix, though a delay before animation starts was noted, and one tester reported issues with demo patterns progressing.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a hardware implementation of the Simon Says memory game. The game uses four buttons and four LEDs to display a growing sequence of colors, each with a corresponding tone played on a speaker. It also supports a two-digit 7-segment display for showing the score. The design requires an external 50 kHz clock and is documented with wiring instructions, including a Wokwi online simulation for reference.
tt05of/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed wokwi because the source only links an online simulation, not creation in Wokwi; added puzzle and display tags.

tt05of/tt_um_urish_skullfet.summary: This project contains hand-crafted, skull-shaped MOSFET transistors implemented in a custom description language. It includes three devices: a NOT gate, a NAND gate, and an SR flip-flop, with inputs and outputs exposed on the chip pins. Testing involves applying input values and observing the outputs, and pulsing set/reset for the flip-flop. Silicon tests confirmed that the inverter and NAND work perfectly, and the flip-flop outputs are inverted as noted by the author.
tt05of/tt_um_urish_skullfet.review_notes: Added silicon-tested (both tester and author reports confirm working silicon).

tt05of/tt_um_uwuifier.summary: This design operates on a UART signal and transforms the text into 'uwu' speak. It interfaces via UART at 115200 baud with a 6 MHz clock, using dedicated receive and transmit pins. It is intended to be connected inline with a UART transceiver to modify data in real time. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester using a serial terminal to send data and receiving the uwuified version back.
tt05of/tt_um_uwuifier.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

tt05of/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This design shows the time on a VGA screen using a 31.5 MHz clock, with pins for hsync, vsync, and 6-bit color output (two bits per RGB channel). It uses a pre-generated font loaded into registers and 'races the beam' to generate the display. External hardware includes an R2R DAC to convert the digital color outputs to analog VGA signals and a VGA monitor. The design supports adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds via input pins.
tt05of/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (misleading; it is a time display) and added rtc.

tt05of/tt_um_vhdl_seven_segment_seconds.summary: This VHDL demo counts from 0 to 9 on a 7-segment display, incrementing once per second with a 10 MHz clock. It uses a clock divider and combinational logic to convert binary to decimal, and the lower 8 bits of the counter are available on bidirectional pins. The counting speed can be adjusted by setting input pins that program a comparison value. Silicon testing confirmed it counts from 0 to 9 once per second.
tt05of/tt_um_vhdl_seven_segment_seconds.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and education tags; added vhdl and silicon-tested.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_376553022662786049.summary: This project implements several test clusters featuring various spike trains for neuro-inspired computing research. It includes neuron clusters of different sizes, an LFSR, flip-flops, and a multiplexer, with inputs and outputs exposed on the chip pins. The design is tested by providing input clock frequencies to the neuron clusters and observing outputs via an oscilloscope to generate raster spiking plots. It is implemented in Wokwi and is intended for investigating spike-based information representation, with no silicon test results provided.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_377426511818305537.summary: This design is a configurable pseudo-random binary sequence generator built around a Galois LFSR with XOR taps, supporting polynomial sizes up to 16 bits. It is configured over an SPI mode 0 interface with four registers controlling command/address, clock divider, polynomial enable bits, and tap selection. Outputs include differential PRBS and look-ahead versions of the next bit, and a fail-safe all-zeros check prevents lock-up. It requires an external SPI controller, a clock input, and a logic analyzer to observe the generated sequence.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_377426511818305537.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file tag and added canonical tags for the documented PRBS/LFSR, SPI, clock divider, and Wokwi implementation.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_378231665807713281.summary: This project is a simple test of a memory cell, with inputs for data and address selection and a write/read control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a brief description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of how the cell operates or how to test it. No external hardware is required. Due to the lack of documentation, the exact functionality and testing procedure are unclear.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_378231665807713281.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc tag as the documentation, while minimal, adequately describes the design's purpose and interface.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379319062779062273.summary: This project implements a binary counter that drives a 7-segment display, incrementing with each clock cycle. The design is described only as a binary counter connected to the clock, with separate outputs for each segment and the decimal point. The documentation is very sparse and explicitly leaves the test instructions as a placeholder with no external hardware details. Beyond the basic counter and display function, no further specifics are available.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379319062779062273.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; kept the rest as supported.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379764885531576321.summary: This project uses a linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) to implement a counter that displays its value on a 7-segment display. It includes a synchronous reset input and increments the count on each positive clock edge. Silicon testing confirmed that it counts up, repeating from 0 to 9. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond the display.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379764885531576321.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; 7-segment already captures the output.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379824923824476161.summary: This project implements an analog clock controller that drives LEDs to represent the time, with a 1 Hz internal clock input. It includes counters for seconds, minutes, and hours, and outputs to 16 LEDs that indicate the hour and the last 15-minute increment. Input pins allow stopping the clock and manually incrementing the minute or hour counters. The design requires 16 external LEDs for display and is intended to simulate an analog clock face.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379824923824476161.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and decoder (unsupported); added rtc and led.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379889284755158017.summary: This project controls a 7-segment display to show the author's initials and a date (10/28). The documentation is essentially a template with no explanation of how the circuit works or how to test it. The only provided information is the pin mapping for the segments and decimal point. It appears to be a static display project, but no further details are available.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_379889284755158017.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added text since the display shows characters.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380005495431181313.summary: This project is a water pump controller designed for camping vans, with inputs for multiple tap switches, a high-pressure switch, and a timer enable. It includes a timer that warns via a buzzer when water runs too long and automatically shuts off the pump after a timeout, with configurable settings. The controller outputs signals for the pump, status LEDs, and buzzer, and can be tested with LEDs or a 7-segment display and DIP switches. It requires a 32.768 kHz clock and external hardware such as tap switches and a pump for full operation.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380005495431181313.review_notes: Removed industrial, sensor-interface, and fsm tags not supported by source.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380055891603379201.summary: This project implements a hexadecimal countdown from F to 0 on a 7-segment display, controlled by a state machine that decrements on each clock pulse. An activation signal starts the countdown, and a reset returns the display to F. Silicon testing confirmed that it works as described, counting down when the activation input is high. It requires a 1 Hz clock signal and no additional external hardware.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380055891603379201.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; 7-segment already captures the output.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380119282165535745.summary: This project is a simple counter that displays a digit on a 7-segment display, counting from 0 to 9 and wrapping around, with one step per clock cycle. It uses SR flip-flops to avoid combinational logic in the clock path, which previously caused glitches. Testing involves pressing reset and then clocking to advance the count. No external hardware is required beyond the display.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380119282165535745.review_notes: Removed redundant 'display' tag; 7-segment already covers the output.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380120751165092865.summary: This project drives a WS2812B LED strip with random colors that update periodically. It uses a 16-bit linear-feedback shift register to generate pseudo-random bits, a 5-bit counter to create the 1.25 µs pulses required by the WS2812B protocol, and a 16-bit ripple counter to control the refresh rate. The design requires a 20 MHz clock and a WS2812B LED strip connected to the output, with optional feedback from the strip's data output. Testing involves setting the clock, connecting the strip, and observing random colors with adjustable refresh frequency.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380120751165092865.review_notes: Removed signal-generator tag; design is a WS2812B driver, not a general signal generator.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380145600224164865.summary: This design converts a 4-bit binary input into a 7-segment display pattern using a simple combinational circuit of OR and AND gates. It is tested by setting the first four switches to a binary value from 0 to 15 and observing the display. No external hardware beyond the switches and a 7-segment display is required. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation for digits 0 through 9, but values 10 to 15 do not display, which the testers note may be intentional but would be nicer as hexadecimal.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380145600224164865.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd and education tags; added silicon-tested per the working test report.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380197591775930369.summary: This project blinks the letter A on a 7-segment display, with each output pin driving one segment plus the decimal point. The documentation consists only of placeholder text, so the internal logic and intended test procedure are not described. It needs only a 7-segment display connected to the eight outputs. A silicon test report confirms that it did blink an A, but the lack of documentation makes the design's details unclear.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380229599886002177.summary: This design generates pseudo-random bit streams whose probability of a one equals the product of two 2-bit input vectors, implementing stochastic multiplication based on a published PN-sequence method. It is used by setting inputs A and B, applying a clock, and toggling reset low to start the PRBS generators, with outputs providing the product stream and individual operand streams. No external hardware is strictly required, and some outputs are also mapped to 7-segment segments. The documentation is brief and cites the underlying paper, but does not describe the internal implementation or provide silicon test results.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380229599886002177.review_notes: Removed lfsr as unstated and dsp as unsupported application framing; the add list must stay canonical.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380361576213660673.summary: This is a hardware implementation of two-player ping pong rendered on a 16x24 LED matrix, using up/down counters for each paddle and the ball plus an input register to debounce buttons. It requires substantial external hardware: a 16-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register, a 5-to-24 decoder, the LED matrix, eight buttons, BCD counters with 7-segment displays for scoring, and a timing unit to generate the enable and clock signals. Testing can start simply by hooking up left/right buttons for player one and monitoring the horizontal position bits, but full functionality needs the complete external support circuitry. The design is notable for its detailed pin-level documentation and its reliance on external multiplexing and decoding to drive the matrix.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380361576213660673.review_notes: Added button and 7-segment interface tags supported by the pin descriptions; removed redundant display tag.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408396356749313.summary: This project is a simple ring oscillator that outputs a square wave on pins 0 through 3, with the pins phase shifted relative to one another. It is tested simply by applying power, with no other control inputs described. No external hardware is needed beyond observing the outputs. The documentation is very thin and does not specify the oscillation frequency or the exact phase relationship, so those details cannot be confirmed.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408396356749313.review_notes: Removed unsupported analog tag, added silicon-tested based on multiple shuttle resubmissions.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408409844584449.summary: This project demonstrates one of each basic logic gate together with some flip-flops, intended as a gate-level playground. The documentation is placeholder text, so the exact circuit and test method are not described. It appears to use the eight outputs for 7-segment segments, but the connection to the logic is unclear. The author's silicon test report notes a 1 Hz clock while tracing the logic through the Wokwi diagram, and that momentary push-button mode helped separate gate tests from flip-flop tests.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408409844584449.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added silicon-tested tag based on author's working report.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408455148316673.summary: This design combines a tapped ring oscillator with a glitchless clock source switch, allowing selection between two external clocks. To test the oscillator, one of the three inverted taps is fed back to input 0, while the clock switch is tested by using input 1 to select between clock0 and clock1, with the selected clock appearing on output 3. No external hardware beyond clock sources and feedback wiring is required. The documentation is concise but describes both functional blocks and their test procedure clearly.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408455148316673.review_notes: Removed analog (digital Wokwi design) and added clock-domain-crossing for the glitchless clock switch.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408486941145089.summary: This project is a Tiny Tapeout 5 workshop design whose first three output bits form a binary counter that can be preset with the first three input bits, while the remaining input bits pass through to the outputs. The documentation does not explain how to test it, leaving the test procedure unspecified. No external hardware is described, though the outputs are mapped to 7-segment segments. The design appears to be a teaching example from a workshop, but the sparse documentation limits what can be said about it.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408486941145089.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added counter, workshop, wokwi, and 7-segment tags supported by the source.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408594272345089.summary: This design divides the input clock by successive powers of two, with CLK/2 on output 7 down to CLK/256 on output 0. The documentation is placeholder text and does not describe the internal implementation or how to test it. It requires only a clock input and observation of the divided outputs, with no other external hardware mentioned. Because the documentation is essentially empty, the summary is inferred from the title and pin names.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408594272345089.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the supplied documentation is placeholder text.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408774591779841.summary: This Verilog design generates a sawtooth waveform for audio by incrementing a counter from 0 to 25,000,000 and feeding the value into a PDM modulator, with the frequency set by a 4-bit left-shift amount. It is tested by adding an RC low-pass filter with a cutoff around 30 kHz to output pin 7, which can be probed with an oscilloscope or connected to an audio amplifier to listen to the result. The design outputs both PCM bits and a PDM stream, and follows the Tiny Tapeout audio pinout recommendation. It is notable for being a straightforward audio waveform generator that requires external filtering and amplification to be useful.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408774591779841.review_notes: Removed pwm/synthesizer/dac which are unsupported; kept signal-generator and audio.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408784463076353.summary: This is a simple binary counter implemented in Wokwi that drives a 7-segment display. The eight outputs map directly to the seven segments and decimal point, and the design counts in binary at a 10 Hz clock. It requires no external hardware and is tested simply by turning it on. The documentation is very thin and the description is informal, so little can be said about its internal structure.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408784463076353.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; 7-segment is the specific supported output interface.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.summary: This design displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display based on a 6-bit binary value entered on DIP switches. It drives the display one segment at a time, so a high clock rate is needed to see the full character. The character set covers a-z plus space, underscore, hyphen, period, exclamation mark and quote. Silicon tests report it working, and it is notable as a simple character generator with a documented mapping table.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.review_notes: Removed text (7-segment output only) and added silicon-tested per test reports.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408936929183745.summary: This project adds two 4-bit numbers entered on the eight inputs and shows the 5-bit sum on the outputs, which are wired to a 7-segment display. It was created for Supercon 2023 as a tapeout test of basic logic gates that add things. The documentation does not explain how to test it beyond a placeholder, and the internal implementation is not described. It appears to be a simple educational adder demonstration rather than a complex design.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380408936929183745.review_notes: Removed unsupported ALU/display tags and added logic-gate/combinational/education based on the gates and Supercon description.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409393770716161.summary: This design generates a VGA signal that displays a white pixel on a blue background, reusing VGA Flappy Bird code from Cutout1. It correctly times the sync and color signals for VGA output on the eight pins, which match the Tiny VGA pinout. It requires an external VGA adaptor and a digital-to-analog converter to connect to a monitor. The project was submitted for Supercon 2023 and is notable for being a minimal VGA demonstration on a Tiny Tapeout tile.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409393770716161.review_notes: Removed display because the output is specifically VGA, already covered by vga and video.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409481852161025.summary: This project is titled test001 and is described only as a test Tiny Tapeout design. The documentation consists of placeholder text asking how the project works and how to test it, with no actual explanation. The pin names map the eight outputs to the segments and dot of a 7-segment display, but nothing states what is driven onto them. There is not enough information to determine the design's function or how it should be used.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409488188706817.summary: This design implements four basic logic gates: an AND of inputs 0 and 1, a NAND of inputs 2 and 3, an OR of inputs 4 and 5, and an XOR of inputs 6 and 7, with the results on outputs 0 through 3. It demonstrates simple combinational logic and is intended for education. The design was created as part of a Supercon workshop using the Wokwi simulator. Silicon test reports say each gate worked as expected.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409488188706817.review_notes: Removed unsupported template tag and added silicon-tested tag plus mention based on the provided report.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409528895479809.summary: This project is titled RBUART and implements a low baud rate UART that outputs ASCII characters. The documentation explains that connecting the TX and RX pins to a computer's TX and RX pins should show the characters being printed. The output pins are named for 7-segment display segments a through g plus the dot. The design is built in Wokwi and has no silicon test reports.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409528895479809.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the actual UART documentation rather than placeholder text.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409532780455937.summary: This Wokwi design has outputs labeled as seven-segment display segments a through g plus a dot. The documentation is placeholder text and does not explain how the design works or how to test it. The title mentions a triple OR gate, but no details are provided. There is not enough information to determine the actual behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409532780455937.review_notes: Removed unsupported hardware-trojan, security, and comparator tags; added 7-segment and insufficient-doc.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409568391147521.summary: This design is a simple hardware trojan example based on a Medium article by Ryan Cornateanu. It provides two four-input circuits, one normal and one containing an embedded hardware trojan, selected via DIP switches. The outputs are shown on a 7-segment display, with the normal circuit driving some segments and the trojan circuit driving others. It is built with Wokwi and requires only the Tiny Tapeout carrier board for testing.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409568391147521.review_notes: Replaced unsupported LFSR/clock-generator/education tags with hardware-trojan, security, dip-switch and 7-segment supported by the source.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409904919056385.summary: This design implements a 4-bit LFSR configured as a PRBS with polynomial X^3+X^2+1, using XNOR gates to avoid synthesis warnings. It has clock and reset inputs, and outputs for seven segments of a 7-segment display plus a PRBS output. The reset sets four D flip-flops to zero to ensure oscillation starts. The design is intended to verify the design flow for teaching lower division college students IC design.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380409904919056385.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the PRBS and 7-segment display description.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380410498092232705.summary: This design sends the string 'Hello\n' over UART using a shift register with hardcoded initial values loaded into a looped feedback path. It also fills remaining die space with an 'RNN' module made from flip-flops feeding into each other, driven by inputs 0-3 and producing outputs 0-3. To test UART, connect the UART output to a microcontroller or scope, set load/enable low then high, set output enable high, and observe the string. The design has been silicon-tested and reported working by a tester who connected it to a serial port and saw it print Hello.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380410498092232705.review_notes: Replaced counter/clock-generator tags with tags supported by the UART shift-register and flip-flop RNN documentation, and corrected the summary which described unrelated counter and display behavior.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380412382001715201.summary: This project is a naive 8-bit binary counter built from eight chained D flip-flops that count the clock input. Its eight outputs drive the segments and dot of a 7-segment display, and it lacks features such as a deterministic initial state or a reset. It was constructed during the Hackaday Supercon 2023 ASIC workshop as a rapid learning exercise. Testing consists of pulsing the clock and monitoring the outputs for the binary value, and silicon testers report it counts correctly.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380412382001715201.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a placeholder submission, contradicting the actual counter documentation and working silicon reports.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380416099936681985.summary: This design counts seconds and displays the value on a 7-segment display, with the lower counter bits also available on the bidirectional pins. The input pins program a 24-bit compare register so the counting rate can be changed from the default one-second interval. It is a standard Tiny Tapeout Verilog demo intended to show clock division and binary-to-decimal conversion. The documentation is complete and describes both the default and programmable counting behavior.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380416099936681985.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and template tags; source describes a counter/timer demo, not a clock generator or template.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380416361853146113.summary: This project is titled "IDK WHAT TO DO" and its description states the author does not yet know what it does. The documentation consists only of the default placeholder text for how it works and how to test it. The pin names map the outputs to 7-segment display segments, but nothing indicates what is driven onto them. There is essentially no information about the design's function or usage.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380416616536542209.summary: This project is titled "TT05 Submission" and its description states the author does not yet know what it does. The documentation consists only of the default placeholder text for how it works and how to test it. The pin names map the outputs to 7-segment display segments, but nothing indicates what is driven onto them. There is essentially no information about the design's function or usage.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380438365946734593.summary: This project implements a UART transmitter using registers made from D-flip flops and multiplexers, based on an example from a digital design guide. It continuously sends the characters QSM when enabled. To use it, a clock signal must be connected, and the Load and Output Enable pins must be toggled in a specific sequence. An external UART receiver is required to observe the transmitted data.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380438365946734593.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register and multiplexer tags; kept flip-flop and education which are supported.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380465686251921409.summary: This project is a counter designed for the Tiny Tapeout shuttle, with outputs connected to a 7-segment display. The documentation is essentially a template with placeholder text, providing no details on how the counter works or how to test it. The only concrete information is the pin names, which indicate the seven segments and decimal point. It appears to be an incomplete or template project.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380465686251921409.review_notes: Removed redundant generic display tag; 7-segment already covers the output.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380477805171811329.summary: This project combines a 2-bit ALU and a dice function, and can translate binary code into a single-digit display. The documentation is mostly placeholder text, with no explanation of how the ALU or dice operate or how to test them. The only pin listed is the decimal point of a 7-segment display, suggesting the output is shown on such a display. The design is described as 'extremely professional' and 'Steve Jobs approves', but lacks technical details.

tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380490286828784641.summary: This is a remake of Matt Venn's original TT02 7-segment Wokwi project, with the multiplexer select lines inverted at reset so that transitions occur on the opposite clock edge. It functions as a counter that drives a 7-segment display. Testing involves manually clocking the design to see the incrementing output on the display. The project is a minor variation of an existing design and includes links to the original Wokwi project.
tt05of/tt_um_wokwi_380490286828784641.review_notes: Removed multiplexer and retro tags not supported by the design's purpose.

tt05of/tt_um_wrapper_inputblackboxoutput.summary: Byte Computer is an 8-bit Turing complete computer implemented in Verilog, featuring an in-order, non-pipelined architecture with no register file, cache, or branch predictor. It fetches instructions from external memory, decodes and executes them, and repeats until a halt instruction is encountered. Testing requires external memory and control logic, typically provided by a microcontroller, which must be preloaded with a program. The design is notable for its simplicity and small size, making it suitable for Tiny Tapeout.
tt05of/tt_um_wrapper_inputblackboxoutput.review_notes: Removed memory, microcontroller and esoteric because they are not supported by the source; cpu was already present and is correct.

tt05of/tt_um_wta.summary: This project implements a Winner-Take-All (WTA) network that takes an 8-bit current input, splits it into two 4-bit values, and outputs the 4 bits of the higher value, with preference to the most significant bits in case of a tie. It includes outputs for membrane potential and spike bits, though the spike outputs are mostly unspecified. Testing involves resetting the design and observing the comparator and result values. The design is a simple digital implementation of a neural network concept.
tt05of/tt_um_wta.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network tag; source only supports a WTA comparator/neural-network concept.

tt05of/tt_um_yubex_metastability_experim.summary: This design evaluates whether metastability in flip-flops can be used as a true random number generator source in an ASIC. It uses a toggle flip-flop to create edges, a programmable delay line made of inverter pairs, and two metastable flip-flops; metastability is detected when their outputs differ. The design has manual and auto trigger modes, and the delay is controlled by a 6-bit input. Testing involves selecting a mode, adjusting the delay, and observing the 7-segment display for metastability indication; no external hardware is required.
tt05of/tt_um_yubex_metastability_experim.review_notes: Removed trng because the design only evaluates metastability as a possible TRNG source, not a TRNG implementation.

tt06/tt_um_3515_sequenceDetector.summary: This project implements a finite state machine in Verilog that detects the overlapping bit sequence '1001' and indicates detection by displaying '8.' on a 7-segment LED display, otherwise showing '-'. The design includes a test mode where holding the condition inputs high allows individual segment testing or digit display by varying the bidirectional pins. It needs an external 7-segment LED display wired to the eight outputs and a switch or signal source to drive the serial input. The documentation is clear about operation and testing, though it is a straightforward educational FSM exercise.
tt06/tt_um_3515_sequenceDetector.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not state an educational purpose.

tt06/tt_um_4bit_cpu_with_fsm.summary: This is a small 4-bit CPU implemented with a finite state machine that performs simple arithmetic and logic operations, along with storing, loading, and shifting values. It is controlled through input pins for storage address, input data, write access, and a 4-bit operation code, with results presented as an 8-bit output. Testing involves supplying values and opcodes in sequence, storing and loading intermediate results as needed for multi-operand operations. The documentation is brief and the design appears to be a compact processor without external hardware requirements beyond switches and LEDs.
tt06/tt_um_4bit_cpu_with_fsm.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added verilog tag.

tt06/tt_um_7seg_animated.summary: This design animates a 7-segment display by reading input switches to form a custom character and then illuminating the segments sequentially at roughly 0.12 seconds per segment. Inputs 0 through 6 map directly to the seven segments, input 7 enables the display and starts the animation, and the bidirectional pins optionally control an experimental PWM dimming feature. It requires an external 7-segment display and switches for the inputs, and a silicon test report confirms it is working. The design is a simple visual demonstration with a PWM dimming experiment.
tt06/tt_um_7seg_animated.review_notes: Removed led tag (drives 7-segment display) and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

tt06/tt_um_8bitALU.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit unsigned arithmetic logic unit written in Verilog, with a single input and output pin listed in the pinout. The documentation consists almost entirely of images showing the design and test setup, with no textual explanation of the supported operations or control scheme. Testing is described as using an ADALM2000 instrument, but the images are not accessible in the provided text. The documentation is too thin to determine the exact instruction set or how the single input pin selects operations.
tt06/tt_um_8bitALU.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate and insufficient-doc tags; summary already matches the source.

tt06/tt_um_8bit_cpu.summary: This is an 8-bit single-cycle microprocessor with a register file and ALU, designed to execute a simple instruction set supporting basic ALU operations, load/store, and carry status checks. It is controlled through input pins for register addresses, opcode, and data, with outputs providing register data or processor status. The design was tested with twelve testbenches covering ALU operations, data movement, and load/store, though timing interactions between instructions were not exhaustively verified. It lacks a program counter and external memory, so jump operations are omitted, and it operates entirely in simulation without external hardware.
tt06/tt_um_8bit_cpu.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not state an educational purpose.

tt06/tt_um_ADPCM_COMPRESSOR.summary: This design accepts a pulse-density-modulated microphone signal and produces a 4-bit ADPCM encoded output at a lower sampling rate, using a CIC decimation filter followed by ADPCM encoding. It requires two synchronized external clocks, with slow_clk running at one-eighth the frequency of clk, and a block enable signal to start compression. The encoded output streams from the encPcm pins with an outValid flag, and can be stored or decoded for playback. The design is notable for implementing audio compression on a small tile budget and requires an external PDM microphone.
tt06/tt_um_ADPCM_COMPRESSOR.review_notes: Summary was already four sentences; no factual changes needed.

tt06/tt_um_ALU.summary: This is a 3-bit ALU that computes addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulo in parallel, with a 3-bit selector choosing which result appears on the 6-bit output. Inputs A and B are set with switches, and the selector uses three more switches to pick one of the five operations, with the result shown on six LEDs. The documentation explains the selector encoding and provides examples, and the design is purely combinational. It is an educational project requiring external switches and LEDs for input and output.
tt06/tt_um_ALU.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not state an educational purpose; added combinational based on the parallel operation description.

tt06/tt_um_ALU_DECODERS.summary: This combinational design implements a 3-bit ALU supporting subtraction, addition, XOR, and AND, with its output routed to both an octal decoder and a Gray code decoder for display on two 7-segment displays. A selector chooses the ALU operation and another selects whether the octal or Gray decoder drives the displays, with the Gray decoder specially mapped to decimal for the displays. Testing requires setting the two 3-bit numbers and the selectors, then observing the result on the external displays. External hardware includes two common-cathode 7-segment displays, fourteen 330-ohm resistors, and a DC power source.

tt06/tt_um_BoothMulti_hhrb98.summary: This project implements a Booth-4 signed multiplier in Verilog, taking two 4-bit inputs X and Y and producing an 8-bit product Z. The Booth algorithm reduces the number of partial products by using shifting and addition/subtraction based on recoded multiplier bits. Testing is described as applying physical inputs via a testbench and observing the output, though no detailed test procedure or results are provided. The documentation is minimal and the design appears to be a compact multiplier.
