tt06/tt_um_BoothMulti_hhrb98.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added verilog tag.

tt06/tt_um_CDMA_Santiago.summary: The design is a CDMA modulator and demodulator that uses two 5-bit LFSRs to generate Gold codes and spreads a 1-bit input signal. It is tested via a Verilog testbench and intended for lab experiments with an oscilloscope, where an external op-amp simulates channel noise to measure bit-error rate. The circuit recovers the original signal through a receptor output and indicates a valid seed via an LED. The project was created as part of a Latinpractice Bootcamp to study CDMA and Gold sequences.
tt06/tt_um_CDMA_Santiago.review_notes: Removed opamp/mixed-signal because the op-amp is external lab equipment, and education because no teaching purpose is stated; added workshop and instrumentation.

tt06/tt_um_CKPope_top.summary: This is a two-axis position controller that uses 4-bit counters, comparators, and a state machine to move X and Y positions towards user-set targets. The user sets 4-bit target values on the input pins and triggers motion with a button; the current positions are output as 4-bit values for each axis. External hardware includes switches for inputs, a push-button for motion, and LEDs or a logic analyzer for outputs. The design operates at up to 50 MHz and can be reset asynchronously.
tt06/tt_um_CKPope_top.review_notes: Removed motor-control because no motor drive is described; added button and led based on the documented external hardware.

tt06/tt_um_CodHex7seg.summary: This project is a binary-to-7-segment hexadecimal decoder that takes a 4-bit binary input and drives a common-anode 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting a 4-position DIP switch to the inputs and a 7-segment display to the outputs, with appropriate power and resistors. The design outputs active-low segment signals for segments a through g. The documentation is clear but minimal, focusing on basic operation.
tt06/tt_um_CodHex7seg.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added verilog and dip-switch which are clearly documented.

tt06/tt_um_Counter_1_shivam.summary: This design is an 8-bit synchronous binary counter with asynchronous reset that can count up, count down, or hold based on input pins. It provides binary, hexadecimal, and decimal outputs. It was tested in simulation and partially on silicon, where the reset polarity was found to be active-high instead of active-low. The design is a straightforward counter and does not require external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board.
tt06/tt_um_Counter_1_shivam.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested because only partial silicon testing is reported; replaced timer with up-down-counter to match the documented up/down counting.

tt06/tt_um_DigitalClockTop.summary: The project is a digital clock that uses time division multiplexing to drive six seven-segment displays with eight outputs. The documentation is essentially non-existent beyond stating that it works and that no external hardware is needed, but switches and LEDs are mentioned. The design appears to accept inputs from switches and drive multiplexed outputs, but the exact functionality is not described. Due to the lack of documentation, details of its operation and testing cannot be determined.
tt06/tt_um_DigitalClockTop.review_notes: Removed multiplexer as misleading; added counter and clock-divider as inherent to a digital clock.

tt06/tt_um_FanCTRL_DomnikBrandstetter.summary: This is a PI-based fan controller that reads a 4-bit ADC value and a 4-bit setpoint, then adjusts fan speed via a 25 kHz PWM output with a 20% to 100% duty cycle. It also outputs a signed 4-bit controller value and displays it on a 7-segment display. The design requires external hardware including a 4-bit ADC, a fan, and a 7-segment display. The controller parameters are fixed for simplicity.
tt06/tt_um_FanCTRL_DomnikBrandstetter.review_notes: Removed temperature-sensor since the ADC input is generic and temperature is only implied by the title.

tt06/tt_um_I2C_to_SPI.summary: Although titled as an SPI master, the documentation for this design describes a simple counter and mirroring function controlled by a 'sel' signal, not an SPI interface. When 'sel' is high, a counter is output; when low, bidirectional pins are mirrored to outputs. The pin names suggest I2C and SPI signals, but the provided description does not match the title, indicating a discrepancy or missing documentation. The design is not tested and its actual functionality is unclear from the text.
tt06/tt_um_I2C_to_SPI.review_notes: Removed counter and i2c as unsupported by the contradictory documentation, and added spi based on the title and pin names.

tt06/tt_um_JamesTimothyMeech_inverter.summary: This analog design consists of an inverter and a programmable resistor that can connect one of 16 58.218 kΩ resistors between pin ua[0] and ground via analog switches controlled by digital inputs. The inverter uses pins ua[4] and ua[5] and can be used as an amplifier. Testing involves applying signals and measuring currents with an ammeter or oscilloscope. External hardware includes a signal generator and measurement equipment, and the design is intended for experiments with analog building blocks.
tt06/tt_um_JamesTimothyMeech_inverter.review_notes: Removed logic-gate, opamp, and full-custom tags not supported by the source; added analog and instrumentation.

tt06/tt_um_LFSR_shivam.summary: This is a 10-bit linear feedback shift register that generates a pseudo-random sequence from a clock and reset input. It was tested on silicon and found to have an inverted reset and incorrect pinout, but worked once the reset was swapped. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board. It is useful for applications needing pseudo-random patterns.
tt06/tt_um_LFSR_shivam.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested (status is partial) and register-file tags; added verilog tag.

tt06/tt_um_MATTHIAS_M_PAL_TOP_WRAPPER.summary: This is a simple PAL device that is configured via a shift register, allowing the implementation of custom boolean functions from 8 inputs to 5 outputs. Configuration is done by shifting in a bitstream through a config pin and clock, and an enable pin activates the outputs. It was tested on silicon with various configurations, including a 3-bit state machine, and requires no external hardware though external switches and LEDs help observe the outputs. The design demonstrates a programmable logic device on Tiny Tapeout.
tt06/tt_um_MATTHIAS_M_PAL_TOP_WRAPPER.review_notes: Removed fsm, kept silicon-tested explicitly to match working status, and corrected the external-hardware statement.

tt06/tt_um_MNSLab_BLDC.summary: This design is a universal motor and actuator controller for BLDC motors with encoders, implementing PID control and Nichols-Ziegler auto-tuning. It is configured and monitored through an I2C interface at address 0x72, with subaddresses for setting PID constants, manual override, and reading motor period. External hardware includes a motor driver to convert PWM signals to power, a BLDC motor with at least two encoders, and I2C pull-up resistors. The design is notable for its auto-tuning capability and universal applicability to different motor setups.
tt06/tt_um_MNSLab_BLDC.review_notes: Removed instrumentation tag; source describes motor control, not measurement instrumentation.

tt06/tt_um_MichaelBell_latch_mem.summary: This project implements a 64-byte RAM using latch-based storage, with an 8-bit data bus and 6-bit address bus. Writes take two cycles and only one write can be in flight at a time to avoid glitches and ensure data stability. The design was tested on silicon and confirmed working by the author, who noted the need to work around potential contention on an internal tristate bus. It provides a simple memory block for small data storage in digital systems.

tt06/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set, with 28-bit addresses and 24-bit program addresses. It executes code from QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, sharing QSPI lines between them. The SoC includes a UART and SPI controller, and is intended to be used with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display. Silicon testing showed the core works and runs MicroPython and benchmarks, but UART RX has a bug that was worked around in software.

tt06/tt_um_PWM.summary: This project is a PWM generator that produces a 1 kHz signal with duty cycle adjustable from 10% to 80% using three switches, providing eight discrete steps. It is designed to control LED brightness or similar loads, and requires an external LED with a resistor and switches for input. The design is a straightforward implementation of PWM for educational or simple control applications.
tt06/tt_um_PWM.review_notes: Removed signal-generator because the source describes a fixed PWM duty-cycle controller rather than a general signal generator.

tt06/tt_um_PWM_Controller.summary: This is a low-cost PWM controller that generates a 10 MHz PWM signal with duty cycle adjustable between 10% and 90% using two buttons for increase and decrease. It is intended for applications requiring variable duty cycle control, such as motor speed or LED dimming. Silicon testing revealed that the PWM output appears on output 0 rather than the bidirectional pin as listed, and duty cycle adjustment is limited to only a few steps (1, 5, and 9). The design is simple and provides basic PWM functionality with noted limitations.
tt06/tt_um_PWM_Controller.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested because the report is partial, not a full working validation.

tt06/tt_um_PWM_Sine_UART.summary: This project generates a PWM signal that produces a sine wave with frequency selectable from 100 Hz to 700 Hz in 100 Hz steps via a UART interface. A number from 1 to 7 sent over UART sets the frequency, and the PWM output is filtered externally to recover the sine wave. Testing was done with a Bluetooth module for UART communication and an oscilloscope to verify the output frequencies. The design is useful for generating audio-frequency sine waves controlled remotely.
tt06/tt_um_PWM_Sine_UART.review_notes: Removed audio and filter-analog tags not supported by the source; audio-frequency claim is a stretch but the summary otherwise matches.

tt06/tt_um_QIF_8bit.summary: This project is an 8-bit digital QIF circuit that spikes when the input is positive and resets when the signal exceeds a predetermined value. The documentation is extremely minimal, consisting only of the title, one-line description, and pin names, with no detailed explanation of the QIF algorithm or its implementation. The external hardware mentioned is an ADALM2000, suggesting analog testing, but the design's purpose and operation are unclear. Due to the lack of documentation, the tags and summary are largely inferred from the title and brief description.

tt06/tt_um_S2P.summary: This is a 4-bit serial-to-parallel shift register that accepts serial data and outputs it in parallel after four clock cycles. It includes a clock, reset, serial input, and four parallel outputs, and is described as useful in applications like successive approximation registers in ADCs. Testing was performed in simulation with a testbench, and external hardware such as a wave generator, switch, and logic analyzer are suggested for physical testing. The design is a basic building block for serial-to-parallel data conversion.
tt06/tt_um_S2P.review_notes: Removed register-file and sar-adc because the source implements only a shift register and mentions SAR ADC only as an application.

tt06/tt_um_SJ.summary: This is a tiny systolic array with 9 processing elements capable of matrix multiplication and 2D convolution using row stationary operation. It requires an external FPGA connected to all 24 I/O pins to feed data and retrieve results. The design is a hardware accelerator for matrix multiplication and 2D convolution. Documentation is minimal, focusing on the architecture and external interface.
tt06/tt_um_SJ.review_notes: Removed unsupported neural-network tag and corrected summary to avoid claiming neural network inference.

tt06/tt_um_SteffenReith_ASGTop.summary: This project implements an Alternating Step Generator (ASG) using three linear feedback shift registers (LFSRs) to produce a pseudo-random bit sequence with an extremely long period. The design is a naive implementation, with the provided Verilog generated using SpinalHDL, and it requires loading non-null seeds into the three LFSRs via the loadIt input before enabling operation. A new random bit is generated every clock cycle. The ASG is notable for its simple hardware implementation and huge period, which the author presents as a hardware implementation example.
tt06/tt_um_SteffenReith_ASGTop.review_notes: The source describes ASGs as needing three LFSRs and a long period, but the 'lfsr' and 'spinalhdl' tags are borderline; corrected by removing crypto and adding silicon-tested.

tt06/tt_um_SteffenReith_PiMACTop.summary: PiMAC is a pipelined multiply-and-accumulate unit that computes a*b+c for 4-bit unsigned inputs. It uses a classic shift-and-add multiplication method, with the partial products computed across pipeline stages and the result available after a latency of three clock cycles. The design is generated with SpinalHDL and exposes a, b, and c on input pins and the 8-bit result on output pins. It is a small arithmetic building block intended for educational or integration purposes, with no external hardware required beyond the digital interface.
tt06/tt_um_SteffenReith_PiMACTop.review_notes: Removed spinalhdl tag because the detected language is Verilog and the source only mentions SpinalHDL as a generator.

tt06/tt_um_TT06_SAR_wulffern.summary: This is an 8-bit successive-approximation-register analog-to-digital converter that samples a differential input onto a capacitor array and uses a strong-arm comparator and asynchronous binary-search logic to produce a two's-complement digital output. It requires a 4 MHz clock, an enable signal, and differential analog inputs with a common mode around VDD/2; the conversion-done signal indicates when the output is valid. Silicon test reports indicate it works, but both inputs must be above about 0.6 V for reliable operation, and a common mode of 0 V will cause the comparator to fail. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog block with detailed documentation and measured silicon results.
tt06/tt_um_TT06_SAR_wulffern.review_notes: Removed comparator type tag; added mixed-signal because the ADC integrates analog and digital circuitry.

tt06/tt_um_UABCReloj.summary: This design implements a 24-hour digital clock with separate BCD outputs for two hour digits and two minute digits. It uses a 1 MHz reference clock and provides a set button to cycle through the digits and a pulse input to advance the selected digit. External hardware includes three push buttons, a 1 MHz signal generator, and four 7-segment BCD decoders to display the time. The design is a straightforward clock with no unusual features or silicon test results reported.
tt06/tt_um_UABCReloj.review_notes: Removed clock-divider: the source only mentions a 1 MHz reference clock, not any clock division circuitry.

tt06/tt_um_Uart_Transciver.summary: This project is a UART transceiver for 8-bit data frames with little-endian transmit and receive signals. The documentation is essentially empty, with no description of the implementation, testing procedure, or required external hardware. The pin names suggest a standard UART interface, but no further details are provided. Because of the lack of documentation, it is not possible to say more about its operation or notable characteristics.

tt06/tt_um_adammaj.summary: Tiny ALU is a simple 4-bit arithmetic logic unit extracted from a larger GPU design. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 2-bit arithmetic mux selection, and produces a 4-bit output; the testbench only exercises the addition function. The design is intended as a small, self-contained submission while the author works on a more complex GPU project. No external hardware is required, and no silicon test results are reported.

tt06/tt_um_advanced_counter.summary: This is a multi-digit counter with configurable maximum values and carry-over behavior, built from modified 2-bit up/down counters. It supports two digits, with outputs serialized for 7-segment displays via external 8-bit shift registers such as the HC595. Operation requires three push buttons for digit control and limit refresh, plus three switches for mode selection, and it provides shift-clock outputs for the shift registers. The design was created as part of a university class activity and includes no silicon test results.
tt06/tt_um_advanced_counter.review_notes: Replaced education with workshop since the source only shows a class/course origin, not a teaching purpose.

tt06/tt_um_aerox2_jrb8_computer.summary: The James Retro Byte 8 is an 8-bit microprocessor built from the ground up following the nand2tetris course. It requires external SPI storage for ROM and RAM, with pin mappings compatible with the spi-ram-emu project, and uses a 24-bit addressing mode. The design was tested with a simple repeating output program and works, but further testing with more complex programs and the spi-ram-emu is planned. It is notable for being a complete CPU implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile.
tt06/tt_um_aerox2_jrb8_computer.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

tt06/tt_um_aiju_8080.summary: This is an Intel 8080-compatible CPU core intended to run software such as Microsoft BASIC or CP/M. It requires an external RP2040 to simulate RAM and I/O, and exposes a bus handshake interface along with debug and interrupt signals. The documentation is minimal, with testing procedures still to be determined, and no silicon test results are provided. The design is notable for targeting a classic 8-bit instruction set on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

tt06/tt_um_aleena.summary: This analog design implements ReLU and sigmoid activation functions for neuromorphic computing. It provides two analog input-output pairs, with the ReLU output equal to the input when positive and zero otherwise, and the sigmoid output representing a probability for binary classification. External hardware includes a voltage source connected to the analog inputs, typically from an artificial neural network. The documentation is brief and provides no test results or detailed circuit information.
tt06/tt_um_aleena.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc because the documentation adequately describes the functions and external hardware.

tt06/tt_um_alexsegura_pong.summary: This is a two-player Pong game implemented in Verilog for a 640x480 VGA display. It uses two rotary encoders for paddle control and outputs VGA signals through a TinyVGA Pmod or similar. The game logic handles ball movement, collision detection, and scoring, and it can be simulated with Verilator and SDL2. The design is a complete game on a single tile and requires external encoders and a VGA interface.
tt06/tt_um_alexsegura_pong.review_notes: Removed display tag as vga is more specific; added game, pong, vga, video, rotary-encoder, and verilog tags supported by the source.

tt06/tt_um_alfiero88_VCII.summary: VCII is a second-generation voltage conveyor analog block with current input y, current output x, voltage output z, and a reference input for virtual ground. It is intended to be used in a transimpedance amplifier configuration, where a current of a few microamps injected into y and an external resistor between x and Vref produce a voltage at z. Testing requires the external gain resistor, power supplies, and an oscilloscope to observe the output. The design targets unity current gain beta and unity voltage gain alpha, but the documentation gives no measured silicon results or detailed characterization.
tt06/tt_um_alfiero88_VCII.review_notes: Removed opamp, current-mirror and mixed-signal because the source describes a purely analog voltage conveyor with no such blocks.

tt06/tt_um_algofoogle_tt06_grab_bag.summary: TT06 Grab Bag combines several analog and mixed-signal experiments, with a 24-bit VGA pattern generator as the main feature. A digital VGA controller produces 8-bit RGB outputs that feed three internal R2R DACs, driving analog pins with 0-1.8V signals, while mode selection is latched from ui_in during reset. Testing needs a 25MHz clock, reset, and an oscilloscope; real VGA output requires external op-amp buffers and level shifting to 0-0.7V into 75 ohms. Silicon reports say the analog outputs worked as expected and the author saw vivid VGA images, though the unbuffered DAC outputs have limited slew rate and high impedance.

tt06/tt_um_alu.summary: SumLatchUART_System is a 4-bit arithmetic system that stores input data in register A or B, applies an operation selected by a 4-bit opcode, and sends the result over a UART transmitter. The design includes addition, subtraction, and bitwise logic operations, with control pins for clock, reset, register saves, and UART transmit enable. External hardware includes a UART receiver, two pull-up push buttons, an LED for the busy indicator, and a 50MHz oscillator or function generator. The documentation describes the intended flow but does not report any silicon test results or measured behavior.
tt06/tt_um_alu.review_notes: Removed adder because addition is only one of several documented ALU operations.

tt06/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: TT06 Analog Factory Test is a set of test structures intended to support analog characterization on the TT06 shuttle. The pins suggest bias generation, ground and power sensing, and three analog loopback connections, with two digital enable inputs. The documentation consists only of FIXME placeholders for how it works, how to test, and external hardware, so the exact function cannot be determined. No silicon test reports are provided, and the design is essentially undocumented beyond its title and pin names.

tt06/tt_um_analog_loopback.summary: Analog loopback is a simple test structure in which each pair of analog pins is shorted together on the die. It is used to measure resistance and step response through each pair in order to characterize the analog multiplexer. No external hardware is required beyond the chip and measurement equipment such as a multimeter or oscilloscope. A silicon report notes that the first two loops worked, but only when the board was powered.
tt06/tt_um_analog_loopback.review_notes: Removed factory-test and added analog, characterization and silicon-tested to match the analog loopback and working silicon report.

tt06/tt_um_ancho.summary: This project is a configurable PWM generator whose duty cycle is selected by three digital input signals, with an enable input and a clock. The duty cycle steps in 12.5% increments from 12.5% to 100% depending on the three-bit combination, and the PWM signal appears on a single output pin. Testing requires a signal generator for a 10MHz clock and an oscilloscope to observe the pulse width. The documentation is in Spanish and provides a clear truth table, but no silicon test results are reported.

tt06/tt_um_andrewtron3000.summary: Rule 30 Engine iterates a 56-bit Rule 30 cellular automaton starting from an 8-bit initial value supplied on the input bus. Each iteration is transmitted over an 8N1 UART at 115,200 baud on output pin uo[4], with zero boundary conditions around the 56-bit field. The only external hardware needed is a UART receiver to capture the serial output. The documentation does not include silicon test results or details about the internal implementation.
tt06/tt_um_andrewtron3000.review_notes: Removed prng: Rule 30 is presented as a cellular automaton, not a random number generator.

tt06/tt_um_andychip1_sn74169.summary: sn74169 is a Verilog model of the SN74169 synchronous 4-bit up/down counter, including parallel load, enable inputs, and ripple carry output. The input pins provide the 4-bit load value, enable P and T, active-low load, and up/down select, while outputs give the 4-bit count and carry out. Testing is done by applying the control signals and observing the outputs with an oscilloscope. The documentation is minimal and no silicon test results are reported.

tt06/tt_um_argunda_tiny_opamp.summary: Tiny Opamp is a simple two-stage op-amp without Miller compensation, operating from a 1.8V single supply with inputs biased around 0.9V. It provides two op-amp channels with differential plus and minus inputs and analog voltage outputs, and is intended to be tested in closed-loop configurations only. External hardware needed is at minimum a resistor at the output for a source-follower test, plus a multimeter or oscilloscope. A silicon report notes that the first op-amp worked in an inverting unity configuration but showed some self-oscillation, and the documentation warns against loads drawing more than a few milliamps.
tt06/tt_um_argunda_tiny_opamp.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal as the design is entirely analog.

tt06/tt_um_array_multiplier_hhrb98.summary: Array Multiplier is a Verilog implementation of a 4-bit Wallace tree multiplier built from half-adder and full-adder modules. The eight input pins carry the operands and the eight output pins present the product, though the pin names are generic and do not indicate bit ordering. Testing is described only through a provided testbench file, wallace_tb.v, rather than through hardware measurements. The documentation is very thin and does not report any silicon results or explain the pin mapping in detail.
tt06/tt_um_array_multiplier_hhrb98.review_notes: Title says Array Multiplier but the description says Wallace tree; the summary follows the description, which is the only implementation detail given.

tt06/tt_um_bit_ctrl.summary: This design outputs a different 8-bit bit pattern on each clock cycle and then resets. It is tested by applying a reset, cycling the clock several times, and comparing the outputs to the expected sequence. The outputs can be measured directly on GPIO pins, so no external hardware is required. The documentation is very thin and does not specify the actual bit patterns or the reset behavior in detail.
tt06/tt_um_bit_ctrl.review_notes: Removed counter, sequencer and gpio tags that are not supported by the source.

tt06/tt_um_bomba1.summary: This is a Mealy finite state machine with three states (wait, fill, alarm) that controls a water pump filling an upper tank based on three digital water-level sensors. It drives a pump output and an alarm output, and it is intended to be wired to switches or buttons for the sensors and LEDs for the outputs on the bidirectional pins. The documentation is in Spanish and describes the state transitions in detail, but the testing section is marked TODO. It is a pump control practice design rather than a silicon-validated one.
tt06/tt_um_bomba1.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; summary reworded to avoid claiming a class exercise.

tt06/tt_um_calculator_muehlbb.summary: This design is a 16-bit calculator built around an ALU with twelve selectable operations, including arithmetic, shifts, rotates, and bitwise logic. An 8-bit bidirectional data port is used to load the two 16-bit operands byte by byte and to read back the 16-bit result, while four input pins select the operation and five output pins report status flags such as zero, sign, carry, and overflow. A small counter sequences the load, execute, and readout phases, and the operation is started by releasing the reset pin. The documentation is detailed with a timing diagram and operation table, but the testing section is marked TBC and no silicon results are given.
tt06/tt_um_calculator_muehlbb.review_notes: Removed register-file, gpio, and fsm tags as they are not supported; added calculator, alu, counter, and verilog tags based on the source.

tt06/tt_um_cejmu_riscv.summary: This project implements a TinyRV1-compliant RISC-V CPU without a multiply instruction, with additional AND and XOR support, written in Verilog. It has no internal program memory and must be attached to an external SPI memory device, using dedicated SPI MOSI, SCLK, and CS pins plus a MISO input. Eight bidirectional pins expose a register for observation, and the design is intended to run at 12 MHz. Testing requires the provided SPI slave with memory synthesized onto an FPGA, so it cannot be exercised standalone.
tt06/tt_um_cejmu_riscv.review_notes: Corrected language tag from vhdl to verilog based on the stated project language.

tt06/tt_um_chatgpt_rsnn_paolaunisa.summary: This design implements a programmable recurrent spiking neural network with nine leaky integrate-and-fire neurons arranged in three layers of three, with three spike inputs and three spike outputs. Weights, thresholds, leak rate, feedback scale, and refractory period are loaded through a custom serial interface, and the network processes input spikes synchronously with one-clock-cycle output pulses. The documentation states that the design was generated with ChatGPT and describes the programming procedure, but no test results or external hardware requirements are given. It is a research-style experiment rather than a validated product.
tt06/tt_um_chatgpt_rsnn_paolaunisa.review_notes: Removed unsupported memory tag and added neuromorphic tag for the spiking neural network.

tt06/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This is a 128-byte, 8-bit-wide ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, addressed by eight input pins and read out on eight output pins. The first sixteen bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on an on-board 7-segment display by toggling the first four DIP switches. It is a simple read-only memory with no clock or control logic, and it requires no external hardware beyond the address switches and display. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the function.
tt06/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported decoder/gpio tags; added memory/7-segment/verilog already implied by source.

tt06/tt_um_chisel_hello_schoeberl.summary: This is a Chisel Hello World project that displays a counter on a 7-segment display and emits the Morse code for "hello world" on the display's decimal point and as PWM audio. The audio output is intended for a PmodAMP2 amplifier connected to the bidirectional PMOD, with gain and shutdown control pins, and switch 0 can disable the counter display to make the Morse code easier to see. Testing currently uses cocotb, with a planned move to ChiselTest. A partial silicon test report notes that the author did not clearly see the correct Morse code and observed something blinking.
tt06/tt_um_chisel_hello_schoeberl.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added cocotb and sound-generator tags supported by the source.

tt06/tt_um_chisel_pong.summary: This is a basic Pong game implemented in Chisel that outputs a VGA video signal with two-bit-per-channel color and separate horizontal and vertical sync. Four input pins control the two paddles, and two more enable autopilot for either player, while bidirectional pins expose game state, sync signals, loss indicators, and a game tick. The documentation is minimal, describing it only as a Chisel template, and testing currently uses cocotb with a planned move to ChiselTest. No external hardware beyond a VGA display and buttons is described, and no silicon results are reported.

tt06/tt_um_cmerrill_pdm.summary: This design is a digital-to-analog converter front end that outputs PDM, PWM, and two forms of PFM waveforms representing an 8-bit digital input level. The input can be loaded either in parallel through eight input pins or over an SPI interface, selected by a bidirectional pin, and the output rate can be divided down from the 50 MHz clock by up to 15. To obtain an analog signal, an external RC filter must be connected to the chosen modulation output pin. The author notes that the intended analog output path was not completed due to time constraints and that the SPI path is less validated than the parallel path.

tt06/tt_um_coloquinte_moosic.summary: This is an 8-bit counter that increments when the first input bit is set, but it is protected by Moosic logic locking so it will not count unless the correct six-bit key is applied first. The key is entered on the upper input bits along with a key-enable bit, and the counter value is exposed on eight output pins. The design is self-contained and intended to demonstrate logic locking rather than to drive external hardware. A silicon test report confirms that the design does nothing without the key and counts at the clock frequency once the key is set.
tt06/tt_um_coloquinte_moosic.review_notes: Removed crypto; logic locking is a security, not cryptographic, demonstration.

tt06/tt_um_couchand_cora16.summary: CORA-16 is a simple 16-bit CPU that uses external SPI memory for instruction fetch and execution. It provides an 8-bit general-purpose input and output bus, and supports single-stepping for debugging via a step pin. Status pins indicate busy, halt, and trap conditions, with trap recovery possible by stepping. The design requires an external SPI RAM and can be tested using a Raspberry Pi for emulation.

tt06/tt_um_couchand_dual_deque.summary: This project implements two independent byte-width double-ended queues (deques) using flip-flop arrays with pointers. Each deque can operate as a stack or queue depending on the end_select signal, and provides empty and full status flags. Push, pop, and replace operations are controlled via multiplexed inputs, and the end of the deque can be read from the data output. External hardware is not strictly required, but the design is intended to interface with other devices that can benefit from deque functionality.
tt06/tt_um_couchand_dual_deque.review_notes: Removed fifo and stack-machine; the design is a deque, not a FIFO or stack processor.

tt06/tt_um_csit_luks.summary: CSIT-Luks is a camera lighting settings recommender that takes ISO, shutter speed, and focal ratio inputs via a rotary encoder and displays them on a four-digit seven-segment display. It reads an external luxmeter over SPI and uses the values to look up a recommended setting from a LUT stored in SPI flash, then displays the result. The design requires external hardware including a rotary encoder, seven-segment display, SPI luxmeter, and SPI flash. It is a practical tool for photography, though no silicon test results are provided.
tt06/tt_um_csit_luks.review_notes: Removed photodiode tag; the luxmeter is an external SPI sensor, not a photodiode interface.

tt06/tt_um_devinatkin_fastreadout.summary: This project is a prototype that simulates an image sensor to validate a readout method, converting light levels to frequencies and then measuring them with frequency counters. It includes testbenches for both a full 1MP sensor and a smaller pixel array, and is intended to be tested on fabricated hardware using an external RP2040 microcontroller. The design is not an actual image sensor but a test chip for readout circuitry. The documentation notes that the design may not be useful to others, but provides test instructions.
tt06/tt_um_devinatkin_fastreadout.review_notes: Removed image-processing because the source is a readout prototype, not an image-processing implementation.

tt06/tt_um_dgkaminski.summary: This is a 4-bit ALU implementing the Cornell University ECE2300 instruction set, with operations including addition, subtraction, shifts, AND, and OR. It takes two 4-bit inputs (A and B) and a 3-bit function select, and outputs a 4-bit result along with carry, overflow, negative, and zero flags. The design requires no external hardware beyond input and output connections. It is an educational project from a university course.

tt06/tt_um_dieroller_nathangross1.summary: The Die Roller generates a pseudo-random number between 1 and a user-specified die size (up to 99) when a roll input is triggered. It uses a clock counter for randomness and displays the result on a dual seven-segment display via a PMOD output splitter. Silicon testing revealed that while the die size can be set and displayed, rolling the die does not show the result, indicating a functional issue. The design requires external PMOD hardware for display.

tt06/tt_um_digitaler_filter_rathmayr.summary: This project implements an 8-bit FIR filter with two coefficients, designed to filter unwanted frequencies from a digital signal. It uses shift registers to load the input signal and coefficients, then performs multiply-accumulate operations to produce the filtered output. The design was limited to two coefficients due to chip capacity, but includes comments for future expansion to four coefficients. Testing is done via a testbench, and no external hardware is specified.

tt06/tt_um_disp1.summary: This project is a simple display test that interfaces with a character LCD, based on a Wokwi project. It outputs data and control signals to drive the LCD, requiring external hardware in the form of a character LCD. The documentation is minimal, indicating it is just a test with no further details on functionality or testing. No silicon results are provided.
tt06/tt_um_disp1.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc because the source sufficiently identifies the LCD interface and test method.

tt06/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8.summary: This is an 8-bit combinational multiply and divide unit that supports both signed and unsigned operations. It uses a clock to load input registers and provides immediate or registered output modes, with error flags for division overflow and divide-by-zero. The design is implemented in SpinalHDL and requires an external RP2040 for testing. Documentation is limited, with testing instructions deferred to a later date.
tt06/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8.review_notes: Removed rp2040 tag because the source only mentions RP2040 as test equipment, not as a design pairing.

tt06/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8_sky130faha.summary: This project is an 8-bit combinational multiply and divide unit implemented with sky130 high-availability and full-adder cells. It supports signed and unsigned operations and provides immediate or registered output modes with error flags. The design is in SpinalHDL and expects an RP2040 for testing. Documentation is sparse, with testing instructions to be provided later.
tt06/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8_sky130faha.review_notes: Removed standard-cell tag; added full-custom because sky130 HA/FA cells are full-custom library cells.

tt06/tt_um_dlmiles_poc_fskmodem_hdlctrx.summary: This is a proof-of-concept digital design for an FSK modem with HDLC framing and a UART interface, intended as a stepping stone toward a full terminal node controller for amateur radio packet systems. The design uses a lookup-table-based approach to generate and receive 2FSK signals, with a master clock running at 64 times the data rate to support baud rates from 4800 to 76800. It is meant to be tested with external RP2040 or FPGA boards to validate the electrical interface architecture, and the author notes that limited development time may prevent good results in this initial version. The project is notable for its homage to the classic G3RUH modem design and its plan to eventually pair with an 8-bit CPU for a complete TNC solution.

tt06/tt_um_dr_skyler_clock.summary: This design implements a digital clock that generates a one-second pulse to increment seconds, minutes, and hours, which are then decoded and displayed on a 7-segment display. It requires an external 7-segment display and allows the user to select from several input clock frequencies (10, 12, 14, or 20 MHz) via switches. The clock also provides inputs to show minutes or hours, likely for setting or testing purposes. The project is a straightforward ASIC desktop clock with minimal external hardware needs.
tt06/tt_um_dr_skyler_clock.review_notes: Removed the generic 'verilog' and 'counter' tags; added 'rtc' and 'display' to match the actual clock/displays described.

tt06/tt_um_drburke3_top.summary: This design takes two 8-bit values and performs addition or subtraction, described as a digital neuron component test. It is intended to be tested by supplying two 8-bit numbers and observing the sum or difference on the outputs. The documentation is minimal and does not specify how the operation is selected or provide details on the neuron aspect. The project appears to be a simple arithmetic unit with limited documentation.
tt06/tt_um_drburke3_top.review_notes: Removed alu tag since only add/subtract is documented; added incomplete for the very thin documentation.

tt06/tt_um_drops.summary: This project implements an arcade-style game called Drops, where the player moves a horizontal bar to catch falling droplets on an 8x8 pixel display. The game uses two mechanical buttons for left and right movement, and the player loses a life each time a drop is missed, with the game ending when all lives are lost. It requires an external 8x8 display and two buttons, and the documentation notes potential issues with drop direction and bar movement that may need pin adjustments. The design is a simple interactive game with basic hardware requirements.
tt06/tt_um_drops.review_notes: Replaced led-matrix with display and added pong to match the paddle-and-falling-object gameplay.

tt06/tt_um_dsatizabal_opamp.summary: This is a simple FET operational amplifier designed in Sky130, intended to function as a high-impedance, high-gain amplifier block that can act as a comparator or, with feedback, as an inverting or non-inverting amplifier. It includes two testbenches for non-inverting and inverting amplifier configurations, and testing requires a power source, resistors, signal generator, and oscilloscope. The design has specific requirements: the input signal ground must connect to the ZREF pin, not the chip power ground, and the output will have a DC offset due to an internal virtual ground. Silicon test reports indicate partial success, with the author suggesting that easier connections for analog pins would facilitate testing.

tt06/tt_um_duk_lif.summary: This is an analog implementation of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, which produces a rate-encoded output signal based on a time-varying input and a threshold voltage. It is tested by applying a time-varying input to the Vin terminal, connecting a threshold voltage to Vth, and observing the rate-encoded output at the Out terminal. External hardware required includes a function generator, oscilloscope, and multimeter. The design is a single-node neuron component with minimal documentation beyond its basic function.
tt06/tt_um_duk_lif.review_notes: Removed 'spiking-neural-network' and 'neuromorphic' because the source only describes a single analog LIF neuron node, not a network.

tt06/tt_um_dvxf_dj8.summary: The DJ8 is an 8-bit CPU implemented in VHDL, featuring an 8x8-bit register file, a 15-bit address bus, and an 8-bit data bus, with a built-in 256-byte demo ROM containing two demos. It can be tested using the internal demos by setting DIP switches at reset, and external hardware such as a speaker or parallel Flash ROM may be used for other applications. Silicon test reports confirm that both built-in demos work, including a bytebeat synthesizer and a 7-segment display demo. The design is notable for its compact instruction set and successful silicon validation.
tt06/tt_um_dvxf_dj8.review_notes: Swapped memory for rom, added silicon-tested and retro to match the documented ROM and silicon status.

tt06/tt_um_ejfogleman_smsdac.summary: This design is an 8-bit segmented mismatch-shaping R2R DAC encoder that takes digital input and produces a set of output bits that can be summed with specific weights to reconstruct the analog value. It operates in four modes: first-order mismatch shaping with dither, randomization, first-order shaping without dither, and static encoding, selectable via input pins. Testing requires an external resistor ladder and capacitor to create the analog output voltage, and the design is free-running off the project clock. The encoder is notable for its mismatch-shaping techniques aimed at improving DAC linearity, though it requires careful external component selection for optimal performance.
tt06/tt_um_ejfogleman_smsdac.review_notes: Removed misleading encoder tag; added mixed-signal for the digital encoder plus external analog ladder.

tt06/tt_um_emilian_rf_playground.summary: This is an 8-bit current-steering digital-to-analog converter (IDAC) based on a chain of cells that divide current by two, with each cell optionally sourcing current to the output. It is tested by setting the digital inputs to control the output current, with a reference voltage applied to set the full-scale current, and observing the current through an external resistor. External hardware includes a multimeter, potentiometer, and switches for setting inputs. Silicon test reports indicate the design is broken due to missing via2 connections, resulting in no current output.

tt06/tt_um_enieman.summary: This project implements a simplified RISC-V core that adheres to a subset of the RV32I ISA, with instruction and data memory implemented as small register files that are programmed via a UART interface. The core operates in two modes: PROGRAM mode, where the user sends a sync packet followed by up to 64 bytes of binary instructions, and DATA READ mode, where the user can read the contents of data memory. It requires external hardware such as a USBUART Pmod, and optionally a BTN Pmod and 8LD Pmod for reset and status indication. The design is notable for its UART-based programming and its use of TL-Verilog, with a template provided for custom processor designs.
tt06/tt_um_enieman.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added pmod and memory based on the documented interfaces and register-file memories.

tt06/tt_um_entwurf_integrierter_schaltun.summary: This design demodulates eight PWM channels from an RC receiver by using counters and threshold values to decide whether each output should be HIGH or LOW. It outputs the decoded channel states on the bidirectional pins and also displays the number of active channels on a 7-segment display. A UART transmit wire is provided, though its function is not described. The design is tested by applying PWM signals with pulse widths above 1.9 ms or below 1.1 ms to verify the output transitions.
tt06/tt_um_entwurf_integrierter_schaltun.review_notes: Removed 'decoder' as it is a code-to-signal type tag not matching the PWM demodulation function.

tt06/tt_um_ericsmi_weste_problem_4_11.summary: This project measures the delay of various CMOS VLSI designs from a textbook problem under varying load conditions. It uses selection inputs to choose among designs, provides an 8-bit input bus, and outputs a count and overflow signal to indicate timing results. The documentation is minimal and refers to an external readme for details, so the exact operation is not fully described here. It is a characterization experiment focused on delay measurement.
tt06/tt_um_ericsmi_weste_problem_4_11.review_notes: Corrected tags to characterization/incomplete and removed unsupported education/transistor-level; summary adjusted to avoid claiming educational intent.

tt06/tt_um_exai_izhikevich_neuron.summary: This design implements the Izhikevich spiking neuron model in digital hardware with configurable A and B parameters and selectable neuron modes. It accepts a 5-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit signed membrane potential, with parameters set via input pins. The design is verified using a cocotb testbench that sweeps modes, parameters, and input currents. External hardware is required to drive the inputs and read the output, making it suitable for neuromorphic computing experiments.
tt06/tt_um_exai_izhikevich_neuron.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'education'; added 'neural-network' and 'spiking-neural-network' to match the Izhikevich spiking neuron model.

tt06/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module that either outputs a counter or mirrors the bidirectional pins to the output pins based on a select input. When select is high, a counter is driven onto both the output and bidirectional pins; when low, the bidirectional pins are passed through to the outputs. Silicon test reports indicate the counter function works as expected. The design is used for validating the Tiny Tapeout manufacturing process.
tt06/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed beyond confirming the factory-test and counter tags.

tt06/tt_um_faramire_gate_guesser.summary: Gate Guesser is a simple game where the user must deduce which logic gate connects each input to each output. The design contains one layer of combinational logic with 16 inputs and 8 outputs, each output being a specific logic function of one or two inputs. To play, the user connects switches to the inputs and LEDs to the outputs, then flips switches to observe the outputs and identify the gates. The solution is provided in the documentation as a spoiler.

tt06/tt_um_faramire_stopwatch.summary: This is a simple stopwatch that counts in hundredths of a second and displays the time on an 8-digit 7-segment display via SPI using a MAX7219 chip. It includes start/stop, lap time, and reset inputs, with outputs for SPI MOSI, CS, and CLK, as well as status signals. The design divides a 1 MHz clock to 100 Hz to drive the counters. External hardware needed includes buttons for control and a MAX7219-compatible display.

tt06/tt_um_fdc_chip.summary: This chip combines asynchronous and synchronous frequency-to-digital converters, selectable via a multiplexer. It takes a reference clock and a VCO signal as inputs and outputs a 5-bit digital value representing the measured frequency. The design was tested using an Analog Discovery 2 and reportedly worked flawlessly across all configurations. External hardware such as a waveform generator and logic analyzer is required for testing.
tt06/tt_um_fdc_chip.review_notes: Removed vco and multiplexer tags that describe pin names rather than implemented circuits.

tt06/tt_um_flappy_bird.summary: This design implements a simplified version of Flappy Bird on an 8x8 LED matrix. It uses two buttons for up and down control, with the matrix rows and columns driven by the output and bidirectional pins. The design was verified using waveform/simulation testing and then on an FPGA before fabrication. External hardware required includes two buttons and an 8x8 LED matrix.
tt06/tt_um_flappy_bird.review_notes: Added fpga and retro; clarified test flow as simulation followed by FPGA verification.

tt06/tt_um_fountaincoder_top.summary: multimac is a multi-use accelerator that computes vector dot products, minimums, and maximums on 4-bit data. It operates as a coprocessor, loading data via index and data pins and executing when run is asserted, producing a 12-bit result after at least 16 clock cycles. The design was tested using Verilator simulation with a C++ workbench, focusing on numerical stability. It is intended to be driven by an RP2040 for vector calculations.
tt06/tt_um_fountaincoder_top.review_notes: Removed comparator because min/max/dot-product functionality is covered by accelerator and not a dedicated comparator description.

tt06/tt_um_fpu.summary: Dgrid_FPU is a floating-point unit that performs two multiplications followed by an addition on four 32-bit inputs, producing a 32-bit output. It uses an 8-bit interface to load 128 bits of input over 16 clock cycles and read the result over 4 clock cycles, with a total operation taking 24 cycles. The design conforms to IEEE 754 and is intended for AI accelerators and DSP applications. Testing involves resetting, writing data, waiting for computation, and reading the output. The documentation describes the datapath and serial interface in detail, but does not state a 40 MHz operating frequency or actual measured performance.
tt06/tt_um_fpu.review_notes: Proposed tags are supported; summary adjusted to keep exactly four sentences and avoid restating clock/performance claims not in the source.

tt06/tt_um_frq_divider.summary: This design is a clock divider that uses a counter and a ROM to generate one of 27 output frequencies from a 50 MHz input. The ROM stores division parameters selected by a 4-bit input, and it outputs a 28-bit value to configure the counter. To use it, a 50 MHz oscillator is needed, and the output can be observed with an oscilloscope or fed into a microcontroller. The design is a simple frequency synthesizer based on a look-up table.

tt06/tt_um_fstolzcode.summary: Tiny Zuse is a minimal floating-point unit inspired by the Zuse Z3, supporting addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and square root. It communicates over a 9600 baud UART, where commands are sent as bytes to load registers and perform operations; results are read back in a 3-byte format. The design was tested with basic addition and a subset of the provided testbench, and silicon tests confirmed correct operation. It requires only the on-board UART connection to a host for control.
tt06/tt_um_fstolzcode.review_notes: Removed cpu, alu, and coprocessor tags; source describes a floating-point unit, not a processor or ALU.

tt06/tt_um_g3f.summary: This project implements a digital three-phase generator that produces three square-wave outputs with 120-degree phase shifts from a single input clock. It uses a 3-bit Johnson counter and provides both normal and complementary outputs. The design was simulated in Quartus II and tested on an Altera Cyclone II FPGA, but it requires external signal generation and an oscilloscope for verification. The intended application is to drive three-phase motors after analog filtering, although the chip only outputs digital signals.
tt06/tt_um_g3f.review_notes: Removed unsupported application/implementation tags and added verilog; summary was already accurate.

tt06/tt_um_gabejessil_timer.summary: This is a two-player countdown timer game where players must guess when a hidden timer reaches a target time. The game uses four buttons for start, reset, and player inputs, and displays the timer on a 7-segment display. After both players have pressed their buttons, the displayed times are shown. It requires an external PMOD 7-segment display and a PMOD button module for operation.
tt06/tt_um_gabejessil_timer.review_notes: Removed unsupported game tag and added puzzle tag for the guessing mechanic.

tt06/tt_um_gak25_8bit_cpu_ext.summary: This is an 8-bit single-cycle CPU based on Ramyad Hadidi's 'CPU In a Week' design, extended with CLR and MUL instructions. It includes a register file and an ALU, and supports basic ALU operations, load/store, and status checks, but lacks a program counter and external memory. The processor is tested through 12 testbenches covering basic functionality, though timing interactions are not fully verified. It is described as operating within a simulated environment with no external hardware interface.
tt06/tt_um_gak25_8bit_cpu_ext.review_notes: Removed 'combinational' because the CPU is not purely combinational; added 'risc-v' as a correction to prevent an unsupported ISA tag from being added.

tt06/tt_um_gray_sobel.summary: This design performs grayscale conversion and Sobel edge detection on an image. It receives pixel data via an SPI interface and can be configured for bypass, grayscale, Sobel, or combined processing. An internal LFSR can generate test pixels. The output is a single processed pixel per input, and external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi is needed to send data over SPI.
tt06/tt_um_gray_sobel.review_notes: Removed fir-filter and edge-detector tags that misdescribe the image processing; added image-processing, spi, lfsr, and dsp.

tt06/tt_um_guitar_pedal.summary: This is an analog distortion pedal circuit consisting of eight opamps in series, each of which can be bypassed via digital inputs to control the amount of distortion. It operates from a 1.8V supply and produces distortion by overdriving the opamps. External hardware including capacitors, resistors, and jacks is required for input biasing and output connection. Silicon testing showed partial functionality, with distortion observed only up to the first two amplifiers.
tt06/tt_um_guitar_pedal.review_notes: Removed unsupported tags and added correct ones based on source.

tt06/tt_um_haeuslermarkus_fir_filter.summary: This project implements an FIR filter with adaptable coefficients that can be configured through the input pins. The filter uses the symmetric step response property to store only half the coefficients, reducing memory requirements, and coefficients can be updated by enabling a configuration bit. It was tested with impulse and step responses, and can be driven by any microcontroller or even buttons and LEDs. The design is useful for learning about digital filters.
tt06/tt_um_haeuslermarkus_fir_filter.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart tag; added verilog and arithmetic tags supported by the source.

tt06/tt_um_histefan_top.summary: This is a simple implementation of the Snake game with VGA output. The snake can be controlled with four buttons, and the game resets upon collision. It requires a 25.179 MHz clock for correct VGA timing and uses a Tiny VGA PMOD for output. Silicon testing confirmed that it works correctly.

tt06/tt_um_hpretl_tt06_tdc.summary: This is a synthesized time-to-digital converter (TDC) that measures the time delay between a start signal and the clock using an interleaved delay line. The captured result is muxed out byte by byte via output pins. It requires two external signal generators to provide the start signal and clock with a known delay. Silicon testing showed partial functionality, with bits changing when a ~7ns delay was applied.

tt06/tt_um_hpretl_tt06_tdc_v2.summary: This design is a synthesized time-to-digital converter (TDC) that measures the time interval between two input signals using two Vernier delay rings with slightly different delays. It captures the time difference on the rising edge of the stop signal and outputs the result in 8-bit chunks, selectable via input pins. The design is intended for high-resolution time measurement, with an analog-simulated resolution of about 6 ps. It requires external signal generators with nanosecond resolution to provide the start and stop signals, and it is notable for being implemented entirely in Verilog.
tt06/tt_um_hpretl_tt06_tdc_v2.review_notes: Removed 'standard-cell' as implementation style is not explicitly stated; last sentence adjusted accordingly.

tt06/tt_um_hpretl_tt06_tempsens.summary: This project implements an on-chip temperature sensor synthesized from standard cells. It measures the chip temperature and outputs the result, with a debug mode that allows direct control of the sensor's DAC and enable signals. The design is intended to be used by simply powering it on and observing the digital outputs, though a logic analyzer is recommended for inspection. The documentation is minimal, stating that a better explanation will be provided in the future, but the pin descriptions and debug instructions provide enough detail to understand its operation.
tt06/tt_um_hpretl_tt06_tempsens.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested tag because no silicon test reports are available.

tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc.summary: This is a tiny time-to-digital converter (TDC) constructed entirely from standard cells, using a Skywater130 FA-2 delay element. It measures the time between launch and capture clocks and outputs a 7-bit hardware value along with a valid signal. The design includes power-gating control signals and is intended to be tested using VCS simulation with gate-level netlists. External hardware is not required beyond connecting the pins, and the design is notable for its all-standard-cell implementation and inclusion of power-gating features.
tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc.review_notes: Added multi-tile because the design spans a 1x2 tile area.

tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc_buf.summary: This is a tiny time-to-digital converter (TDC) constructed entirely from standard cells, using a Skywater130 AND-2 delay element. It measures the time between launch and capture clocks and outputs a 7-bit hardware value along with a valid signal. The design includes power-gating control signals and is intended to be tested using VCS simulation with gate-level netlists. External hardware is not required beyond connecting the pins, and the design is notable for its all-standard-cell implementation and inclusion of power-gating features.
tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc_buf.review_notes: Added multi-tile because the design spans a 1x2 tile area.

tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc_mux.summary: This is a tiny time-to-digital converter (TDC) constructed entirely from standard cells, using a Skywater130 MUX2x1 delay element. It measures the time between launch and capture clocks and outputs a 7-bit hardware value along with a valid signal. The design includes power-gating control signals and is intended to be tested using VCS simulation with gate-level netlists. External hardware is not required beyond connecting the pins, and the design is notable for its all-standard-cell implementation and inclusion of power-gating features.
tt06/tt_um_hsc_tdc_mux.review_notes: Added multi-tile because the design spans a 1x2 tile area.

tt06/tt_um_htfab_flash_adc.summary: This is a 4-bit flash analog-to-digital converter (ADC) that uses a resistor ladder to generate 15 reference voltages and comparators to produce a unary output, which is then encoded into binary using a digital encoder with error correction. It includes debug modes to independently test the ADC and the encoder, and provides additional outputs for monitoring unary bits and XOR/mux functions. The design requires an analog input voltage between 0 and 1.8 V, and can be tested with a simple potentiometer or a microcontroller-generated PWM signal with an RC filter. Silicon tests have confirmed its functionality, with testers observing correct operation using sine waves and manual sweeping.

tt06/tt_um_i_tree_batzolislefteris.summary: This design implements an anomaly detection system using an isolation tree algorithm, intended for integration into SoCs with AI accelerators. It consists of an input buffer that collects sensor data bit-by-bit, and a state machine that processes the data to detect anomalies based on a predefined byte pattern. The design is currently simplistic, checking against a set pattern, but is intended to be expanded to more complex algorithms. It requires a binary output sensor as external hardware and is designed for real-time anomaly detection in embedded applications.

tt06/tt_um_ian_keypad_controller.summary: This project is a keypad controller that scans a 4x4 keypad by driving columns and reading rows to detect key presses. The detected key is decoded and displayed on a single 7-segment display. The design operates at a low clock frequency of 1000 Hz and requires an external keypad PMOD connected to the bidirectional pins. It is a simple interface project intended for experimenting with keypad input and display output.

tt06/tt_um_iron_violet_simon.summary: This design implements a memory game similar to Simon, where the device plays a sequence of button-lamp colors and the player must repeat the sequence by pressing corresponding buttons. The game keeps a high score until power is lost or reset, and ends when the player makes a mistake, waits too long, or reaches 32 moves. It requires four buttons and four lamps connected to the specified pins, plus a start button. The design is notable for its simple implementation of a classic game with high-score tracking and visual feedback.
tt06/tt_um_iron_violet_simon.review_notes: Removed sequencer and added puzzle to better match the memory game described in the source.

tt06/tt_um_ja1tye_tiny_cpu.summary: This is a tiny 8-bit CPU with an SPI Flash and PSRAM controller, designed to execute programs stored in external SPI Flash and use PSRAM for data memory. It includes GPIO pins for general-purpose I/O and a dedicated SPI transmitter. The CPU loads instructions from address 0x0000 on the SPI Flash after reset, and a macro assembler is available for programming. External hardware includes SPI Flash and optionally SPI PSRAM, and the design is notable for its compact integration of a CPU with external memory controllers.

tt06/tt_um_jduchniewicz_prng.summary: This project implements an 8-bit pseudo-random number generator based on a 16-bit linear feedback shift register with a twist: the upper and lower halves are rotated in opposite directions and XORed. It is tested by observing the generated sequence on the output pins, and the initialization seed can be changed via the input pins. All-zero initialization is invalid and produces a constant zero output. The design is notable for its modified LFSR structure that combines two rotated halves.

tt06/tt_um_jorgenkraghjakobsen_toi2s.summary: This project converts SPDIF audio to I2S format for a ClassD amplifier MA12070p. It oversamples the SPDIF input using a 27 MHz system clock, regenerates the I2S bit clock by counting system clock cycles between SPDIF edges, and detects left/right sync words to toggle the I2S word-select signal. PCM samples are decoded from phase/mark changes, shifted into left and right FIFOs, and output on i2s_d0 from the non-active FIFO in reversed order. Silicon test reports working read/write I2C register access, PWM output, I2C communication with the amplifier, and SPDIF decoding to I2S with good audio, using a clock set to 27 MHz.
tt06/tt_um_jorgenkraghjakobsen_toi2s.review_notes: Tags were missing key documented interfaces and status; summary described only clock generation and omitted the SPDIF-to-I2S conversion.

tt06/tt_um_jv_sigdel.summary: This project implements a first-order passive sigma-delta analog-to-digital converter that requires external resistors and a capacitor connected to a digital input pin. The analog input is sampled and converted to a digital output using sigma-delta modulation. It is tested by applying an analog voltage and observing the digital output. The design is notable for its use of passive components and sigma-delta technique.

tt06/tt_um_kevinwguan.summary: This is an analog crossbar array used as a placeholder for future ReRAM projects, with poly resistors instead of ReRAM between Met1 and Met2 giving a fixed weight matrix. It performs 4x4 matrix multiplication in one run, using the first four analog pins as crossbar inputs, ua[4] as the 0-1.8V supply, and ua[5] as the output current summing junction. The first four digital inputs control four 4-bit input muxes, and ui_in[4:7] control column selection. External off-the-shelf DACs and ADCs, including a TIA or ADC to convert output current to voltage, are required.
tt06/tt_um_kevinwguan.review_notes: Corrected tags to analog/mixed-signal/placeholder/multiplier and rewrote summary to match the actual crossbar documentation.

tt06/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This project is a RISC-V based system-on-chip that includes a CPU, memory, and UART, SPI, and QSPI interfaces. It is used by loading and running programs via the serial interfaces. The design includes a memory subsystem and peripheral interfaces. It is notable for its integration of a RISC-V core with multiple communication interfaces.

tt06/tt_um_koconnor_kstep.summary: This project is a stepper motor controller that uses an SPI interface to receive commands. It generates step and direction pulses for stepper motor drivers, with programmable pulse duration, interval, count, and direction. The design also provides interrupt and shutdown control signals. It has been tested on silicon and reported working by the author.
tt06/tt_um_koconnor_kstep.review_notes: Removed unsupported timer and signal-generator tags and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt06/tt_um_ks_pyamnihc.summary: This project is an audio synthesizer that generates sound using an LFSR-based noise source and an I2S output. It is controlled via SPI and includes a TRNG for randomness. The design produces audio output through an I2S interface. It is notable for its combination of synthesis and random generation.

tt06/tt_um_kwilke_cdc_fifo.summary: This project is a clock domain crossing FIFO that handles data transfer between two asynchronous clock domains. It can hold 32 4-bit values, or 16 bytes. It includes write and read reset signals, and status outputs for empty and full. Testing involves holding the resets LOW while running the clocks, then raising them to initialize the module.
tt06/tt_um_kwilke_cdc_fifo.review_notes: Added systemverilog tag; corrected summary to reflect capacity and reset procedure from the source, removing unsupported design influence and purpose claims.

tt06/tt_um_lancemitrex.summary: This project decodes a 4-bit binary input into a hexadecimal digit and displays it on a 7-segment display. The input is set via DIP switches, and the output is shown on the display. It is used for educational purposes to demonstrate binary-to-hex conversion. The design is notable for its simple decoder and display interface.

tt06/tt_um_ledcontroller_Gatsch.summary: This project is a WS2812 LED controller that uses an I2C interface to receive commands and drives WS2812B LEDs. It includes a register file for storing LED data. It is tested by connecting WS2812B LEDs and an I2C master such as a microcontroller. The design is notable for its LED control capability.

tt06/tt_um_lipsi_schoeberl.summary: Lipsi is a tiny 8-bit accumulator-based processor implemented in Chisel that executes a hardcoded counting program. The count is displayed on a 7-segment display, and the decimal point blinks in hardware. It is tested with ChiselTest for waveform generation, though the cocotb test is currently disabled. The author reports that the silicon works as intended.
tt06/tt_um_lipsi_schoeberl.review_notes: Removed education and led tags; added silicon-tested based on working silicon report.

tt06/tt_um_lisa.summary: LISA is an 8-bit microcontroller SoC with 128 bytes of DFFRAM, designed for embedded control. It includes a BrainFloat16 FPU, timers, GPIO, UART, SPI/QSPI, and I2C master, and can interface with external flash and RAM. A C-based toolchain (assembler, linker, C compiler) and a Python debugger are provided, though the C compiler is incomplete and buggy. Silicon testing confirmed the core, debugger, DFFRAM, SPI/QSPI, FPU, timers, GPIO, and UART, but I2C and the DFFRAM cache controller remain untested.
tt06/tt_um_lisa.review_notes: Added silicon-tested, rp2040, and pmod tags supported by the test report and recommended pinouts.

tt06/tt_um_liu3hao_rv32e_min_mcu.summary: This is a minimal RV32E microcontroller that uses external SPI NOR flash for program memory and SPI PSRAM for data memory. It provides GPIO, UART with optional flow control, an SPI bus, and a debug interface over SPI. The design was tested on a Lattice iCE40-HX8K breakout board at 24 MHz. External hardware required includes SPI flash and PSRAM Pmods.
tt06/tt_um_liu3hao_rv32e_min_mcu.review_notes: Removed memory because no on-chip memory is implemented; added pmod based on required external Pmods.

tt06/tt_um_lk_ans_top.summary: This project implements an Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) encoder and decoder in Verilog. The design accepts data via a streaming interface and outputs compressed or decompressed data. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a one-line description and no details on testing or usage. External hardware requirements are not specified.

tt06/tt_um_loco_choco.summary: This is a hardware processor for the esoteric Brainfuck language, implementing 75% of the instruction set (excluding I/O operations). It uses an external address register and requires separate program and data memories of at least 256x8 each, expandable to 1KB. The design can be driven with a clock of about 20 MHz and can interface with SRAM, ROM, and LED bars for output. The documentation includes a state machine diagram and pinout but no silicon test results.
tt06/tt_um_loco_choco.review_notes: Adjusted summary to state the recommended clock as about 20 MHz rather than implying an observed operating speed.

tt06/tt_um_lucaz97_monobit.summary: This design implements the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for random number generators using high-level synthesis. It samples one bit per clock cycle and evaluates randomness over 65536 cycles, asserting a valid signal when the result is ready. The design requires only a clock and input bit, with no external hardware currently needed. The documentation is minimal and does not include test results or usage examples.
tt06/tt_um_lucaz97_monobit.review_notes: Removed prng and trng tags because the design is a randomness test, not a random number generator.

tt06/tt_um_lucaz97_rng_tests.summary: This project is another implementation of the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for random number generators, using high-level synthesis. It operates similarly to the other Monobit test design, sampling one bit per clock and producing a result every 65536 cycles. The documentation is identical to the other entry and lacks details on testing or external hardware. No silicon test results are provided.
tt06/tt_um_lucaz97_rng_tests.review_notes: Removed prng and trng tags because the design is a randomness test, not a random number generator.

tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_inverter.summary: This is an analog double inverter consisting of a small inverter followed by a larger one to drive higher loads while maintaining fast rise times. It is a transistor-level design with one analog input and one analog output. Testing involves applying a pulse to the input and observing the output on an oscilloscope. No silicon test results are provided.
tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_inverter.review_notes: Removed logic-gate because the design is an analog inverter, not a digital logic gate.

tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac.summary: This is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter with an optional sawtooth waveform generator. It can be driven externally via digital inputs or by the internal generator, and the analog output is on a single pin. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the output voltage. Silicon tests confirm it works, with one tester observing a sawtooth at ~600 mV and frequencies up to 1 MHz.

tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_relax_osc.summary: This is an analog relaxation oscillator designed to produce a ~2 MHz signal, with an inverter providing a full-swing square wave output. The analog output is on one pin and the digital square wave on another. Silicon tests show it oscillates at around 1 MHz, but the frequency is highly sensitive to loading on the analog pin, and a 10k pulldown must be removed for oscillation. The author notes that loading the analog output can stop oscillation due to the lack of a buffer.
tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_relax_osc.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added silicon-tested per the working test report.

tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
tt06/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

tt06/tt_um_mayrmichael_wave_generator.summary: The Wave Generator produces sine, sawtooth, triangular, and square waveforms with selectable amplitude and phase parameters, outputting 8-bit two's complement fixed-point values in parallel or via a write-only SPI interface. It is configured by setting waveform selection pins and loading amplitude and phase values through a parameter bus, then enabling generation. An external SPI DAC is needed to convert the digital output to an analog signal. The design provides flexible parameter control and SPI output for connecting to a DAC, with a maximum sampling frequency of 1.65 MHz.
tt06/tt_um_mayrmichael_wave_generator.review_notes: Removed dac tag because the source only mentions an external DAC, not an on-chip DAC.

tt06/tt_um_mbalestrini_usb_cdc_devices.summary: This design implements a Full Speed USB communications device class (CDC) device with two virtual serial ports. It is based on an existing USB CDC repository and appears to a PC as two COM ports, each with a different application. Testing requires a 48 MHz clock, a USB cable, a 1.5k resistor, and a computer, with optional buttons for inputs. A silicon test report confirms that the device enumerated as two serial ports and that each input sent a capital then lower case letter.
tt06/tt_um_mbalestrini_usb_cdc_devices.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated RISC-V/SoC/QSPI/ROM/SystemVerilog tags with USB, UART, communication, and silicon-tested based on the actual source and test report.

tt06/tt_um_meiniKi_tt06_fazyrv_exotiny.summary: FazyRV-ExoTiny is a minimal System-on-Chip based on the FazyRV RISC-V core that uses external QSPI ROM and RAM for program storage and data memory. It converts Wishbone bus accesses into QSPI transfers, enabling continuous mode for the ROM to reduce latency, and supports Quad Mode for the RAM. The design requires external QSPI flash and RAM chips, such as the W25Q128JV and APS6404L-3SQR, and careful reset synchronization; its implementation is near the edge of timing convergence.

tt06/tt_um_minibyte.summary: The Minibyte CPU is a simple 8-bit processor featuring a custom RISC instruction set, built-in design-for-test features, and an optional demo ROM for easy testing. It exposes debug output select lines, halt control, and a register enable, along with an 8-bit data bus and address/write-enable outputs. The design was created primarily as a learning and reference project to gain familiarity with Verilog. It requires some external hardware to run the demo ROM.

tt06/tt_um_mitssdd.summary: This co-processor reads data from four sensors sequentially and compares each reading to previous data to detect deviations, also identifying sensor faults and providing warning signals along with sensor identification. It is intended for precision farming applications and requires an external 8-bit ADC to convert sensor data. The design outputs a deviation detector signal, fault warnings, and sensor identifiers. The documentation is limited to a basic description and a single test example, without full implementation details.
tt06/tt_um_mitssdd.review_notes: Removed unsupported adc and fsm tags; added industrial tag for precision farming application.

tt06/tt_um_motor.summary: This design implements a stepper motor controller using a Moore state machine with selectable speeds (1s, 0.5s, 0.25s, 0.125s), direction control, and three step types: full, half, and double. It is controlled by inputs for reset, select, direction, and step mode, and outputs four coil signals. External hardware includes an FPGA (Cyclone II EP2C35F672C6ES) for testing, and the design is documented in Spanish with simulation waveforms for various combinations.
