The project appears to be an educational exercise, providing a didactic implementation of stepper motor control.
tt06/tt_um_motor.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

tt06/tt_um_moving_average_master.summary: This design implements a 10-bit moving average filter that smooths input data streams using registers and a finite state machine, with the filter width determined by the FILTER_POWER parameter. It processes digital input values presented on the ui_in port and produces smoothed outputs on uo_out, with control signals on uio_in to select filter width and operation. The design includes strobe input and output for data synchronization. Testing involves providing varying input patterns and filter widths to evaluate the filter's response.
tt06/tt_um_moving_average_master.review_notes: Corrected tags: removed unsupported fir-filter and incorrect combinational, added dsp; summary unchanged.

tt06/tt_um_mult_2b.summary: This project is a simple 2-bit multiplier implemented using combinational logic gates, specifically AND gates and half adders made from AND and XOR gates. It takes two 2-bit inputs (a and b) and produces a 4-bit product output, with a full truth table provided in the documentation. External hardware required includes a 4-position DIP switch for inputs and 4 LEDs for outputs, both with appropriate resistors. The design is presented as a practical and didactic exercise to go from Verilog description to a physical circuit.

tt06/tt_um_mw73_pmic.summary: This power management IC generates two complementary PWM outputs with duty cycles controlled by an external ADC, using a heartbeat signal to periodically initiate ADC conversions and update the PWM. It reads an 8-bit parallel ADC (AD7819) and drives a high-side driver (MCP14700) for a half-bridge configuration, with a built-in dead zone to prevent shoot-through. The design uses state machines to sequence the ADC read and PWM update so the two outputs remain 180 degrees out of phase. External hardware includes the specified ADC and high-side driver.
tt06/tt_um_mw73_pmic.review_notes: Added driver tag for the explicit external gate-driver outputs; summary lightly qualified to match source.

tt06/tt_um_neurocore.summary: Neurocore implements a 2x2 systolic array multiplier that computes the product of two 2x2 matrices using 16-bit floating-point arithmetic. It communicates over a UART interface, receiving matrix elements as two 8-bit frames each and returning the result in the same format. The design is intended for matrix multiplication tasks. Testing requires an external UART connection to send and receive data according to the documented protocol.
tt06/tt_um_neurocore.review_notes: Removed neural-network and dsp tags not supported by the source; summary now avoids implying those applications.

tt06/tt_um_nicklausthompson_twi_monitor.summary: The TWI Monitor passively observes I2C bus traffic and converts captured frames into a three-byte UART output representing address, data, and acknowledgment bits. It operates at 50 MHz with a UART baud rate of 115,200 and does not act as an I2C slave. The design was tested on an FPGA and can capture single frames but not repeated frames. External hardware includes an I2C source such as an Arduino and a UART-to-USB adapter for viewing the output on a PC.

tt06/tt_um_noritsuna_i4004.summary: This project is a Verilog implementation of the Intel 4004, a 4-bit microprocessor, designed for the Tiny Tapeout platform. It requires external hardware, specifically an MCS4 memory system, to function. The documentation is minimal, providing only a link to a Japanese Wikipedia page and no testing instructions. The design's operation and verification are not detailed in the provided documentation.

tt06/tt_um_nubcore_default_tape.summary: This Verilog design displays the string 'dEFAULt123' on a 7-segment LED display. Its outputs drive segments a through g and the dot. The documentation is extremely sparse, with no explanation of how the design works or how to test it beyond powering it on. No external hardware requirements are stated beyond the 7-segment display itself.
tt06/tt_um_nubcore_default_tape.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc since the display function is clearly stated; summary trimmed to four supported sentences.

tt06/tt_um_nurirfansyah_alits01.summary: This is an analog voltage-controlled ring oscillator (VCRO) that uses transmission gates as delay control elements, based on a published paper. It provides an analog output and requires external control voltages on two pins, with the sum ideally equal to the 1.8V supply. The design is intended for testing and characterization of the oscillator's frequency tuning range. It is a transistor-level analog circuit with no digital interface.

tt06/tt_um_obriensp_be8.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU based on Ben Eater's breadboard CPU design, featuring a built-in debugger accessible via I2C at address 0x2A. The debugger allows pausing the CPU, loading programs, and inspecting or modifying registers. The CPU has 8 input and 8 output pins for external data, and it can be halted via a dedicated pin. Silicon testing confirmed it works when connected to a BusPirate over I2C.

tt06/tt_um_obriensp_be8_nomacro.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU based on Ben Eater's breadboard CPU design, featuring a built-in debugger accessible via I2C at address 0x2A. The debugger allows pausing the CPU, loading programs, and inspecting or modifying registers. The CPU has 8 input and 8 output pins for external data, and it can be halted via a dedicated pin. Silicon testing confirmed it works when connected to a BusPirate over I2C.

tt06/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: Oscillating Bones is a ring oscillator built from a chain of 21 SkullFET inverters, producing a square wave output around 90 MHz. It provides divided frequency outputs at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 of the base frequency. Silicon tests measured frequencies between about 87 and 91 MHz on the base and divided outputs, with some testers observing lower frequencies on divided outputs. It requires an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe the output waveforms.
tt06/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Summary corrected: the 87-91 MHz range applies to the base frequency, while lower readings were on divided outputs.

tt06/tt_um_otp_encryptor.summary: This design implements an 8-bit encryption and decryption unit using pseudorandom one-time pads. It accepts plaintext or ciphertext on 8 input pins, uses a control pin to select encryption or decryption, and outputs the result on 8 output pins. For encryption, it generates a random pad, XORs it with the plaintext, and stores the pad in an internal register file, outputting the register index. For decryption, it uses the provided index to retrieve the pad and recover the plaintext.

tt06/tt_um_pckys_game.summary: This is a game where the player tries to guess a pseudo-random 8-bit number by successive approximation, similar to the algorithm used in SAR ADCs. The player inputs an 8-bit guess via DIP switches, and a 7-segment LED indicates whether the guess is above, below, or equal to the secret number. The secret number is generated upon reset, and the player can keep guessing until they find it. Silicon testing confirmed it works on the demo board using its DIP switches and 7-segment LED.

tt06/tt_um_petersn_micro1.summary: This project is a simple computer that renders to VGA, designed in the last 14 hours before the submission deadline. It requires an external SPI SRAM and an external VGA breakout board to operate. The documentation is minimal and does not explain how the computer works or how to test it. The design is notable for being created under extreme time pressure, but its functionality is uncertain.
tt06/tt_um_petersn_micro1.review_notes: Removed unsupported cpu and memory tags; added incomplete because the source admits the design may not work and documentation is TODO.

tt06/tt_um_ppca.summary: This design implements a simple shooting game in a 32x32 grid where the player controls a cannon to hit a randomly placed target. The cannon can be moved left or right and aimed in seven different directions, and the projectile bounces off side walls. The game outputs the target coordinates and a hit/miss result, and is controlled via five input pins. The design is a projectile positioning calculation accelerator, but the documentation focuses on gameplay rather than hardware implementation.
tt06/tt_um_ppca.review_notes: Removed accelerator because the project is a game; added puzzle for the aiming/trajectory gameplay.

tt06/tt_um_ps2_morse_encoder_top.summary: This project converts PS/2 keyboard input into Morse code output, supporting alphanumeric characters. It provides separate outputs for dits and dahs, a combined Morse output, and a 600Hz square wave for a buzzer. The design has two modes: one triggered by Enter and another by Space, and it generates Morse at approximately 15 WPM. Silicon testing confirmed it works at 1MHz, and it requires a PS/2 keyboard and an optional buzzer or speaker.

tt06/tt_um_psychogenic_wowa.summary: This mixed-signal design implements a simple ADC using an analog comparator, an R2R DAC, and digital control logic. It performs a search to determine the digital value corresponding to an analog input, with optional comparator calibration. The design includes a p3 opamp for testing and provides analog pins for inspection. Silicon testing showed good conversions at 10MHz, and it requires an external voltage source and a way to read the digital outputs.
tt06/tt_um_psychogenic_wowa.review_notes: Removed incorrect sar-adc tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

tt06/tt_um_qubitbytes_alive.summary: This design plays a tune through a speaker or piezo buzzer connected to a bidirectional pin. It uses a 7-segment display to indicate the current song part and activity, and requires a 100kHz clock for correct pitch. The reset button restarts the song, and if the display shows '0', the user should press reset. Silicon testing confirmed it successfully played a tune, and it was created by a beginner who learned Verilog within 24 hours.
tt06/tt_um_qubitbytes_alive.review_notes: Added audio tag because the design is a song player; kept music, speaker, 7-segment, buzzer, verilog.

tt06/tt_um_ram.summary: This project is a 4-bit RAM with 4 address bits and 4 data input bits, providing 4 data output bits. It includes a write enable input and is clocked. Testing requires setting the address and data inputs, and the write enable, then reading the output. External hardware such as a microcontroller or switches is needed to provide inputs and addresses. The documentation is very brief and does not provide detailed implementation or test information.

tt06/tt_um_rejunity_1_58bit.summary: This design implements a matrix multiplication accelerator for ternary (1.58-bit) weights and 8-bit activations, targeting LLM inference. It uses a systolic array architecture and accepts packed weight data on input pins and activation data on bidirectional pins. Results are output on 8 output pins, and an enable pin strobes the operation. An external microcontroller is required to feed data and retrieve results.
tt06/tt_um_rejunity_1_58bit.review_notes: Removed neural-network because a matrix multiplication block is not a generic artificial neural network; added the more specific mac-unit.

tt06/tt_um_rejunity_current_cmp.summary: This analog design implements a current comparator that compares two currents formed by summing eight digital inputs each. The excitatory and inhibitory currents are set via input and bidirectional pins, and the comparator output is an analog voltage representing a sigmoid-like function. It includes debug analog pins for monitoring internal signals. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the output voltage, and the design is intended for experimentation with analog neural network primitives.
tt06/tt_um_rejunity_current_cmp.review_notes: Removed neural-network and neuromorphic because the comparator is not an ANN or neuromorphic system; added the canonical comparator-analog tag.

tt06/tt_um_rejunity_fp4_mul_i8.summary: This design implements a matrix multiplication accelerator for 4-bit floating point (E3M0) weights and 8-bit activations. It uses a systolic array architecture and accepts packed weight data on input pins and activation data on bidirectional pins. Results are output on 8 output pins, and an enable pin strobes the operation. An external microcontroller is required to feed data and retrieve results.

tt06/tt_um_rgbled_decoder.summary: This design decodes SPI input to drive a string of WS2812B RGB LEDs. It shifts 240 bits from SPI into an internal register and generates the precise pulse-width modulated output required by WS2812B LEDs. The output pin connects directly to the LED data line, and a reset pulse is generated after each full transmission. It requires an SPI master and a string of up to 10 WS2812B LEDs.

tt06/tt_um_rng.summary: This design generates a pseudo-random bit stream using an LFSR whose behaviour is selected by a mode input and seeded by four input bits. The eight output bits can be observed on LEDs or a display connected to the chip. Testing consists of varying the seed and mode and watching the output bits change. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the modes or the LFSR polynomial in detail.

tt06/tt_um_rng_3_lucaz97.summary: This design samples an input bit and evaluates whether the bit source is random using the Monobit test from NIST 800.22. It produces an is_random output that is valid only when the valid signal is high. The result is updated every 65536 cycles. The design is written in Verilog and currently requires no external hardware.
tt06/tt_um_rng_3_lucaz97.review_notes: Tags described an oscillator/DAC that does not exist; corrected to randomness-testing tags.

tt06/tt_um_s1pu11i_simple_nco.summary: This design is a simple numerically controlled oscillator that can output sine, square, or sawtooth waveforms. The sine wave is generated from a lookup table, while square and sawtooth are derived from the phase accumulator. The output is unsigned 8-bit, and the mode is selected via uio[1:0]. The frequency word is 16 bits, split into lower and upper parts updated through the input pins.
tt06/tt_um_s1pu11i_simple_nco.review_notes: Replaced incorrect UART/ADC/SPI tags with NCO and waveform generator tags based on the documentation.

tt06/tt_um_sanojn_tlv2556_interface.summary: This design is a UART interface to a TI TLV2556 ADC, allowing ADC values to be read over a serial connection. The UART settings are static, and the interface supports prompting a conversion and receiving the measured value in human-readable form. It requires a 48 MHz clock and a TLV2556 ADC connected to the appropriate pins. The design also supports a continuous mode that loops through all channels and prints measured values.
tt06/tt_um_sanojn_tlv2556_interface.review_notes: Corrected tags to reflect the UART-to-ADC interface; removed unrelated game and display tags.

tt06/tt_um_sanojn_ttrpg_dice.summary: This is a TTRPG dice roller with a simple I2C peripheral, implemented in Verilog. It supports rolling d4 through d20 using button inputs and can drive a two-digit 7-segment display for multi-digit results. The design includes an I2C slave, a PWM-capable GPIO, and configuration pins for display polarity. Silicon test reports are mixed, with one tester reporting no output and the author reporting all functions working.
tt06/tt_um_sanojn_ttrpg_dice.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated SAP-1 CPU; corrected to the documented dice roller and I2C peripheral.

tt06/tt_um_sap_1.summary: This design implements a SAP-1 computer, a simple as possible 8-bit computer architecture based on the Malvino and Brown book and popularized by Ben Eater. It includes modules such as a clock, program counter, registers, adder, multiplier, divider, memory, instruction register, bus, and controller. The computer can perform addition and subtraction, with operations coordinated by a controller through six stages. The output is read from the 8-bit bus using an oscilloscope.
tt06/tt_um_sap_1.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the source; corrected to reflect the SAP-1 computer.

tt06/tt_um_scorbetta_goa.summary: This design implements a single neuron using fixed-point arithmetic. It uses an external FPGA clock for the core and an on-board RP2040 clock for debug purposes. Control and status are exchanged over an SCI interface that requires synchronization. The design is written in Verilog and includes debug outputs.
tt06/tt_um_scorbetta_goa.review_notes: Tags were for a PWM/button design; corrected to neural-network and clocking/synchronization tags.

tt06/tt_um_seven_segment_fun1.summary: This project displays many different animations on a 7-segment display, implemented in Verilog. It is essentially a counter whose speed can be changed, combined with switchable animations. Four buttons control incrementing/decrementing the animation and speed. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester could not see speed changes.
tt06/tt_um_seven_segment_fun1.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated multiplier; corrected to the documented 7-segment animation project.

tt06/tt_um_shivam.summary: This Verilog module generates a PWM signal with an adjustable duty cycle from a 50 MHz clock input. Two debounced button inputs increase or decrease the duty cycle, and the PWM output runs at 5 MHz. The duty cycle can vary from 0% to 90% in 10% increments. Hardware testing confirmed the buttons adjust the PWM, though the documented pinout is incorrect.
tt06/tt_um_shivam.review_notes: Replaced incorrect empty-draft tags with tags supported by the PWM documentation and working silicon report.

tt06/tt_um_signed_unsigned_4x4_bit_multi.summary: This combinational multiplier takes a 4-bit multiplicand and 4-bit multiplier and produces an 8-bit product. A signed_mode input selects whether the operands are treated as unsigned or signed using the Modified Baugh-Wooley algorithm. In unsigned mode the multiplier uses an array of full-adder and AND-gate cells, with a ripple-carry adder forming the upper product bits. It can be tested on a Tiny Tapeout demoboard by setting the switches and reading the product on a 7-segment display.
tt06/tt_um_signed_unsigned_4x4_bit_multi.review_notes: Replaced incorrect empty-draft tags with tags matching the documented and silicon-tested multiplier.

tt06/tt_um_silicon_tinytapeout_lm07.summary: This design reads 8-bit temperature data from an LM70 sensor over SPI and displays it on a 7-segment display. It can be tested without external hardware by using an RP2040 to emulate the sensor and provide the clock, with modes to show MSB or LSB. External hardware includes an LM70 sensor and a 7-segment display. Silicon testing confirmed it works when connected to a real LM70 sensor.
tt06/tt_um_silicon_tinytapeout_lm07.review_notes: Removed redundant generic display tag and added silicon-tested and rp2040 tags supported by the test report and procedure.

tt06/tt_um_simplez_rcoeurjoly.summary: Simplez is a small CPU implemented in Verilog, with a single tile. Its pins include a serial receive input, a serial transmit output, and a stop indicator. The documentation is very thin, consisting only of links to an external GitHub repository, so the design's operation and test procedure are not described here. External hardware details are likewise not given in the source.
tt06/tt_um_simplez_rcoeurjoly.review_notes: Removed led and uart because neither is supported by the source; the only documentation is external links.

tt06/tt_um_soundgen.summary: This design plays a prelude.wav file in an endless loop using a sine lookup table with varying frequency, output as a PWM signal. It is intended to be tested by connecting a piezo speaker to the PWM pins and listening. External hardware required is a piezo. A silicon test report indicates the design is broken, with no output observed.
tt06/tt_um_soundgen.review_notes: Adjusted tags to match the stored-waveform PWM audio source rather than implying generic synthesis.

tt06/tt_um_spi_pwm_djuara.summary: This design is an SPI-controlled PWM generator and 8-bit IO controller with two SPI interfaces for testing. It contains eight registers that configure PWM on-time and cycle, and eight IO pins that can be set as inputs or outputs. Testing involves reading an ID register and writing/reading back registers via SPI. External hardware needed is an SPI master device.

tt06/tt_um_spiff42_exp_led_pwm.summary: This is an 8-channel PWM controller for LED brightness, using an exponential (X^3) duty cycle curve to provide linear perceived brightness with 8-bit input. It can be controlled either by the ui inputs or via I2C, with the first I2C write switching to I2C mode. Testing can be done by adjusting DIP switches to see different brightness levels on a 7-segment LED display. External hardware includes LEDs and optionally an I2C master.
tt06/tt_um_spiff42_exp_led_pwm.review_notes: Removed display and 7-segment tags not supported as design interfaces.

tt06/tt_um_ss_register.summary: This project implements a serial-in serial-out shift register with four internal registers and selectable left or right shifting. It has inputs for data, clock, reset, enable, and shift direction, and a single data output. Testing involves applying clock edges with reset low and enable high, and observing the shifted data. External hardware may include a signal generator for clock and buttons or switches for inputs.
tt06/tt_um_ss_register.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the source describes a shift register only.

tt06/tt_um_stepper.summary: This design is a state machine that controls a bipolar stepper motor with four output bits, plus enable and direction inputs. It requires an external clock to set the step rate. Testing involves verifying the output waveforms for enable and direction. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation.
tt06/tt_um_stepper.review_notes: Removed unsupported robotics, industrial, and gpio tags and added canonical tags for the documented stepper motor control, FSM, Verilog implementation, and silicon-tested status.

tt06/tt_um_thorkn_audiochip_v2.summary: AudioChip_V2 generates two audio waveforms as PWM outputs, intended for use in modular synthesizers. It has 12 frequency input bits and ADSR control inputs to alter the waveforms. Testing requires attaching low-pass filters to the PWM outputs to hear analog audio. External hardware includes low-pass filters.
tt06/tt_um_thorkn_audiochip_v2.review_notes: Added spinalhdl tag because the source explicitly states SpinalHDL was used.

tt06/tt_um_timer_counter_UGM.summary: This design implements a timer and counter with a 4-digit 7-segment display interface, controlled by start, stop, and mode buttons. It includes debouncing logic and can operate in manual or automatic modes. The display blinks when idle or in manual mode, and digits are driven through BCD conversion and multiplexing. The design is documented in detail.
tt06/tt_um_timer_counter_UGM.review_notes: Removed bcd because it is mentioned only as an internal display conversion, and added button for the physical control inputs.

tt06/tt_um_tiny_shader_mole99.summary: Tiny Shader is a programmable shader unit that executes a 10-instruction shader per pixel to generate images and animations, output via VGA at 640x480 with an internal resolution of 64x48. It includes an SPI interface for loading new shaders and setting a user register. Testing requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally an SPI controller. Silicon testing confirmed all features work, including custom shader upload and animation.

tt06/tt_um_toivoh_retro_console.summary: The Retro Console is an 8.5-bit retro game console implemented in Verilog across a 3x2 tile area. Its PPU generates pixels from tile, map, sprite and palette data and outputs them as VGA, while its synth mixes four voices at 96 kHz. An RP2040-based RAM emulator provides program and graphics data, and VGA output requires a Pmod; audio output is left to the RP2040 and is still to be determined. Silicon tests confirm the graphics work, but the synth portion has not been tested.
tt06/tt_um_toivoh_retro_console.review_notes: Removed memory (external RAM emulator, not on-chip memory); added silicon-tested and display.

tt06/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: VGA Experiments in Tennis is a simple Pong-like game implemented in Verilog. It uses VGA output to display paddles and a ball, with inputs for paddle movement, score reset, and speed selection. The design requires a VGA Pmod and buttons for gameplay, and supports both Mole99 and Digilent pin mappings. Silicon tests confirm it works with both Mole99 and Digilent VGA Pmods.
tt06/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported gamepad tag; added silicon-tested from the working silicon reports.

tt06/tt_um_tommythorn_4b_cpu_v2.summary: Silly 4b CPU v2 is a minimal 4-bit CPU inspired by the PDP-8, implemented in Verilog. It features 8 words of 6-bit memory, a 4-bit accumulator, and a 3-bit program counter, and can execute simple programs like Fibonacci. The CPU is controlled via input pins for commands and arguments, and outputs the accumulator and program counter. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected.
tt06/tt_um_tommythorn_4b_cpu_v2.review_notes: Added silicon-tested because the source includes a working silicon test report.

tt06/tt_um_tommythorn_ncl_lfsr.summary: This project is a small example of self-timed logic using dual redundant encoding to distinguish data and null states. It implements an LFSR in NCL logic. The documentation is incomplete and notes that the design is a trivial example. Silicon testing showed the C-gate works but the oscillator does not behave as expected.
tt06/tt_um_tommythorn_ncl_lfsr.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the NCL LFSR self-timed logic design.

tt06/tt_um_topTDC.summary: Convertidor de Tiempo a Digital (TDC) is a time-to-digital converter that measures the width of an input pulse and transmits the digital value via RS232. It includes a counter, a state machine, and an RS232 transmitter operating at 9600 baud with odd parity. The design is intended for interfacing with time-output sensors and was tested in simulation and on an FPGA development board.

tt06/tt_um_triple_watchdog.summary: Triple Watchdog is a redundant watchdog timer implemented in Verilog, consisting of three watchdog modules operating in lockstep. Each watchdog must be kicked by writing a different value to the input within a 1 ms timeout; otherwise, it sets an output pin high. The design is intended as part of a larger fault-tolerant supervisor system. No silicon test reports are provided.
tt06/tt_um_triple_watchdog.review_notes: Removed interrupt-controller because the source describes watchdog timers, not interrupt handling.

tt06/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.summary: Dickson Charge Pump is an analog circuit that boosts the input voltage to approximately 5.4 V using a 3-stage Dickson charge pump. The output voltage is divided by 6 for measurement due to the 1.8 V analog pin limit. It requires a 2 MHz clock input and was tested at various frequencies, showing best performance at 5-10 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, with output voltage around 4.3 V at optimal frequencies.
tt06/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon reports.

tt06/tt_um_urish_dffram.summary: DFFRAM Example (128 bytes) is a 128-byte RAM module implemented using a 32x32 1RW DFFRAM macro. It provides an 8-bit address bus, 8-bit data input, and 8-bit data output, with a write-enable pin. The RAM contents are not reset by the system reset. The design is a simple memory block for integration into larger systems.
tt06/tt_um_urish_dffram.review_notes: Removed sram and register-file because the source specifies a DFFRAM macro and a RAM module.

tt06/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: Simon Says game is a memory game implemented in Verilog where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors. It uses four LEDs, four buttons, a speaker for tones, and a two-digit 7-segment display for the score. The design requires external hardware including buttons, LEDs, and optionally a speaker and 7-segment display. Silicon tests confirm it works with a Simon Says PMOD.

tt06/tt_um_urish_spell.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal, stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It features 32 bytes of program memory, 32 bytes of stack, and 8 I/O pins, with a serial interface for loading programs and inspecting state. The design is tested by loading and executing SPELL programs, and silicon tests confirm it can run a program that spells 'SPELL' on a 7-segment display. It is an esoteric stack-machine processor implemented in Verilog.
tt06/tt_um_urish_spell.review_notes: Removed unsupported security tag and added silicon-tested and 7-segment evidence from the test report.

tt06/tt_um_vaf_555_timer.summary: This analog block reimplements the behaviour of a 555 timer, with threshold, trigger, discharge, reset and output pins exposed for external RC networks. It is intended to be wired on a breadboard with through-hole resistors and capacitors and configured in astable or monostable circuits taken from a 555 datasheet. A tester built the suggested astable circuit with 4.7k resistors and roughly 15uF capacitance and observed about 10Hz on the output. Silicon tests confirm it works, and its maximum frequency was not established.
tt06/tt_um_vaf_555_timer.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to reflect the silicon test result.

tt06/tt_um_vks_pll.summary: This analog tile collects separate PLL building blocks: two phase frequency detectors, a charge pump, a ring-oscillator VCO and four D flip-flop frequency dividers, each contributed by a different participant of the Saudi Semiconductor Program. Testing requires a two-channel function generator to drive the PFD and divider inputs and a two-channel oscilloscope to observe the QA/QB pulses, charge-pump output and divided frequencies. The VCO is tuned by a control voltage around 0.75V to 1V, and the dividers are expected to produce one-eighth of a 40 to 80MHz input. The blocks are documented individually but are not wired together into a complete closed-loop PLL on this tile.
tt06/tt_um_vks_pll.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and education tags; added mixed-signal because the tile combines analog and digital PLL blocks.

tt06/tt_um_voting_thingey.summary: This Verilog design implements modified-consensus voting for redundant microcontrollers, treating each of the eight inputs as a vote where 1 means fail and 0 means pass. The number of active voters and the failure threshold are configurable, so a system can, for example, fail when three of eight voters report a fault. It is aimed at safety-critical hardware where redundant controllers guard against single-point faults. Verification is done through unit tests run with make in the test subfolder, and no external hardware is described.
tt06/tt_um_voting_thingey.review_notes: Removed arbiter, error-correction and fsm because the source describes configurable consensus voting, not those specific hardware functions; added industrial for the safety-critical hardware application.

tt06/tt_um_wallace_hhrb98.summary: This project is a 4-bit Wallace tree multiplier written in Verilog, built from instantiated half-adder and full-adder modules. It takes two 4-bit operands on the eight input pins and presents the product on the eight outputs. A testbench named wallace_tb.v is provided to exercise the design. The documentation is brief and does not report synthesis results or silicon measurements.
tt06/tt_um_wallace_hhrb98.review_notes: Removed adder tag; adders are only internal components of the multiplier.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_384437973887503361.summary: This Wokwi project is a 3-bit asynchronous down counter in which each flip-flop clocks the next, with a button used to advance the count. It is intended to drive a 7-segment display as external hardware. A tester ran it through the Commander application and found that ui_in[0] acts as the clock rather than the real clock, and that the observed output sequence 102, 63, 7, 79, 109, 6, 125, 91 repeats, suggesting the output bits are scrambled relative to the intended display. The silicon behaviour therefore only partially matches the intended counter.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_384437973887503361.review_notes: Removed 7-segment output tag because no output pins are detected; the silicon test is partial, not a silicon-tested claim.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_384711264596377601.summary: This Wokwi design is a digital dice that displays the word roll and lights the number 6 as a lucky result. The user interacts with it through a switch. The documentation gives no further detail on the internal logic or how the value is generated. No external hardware beyond the on-board display and switch is mentioned.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_384711264596377601.review_notes: Removed unsupported prng/7-segment/led tags and added display, game and button tags.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_384804985843168257.summary: This Wokwi project lets a user select a number from 1 to 8 with DIP switches and indicates whether it is even or odd using LEDs and a 7-segment display, with logic gates such as AND, OR, XOR, NAND and NOT involved. Switching on 2, 4, 6 or 8 is intended to light all blue LEDs and show 8 on the display. A tester confirmed that the odd/even detection works on silicon but that the 7-segment output does not match the Wokwi simulation because the display is wired differently on the board. The project is a logic-gate teaching exercise and needs an external seven-segment display.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_390913889347409921.summary: This Wokwi puzzle uses eight DIP switches, each mapped to a Notre Dame dormitory, and lights an LED when a valid combination of three dorms is selected. The valid set requires one of the best male dorms, one of the best female dorms and the best gender-neutral dorm, for example Alumni, Flaherty and Fischer Grad. It is intended as a trial-and-error exercise for students learning about logic gates. One external LED is needed, and no silicon test results are reported.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_392873974467527681.summary: This Wokwi design drives a 7-segment display to spell out PILIPINASLASALLE one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. Setting input pin 7 high enables a manual mode in which pins 0 to 3 select a BCD value that maps to a specific character according to a documented table. It is based on an earlier Wokwi project and requires an external 7-segment display. Multiple testers, including the author, report that the message appears correctly on silicon and that manual mode works, although one tester noted the reset signal appears to have no effect and the sequence starts at a random point.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_392873974467527681.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design only consumes a clock; added silicon-tested based on the working test reports.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_393815624518031361.summary: This Wokwi project is described only as a microchip that lights an LED digital number and an LED, controlled by flicking switches in the simulation. No pin functions, logic details or external hardware requirements are documented. Testing is limited to starting the Wokwi simulation and toggling switches. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, so the design's actual behaviour cannot be determined.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_393815624518031361.review_notes: Trimmed tags to what the thin documentation actually supports.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394618582085551105.summary: This design scans a 4x4 keypad matrix and displays the pressed key on a 7-segment display. It uses a 16-bit register to store the key state and combinatorial logic to drive the segments. External hardware includes a 4x4 keypad matrix and a 7-segment display. The design lacks debouncing and latching, making it a simple demonstration of keypad interfacing.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394640918790880257.summary: This project implements a 4-digit password locker using a 4x4 matrix keypad. It registers a password and then compares subsequent entries, indicating success via an output pin. External hardware includes a keypad, a reset button, and LEDs. The design uses shift registers and state machines to manage password registration and verification.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394704587372210177.summary: This is a 32-bit Fibonacci linear feedback shift register with taps at bits 32, 30, 26, and 25. It includes a fail-safe to prevent all-zero lock-up and allows manual initialization via input pins. The design outputs the lower 8 bits and can be tested with a logic analyzer. Silicon testing confirmed it generates a random-looking output.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394704587372210177.review_notes: Added silicon-tested because the source reports working silicon test results.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394707429798790145.summary: This is a 32-bit Galois linear feedback shift register with taps at bits 32, 30, 26, and 25. It includes a fail-safe to prevent all-zero lock-up and allows manual initialization via input pins. The design outputs the lower 8 bits and can be tested with a logic analyzer. No silicon test results are provided.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394830069681034241.summary: This design implements an 8-bit cyclic redundancy check for error detection in serial data streams. It takes a serial input and provides an 8-bit CRC output. External hardware includes LEDs, a clock source, and switches for reset and input. Silicon testing showed it functioned correctly compared to a software model.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394830069681034241.review_notes: Removed error-correction since CRC only detects errors, and added silicon-tested to match the working status.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394888799427677185.summary: This design implements a 4-bit stochastic multiplier using a traditional architecture. It converts two 4-bit binary-weighted vectors into 1-bit serial stochastic streams using a PRBS and a comparator, then multiplies them with a two-input AND gate. The serial multiplier output and the intermediate stochastic streams and PRBS signals are brought to the outputs for observation. External hardware includes an ADLAM2000 for control and analysis of the stochastic bitstreams.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394888799427677185.review_notes: Fourth sentence claimed a study context not stated in the source; replaced with a supported output statement.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394898807123828737.summary: This is a compact 4-bit stochastic multiplier that uses the Schmitt trigger on input pins as a stochastic resonator. It converts two 4-bit binary vectors into 1-bit serial stochastic streams using a PRBS and comparator, then multiplies them with an AND gate. External hardware includes an ADLAM2000 for control and analysis. The design explores a more compact architecture for stochastic computing.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_394898807123828737.review_notes: Added mixed-signal because the documented Schmitt trigger use is analog input conditioning for a stochastic resonator.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395034561853515777.summary: This is a 2-bit binary calculator that can add, subtract, or multiply two 2-bit numbers. The result is displayed on a 7-segment display. External hardware includes DIP switches for input and a 7-segment display. Silicon testing partially confirmed correct operation for addition and multiplication.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395034561853515777.review_notes: Removed alu tag; no ALU is mentioned in the source.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054466384583681.summary: This project is a 1-bit ALU intended as a test tapeout. The documentation is minimal, providing only the title and one-line description. No functional details, pinout, or test information are given. It appears to be an experimental design with insufficient documentation to describe its operation.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054466384583681.review_notes: Replaced placeholder with insufficient-doc and adjusted the final sentence to match the source.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054508867644417.summary: This design is a 2-bit multiplexer with output enable. It selects between two 2-bit inputs based on a select signal and provides both true and complemented outputs, along with parity and population count. The outputs can be tri-stated via an output enable pin. No external hardware is specified, and no silicon test results are provided.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054508867644417.review_notes: Removed sequential-logic (design is combinational) and added combinational; also dropped 'synchronous' from the summary since no clocked logic is described.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054564978002945.summary: This design is a driver for a hexagonal charlieplexed LED matrix with columns of 3-4-5-4-3 pixels. It accepts serial data on ui[0] while ui[1] is low, loading the pattern column-wise, and then drives the matrix through five bidirectional pins when ui[1] is high. Testing requires an external charlieplexed LED display (or individual LEDs) connected to the uio pins, with the clock pulsed at 100 Hz or more. The project is implemented in Wokwi.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054564978002945.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register tag; no canonical charlieplexing tag exists.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054820631340033.summary: This project is a placeholder created during a Hackaday workshop, with no functional description provided. The documentation explicitly states that the author refuses to describe how it works or how to test it. No pins or external hardware are specified. As a result, there is insufficient information to determine the design's purpose or capabilities.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054820631340033.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and education tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054823569451009.summary: This is a default Tiny Tapeout project that displays three segments lighting up on a 7-segment display. It is intended to be used as a template for building more complex 7-segment projects. No specific inputs or outputs are documented beyond the display segments. The design is a starting point for beginners and was created at a Hackaday workshop.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054823569451009.review_notes: Removed workshop and education tags because the source only mentions Hackaday and template use, not a workshop or educational intent.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054823837887489.summary: This design simulates rolling a dice, displaying the result on a 7-segment display. Pulling input 0 high causes the dice to roll, and releasing it stops the roll. It requires an external 7-segment display connected to outputs 0-6 and a button connected to input 0. Silicon tests confirm it works, though the author notes that using the microswitch to stop the roll is a bit annoying.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395054823837887489.review_notes: Removed prng tag as the source does not document any pseudorandom generator.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055035944909825.summary: This project is titled 'Some_LEDs' and described as 'Nothing special'. The documentation states that the author does not yet know how it works and that testing involves connecting the right things. No pins or external hardware are specified. There is insufficient information to determine the design's functionality or purpose.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055035944909825.review_notes: Removed unsupported led, template and education tags; added insufficient-doc.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055341723330561.summary: This is the example project from the Wokwi Hackaday Europe workshop, with no modifications. It displays segments on a 7-segment display based on the states of switches 0-7. Testing involves flipping the switches to turn on the corresponding segments. The design serves as a starting point for workshop participants.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055351144787969.summary: This project was designed during a Hackaday workshop, but the documentation consists only of 'TODO' placeholders for how it works, how to test, and external hardware. No pins or functional details are provided. There is insufficient information to determine what the design does.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055351144787969.review_notes: Removed unsupported tags and added correct ones based on source.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055359324730369.summary: This design shows two animations on a 7-segment display: alternating letters F and H, or a rotation animation. It divides a 10 kHz clock input based on input 7 and uses input 0 to select the mode, input 1 for blinking the dot, input 5 to pause, and input 6 for debug. Testing requires applying a 10 kHz clock and observing the display; silicon tests confirm it works correctly. The project was created during the Hackaday Conference 2024.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055359324730369.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter tag and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055455727667201.summary: This design implements two pseudorandom number generators (PRNGs) using scan flip-flops and XOR gates, one with and one without a hardware trojan. It includes scan chain inputs for setting the PRNG state and an external trigger for the trojan, with outputs for both PRNGs and test points for inverters. Testing involves providing a clock, setting the scan inputs, toggling scan enable, and using a pattern generator and logic analyzer. The project is notable for demonstrating a hardware trojan in a PRNG context.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055455727667201.review_notes: Removed lfsr (not stated in source) and crypto (no cryptographic function documented).

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055722430895105.summary: This design tests servo signals by lighting up eight LEDs according to the pulse width of the input signal. A 1 ms pulse (0 degrees) lights no LEDs, while a 2 ms pulse (180 degrees) lights all eight. It requires an external 4 kHz clock, eight LEDs with resistors, and a servo signal on input 0. The design uses flip-flops to process the servo signal and is implemented in Wokwi.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395055722430895105.review_notes: Removed PWM and motor-control tags not supported by the LED-only output; added instrumentation.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395058308283408385.summary: This project is a deliberately useless test design created for a Tiny Tapeout Hackaday event. It has two inputs labeled a and b and eight outputs labeled 0 through 7, but the documentation states that it does not function and should not be used. There is no meaningful behavior to test, and the author notes that any disappointment is the user's own fault. The design serves only as a placeholder or joke submission.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395058308283408385.review_notes: Removed unsupported template tag and added insufficient-doc to match the very thin documentation.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395061443288867841.summary: This design converts a 4-bit binary-coded decimal input into the seven segment drive signals for a single common-cathode 7-segment display. It uses combinational logic gates to map input values 0 through 9 to the appropriate segment patterns. The design requires an external DIP switch for the BCD input and a common-cathode 7-segment display for output. A silicon test report confirms that the fabricated chip works as described.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395134712676183041.summary: This project contains a set of digital inverters of different sizes, along with a D flip-flop, intended for analog characterization on a digital Tiny Tapeout tile. Inputs and outputs are connected to the inverters, with some bidirectional pins allowing flexible configurations such as paralleling inverters or building an amplifier. Testing requires a signal generator and an oscilloscope to measure propagation delays and analog behavior. The design is notable for comparing digital inverter measurements with those from an analog tile, and it originated from a TT06 submission.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395134712676183041.review_notes: Removed instrumentation tag not supported by the source; added silicon-art for the decorative inverter array.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395142547244224513.summary: This design displays the letters 'E', 'F', 'A', and 'b' on a 7-segment display using a D flip-flop ring counter. It is controlled by input switches for run, reset, initial state selection, and blink control, and works best with a slow clock or manual stepping. The project is a demonstration for the EFAB webinar and has been tested on silicon, with multiple reports confirming that it works as described. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and switches for input.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395142547244224513.review_notes: Removed education tag not supported by source; added counter for the ring counter.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395179352683141121.summary: This project implements a 4-bit combination lock with a maximum of three unlock attempts and a master reset. The user sets a password, then enters attempts via input pins; after three failures the lock becomes locked until reset. External hardware such as buttons or switches is required for physical operation, and a microcontroller is recommended for admin reset control. Silicon testing confirms that setting the password, unlocking, and the lockout after three wrong attempts all function correctly.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395179352683141121.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; silicon-tested matches the working status.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395263962779770881.summary: This design is a hardware implementation of the Bivium-B stream cipher used as a non-linear feedback shift register (NLFSR). It includes a 177-bit NLFSR with feedback taps and an output function, and it provides eight outputs that expose internal register values for self-testing. The circuit can be initialized to all zeros and then run, with outputs compared against a Python simulation. External hardware such as a logic analyzer is needed to observe the outputs, and the design is implemented in Wokwi.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395263962779770881.review_notes: Removed incorrect LFSR and PRNG tags; added shift-register and corrected summary wording.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395355133883896833.summary: This project is a simple 1-bit comparator that compares two input bits and indicates whether they are equal or which one is greater. It has two inputs (A and B) and three outputs: one for equality, one for A greater than B, and one for B greater than A. The design is purely combinational and can be tested by applying all four input combinations and observing the outputs, with LEDs recommended for visual indication. It is a basic educational logic circuit with no external hardware required beyond input switches and output LEDs.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395355133883896833.review_notes: Removed logic-gate (it is a comparator, not a gate) and added combinational.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395357890431011841.summary: This design is a hardware implementation of the Trivium stream cipher used as a non-linear feedback shift register (NLFSR). It contains a 288-bit NLFSR with three feedback taps and an output function, and it provides eight outputs that expose internal register values for self-testing. The circuit can be initialized to all zeros and then run, with outputs compared against a Python simulation. External hardware such as a logic analyzer is needed to observe the outputs, and the design is implemented in Wokwi.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395357890431011841.review_notes: Removed incorrect LFSR and PRNG tags; added shift-register and corrected summary wording.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395414987024660481.summary: This design uses a chain of flip-flops to display the word 'HELP' on a 7-segment display, with each flip-flop representing one letter and the last one blanking all segments. It has only seven outputs for the segments and no inputs, so it simply shows the sequence after reset. The project is a minimal demonstration and has been tested on silicon, with the author confirming that it displayed 'HELP'. No external hardware is required beyond the 7-segment display.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395414987024660481.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and kept silicon-tested as the author reported working silicon.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395444977868278785.summary: This project attempts to recreate the decoding logic of the vintage HP 5082-7500 display, a custom ASIC from the 1970s, on modern silicon. The design is incomplete and currently does not work, as indicated by the title. It would require a 4-bit BCD input and an LED dot-matrix display for testing, but no functional behavior is documented. The project is notable only as an unfinished attempt to reproduce historical logic.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395444977868278785.review_notes: Removed the erroneous retro removal note; display tag was already present, so no tag changes were needed.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395514572866576385.summary: This is a simple parity generator that takes 8 input bits and produces outputs on 4 output pins. It is implemented as a Wokwi learning exercise. The design is tested by setting input switches and observing the output LEDs. The documentation is minimal and does not specify the exact parity function or output encoding.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395514572866576385.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate and combinational tags; kept parity, wokwi, education.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395522292785089537.summary: This design displays the characters 'CIt' on a 7-segment display using a D flip-flop ring. It is implemented in Wokwi and has a 1 Hz clock. The inputs include a run signal and four state initialization bits, while the outputs drive the seven segments plus an eighth segment. The documentation is brief and does not provide a schematic or detailed explanation of the state machine.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395522292785089537.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added counter for the flip-flop ring sequencing.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395567106413190145.summary: This project implements a 4-bit full adder and subtractor with an externally triggered hardware trojan inserted in the critical path. It includes LFSR outputs and inputs, and displays results on a 7-segment display. Testing requires DIP switches, an external trigger signal, and a pattern generator and logic analyzer. The design demonstrates a hardware trojan in a simple arithmetic circuit.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395567106413190145.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'security' tag; 'silicon-tested' was not added since no silicon reports exist.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395599496098067457.summary: This design implements an even and odd BCD counter that can be selected via two inputs. When input 1 is high, the even counter is active; when input 2 is high, the odd counter is active. The outputs are 7-bit BCD values intended to drive a 7-segment display. Testing involves setting the inputs and observing the count on a connected 7-segment display.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395599496098067457.review_notes: Removed parity tag because the source describes even/odd BCD counting, not parity logic.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395614106833794049.summary: This project aims to create a modern take on 74-series universal gate chips, eventually becoming a Wokwi port of unigate-gf. It provides various logic functions through configurable inputs and bidirectional pins. The design is tested by running a testbench in the test directory. The documentation is sparse and does not detail the exact functionality or pin mappings.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395614106833794049.review_notes: Removed wokwi: the project is currently a Verilog design and only planned as a Wokwi port.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395615790979120129.summary: This design controls the direction of a DC motor using logic gates, with inputs and outputs mapped to specific pins. It is implemented in Wokwi and includes a schematic link. The documentation is in Spanish and describes the logic for changing rotation direction, but it is somewhat disorganized and includes irrelevant information about an LFSR. Testing requires external hardware such as a motor driver and motor.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395615790979120129.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the rest of the tags and summary are supported.

tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395618714068432897.summary: This project is titled '32b Fibonacci Original' and described as 'Fibonacci Serie'. It has two inputs and eight outputs, but the documentation is essentially absent, providing no details on functionality or testing. The design is likely a sequence generator based on the Fibonacci series. Without further documentation, the exact behavior and usage cannot be determined.
tt06/tt_um_wokwi_395618714068432897.review_notes: Removed speculative LFSR/PRNG/counter/sequencer tags; added wokwi and incomplete.

tt06/tt_um_wuehr1999_servotester.summary: This design generates a 50 Hz PWM signal for testing RC servos, with the pulse width controlled by an 8-bit input. It uses a 10 MHz clock to create the timing and outputs the servo pulse on a bidirectional pin. The position is also indicated on a 7-segment display. Testing requires an RC servo connected to the output pin.
tt06/tt_um_wuehr1999_servotester.review_notes: Removed 7-segment tag because the design does not implement a 7-segment display interface.

tt06/tt_um_zhwa_rgb_mixer.summary: This design reads three digital encoders, debounces the inputs, and outputs three PWM signals to control LED brightness. It is a Zero to ASIC demo project implemented in Verilog. Testing involves twisting each encoder and observing the brightness change on connected LEDs. External hardware includes three digital encoders and LEDs attached to the outputs.
tt06/tt_um_zhwa_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed unsupported rgb-led/asic; added rotary-encoder and led based on pins and text.

tt07/tt_um_28add11_QOAdecode.summary: This chip decodes the QOA audio format, a simple format for 16-bit PCM audio, via an SPI slave interface. It acts as a co-processor, requiring an external microcontroller to handle file I/O and streaming. The design has been tested in silicon and works, achieving up to 176,056 samples per second. It is notable for its compact implementation and potential for real-time audio streaming.
tt07/tt_um_28add11_QOAdecode.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag; added rp2040 and corrected summary wording.

tt07/tt_um_6bitaddr.summary: This project implements a 6-bit ripple carry adder with a carry input and carry output, using continuous assignment without a clock. It takes two 6-bit numbers on the input and bidirectional pins and produces their sum on the output pins. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. Silicon tests confirm that the adder works correctly, with one tester noting it works eventually.
tt07/tt_um_6bitaddr.review_notes: Removed alu since the design is a plain adder, and added silicon-tested to match the working status.

tt07/tt_um_8bit_vector_compute_in_SRAM.summary: This design implements an 8-bit vector compute-in-SRAM with eight multiply-and-add units and an adder tree that sums the results without precision loss. Weights and activations are programmed via operation codes, with weights remaining stationary for reuse. The design is tested through a Python test suite that covers individual MAC operations, weight loading, adder tree functionality, and readout, though most tests are commented out due to limited external signal access. It operates entirely within its own resources and does not interface with external hardware, though external signals might be needed to orchestrate multiple units with a control processor.
tt07/tt_um_8bit_vector_compute_in_SRAM.review_notes: Removed unsupported neural-network, machine-learning, and dsp tags; added systolic-array and compute-in-sram.

tt07/tt_um_8bitadder.summary: This project implements an 8-bit ripple carry adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using a cascade of full adders. The sum is output on the 8 output pins, and the design is purely combinational with no clock. It requires no external hardware, though switches and LEDs can be used for demonstration. Silicon tests confirm that the adder works correctly, with multiple testers verifying the sum of two 8-bit inputs.
tt07/tt_um_8bitadder.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu tag and added silicon-tested based on working test reports.

tt07/tt_um_Burrows_Katie.summary: This analog project models a quadratic integrate-and-fire (QIF) spiking neuron, where the output spikes and resets to a known value when the input crosses a threshold voltage. It uses five analog pins for differential input and output signals and is based on a published compact digital implementation of a QIF neuron. Testing involves applying an 8-bit digital signal and observing whether the output spikes when the voltage crosses the threshold. External hardware listed is an ADLAM2000.
tt07/tt_um_Burrows_Katie.review_notes: Replaced incorrect instrumentation-amplifier tags and summary with the actual QIF spiking neuron content from the source.

tt07/tt_um_CktA_InstAmp.summary: This analog project implements an instrumentation amplifier for electrocardiogram signal acquisition, using a three-opamp array to extract low differential signals from noisy common-mode environments. The differential gain is digitally selectable via two input bits, providing 0 dB, 26 dB, or 46 dB gain, with a common-mode rejection ratio of 120 dB. Testing requires a balun, vector network analyzer, and power supplies to measure differential and common responses. The design includes a sense circuit to stabilize the analog ground and is intended for biomedical applications.

tt07/tt_um_DanielZhu123.summary: This SystemVerilog design implements a calculator that performs addition, AND, OR, and XOR operations on two input numbers, with the result displayed on a 4-digit Nixie tube display. It uses a 100 Hz clock and provides control signals for selecting numbers, positions, signs, and modes. Testing involves applying inputs and predicting the output to verify against the display. The design requires external Nixie tubes and associated driver hardware.
tt07/tt_um_DanielZhu123.review_notes: Replaced logic-gate with 7-segment to match the numeric display output.

tt07/tt_um_KolosKoblasz_mixer.summary: This analog project implements a Gilbert cell mixer for up and down conversion of signals, with both internal and external local oscillator options. The digital control part can generate internal LO signals at different frequencies or pass an external LO to the analog mixer. Testing requires biasing the input ports with 900-950 mV and applying a differential signal of about 20 mV peak-to-peak, typically using a custom interface PCB. Silicon tests confirm successful downconversion from 32 MHz RF and 30 MHz LO to a 2 MHz IF, and the author notes it works well with both internal and external LO sources.
tt07/tt_um_KolosKoblasz_mixer.review_notes: Removed audio tag; added silicon-tested based on working silicon reports.

tt07/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.summary: This design reads run-length encoded video data from a QSPI flash memory and outputs it to a 640x480 VGA display, suitable for playing the Bad Apple music video. It requires external QSPI and VGA PMODs, and the SPI read latency is configurable via input pins. The design operates at 25.175 MHz and was successfully tested on silicon, playing Bad Apple, though there were minor issues with short back-to-back runs that the author believes are fixed in a later version. The documentation notes the flash must support the h6B Fast Read Quad Output command with 8 dummy cycles.
tt07/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.review_notes: Removed 'memory' and 'demoscene' as unsupported; added 'silicon-tested' to match the working silicon report.

tt07/tt_um_PS_PWM.summary: This Verilog design generates phase-shifted PWM signals for controlling two PMOS and two NMOS transistors in a power converter, with configurable duty cycles and dead time to prevent cross-conduction. It includes a shift register for serial control, internal generation of phase-shifted triangular waveforms, and output multiplexing. The design operates at a 1000 Hz clock and requires no external hardware. Testing involves verifying the PWM outputs against the input duty cycles and control signals.

tt07/tt_um_PUF.summary: This design implements a ring-oscillator physically unclonable function (PUF) using reversible logic for fault tolerance, with 64 ring oscillators divided into two groups of 32. Challenges are generated by an LFSR, and responses are derived from frequency differences between selected oscillators, producing unique outputs per challenge. The design was tested on Vivado and OpenRoad, and requires no external hardware. It is notable for combining reversible logic with a PUF architecture to enhance security and fault tolerance.

tt07/tt_um_Saitama225_comp.summary: This is an analog comparator built by the MNEL team from USFQ that compares two voltages or currents and outputs a binary signal indicating which input is greater. It is tested by applying known input voltages and verifying that the output transitions at the expected threshold across the full input range. No external hardware is required beyond the analog input, reference, and output pins. A silicon test report notes the design was broken because the supply voltage appeared higher than the 1.8V rating of the transistors.
tt07/tt_um_Saitama225_comp.review_notes: Removed unsupported education/transistor-level and redundant comparator; added silicon-tested per report.

tt07/tt_um_TD4_Assy_KosugiSubaru.summary: This is a 4-bit CPU implemented in Verilog with 4 input ports and 4 output ports, running from a 10 Hz clock. It is tested by setting the inputs and observing the outputs, with pins exposing data, address, carry flag, and ALU-to-register signals. The documentation does not specify any external hardware, and the description is very brief. The design appears to be a small educational processor, but the limited documentation makes its full instruction set and behavior unclear.

tt07/tt_um_The_Chairman_send_receive.summary: This Verilog project is a dual-mode sender or receiver that transmits bits between two chips, selected by a mode pin. In sender mode it can read from DIP switches or a 4-button PMOD keypad, and in receiver mode it drives an LCD display value from the received bits. Testing requires two chips connected with a specially crafted crossover cable so that all data pins map correctly between sender outputs and receiver inputs. External hardware includes a PMOD 4-button keypad, and the documentation notes the need for careful wiring.
tt07/tt_um_The_Chairman_send_receive.review_notes: Added dip-switch because the sender side explicitly supports reading from the carrier chip's DIP switches.

tt07/tt_um_VishalBingi_r2r_4b.summary: This is a 4-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter with an integrated sawtooth waveform generator, implemented in analog. It can be driven externally by setting the external data pin high and applying 4 input bits, or it can generate a sawtooth internally when external data is low, with frequency set by loading a divider. Testing requires a multimeter on the analog output pin to observe the voltage or sawtooth waveform. A silicon test report confirms it worked at a 10 kHz clock, producing the expected sawtooth wave.
tt07/tt_um_VishalBingi_r2r_4b.review_notes: Removed unsupported instrumentation; added silicon-tested per working report.

tt07/tt_um_adennen_inverter.summary: This is an analog buffer made from two inverters, one large and one small, connected together, originating from Matt's analog course. The analog input is on ua[1] and the output is on ua[0], and it is tested simply by applying an input signal and observing the buffered output. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and does not provide measured performance or silicon test results.
tt07/tt_um_adennen_inverter.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag because the design is an analog buffer, not a logic gate.

tt07/tt_um_adia_psu_seq_test.summary: This Verilog design is a sequencer for a 9-step 4-phase combined power-clock supply intended for adiabatic circuits, running at 32 MHz with each phase at 1/32 of that rate. It generates control signals for phases 0 and 1, with a select pin routing one phase to the output pins, and also provides digital sync signals for latching data into or out of adiabatic gates. The project is free-running: after a reset, the user selects a phase and monitors the outputs. No external hardware is necessary, and the design is explicitly a test of the power supply sequencer concept.
tt07/tt_um_adia_psu_seq_test.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and synchronizer because the design sequences an external power-clock and emits timing markers, not a general clock generator or CDC synchronizer.

tt07/tt_um_adonairc_dda.summary: This Verilog project implements a digital differential analyzer solver for the van der Pol oscillator using 16-bit posit (16,1) arithmetic. It communicates over SPI, receiving the oscillator parameter and returning the X and Y state variables as 32-bit words for each time step, with simulation stopped by ending SPI communication. Testing requires an SPI master, and a controller using an FTDI FT232H is available on GitHub, with the top row of a PMOD used for SPI signals. The core solver is implemented in Verilog.
tt07/tt_um_adonairc_dda.review_notes: Replaced the unsupported floating-point tag with physics and fixed-point; also removed an unsupported claim about posit novelty from the summary.

tt07/tt_um_afasolino.summary: This Verilog module converts two 16-bit fixed-point numbers in 0.15 format to 16-bit posit (16,1) format and adds them, producing a posit result. It is tested by providing two fixed-point input values and observing the addition result on the output pins, with handshake signals for data valid and read ready. The design combines a fixed-to-posit converter using a leading zero counter and a posit adder based on a published architecture. No external hardware is mentioned, and the documentation is technical but brief.

tt07/tt_um_agurrier_mastermind.summary: This TL-Verilog project implements the Mastermind game, where the user guesses a hidden four-color combination using eight color inputs and receives feedback on correct colors and positions via eight LEDs. A random answer is chosen by pressing a button, guesses are made with four button presses, and the game indicates a win or loss after ten rounds. External hardware includes two Pmod BTN modules for eight push buttons, a Pmod8LD for eight LEDs, and a splitter cable. The design is a complete interactive game with clear testing instructions.
tt07/tt_um_agurrier_mastermind.review_notes: Removed verilog tag since language is TL-Verilog; re-added supported game interface tags.

tt07/tt_um_aidenfoxivey.summary: This Verilog design is a parallel implementation of CRC-8 following the CCITT specification with a start value of 0x00 and polynomial 1+x^1+x^2+x^8. It accepts two bytes on the input pins when enabled, updates the internal CRC value, and outputs the current CRC on eight output pins, with a reset pin to restart at 0x00. Testing is done by running make in the test directory, and no external hardware is required because the design only needs a small buffer for the CRC value. The documentation is clear and includes a reference to an online CRC calculator.
tt07/tt_um_aidenfoxivey.review_notes: Removed combinational tag since the design stores CRC state, and added sequential-logic.

tt07/tt_um_ajstein_stopwatch.summary: This design implements a decimal stopwatch that counts from 0 to 9 and loops, driven by the 20 MHz ASIC clock. It is a first Tiny Tapeout experiment with no external inputs or outputs required, and the documentation notes limited testing infrastructure. Testing can be done in simulation via a linked MakerChip sandbox or on a Tiny Tapeout demo board using an FPGA harness and dfu-util. The project is notable mainly as a simple counter with no silicon test results reported.
tt07/tt_um_ajstein_stopwatch.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and clock-divider tags; kept counter and timer.

tt07/tt_um_alfiero88_CurrentTrigger.summary: This analog block is a current-mode Schmitt trigger that converts input currents into a digital output with hysteresis, using internally set reference currents and an adjustable falling-edge threshold via an external voltage. It is intended to detect current-mode signals from devices such as photodiodes, SPADs and silicon photomultipliers for LIDAR, medical and particle-physics applications. Testing requires a current source or voltage source with series resistance in the tens of microamperes range, a tunable voltage supply for references, and a fast oscilloscope on the output. The design is notable for targeting single-photon and rare-event detection front ends, though no silicon test results are provided.

tt07/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray-casting graphics engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, rendering textured walls with flat floor and ceiling by racing the beam. The player point of view is controlled over SPI, and an optional external QSPI ROM can supply textures instead of the internally generated ones. It needs a Tiny VGA PMOD on the dedicated outputs, an SPI host for control, and a clock around 25.175 MHz for standard 640x480 VGA. Silicon reports say it works without the glitches of the earlier TT04 version, including external SPI textures, though a clock hack was needed and the SPI peripherals still need full testing.

tt07/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: This is an analog factory test structure for Tiny Tapeout analog support, with pins for bias current, ground and power sense, and three loopback connections. The documentation consists only of FIXME placeholders, so the exact operation and test procedure cannot be determined from the provided text. External hardware requirements are likewise undocumented. Because essentially no usable documentation is present, the tags and summary are inferred from the title and pin names alone.

tt07/tt_um_analog_rf_readout_circuit.summary: This analog block selects among different peripheral circuits, including RF-based transmission, depending on the chosen mode. The documentation is very thin, giving only that a mode must be selected with the proper input to activate the required RF transmission peripheral. Testing is said to require a VNA, multimeter and oscilloscope, but no pin-level detail or measured results are provided. The design is notable only as an RF peripheral experiment, and the available documentation is insufficient to describe its operation precisely.

tt07/tt_um_asinghani_tinywspr.summary: TinyWSPR is a Chisel-based WSPR beacon that transmits Weak Signal Propagation Reporter radio signals, recommended for the 20m and 40m bands. Configuration is loaded one byte at a time over the config pins, covering callsign, grid square, power level, symbol time, divisor and deviation, after which the RF start pin triggers transmission at the correct time. An external lowpass filter is absolutely required to remove harmonics from the square-wave transmitter, along with a properly tuned antenna. The design places a complete WSPR encoder and transmitter into a small digital block.
tt07/tt_um_asinghani_tinywspr.review_notes: Removed modulator and clock-divider as unsupported, and removed the unsourced silicon-test sentence from the summary.

tt07/tt_um_brucemack_sb_mixer.summary: This analog block is a double balanced mixer that takes an RF input with DC bias and a digital local-oscillator signal to produce a differential intermediate-frequency output. It also includes a quadrature divider that generates I and Q phase outputs from a clock input. The design was simulated at 7 MHz, and the documentation gives no test procedure or external hardware beyond the RF and LO sources implied by the pins. No silicon test results are provided, so the summary is based mainly on the title and pin names.
tt07/tt_um_brucemack_sb_mixer.review_notes: Removed unsupported audio/demodulator tags and added mixer.

tt07/tt_um_btflv_subleq.summary: This design implements a Subleq CPU, a one-instruction set computer, using an external SPI FRAM for memory. It includes a UART interface with a baud rate of 115200 at a 10 MHz clock, and SPI signals for communicating with the FRAM. Testing involves loading compiled Subleq code into the FRAM via an Arduino and running the CPU. The documentation describes the Subleq architecture, toolchain, and external hardware requirements.
tt07/tt_um_btflv_subleq.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the Subleq CPU design with FRAM and UART; removed unsupported tags and added accurate ones.

tt07/tt_um_calonso88_74181.summary: This design replicates the classic 74181 4-bit slice ALU twice to form an 8-bit arithmetic logic unit, with an SPI slave peripheral for loading and reading registers and a multiplexer driving a 7-segment debug display. It supports all four SPI modes with eight configurable read/write registers and eight read-only status registers, and is controlled from an RP2040 using SPI1. Silicon reports confirm the SPI interface works when the SPI clock is at least five times slower than the ASIC clock, though the ALU itself was not verified by the independent tester. The project is notable as a faithful reproduction of a historic ALU part with a practical SPI debug interface.

tt07/tt_um_ccattuto_charmatrix.summary: This design drives a chain of up to four Pixie Chroma WS2812B LED-matrix displays, showing characters received over a 9600-baud 8N1 UART and shifting them left as new ones arrive. It includes reusable blocks such as a WS2812B driver, UART receiver and transmitter, an LFSR-based pseudo-random color selector, and a 5x7 character ROM, with options for dimming, fixed or random colors, and internal or UART-triggered refresh. External hardware needed is one to four chained Pixie Chroma displays with adequate power and a UART terminal or adapter. Silicon testing by the author confirmed working operation with two chained devices, and the project is notable for its cocotb tests of the UART and WS2812B protocol.

tt07/tt_um_ccattuto_conway.summary: This design simulates Conway's Game of Life on a 32x16 grid with periodic boundary conditions. It outputs the state to an ANSI serial terminal over UART and also provides VGA output via the bidirectional pins. The initial state is pseudo-randomly generated using an LFSR, and the simulation can be controlled via single-character commands over UART. Partial silicon testing confirmed that the terminal output works as expected.
tt07/tt_um_ccattuto_conway.review_notes: The vga and text tags are not clearly supported: the design outputs VGA-style signals for a TinyVGA Pmod, but the primary documented interface is ANSI terminal over UART, and no text rendering hardware is described.

tt07/tt_um_chess.summary: This is a chess move generator implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a 256-bit chessboard and a 64-bit square-enable mask to compute attacks and arbitrate the most promising move. The design is intended to be driven by an external RP2040 microprocessor, as the chip lacks the space to run the full game logic. It is tested using a provided test suite.
tt07/tt_um_chess.review_notes: Removed fsm (not described) and added rp2040 and arbiter which are supported by the source.

tt07/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip.
