The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

tt07/tt_um_cm_1.summary: This is a proof-of-concept experiment with GDS-level open-source countermeasure implementation. It exposes a set of customized hardened matrices that can be selected via the MAT_SEL input. The design is intended for fab testing and research purposes, allowing comparison of the observed input-to-output mapping with a reference model. No external hardware is required.

tt07/tt_um_davidparent_hdl.summary: This design generates a PRBS31 signal using a Fibonacci LFSR and also analyzes it with a similar structure. It includes two 7-bit vectors that are converted to pseudo-random signals by comparison with the PRBS, which can be used as an alternative to a PWM DAC. A 131-bit PRBS generator is also included. The design requires an external ADALM2000 for testing.
tt07/tt_um_davidparent_hdl.review_notes: Removed instrumentation tag not supported by the source; added signal-generator for the PRBS output.

tt07/tt_um_delay_line_tmng.summary: This project implements a single NAND gate that is time-multiplexed using a giant shift register to emulate complex logic. The design achieves a time/space tradeoff by feeding inputs from and writing results to the shift register. It requires an external FPGA or similar to drive the inputs at high precision to feed instructions. Silicon testing showed it works as expected even at high frequencies.
tt07/tt_um_delay_line_tmng.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag based on author's working report.

tt07/tt_um_devinatkin_dual_oscillator.summary: This analog project generates two sinusoidal oscillators centered around 0.9V, targeting 20MHz and 21MHz. The oscillators are based on ring oscillators and should oscillate regardless of chip corner, though frequency varies. Silicon testing showed they run slower than intended (approx 13 and 14.2MHz) with waveforms between sinusoidal and triangular. No external hardware is required for operation.
tt07/tt_um_devinatkin_dual_oscillator.review_notes: Removed broad signal-generator; added silicon-tested per working report.

tt07/tt_um_dpetrisko_ttdll.summary: This is an all-digital delay-locked loop (DLL) test design featuring tunable, hierarchical oscillation blocks. It demonstrates a clock generator and a 90-degree delay line using delay elements and control registers. The design is validated in TSMC-28 and is being tested on open tools and an open PDK. It requires an external oscilloscope for visualizing waveforms and uses bsg_tag for hardware testing.
tt07/tt_um_dpetrisko_ttdll.review_notes: Tags are all supported; no changes needed beyond confirming the existing set.

tt07/tt_um_drburke3_top.summary: This design is a fast magnitude comparator intended for digital neuron threshold detection. It compares two 8-bit inputs and outputs less-than, equal, and greater-than signals. The design is based on a bit-sliced expandable structure expressed in AND-INV form to leverage ABC9 logic optimization. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation, though documentation on output bit mapping was unclear.
tt07/tt_um_drburke3_top.review_notes: Removed neural-network tag (comparator building block, not a network) and added silicon-tested and combinational tags supported by the source.

tt07/tt_um_dusterthefirst_project.summary: This project implements a Manchester decoder and parser for 433MHz transmissions, such as those from a thermostat. It uses two state machines: one for decoding the Manchester signal and another for parsing the data frames. The decoded data is accessible via parallel output lines based on an address. External hardware required is a 433MHz receiver connected to the digital input pin.
tt07/tt_um_dusterthefirst_project.review_notes: Added sensor-interface for the external receiver input; existing tags and summary are supported.

tt07/tt_um_dvxf_dj8v_dac.summary: DJ8 is an 8-bit CPU with an 8x8-bit register file, a 15-bit address bus, an 8-bit data bus, and an integrated 8-bit R-2R DAC. It includes a built-in 256-byte demo ROM with two demos selected via DIP switches at reset, one of which drives a speaker through the DAC. External hardware can include a parallel Flash ROM and optional SRAM for larger programs, plus a speaker and amplifier for the audio demo. The design is notable for combining a full CPU with an analog DAC on a single Tiny Tapeout tile and for having prior VHDL and Verilog implementations.
tt07/tt_um_dvxf_dj8v_dac.review_notes: Removed audio and memory tags not supported by the design's own interfaces; added silicon-tested based on the author's working report.

tt07/tt_um_eater_8bit.summary: This project recreates Ben Eater's 8-bit breadboard computer as a Tiny Tapeout ASIC in SystemVerilog. It is programmed through a dedicated prog_mode pin, four address bits, and eight bidirectional data lines, with a 4-bit address space limiting internal RAM to 16 bytes. An RP2040 or similar microcontroller is needed to load programs, and an external output register on a breadboard connects to the 8-bit I/O lines. The design is notable as an educational ASIC implementation of a well-known instructional computer.

tt07/tt_um_ejfogleman_smsdac8.summary: This is an 8-bit segmented mismatch-shaping R2R DAC encoder implemented in Verilog. It accepts 8-bit digital input and produces a segmented output that must be summed by an external resistor ladder to create the analog voltage, with optional buffering and retiming recommended for best performance. The output swing is 0.25 to 0.75 of the IO supply, and resistor mismatch appears as first-order shaped noise removable by lowpass filtering. The design is notable for using mismatch-shaping and dithering techniques to achieve 8-bit linearity without precise resistor matching.
tt07/tt_um_ejfogleman_smsdac8.review_notes: Removed unsupported sigma-delta and generic encoder tags; added mixed-signal since the encoder drives an external analog resistor ladder.

tt07/tt_um_emern_top.summary: badGPU is a basic GPU that rasterizes up to four triangles at 640x480 60Hz with 6-bit color, controlled by a host microcontroller over SPI. It supports a programmable background color and uses polygon ordering instead of a Z-buffer, with vertices limited to 80 X and 60 Y positions. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD, a VGA screen, and an SPI-capable microcontroller, and it asserts an interrupt during blanking to accept new commands. It is notable for fitting a simple polygon rasterizer into a 4x2 tile Tiny Tapeout design.
tt07/tt_um_emern_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported accelerator tag and redundant generic display/video tags; added verilog.

tt07/tt_um_ender_clock.summary: This project is a clock design intended to drive a USB digital tube display. It exposes an 8-bit address input and an 8-bit data output, suggesting a memory-mapped interface to external display hardware. The documentation is very thin, stating only that it is a clock and that a PCB and 3D shell will be published separately. External hardware includes the PCB, shell, and digital tube, but no further implementation details are provided.

tt07/tt_um_explorer.summary: Explorer implements a 2D voxel raycasting terrain renderer in hardware, based on the 1992 Voxel Space algorithm used in Comanche. It is written in Silice and interfaces with a QSPI PSRAM for terrain data and an SPI ST7789V screen for output, with four buttons as inputs. Terrain data must be uploaded to the PSRAM before operation, planned from an RP2040 on the PCB, and the design has been tested successfully at 17MHz. It brings a classic software rendering algorithm into a hardware implementation on Tiny Tapeout.
tt07/tt_um_explorer.review_notes: Removed unsupported game tag and added silicon-tested and retro tags supported by the source.

tt07/tt_um_factory_test.summary: The TinyTapeout 7 Factory Test module is a simple design for testing all I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes selected by rst_n and sel: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required, and the design has been reported working by multiple testers. It is notable as a dedicated factory test and bring-up utility rather than a functional application.
tt07/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Added silicon-tested to match the working silicon test reports.

tt07/tt_um_fp_mac.summary: This is a simple FP8 multiply-accumulate module implemented in Verilog, taking two 8-bit floating-point inputs and producing an 8-bit result after three clock cycles. It includes a partial register at address 0x00 as the starting value and is intended as a building block for systolic arrays and hardware accelerators. The design is self-contained and requires only an output buffer to store partial products and results. Testing is done by running make in the test directory, and the documentation is otherwise brief.
tt07/tt_um_fp_mac.review_notes: Removed chisel tag because the project language is Verilog; corrected summary to match.

tt07/tt_um_htfab_fprn.summary: The Field Programmable Resistor Network is an analog design consisting of resistors and pass-gate switches arranged in a matrix, with latches that hold the configuration. Cells are selected via H_GATE and V_GATE inputs, and the network can be configured as a makeshift DAC by controlling the bitstream. The output voltage is measured externally at the analog pin, requiring a multimeter or microcontroller ADC. Silicon tests confirmed the R2R DAC mode works after cutting a 10k pulldown resistor on the demoboard, and the design is notable for its configurable analog resistor network.
tt07/tt_um_htfab_fprn.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added silicon-tested and mixed-signal based on test reports and analog/digital nature.

tt07/tt_um_jleightcap.summary: fractran-tt is a hardware implementation of John Conway's esoteric Turing-complete language Fractran, written in Clash. It operates on streams of prime factor degrees, using an 8-bit accumulator stream and fraction stream as inputs and producing a factorized result stream, with sentinel values for STOP and HALT. The internal logic is small and requires external support circuitry such as a fraction counter, degree pointer, fraction ROM, and banked accumulator RAM. The design is notable for implementing an unusual mathematical language directly in hardware.

tt07/tt_um_jorga20j_prng.summary: This project implements an 8-bit pseudo-random number generator based on the Xorshift algorithm. It accepts an 8-bit seed on the input pins and, after a two-cycle latency, produces a new pseudo-random 8-bit value on the output pins every clock cycle. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware; it can be tested by applying a seed and observing the output sequence. Silicon tests confirm that it works as intended, with the same seed always producing the same first random output.
tt07/tt_um_jorga20j_prng.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag to match the working silicon test reports.

tt07/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.summary: This is a baremetal RISC-V RV32E system-on-chip that includes a UART, a QSPI memory controller for PSRAM and flash, a generic SPI interface, and a sigma-delta audio emulator. It is designed to run firmware from external NOR flash and requires a PMOD with flash and PSRAM for operation. The design is reported working by the author, with MicroPython for RV32E running and playing audio. It is a KianV baremetal edition SoC occupying a 3x2 tile area.
tt07/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.review_notes: Replaced the unsupported compactness claim with the documented tile size.

tt07/tt_um_lcasimon_tdc.summary: This analog block implements the fine-resolution part of a time-to-digital converter using time interpolation. It converts an input pulse of 20 to 60 nanoseconds into a periodic square wave with a period 90 times longer, allowing a low-frequency counter to measure the pulse width with high resolution. The circuit requires external hardware including a digital signal generator, a 13uA current source, and an oscilloscope for testing. It is an analog design intended for applications such as digital communications, radar, and particle physics.
tt07/tt_um_lcasimon_tdc.review_notes: Proposed tag 'time-to-digital-converter' is outside the canonical vocabulary; the closest canonical tag is 'oscillator'.

tt07/tt_um_lfsr.summary: This design is a linear feedback shift register random number generator that interfaces via a Wishbone bus to fit within the Tiny Tapeout pin constraints. It allows loading a seed through the bus and then outputs a pseudo-random bit stream. Testing uses a cocotb testbench, and a microcontroller on the development board applies the correct startup signals. The design is a compact digital implementation of an LFSR with a bus interface.
tt07/tt_um_lfsr.review_notes: Simplified test sentence so it is directly supported by the source.

tt07/tt_um_lisa.summary: This is an 8-bit microcontroller system-on-chip called LISA, featuring a Tiny Tapeout Logic Controller and multiple communication interfaces including SPI, UART, and I2C. It is supported by a custom C-based assembler, linker, and a Python-based debugger for programming and debugging. The design requires external SPI flash and SRAM for program storage and data memory. The toolchain is partially functional, with the C compiler still under development and lacking floating-point support.

tt07/tt_um_litneet64_ro_puf.summary: This project implements a ring-oscillator-based physically unclonable function (PUF) with 8 bits of challenge-response pairs. It uses 32 ring oscillators per bit, selected by the challenge, and races counters to produce a response bit. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by applying challenges and observing responses, though responses may vary with temperature. The author seeks collaboration to characterize the PUF's uniqueness, reliability, and entropy across many devices.
tt07/tt_um_litneet64_ro_puf.review_notes: Removed crypto and trng because the source describes a PUF for identification/authentication and nonce generation, not a cipher or true random source; added characterization for the explicit process/PUF characterization effort.

tt07/tt_um_macros77_subneg.summary: This is an implementation of a simple 8-bit SUBNEG CPU that requires external parallel SRAM for program and data storage. It provides control signals for interfacing with external SRAM and latches, and the program must be loaded into SRAM by an external device before enabling the CPU. The design outputs internal state bits for debugging and requires additional hardware such as a 3.3V SRAM, address latch, and output latch. It is a minimal CPU design intended for educational or experimental use.
tt07/tt_um_macros77_subneg.review_notes: The fsm, subtractor, and latch tags are unsupported or misattributed: no FSM or subtractor is described, and latches are external components.

tt07/tt_um_maheredia.summary: This project generates GPS intermediate frequency signals with configurable parameters including satellite ID, code phase, Doppler shift, and SNR. It includes a register bank configurable via UART and a core with a Gold code generator, NCO, and PRNGs for noise generation. The design outputs sine and cosine signals with and without noise, and can be used to test GPS receiver search algorithms. External hardware such as a microprocessor or FPGA can be used to provide the navigation message input.
tt07/tt_um_maheredia.review_notes: Removed unsupported communication and lfsr tags; added instrumentation and rf based on the GPS test-signal purpose.

tt07/tt_um_mandelbrot_accel.summary: This accelerator calculates the Mandelbrot set iteration z = z^2 + c using 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point arithmetic, performing one iteration per clock cycle. It accepts the complex number c via a shift register interface and outputs the iteration count and an unbounded flag when the result exceeds the bound. The design requires no external hardware and was tested by generating a 256x256 image of the Mandelbrot set, taking about 24 minutes when manually clocked. It is notable for implementing floating-point arithmetic in a compact hardware design.
tt07/tt_um_mandelbrot_accel.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added image-processing tag based on use case.

tt07/tt_um_maxluppe_NIST.summary: This project implements four NIST statistical tests (Frequency, Block Frequency, Runs, and Longest Run of Ones) to evaluate random bit sequences. It also includes an analog LFSR with configurable delay lines that can act as a conventional LFSR, oscillator, or chaotic oscillator. The design accepts random bits as input and outputs test results, and requires external hardware for configuration and monitoring. It is based on published works on low-cost on-chip randomness tests.
tt07/tt_um_maxluppe_NIST.review_notes: Removed trng and prng because the source describes an LFSR/delay-line circuit with NIST randomness tests, not a random number generator; added characterization for the statistical test purpose.

tt07/tt_um_maxluppe_digital_analog.summary: This design implements two digital-to-analog converters and three analog comparators using only standard logic cells, based on published work by Sala et al. and Yang et al. Two 5-bit counters drive the DACs to generate analog ramp signals that exercise the comparators. A SEL pin selects whether the counters operate together for a 10-bit sequence or independently. An oscilloscope is required to observe the DAC and comparator outputs, and the design is notable for being fully synthesizable from standard cells rather than custom analog blocks.
tt07/tt_um_maxluppe_digital_analog.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal because the design is entirely digital standard-cell logic; added signal-generator for the ramp generation.

tt07/tt_um_mini_aie_2x2.summary: This project is a minimal coarse-grained reconfigurable array inspired by AMD's AI engine architecture, containing a 2x2 array of compute tiles connected by a simplified packet-switched network-on-chip. Two interface tiles connect the array to external memory and a host, and packets are routed through the NoC and processed in a pipelined manner. Eight data inputs, eight debug outputs and eight data outputs are exposed on the pins. The documentation does not describe a concrete test procedure, so how the design is exercised on silicon is unclear.
tt07/tt_um_mini_aie_2x2.review_notes: Removed dsp because the source does not mention digital signal processing.

tt07/tt_um_mitssdd.summary: This co-processor reads data from four sensors sequentially and compares each reading to previous data to detect deviations, also identifying sensor faults and providing warning signals along with sensor identification. It is intended for precision farming applications and requires an external 8-bit ADC to convert sensor data. The design outputs a deviation detector signal, fault warnings, and sensor identifiers. The documentation is limited to a basic description and a single test example, without full implementation details.
tt07/tt_um_mitssdd.review_notes: Removed unsupported adc and fsm tags; added industrial tag for precision farming application.

tt07/tt_um_mixed_signal_pulse_gen.summary: This mixed-signal block generates pulses whose period, duty percentage and count are configured through digital input pins. It exposes analog input and output lines alongside PWM outputs and several analog voltage outputs. The documentation is extremely thin, stating only that a pulse is generated when an input is given and that testing consists of providing an input. No external hardware is listed, but the sparse description makes the exact behavior and intended use difficult to determine.

tt07/tt_um_mos_bandgap.summary: This analog block implements a bandgap voltage reference using only MOSFETs, with a second output for a DTMOS variant. The documentation points to an external paper for the operating principle and provides no further explanation of the circuit. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the bandgap outputs and a hot air gun to heat the chip and observe temperature behavior. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog reference submitted to a digital-oriented shuttle.
tt07/tt_um_mos_bandgap.review_notes: Removed transistor-level and temperature-sensor because the source only says MOSFET-only bandgap and uses heating for test, not a discrete-transistor or temperature-sensing design.

tt07/tt_um_multiplier_mbm.summary: This design multiplies two 8-bit signed numbers to produce a 16-bit product using a modified Booth encoding algorithm. The Booth-recoded bits feed a Dadda multiplier design, and the partial products are added in a carry-lookahead adder. The multiplicand is applied on the eight input pins while the product is split across the output and bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required.
tt07/tt_um_multiplier_mbm.review_notes: Removed incorrect ALU tag and DSP/accelerator wording, and corrected the unsupported 32-bit product claim.

tt07/tt_um_neural_network.summary: This project implements a reusable neural network of four neurons whose weights and biases are loaded serially through a shift register under state-machine control. An 8-bit input is captured, four inputs are shifted in, and twenty parameters per layer are fed in a defined order, with neuron outputs fed back to the next layer. The state machine cycles through input, buffer and output states, and the finished state exposes the four neuron outputs on the output pins. Testing is intended with an FPGA to feed weights correctly, and the weights must first be trained externally in Python or Matlab.
tt07/tt_um_neural_network.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added fixed-point based on power-of-2 weight multiplication.

tt07/tt_um_njp_micro.summary: This design is a microcode-based shift-and-add multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product. The documentation is minimal, describing only that the inputs are supplied and the product returned, with a reset required before operation. Switches and LEDs are suggested as external hardware for driving inputs and observing outputs. The very low 1 kHz clock and sparse description suggest an educational demonstration rather than a high-performance arithmetic unit.
tt07/tt_um_njp_micro.review_notes: Removed unsupported instruction-decoder and alu tags; the design is a multiplier.

tt07/tt_um_nurirfansyah_alits02.summary: This analog test circuit contains a transmission-gate VCO with on-chip capacitors for linearization, plus a phase detector and a second VCO forming parts of a phase-locked loop. Six analog pins expose the VCO outputs, control inputs, the PLL VCO output and the differential PLL filter nodes. Testing requires a typical experimental PLL or VCO bench setup, and no digital control pins are provided. The submission is an analog exploration of PLL and VCO building blocks on a shared shuttle.
tt07/tt_um_nurirfansyah_alits02.review_notes: 'transistor-level' is unsupported by the source, which says only VCOs, transmission gates and a phase detector.

tt07/tt_um_obriensp_pll.summary: This project exposes a VCO and a phase-frequency detector as building blocks of a phase-locked loop, with analog control and output pins plus digital select and clock inputs. An oscilloscope, function generator and bench power supply are suggested but not required for testing. A silicon test report confirms the VCO works, producing 13 kHz to 66 MHz, though the usable control range was 0.4 V to 1.0 V rather than the documented 1.0 V to 1.8 V. The phase-frequency detector was not tested by the reporter, and the design is notable for including measured silicon results.

tt07/tt_um_pa1mantri_cdc_fifo.summary: This SystemVerilog design implements a 4-bit asynchronous FIFO that buffers data between independent write and read clock domains. It uses a dual-port RAM for storage, with binary-to-gray and gray-to-binary converters plus synchronizers to safely pass pointers across domains. Write and read operations are controlled by increment pulses, with full and empty flags indicating status, and resets are held low during initialization. No external hardware is required, and the design is a standard clock-domain-crossing building block with clear usage instructions.

tt07/tt_um_pongsagon_tiniest_gpu.summary: This design is a minimal GPU implemented in Verilog that renders a single triangle. It outputs RGB color bits along with horizontal and vertical sync signals through its pins. The documentation is very sparse, providing only the title and pin names, so details about the rendering pipeline and testing are not available. No silicon test results are reported for this design.
tt07/tt_um_pongsagon_tiniest_gpu.review_notes: Removed vga because the source only shows RGB/sync pins without naming a VGA interface.

tt07/tt_um_pwm_elded.summary: This project implements a pulse-width modulation (PWM) modulator in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit duty cycle input on the ui pins and produces a PWM output on uo[0]. The design is intended to be tested on a Xilinx Basys 3 FPGA board. The documentation is minimal, consisting of a one-line description and a brief note on testing, with no further details on implementation or verification.
tt07/tt_um_pwm_elded.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and fpga tags; the design is a PWM modulator in Verilog.

tt07/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.summary: This design is a 16-bit counter with count enable and multiplier enable inputs. It accepts 3-bit operands m_a and m_b for the multiplier. The counter outputs its lower 8 bits on uo and upper 8 bits on the bidirectional pins. The documentation is extremely thin, describing it only as "like a 16-bit counter" and providing no details on the multiplier functionality or testing.
tt07/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source only supports counter and multiplier functionality.

tt07/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.summary: This design implements an iterative multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) unit intended for machine learning accelerators. It performs a 7x8-bit multiplication and adds a third operand provided on the bidirectional pins, with the result output on uo_out. The design uses a reset to latch the first operand and then accepts the second operand each clock cycle. Testing is described as complex, with full instructions to be added later, and it requires a CPU to supply input data.
tt07/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.review_notes: Removed alu, dsp, and neural-network as unsupported by the source, which describes a MAC unit for ML accelerators.

tt07/tt_um_rejunity_analog_dac_ay8913.summary: This is an analog logarithmic 4-bit DAC designed for the AY-8193 sound generator. It uses current steering to convert digital inputs into an analog output current on ua[0]. The design can be tested by setting input or bidirectional pins to regulate current and measuring the output with an oscilloscope or by connecting an amplifier and speakers. The documentation is brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing notes.
tt07/tt_um_rejunity_analog_dac_ay8913.review_notes: Removed chiptune (no music generation described) and added sound-generator; summary sentence about input pins corrected to match pin list.

tt07/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This project is a reimplementation of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a 3-voice PSG chip from General Instruments and a smaller variant of the AY-3-8910 or its analog YM2149. It uses a simple 8-bit R2R DAC driven externally or by an OpenLane-generated sawtooth waveform generator. The analog outputs are on the ua pins and the PWM outputs are on the uo pins. Testing requires a multimeter to measure the output voltage on analog pin 0.
tt07/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Removed 'dac' and 'synthesizer' tags not supported by the AY-3-8913 PSG project; summary rephrased with source-supported wording.

tt07/tt_um_rejunity_vga.summary: This design generates a checkers pattern on a VGA screen. It outputs RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires a TinyTapeout VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for testing. Silicon test reports indicate that it works and produces a pattern similar to the default checkers from vga-playground.com, with a noted transparency effect.

tt07/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

tt07/tt_um_revenantx86_tinytpu.summary: This design is a tiny TPU accelerator that supports 2x2 matrix multiplication using 8 input pins and 2 output pins. The matrix data is likely serialized over these pins. The design is intended to be tested with a provided test file that multiplies random matrices. No external hardware is required, but a driver is needed to convert and push matrices as input and read the output; the documentation notes the project will be updated for more complex computations.
tt07/tt_um_revenantx86_tinytpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported neural-network and machine-learning tags; summary is supported by the source.

tt07/tt_um_riscv_spi_wrapper.summary: This project is a RISC-V RV32I CPU core with a bare-bones SPI wrapper that allows uploading programs to instruction memory and echoing data. The CPU is a 5-stage pipeline supporting most of the base integer instruction set, with 16 words of instruction memory and 8 words of data memory. The SPI wrapper starts in boot mode, requiring the user to upload a program and then enter echo mode to release the CPU from reset. Testing involves preparing a RISC-V binary, programming via SPI commands, and observing the passed/failed signals that check if register 10 equals 45.

tt07/tt_um_rnunes2311_12bit_sar_adc.summary: This is a 12-bit differential (11-bit single-ended) successive-approximation-register ADC implemented with custom metal-fringe capacitors and a calibrated comparator. It samples the input for two clock cycles, performs a binary search conversion over 16 cycles, and outputs the result in two 6-bit halves on the DATA pins synchronized to CLK_DATA. The design supports both differential and single-ended modes, with an offset calibration feature enabled by EN_CAL_OFFSET. Silicon tests show it works at 10-20 MHz but with noticeable noise and missing codes, requiring averaging for accurate results.
tt07/tt_um_rnunes2311_12bit_sar_adc.review_notes: Removed unsupported dac/comparator/transistor-level/characterization tags; added silicon-tested per the working test reports.

tt07/tt_um_router.summary: This is a 1-to-3 router that directs 3-bit data packets to one of three outputs based on control signals. It accepts data_in, pkt_valid, and read_enb signals, and provides data_out, vld_out, err, and busy status. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it routes data to three directions and suggesting to give input to data_in. No external hardware or detailed testing procedure is described.

tt07/tt_um_rtmc_top_jrpetrus.summary: This is a real-time motor controller designed to drive stepper motors with precise timing between steps. It interfaces with an RP2040 via SPI for register programming and control, and provides 8 motor control outputs along with general-purpose I/O. External hardware includes a 28BYJ-48 stepper motor with a ULN2003 driver, and optionally a second motor. The design is intended for use with the Tiny Tapeout demo board, and MicroPython support is planned but not yet available.

tt07/tt_um_seanyen0_SIMON.summary: This is an implementation of the classic SIMON memory game, where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of button presses. It uses four buttons for input and a 7-segment display to show the current sequence length or an 'L' upon losing. The design requires a Digilent PmodBTN for button input and has been tested successfully by multiple users. It is a simple, self-contained game with no additional external hardware beyond the Pmod.
tt07/tt_um_seanyen0_SIMON.review_notes: Removed verilog tag because the source language is TL-Verilog, which is not in the canonical vocabulary.

tt07/tt_um_serdes.summary: This project implements a Serializer/Deserializer (SerDes) that converts 8-bit parallel data into a 10-bit serial stream using 8b/10b encoding and decodes it back. It includes data, serial, parallel, and serialization enable control signals plus a synchronous reset, with latch and shift-register elements synchronizing the paths. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware, making it suitable for integration into larger systems. The documentation is thorough but contains no silicon test results.
tt07/tt_um_serdes.review_notes: 'encoder' is not supported by the design, which uses 8b/10b encoding but no encoder primitive; the other tags are fine.

tt07/tt_um_shadow1229_vga_player.summary: This is a video and audio player that reads binary 80x60 pixel video and PCM/PWM audio data from an external SPI NOR flash chip and outputs it as 640x480 VGA with audio. It supports configurable audio type (PCM or PWM), VGA PMOD type, and pixel colors via input pins. External hardware includes a VGA monitor, a Tiny VGA PMOD, an SPI flash chip (W25Q128JVSSIQ), and for PWM audio an external DAC. The design is notable for streaming video and audio data from external flash to a VGA display.
tt07/tt_um_shadow1229_vga_player.review_notes: Removed 'memory' because the flash is external hardware rather than an on-chip memory block.

tt07/tt_um_spacecat_chan_john_pong_the_s.summary: This is a simple Pong game where the ball is represented by an image of the Polish pope, output over VGA. It supports two players via button inputs or an AI opponent, selectable by a pin. The design requires external hardware for VGA digital-to-analog conversion, a VGA monitor, and buttons for player input. The game logic runs once per frame during vertical sync, and it outputs one pixel per clock cycle.

tt07/tt_um_template.summary: This is a configurable digital clock that defaults to 20 MHz but can be set to 10, 12, or 14 MHz via input pins. It supports display of minutes or hours on a 2-digit 7-segment display, with an option for 4-digit mode, and includes an Arduino mode. External hardware includes a PMOD 2-segment display (and possibly a 4-segment display). The design is simple and intended for basic timekeeping with adjustable speed for setting.
tt07/tt_um_template.review_notes: Replaced clock-generator with rtc because the source describes a timekeeping clock, not a clock signal generator.

tt07/tt_um_thatoddmailbox.summary: This is a small System-on-Chip (SoC) built around DuckCPU, a custom 8-bit CPU inspired by the Zilog Z80 and Sharp LR35902. It includes peripherals such as UART, SPI, and GPIO, and uses a reserved SPI interface for external flash and RAM. The design is intended for learning purposes and requires external SPI flash and RAM ICs, as well as a USB-to-UART circuit for programming via a bootloader. Detailed documentation is promised after tapeout.

tt07/tt_um_tinytapeout_dvd_screensaver.summary: This project displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a 640x480 VGA screen, mimicking a DVD screensaver. It includes options to tile the logo across the screen and enable color output via input pins. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, and has been tested successfully by multiple users. It is a simple visual demo with no additional external hardware.
tt07/tt_um_tinytapeout_dvd_screensaver.review_notes: 'video' is redundant with 'vga'; the rest of the tags and summary are supported.

tt07/tt_um_tnt_diff_rx.summary: This is a small analog test module for a differential input receiver. It takes differential clock and data inputs along with a bias current and bias select, and produces an 8-bit output. The documentation is essentially missing, with all sections marked FIXME, so its internal operation and intended use cannot be determined. It is likely a characterization or test vehicle for a differential receiver cell, but no test procedure or external hardware requirements are described.

tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816.summary: Basilisc-2816 is a small 2-bit serial CPU that executes 8/16-bit instructions and communicates with external memory over a serial interface. It includes a memory interface, arbiter, prefetcher, decoder, scheduler, ALU, and register file, and uses the demo board USB pins for memory transactions and debug signals. The design requires an external RP2040 microcontroller, such as on the Tiny Tapeout 7 demo board, to act as a RAM emulator. The documentation describes the architecture in detail but provides no test procedure, and no silicon results are reported.
tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816.review_notes: Removed uart and memory tags as unsupported; added instruction-decoder and pipeline based on the documented architecture.

tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816_cpu_OL2.summary: This is version 0.1b of the Basilisc-2816, a small 2-bit serial CPU that executes 8/16-bit instructions and communicates over a serial interface. It uses UART pins for memory transactions and debug signals. The documentation for this specific version is minimal, with no test procedure or silicon results provided. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs at 50 MHz.
tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816_cpu_OL2.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu, register-file, memory and rp2040 tags; summary rewritten to avoid invented RP2040 and architecture claims.

tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816_cpu_exp.summary: This is an experimental version 0.1c of the Basilisc-2816, a small 2-bit serial CPU that executes 8/16-bit instructions and communicates over a serial interface. It uses UART pins for memory transactions and debug signals. The documentation for this specific version is minimal, with no test procedure or silicon results provided. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs at 50 MHz.
tt07/tt_um_toivoh_basilisc_2816_cpu_exp.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu, register-file, memory and rp2040 tags; summary rewritten to avoid invented RP2040 and architecture claims.

tt07/tt_um_tt7_meonwara.summary: This design implements a direct digital synthesizer (DDS) with a resistive digital-to-analog converter to produce an analog sine wave output. The output frequency is controlled by the 8 input switches, and with a 40 MHz clock, a rail-to-rail sine wave can be observed on the analog pin ua[0]. The DAC output has an impedance of about 10 kOhm, and an external capacitor to ground can be added to smooth or filter the waveform. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation and testing.
tt07/tt_um_tt7_meonwara.review_notes: Removed the unsupported nco tag; the design is described only as a DDS with resistive DAC.

tt07/tt_um_twin_tee_opamp_osc.summary: This analog design uses a Twin Tee notch filter with an opamp to generate a sine wave at approximately 4.93 MHz. A 20-bit digital counter is connected to the oscillator output, with the top 8 bits driving the LEDs, so the most significant bit flashes about 5 times per second. An oscilloscope is required to observe the sine wave, and the design is sensitive to loading, so it should be started with no scope connected. Silicon testing by the author shows it oscillates at about 4.6 MHz and the counter works, though the sine wave quality is moderate.

tt07/tt_um_underserved.summary: Underserved is a Tiny Tapeout implementation of SERV, a compact RISC-V CPU that boots from an external SPI flash memory in XIP mode and executes instructions directly from it. It provides GPIO pins that can be used for various purposes, such as bitbanged UART, and uses SPI pins for flash communication. The design expects a compatible SPI flash memory and can be tested using a testbench with a flash model, with FuseSoC used for simulation and linting. The documentation is thorough, describing the boot process and test setup, but no silicon results are reported.

tt07/tt_um_unisnano.summary: This design implements a UART menu system that waits for user input characters (1-7) and responds with either informative text or toggles output bits. It uses a basic UART driver for TX and RX, operating at 115200 bps with a 50 MHz clock, and requires an external UART transceiver connected to the recommended pins. Two output pins can drive LEDs through MOSFET drivers, and the design is controlled by sending single characters without line endings. The documentation is minimal but provides enough information to understand and test the functionality.
tt07/tt_um_unisnano.review_notes: Removed button tag; no button interface in pins or text.

tt07/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.summary: This is a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that steps up the input voltage to approximately 5.44 V, with the output divided by two due to the analog pin voltage limit. It requires a 2 MHz clock signal to operate, and the divided output voltage can be measured at the ua[0] pin. Silicon testing by the author shows that at 7.5 MHz the output is about 4.55 V, slightly higher than simulation predicted. The design is a straightforward analog power circuit with no digital interface beyond the clock.

tt07/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a hardware implementation of the Simon Says memory game, where the player must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors and tones. The game uses four buttons, four LEDs, a speaker, and optionally a two-digit 7-segment display for the score, all connected to the specified pins. It requires a 50 kHz clock and can be simulated online via Wokwi, with the wiring diagram provided. Silicon testing by the author confirms the game works as expected, including improved UX for slow players.
tt07/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed 'memory' since it is a game title word, not a memory hardware block.

tt07/tt_um_urish_spell.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It executes a cryptic program stored in volatile program memory, using a stack machine architecture with a shift register for serial access. The design provides 256 bytes of program memory, 32 bytes of stack memory, and 32 bytes of data memory, with 8 bidirectional pins and up to 8 output-only pins. Silicon test reports confirm the design works, with successful communication and demo program execution at 10 MHz and overclocking tests up to 156 MHz.
tt07/tt_um_urish_spell.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart and security tags; added stack-machine and silicon-tested; corrected summary to match silicon status and remove invented external hardware claim.

tt07/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
tt07/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

tt07/tt_um_vga_perlin.summary: This project implements a VGA graphics controller with a machine-learning accelerator. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is designed for educational purposes. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

tt07/tt_um_vga_snake.summary: This is a simple Snake game with VGA output, controlled by four directional buttons. It requires an external VGA monitor and buttons for interaction. A silicon test report notes that the game loads but runs too fast, causing the snake to crash quickly. The design is implemented in Verilog.
tt07/tt_um_vga_snake.review_notes: Removed unsupported FSM, counter, and GPIO tags; added silicon-tested and corrected summary to include the partial silicon report.

tt07/tt_um_vzayakov_top.summary: This is a Pong game with VGA output, controlled by two players. The game uses a finite state machine and counters to manage game logic and display. It requires external VGA monitor and buttons for interaction. No silicon test report is provided, so its hardware behavior is not confirmed.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.summary: This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display. It uses a modulo-12 counter to select which character to display and has logic to light the appropriate segments. It is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by running the clock to scroll text or using pins to manually select characters. Silicon test reports confirm the design is working on fabricated hardware.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.review_notes: Corrected tags to match the modulo-12 counter and silicon-tested status, and removed the false no-report claim from the summary.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397142450561071105.summary: This circuit is a padlock that lets you set a code for a safe using pins 2 to 4 and pin 7. Pin 1 resets the safe, and the clock button is used to enter the code. The seven-segment display shows "L" for locked when pin 1 is on and the clock button is pressed. A partial silicon test report notes errors where the saved code inverts each clock cycle and the third code bit is ignored, so some invalid codes are accepted.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397142450561071105.review_notes: Replaced invented game/debouncer/edge-detector tags and summary with the actual padlock functionality and partial silicon status.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397268065185737729.summary: This circuit uses a circular buffer of D flip-flops as a selector and D flip-flops for player memory, with combinational logic for the display. It is implemented in Wokwi and is a small game where the player toggles a switch at the right moment to light the segments forming a '0'. Silicon test reports confirm the design works on fabricated hardware. The reset signal initializes the circular buffer and clears the player memory.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397268065185737729.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate tag, added game/puzzle/silicon-tested tags, and corrected the summary's false claim that no silicon test report exists.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397774697322214401.summary: This is a basic first test design that uses a pair of inverters and a pair of AND gates to detect a secret code on three input pins. It requires no external hardware and is intended as a learning exercise for the Tiny Tapeout process. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is a simple combinational logic circuit. A silicon test report confirms that setting the inputs to the secret code shows an L on the display.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_397774697322214401.review_notes: Removed security tag and added silicon-tested; corrected summary to reflect the provided working silicon test report.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399163158804194305.summary: This configurable timer counts down from a value placed on inputs 0 through 7 and displays the remaining time in binary form. The start input loads the configured value and begins the countdown, and the end flag is raised when the count reaches zero. An out_state signal reports the running state. The design is implemented in Wokwi; no silicon test report is provided, so hardware behavior is not confirmed.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399163158804194305.review_notes: Removed led output tag since LEDs are external recommendations only; added counter, sequential-logic and gpio and corrected unsupported educational/clock-generator claims.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399169514887574529.summary: This design implements a 4-bit Gaussian blur filter that accepts nine pixel values serially through a free-running shift register and outputs the blurred center pixel. After nine clock cycles the shift register is full and the output can be sampled, with the last shift register stage also exposed for testing. The design is written in Wokwi and runs at 100 kHz on a single tile. An FPGA is suggested as useful external hardware for driving the pixel stream, and the documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the operation.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399192124046955521.summary: This project implements a 1-bit error detection and correction module with a transmitter that generates four redundant bits from an 8-bit input to form a 12-bit codeword, a built-in self-test block that can inject errors, and a receiver that corrects any single-bit error. The BIST block outputs either the redundant bits or the error position on four bidirectional pins depending on whether an error was inserted. Testing requires twelve LEDs, a 7-segment display, counters, and digital input switches. The design was made in Wokwi and has been silicon tested, with the author reporting it works.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399192124046955521.review_notes: Added silicon-tested based on the working author report.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399336892246401025.summary: This project is described as a UART for connecting two digital devices, using switches to select an ASCII character and a 7-segment display to show the result. The documentation is very thin, consisting of only a few sentences that do not explain the baud rate, framing, or register interface. The pin names are generic (in1 through in8, out1 through out3) and do not clearly map to UART signals. External hardware listed includes an Arduino, a 7-segment display, and eight switches, but the design's actual behavior cannot be fully determined from the provided text.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399336892246401025.review_notes: Added UART/communication/gpio tags; removed 7-segment as an output tag.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399447152724198401.summary: This design is a simple 8-bit register that stores the eight input bits on the eight outputs when a clock pulse occurs. It is built from D-type flip-flops and is intended as a basic educational example. Testing is done by setting the inputs and using a push button to save and hold the value. The documentation is minimal and the design is very simple, with no external hardware required beyond the clock and input switches.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399447152724198401.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; design is a single register, not a register file.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399469995038350337.summary: This project sequentially spells out a hidden message on a 7-segment display by inverting the segment outputs, so the viewer must invert the segments to decipher the text. It uses the eight outputs a through g plus dot and runs at 1 Hz on a single tile. The documentation is very brief and does not state what the message is or how the sequence is generated. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design appears to be a small novelty or puzzle.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399488550855755777.summary: This is an 8-bit binary counter designed by a 9-year-old following instructions and a picture, with outputs Q0 through Q7 counting upward. It is tested by connecting an LED Pmod and observing the binary count, and multiple silicon test reports confirm that it works correctly at 1 Hz. The design is notable as a beginner-friendly educational project and has been verified by several testers. No complex external hardware is required beyond the LEDs.

tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399518371950068737.summary: This project implements a full-adder directly from Karnaugh maps for both the sum and carry-out outputs, taking inputs A, B, and C-IN. It behaves as a standard full-adder and requires no external hardware. The design is a straightforward combinational circuit built from K-map-derived logic. The documentation is short but sufficient to understand the function.
tt07/tt_um_wokwi_399518371950068737.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added logic-gate for the full-adder.

tt07/tt_um_xeniarose_sha256.summary: This project is a minimal SHA-256 hash core implemented in Verilog with a single-cycle-round architecture. It occupies a 2x2 tile area and uses an addressed register bus with 6-bit register addressing, a read/write select, an IO clock, and 8-bit data lines. The documentation is incomplete, with TODO placeholders for how-it-works and testing instructions. No external hardware is needed beyond a method of interacting with the bus to transfer commands and data.
tt07/tt_um_xeniarose_sha256.review_notes: Replaced tags that described an unrelated factory-test counter with crypto/hash/multi-tile/incomplete tags matching the SHA-256 core.

tt08/tt_um_08_sws.summary: This analog design generates a stepwise approximation of a sine wave, with the output frequency depending on the clock. It is intended as a sine wave synthesizer and uses analog pins for bias and current outputs. Testing requires a 1 kΩ resistor from the output pins to ground. The documentation is brief and does not provide detailed specifications or test results.
tt08/tt_um_08_sws.review_notes: Removed oscillator, clock-generator, dac and mixed-signal: none are supported by the analog sine synthesizer documentation.

tt08/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunter.summary: This design implements a 16-microphone delay-and-sum beamformer that processes PDM input from up to 16 digital microphones. It converts the PDM data to PCM using a 3-stage CIC filter and outputs the result as an I2S stream. The design requires external digital microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver. It is notable for its high channel count and integrated filtering.
tt08/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunter.review_notes: Removed incorrect filter tags and asic; added pdm and beamformer, but note these are not in the canonical vocabulary and should be reviewed.

tt08/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game with VGA output. The player uses four buttons to move tiles in four directions, merging matching numbers to reach 2048. It includes a debug mode for unit testing and requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester successfully playing a game.

tt08/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.summary: This design is a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder that computes the sum of two 4-bit inputs plus a carry-in. It provides sum and carry-out outputs and can be used as a building block for larger adders. The design was tested on an FPGA but has no silicon test report. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand its function.
tt08/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the design is an adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

tt08/tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.summary: This design is an ASIC implementation of a university CPLD project that drives four multiplexed seven-segment displays and scans a multiplexed keypad. It uses a simple SPI protocol to receive commands for display data and keypad column selection, and it outputs keypad row data on MISO. The design requires external hardware including displays, a keypad, and an SPI master, and it must be clocked by the SPI clock. Silicon testing showed it functional up to 3.7 MHz, but auto-clocking must be disabled.
tt08/tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed.

tt08/tt_um_LnL_SoC.summary: This design is a tiny system-on-chip featuring a 16-bit microprocessor, boot ROM, PWM, timer, and SPI interface. The CPU runs a built-in program that reads from an 8-bit input port and writes to an 8-bit output port, and it also exercises the SPI, PWM, and timer peripherals. The design is intended to test the microprocessor on silicon and requires external hardware such as a keypad and display. The documentation is detailed but the external hardware is not fully specified.
tt08/tt_um_LnL_SoC.review_notes: Removed microcontroller in favor of soc/cpu; added education and pwm tags supported by the source.

tt08/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.summary: This design plays Pachelbel's Canon while displaying synchronized visuals on a VGA screen. It uses a PWM output for audio and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a Tiny Audio Pmod. Silicon testing showed it works, though one tester noted the audio was out of sync until manually reset. The design is a demonstration of audio and video capabilities on Tiny Tapeout.
tt08/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.review_notes: Removed generic graphics tag; added silicon-tested and verilog tags supported by the silicon reports and language.

tt08/tt_um_MichaelBell_mandelbrot.summary: This design computes and displays the Mandelbrot fractal on a VGA screen using a racing-the-beam technique. It uses 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic and a maximum iteration depth of 14, with configurable position and zoom via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 100 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it broadly works, though the demo mode can sometimes get stuck zooming into the wrong offset.

tt08/tt_um_NicklausThompson_SkyKing.summary: This design displays a static image of a plane flying into the sunset with a text overlay that types out character by character. It also includes demos for oscilloscope XY display PMODs, which can be selected via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for the main demo and additional PMODs for the XY demos. The text animation may complete before the VGA monitor recognizes the signal, so viewing in a VGA playground is recommended.

tt08/tt_um_Richard28277.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ALU that performs arithmetic and logical operations on two 4-bit inputs, selected by a 4-bit opcode. The 8-bit result is output on the uo pins and the lower four bidirectional pins, while carry-out and overflow flags appear on two of the bidirectional pins. Testing involves setting the a and b inputs and the opcode, then observing the result and status flags. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward combinational ALU.
tt08/tt_um_Richard28277.review_notes: Removed adder because the documentation does not specifically claim adder functionality.

tt08/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.summary: This is a standalone VGA and sound demo that fits in two tiles, developed for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition. It generates a 640x480@60Hz VGA signal with a non-standard 1220-pixel horizontal resolution and RGB222 dithered graphics, plus 3-channel synthesized audio via a 16-bit sigma-delta DAC on a single pin. It requires a 48 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for sound. Silicon tests confirm both graphics and sound work as expected, matching FPGA simulations.

tt08/tt_um_a1k0n_nyancat.summary: This design displays the classic Nyan Cat animation on a VGA monitor with accompanying music. It uses a 2x2 Bayer dithering matrix for color rendition and generates sound from a MIDI file using square waves with exponential decay envelopes, a low-pass filter, and a sigma-delta DAC. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for audio. Silicon tests confirm it works, and it was originally intended for one tile but expanded to two.

tt08/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.summary: This project renders a 3D torus (donut) on a VGA display using a raymarching technique with a CORDIC unit to calculate distances. It runs at a non-standard 1220x480 resolution and uses spatial and temporal dithering to improve appearance despite low horizontal resolution. It requires a 48 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output. Silicon tests show it works but may have minor glitches at 48 MHz; running at 45 MHz avoids them.
tt08/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.review_notes: Added silicon-tested: the source reports working silicon results from testers and the author.

tt08/tt_um_alexjaeger_ringoscillator.summary: This is a simple analog ring oscillator that outputs a nominal 5 MHz clock signal on a single analog pin. It requires no external hardware and is automatically enabled when selected on the evaluation board. Silicon tests show it oscillates at around 4.5-4.6 MHz with an amplitude of about 0.6-1.6 V, depending on the setup. The design is notable for its simplicity and use of analog circuitry.
tt08/tt_um_alexjaeger_ringoscillator.review_notes: Added silicon-tested because the source includes multiple working silicon test reports.

tt08/tt_um_algofoogle_tt08_vga_fun.summary: This project implements rough 24-bit VGA DACs with a digital control block for testing various patterns. It includes current-steering DACs for red and green channels and a segmented current-switching DAC for blue, with analog outputs on ua pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a VGA monitor, and external op-amp circuits to convert the analog outputs to the 0-0.7V range required by VGA. Silicon tests confirm the digital output works and the analog outputs show good rise/fall times, but external buffering is needed for direct VGA connection.

tt08/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: This project provides test structures for Tiny Tapeout analog support, including bias generation, power supply sensing, and loopback connections. The documentation is incomplete, with sections marked as FIXME, so the exact functionality and usage are not fully described. It appears to be intended for factory testing of analog infrastructure. No external hardware or testing procedure is specified in the available documentation.

tt08/tt_um_benpayne_ps2_decoder.summary: This PS2 decoder reads scan codes from a PS2 keyboard, debounces and synchronizes the signals, and outputs the data byte along with valid, interrupt, and data-ready signals. It includes a FIFO to queue received bytes, and the host can read data by asserting chip select. It requires a PS2 keyboard and level shifting from 5V to 3.3V, and is intended for interfacing with retro computers. The design is a straightforward implementation of the PS2 protocol.
tt08/tt_um_benpayne_ps2_decoder.review_notes: Removed 'decoder' because it is a type tag for code-to-signal decoding, not a PS/2 protocol decoder; no canonical replacement exists.

tt08/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.summary: This Morse code keyer converts paddle or straight-key inputs into Morse code outputs, including an auxiliary Morse output, a buzzer tone, and a 7-segment display showing the last character. It supports iambic keying types A and B, and adjustable speed from about 7 to 110 WPM via dip switches. It uses a 12 MHz clock and requires a 12 MHz input clock plus external hardware such as a companion PCB for radio interfacing. The design includes a warning against using the auxiliary output directly for radio transmission.
tt08/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.review_notes: Corrected the invented PS2 PMOD hardware mention; the source only documents a companion PCB for radio interfacing and 12 MHz clock.

tt08/tt_um_bgr_agolmanesh.summary: This project is a bandgap voltage reference designed in Skywater 130nm CMOS to provide a stable 1.17V output over a 0-80°C temperature range. It includes a startup circuit and operates from a 1.8V supply, consuming 0.35 mW. Testing requires a temperature chamber, power supply, and measurement equipment to verify temperature stability, line and load regulation, and power consumption. Silicon tests show it can be unstable depending on load, sometimes latching to 0.46V instead of 1.17V.
tt08/tt_um_bgr_agolmanesh.review_notes: Removed temperature-sensor because the design is a voltage reference, not a temperature sensing circuit.

tt08/tt_um_brailliance.summary: Brailliance converts an ASCII character into its 8-bit Braille representation, where the first two bits of each output byte are zeroed for redundancy. The design is implemented in Verilog and uses a 5 MHz clock. External hardware such as LEDs or solenoid actuators can be used to display the Braille output. This project serves as an educational tool for ASCII-to-Braille conversion.
tt08/tt_um_brailliance.review_notes: Removed display and education tags as they are not supported by the source.

tt08/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_with_NE.summary: The design implements a two-player Pong game that uses two NES controllers for input and outputs a VGA video signal.
tt08/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_with_NE.review_notes: Removed gpio tag because the bidirectional pins are dedicated to NES controller signals.

tt08/tt_um_bytex64_munch.summary: Munch displays a munching squares animation on a VGA monitor while generating simple music through an audio PMOD. It uses the Tiny VGA and TT Audio pinouts and is implemented in Verilog. The author notes it works but requires a manual reset to sync the music properly. The design targets a 25.175 MHz input clock and was tested on fabricated silicon with partial success.
tt08/tt_um_bytex64_munch.review_notes: Added silicon-tested, audio, and music; expanded summary to four sentences.

tt08/tt_um_cattuto_sr_latch.summary: This experiment implements a 512-bit shift register using D latches instead of flip-flops, with a single pulse rippling through the register to perform the shift. It has one input, one output, and an edge-triggered control signal that updates the shift on either a rising or falling edge. Testing involves shifting zeros in until the register is empty, then shifting in a pattern and observing it appear on the output after 512 control transitions. No external hardware is required.
tt08/tt_um_cattuto_sr_latch.review_notes: Added incomplete because the source explicitly frames the design as an experiment.

tt08/tt_um_cejmu.summary: This design bundles four educational modules selected by an internal multiplexer: a vending machine state machine, a coin acceptor decoder, a 24-bit ripple carry adder, and a 24-bit carry lookahead adder. The adders are tested by feeding 24-bit operands in 8-bit chunks and reading the 25-bit result in 8-bit chunks. An oscilloscope can be used to measure the difference in execution speed between the two adder types. The coin acceptor decoder is designed for the HX-916 model.
tt08/tt_um_cejmu.review_notes: Removed multiplexer tag as it is an internal selection mechanism, not a primary design feature.

tt08/tt_um_cfib_demo.summary: This demoscene competition entry generates a pseudo-random soundtrack via PWM and displays a waveform on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA Pmod on uo_out and Mike's audio Pmod on uio_out[7]. The design is written in Verilog and runs from a 50 MHz clock with asynchronous reset. A silicon test report confirms the design is working.
tt08/tt_um_cfib_demo.review_notes: Removed waveform-generator (not a general waveform generator) and added silicon-tested per the working test report.

tt08/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

tt08/tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.summary: This design is a clock divider with lag correction that interfaces with PDM microphones and an I2S receiver. It takes bit clock and LR clock inputs, along with PDM data from up to eight microphones, and outputs PCM audio for each microphone plus a beamformed PCM output. The documentation is too vague to describe its exact operation.
tt08/tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported i2s/dsp tags and added pdm based on PDM microphone inputs.

tt08/tt_um_comm_ic_bhavuk.summary: Comm_IC combines UART, SPI, and I2C communication protocols into a single design that is selected via input data bits.
tt08/tt_um_comm_ic_bhavuk.review_notes: Added missing canonical tags for the implemented communication protocols and language.

tt08/tt_um_crispy_vga.summary: Crispy VGA takes a standard Tiny Tapeout VGA signal as input and adds a programmable amount of random noise to the video and audio signals before passing them to the output. The uio_in[0] through uio_in[4] inputs individually toggle noise on the hsync, B, G, R, and vsync signals. The uio_in[5] input sets the noise level applied to the R, G, and B wires to high or low, and the uio_in[0:5] inputs set successively increasing noise levels on the audio signal. Testing requires plugging an existing Tiny Tapeout VGA project into the input, connecting the output to a VGA monitor, and selecting the control bits for the desired noise level.
tt08/tt_um_crispy_vga.review_notes: Summary expanded to four sentences covering the documented noise controls and test setup.

tt08/tt_um_daosvik_aesinvsbox.summary: This circuit computes the inverse S-box of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It takes an 8-bit input byte on ui[0] through ui[7] and produces an 8-bit output byte on uo[0] through uo[7]. The result can be read back from uo_out (unregistered) or uio_out (registered). No external hardware is required.
tt08/tt_um_daosvik_aesinvsbox.review_notes: Removed lookup-table tag as unsupported; summary expanded to four supported sentences.

tt08/tt_um_ddc_arghunter.summary: This design converts I2S audio input to PDM output using an inverted CIC filter and modulator. It also supports up to eight PDM microphones, producing per-microphone PCM outputs and a beamformed PCM output, with delay selection controlled by five pins. The design is intended for use with an I2S output device and PDM input devices, such as microphones and a clock generator. The documentation is minimal beyond the pin descriptions and a brief explanation of the core conversion method.
tt08/tt_um_ddc_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported fir-filter and delay-line tags; added sigma-delta for the PDM modulator.

tt08/tt_um_demosiine_sda.summary: DemoSiine is a demoscene-style audio-visual project that generates a 640x480 VGA video signal and a looping ~28 second audio track. The video output includes dynamic wavy sine layers and a rainbowy overlay, with user controls to enable/disable layers, pause the animation, and toggle styles. The audio engine drives a frequency synthesizer to produce the soundtrack. It requires external hardware: a TinyVGA PMOD for video output, a TT Audio PMOD for audio output, and switches for input control.
tt08/tt_um_demosiine_sda.review_notes: Removed button (inputs are switches); added pmod, music, and video to match the PMOD hardware and audio/video outputs.

tt08/tt_um_dendraws_donut.summary: The donut project displays a rendered donut on a VGA screen. It uses hand-crafted ellipses to create the donut shape and outputs a standard VGA signal with 2-bit RGB color, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design operates with a 50.35 MHz clock and requires a TinyVGA PMOD connected to the output pins for display. The documentation is sparse, providing only a brief description and testing instructions.
tt08/tt_um_dendraws_donut.review_notes: Removed demoscene as unsupported; added pmod because the TinyVGA PMOD is required.

tt08/tt_um_devstdin_LDO_OSC.summary: This analog project provides three building blocks: a low-dropout regulator (LDO), a bandgap current reference, and an oscillator. The LDO output and oscillator output are accessible on pins, and the oscillator can be enabled and reset via digital inputs. Silicon test reports indicate the LDO outputs around 1.8V and the oscillator runs at approximately 5.2-5.8 MHz. The design is intended as analog IP for integration into larger systems.
tt08/tt_um_devstdin_LDO_OSC.review_notes: Removed unsupported power-management tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

tt08/tt_um_dlfloatmac.summary: This design implements a multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit for 16-bit DLFloat (a custom floating-point format). It accepts two sets of eight FP16 inputs via the ui and uio pins and outputs a 16-bit result in two 8-bit halves over two clock cycles. An external FPGA is required to drive the inputs and capture the output, as the data is presented in a multiplexed manner. A silicon test report confirms functionality, noting a timing discrepancy in the provided cocotb test that was resolved.
tt08/tt_um_dlfloatmac.review_notes: Summary is supported, but the term 'FP16' in the pin names is treated as the input format, not strict IEEE FP16.

tt08/tt_um_dlmiles_poc_fskmodem_hdlctrx.summary: This project is a proof-of-concept digital FSK modem with HDLC framing and UART interface, targeting amateur radio packet communication at data rates from 4800 to 64000 baud. It uses a lookup-table-based waveform generator for 2FSK modulation and includes UART flow control signals. The design is intended to be paired with a future CPU to form a complete terminal node controller (TNC). Testing requires external hardware such as an RP2040 or FPGA to validate the interface.
tt08/tt_um_dlmiles_poc_fskmodem_hdlctrx.review_notes: Removed rom (only in original hardware description) and added demodulator and incomplete.

tt08/tt_um_dlmiles_tt08_poc_uart.summary: The UART project is a UART data terminal equipment (DTE) implementation in SpinalHDL. It provides standard UART signals such as TxD, RxD, RTS, CTS, DSR, DCD, DTR, and RI, along with interrupt outputs. The design is intended to connect to a standard Tiny Tapeout PCB and interface with an RP2040's UART. Documentation is minimal, with only pin mappings and a brief note that docs are to follow.

tt08/tt_um_dmtd_arghunter.summary: The DMTD project is described as a Dual Mixer Timer Differential, but the documentation is extremely sparse, elaborating only that it involves I2S and PDM audio interfaces with microphone inputs and beamformed output. The pinout is identical to another audio project, suggesting it may reuse that interface. External hardware required includes microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver. The documentation is essentially placeholder text, providing no real explanation of functionality.
tt08/tt_um_dmtd_arghunter.review_notes: Removed dsp tag unsupported by text; attempted pdm add is not in vocabulary.

tt08/tt_um_dpmu.summary: This project is titled DPMU (Dynamic Power Management Unit) and is implemented in SystemVerilog. The pin names are generic, and there is no documentation describing its functionality, interface, or how it should be tested. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may indicate an error or a very slow control loop. Due to the lack of documentation, it is not possible to provide a meaningful summary.

tt08/tt_um_dpmunit.summary: This project is titled DPM_Unit and is described as a Design and Implementation of Dynamic Power management unit, implemented in SystemVerilog. The pin names are generic, and there is no documentation describing its functionality, interface, or how it should be tested. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may indicate an error or a very slow control loop. Due to the lack of documentation, it is not possible to provide a meaningful summary.

tt08/tt_um_edwintorok.summary: This design is a competition entry for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene, producing a VGA output and audio PWM signal. It is intended to be connected to a VGA PMOD for 640x480 video and an audio PMOD for sound. The design uses HardCaml and operates at 25.25 MHz, with a test mode pin. The documentation is minimal, providing only pinouts and external hardware requirements, so the visual and audio content is not described.
tt08/tt_um_edwintorok.review_notes: Removed unsupported lfsr tag; added demoscene, vga, audio, pwm, and graphics based on source evidence.

tt08/tt_um_emilian_muxpga.summary: This project is a resubmission of a TinyFPGA design for Tiny Tapeout 8, implemented in Verilog. It provides four inputs, two command pins, and eight outputs, and is configured and then observed via the outputs. No special external hardware is required, and the design includes tests. The documentation is very brief, so the exact function of the FPGA configuration is not detailed.
tt08/tt_um_emilian_muxpga.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and template tags; added incomplete due to very thin documentation.

tt08/tt_um_emmyxu_obstacle_detection.summary: This Verilog design takes two sensor inputs and a reset, and outputs two signals intended for motors or buzzers. It compares each sensor value against a threshold and, if only one side is active, sends a signal to the opposite motor; if both are active, it sends a signal to both motors. Testing involves driving the sensor pins with 0 or 1 and reading the outputs; a reset pin clears all outputs. External hardware includes ultrasonic sensors, a microcontroller, and haptic motors.

tt08/tt_um_ephrenm_tsal.summary: This design implements the Tractive System Active Light (TSAL) function for a Formula SAE electric vehicle, as required by FSAE rule EV.5.9. It reads a 12-bit value from an external AD7476A ADC via a serial interface and compares it to a threshold; if below the threshold, it drives a green LED continuously, and if above, it flashes a red LED at 4 Hz. Testing requires a PMOD AD1 and simulation for at least one second to verify blink timing. The design is intended to be hard-wired in the vehicle and uses a Tiny Tapeout chip for the digital logic.
tt08/tt_um_ephrenm_tsal.review_notes: Removed timer tag; the blink function is part of the TSAL logic, not a separate timer peripheral.

tt08/tt_um_ezchips_calc.summary: This is an 8-bit calculator design originating from a ChipCraft lab exercise. It is implemented in Verilog and tested using Makerchip simulation. No external hardware is required, and all pins are marked unused in the provided pin list. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note about simulation testing.
tt08/tt_um_ezchips_calc.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added incomplete due to minimal documentation and unused pins.

tt08/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module designed to verify all I/O pins of a Tiny Tapeout ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both outputs and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by the reset and select pins. It is used during manufacturing test to confirm connectivity and functionality of every pin.
tt08/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed gpio: the pins are factory test I/O, not a general purpose GPIO interface.

tt08/tt_um_faramire_rotary_ring_wrapper.summary: This Verilog design uses a rotary encoder to control a ring of 12 WS2812B LEDs. Rotating the encoder selects which LED is lit, and a button inverts the LED state. The user can select the color (green, red, or blue) via three input pins and set the intensity with two additional pins. The chip outputs a WS2812B serial data stream on one pin to drive the LED chain, and it also outputs the current count value. External hardware includes a rotary encoder and a WS2812B LED ring.

tt08/tt_um_faramire_stopwatch.summary: This is a simple stopwatch that counts in hundredths of a second and displays the time on an 8-digit 7-segment display via SPI using a MAX7219 chip.
