tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural.summary: This is a 4x4 unsigned array multiplier implemented in Verilog using structural design with carry-save adders and a final carry-propagate adder. It takes an 8-bit input split into two 4-bit operands and outputs an 8-bit product. The design is a class project (ECE2204) and includes a testbench for verification. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not state an educational purpose, and added the supported canonical tags.

tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural_GnahsLl.summary: This project is a 4x4 array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers using a series of full adders to produce an 8-bit product. The design is combinational and the documentation includes a block diagram and a testing procedure with example inputs. No external hardware is required.

tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural_sarahhe.summary: This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It uses partial products and full adders to sum them, with carry propagation between stages. The design is verified with a Verilog testbench and Python script, and no external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural_sarahhe.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational purpose.

tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural_section.summary: This project implements a 4-bit array multiplier using structural Verilog. It takes two 4-bit inputs and computes their 8-bit product using partial products and adders. The design is combinational and does not use clock or reset signals. Testing can be done by applying inputs and observing the output, and no external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_array_mult_structural_section.review_notes: Removed education tag because the documentation does not mention teaching or learning intent.

tt09/tt_um_array_secD7.summary: This project implements a 4x4 array multiplier in Verilog that computes the product of two 4-bit binary numbers using partial products and full adders. The multiplier generates partial products by ANDing each bit of one input with all bits of the other, then sums them with full adders in a staged manner. The design is combinational and purely digital, producing an 8-bit product output. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.

tt09/tt_um_arry_mult_structural.summary: This project implements a 4x4 structural array multiplier in Verilog that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers using full adders. The design generates partial products by ANDing each bit of one operand with all bits of the other, then sums them in a staged manner. The circuit is combinational and purely digital, producing an 8-bit product. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.

tt09/tt_um_asheldon44_dsm_decimation_fil.summary: This design implements a digital low-pass and decimation filter intended for the output of a delta-sigma analog-to-digital converter. It accepts 1-bit modulator data at 50 MHz and produces 16-bit filtered data on the GPIOs at 781.25 kHz. The analog portion is not included and is hoped for on a future shuttle. It is implemented in Verilog and can be tested by feeding a modulated input and observing the filtered output.
tt09/tt_um_asheldon44_dsm_decimation_fil.review_notes: Removed unsupported FIR/IIR/analog-filter tags; corrected summary to match the documented decimation filter behavior.

tt09/tt_um_b_0_array_multiplier.summary: This project is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that takes two 4-bit binary inputs and produces an 8-bit product. It uses full adders to combine partial products and generate the final multiplication result. The design is implemented in Verilog. It is intended as a lab exercise for a group project.
tt09/tt_um_b_0_array_multiplier.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the array multiplier design.

tt09/tt_um_b_10_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4x4 array multiplier, a combinational digital circuit for multiplying two binary numbers. It generates partial products and adds them using full adders arranged in a systematic array to produce the final product. The design is purely digital and produces an 8-bit product. The source includes a structural description and a diagram of the 4x4 array multiplier.
tt09/tt_um_b_10_array_multiplier.review_notes: Added structural tag because the source describes an array of full adders; corrected the summary wording from 4-bit multiplier to 4x4 array multiplier.

tt09/tt_um_b_12_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4-bit binary multiplier using a combinational array structure. It multiplies two 4-bit numbers by generating partial products and summing them with full adders. The design is purely digital and produces an 8-bit product. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.

tt09/tt_um_b_2_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4-bit binary multiplier using a combinational array structure. It multiplies two 4-bit numbers by generating partial products and summing them with full adders. The design is purely digital and produces an 8-bit product. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.

tt09/tt_um_b_6_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs, m and q, and produces an 8-bit product p. Partial products are generated by ANDing each bit of m with all bits of q and summed with a series of full adders. The design is purely combinational and produces an 8-bit product. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.
tt09/tt_um_b_6_array_multiplier.review_notes: Added structural tag; summary corrected to match the documented 4x4 inputs and 8-bit output.

tt09/tt_um_b_8_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4-bit binary multiplier using a combinational array structure. It multiplies two 4-bit numbers by generating partial products and summing them with full adders. The design is purely digital and produces an 8-bit product. It is a structural implementation suitable for learning about binary multiplication.

tt09/tt_um_brandonramos_opamp_ladder.summary: This project implements a 2-bit flash ADC that converts a 1.8 V to 0 V analog signal into an encoded 2-bit digital output. The analog input is applied to analog pin 0, and the encoded bits appear on the two dedicated outputs. It is an analog design occupying a 1x2 tile area with two analog pins. Testing is done by sweeping the analog input voltage and observing the encoded output bits.
tt09/tt_um_brandonramos_opamp_ladder.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated 4-bit multiplier; replaced with ADC-appropriate tags and summary.

tt09/tt_um_c13_array_mult.summary: This project implements a 4x4 multiplier in structural Verilog, producing an 8-bit product from two 4-bit inputs. It is built from an array of full adders that combine partial products, following a classic textbook multiplier structure. The design is intended as a lab exercise and is tested by applying input pairs and comparing the output to the expected product. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is sufficient to understand the basic operation.
tt09/tt_um_c13_array_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added combinational tag.

tt09/tt_um_c1_array_mult_structural.summary: This design is a 4x4 array multiplier that computes the product of two 4-bit binary numbers using full adders. It was created as a lab exercise to demonstrate binary multiplication and the role of full adders in digital circuits. Testing involves applying various input combinations and comparing the output to the expected product, which is 8 bits wide. No external hardware is needed, and the documentation provides a clear explanation of the design and test procedure.
tt09/tt_um_c1_array_mult_structural.review_notes: Removed alu because it is a multiplier, not an ALU, and added workshop for the lab context.

tt09/tt_um_c7_array_mult.summary: This project is a 4-bit multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers using full adders to produce an 8-bit product. It is tested by specifying two 4-bit inputs in a Python test script and verifying the output against the expected product. The design requires no external hardware. The documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the function and testing method.
tt09/tt_um_c7_array_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added combinational tag.

tt09/tt_um_c_2_array_mult.summary: This is a 4x4 array multiplier implemented in Verilog that multiplies two 4-bit numbers to produce an 8-bit product. The design is based on a standard array multiplier structure using full adders. Testing is performed by adding test cases in a Python script and following the instructions in the test README. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is minimal but adequate.
tt09/tt_um_c_2_array_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added combinational tag.

tt09/tt_um_c_4_4b_mult.summary: This project implements a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using full adders. The inputs are split into two 4-bit portions, and the multiplication is performed through adder logic. Testing is done using a testbench with idle cases. No external hardware is needed, but the documentation is very sparse and lacks detail on the exact implementation and test procedure.
tt09/tt_um_c_4_4b_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag (design is a multiplier only) and added incomplete for the very thin documentation.

tt09/tt_um_carryskip_adder8.summary: This design is an 8-bit carry-skip adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using a combination of ripple-carry and skip logic to reduce carry propagation delay. The adder is divided into two 4-bit sections, and the final sum is registered and output synchronously with the clock. Testing involves applying input values to the ui_in and uio_in pins and verifying the sum on uo_out after each clock edge. No external hardware is required, and the documentation provides a clear explanation of the operation and test method.
tt09/tt_um_carryskip_adder8.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added combinational tag.

tt09/tt_um_carryskip_adder9.summary: This project implements an 8-bit carry-skip adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using ripple-carry and skip logic for improved performance. The design splits the addition into two 4-bit sections and registers the output in sync with the clock. Testing is done by applying inputs to ui_in and uio_in and checking the sum on uo_out after each rising edge. No external hardware is needed, and the documentation is identical to another project, suggesting it may be a duplicate or shared design.
tt09/tt_um_carryskip_adder9.review_notes: Removed alu tag; added combinational tag.

tt09/tt_um_ccu_goatgate.summary: This project is a tiny encryption core that takes a 4-bit input and a 4-bit key to produce a 4-bit encrypted output. It is intended to be tested by sending randomized 4-bit inputs and keys and observing the output. The design requires no external hardware, though memory may be needed to supply test data. The documentation is very limited, providing only a high-level description without details on the encryption algorithm or test methodology.
tt09/tt_um_ccu_goatgate.review_notes: Removed unsupported security tag and added verilog tag.

tt09/tt_um_cdc_test.summary: This design is a VGA demo that displays an image of a plane flying into the sunset. It runs automatically and outputs VGA signals on the uo pins, requiring a VGA PMOD connected to the output. The project is a re-run of a previous demo and mentions an unsuccessful attempt at a clock domain crossing project. The documentation is minimal, focusing on the visual output rather than technical details.
tt09/tt_um_cdc_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'text' tag and added 'silicon-tested' based on the TT08 re-run statement.

tt09/tt_um_cellular_alchemist.summary: This project implements a Hopfield neural network on-chip using Izhikevich-type regular spiking and fast spiking neurons with on-chip Hebbian learning for pattern storage and retrieval. It accepts a learning enable signal and a 4-bit pattern input, and outputs spikes from seven neurons via bidirectional pins. The design is a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron model and is intended to be tested, though the documentation provides little detail on the test procedure. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is sparse and lacks specifics on operation and verification.
tt09/tt_um_cellular_alchemist.review_notes: Removed machine-learning tag (neuromorphic spiking design) and added incomplete for the sparse documentation.

tt09/tt_um_chip4lyfe.summary: This design implements a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron network inspired by snnTorch. It accepts an 8-bit input current split between two input neurons, and each neuron integrates the current, decays its state by bit-shifting each clock cycle, and emits a spike when its state reaches or exceeds a threshold of 8. The network has multiple layers, with spike outputs for each layer and state variable outputs for the output layer neurons. The documentation provides no testing procedure or external hardware requirements, and the design is a compact digital implementation of a spiking neural network building block.

tt09/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

tt09/tt_um_claudiotalarico_counter.summary: This project is a 4-bit up/down binary counter with enable and test mode. It uses input pins for test, up/down selection, and enable, and outputs the 4-bit count value. Testing requires connecting the enable pin to VDD, test to GND, up/down to a switch, reset to an RC startup circuit, and a 50 MHz clock, with the outputs connected to LEDs. The design is a straightforward digital building block with minimal documentation beyond basic operation.
tt09/tt_um_claudiotalarico_counter.review_notes: Removed dip-switch tag; the source only mentions a generic switch.

tt09/tt_um_control_block.summary: This design implements the control block for an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture. It uses a 6-stage sequential counter and a lookup table to generate control signals from a 4-bit opcode, with outputs for various register and memory control lines as well as a halt signal. Testing involves applying opcodes and monitoring the control signal outputs, optionally using a logic analyzer or slowing the clock. The project is part of a course (ECE 298A) and is intended to be integrated with other CPU sub-blocks.
tt09/tt_um_control_block.review_notes: Removed instruction-decoder as the block is a control unit; added sequential-logic for the micro-instruction counter.

tt09/tt_um_couchand_analog_switch.summary: This is a simple analog switch that connects or disconnects two analog pins (X and Y) based on a digital control input. When the control input is high, X and Y are connected; when low, they are isolated. The design also provides an inverse of the control signal as a digital output. Testing involves applying a digital high to X, a pull-down resistor on Y, and toggling the control input to verify connectivity and the inverse output.
tt09/tt_um_couchand_analog_switch.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and dip-switch tags; the design is a simple analog passgate switch.

tt09/tt_um_couchand_cora16.summary: CORA-16 is a 16-bit CPU that uses external SPI memory for instruction fetch and execution. It features a byte-wide general-purpose input and output bus, and supports single-stepping for debugging via a step pin. Status pins indicate busy, halt, and trap conditions, with trap recovery possible by stepping. The design requires an external SPI RAM, such as a Raspberry Pi acting as an emulator, to load and run programs.
tt09/tt_um_couchand_cora16.review_notes: Removed memory tag because the design uses external SPI RAM rather than implementing memory; added instruction-decoder as core CPU logic.

tt09/tt_um_d_4_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4x4 structural array multiplier using full adders and AND gates. It takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product. The design is built from basic logic gates and full adders, forming partial products and summing them with carry propagation. It is an educational project (ECE-UY 2204) intended to demonstrate digital arithmetic design, and testing involves applying input values and comparing the output to expected results.
tt09/tt_um_d_4_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed education because the source does not state an educational purpose, and added the supported canonical tags.

tt09/tt_um_db_MAC.summary: This design implements an 8-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit for unsigned integers using Vedic multipliers and reversible gates. Inputs are registered on half a clock cycle, and the MAC operation is performed with the multiplier and adder each taking half a clock cycle. The result is output on dedicated and bidirectional pins. The project explores reversible gates for energy efficiency and requires no external hardware.
tt09/tt_um_db_MAC.review_notes: Removed low-power because the source only mentions exploring reversible gates for energy efficiency, not a low-power implementation.

tt09/tt_um_delta_liafn.summary: This design implements a delta recurrent neural network (Delta RNN) combined with a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron. It accepts an 8-bit input current, computes the difference between previous and current states, and generates a spike when that difference exceeds a set delta threshold. Outputs include the state variable and the difference in states. The documentation provides no testing procedure or external hardware requirements, and the design is a compact digital implementation of a spiking neural network component.

tt09/tt_um_devinatkin_basys3_uart.summary: This project runs the main peripherals of a Basys 3 FPGA board over a 115200 baud UART link. It handles 16 LED inputs, 16 switch outputs, 12 seven-segment display inputs, and 5 button outputs, all communicated via UART TX and RX routed to the bidirectional PMOD bus. Testing can be done with an associated PMOD board or by interacting with the UART, expecting messages like "LD: 0xFFFF" and "SW: 0xFFFF". The design enables remote control of Basys 3 peripherals through a serial connection.
tt09/tt_um_devinatkin_basys3_uart.review_notes: Removed unsupported dip-switch tag and added pmod because the UART is routed to the PMOD bus.

tt09/tt_um_dff_mem.summary: This project implements a 16-byte RAM built from D flip-flops. It supports read and write operations with a 4-bit address, active-low chip enable and load signals, and an 8-bit data input. Read operations are asynchronous, and the output is high-impedance when not enabled. The design is intended for integration into an 8-bit processor and includes CocoTB testbenches that verify write and read functionality across all addresses.
tt09/tt_um_dff_mem.review_notes: Removed sram (built from DFFs) and added cocotb per documented testbenches.

tt09/tt_um_digital_clock_example.summary: This design implements a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format. It uses SPI to drive a MAX7219 7-segment display driver because there are not enough output pins to directly control six 7-segment displays. The time can be set using dedicated buttons for hours and minutes, with a fast/slow adjustment mode and a 12-hour mode option. The design requires an external MAX7219 module and a 32.768 kHz reference clock for accurate timekeeping.
tt09/tt_um_digital_clock_example.review_notes: Removed rtc and clock-generator tags that are not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_dlmiles_dffram32x8_2r1w.summary: This project implements a 32x8 dual-port-read single-port-write RAM using D-type flip-flops, described by the author as a 'really bad implementation' due to its inefficiency. The RAM has two read ports (A and B) and one write port (A), with configurable features such as read buffering, write-through policy, and page selection via configuration bits latched on reset release. It is intended to be tested with standard Tiny Tapeout hardware and an RP2040, and a MicroPython interface is planned. The design is notable for its use of flip-flops instead of dedicated RAM blocks and its flexible read/write policies.
tt09/tt_um_dlmiles_dffram32x8_2r1w.review_notes: Removed register-file (it is a RAM array, not a register file) and added sram as the canonical memory-block tag.

tt09/tt_um_dog_BILBO.summary: This design implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer (CBILBO) for memory testing, using shift registers, multiplexers, and feedback logic. It provides a way to observe and control internal memory elements for test purposes. The project includes input and output paths for Tiny Tapeout and supports asynchronous reset. No external hardware is required for testing, and the design is intended to be verified through simulation of its shifting and feedback behavior.
tt09/tt_um_dog_BILBO.review_notes: Removed scan-chain (unsupported); added bist, shift-register, and memory.

tt09/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture, developed as part of a university course. It includes a control unit, program counter, instruction register, 16-byte memory, arithmetic logic unit with carry and zero flags, accumulator, and output register. The CPU can execute a small instruction set and provides outputs for the accumulator and flags. It is intended for educational purposes and can be tested by providing opcodes and observing outputs.
tt09/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file tag; added risc-v tag noting the architecture is not RISC-V, correcting a potential misattribution.

tt09/tt_um_ericsmi_mips.summary: This is the MIPS processor core example from the Weste & Harris textbook, written by Max Yi and David Harris. It implements a subset of the MIPS architecture with separate memory address, read, and write interfaces. The design requires an external program store to function. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it needs a program store and that testing should be done 'carefully'.

tt09/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module designed to verify all I/O pins of the ASIC. It operates in three modes: mirroring the dedicated inputs to the outputs, mirroring the bidirectional pins to the outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both the outputs and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by the rst_n and sel pins. It requires no external hardware and is used during chip bring-up to confirm pin functionality.
tt09/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed gpio because the design is a factory test module, not a general purpose IO interface.

tt09/tt_um_flyingfish800.summary: This is a simple Verilog test project that accumulates the value on the dedicated input pins into an internal register every clock cycle. The least significant bits of the accumulated value are output on the dedicated output pins, while the most significant bits are output on the bidirectional pins. It is intended as a basic demonstration and requires switches on inputs and LEDs on outputs for testing. The design is minimal and serves as a template or experiment.
tt09/tt_um_flyingfish800.review_notes: Removed alu, register-file, counter, and education tags because the source describes only a simple accumulator/test design.

tt09/tt_um_four_bit_multiplier_nasan016_.summary: This project implements a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product. It uses a manual structural design with AND gates and full adders to compute the multiplication. The design was created for a digital logic course lab and includes a Python test script for verification. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_four_bit_multiplier_nasan016_.review_notes: Removed 'alu' since the design is a dedicated multiplier, not an ALU; 'adder' is already present.

tt09/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an external signal by counting pulses over 100 ms periods and displays the result on a 128x32 SSD1306 OLED display using an emulated 7-segment format. It requires an external 1 MHz clock, a PMOD OLED display, and the signal to be measured connected to the input pin. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and uses SPI to communicate with the OLED. No silicon test results are provided, so the actual performance is not documented.

tt09/tt_um_gfcwfzkm_scope_bfh_mht1_3.summary: This design implements a basic oscilloscope and signal generator on an ASIC, using an external ADC, DAC, FRAM, and HDMI Pmod. It samples input signals, buffers them in FRAM, and displays waveforms on an HDMI screen, with the display rotated 90 degrees due to memory constraints. The signal generator uses direct digital synthesis to produce sine, square, triangle, and sawtooth waves, and the oscilloscope supports trigger functionality. The design requires multiple external Pmods and outputs settings via UART.
tt09/tt_um_gfcwfzkm_scope_bfh_mht1_3.review_notes: Removed nco (DDS, not NCO) and added pmod, button, dip-switch, and oscilloscope.

tt09/tt_um_gmejiamtz.summary: This project implements a small Configurable Logic Block (CLB) with a 3-input Look-Up Table (LUT3). It takes two 8-bit inputs: one for the LUT configuration and control signals, and another for the boolean function arguments. The output is the evaluation of the configured boolean function. The design can be tested by setting the LUT to implement a NAND3 function and using switches and LEDs for input and output.

tt09/tt_um_histogramming.summary: This project implements a histogramming unit, but the documentation is essentially empty, providing no details on its functionality, interface, or usage. The pin names are generic and do not indicate specific behavior. It is not possible to determine how the design works or how to test it from the available information.

tt09/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

tt09/tt_um_htfab_hybrid.summary: This analog telephone hybrid converts two unidirectional signal paths into a single bidirectional line, using a transformer-based circuit. It is tested by connecting a wire between LINE1 and LINE2, then verifying that signals applied to IN1 appear at OUT2 and vice versa. External analog test equipment such as a function generator and oscilloscope is required for evaluation. Silicon measurements show operation up to about 3 kHz with 12–15 dB isolation, and the design requires band-limited input signals to maintain directionality.
tt09/tt_um_htfab_hybrid.review_notes: Removed unsupported tag and added correct ones based on source.

tt09/tt_um_hybrid_adder.summary: This 8-bit hybrid adder combines a 4-bit Kogge-Stone adder with a 4-bit carry-lookahead adder to balance gate efficiency and latency. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and produces the sum on uo_out. Testing requires only applying 3.3V logic levels to the inputs and reading the outputs. The design is described as faster than an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder and more gate-efficient than an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder.
tt09/tt_um_hybrid_adder.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source documents only an adder, not an ALU.

tt09/tt_um_idann.summary: This design implements a forward pass for a simple artificial neural network with 4 input neurons, 8 hidden neurons, and 1 output neuron, and also computes the mean squared error loss. It accepts a 4-bit input on ui_in[3:0] and uses ui_in[7] to start the computation, with the result and state available on the output pins. External hardware consists of switches to set the input value and a button or switch to trigger the forward pass. The design is intended for inference and loss calculation, and can be simulated by modifying the test script.
tt09/tt_um_idann.review_notes: Replaced accelerator with edge-ai to match the small embedded ANN inference design.

tt09/tt_um_instrumented_ring_oscillator.summary: This instrumented ring oscillator allows selection of the number of stages and initial state via input pins, and outputs 16 phases for observation. It is intended for studying the decay or persistence of high-frequency modes, not as a reliable clock source. Testing involves connecting a logic analyzer or oscilloscope to the outputs, configuring the stage count and seed, then enabling the oscillator and observing whether it stabilizes to the longest period or retains high-frequency modes. External hardware such as a logic analyzer or multi-channel oscilloscope is recommended for capturing the phase outputs.

tt09/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.summary: This project is a 1-bit AM software-defined radio pipeline written in Verilog. It uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC frontend, oversampled and decimated 4096 times to gain extra precision. The core includes an SPI interface for setting demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs demodulated audio via PWM. The design spans 3x2 Tiny Tapeout tiles and is based on a Hackaday project by Alberto Garlassi.
tt09/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.review_notes: Removed risc-v, cpu, soc, uart, qspi, and memory tags as unsupported; added radio, rf, dsp, spi, adc, demodulator, nco, audio, pwm, and multi-tile tags based on the source documentation.

tt09/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.summary: This is a software-defined radio core for AM reception that uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC and performs digital bandpass filtering and envelope detection. It is configured via a SPI interface to set the demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs a PWM signal representing the demodulated audio. External hardware includes a comparator, resistor bias network, RC network, SPI microcontroller, and an RF amplifier. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile size, trading off selectivity compared to a previous larger implementation.
tt09/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.review_notes: Removed comparator/adc (external components, not on-chip); added pwm and rf tags.

tt09/tt_um_juarez_jimenez.summary: This design implements a linear feedback shift register with synaptic neuron-inspired behavior, where bit transitions generate excitatory or inhibitory signals that modify the feedback path. It accepts an 8-bit seed on the input pins and produces an 8-bit pseudo-random output sequence on uo_out. Testing involves providing a clock and reset, setting the seed, and observing the output sequence over multiple cycles. No external hardware is required, and the design allows customizable seed values to vary the output sequence.

tt09/tt_um_kailinsley.summary: This project implements a dynamic threshold leaky integrate-and-fire model that simulates a spiking biological neuron. The documentation is essentially placeholder text and does not describe how the model works or how to test it. The pin names suggest eight inputs and eight outputs, but their functions are not explained. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design cannot be evaluated from the available information.
tt09/tt_um_kailinsley.review_notes: Replaced insufficient-doc with incomplete because the documentation is placeholder text rather than sparse.

tt09/tt_um_kashmaster_carryskip.summary: This 8-bit carry-skip adder uses two 4-bit sections with skip logic to reduce carry propagation delay compared to a ripple-carry adder. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and outputs the registered sum on uo_out after each rising clock edge. Testing can be done by applying input values and verifying the output against expected sums, either manually or with a testbench. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_kashmaster_carryskip.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source documents only an adder, not an ALU.

tt09/tt_um_kev_ma_matmult222.summary: This design multiplies two 2-bit 2x2 matrices, accepting matrix A on the standard input pins and matrix B on the bidirectional pins, and outputting the result matrix C on the standard output pins. Each matrix element is 2 bits, and the pin mapping is explicitly documented. Testing requires pulling pins high or low to set the input matrices and reading the output pins for the product. No external hardware is needed.
tt09/tt_um_kev_ma_matmult222.review_notes: Removed accelerator and alu as unsupported; added combinational for the purely combinational matrix multiply.

tt09/tt_um_kmakise_sram.summary: This project is a test harness for an OpenRAM SRAM macro (32x16) that communicates via UART, with separate address and data phases for read and write operations. It includes a DPU that can read, operate on, and write back data in the SRAM. Testing requires sending UART commands, ensuring the first command is sent only when uart_ready is high. Silicon tests confirmed random read/write functionality at 25 MHz and up to 75 MHz, with errors appearing at 100 MHz.
tt09/tt_um_kmakise_sram.review_notes: Removed unsupported accelerator tag and added silicon-tested based on the working silicon report.

tt09/tt_um_koggestone_adder8.summary: This project implements an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder in Verilog. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces their sum, but lacks a carry-out so sums above 255 are not representable. The design is intended as a class exercise and includes a testbench that iterates through all input combinations, skipping cases where overflow would occur. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
tt09/tt_um_koggestone_adder8.review_notes: Removed alu (single adder only); added workshop for the class context.

tt09/tt_um_led_cipher.summary: This design is a nibble-serial implementation of the LED block cipher, which encrypts a 64-bit plaintext block using a 128-bit key. It serializes both data input and output to fit within the limited I/O pins, controlled by a simple handshake protocol. The cipher requires external hardware, such as a Raspberry Pi, to provide the serial data and control signals. The design is notable for its compact implementation, reusing datapath logic across nibbles, at the cost of increased latency.

tt09/tt_um_led_matrix_ayla_lin.summary: This project drives a 32x8 LED matrix using a MAX7219/7221 controller via SPI. It displays an animation that alternates between a beaver logo and the letters 'BWSI', with bitmaps stored in an internal ROM. The design is intended to be tested on an FPGA connected to a breadboard, requiring external hardware including the LED matrix, the MAX7219/7221 chip, and a 5V power source. The SPI interface handles both configuration and bitmap data transmission.

tt09/tt_um_levenshtein.summary: This design implements a fuzzy search engine based on the bit-vector Levenshtein distance algorithm. It finds the closest matching word in a dictionary stored in external QSPI PSRAM, communicating with the host via SPI. The design requires a specific QSPI PSRAM PMOD that supports quad-mode operations and runs at half the clock speed of the chip. It is notable for being a hardware implementation of a string matching algorithm, with a provided client tool for testing.
tt09/tt_um_levenshtein.review_notes: Removed memory tag because the design only interfaces to external PSRAM rather than implementing memory.

tt09/tt_um_lfsr_stevej.summary: This project implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates a pseudo-random sequence. It accepts an 8-bit seed value and a write-enable signal to load the seed, and outputs the current LFSR state on eight output pins. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond reading the output pins. It can be used as a basic pseudo-random number generator.

tt09/tt_um_liaf.summary: This project simulates a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit input current and updates an internal state variable, producing a spike output when the state exceeds a threshold. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed usage or testing instructions. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_liaf.review_notes: Tags were already correct; no changes needed.

tt09/tt_um_lif1.summary: This project implements a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) circuit in Verilog. It detects pre- and post-synaptic spikes, measures the time difference between them, and adjusts a synaptic weight using an exponential trace model. The design is still under development and testing is incomplete. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_lif1.review_notes: Removed machine-learning; STDP is neuromorphic only.

tt09/tt_um_lif_ZB.summary: This project is a tutorial implementation of a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit input current and updates an internal state variable, producing a spike output when the state exceeds a threshold. The documentation is very sparse, with only a brief description and no detailed testing instructions. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_lif_ZB.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added incomplete because the test instructions are placeholder text.

tt09/tt_um_lif_clarencechan28.summary: This project implements a single-layer perceptron in Verilog. It takes 8 bits of input and 8 bits of weights, and classifies the input into one of two classes based on a weighted sum and threshold. The design is tested using a Python script that initializes inputs and expected outputs, and then runs a makefile-based test. No external hardware is required.

tt09/tt_um_lif_network_MR.summary: This project implements a small spiking neural network based on the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model. It consists of three input neurons that receive 5-bit input currents, and one output neuron that integrates weighted spikes from the input neurons. The design can be tested in simulation or on an FPGA, with LEDs and switches for input and output. It is suitable for basic pattern recognition or response simulations.

tt09/tt_um_lif_sfiguerr.summary: This design implements an adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire neuron in Verilog, where the firing threshold adapts based on recent spike activity so that sustained input produces progressively fewer spikes. It accepts an 8-bit input current on ui_in, exposes an 8-bit membrane state variable on uo_out, and emits a spike on uio[7]. Testing is done with the provided test.py by applying varying input currents and comparing observed outputs against expected values. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is limited to a brief description and test instructions.
tt09/tt_um_lif_sfiguerr.review_notes: Removed fsm tag because the source does not describe a finite state machine.

tt09/tt_um_lif_tk.summary: This project implements eight leaky integrate-and-fire neurons connected in a ring topology, with configurable base current, coupling strength, and one of five firing patterns (independent, wave, synchronous, clustered, burst). Inputs are split across ui_in for pattern select and base current scaling, and uio_in for coupling strength, while spike outputs appear on uo_out and the first neuron's membrane potential on uio_out. Testing involves applying reset and enable, selecting a pattern and current, and monitoring the spike outputs for the expected propagation or synchronization behavior. No external hardware is needed.
tt09/tt_um_lif_tk.review_notes: Removed oscillator and synchronizer tags unsupported by the source; dropped unsupported 'notable' claim.

tt09/tt_um_lifn.summary: This design is a simple leaky integrate-and-fire neuron implemented in Verilog that integrates an 8-bit input current into a membrane potential, leaks it over time, and fires a spike when a threshold is reached before resetting. The input current is applied on ui_in, the membrane state is exposed on uo_out, and the spike appears on uio[7]. The testing section only says 'Do something', so no concrete test procedure is documented. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is too thin to describe the implementation details beyond the general LIF behavior.

tt09/tt_um_lrc_stevej.summary: This design computes a running longitudinal redundancy check (LRC) over a stream of bytes, updating the code each time a new byte is presented on the input pins. A byte is supplied on ui_in and the current LRC is read from uo_out, with the running value resetting when the chip is reset. No external hardware is needed, and the design is a straightforward checksum generator. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the function and basic usage.
tt09/tt_um_lrc_stevej.review_notes: Removed crc since the design is an LRC, not a CRC.

tt09/tt_um_lsnn_hschweig.summary: This project implements a leaky spiking neural network (LSNN) neuron with a 12-bit membrane potential, configurable decay, adaptive threshold with optional learning, a three-cycle refractory period, and a 7-bit spike counter. Input current is applied on ui_in, the membrane potential and refractory indicator are output on uo_out, and the spike plus spike counter appear on uio_out, with learning enabled via uio_in[0]. Testing covers reset behavior, basic spiking, learning mode, and spike-count verification entirely through digital I/O. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_lsnn_hschweig.review_notes: Removed redundant neural-network tag and unsupported 'notable' claim.

tt09/tt_um_m4rthaswur1d.summary: This design is a structural 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned factors, m and q, on ui_in and produces their 8-bit product p on uo_out. It works by generating partial products and summing them with full adders in a classic array arrangement. Testing is suggested with a testbench of ten varying 4-bit factor pairs compared against their expected products. No external hardware is needed, and the design is a simple educational arithmetic block.
tt09/tt_um_m4rthaswur1d.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source describes only a multiplier.

tt09/tt_um_matrix_mult.summary: This design multiplies a 2x2 matrix by a 2x1 vector, with 2-bit elements, producing a 2-element output vector. Matrix elements are supplied on ui_in, the input vector on uio_in, and the output vector is split across uo_out and uio_out. The documentation is inconsistent: the 'How it works' section describes treating inputs as current injection into a LIF neuron, which does not match the title or pin descriptions, and the test section only says 'Test it'. External hardware is listed as 'Possibly', and the documentation is too thin and contradictory to describe the design reliably.
tt09/tt_um_matrix_mult.review_notes: Escalated because the source is contradictory about whether this is a matrix-vector multiplier or a LIF neuron circuit.

tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.summary: This analog design contains two ring oscillators, one built from 18 inverters and a NAND enable gate targeting roughly 600 MHz, and one from 36 inverters targeting roughly 300 MHz, each followed by a two-stage driver to drive the analog pads. Ring 1 is enabled via ui[0] and observed on uo[0], while ring 2 is enabled via ui[1] and observed on uo[1]. Testing requires an oscilloscope to measure the attenuated analog output, and the documentation notes that the 300 MHz oscillator had a missing contact in TT08 and was fixed for TT09. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog oscillator experiment with known silicon issues.
tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.review_notes: Removed incorrect clock-generator tag and added silicon-tested tag per documentation.

tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_double_inverter.summary: This analog design is a pair of inverters wired between two analog pins, with a small inverter driving a larger one to form a buffer. A signal is applied to ua[1] and the inverted output is observed on ua[0], with simulated rise time under 4 ns. Testing requires a signal generator and an oscilloscope. The design is a minimal transistor-level analog building block with limited documentation beyond its basic function.
tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_double_inverter.review_notes: Removed logic-gate and driver tags; the source describes an analog inverter pair, not digital logic or a driver stage.

tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.summary: This design is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) with a 3.3V output, driven either externally or by an internal sine waveform generator. Silicon tests confirm a smooth sine wave over the full 3.3V range, with a slight nonlinearity at the mid-code transition. It requires an external multimeter to measure the output voltage. The design uses level shifting drivers to achieve the 3.3V output.
tt09/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.review_notes: Removed transistor-level, which is not supported by the R2R ladder description; silicon-tested was already correctly applied.

tt09/tt_um_mbkmicdec_ringosc.summary: This project is an analog design planned to contain a simple ADC, with a single analog output pin ua[0]. The documentation states only that it is planned to contain a simple ADC, with testing and external hardware both marked 'TBC'. There is essentially no usable documentation describing the implementation, pin functions, or test procedure. As a result, the design cannot be evaluated beyond its stated intent.
tt09/tt_um_mbkmicdec_ringosc.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal: no digital circuitry is documented, only an analog output pin.

tt09/tt_um_michaelmcculloch_alu.summary: This project implements a 6-bit input ALU that selects an operation based on a 4-bit RISC-V opcode and produces an 8-bit output. Inputs A and B are provided through the bidirectional pins and the dedicated input pins, while the opcode is set on the remaining input pins. Testing involves applying input values and opcodes and observing the output, optionally with LEDs connected for visual feedback. The design is a straightforward iterative ALU with no external hardware required.
tt09/tt_um_michaelmcculloch_alu.review_notes: Removed risc-v tag because the design is an ALU using RISC-V-style opcodes, not a RISC-V core.

tt09/tt_um_mickey_pll.summary: This analog project is a 100 MHz voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) whose frequency can be tuned from approximately 100 MHz to 180 MHz by varying the control voltage. It provides analog outputs such as the VCO output and a digital output, along with control and reference pins. Testing is done by applying a 1.0 V control voltage and observing the output pins. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_mickey_pll.review_notes: Title says PLL but documentation only describes a VCO; removed pll and transistor-level tags.

tt09/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.summary: This is an experimental microtile container that places ring oscillators in a separate tile to add power stress. It has 8 digital inputs, 8 digital outputs, and 2 select pins, but the documentation states that there is nothing to test and it serves as an experimental basis. The design is a Verilog module clocked at 20 MHz. No external hardware or specific testing procedure is described.
tt09/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.review_notes: Removed unsupported TDC and multi-tile tags; added incomplete since the design is explicitly an untested experimental basis.

tt09/tt_um_mikegoelzer_7segmentbyte.summary: This design drives a two-digit 7-segment display to show the hexadecimal representation of an 8-bit input byte. The byte is latched on a rising clock edge when the write enable signal is high, and the display is continuously driven with segment outputs and a digit select signal. Testing requires connecting a 7-segment display and manipulating the input and write enable pins to verify latching and display updates. The project uses a simple interface with a standard 7-segment display.
tt09/tt_um_mikegoelzer_7segmentbyte.review_notes: Removed driver (no driver stage); added pmod for the linked Pmod SSD display; reworded final sentence to avoid unsupported 'notable' claim.

tt09/tt_um_mroblesh.summary: This project implements an 8-bit frequency encoder and decoder for a 1-bit frequency channel, with a selector pin to choose between encoding and decoding modes. The documentation also mentions that it treats an 8-bit input voltage as a current injection to a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, but the connection between the two functions is unclear. Testing instructions are minimal, stating only 'Do something', and no external hardware is specified. The design appears to be a mixed-signal or neuromorphic experiment with incomplete documentation.
tt09/tt_um_mroblesh.review_notes: Removed encoder/decoder tags because they do not match the canonical meanings; added neuromorphic and spiking-neural-network tags based on the LIF neuron description.

tt09/tt_um_multiplier.summary: This project is a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using full adders to sum partial products. It is a combinational circuit with no clock, and testing can be done by applying input values and comparing the output to the expected product, either through a provided test script or by internal debugging. The design includes a schematic diagram and requires no external hardware. The documentation explains the partial-product and full-adder structure of the multiplier.
tt09/tt_um_multiplier.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state a teaching or learning intent.

tt09/tt_um_murmann_group.summary: This Verilog design implements a decimation filter for both incremental and regular delta-sigma modulators, reducing oversampled data while preserving signal accuracy. For incremental modulators the output updates after accumulating 16 input samples, while for regular modulators the output update is controlled by the reset signal. The filter provides a 16-bit decimated output and is clocked at 50 MHz. No silicon test reports are included, but the design targets ADC signal processing by converting a high oversampled data rate into a lower downsampled rate.
tt09/tt_um_murmann_group.review_notes: Summary corrected: the regular-modulator mode is described in the source as internal timing controlled by the reset signal, not an internal reset signal, and the unsupported claim that testing details are not provided was dropped.

tt09/tt_um_my_elevator.summary: This project simulates an elevator control system that displays floor numbers on a 7-segment display based on switch inputs. The user selects a floor using the board switches, and the display increments or decrements according to the elevator's state (moving up, moving down, or idle). Testing involves using the switches to select floors and observing the display, which requires an external LED display. The design is a simple state machine demonstration with no additional hardware beyond the display.
tt09/tt_um_my_elevator.review_notes: Removed industrial (no industrial application stated); added fsm for the elevator state machine.

tt09/tt_um_nomuwill.summary: This project implements a 16-bit Izhikevich neuron model in Verilog, which simulates spiking neuron dynamics using 16-bit arithmetic. It accepts an 8-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit state variable along with a spike signal. Testing is done via a supplied testbench that checks reset behavior, sub-threshold non-spiking, and supra-threshold spiking conditions. The design is notable for its efficient implementation of a biologically plausible neuron model, with no external hardware required.
tt09/tt_um_nomuwill.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag; the design is a spiking neuron model, not a DSP block.

tt09/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: Oscillating Bones is a ring oscillator built from a chain of 21 SkullFET inverters, producing a square wave output around 90 MHz. It provides divided frequency outputs at 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 of the base frequency. Silicon tests measured frequencies between about 87 and 91 MHz on the base and divided outputs, with some testers observing lower frequencies on divided outputs. It requires an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe the output waveforms.
tt09/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Summary corrected: the 87-91 MHz range applies to the base frequency, while lower readings were on divided outputs.

tt09/tt_um_patdeegan_anamux.summary: This analog module provides switchable passgates to route 4 or 8 analog signals, functioning as a multiplexer or analog switches for debug and inspection. It includes a ring oscillator and a digital block to generate one-hot control signals, allowing high-speed operation. Testing involves characterizing the passgates and chaining multiplexers, as demonstrated in a video. External analog hardware is required for full evaluation.
tt09/tt_um_patdeegan_anamux.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag; added analog, multiplexer, ring-oscillator, and counter tags supported by the documentation.

tt09/tt_um_perceptron_mtchun.summary: This project implements a perceptron neuron in Verilog that is trained to produce a NAND gate function. It has eight input pins for the current bit, eight output pins for the state variable bits, and one bidirectional pin for the output bit. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of placeholder sections, so it is unclear how the training is performed or how the design is used. The design is notable for demonstrating a basic neural network element in hardware, but without detailed documentation, its operation and intended use are ambiguous.
tt09/tt_um_perceptron_mtchun.review_notes: Replaced incomplete with insufficient-doc because the source is placeholder documentation rather than an unfinished design.

tt09/tt_um_pid_controller.summary: This design implements a hardware PID controller in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit setpoint and an 8-bit feedback signal as inputs and produces an 8-bit control signal output. The controller uses proportional, integral, and derivative terms to adjust the output based on the error between setpoint and feedback, but it only outputs positive values, making it suitable for systems that naturally tend in one direction, such as heating. The design is intended for simulation testing and can be deployed with sensors and actuators for real-world control applications.
tt09/tt_um_pid_controller.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm tag; summary is supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_prefix8.summary: This project is an 8-bit prefix network-based adder designed with the aid of a large language model to achieve a balance between power, performance, and area. It takes two 8-bit operands (a and b) and produces an 8-bit sum output. The design uses specific modules (Square, BigCircle, SmallCircle, Triangle) to generate carries and sums. The test procedure applies all possible input combinations and verifies the sum against the expected result, ensuring correct functionality.
tt09/tt_um_prefix8.review_notes: Removed alu, machine-learning and pipeline tags not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_program_counter_top_level.summary: This project implements a synchronous 4-bit counter with control signals for counting, loading, and output enable. The counter increments on each clock cycle when the count enable is asserted, can load a 4-bit value when the load enable is asserted, and can be disabled to put the output in high-impedance. It includes a reset that clears the counter to zero. The design is tested by observing the output on dedicated pins while manipulating the control signals to verify counting, pausing, loading, and output disabling.

tt09/tt_um_project.summary: This project implements a basic leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in SystemVerilog. It integrates input current by addition and leaks by dividing by two at each time step, with an enable pin advancing time roughly once per second when clocked at about 50 MHz. The neuron fires a spike when the integrated value exceeds a threshold, and it includes a timeout to prevent constant output from overstimulation. Testing involves manually setting input switches to provide current and observing spike output on LEDs, with a dedicated LED indicating time steps.

tt09/tt_um_purdue_socet_uart.summary: This project is a general-purpose UART with FIFO buffers, developed by Purdue's SoCET team. It supports standard UART signals (rx, tx, cts, rts) and includes FIFO buffers for both transmit and receive paths. The design allows configuration of baud rate and operation mode (idle, transmit, receive, buffer clear) through control pins. It can be tested by connecting to another UART or a USB-to-serial adapter, and it provides error and buffer status flags.
tt09/tt_um_purdue_socet_uart.review_notes: Removed driver tag as the UART is a communication interface, not a generic driver output stage.

tt09/tt_um_pwm_top.summary: This design is a versatile PWM generator with adjustable frequency and duty cycle. It takes a 6-bit divisor input to set the frequency by dividing the clock, and two control inputs to increase or decrease the duty cycle by 10% steps. The PWM output can be used to drive RGB LEDs, servomotors, and other devices, but external power is recommended for the driven device. The design is intended to be tested by applying a clock, setting the divisor, and adjusting the duty cycle while observing the PWM output.

tt09/tt_um_r2r_dac.summary: This is a simple 4-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter implemented as an analog design. It accepts a 4-bit digital input on pins A0 to A3 and produces an analog output voltage on a single output pin. The design is tested by applying a sequence of digital codes from 0000 to 1111 and observing the corresponding analog output, typically with an ADALM2000 in digital mode. The converter provides a basic method to generate analog signals from digital values.

tt09/tt_um_rburt16_opamp_3stage.summary: This project is a test chip for a 3-stage PMOS operational amplifier. It provides three analog pins: an output, an inverting input, and a non-inverting input. The documentation is minimal, indicating it is primarily a test vehicle for the amplifier topology. No silicon test results are reported.
tt09/tt_um_rburt16_opamp_3stage.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added incomplete for thin test-chip documentation.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_colorbars.summary: This design generates a VGA test pattern resembling NTSC color bars, with optional station ID display, scrolling ID, and scrolling bars. It is configured through input pins for showing the ID, using a custom ID, scrolling the ID, and scrolling the bars, and it outputs RGB and sync signals on the Tiny VGA pinout. A TinyVGA PMOD is required to connect to a VGA monitor, and the colors are explicitly not accurate to real NTSC color bars. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester noted the clock must be manually set to 25 MHz in the commander app.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_styler.summary: The Styler chip manipulates 16x16 character glyph bitmaps based on text mode attributes such as bold, faint, italic, underline, and blink. It has registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and it interfaces via 8 bidirectional data pins and several control inputs. The typical use involves writing a scanline number, reading back a logical scanline, and then manipulating bitmap halves to apply visual effects. The chip is intended as part of a larger text mode video display hardware system, and testing is covered by provided test scripts.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_tt09ball_gdsart.summary: This design drives a seven-segment display from an 8-byte ROM containing the characters '9', blank, 'C', 'I', 'Г', 'П', 'O', blank, which spell out a message as part of a GDS artwork. An octal counter cycles through the ROM addresses automatically, but the counter can be bypassed by setting ui_in[3] high and providing a 3-bit address on ui_in[2:0]. Testing involves pulsing the clock to advance the display or manually selecting addresses to verify the ROM contents. The design is notable for being a carrier for the 'THE STRONGEST' GDS art and requires an external seven-segment display or chip decapping tools to observe the output.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_tt09ball_screensav.summary: This design generates a 640x480 VGA signal displaying a bouncing DVD-style logo with an animated color gradient. Two inputs control the behavior: ui_in[0] tiles the logo across the screen, and ui_in[1] switches to a solid color instead of the gradient. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor via a TinyVGA Pmod and observing the animation. The design is notable for being a compact VGA screensaver implementation that fits on a single tile and requires the TinyVGA Pmod as external hardware.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_decoder.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large selection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to show the first flag, move to the next or previous flag, or select a flag by index. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a monitor. The design is extensible by adding new flag modules and updating the index, as described in the documentation. No silicon test reports are provided, but the documentation is clear about usage and configuration.
tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed overly generic video tag and added pmod tag supported by external hardware.

tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_experim.summary: This design is a configurable VGA signal generator that allows full control over display timings, sync polarities, and test patterns. It can be programmed via a register interface using ui_in and uio pins to set parameters such as visible width, porches, and sync widths, and it includes 32 test patterns like checkerboards, grids, and color bars. Testing involves connecting a VGA monitor through a TinyVGA Pmod and using the inputs to select patterns or modify timing registers. The design is notable for its flexibility in experimenting with VGA signal generation, requiring only the TinyVGA Pmod as external hardware.
tt09/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_experim.review_notes: Removed 'education' because the source only says experimentation, not teaching or learning.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.summary: This design is a replica of the Atari 2600 video game console system-on-chip, implemented in Verilog. It accepts joystick inputs, switches, and a reset signal, and outputs VGA video and PWM audio, with QSPI pins for external memory. It is tested by connecting a TinyVGA Pmod, Tiny Audio Pmod, and a VGA display, then playing games. The design is notable for being a complete recreation of a classic console on a Tiny Tapeout tile, requiring external hardware for video, audio, and game storage.
tt09/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.review_notes: Removed cpu because the source does not document an implemented processor core.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This Verilog implementation is a replica of the classic AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a 3-voice PSG chip from General Instrument. It provides three square-wave tone generators, a white noise generator using a 17-bit LFSR, an envelope generator with 10 shapes, and 16 volume levels, controlled through 14 registers. The design outputs digital 8-bit audio and a PWM pseudo-analog audio signal, and can be configured with an external clock divider. It is intended for hardware preservation and educational purposes, with a test suite for regression testing against the original chip behavior.
tt09/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Replaced incorrect neural-network/machine-learning/decoder tags with sound-generator, music, audio, pwm, lfsr, verilog, retro, and dac based on the source.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_decoder.summary: This design unpacks ternary, quinary, and septenary packed weights, converting them from a compressed format of 1.6 to 2.6 bits per parameter into an unpacked representation. It takes 8 bits of packed weight data on the input pins and outputs the unpacked values on both the output and bidirectional pins, with a control input to select between ternary and septenary modes. Testing requires providing packed weights on the input Pmods, and external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi Pico is needed to supply the data. The design is notable for its application in neural network quantization, but the documentation is minimal and lacks detailed usage instructions.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_e2m0_x_i8_matmul.summary: This design implements a systolic array for matrix multiplication using reduced-precision packed weights of 2.6 bits per parameter (septenary and quinary formats) and INT8 activations. It accepts packed weights on the input pins and activations on the bidirectional pins, and outputs the multiplication results on the output pins, with a strobe enable pin to start receiving results. Testing requires an external processor such as an RP2040 to feed weights and activations and to fetch the results. The design is notable for its use of compressed weights to reduce memory footprint in neural network acceleration, but it requires external hardware for operation.
tt09/tt_um_rejunity_e2m0_x_i8_matmul.review_notes: Removed fixed-point tag unsupported by source; added rp2040 since the source names it as required external hardware.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This design is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square wave tone generators and one noise generator with white and periodic noise types. It is programmed via an 8-bit data bus and provides both digital 8-bit audio and PWM audio outputs, with separate channel outputs for external mixing. Testing involves sending register write commands and observing the audio output, which can be connected to a DAC, RC filter, or amplifier. The design is notable for its faithful reproduction of the original chip's behavior, thorough test suite, and educational documentation, requiring external hardware such as a microcontroller and audio output circuitry.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_vga_logo.summary: This design displays a 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor, using compressed data and dithered colors to fit into a single tile. It generates standard VGA signals including red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for operation, and it has been tested successfully by a silicon tester who confirmed the video works as expected. Notable features include the large resolution crammed into a small area and the use of dithering for color effects.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.summary: This design is an audio/visual demo that generates VGA video and PWM audio outputs, forming an 8-part megademo. It uses eight PWM audio pins and standard VGA pins for red, green, blue, and sync signals. The demo requires external hardware: a VGA PMOD and audio output hardware. Silicon tests report that both audio and video work as expected, and one tester described it as a very nice demo with polished graphics and audio.

tt09/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

tt09/tt_um_riscv_mini.summary: This design is a compact 8-bit RISC-V processor core that uses a customized compressed instruction set (RVC) with 16-bit instructions to fit Tiny Tapeout constraints. It includes a control unit, an 8-register file, an ALU, and a single-cycle datapath, and it executes R-Type, I-Type, L-Type, S-Type, and B-Type instructions. Testing is done by setting the instruction on the input pins and clocking once to receive the result on the output pins, with different instruction types producing different outputs. The design is a compact RISC-V core optimized for area, but it lacks detailed documentation on its instruction encoding and limitations.
tt09/tt_um_riscv_mini.review_notes: Removed education tag not supported by the source; adjusted summary wording.

tt09/tt_um_ronikant_jeremykam_tinyregist.summary: This design provides three types of registers for a basic 8-bit CPU: a general-purpose register, a memory address register, and an instruction register. The registers are selected using two control pins (uio[6] and uio[7]), and data can be written to or read from the selected register via the input and output pins. Testing involves selecting a register and verifying that data is stored and retrieved correctly. The design is notable for being a simple building block for CPU designs, but it has minimal documentation and requires external control logic to be useful.
tt09/tt_um_ronikant_jeremykam_tinyregist.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the register-file and cpu tags are supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.summary: This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer input, returning the orbit length and an indicator of the maximum value reached. The input number is uploaded byte-by-byte into a 144-bit register via an address bus, and the computation is started with a pin; the busy indicator is polled until completion, after which the results are read back in 16-bit chunks. The design is intended for brute-force searching of path records, and the documentation explains the state machine and I/O protocol in detail. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
tt09/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.review_notes: Removed alu and register-file tags not supported by the source; added fsm, verilog and esoteric.

tt09/tt_um_samkho_two_channel_square_wav.summary: This design generates two independent square waves using 8-bit reloadable countdown timers, with periods proportional to the input values plus one. It also provides a 2-bit sum output of the two square waves. The design is tested by applying arbitrary 8-bit values to the inputs and probing the outputs with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. External hardware is not required, but the intended use is to drive speakers via resistor dividers and an amplifier.
tt09/tt_um_samkho_two_channel_square_wav.review_notes: Removed oscillator and retro tags not supported by the source; added sound-generator for the speaker-driving tone generation.

tt09/tt_um_schoeberl_test.summary: This is a test project created to explore the Chisel hardware construction language. It has 8 inputs, 8 bidirectional pins, and 8 outputs, but the documentation does not describe any specific functionality beyond being a test. The project includes a ChiselTest that can be run with sbt test. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable only as a learning exercise.
tt09/tt_um_schoeberl_test.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; source explicitly says it is just a Chisel test project.

tt09/tt_um_sebastienparadis_hamming_top.summary: This project implements a (7,4) Hamming encoder and decoder with a shared input bus, where the mode is selected by the most significant input bit. In encode mode, it takes a 4-bit input and produces a 7-bit encoded output; in decode mode, it takes a 7-bit input and outputs the corrected 7-bit codeword. Testing involves applying known data and verifying the encoded output, then flipping one bit in the encoded input to confirm error correction. No external hardware is specified, and the design is a straightforward implementation of a classic error-correcting code.

tt09/tt_um_secA_11_nyancar_alanz23.summary: This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit unsigned binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It uses an array of AND gates and full adders to generate and sum partial products. The design is tested by applying two 4-bit inputs and observing the 8-bit output. No external hardware is needed, and the project appears to be a class assignment for a digital logic course.
tt09/tt_um_secA_11_nyancar_alanz23.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source describes only a multiplier.

tt09/tt_um_secA_group5_array_multiplier.summary: This project is a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned numbers and outputs their 8-bit product. It is built from 12 full adders and 16 AND gates, following a structural array multiplier architecture. Testing is done by applying two 4-bit inputs via the ui_in pins and reading the product on the uo_out pins. No external hardware is required, and the design is a typical class project for learning digital arithmetic.
tt09/tt_um_secA_group5_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

tt09/tt_um_secB_15_array_multiplier.summary: This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers to produce an 8-bit result. It generates 16 partial products using AND gates and sums them with full adders. The design is tested by applying various 4-bit inputs in a simulation environment and verifying the product. No external hardware is needed, and the project is a standard educational implementation of an array multiplier.
tt09/tt_um_secB_15_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

tt09/tt_um_secd_8_array_mult.summary: This project implements a 4-bit array multiplier that computes the product of two 4-bit unsigned numbers, outputting an 8-bit result. It uses partial product generation with AND gates and summation with full adders. Testing is done by applying an 8-bit input representing two 4-bit numbers and checking the 8-bit output. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward educational example of a structural multiplier.
tt09/tt_um_secd_8_array_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

tt09/tt_um_section_d_group_fifteen_array.summary: This is a 4x4 array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit unsigned binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It is implemented structurally using logic gates and 1-bit full adders, following a partial product and addition approach. The design can be tested via an automatic testbench or by building the circuit from provided schematics. No external hardware is used, and the project is a class assignment for a digital logic course.
tt09/tt_um_section_d_group_fifteen_array.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

tt09/tt_um_senolgulgonul.summary: This design displays the letters of 'SEnOLGULGONUL' on a 7-segment display using an internal three-gate oscillator. It requires external resistors and a capacitor to complete the oscillator circuit, and the outputs connect directly to a 7-segment display. Testing involves connecting the external components and observing the letters on the display. The project is notable for using a simple gate-based oscillator to drive a text display.
tt09/tt_um_senolgulgonul.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator tag; the source specifies a three-gate oscillator.

tt09/tt_um_shifter.summary: This project implements a shifter that outputs the result of shifting the 8-bit input right by the number of positions specified on the 8-bit bidirectional input. The design is tested by setting switches on the inputs and observing the shifted value on LEDs connected to the outputs. No external hardware beyond switches and LEDs is required. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic operation.
tt09/tt_um_shifter.review_notes: Removed barrel-shifter and education tags as unsupported by the minimal documentation.

tt09/tt_um_snn_with_delays_paolaunisa.summary: This project implements 18 programmable digital LIF neurons with programmable delays and 144 synapses arranged in three fully connected layers. Input spikes are weighted and accumulated into membrane potentials, with weights, thresholds, decay, refractory periods, and delays programmable over SPI. Internal membrane potentials or output spikes can be read through SPI selection. The design is implemented in Verilog and is not reported as tested on silicon.
tt09/tt_um_snn_with_delays_paolaunisa.review_notes: Added verilog and neuromorphic tags; replaced a generic neural-network tag and made the summary match the documented LIF/SPI behavior.

tt09/tt_um_stochastic_integrator_tt9_CL1.summary: This design implements a stochastic integrator using Euler's definition of integration in the stochastic domain.
