It follows unipolar probability and uses LFSR-based stochastic computing. The design has two serial inputs and multiple serial outputs for different integrator configurations. Testing involves setting one input high and the other low to observe the integration behavior.
tt09/tt_um_stochastic_integrator_tt9_CL1.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the source; corrected to reflect the stochastic integrator.

tt09/tt_um_systolicLif.summary: This project implements a systolic array model of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons in Verilog. The design uses weight-stationary multiply-accumulate (MAC) units with bypass logic to prevent overstimulation of the LIF neurons. The user input ui_in drives the MAC inputs, and the output bits indicate the LIF state and spike events. The design has not been tested on silicon.
tt09/tt_um_systolicLif.review_notes: Removed unsupported SPI tag and added systolic-array and mac-unit tags; summary corrected to match the actual LIF/MAC design.

tt09/tt_um_tim2305_adc_dac.summary: This design implements an 8-bit R2R DAC and a 4-bit flash ADC. The DAC inputs are connected directly to digital input pins and its output can be connected to the analog pin via a transmission gate. The flash ADC has an input range of 0-1 volts with reference voltages set by a resistive divider, and its output is multiplexed on three 4-bit buses. The design can be tested by setting the DAC output and reading the ADC output.
tt09/tt_um_tim2305_adc_dac.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the source; corrected to reflect the ADC/DAC design.

tt09/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout.summary: This design is a ternary matrix multiplication processor. It loads weights into an internal register array and performs matrix multiplication using a pipelined architecture. The module can continuously accept new input vectors while completing previous computations. Outputs are produced as 8-bit integers representing the matrix multiplication result.
tt09/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout.review_notes: Removed incorrect neural network tags and added accelerator, verilog, and pipeline tags.

tt09/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout_csa.summary: This project is a ternary matrix multiplication processor using carry-save adders, written in Verilog. It loads weights into an internal register array and multiplies input vectors by those weights, summing the products to produce 8-bit integer outputs. The datapath is pipelined so it can accept new input vectors while computing on previous ones, producing continuous results. Testing is done by driving the inputs from an external MCU such as a Raspberry Pi over GPIO, and no silicon test reports are available.
tt09/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout_csa.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a spiking neural network that does not appear anywhere in the source.

tt09/tt_um_tinysynth.summary: This design is a tiny square wave oscillator that accepts MIDI commands. It receives MIDI commands over UART and generates a corresponding square wave signal using PWM. The design is written in Chisel. External hardware includes a Pmod AMP2 connected to the PMOD connector.
tt09/tt_um_tinysynth.review_notes: Removed incorrect neural network tags and added music, pwm, uart, sound-generator, and chisel tags.

tt09/tt_um_tinytinfoil_saradc_dac.summary: This project is an analog test structure for a C2C array of MIM capacitors used in a CDAC chain. It was created to determine how much bad layout affects the performance of a SAR ADC. The design intentionally uses bad layout to assess noise susceptibility. The test involves clocking the digital pins to observe which areas are most susceptible to noise.
tt09/tt_um_tinytinfoil_saradc_dac.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary are completely unrelated to the source documentation.

tt09/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros modified to remove the LVT implant from the bitcell. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
tt09/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

tt09/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
tt09/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

tt09/tt_um_tobimckellar_top.summary: This design is a basic PWM controller that generates a pulse-width modulated output on uo[7] when enabled by ui[7]. The six-bit input ui[5:0] sets the duty cycle in manual mode, or the frequency of an internally generated triangular reference when ui[6] is high, producing a breathing effect. It is tested by enabling the output and observing the PWM signal on uo[7] while flipping the input switches. No external hardware is required, though an LED and resistor are suggested for visual feedback.
tt09/tt_um_tobimckellar_top.review_notes: Removed signal-generator (PWM only); added led per the stated LED-control purpose.

tt09/tt_um_toivoh_demo.summary: Sequential Shadows is a demoscene demo that combines a ray caster, synthesizer, music sequencer, and audio visualizer to produce a real-time audiovisual experience. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and Mike's audio PMOD for sound, and it includes controls for pausing, stepping frames, and disabling bass or drums. The design was developed for the TT08 demo competition and was tested on hardware by both the author and an independent tester, who confirmed it works as simulated. The demo is best viewed with the monitor rotated 90 degrees and includes flashing lights by default.

tt09/tt_um_toivoh_pio_ram_emu_example.summary: This design demonstrates the use of a PIO-based RAM emulator on the RP2040 to store a 320x480 2-bit-per-pixel frame buffer and continuously output a 640x480 VGA signal. The logic computes a Julia fractal and writes it to the frame buffer, with user input via buttons to adjust parameters. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for VGA output and the RAM emulator running on the RP2040, and includes helper modules and a simulation model for testing. The design serves as an example for using the RAM emulator and includes test infrastructure.

tt09/tt_um_tommythorn_cgates.summary: This design implements two different C-gate (Muller C-element) circuits—one using a latch and one using combinatorial logic—and uses them to build 4-, 16-, and 64-stage rings. The C-gate outputs are directly observable, and the ring outputs toggle at frequencies related to the stage delays. Testing involves verifying the C-gate behavior and measuring ring frequencies, which requires an oscilloscope for the faster rings. Silicon tests show the C-gates work, but the fastest ring output was too fast to observe reliably.
tt09/tt_um_tommythorn_cgates.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator and delay-line tags; added asynchronous, latch, combinational, logic-gate, and silicon-tested tags.

tt09/tt_um_tommythorn_workshop.summary: This is a workshop demo design with a UART receiver on ui[0], a UART transmitter on uo[0], and a PDM output on uo[1]. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is magic and suggesting connecting the TX pin to a terminal. No external hardware is listed, and the design appears to be a workshop example. Due to the lack of detail, its exact functionality cannot be determined.
tt09/tt_um_tommythorn_workshop.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added incomplete due to very thin documentation.

tt09/tt_um_tt09_array_multiplier.summary: This design implements a 4x4 array multiplier using structural logic, taking two 4-bit inputs m and q and producing an 8-bit product p. It uses a grid of AND gates and full adders to sum the partial products along diagonals. The design is purely combinational and is tested by applying an 8-bit input where the lower four bits are m and the upper four bits are q, then observing the product on the outputs. No external hardware is required.

tt09/tt_um_two_lif_stdp.summary: This design implements two Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neurons connected by a synapse with Spike-Timing-Dependent Plasticity (STDP). It uses 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic for neuron states and synaptic weights, with the first neuron receiving an 8-bit input current and the second neuron receiving weighted input from the first. The synapse weight and neuron states are output for monitoring, and spike outputs are available on bidirectional pins. Testing can be done with a logic analyzer or signal generator, but no external hardware is required for basic operation.

tt09/tt_um_uart_mvm.summary: This design performs matrix-vector multiplication, receiving the matrix and vector via UART and outputting the result via UART. Internally, it uses AXI-Stream to pass data between the UART modules and the multiplication core. The design is tested with a provided testbench using iverilog. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_uart_mvm.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; the source describes matrix-vector multiplication, not digital signal processing.

tt09/tt_um_uart_mvm_sys.summary: This design performs matrix-vector multiplication, receiving the matrix and vector via UART and outputting the result via UART. Internally, it uses AXI-Stream to pass data between the UART modules and the multiplication core. The design is tested with a provided testbench using iverilog. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_uart_mvm_sys.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; the source describes matrix-vector multiplication, not digital signal processing.

tt09/tt_um_udxs.summary: This design implements a basic perceptron with a ReLU activation layer, using a single-cycle multiply-accumulation unit. It takes four signed 4-bit weights and four signed 4-bit inputs, and outputs a 16-bit ReLU result. The design is tested by providing weight-input pairs cycle-by-cycle and sampling the output, then resetting for a new invocation. No external hardware is required.
tt09/tt_um_udxs.review_notes: Added verilog and machine-learning tags that were clearly supported but missing.

tt09/tt_um_underserved.summary: This design is a RISC-V based system that boots from an SPI flash memory in XIP mode and executes instructions from there. It provides GPIO pins that can be used for various purposes, such as bitbanged UART. The design is tested with a testbench that includes a model of an SPI flash, and it can be run using FuseSoC. External hardware requires a compatible SPI flash memory.

tt09/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.summary: This is a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that boosts the input voltage to approximately 9.6 V, with the output divided by two and available on the analog pin ua[0]. It requires a 2 MHz clock signal to operate. In the TT09 shuttle, the analog pin voltage is limited to VDDIO/VDDA, so the output is divided by three instead. The design is tested by applying a clock and measuring the divided output voltage.
tt09/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (clock is an input, not generated); charge-pump already present.

tt09/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator with up to 3853 inverter stages. By connecting one of the output pins to the ring_in input or enabling internal loopback, a ring of a specific length is formed, and the output frequency can be measured. External hardware such as an oscilloscope or logic analyzer is required to measure the frequency and delay between different points in the chain. The design is notable for its large number of stages and the ability to select from many tap points.
tt09/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag; the design is an inverter-chain ring oscillator, not a logic gate implementation.

tt09/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

tt09/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
tt09/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

tt09/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
tt09/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

tt09/tt_um_wallento_4bit_toycpu.summary: This is a 4-bit toy CPU based on a design from a German textbook, featuring a 4-bit accumulator and 4-bit instructions with 4-bit operands. It uses external memory and requires a testbed to drive the pins, including a microcontroller program to handle the clock, reset, and tristate data bus. The internal 19-bit state can be scanned out for debugging and visualization. The design is intended as an educational tool to transition from digital design to microprocessors.

tt09/tt_um_warp.summary: This is a demo design that generates VGA video and audio output, intended for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition. It requires external VGA and audio PMODs to be plugged into the board for testing. The design can also be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio portion can run on an ULX3S using its DAC. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed technical information about the implementation.
tt09/tt_um_warp.review_notes: Removed pmod (external hardware, not a design interface) and added fpga and music tags supported by the documentation.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_411379488132926465.summary: This project is a union of projects done in a class, as indicated by its title and description. It has 8 input pins and 7 output pins, and requires external hardware such as 7-segment displays and LEDs. The documentation is very sparse, providing only pin names and a list of external hardware, with no explanation of functionality or how to test it. Therefore, it is difficult to determine what the design actually does beyond being an educational exercise.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_411379488132926465.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc tag because documentation is very thin and lacks functional description.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_411783629732984833.summary: This design is a binary counter built from D flip-flops, with additional logic gate examples on the bidirectional pins. It is intended to be tested by connecting a 1 Hz oscillator to the clock pin and observing the output on LEDs, which count from 0 to 15 and roll over. External hardware includes a 555 timer for the oscillator, DIP switches or pushbuttons for input, and LEDs with resistors for output. The project is a first-time Tiny Tapeout submission.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_411783629732984833.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added dip-switch and button tags supported by the documentation.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_412367067047460865.summary: This project is a simple single gate design created for workshop validation. It has two input pins and one output pin, and requires external hardware such as an LED display and input switches for testing. The documentation is extremely minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note to look at the Wokwi project. It appears to be a basic test design with little original functionality.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_412367067047460865.review_notes: Replaced unsupported template tag with workshop based on the explicit workshop validation description.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_412635532198550529.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU trainer that executes opcodes fed via input pins, with an 8-bit accumulator and four 8-bit working registers. It supports arithmetic and logical operations, shifts, and provides carry and zero flags. The design is tested by providing a 10 kHz clock, loading opcodes and immediate data, and observing results on a 7-segment display or via output pins. It is intended as an educational tool for learning CPU operation.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413385294512575489.summary: This design consists of a string of inverters intended to function as a delay line or ring oscillator, with an XOR gate on the bidirectional pins that could be used as a mixer. The outputs are derived from the inputs according to a specific logic function: OUT1 = IN3 ? (IN0 & IN1) : IN2, and OUT0 and OUT2 are the inverse of OUT1. Testing requires basic DC logic signals on the input pins, and no specific external hardware is needed beyond switches or digital inputs. The documentation is brief and the design appears to be an experiment.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386973689694209.summary: This project counts the number of input switches that are turned on, providing the count on its output pins. It is tested by simply flipping the switches and observing the output. No external hardware is required. The design is a straightforward circuit created in Wokwi.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386973689694209.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and speculative learning-exercise wording.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386988538584065.summary: This Wokwi project implements a simple combinational logic circuit that converts the ASCII binary representation of the letter 'A' (0x37) to the letter 'V' (0x56). The design is described as 'basic (broken) logic', suggesting it may not function correctly. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and a test procedure. No external hardware is specified.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386988538584065.review_notes: Removed unsupported 7-segment, education, and template tags; added wokwi, logic-gate, and incomplete; corrected summary to remove invented DIP switch and 7-segment display.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386991502909441.summary: This design displays the contents of a register map on a charlieplexed 8x7 LED display and can generate waveforms for PWM, UART, and WS2812 in response to a trigger. A SPI serial connection is used to set values in the register map, with CS active low, SPI mode 0, and MSB first. Auxiliary functions such as LFSR, PWM, frequency counting, and ultrasonic distance sensing are implemented as space and time permit. Testing uses SPI to read and write registers and observe the LEDs or serial response, with a charlieplexed 7x8 LED display as external hardware.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413386991502909441.review_notes: Removed unsupported ws2812/led/uart interface tags and corrected the summary, which had invented a WS2812 driver as the main function.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.summary: This Wokwi project uses simple logic gates to display the letter 'P' on a 7-segment display when the 8-bit input equals 0x46. The design requires external hardware including a breadboard, 1.8V power supply, connector wires, an 8-position DIP switch, and a 7-segment display. The documentation describes the basic function and test procedure, noting that with all inputs at 0x00 the display shows the inverse of the P pattern. The design is a simple combinational logic demonstration.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and template tags and added combinational; summary otherwise matches the source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387014781302785.summary: This Wokwi project displays the letter L on a seven-segment display when the input bits 00101111 are entered on IN0 through IN7. The display only appears while the Step button is pressed, and releasing it clears the display. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic function and test procedure. The design requires external hardware including a DIP switch, a push button, and a seven-segment display.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387014781302785.review_notes: Corrected the summary's wrong bit pattern and letter, and replaced unsupported logic-gate/template tags.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387015959903233.summary: This Wokwi project implements the 'secret code' exercise from the TinyTapeout workshop. If the correct code 10101010 is set on IN0 through IN7, the design outputs 10001100 on OUT0 through OUT7 to display the letter 'r' on a 7-segment display. Any other input outputs 00000000. External hardware includes a DIP switch for inputs and a 7-segment display for outputs.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387015959903233.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated shift-register/led/clock-generator/template tags with wokwi, 7-segment, dip-switch, education, workshop, comparator, and sequential-logic.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387032609197057.summary: This design connects a bunch of AND gates together to make a really big AND gate. It displays 1 on a 7-segment display if all inputs are high, and 0 otherwise. The design is created using the Wokwi simulator. The documentation is present and describes the testing procedure.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387032609197057.review_notes: Removed incorrect interface/communication tags and added logic-gate, education, and wokwi tags.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387064715554817.summary: This Wokwi project drives a string of D flip-flops so that LED segments illuminate in a circle. A clock input advances the pattern, and a reset clears the flip-flops if more than one segment is lit. Testing is done by turning on the clock switch or pressing the step button. External hardware includes a clock, a button and a 7-seg LED.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387064715554817.review_notes: Removed logic-gate/template; design is a flip-flop ring driving LED segments.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387065339458561.summary: This design converts an SPI-style APA102 LED protocol stream into a single-line WS2812 output. It is hard-coded for seven LEDs, waits for a 32-bit low start condition, shifts in the pixel data, and forwards it to the WS2812 output until a stop condition is recognized. It ignores the APA102 intensity byte and also emits a continuous UART output of "Arglius Barglius" at approximately 115200 baud. Testing requires an SPI driver and a string of at least seven WS2812 LEDs, and no silicon results are reported.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387065339458561.review_notes: Tags were unrelated (wokwi/logic-gate/template/incomplete); replaced with the actual APA102-to-WS2812 translator tags and summary.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387065963362305.summary: This is a Wokwi project whose documentation is very thin, stating only that the various inputs will be used to determine whether there is success on the output. Testing is described as changing the inputs to change the output. No external hardware is needed. The exact function of the design is not described in the source.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387065963362305.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate/education/template tags and rewrote summary to match the sparse source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387076188030977.summary: This is a Wokwi project that currently does nothing, as stated in its documentation. It has two inputs and one output, with external buttons and an LED suggested for testing. The design is incomplete and not yet functional. It is a placeholder or starter project.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387076188030977.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate and education tags; added incomplete tag based on explicit statement that it doesn't work yet.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387093939376129.summary: This Wokwi project is intended to implement eight-input logic gates using all eight inputs of the tile. The documentation states the gates are planned but not yet built, so the design is essentially a hello-world placeholder. Testing would involve setting the eight input pins and observing the corresponding outputs. No external hardware is required, and the project is notable only as an introductory template.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387093939376129.review_notes: Removed unsupported template/education tags; added logic-gate and incomplete.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387120998931457.summary: This design demonstrates trivial AND gates and inverters on a Tiny Tapeout tile, with OUT0 combining IN0 and a reset signal, OUT1 combining IN0 and IN1, OUT2 and OUT3 inverting IN2 and IN3, and OUT4 through OUT7 passing inputs straight through. It is meant to illustrate logical inputs and outputs, the tool flow, and 3D visualization. Testing uses a reset pushbutton, DIP switches for inputs, and an LED display for outputs. The project is a simple educational gate sample rather than a functional application.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387122850717697.summary: This project is described as an introduction to Tiny Tapeout built around AND gates that do not do much. The author states they are still figuring out how it works, and the pin list is inconsistent, with uo[3] labelled OUT4. Testing is said to involve flipping DIP switches, and a 7-segment display is listed as external hardware. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual logic function.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387122850717697.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were mostly appropriate, but the 7-segment tag was not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387152803294209.summary: This design proposes a pseudo random generator built from two ring oscillators whose outputs are sampled by a D flip-flop at a 10 kHz clock. OUT0 and OUT1 are described as complementary random outputs. The documentation says only that power should be connected and that the oscillators will in theory start oscillating. No external hardware is required, but the design is speculative and no silicon results are reported.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387152803294209.review_notes: Removed redundant oscillator tag since ring-oscillator is already present.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387186248679425.summary: This project is titled Drew's First Wokwi Design and its documentation says only that it is a thing that does stuff. Testing is described as hooking it up to things and seeing if it does stuff, and the external hardware is called a mystery. The pin list includes eight inputs, eight bidirectional pins and eight outputs, but no function is specified. The documentation is essentially unusable for determining what the design does.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387190167208961.summary: This design places four NAND gates on a tile, with each gate taking two input pins and driving one output pin. The description says it is a bunch of NANDs intended to test the tool chain for now. Testing is described informally as manually connecting the NAND inputs. No external hardware is specified, and the project is a simple tool-chain exercise rather than a useful circuit.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387190167208961.review_notes: Removed education as unsupported; kept logic-gate and wokwi.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387214966034433.summary: This project drives a seven-segment display to spell the letters J, O and N depending on which of three input pins is asserted. Pin 1 outputs J, pin 2 outputs O and pin 3 outputs N according to the documentation. A seven-segment display is the only external hardware required. The design has minimal documentation and no reported silicon results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387214966034433.review_notes: Removed education tag not stated in source; keep 7-segment/display/text/wokwi.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387224567846913.summary: This design steps through the five letters of the name AAron on a seven-segment display each time a clock button is pressed. The documentation notes that the letters for 0 and 1 are the same, so the sequence has a quirk. A seven-segment display is the only external hardware needed. It is a simple character-sequencing project with no reported silicon results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387224567846913.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added button tag for the clock button input.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387348132056065.summary: This project implements a simple set-reset latch using two input pins and two output pins. IN1 acts as the set input, driving OUT0 high and OUT1 low, while IN0 acts as the reset input, driving OUT0 low and OUT1 high. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal and does not describe behaviour when both inputs are asserted or released.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387348132056065.review_notes: Removed unsupported flip-flop and education tags.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387352465821697.summary: This design is a six-bit shift register that takes a clock and serial data input and presents the six stored bits on output pins 0 through 5. Testing is done by applying a clock and data on inputs 0 and 1 and observing the outputs. Most other pins are marked as not connected, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief and gives no timing or reset details.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387352465821697.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; shift-register and wokwi remain supported.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387462882977793.summary: This design implements two NAND gates using Wokwi, with the first gate taking inputs from pins 0 and 1, the second from pins 2 and 3, and their outputs combined to drive output pin 1. The documentation says to set pins 1-7 high for testing, which does not match the described pin usage. The project appears to be a beginner-level logic gate experiment.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387462882977793.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state a teaching or learning purpose.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387481972305921.summary: This design implements three AND gates in a Wokwi simulation, with two AND gates driving OUT1 and OUT2 and a further AND of the gates driving OUT3. The inputs are labeled IN0 through IN7 and the outputs OUT0 through OUT7. Testing is done by switching the dipswitch, and the listed external hardware includes a 7-segment display, dipswitch and pushbutton. Documentation is very thin and no silicon test reports are available.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413387481972305921.review_notes: Summary was corrected to match the three AND gates and pin names; no workshop tag added since the source does not state one.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413391266378724353.summary: The project documentation states that the design does nothing and does not work. It is described as untestable, and no external hardware is used. The submission is a Wokwi project with very thin documentation. It appears to be a placeholder or incomplete design.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413391266378724353.review_notes: Summary was only one sentence; expanded to four sentences using only source-supported statements.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413407859783959553.summary: This design implements a reconfigurable digitally controlled oscillator that can operate as a ring oscillator or a clock divider. The ring oscillator is formed by chaining five inverters, and its frequency is set by the inverter cell delay. A D flip-flop chain divides the clock, with the division ratio selected by the s0, s1 and s2 inputs. The design is created using the Wokwi simulator and has no reported silicon test results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413407859783959553.review_notes: Added ring-oscillator and clock-divider tags and rewrote the summary to remove unsupported or garbled sentences.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413471588783557633.summary: This design implements an 8-bit shift register. The documentation is extremely sparse, with only 'This just works2' repeated. No external hardware or detailed testing instructions are provided.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413471588783557633.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file and uart tags; added insufficient-doc due to very thin documentation.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413686101237123073.summary: This design is a comparator circuit built in Wokwi, with inputs A_IN and B_IN and outputs LT, GT, and EQ. The documentation is insufficient to fully describe its functionality, as both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections say 'Will deal with this later'. The external hardware section is left as boilerplate placeholder text. The project appears to be incomplete.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413686101237123073.review_notes: Removed placeholder tag not supported by source; expanded summary to four sentences.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413849515516143617.summary: This design implements a phase frequency detector and a zero dead zone PFD. The basic PFD drives UP high when the VCO input leads and DN high when the reference input leads. A second PFD block provides additional UP2, DN2, and Reset outputs. The design is implemented in Wokwi and is not reported as tested on silicon.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413849515516143617.review_notes: Corrected pll and analog tags to phase-detector/sequential-logic; summary reflects only the documented PFD function.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413871526879619073.summary: This design is a 4-1 multiplexer built in Wokwi, with inputs a, b, c, and d selected by s1 and s2 and the result driven on output out. The documentation is very thin, but the pin names and title make the function clear. The project appears to be a simple combinational logic design.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413871526879619073.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc because the multiplexer function is clear from the title and pin names.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413872016164217857.summary: This design is a 2-bit adder that takes two single-bit inputs (in0 and in1), treating each as 0 or 1, and displays their sum as a decimal integer on a 7-segment display. It is implemented in Wokwi. The design assumes a bit is 1 if the input is ON, else 0. Testing involves connecting in0 and in1 to ON-OFF switches.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413872016164217857.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and bcd tags; summary expanded to four sentences based on source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413879612498222081.summary: This design is an 8-bit clocked display that uses flip-flops to latch input values and drive output pins. It allows output displays when the switch is clicked or the clock signal toggles. The design can be reset using the reset button. It is implemented in Wokwi and demonstrates sequential logic with flip-flops.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_413879612498222081.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file, 7-segment, and clock-generator tags; summary expanded to four sentences.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124597390729217.summary: This project is a placeholder Wokwi design with no implemented functionality. The documentation states that it does not work yet and that testing is to be determined. It requires no external hardware. The design is notable only as an incomplete submission.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124597390729217.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added placeholder/insufficient-doc tags.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124843472659457.summary: This design implements a 2-bit adder that takes two 2-bit numbers as inputs and produces a 2-bit sum. It is tested by setting all inputs and observing the outputs. External hardware needed includes buttons for inputs and LEDs for outputs. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed implementation or test results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124843472659457.review_notes: Removed alu, education, button and led tags that are not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124872671308801.summary: This circuit generates Morse code for the letters J and R using a 4-bit synchronous counter and logic gates. It can be tested by connecting a 7-segment display and using a button to select between J and R. External hardware required includes a button, a 7-segment display, and a clock. The design is a simple example of Morse code generation.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414124872671308801.review_notes: Removed education and clock-generator tags not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414125058137148417.summary: This project is described as a basic project with minimal documentation. It has three pins and the documentation states it is Aditya's init and a basic project. External hardware is listed as 'Need to fill in'. The design is too poorly documented to determine its function or purpose.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414125777368065025.summary: This project implements a full adder that takes two 1-bit inputs X and Y plus a carry-in, and produces a sum and carry-out. It is tested by checking that the sum of X and Y equals the output sum. No external hardware is mentioned. The documentation is brief and does not include silicon test results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414125777368065025.review_notes: Removed alu; a 1-bit full adder is not an ALU.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414126546375915521.summary: This design is a 2-bit full adder that adds two numbers. It is tested by applying two input signals and observing the outputs. The documentation mentions external hardware but does not specify any. The project lacks detailed implementation notes and test results.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414126546375915521.review_notes: Removed alu and education tags not supported by the source.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414127944900611073.summary: This project is titled 'gta6' and involves guessing a pin that lights an LED. It is tested by picking a pin and seeing if it lights up. No external hardware is required. The documentation is extremely sparse and does not describe any actual game functionality.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414127944900611073.review_notes: Removed led tag due to lack of clear LED output evidence; added game and puzzle tags based on the guessing interaction.

tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414174625969437697.summary: This design uses a 3-bit clock divider to spell a name by displaying a counter on a 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting a 7-segment display and a reset button, and observing the counter increment and reset. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and a reset button. The project is a simple example of sequential logic.
tt09/tt_um_wokwi_414174625969437697.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added incomplete because the name-spelling behavior is not documented.

tt09/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
tt09/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

tt09/tt_um_znah_vga_ca.summary: This design generates a VGA signal that displays 1D elementary cellular automata. It is used by plugging it into a VGA PMOD and a display. External hardware required is a VGA PMOD. The project is notable for its creative visual output and is implemented in Verilog.
tt09/tt_um_znah_vga_ca.review_notes: Removed unsupported signal-generator tag; added vga, cellular-automaton, video, display, and verilog tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_08_sws.summary: This analog design generates a stepwise approximation of a sine wave, with the output frequency depending on the clock. It is intended as a sine wave synthesizer and uses analog pins for bias and current outputs. Testing requires a 1 kΩ resistor from the output pins to ground. The documentation is brief and does not provide detailed specifications or test results.
ttcad25a/tt_um_08_sws.review_notes: Removed oscillator, clock-generator, dac and mixed-signal: none are supported by the analog sine synthesizer documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.summary: This design recreates the Crossy Road game on an ASIC, where a chicken crosses roads while avoiding cars. It is controlled by a move button and outputs VGA video to a display. External hardware needed includes a debounced button and a 25 MHz clock. The project is a complete game implementation in Verilog.
ttcad25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.review_notes: Added retro tag for the arcade-style game recreation; removed unsupported 'notable' claim from summary.

ttcad25a/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunt.summary: The design is a 16-microphone delay-and-sum beamformer that processes PDM inputs and outputs beamformed audio via I2S. It expects a 3.072 MHz bit clock and 48 kHz LR clock, and can use up to 16 digital microphones. Documentation is minimal placeholder text, so the internal beamforming details and test procedure are not described. The project is notable for targeting a high microphone count in a small digital design.
ttcad25a/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunt.review_notes: Added 'incomplete' because the source documentation is placeholder text and the design is unfinished.

ttcad25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttcad25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttcad25a/tt_um_2x2MatrixMult_Vort3xed.summary: This project implements a 2x2 matrix multiplier that receives two matrices over UART and transmits the resulting matrix back. It also provides the four result bytes on parallel output pins, and operates with a 100 MHz clock and a 115200 baud UART interface. The design was tested using a USB-UART bridge and documented with example test cases, including notes on overflow for results exceeding 255. The project credits mentorship and was completed as a student project.
ttcad25a/tt_um_2x2MatrixMult_Vort3xed.review_notes: Removed 'alu' and 'accelerator'; 'fsm' is already present and supported by the documented state machine.

ttcad25a/tt_um_4Bit_SAR_ADC.summary: This is a 4-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter that converts a constant analog input voltage to a 4-bit digital output. It requires an external sample-and-hold circuit to keep the input stable during the 5-clock-cycle conversion, and a 5 MHz clock, producing a 1 MHz conversion rate. The digital result appears on four output pins along with an end-of-conversion signal. The design is an analog implementation and its digital outputs are the ADC result.
ttcad25a/tt_um_4Bit_SAR_ADC.review_notes: Removed redundant duplicate tag 'adc'; no other changes needed.

ttcad25a/tt_um_DaDDS.summary: DaDDS is an 8-bit direct digital synthesizer intended as an RF transmitter with on-off keying and frequency-shift keying modulation. It uses a 60 MHz clock and outputs an 8-bit DAC word, and includes UART control for setting frequency and modulation parameters. The documentation is sparse, consisting mainly of images that are not accessible in the provided text, so the exact control protocol and test method are not fully described. External hardware suggested includes a DAC and RF circuitry in a typical application diagram.
ttcad25a/tt_um_DaDDS.review_notes: Removed synthesizer (audio connotation) and added signal-generator for the DDS waveform generation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.summary: This design is a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder that computes the sum of two 4-bit inputs plus a carry-in. It provides sum and carry-out outputs and can be used as a building block for larger adders. The design was tested on an FPGA but has no silicon test report. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand its function.
ttcad25a/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the design is an adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.summary: This design is an ASIC implementation of a university CPLD project that drives four multiplexed seven-segment displays and scans a multiplexed keypad. It uses a simple SPI protocol to receive commands for display data and keypad column selection, and it outputs keypad row data on MISO. The design requires external hardware including displays, a keypad, and an SPI master, and it must be clocked by the SPI clock. Silicon testing showed it functional up to 3.7 MHz, but auto-clocking must be disabled.
ttcad25a/tt_um_JAC_EE_segdecode.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed.

ttcad25a/tt_um_LnL_SoC.summary: This design is a tiny system-on-chip featuring a 16-bit microprocessor, boot ROM, PWM, timer, and SPI interface. The CPU runs a built-in program that reads from an 8-bit input port and writes to an 8-bit output port, and it also exercises the SPI, PWM, and timer peripherals. The design is intended to test the microprocessor on silicon and requires external hardware such as a keypad and display. The documentation is detailed but the external hardware is not fully specified.
ttcad25a/tt_um_LnL_SoC.review_notes: Removed microcontroller in favor of soc/cpu; added education and pwm tags supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_MAC_Accelerator_OnSachinS.summary: This project implements a multiplication and accumulation (MAC) operation in Verilog. The documentation states only that it multiplies and accumulates the data. Testing is suggested using a memory operation, and no external hardware is specified. The exact interface and behavior of the design are not fully described in the source.
ttcad25a/tt_um_MAC_Accelerator_OnSachinS.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and memory tags; kept mac-unit and multiplier, added verilog and insufficient-doc.

ttcad25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.summary: This design plays Pachelbel's Canon while displaying synchronized visuals on a VGA screen. It uses a PWM output for audio and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a Tiny Audio Pmod. Silicon testing showed it works, though one tester noted the audio was out of sync until manually reset. The design is a demonstration of audio and video capabilities on Tiny Tapeout.
ttcad25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.review_notes: Removed generic graphics tag; added silicon-tested and verilog tags supported by the silicon reports and language.

ttcad25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_mandelbrot.summary: This design computes and displays the Mandelbrot fractal on a VGA screen using a racing-the-beam technique. It uses 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic and a maximum iteration depth of 14, with configurable position and zoom via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 100 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it broadly works, though the demo mode can sometimes get stuck zooming into the wrong offset.

ttcad25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set with Zcb and Zicond extensions, using QSPI flash for program storage and QSPI PSRAM for data memory. It includes a UART and SPI controller, and is intended to be used with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display and game controller. The QSPI clock and data lines are shared between the flash and the RAM, so only one can be accessed simultaneously. Data can be read from flash and RAM, and written to RAM.

ttcad25a/tt_um_NicklausThompson_SkyKing.summary: This design displays a static image of a plane flying into the sunset with a text overlay that types out character by character. It also includes demos for oscilloscope XY display PMODs, which can be selected via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for the main demo and additional PMODs for the XY demos. The text animation may complete before the VGA monitor recognizes the signal, so viewing in a VGA playground is recommended.

ttcad25a/tt_um_Qwendu_spi_fpu.summary: This project is a 32-bit floating point unit accessible over SPI. It features four internal floating point registers that can be written and read over SPI. Every SPI transaction starts with a command byte followed by arguments, and data output requires sending enough bytes to receive the entire response. Testing is best done with the provided Arduino testbench, though the author notes issues with Arduino SPI controllers.
ttcad25a/tt_um_Qwendu_spi_fpu.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the SPI floating point unit described in the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_Richard28277.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ALU that performs arithmetic and logical operations on two 4-bit inputs, selected by a 4-bit opcode. The 8-bit result is output on the uo pins and the lower four bidirectional pins, while carry-out and overflow flags appear on two of the bidirectional pins. Testing involves setting the a and b inputs and the opcode, then observing the result and status flags. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward combinational ALU.
ttcad25a/tt_um_Richard28277.review_notes: Removed adder because the documentation does not specifically claim adder functionality.

ttcad25a/tt_um_Strider93.summary: This project implements a digital LIF neuron with reset by subtraction, configurable leakage and threshold. It takes weight inputs and a spike input, and produces a spike output. The documentation is very thin, with no detailed testing instructions beyond inputting weights and spikes to observe spiking.
ttcad25a/tt_um_Strider93.review_notes: Removed floating-point, spi, and adder tags as unsupported; added neuromorphic and spiking-neural-network tags based on the LIF neuron description.

ttcad25a/tt_um_UartMain.summary: This project implements a simple XOR cipher with a UART interface. It receives a character via UART and returns an encrypted character using a configurable key. The key can be updated by asserting the updateKey input before sending the new key. The default key is b10101010.
ttcad25a/tt_um_UartMain.review_notes: Replaced incorrect VGA/video/display/graphics tags with UART, crypto, cipher, and Verilog.

ttcad25a/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.summary: This is a standalone VGA and sound demo that fits in two tiles, developed for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition. It generates a 640x480@60Hz VGA signal with a non-standard 1220-pixel horizontal resolution and RGB222 dithered graphics, plus 3-channel synthesized audio via a 16-bit sigma-delta DAC on a single pin. It requires a 48 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for sound. Silicon tests confirm both graphics and sound work as expected, matching FPGA simulations.

ttcad25a/tt_um_a1k0n_nyancat.summary: This design displays the classic Nyan Cat animation on a VGA monitor with accompanying music. It uses a 2x2 Bayer dithering matrix for color rendition and generates sound from a MIDI file using square waves with exponential decay envelopes, a low-pass filter, and a sigma-delta DAC. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for audio. Silicon tests confirm it works, and it was originally intended for one tile but expanded to two.

ttcad25a/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.summary: This project renders a 3D torus (donut) on a VGA display using a raymarching technique with a CORDIC unit to calculate distances. It runs at a non-standard 1220x480 resolution and uses spatial and temporal dithering to improve appearance despite low horizontal resolution. It requires a 48 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output. Silicon tests show it works but may have minor glitches at 48 MHz; running at 45 MHz avoids them.
ttcad25a/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.review_notes: Added silicon-tested: the source reports working silicon results from testers and the author.

ttcad25a/tt_um_alexandercoabad_mixedsign.summary: This is an analog design that biases an inverter for linear-mode operation, producing an analog output. It has one analog input and one analog output, and the minimal test suggestion is to add an external 20 nF capacitor, apply a small-signal sine wave, and observe the output with an oscilloscope. The documentation consists primarily of the title and that test description, with no further circuit details. This appears to be a basic analog building block or experiment.
ttcad25a/tt_um_alexandercoabad_mixedsign.review_notes: Removed unsupported opamp/logic-gate/transistor-level tags and added incomplete due to sparse documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_alexjaeger_ringoscillator.summary: This is a simple analog ring oscillator that outputs a nominal 5 MHz clock signal on a single analog pin. It requires no external hardware and is automatically enabled when selected on the evaluation board. Silicon tests show it oscillates at around 4.5-4.6 MHz with an amplitude of about 0.6-1.6 V, depending on the setup. The design is notable for its simplicity and use of analog circuitry.
ttcad25a/tt_um_alexjaeger_ringoscillator.review_notes: Added silicon-tested because the source includes multiple working silicon test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: The design is a resubmission of a simple VGA ray casting game engine that renders textured walls in a 3D-like first-person view without a framebuffer. It is controlled via an SPI interface for player point-of-view and other visual effects registers, and outputs standard VGA signals. Optional external QSPI memory can supply textures, and the chip includes debug and demo modes. This is a more complex design occupying 6x2 tiles and represents an iterative development from earlier Tiny Tapeout versions.

ttcad25a/tt_um_algofoogle_tt08_vga_fun.summary: This project is a test chip for an analog VGA digital-to-analog converter with a digital control block that can generate various test patterns after reset. The digital block drives three color channels, each with eight positive and eight negative polarity bits and an estimated 500 microamp current per channel, converted to voltage through pull-up resistors. The first analog output pin exposes the red channel DAC bias voltage for testing. The source documentation notes that the image will not be very clear due to poor matching and simulated slew worse than 40 ns, and that a VGA connector and probably an op-amp on each analog output are needed.
ttcad25a/tt_um_algofoogle_tt08_vga_fun.review_notes: Removed overly broad display tag; added mixed-signal and characterization supported by the analog/digital test-chip description.

ttcad25a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga.summary: This Verilog design generates VGA timing and RGB222 color output for a Tiny VGA PMOD, displaying a bouncing ball animation over an adaptation of Matt Venn's VGA clock. It supports a 640x480 60Hz mode from a 25MHz clock and includes inputs to adjust hours, minutes, and seconds. Testing requires a VGA monitor and Tiny VGA PMOD, with mode and pmod_select inputs configuring the display. The design is notable for combining a real-time clock display with a simple animation and is intended for the IHP tapeout.
ttcad25a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga.review_notes: clock-generator was a misreading of the VGA clock display; added retro for the recreated clock.

ttcad25a/tt_um_alphaonesoc.summary: AlphaOneSoC is a 32-bit RISC-V SoC based on Michael Bell's TinyQV, implementing the RV32EC ISA. It boots from external QSPI flash or PSRAM and provides UART, SPI, and GPIO interfaces for interaction and debugging. Testing involves flashing instructions into memory and observing outputs via UART, SPI, or GPIO. The design requires a QSPI flash/PSRAM PMOD and is a larger 3x2 tile submission.
ttcad25a/tt_um_alphaonesoc.review_notes: Removed microcontroller (SoC/cpu already cover it) and added multi-tile and qspi, both supported by the pin facts.

ttcad25a/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: This project provides test structures for Tiny Tapeout analog support, including bias generation, power supply sensing, and loopback connections. The documentation is incomplete, with sections marked as FIXME, so the exact functionality and usage are not fully described. It appears to be intended for factory testing of analog infrastructure. No external hardware or testing procedure is specified in the available documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_asgerwenneb.summary: This project is titled 'My Project' and has essentially no documentation, with placeholder text for how it works, how to test, and external hardware. The pin names are generic and provide no information about the design's function. It appears to be an empty or template submission with no described behavior. No meaningful tags or summary can be derived from the available information.

ttcad25a/tt_um_atomNPU.summary: AtomNPU is a 4-bit neural processing unit designed to perform multiply-accumulate operations for neural network computations. It has 4-bit input and weight inputs and produces a 4-bit output, operating at 100 MHz. The documentation is very thin, with only a one-line description and placeholder text, so the exact MAC architecture and test procedure are not specified. It is a compact implementation of a basic NPU building block.
ttcad25a/tt_um_atomNPU.review_notes: Removed unsupported fixed-point tag and added edge-ai and accelerator tags supported by the NPU description.

ttcad25a/tt_um_autosel.summary: This design reads a 16-bit design ID from an I2C EEPROM and generates control signals to select the corresponding Tiny Tapeout project on a multiplexer. It also outputs the read value on a UART for debugging and includes a ring oscillator that can be enabled to provide a clock, avoiding the need for an external clock. It requires an external I2C EEPROM and pull-up resistors on the I2C lines. The design is a prototype for automatic project selection in Tiny Tapeout.

ttcad25a/tt_um_benpayne_ps2_decoder.summary: This PS2 decoder reads scan codes from a PS2 keyboard, debounces and synchronizes the signals, and outputs the data byte along with valid, interrupt, and data-ready signals. It includes a FIFO to queue received bytes, and the host can read data by asserting chip select. It requires a PS2 keyboard and level shifting from 5V to 3.3V, and is intended for interfacing with retro computers. The design is a straightforward implementation of the PS2 protocol.
ttcad25a/tt_um_benpayne_ps2_decoder.review_notes: Removed 'decoder' because it is a type tag for code-to-signal decoding, not a PS/2 protocol decoder; no canonical replacement exists.

ttcad25a/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.summary: The Morse Code Keyer converts dit/dah paddle inputs into Morse code outputs, including auxiliary dit/dah signals, a buzzer tone, and a 7-segment display of the last character. It supports straight key or iambic paddles (types A and B) and adjustable speed from 7 to 110 WPM via dip switches. The design emphasizes proper radio keying practices, warning against using the auxiliary output directly for transmitter control, and recommends a companion PCB for interfacing with radio hardware. It operates at 12 MHz and outputs to a seven-segment display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.review_notes: Added dip-switch and pmod tags supported by the documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_bg_DanielZhu123.summary: This analog bandgap reference is designed to provide a constant 1.2V output from a 3.3V supply. It is tested by placing the chip in an oven and measuring the output voltage across different temperatures. No external hardware is required for basic operation, though a multimeter is needed to measure the output. The documentation is minimal, providing only the basic function and test method, with no details on the circuit topology or performance.
ttcad25a/tt_um_bg_DanielZhu123.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag since the source never claims a discrete-transistor implementation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_bgr_agolmanesh.summary: This project is a bandgap voltage reference designed in Skywater 130nm CMOS to provide a stable 1.17V output over a 0-80°C temperature range. It includes a startup circuit and operates from a 1.8V supply, consuming 0.35 mW. Testing requires a temperature chamber, power supply, and measurement equipment to verify temperature stability, line and load regulation, and power consumption. Silicon tests show it can be unstable depending on load, sometimes latching to 0.46V instead of 1.17V.
ttcad25a/tt_um_bgr_agolmanesh.review_notes: Removed temperature-sensor because the design is a voltage reference, not a temperature sensing circuit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_bilal_trng.summary: This is a true random number generator that samples a noise source with a digital circuit and conditions the data using SHA-256 to produce cryptographic-quality random numbers. It supports raw entropy output for analysis and hashed output for secure applications, with built-in health tests such as the repetition count test. A state machine controls data collection, processing, and transmission of results over UART. Testing requires a UART terminal, and optionally an oscilloscope for debugging the noise source.
ttcad25a/tt_um_bilal_trng.review_notes: Removed bist (health tests are entropy health checks, not chip self-test); no silicon-tested claim since no silicon reports exist.

ttcad25a/tt_um_bitty.summary: This is a 16-bit simple processor with UART receive and transmit data pins and baud-rate selection inputs. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the instruction set, architecture, or internal blocks. UART communication is emulated within the testbench, and no external hardware is required. The design has been resubmitted on multiple shuttle runs but has no silicon test reports.
ttcad25a/tt_um_bitty.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the thin UART processor documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_brailliance.summary: Brailliance converts an ASCII character into its 8-bit Braille representation, where the first two bits of each output byte are zeroed for redundancy. The design is implemented in Verilog and uses a 5 MHz clock. External hardware such as LEDs or solenoid actuators can be used to display the Braille output. This project serves as an educational tool for ASCII-to-Braille conversion.
ttcad25a/tt_um_brailliance.review_notes: Removed display and education tags as they are not supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_branch_pred.summary: This design implements a minimal perceptron-based branch predictor that reads the lower 8 bits of a branch instruction address and its ground truth direction over basic SPI. It uses latch-based memory from a third-party repository and is not single-cycle due to memory architecture constraints. It is tested with CocoTB and a C++ functional simulation that parses Spike execution logs of a RISC-V reference program. The design exposes debug outputs for monitoring internal state and requires external hardware to drive and read its pins.
ttcad25a/tt_um_branch_pred.review_notes: Removed risc-v/cpu/machine-learning tags since the design is a branch predictor block, not a processor or ML hardware; added spi, memory and cocotb which are explicitly documented.

ttcad25a/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.summary: The design implements a two-player Pong game that uses two NES controllers for input and outputs a VGA video signal.
ttcad25a/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.review_notes: Removed gpio tag because the bidirectional pins are dedicated to NES controller signals.

ttcad25a/tt_um_bytex64_munch.summary: Munch displays a munching squares animation on a VGA monitor while generating simple music through an audio PMOD. It uses the Tiny VGA and TT Audio pinouts and is implemented in Verilog. The author notes it works but requires a manual reset to sync the music properly. The design targets a 25.175 MHz input clock and was tested on fabricated silicon with partial success.
ttcad25a/tt_um_bytex64_munch.review_notes: Added silicon-tested, audio, and music; expanded summary to four sentences.

ttcad25a/tt_um_cattuto_sr_latch.summary: This experiment implements a 512-bit shift register using D latches instead of flip-flops, with a single pulse rippling through the register to perform the shift. It has one input, one output, and an edge-triggered control signal that updates the shift on either a rising or falling edge. Testing involves shifting zeros in until the register is empty, then shifting in a pattern and observing it appear on the output after 512 control transitions. No external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_cattuto_sr_latch.review_notes: Added incomplete because the source explicitly frames the design as an experiment.

ttcad25a/tt_um_cejmu.summary: This design bundles four educational modules selected by an internal multiplexer: a vending machine state machine, a coin acceptor decoder, a 24-bit ripple carry adder, and a 24-bit carry lookahead adder. The adders are tested by feeding 24-bit operands in 8-bit chunks and reading the 25-bit result in 8-bit chunks. An oscilloscope can be used to measure the difference in execution speed between the two adder types. The coin acceptor decoder is designed for the HX-916 model.
ttcad25a/tt_um_cejmu.review_notes: Removed multiplexer tag as it is an internal selection mechanism, not a primary design feature.

ttcad25a/tt_um_cfib_demo.summary: This demoscene competition entry generates a pseudo-random soundtrack via PWM and displays a waveform on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA Pmod on uo_out and Mike's audio Pmod on uio_out[7]. The design is written in Verilog and runs from a 50 MHz clock with asynchronous reset. A silicon test report confirms the design is working.
ttcad25a/tt_um_cfib_demo.review_notes: Removed waveform-generator (not a general waveform generator) and added silicon-tested per the working test report.

ttcad25a/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttcad25a/tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.summary: This design is a clock divider with lag correction that interfaces with PDM microphones and an I2S receiver. It takes bit clock and LR clock inputs, along with PDM data from up to eight microphones, and outputs PCM audio for each microphone plus a beamformed PCM output. The documentation is too vague to describe its exact operation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_clock_divider_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported i2s/dsp tags and added pdm based on PDM microphone inputs.

ttcad25a/tt_um_comm_ic_bhavuk.summary: Comm_IC combines UART, SPI, and I2C communication protocols into a single design that is selected via input data bits.
ttcad25a/tt_um_comm_ic_bhavuk.review_notes: Added missing canonical tags for the implemented communication protocols and language.

ttcad25a/tt_um_crispy_vga.summary: Crispy VGA takes a standard Tiny Tapeout VGA signal as input and adds a programmable amount of random noise to the video and audio signals before passing them to the output. The uio_in[0] through uio_in[4] inputs individually toggle noise on the hsync, B, G, R, and vsync signals. The uio_in[5] input sets the noise level applied to the R, G, and B wires to high or low, and the uio_in[0:5] inputs set successively increasing noise levels on the audio signal. Testing requires plugging an existing Tiny Tapeout VGA project into the input, connecting the output to a VGA monitor, and selecting the control bits for the desired noise level.
ttcad25a/tt_um_crispy_vga.review_notes: Summary expanded to four sentences covering the documented noise controls and test setup.

ttcad25a/tt_um_cw_vref.summary: This current-mode bandgap reference provides a stable 1V voltage and 5.6uA current, with an integrated testbuffer for measurement. It is tested by applying external bias and control signals, and requires a multimeter, power supply, and optionally an oven for temperature stability tests. Silicon results show the voltage output at 1.15V and current at 6.9uA, with minor documentation errors noted. The design includes an 8-bit trim for process variations and can be enabled or disabled via a control pin.
ttcad25a/tt_um_cw_vref.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; analog, bandgap, voltage-reference, current-mirror and silicon-tested are supported.

ttcad25a/tt_um_daobaanh_rng.summary: This design is a trial implementation of a lightweight all-digital true random number generator based on ring oscillators. It outputs random data via a UART serial interface, and also provides ring oscillator and random generator outputs for observation. The design is intended for testing and evaluation of TRNG concepts. It uses ring oscillators to generate entropy.
ttcad25a/tt_um_daobaanh_rng.review_notes: Removed prng and crypto tags; added ring-oscillator and uart, which are directly supported by the pins and description.

ttcad25a/tt_um_daosvik_aesinvsbox.summary: This circuit computes the inverse S-box of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). It takes an 8-bit input byte on ui[0] through ui[7] and produces an 8-bit output byte on uo[0] through uo[7]. The result can be read back from uo_out (unregistered) or uio_out (registered). No external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_daosvik_aesinvsbox.review_notes: Removed lookup-table tag as unsupported; summary expanded to four supported sentences.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ddc_arghunter.summary: This design converts I2S audio input to PDM output using an inverted CIC filter and modulator. It also supports up to eight PDM microphones, producing per-microphone PCM outputs and a beamformed PCM output, with delay selection controlled by five pins. The design is intended for use with an I2S output device and PDM input devices, such as microphones and a clock generator. The documentation is minimal beyond the pin descriptions and a brief explanation of the core conversion method.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ddc_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported fir-filter and delay-line tags; added sigma-delta for the PDM modulator.

ttcad25a/tt_um_demosiine_sda.summary: DemoSiine is a demoscene-style audio-visual project that generates a 640x480 VGA video signal and a looping ~28 second audio track. The video output includes dynamic wavy sine layers and a rainbowy overlay, with user controls to enable/disable layers, pause the animation, and toggle styles. The audio engine drives a frequency synthesizer to produce the soundtrack. It requires external hardware: a TinyVGA PMOD for video output, a TT Audio PMOD for audio output, and switches for input control.
ttcad25a/tt_um_demosiine_sda.review_notes: Removed button (inputs are switches); added pmod, music, and video to match the PMOD hardware and audio/video outputs.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dendraws_donut.summary: The donut project displays a rendered donut on a VGA screen. It uses hand-crafted ellipses to create the donut shape and outputs a standard VGA signal with 2-bit RGB color, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design operates with a 50.35 MHz clock and requires a TinyVGA PMOD connected to the output pins for display. The documentation is sparse, providing only a brief description and testing instructions.
ttcad25a/tt_um_dendraws_donut.review_notes: Removed demoscene as unsupported; added pmod because the TinyVGA PMOD is required.

ttcad25a/tt_um_devmonk_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square-wave tone channels, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with ten shapes. It is programmed through a multiplexed data/address bus with bus control pins, and it outputs digital 8-bit audio as well as PWM signals for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to hear the audio, and the design includes a configurable clock divider to match different clock frequencies. The project is notable for its thorough test suite and goal of hardware preservation, fitting on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttcad25a/tt_um_devmonk_ay8913.review_notes: Removed dac since conversion is external; added sound-generator and retro for the classic PSG replica.

ttcad25a/tt_um_devstdin_LDO_OSC.summary: This analog project provides three building blocks: a low-dropout regulator (LDO), a bandgap current reference, and an oscillator. The LDO output and oscillator output are accessible on pins, and the oscillator can be enabled and reset via digital inputs. Silicon test reports indicate the LDO outputs around 1.8V and the oscillator runs at approximately 5.2-5.8 MHz. The design is intended as analog IP for integration into larger systems.
ttcad25a/tt_um_devstdin_LDO_OSC.review_notes: Removed unsupported power-management tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dlfloatmac.summary: This design implements a MAC unit for the 16-bit DL float data type. Inputs are fed as binary or hexadecimal representations of the floating-point format, and outputs are read similarly. An FPGA is required to drive the inputs and capture the 16-bit result, which arrives as 8 bits over two clock cycles. It is implemented in Verilog and spans two tiles.
ttcad25a/tt_um_dlfloatmac.review_notes: Replaced incorrect audio tags with MAC/floating-point/DSP tags and corrected summary to match the DL float MAC description.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dlmiles_poc_fskmodem_hdlc.summary: This project is a proof-of-concept digital FSK modem with HDLC framing and UART interface, targeting amateur radio packet communication at data rates from 4800 to 64000 baud. It uses a lookup-table-based waveform generator for 2FSK modulation and includes UART flow control signals. The design is intended to be paired with a future CPU to form a complete terminal node controller (TNC). Testing requires external hardware such as an RP2040 or FPGA to validate the interface.
ttcad25a/tt_um_dlmiles_poc_fskmodem_hdlc.review_notes: Removed rom (only in original hardware description) and added demodulator and incomplete.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dlmiles_tt08_poc_uart.summary: The UART project is a UART data terminal equipment (DTE) implementation in SpinalHDL. It provides standard UART signals such as TxD, RxD, RTS, CTS, DSR, DCD, DTR, and RI, along with interrupt outputs. The design is intended to connect to a standard Tiny Tapeout PCB and interface with an RP2040's UART. Documentation is minimal, with only pin mappings and a brief note that docs are to follow.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dmtd_arghunter.summary: The DMTD project is described as a Dual Mixer Timer Differential, but the documentation is extremely sparse, elaborating only that it involves I2S and PDM audio interfaces with microphone inputs and beamformed output. The pinout is identical to another audio project, suggesting it may reuse that interface. External hardware required includes microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver. The documentation is essentially placeholder text, providing no real explanation of functionality.
ttcad25a/tt_um_dmtd_arghunter.review_notes: Removed dsp tag unsupported by text; attempted pdm add is not in vocabulary.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dpmu.summary: This project is titled DPMU (Dynamic Power Management Unit) and is implemented in SystemVerilog. The pin names are generic, and there is no documentation describing its functionality, interface, or how it should be tested. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may indicate an error or a very slow control loop. Due to the lack of documentation, it is not possible to provide a meaningful summary.

ttcad25a/tt_um_dpmunit.summary: This project is titled DPM_Unit and is described as a Design and Implementation of Dynamic Power management unit, implemented in SystemVerilog. The pin names are generic, and there is no documentation describing its functionality, interface, or how it should be tested. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may indicate an error or a very slow control loop. Due to the lack of documentation, it is not possible to provide a meaningful summary.

ttcad25a/tt_um_drum_goekce.summary: This design consists of a RAM and an approximate multiplier based on the DRUM technique for approximate applications. It multiplies two operands a and b to produce a result r, with operands and results accessed through an address-mapped RAM. The design is written in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. The documentation notes that product results may differ if the frequency is increased, suggesting approximate behavior under timing variation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_drum_goekce.review_notes: Corrected completely unrelated VGA/video tags and summary to match actual DRUM approximate multiplier with RAM.

ttcad25a/tt_um_edwintorok.summary: This design is a competition entry for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene, producing a VGA output and audio PWM signal. It is intended to be connected to a VGA PMOD for 640x480 video and an audio PMOD for sound. The design uses HardCaml and operates at 25.25 MHz, with a test mode pin. The documentation is minimal, providing only pinouts and external hardware requirements, so the visual and audio content is not described.
ttcad25a/tt_um_edwintorok.review_notes: Removed unsupported lfsr tag; added demoscene, vga, audio, pwm, and graphics based on source evidence.

ttcad25a/tt_um_emilian_muxpga.summary: This project is a resubmission of a TinyFPGA design for Tiny Tapeout 8, implemented in Verilog. It provides four inputs, two command pins, and eight outputs, and is configured and then observed via the outputs. No special external hardware is required, and the design includes tests. The documentation is very brief, so the exact function of the FPGA configuration is not detailed.
ttcad25a/tt_um_emilian_muxpga.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and template tags; added incomplete due to very thin documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_emmyxu_obstacle_detection.summary: This Verilog design takes two sensor inputs and a reset, and outputs two signals intended for motors or buzzers. It compares each sensor value against a threshold and, if only one side is active, sends a signal to the opposite motor; if both are active, it sends a signal to both motors. Testing involves driving the sensor pins with 0 or 1 and reading the outputs; a reset pin clears all outputs. External hardware includes ultrasonic sensors, a microcontroller, and haptic motors.
