ttcad25a/tt_um_enjens.summary: This Verilog design is a clock-driven counter intended to display values on a 7-segment display. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the exact counting or display logic. It uses a 1 Hz clock and has eight outputs that likely drive the display segments. No silicon test results are reported.
ttcad25a/tt_um_enjens.review_notes: Removed unsupported factory-test and current-mirror tags; added 7-segment, clock-divider, and insufficient-doc.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ephrenm_tsal.summary: This design implements the Tractive System Active Light (TSAL) function for a Formula SAE electric vehicle, as required by FSAE rule EV.5.9. It reads a 12-bit value from an external AD7476A ADC via a serial interface and compares it to a threshold; if below the threshold, it drives a green LED continuously, and if above, it flashes a red LED at 4 Hz. Testing requires a PMOD AD1 and simulation for at least one second to verify blink timing. The design is intended to be hard-wired in the vehicle and uses a Tiny Tapeout chip for the digital logic.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ephrenm_tsal.review_notes: Removed timer tag; the blink function is part of the TSAL logic, not a separate timer peripheral.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ezchips_calc.summary: This is an 8-bit calculator design originating from a ChipCraft lab exercise. It is implemented in Verilog and tested using Makerchip simulation. No external hardware is required, and all pins are marked unused in the provided pin list. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note about simulation testing.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ezchips_calc.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added incomplete due to minimal documentation and unused pins.

ttcad25a/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttcad25a/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_faramire_rotary_ring_wrap.summary: This Verilog design uses a rotary encoder to control a ring of 12 WS2812B LEDs. Rotating the encoder selects which LED is lit, and a button inverts the LED state. The user can select the color (green, red, or blue) via three input pins and set the intensity with two additional pins. The chip outputs a WS2812B serial data stream on one pin to drive the LED chain, and it also outputs the current count value. External hardware includes a rotary encoder and a WS2812B LED ring.

ttcad25a/tt_um_faramire_stopwatch.summary: This is a simple stopwatch that counts in hundredths of a second and displays the time on an 8-digit 7-segment display via SPI using a MAX7219 chip. It includes start/stop, lap time, and reset inputs, with outputs for SPI MOSI, CS, and CLK, as well as status signals. The design divides a 1 MHz clock to 100 Hz to drive the counters. External hardware needed includes buttons for control and a MAX7219-compatible display.

ttcad25a/tt_um_favoritohjs_scroller.summary: This design generates a scrolling pixelated cityscape video signal for VGA output. The terrain layers are produced using an LFSR to create deterministic randomness. It requires a Tiny VGA carrier board and a 25.18 MHz clock to display video. Silicon testing confirmed it works and produces a Tetris-like scrolling display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_favoritohjs_scroller.review_notes: Removed demoscene tag; the source does not describe a demoscene-style showcase.

ttcad25a/tt_um_find_the_damn_issue.summary: This 2x2 tile design is a USB to UART/SPI/I2C/JTAG/GPIO adapter implemented in Gatery. It enumerates as a USB CDC device on a host computer and can bit-bang various serial protocols to communicate with external devices. Testing involves connecting a device such as a LIS2DH12 sensor and running example software. An external 1.5k pull-up resistor on USB_DP is required for USB operation. The design is notable for supporting many protocols on a single chip.

ttcad25a/tt_um_flummer_ltc.summary: This design generates Linear Timecode (LTC) for audio and video synchronisation, using counters to track time and frame count and serialising 80-bit biphase mark coded frames. It is driven by a 12 MHz clock and starts counting from 00:00:00:00 after reset, with the frame rate selected by two input pins for 24, 25, or 30 fps. The LTC output appears on a bidirectional pin and can be fed to an audio PMOD for levels usable by audio equipment, or connected directly to a logic analyser. The 29.97 fps mode is documented as not implemented, and the project is a small single-tile Verilog design.
ttcad25a/tt_um_flummer_ltc.review_notes: Removed synchronizer (not a CDC block) and added signal-generator for the LTC waveform output.

ttcad25a/tt_um_fountaincoder_top_ad.summary: This Verilog design implements a temporal adder, where addition is performed over time with an enable signal. It takes 8 input bits and produces 8 output bits, and is intended to be used as a coprocessor for vector calculations driven by an RP2040. The design was tested using cocotb. No external hardware is required beyond the driving microcontroller.
ttcad25a/tt_um_fountaincoder_top_ad.review_notes: Removed accelerator tag because the source describes a coprocessor, not a dedicated compute accelerator.

ttcad25a/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an external signal by counting pulses over 100 ms periods and displays the result on a 128x32 SSD1306 OLED display using an emulated 7-segment format. It requires an external 1 MHz clock, a PMOD OLED display, and the signal to be measured connected to the input pin. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and uses SPI to communicate with the OLED. No silicon test results are provided, so the actual performance is not documented.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gamepad_pmod_demo.summary: This project reads input from a Gamepad PMOD and displays the pressed buttons as green symbols on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout and a 25.175 MHz clock, and is intended to be run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board with both PMODs attached. After reset, pressing a gamepad button causes its corresponding symbol to appear on screen. It is a demonstration of combining the Gamepad and Tiny VGA PMODs, derived from the VGA Playground, and needs both external PMOD boards to operate.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gcd_stephan.summary: This module computes the greatest common divisor of two 15-bit integers, taking the operands across the eight ui and eight uio input pins and returning a 7-bit result on the output pins. A request signal on uio[7] indicates when operands have been presented, and an acknowledge signal on uo[7] indicates when the first operand has been received and when the GCD is ready. The documented test procedure is to hold the first operand, raise request, wait for acknowledge, then present the second operand and read the result. It is a small single-tile Verilog design that expects buttons and LEDs as external hardware, and the documentation gives no details of the internal algorithm.
ttcad25a/tt_um_gcd_stephan.review_notes: Removed alu and synchronizer tags because the source describes a GCD module with a request/acknowledge handshake, not an ALU or clock-domain synchronizer.

ttcad25a/tt_um_georgboecherer_vco.summary: This is an analog voltage-controlled oscillator built from four differential stages with capacitive loading, providing eight output taps with phase differences. The frequency is controlled by a bias current or voltage applied to an analog input pin, and the eight tap signals are buffered to digital outputs. It requires external DC power for control and an oscilloscope for monitoring. Silicon tests show it works, achieving frequencies from 33 kHz to 2.8 MHz depending on bias current, with measured phase relationships among the taps.
ttcad25a/tt_um_georgboecherer_vco.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator and signal-generator tags not supported by the source; added silicon-tested per the working test report.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gfg_development_tinymande.summary: This design generates a Mandelbrot set image and outputs it via a VGA driver, using an external RP2040 to emulate a framebuffer. It includes a serial interface for configuration and control, and the VGA output follows the Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD for display and an RP2040 for framebuffer emulation. The documentation is brief and lacks details on the serial protocol and exact operation, but the core function is clear.
ttcad25a/tt_um_gfg_development_tinymande.review_notes: Removed vga: VGA is only described as an optional output mode for the Mandelbrot image generator.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gregac_tiny_nn.summary: This is a toy neural network accelerator aimed at convolutional neural networks, containing 16-bit floating point add and multiply units using an approximation of the BF16 encoding. It supports a 4x2 convolution operation with streamed image pixels and an accumulate operation with optional bias and ReLU, all controlled by operation codes sent over a 16-bit input formed from ui_in and uio_in. Results are emitted as 16-bit values split over two clock cycles on the 8-bit output, so the user must know which cycles carry valid data. The Verilog is generated from a separate SystemVerilog repository that holds the full verification environment and software, both described as work in progress at tapeout time, and no specific external hardware is required beyond something to drive the sequences, such as the demo board's RP2040.
ttcad25a/tt_um_gregac_tiny_nn.review_notes: Removed dsp and image-processing as unsupported; added tpu and mac-unit which the CNN accelerator description supports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gus16.summary: This project is a 16-bit experimental CPU called GUS16 with a serial port, PWM output, general purpose I/O and an external memory interface, with memory provided off-chip. It includes a bootloader that loads programs over the serial port, and the documented basic test is to connect at 115200 baud, 8N1, and send an 'L', which should be echoed back. More complete testing requires an external board with SRAM and address latches attached to the user PMOD connectors, and that memory board is noted as still pending design. The design is documented in an accompanying PDF and occupies a 1x2 tile area.

ttcad25a/tt_um_gxrii_spi_sevenseg.summary: This is a small SPI slave that receives 6-bit messages and drives the 7-segment display on the Tiny Tapeout carrier board. The first two bits of each message form a command that turns the decimal point on or off, and the remaining four bits select the digit to display; malformed commands turn the decimal point on with the rest of the display blank. The SPI signals SCLK, SS and MOSI are mapped to the clock and two input pins, and the seven segments plus decimal point appear on the eight outputs. It requires the carrier board's seven-segment display and a microcontroller to act as SPI master.

ttcad25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.summary: This is a 16-bit CPU based on the HACK architecture, featuring an ALU, three registers (A, D, PC), and two SPI modules for memory and debug communication. It uses SPI to fetch instructions and data from an external SPI RAM, and a separate SPI debug interface allows reading internal registers. The design requires an external SPI RAM (e.g., 23XX512) and a microcontroller with SPI for debugging. It is notable for fitting a CPU into a single tile and using serial memory access due to pin limitations.
ttcad25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.review_notes: Removed risc-v tag because the HACK architecture is not RISC-V.

ttcad25a/tt_um_hpdl1414_uart_atudoroi.summary: This design is a 115200 baud UART transceiver that stores received characters in a 16-byte buffer and asynchronously drives four HPDL-1414 alphanumeric LED display modules. When the buffer fills, existing characters shift left to make room, a blinking cursor shows the input position, and Ctrl-H performs a backspace for editing. Testing is done by connecting a computer or microcontroller at 115200 baud, sending ASCII characters, and observing them on the HPDL-1414 modules. It requires the external HPDL-1414 PMOD module and uses a 12 MHz clock.

ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.summary: This is a demoscene project that displays a bouncing capsule with background and text on a VGA output, accompanied by PDM audio. It includes input switches to pause, reset, mute, hide elements, lock colors, and disable re-orientation. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD (or compatible) for output. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition and runs at 25 MHz.
ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.review_notes: Removed speaker tag: PDM audio on uio pins is a digital audio output, not a driven speaker stage.

ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_checkers.summary: This project recreates the classic Checkers demo from VGA Playground, with each of its five layers generated by a different Python-based HDL: Amaranth, MyHDL, PyCDE, PyRTL and PyMTL3. It outputs VGA signals on the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout at a 25.175 MHz clock, and the eight input pins can be toggled to change the main, sub, foreground and background colours. The only external hardware needed is the TinyVGA PMOD and a screen, and the design is notable for demonstrating several Python HDLs in a single chip. It is essentially a visual demonstration rather than a functional application.
ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_checkers.review_notes: Removed amaranth/myhdl since only individual layers use them; added demoscene and retro for the classic demo recreation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_dg_dac.summary: This design implements a Dempsey-Gorman 8-bit segmented DAC using two resistor ladders without voltage buffering. It is tested by setting the 8-bit input and measuring the analog output voltage, which should map to the 0V to 3.3V range. External hardware such as a multimeter or oscilloscope is required to measure the output. The documentation is brief but sufficient, referencing an external tutorial for architecture details.
ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_dg_dac.review_notes: Removed unsupported r2r-dac and transistor-level tags; architecture is Dempsey-Gorman, not R-2R.

ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_pi_snake.summary: This analog design implements a voltage divider using precision resistors that meander through geometric shapes to output a voltage of approximately π volts from a 3.3 V supply. The output is a single analog pin, and the design is tested by measuring the voltage with a multimeter. Silicon tests show an output of about 3.16 V, which is close to π when accounting for the actual supply voltage. The project is notable for its creative use of resistor geometry to achieve a mathematical constant.
ttcad25a/tt_um_htfab_pi_snake.review_notes: Removed instrumentation because the design is a voltage divider, not a measurement application; added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

ttcad25a/tt_um_huffman_coder.summary: This ASIC compresses ASCII characters into Huffman codes using a lookup table, taking a 7-bit ASCII character on the input pins with a load strobe on ui[7]. After loading, a Valid_out signal indicates when the Huffman code and its bit length are available on the uo and uio pins. Communication requires an RP2040 or external microcontroller to send ASCII input and read the compressed output. The documentation is brief and does not describe the code table or the internal implementation beyond the lookup table.
ttcad25a/tt_um_huffman_coder.review_notes: Removed encoder; compression, lookup-table, ascii and verilog are all supported.

ttcad25a/tt_um_i2c_peripheral_stevej.summary: This design implements several I2C peripherals: an FNV-1a 32-bit hash calculator, a leading zero counter (LZC), and two constant byte generators (0x55 and 0xAA). It demonstrates address decoding and I2C read/write operations, with each peripheral accessible via specific addresses. The design requires an I2C master device for testing, and Arduino test code is provided. It is a compact example of I2C peripheral integration.

ttcad25a/tt_um_i2c_regf.summary: This block is an asynchronous I2C slave that exposes a register file, intended to configure analog blocks on the same chip. An I2C master writes and reads words to the registers, and an LED is listed as external hardware for testing. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the register map or address. The design is notable for providing a reusable configuration interface for analog circuitry.

ttcad25a/tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.summary: This design converts I2S audio input to PWM output, with support for up to eight PDM microphones and beamforming via delay selection. It outputs PCM data for each microphone and a beamformed PCM output. The documentation is extremely sparse, using placeholder text like 'cool stuff', so the exact functionality and usage are unclear. External hardware needed includes PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver.
ttcad25a/tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.review_notes: Removed pwm and dsp; added insufficient-doc because the documentation is placeholder text.

ttcad25a/tt_um_jayjaywong12.summary: This is a 4-bit vector multiplication engine that multiplies two vectors of up to 32 elements and accumulates the result into an 8-bit output. It is programmed via a register interface using read/write opcodes and a run command, and it operates in two clock cycles. The design is intended to be controlled by an RP2040 and requires no other external hardware. Silicon tests show it works, though timing adjustments were needed.
ttcad25a/tt_um_jayjaywong12.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu/dsp tags and added mac-unit, rp2040, and silicon-tested based on the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_jimktrains_vslc.summary: The VSLC is a small PLC-like stack machine controller with 8 inputs, 8 outputs, and two timers, inspired by relay logic and early PLCs. It is programmed via an external EEPROM over SPI and executes scan cycles to handle small control tasks such as model train crossing gates, flashing lights, and servo actuation. A compiler and disassembler are provided for program development, and the design latches inputs at the start of each scan cycle. Notable features include rising/falling edge detection between scan cycles and complementary timer outputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_jimktrains_vslc.review_notes: Removed rom and motor-control, added industrial, spi, servo, timer, and stack-machine as directly supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_jmack2201.summary: This design displays a bouncing sprite with multiple background options on a VGA output, with sprite ROM, background control registers, and audio ROM configured via SPI. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and an audio Pmod for sound output. The design is controlled by SPI to set the background, sprite image, and sound effects. It is a hardware sprite engine suitable for simple demos.
ttcad25a/tt_um_jmack2201.review_notes: Removed unsupported game/framebuffer tags and added pmod and demoscene based on the documented external hardware and demo purpose.

ttcad25a/tt_um_johshoff_metaballs.summary: This design attempts to render metaballs on a VGA display. It outputs RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Silicon tests show partial functionality: one ball moves as expected, but the other exhibits erratic behavior, and results vary across chips. The documentation is minimal and the design is described as rushed.
ttcad25a/tt_um_johshoff_metaballs.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added 'silicon-tested' to match the reported silicon status.

ttcad25a/tt_um_jp_cd101_saw.summary: This is a digital saw-wave synthesizer with a programmable pulse generator, ADSR amplitude modulation, a one-pole IIR filter, and a first-order delta-sigma audio output. Parameters are set over an SPI slave interface, and a trigger input starts and stops notes; a VST/CLAP plugin generates the SPI commands. It is an educational design that deliberately mirrors the audio pipeline structurally in hardware, and it requires an external lowpass filter, button Pmod, audio Pmod, and SPI master. Testing uses a cocotb testbench that writes audio to a file and compares against a golden reference.

ttcad25a/tt_um_jun1okamura_test0.summary: This design drives a 7-segment display from a counter whose period is either fixed or pseudo-random, selected by an input pin. A second input chooses between a hexadecimal sequence and a fixed text string, and the low 8 bits of a 24-bit counter are exposed on the bidirectional pins. It is tested on the Tiny Tapeout evaluation board by observing the display and changing the two select inputs. The design is notable mainly as a simple display and LFSR demonstration.
ttcad25a/tt_um_jun1okamura_test0.review_notes: Removed lfsr (source only says pseudo-random value) and added bcd for the binary-to-decimal display conversion.

ttcad25a/tt_um_kapilan_alarm.summary: This is a simple alarm clock that compares internal hour and minute counters against user-set alarm values and asserts an alarm output when they match. It is tested with a provided testbench that sets alarm values and observes the alarm and time outputs. The design uses inout pins for some signals due to limited pin availability. The project was sponsored by The MITRE Corporation and MIT/LL Beaver Works Summer Institute.
ttcad25a/tt_um_kapilan_alarm.review_notes: Removed rtc and education tags that lack direct source support; added calculator tag for the numeric-input numeric-display alarm-clock interface.

ttcad25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.summary: This design is a 4-bit ALU slice intended for use in minicomputer or microcomputer CPUs. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 3-bit function code, and produces a 4-bit result along with carry, equal, and zero flags. The design was tested using an Altera FPGA. It provides basic arithmetic and logic functions.
ttcad25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.review_notes: Removed adc, cpu, and education tags not supported by the source; added alu, retro, and fpga.

ttcad25a/tt_um_kch_cd101.summary: This is a digital synthesizer with a programmable pulse-wave generator, ADSR amplitude modulation, a one-pole IIR filter, and a first-order delta-sigma audio output. It is controlled through an SPI slave interface and a trigger input, with a VST/CLAP plugin available to generate SPI commands from a DAW. The design is educational and intentionally maps the audio pipeline directly into hardware, requiring an external lowpass filter, button Pmod, audio Pmod, and SPI master. Testing uses a cocotb testbench that captures audio to a file and compares against a golden reference.

ttcad25a/tt_um_kentrane_tinyspectrum.summary: This is a small square-wave tone generator that produces 16 notes across 4 octaves with an optional tremolo effect. Note and octave are selected by input pins, an enable pin gates the tone, and seven outputs drive LEDs as a simple visualizer while the audio comes from the eighth output. It requires an external RC low-pass filter, a DC blocking capacitor, and a speaker or headphones, and the documentation suggests it could be controlled from a Pi Pico or a small keyboard. The documentation is informal and notes that the project was completed under time pressure.
ttcad25a/tt_um_kentrane_tinyspectrum.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; softened the control sentence to match the source's speculative wording.

ttcad25a/tt_um_keszocze_ssmcl.summary: This design is a 3-bit unsigned multiplier that trades speed for area by streaming operands and results over multiple clock cycles. A start signal begins the operation, the product appears after 18 cycles, and a valid output indicates when the result is ready. It can be driven from the Tiny Tapeout motherboard web interface or with input/output Pmods. The design is notable for its explicit multi-cycle streaming behavior.
ttcad25a/tt_um_keszocze_ssmcl.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu, fsm and education tags and speculative educational wording.

ttcad25a/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, plus UART over the demo board USB. It is a full Linux-capable SoC implemented in Verilog on a 8x2 tile Tiny Tapeout chip.
ttcad25a/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Removed redundant microcontroller tag and corrected the summary to avoid implying built-in flash or an onboard UART bridge.

ttcad25a/tt_um_larva.summary: This project is a RISC-V CPU (LaRVa) with a serial port, JTAG interface, and a few other peripherals, but it requires external memory. An included bootloader allows programs loaded through the serial port to execute, and JTAG provides an additional debug path. A simple test is to connect a serial port at 8-bit, no parity, 115200 bps and send an 'L', expecting the bootloader to reply with another 'L'. More complete testing needs an external board with SRAM memory and address latches attached to the Pmod ports, and the JTAG port can also be used.
ttcad25a/tt_um_larva.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm/sram tags, added gpio and education, and rephrased the summary from source-supported facts.

ttcad25a/tt_um_led_jellyant.summary: This design simply turns on one output pin, as described in its minimal documentation. It has no inputs and only eight output pins, all labeled A[0] through A[7]. The testing instructions state that no action is needed, and no external hardware is required. The project is a minimal LED test with essentially no functionality beyond driving an output high.
ttcad25a/tt_um_led_jellyant.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and gpio tags; added insufficient-doc given the very thin documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_log_afpm.summary: This design is a 16-bit floating-point multiplier that uses logarithmic approximation to reduce hardware complexity and power consumption. It has 8 input pins for operand A, 8 bidirectional pins for operand B, and 8 output pins for the product, with the pins time-multiplexed to handle 16-bit values. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of the algorithm or testing procedure. Notable aspects include the use of approximation for efficiency, but without further documentation, its accuracy and limitations are unclear.
ttcad25a/tt_um_log_afpm.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; no DSP application is described, only a floating-point multiplier.

ttcad25a/tt_um_luke_clock.summary: This design is a VGA-based binary clock implemented in Chisel that displays hours, minutes, and seconds as a matrix of binary squares. It accepts switches to select the time clock source and display mode, and plus/minus buttons to set the time. The VGA output shows the binary time representation, updating every second. External hardware includes a TT VGA PMOD, buttons, switches, and optionally a real-time clock for precision timekeeping.
ttcad25a/tt_um_luke_clock.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated multiplier project; corrected to match the VGA binary clock source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mac.summary: This project implements a Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) unit using a Dadda multiplier and a Kogge-Stone adder. The design includes pipeline registers and an accumulator, and is intended for digital signal processing tasks such as filtering and convolution. A testbench is provided to simulate input scenarios and observe the output behavior. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may be a documentation error.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mac.review_notes: Removed dsp tag since the design is a MAC building block rather than a DSP algorithm; no silicon-tested claim since there are no test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_adjustable_psu_c.summary: This design allows an analog supply to power a digital counter, with the warning that the analog supply resistor must be removed before enabling to avoid destroying the digital logic. It is tested by connecting a variable power supply to the analog supply and observing the counter outputs. External hardware includes a variable PSU. The documentation is minimal and emphasizes the destructive risk if misused.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_adjustable_psu_c.review_notes: Removed 'power-gating' because the source only warns about a destructive supply connection, not a power-gating technique.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.summary: This analog design implements two ring oscillators, one targeting 600 MHz and the other 300 MHz, with enable inputs and analog outputs. Silicon tests show that the first oscillator works at around 500 MHz with reduced amplitude, while the second oscillator is broken due to a missing via. The documentation notes that only analog outputs are connected, not digital ones. The design uses inverter chains with NAND gates for enable and a two-stage inverter driver for the analog outputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested because silicon status is partial; added a supported sentence about the inverter-chain implementation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_level_shifter.summary: This is an analog level shifter experiment that operates down to around 0.2V, designed by Sylvain Munaut. The design improves upon traditional level shifters that only work down to about 1V. The documentation includes a schematic and a graph showing a 0.2V input resulting in a full 1.8V swing output. It is tested by applying an input signal and observing the output, requiring an adjustable power supply, a soldering iron to remove a resistor, and an oscilloscope.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_level_shifter.review_notes: Removed incorrect transistor-level and low-power tags; reordered summary so design precedes testing.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.summary: This design is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) with a 3.3V output, driven either externally or by an internal sine waveform generator. Silicon tests confirm a smooth sine wave over the full 3.3V range, with a slight nonlinearity at the mid-code transition. It requires an external multimeter to measure the output voltage. The design uses level shifting drivers to achieve the 3.3V output.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.review_notes: Removed transistor-level, which is not supported by the R2R ladder description; silicon-tested was already correctly applied.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.summary: This design debounces inputs from three rotary encoders and generates PWM signals to control LED brightness. It is intended for use with external digital encoders connected to the first six inputs. The project is a demo for the Zero to ASIC course. Testing involves twisting the encoders and observing the LED brightness changes.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed unsupported rgb-led and education tags; added rotary-encoder and driver tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_spi_test.summary: This is an SPI test design based on the tt07_alu_74181 project, as stated in the documentation. It includes SPI signals (MISO, MOSI, clock, chip select) and inputs for CPOL and CPHA, but the documentation provides no further details on functionality or testing. The design is likely a test for SPI communication, but its exact behavior is unclear from the available information. No external hardware is required according to the description.
ttcad25a/tt_um_mattvenn_spi_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported communication tag and added insufficient-doc to match very thin documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker connected to the bidirectional pins in a differential PWM configuration. It requires an external piezo speaker or the Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod. The design also copies the input pins to the output pins for testing purposes. It operates with a 100 kHz clock and is intended for audio output.

ttcad25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.summary: This project implements a generic synchronous FIFO buffer with a single clock domain. It buffers data from an 8-bit input to an 8-bit output, with write and read enable signals and full/empty flags. The design is intended as an experimental microtile container. Testing involves writing data until full and reading until empty.
ttcad25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag because the project uses only one tile.

ttcad25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container_gro.summary: This design implements a maze game where the player can walk around and see adjacent walls on a 7-segment display. It uses the first four inputs to move up, down, left, or right. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout PCB. The documentation is minimal and does not provide details on the maze layout or game mechanics.
ttcad25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container_gro.review_notes: Removed multi-tile because the project is 1x1 tiles.

ttcad25a/tt_um_monishvr_fifo.summary: This project implements a synchronous FIFO with a 4-bit data width. It has inputs for write and read control, 4-bit data input, and outputs for full, empty, and 4-bit data output. The documentation mentions that it is based on a debouncing mechanism, but the testing procedure is listed as 'TBA' and no external hardware is required. The design is a basic first-in-first-out memory buffer.
ttcad25a/tt_um_monishvr_fifo.review_notes: Removed redundant memory tag and added debouncer, which is explicitly mentioned in the documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_moody_mimosa.summary: This project implements a Tamagotchi-like artificial creature called Mimosa, which reacts to external stimuli such as tickling, playing, talking, feeding, and temperature changes. It outputs emotional states like sleeping, eating, playing, smiling, babbling, kicking legs, doing nothing, and crying, and includes SPI and UART interfaces for debugging. The design is supported by extensive simulation, FPGA prototyping, and a microcontroller-based logger for debugging. Notable aspects include its complex behavioral model inspired by biological processes and its use of multiple subprojects for testing and emulation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_moody_mimosa.review_notes: Removed game tag because the design is a Tamagotchi-like creature rather than an interactive game implementation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_morningjava_r2r_from_matt.summary: This project is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter that is a duplicate of Matt Venn's design. It accepts eight digital input bits and produces an analog output voltage on one analog pin, with an external data input and a load divider control. Testing involves setting the external data input high, driving the eight inputs, and measuring the analog output with a multimeter. The documentation is minimal and refers to the original project for details, so the design's specifics are not fully described here.

ttcad25a/tt_um_mp_lif_schor.summary: This project implements a mixed-precision leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that can compute either one neuron with a 24-bit membrane value and 8-bit weights or two neurons with 12-bit membrane values and 4-bit weights. It has 4 input pins for weights, a ready output, and two spike outputs for upper and lower neurons. The documentation is minimal, with testing instructions stating to apply weights and observe spikes, and no external hardware is required. The design is notable for its mixed-precision approach, but further details are lacking.

ttcad25a/tt_um_multiplier.summary: This is an 8-bit unsigned binary multiplier implemented in SystemVerilog, with two 8-bit inputs and a 16-bit product split across outputs. The documentation is brief, stating that inputs are given through ui_in and uio_in and the product appears on uo_out and uio_out. No details are provided about the internal Vedic algorithm or testing methodology beyond basic pin usage. No external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_multiplier.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and overly harsh insufficient-doc tags; fixed summary to mention Vedic.

ttcad25a/tt_um_neural_navigators.summary: This design implements a neural network accelerator for MNIST handwriting prediction in Verilog. It uses a 4x2 tile area and runs at 10 MHz, with all pins labeled generically as ui, uio, and uo. The documentation is essentially absent, providing only the title and one-line description, so no details on architecture, usage, or testing are available. The project is notable for targeting a neural network ASIC but lacks sufficient documentation to verify its functionality.
ttcad25a/tt_um_neural_navigators.review_notes: Removed asic tag not supported by source and added insufficient-doc for very thin documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_nithishreddykvs.summary: This Verilog module generates a PWM signal with an adjustable duty cycle controlled by two debounced buttons, using a 50 MHz input clock. The duty cycle can be increased or decreased in 10% steps from 0% to 90%, producing a PWM output. Testing can be done in simulation or on an FPGA, with buttons connected to the inputs and an oscilloscope or LED on the output to verify the waveform. External hardware includes two push buttons, a clock source, a reset, and a device such as an LED or motor to use the PWM signal.
ttcad25a/tt_um_nithishreddykvs.review_notes: Removed clock-generator which is contradicted by pins; kept verilog and corrected summary wording to match source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_noritsuna_Vctrl_LC_oscill.summary: This is a voltage-controlled LC oscillator designed for 2 GHz operation in Skywater 130nm. It has four analog pins: differential outputs vout_p and vout_n, a control voltage input vctrl, and a bias current input ibias. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the title and pin names, with no description of how it works or how to test it. External hardware such as a bias current source and control voltage source would be needed to operate it.

ttcad25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.summary: This Verilog design generates a VGA demo that displays a virtual 7-segment LED display with decimal point, controlled by 8-bit input. It also has a demo mode that counts down from 9 to 0 and toggles the decimal bit, but the reset for this mode is flawed. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD for output and runs at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm the basic display and user input work, but the demo mode does not reset correctly.
ttcad25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.review_notes: Removed 7-segment/display since the seven-segment display is only virtual on VGA; added silicon-tested per test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_nyan.summary: This design plays the Nyan Cat animation and music on infinite repeat. It outputs VGA video signals and a PWM audio signal, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD and Mike's audio PMOD for full functionality. The design runs at 25 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon, with testers reporting that it delighted children. It is a simple, self-contained demo with no inputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_nyan.review_notes: Added silicon-tested and speaker tags to reflect the confirmed silicon status and audio output hardware.

ttcad25a/tt_um_obriensp_jtag.summary: This project implements a JTAG Test Access Port with boundary scan support, wrapping an inner design that drives a seven-segment display from either an internal 4-bit counter or an external 4-bit value. The TAP supports standard instructions including IDCODE, SAMPLE/PRELOAD, EXTEST, INTEST, CLAMP, and BYPASS, and a BSDL file is provided for testing with tools like UrJTAG. The design requires a JTAG adapter connected to specific bidirectional pins. Notable features include the integration of boundary scan for testing both the inner project and external pins.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ole_moller_priority_encod.summary: This Verilog design implements an 8-bit priority encoder that converts the highest-priority set bit into a decimal digit displayed on a 7-segment display. If no bits are set, a decimal point is shown instead of a digit. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display and input switches. It is a simple project for demonstrating priority encoding and 7-segment decoding.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ole_moller_priority_encod.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

ttcad25a/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This design is a stylish ring oscillator built from 21 SkullFET inverters, generating a square wave with a simulated frequency of about 169.2 MHz. It is tested by connecting an oscilloscope to one of the divided outputs, as the full-speed outputs are too fast for GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond an oscilloscope. Notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and the inclusion of frequency dividers for observability.
ttcad25a/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Removed the overbroad clock-generator tag; simulation frequency kept as stated in the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_patater_demokit.summary: This Verilog design outputs a waggling 6-bit rainbow demo on VGA, with effects controlled by input pins. Inputs enable dual mode (horizontal flip per scanline) and horizontal waves, with offsets controlling wave speeds. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and runs at 25.175 MHz. The design can be tested in a VGA playground or with hardware, and an incomplete cocotb testbench is provided.

ttcad25a/tt_um_pdm_correlator_arghunter.summary: This chip performs cross- or auto-correlation on up to eight PDM microphone inputs by XORing pairs of bitstreams and summing the results, with lower sums indicating higher correlation. It outputs PCM data for each microphone and a beamformed PCM output, with delay selection controlled via bidirectional pins. The design requires external PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an SPI port for configuration. The documentation is sparse and contains placeholder text, but the core function and pinout are described.
ttcad25a/tt_um_pdm_correlator_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported tag and added correct ones based on source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_pdm_pitch_filter_arghunte.summary: This project implements a moving average filter and decimator for PDM microphone input, intended to filter out a specific frequency and its harmonics by averaging over a period where the sine wave's energy sums to zero. It outputs PCM data for each microphone plus a beamformed PCM output, with filter and decimator parameters set via an SPI port. The design requires external PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an SPI interface. The documentation contains placeholder text and testing instructions that are still in progress.
ttcad25a/tt_um_pdm_pitch_filter_arghunte.review_notes: Filter is a moving average/IIR style not a FIR; testing section is explicitly unfinished.

ttcad25a/tt_um_project.summary: This is a simple 8-bit shift register that shifts left on each clock cycle and outputs the current value, with new data loaded when a specific bidirectional pin is high. The clock is specified as 1 Hz, making it suitable for visual observation of the shifting bits. Testing involves setting an 8-bit input, asserting the load pin, and watching the output shift. No external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_project.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and register-file tags; summary's educational claim was not supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.summary: This design is a 16-bit counter with count enable and multiplier enable inputs. It accepts 3-bit operands m_a and m_b for the multiplier. The counter outputs its lower 8 bits on uo and upper 8 bits on the bidirectional pins. The documentation is extremely thin, describing it only as "like a 16-bit counter" and providing no details on the multiplier functionality or testing.
ttcad25a/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source only supports counter and multiplier functionality.

ttcad25a/tt_um_quarren42_demoscene_top.summary: This Verilog design displays a parody of the 'graphic design is my passion' meme with bouncing shapes on a VGA monitor. It has no inputs and outputs standard VGA signals, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon. It is a simple graphics demo with no interactive elements.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ran_DanielZhu.summary: This SystemVerilog design generates a random number from 0 to F when a button is pressed, using an inverter ring as the entropy source. It outputs the result on its output pins, intended for a 2-digit LED display. The design runs at 50 MHz and requires external hardware for the button and display. The documentation is very thin, with pin names all labeled '1', so the exact interface is unclear.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ran_DanielZhu.review_notes: Removed game (not an interactive game) and added insufficient-doc for the very thin documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rburt16_bias_generator.summary: This analog test chip evaluates mismatch in a simple CMOS beta multiplier 1uA current source. It contains eight identical cells in one orientation and eight rotated 90 degrees, with all current outputs wired together to a single analog pin. Individual cells can be disabled via digital input pins to measure the current contributed by each cell. A silicon test report confirms the current source is functional, with measured currents around 0.4-0.9 uA per cell, though no external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rburt16_bias_generator.review_notes: Removed unsupported voltage-reference tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rc_oscillators.summary: This project contains six R-C oscillators, three at 500kHz and three at 16MHz, originally designed for the Efabless Frigate project's timing subsystem. Each oscillator is enabled by a digital input and produces an output in the 1.8V domain, with four outputs on digital pins and two on analog pins. The oscillators are intended to measure cross-coupling and frequency variation across the wafer. The design is implemented with analog circuitry and has been validated on fabricated silicon.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This hardware module converts Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is intended to be used by any device that processes Unicode text, and it provides dedicated output pins for status signals like READY, ERROR, and various error types. Testing is supported by a comprehensive test set included in the project's test.py file, covering many edge cases.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction and ascii tags as they are not supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_styler.summary: The Styler chip transforms a 16x16 character glyph bitmap based on text mode attributes such as bold, italic, underline, blink, and cursor display. It contains a 4-bit scanline register, a 6-bit control register, a 16-bit bitmap register, and a 25-bit attribute register, and supports double width/height, mirroring, and various text decorations. The chip is intended to be used as part of a larger text mode video display hardware project, and it is accessed through an address bus and bidirectional data pins. Test cases are to be determined, but the register layout and usage steps are documented.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_styler.review_notes: Removed register-file because the design is a glyph attribute processor, not a general register file.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttcad25a/tt_um_reemashivva_fifo.summary: The design implements an asynchronous FIFO that buffers data between two clock domains with independent read and write clocks. It uses Gray-coded pointers and synchronization logic to prevent metastability, with full and empty flags indicating when the FIFO cannot accept or provide data. The documentation describes how to test by setting write and read enables and observing the flags and data outputs, but the pin list provided in the documentation does not match the actual pin names given in the project metadata. External hardware is minimal, likely just a way to drive the inputs and observe the outputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_reemashivva_fifo.review_notes: Removed generic memory tag; added fifo, asynchronous, clock-domain-crossing, synchronizer, gray-code, and verilog based on source evidence.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_lgn_mnist.summary: This project is an experiment with Deep Differential Logic Networks for classifying hand-written MNIST digits at 16x16 pixels. It accepts an 8-bit input packet shifted in on the input pins and outputs a 4-bit digit plus a 7-bit confidence score. A /WE input pauses the design, and an external MCU is needed to provide input data and read out results. The documentation is sparse and the test procedure is still marked TO DO, with no silicon results reported.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_lgn_mnist.review_notes: Removed unsupported perceptron and UART tags; added image-processing and insufficient-doc, and corrected the summary to match the actual pins and sparse documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_ternary_dot.summary: This project computes a dot product between a binary vector A and a ternary vector B, with ternary weights and 1-bit activations, targeting on-chip neural network inference. The inputs are eight binary elements of A and serial ternary elements of B, and the dot product result is provided on eight output pins. Testing is done via the Commander app to set inputs and weights, with no additional hardware required. The documentation is very brief, only stating the basic function and test method.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_ternary_dot.review_notes: Removed multiplier; added mac-unit and accelerator to reflect the actual dot-product datapath.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_vga_logo.summary: This design displays a 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor, using compressed data and dithered colors to fit into a single tile. It generates standard VGA signals including red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for operation, and it has been tested successfully by a silicon tester who confirmed the video works as expected. Notable features include the large resolution crammed into a small area and the use of dithering for color effects.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.summary: This design is an audio/visual demo that generates VGA video and PWM audio outputs, forming an 8-part megademo. It uses eight PWM audio pins and standard VGA pins for red, green, blue, and sync signals. The demo requires external hardware: a VGA PMOD and audio output hardware. Silicon tests report that both audio and video work as expected, and one tester described it as a very nice demo with polished graphics and audio.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

ttcad25a/tt_um_resfuzzy.summary: This project implements a fuzzy logic system that estimates a risk value based on rainfall and soil moisture inputs. It uses triangular membership functions to evaluate inputs as low, medium, or high, and applies three fuzzy rules to compute a weighted average risk output. The design requires external hardware: eight switches for sensor inputs, one switch for sensor selection, and an 8-bit LED display for the risk output. Testing involves feeding different sensor data and verifying the expected risk levels (high, low, medium).

ttcad25a/tt_um_ring_divider.summary: This design implements a ring oscillator operating in the GHz range, with a divider to produce an observable output frequency around 20 MHz. It includes a test/debug mode and an enable pin to control the oscillator. Testing requires an oscilloscope, power supply, and function generator, and the documentation suggests monitoring supply current to verify functionality. A silicon test report indicates the design is broken: no output was observed, and debug outputs were not accessible due to pin configuration issues.
ttcad25a/tt_um_ring_divider.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal tag; the source describes only a digital ring oscillator and divider.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rkarl_Spiral.summary: This design generates an Archimedean spiral pattern for VGA display, with adjustable foreground/background colors and animation speed via input pins. It requires an external PMOD VGA adapter and optionally switches for control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a short description and basic testing instructions.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rom_test.summary: This is a quick test of a SKY130 ROM compiler, implementing a small ROM array with wordline and bitline controls. It supports two read methods: pullup and precharge, as described in the silicon test reports. The design has minimal documentation, with sections marked as FIXME, so its intended usage and requirements are unclear. Silicon tests indicate it works: the author successfully read the test array using both methods, though the precharge data decays in about 2 ms and always decays to 0x11 on that chip.
ttcad25a/tt_um_rom_test.review_notes: Removed analog tag (digital ROM test structure) and added silicon-tested and incomplete based on the test reports and FIXME documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_roy1707018.summary: This design combines a ring-oscillator-based true random number generator with an ASCON S-box cryptographic substitution block. Sixteen ring oscillators are split into two banks controlled by ui_in bits 0 and 1, and a 64-bit shift register captures their outputs, with bits 2-4 selecting which 8-bit slice is presented. The S-box is enabled by ui_in bit 7 and takes bits 2-6 as its 5-bit input, and the final uo_out is the bitwise XOR of the TRNG and S-box results. It was verified only in simulation with a testbench driving various input values, and no external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_roy1707018.review_notes: Removed prng tag since the design is explicitly a TRNG, not a PRNG.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rte_eink_driver.summary: This is a Verilog driver for the Adafruit 2.13-inch e-ink display, which uses the SSD1680 chipset. It generates eight simple patterns in real time and sends them via SPI, with a special mode to copy SRAM contents to the display. It requires the specific e-ink display and a bundle of jumper wires to connect to the PMOD. The design is notable for its low memory overhead and ability to put the display into deep sleep while retaining the image.

ttcad25a/tt_um_rte_sine_synth.summary: The project implements a monophonic keyboard synthesizer with one octave of notes, generating sine waves using an efficient delta-step method. The 8-bit output is provided directly and also via a PWM generator for audio output, intended for use with Mike Bell's audio PMOD. Testing involves attaching the input PMOD to a row of buttons for playing notes. No silicon test results are mentioned.

ttcad25a/tt_um_samuelm_pwm_generator.summary: This is a configurable PWM generator with a 12-bit period register and a duty-cycle register whose low 7 bits set a 1-99% duty. The sel pin chooses whether the duty or period register is written, wr_en latches the value from the 12 input pins, and out_en gates the pwm_out signal. Testing is done by connecting pwm_out to an oscilloscope and checking that the observed frequency and duty cycle match the programmed values. External hardware consists of a wire for pwm_out plus about 15 input signals from a microcontroller or pattern generator to drive the data and control pins.
ttcad25a/tt_um_samuelm_pwm_generator.review_notes: Removed register-file and counter because the source describes only two configuration registers and no counting circuit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_save_buffer_hash_table.summary: This design implements a hash table with eight slots, 4-bit keys, and 4-bit values, supporting lookup, insert, and delete operations. Commands are issued via CMD and GO signals, with status and output value provided on output pins. The table handles collisions using linear probing and buffers inputs during operation. Testing involves setting keys, values, and commands, then observing status and output. No external hardware is required beyond input switches and output displays.

ttcad25a/tt_um_schoeberl_wildcat.summary: Wildcat is a 3-stage RISC-V CPU implementation written in Chisel. The documentation is extremely sparse, with only a one-line description and a 'TBD' for testing, and the pin names are generic. It may require external flash and RAM PMODs for operation according to the pin description. No further details on functionality, testing, or silicon results are provided.

ttcad25a/tt_um_shiftreg_test.summary: This is a custom high-density shift register implemented as an analog block, with 8 serial inputs, 8 serial outputs, and two clock phases. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, with the how-it-works, how-to-test, and external-hardware sections all left as FIXME. Silicon test reports from the author and an independent tester indicate that shift-register behavior was observed for both the internal-clock and dual-phase-clock variants, with data emerging roughly 36 cycles later, though the micropython-driven timings are described as unreliable. The notable point is that the custom cell works in silicon despite the minimal documentation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_shiftreg_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag and added insufficient-doc; silicon-tested is supported by the working reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.summary: This project implements a basic calculator supporting addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division on positive integers. It scans a 4x4 matrix keypad through the ROW and COL pins and drives a 3-digit seven-segment display via the sseg outputs, with E_1 through E_3 likely acting as digit enables. Testing is done by entering operands through the keypad and checking that the display shows the expected result. External hardware required is a 4x4 matrix keypad and a 3-digit seven-segment display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.review_notes: Removed alu and decoder tags not supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sign_addsub.summary: This is a 4-bit signed adder-subtractor built from multiplexers, half adders, and full adders. Two 4-bit operands a and b are supplied on ui_in, and the two sign bits on uio select one of four operations: A+B, -A+B, A-B, or -A-B, with the 4-bit result on uo and sign outputs on uio. The design was verified in QuestaSim using an extensive testbench covering the operation modes. No external hardware is needed.
ttcad25a/tt_um_sign_addsub.review_notes: Removed alu (only add/subtract, no logic ops) and added systemverilog and combinational tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_silice.summary: Warp is a demoscene demo that generates audio and video output, intended for use with VGA and audio PMODs. It can be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio also runs on an ULX3S. The documentation is minimal and uncertain, with statements like 'Maybe it works?'. External hardware includes VGA and audio PMODs, and the design is written in Silice.

ttcad25a/tt_um_simon2024_c_element_top.summary: This project attempts a standard cell implementation of a Muller C-element. The documentation is incomplete, with TBD sections for how it works and how to test it. No external hardware is listed. The design is written in Verilog and appears to be unfinished.
ttcad25a/tt_um_simon2024_c_element_top.review_notes: Corrected tags to reflect the Muller C-element standard cell attempt; removed unsupported CPU and interface tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_simon_cipher.summary: This is a bit-serial implementation of the SIMON-128 lightweight block cipher, trading throughput for a compact area dominated by flip-flops and multiplexers. A 2-bit control word on ui[7:6] selects idle, plaintext load, key load, or encrypt, with serial data entering on ui[0] and ciphertext emerging on uo[0] over 128 consecutive clock cycles, flagged by a valid bit on uo[7]. The design is verified through a testbench containing example test vectors, and no external hardware is required. The documentation notes a limitation in the key-loading process and includes a debug bit to verify key register loading.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sky130_as_sc_hs.summary: This project is a simple 6-bit MCU implemented with the sky130_as_sc_hs standard cell library. It loads bytecode from an external 25Q32-compatible SPI flash using the SDO, SDI, SCLK and CSb pins. A test program in the repository counts up on the PA lines. The design also exposes GPIO lines for general use.
ttcad25a/tt_um_sky130_as_sc_hs.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an LFSR/PRNG that is not present; corrected to the documented 6-bit MCU.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sky130_as_sc_hs_dyn_test.summary: This project is a test of the sky130_as_sc_hs standard cell library using dynamic D flip-flops. It contains an LFSR that updates on every clock cycle and outputs its state on all output pins. The dynamic DFFs will lose their state if the clock speed gets too low. It can be tested by releasing reset with all ui_in pins zero and observing the outputs with an RP2040 or LEDs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_sky130_as_sc_hs_dyn_test.review_notes: Proposed tags were entirely unsupported; replaced with LFSR, standard-cell and factory-test tags matching the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sonos_flash_party.summary: This project is an experimental SONOS flash controller for Tiny Tapeout using the SkyWater 130 nm process. It generates internal voltages using charge pumps to program and erase the flash cell. The design includes a read mechanism that buffers the drain voltage to produce a digital output. The project is still in development with pre-layout simulation values and no silicon test results.
ttcad25a/tt_um_sonos_flash_party.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary are unrelated to the source documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_space_invaders_game.summary: This is a Verilog implementation of the classic Space Invaders game. The player controls a ship using three input buttons to move left, move right, and shoot, with the game state output on eight pins. It is intended to be played using the TinyTapeout Commander app, which maps keyboard inputs to the ASIC pins, and tested with the TinyTapeout VGA Playground. No external hardware is required beyond the standard TinyTapeout setup, and no silicon test results are mentioned.
ttcad25a/tt_um_space_invaders_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported vga and gpio tags; added button and multi-tile.

ttcad25a/tt_um_spacewar.summary: This project is a scaled-down Spacewar-style design with VGA output, based on the VGA playground controller example. It accepts a SNES gamepad for input and outputs VGA signals, and the pinout also accommodates an audio PMOD. The design was left incomplete when work stopped at the Efabless shutdown, so it only allows moving a square on the screen rather than being a full game. It is configured for the demoscene competition and requires external VGA and gamepad hardware.
ttcad25a/tt_um_spacewar.review_notes: Removed game tag because the source states it is not a complete game; kept incomplete, retro, demoscene, vga, gamepad.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ssp_opamp.summary: This analog project contains three circuits: two two-stage operational amplifiers and one power-on-reset circuit, all designed by participants in an analog IC design training program run by the Saudi Semiconductor Program. The opamp inputs and outputs are exposed on the analog pins, with INP, INN, and separate outputs for each amplifier plus a POR output. Testing is done with a Digilent Analog Discovery, using its waveform generator for stimulus and its oscilloscope for frequency response, transient, and voltage-level measurements. The design is notable as a training-program artifact rather than a production circuit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.summary: This project implements a stochastic multiplier, adder, and self-multiplier using stochastic computing. It takes two serial input streams and produces serial outputs for multiplication, addition, and self-multiplication. The design uses LFSR-based stochastic bit streams and is implemented in Verilog. The documentation includes references to stochastic computing and LFSR design.
ttcad25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.review_notes: The proposed tags were unsupported by the source; corrected to reflect the stochastic computing multiplier/adder design.

ttcad25a/tt_um_strau0106_simple_viii.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit CPU architecture implemented in SystemVerilog. It interfaces with external QSPI flash and RAM memories through dedicated chip select and data pins. The design is intended to be a minimal CPU, but the documentation is very sparse, providing only the title and pin names without detailed operation or testing instructions. No silicon test results are available.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sudana_ota5t_1.summary: This is a simple five-transistor operational transconductance amplifier with an externally supplied bias current. It operates from a 1.8V supply with VSS ground, takes a 1uA bias current on the BIAS pin, and compares the PLUS and MINUS inputs, with the differential output on DIFFOUT. Testing is done by sweeping PLUS from 0 to 1.8V in 10mV steps while MINUS is held at 0.9V and observing that DIFFOUT swings to 1.8V when PLUS exceeds MINUS by 10mV. External hardware needed is a power supply, a sourcemeter for the bias current, and a multimeter to measure voltages.

ttcad25a/tt_um_supermic_arghunter.summary: This project is an 8-channel customizable beamforming signal processor. It accepts PDM microphone inputs and produces beamformed PCM output as well as individual PCM outputs for each microphone. Delay select inputs allow customization of the beamforming behavior. The documentation is largely placeholder text and lacks detailed implementation information.
ttcad25a/tt_um_supermic_arghunter.review_notes: Corrected tags to reflect the beamforming microphone DSP design rather than a CPU.

ttcad25a/tt_um_sushi_demo.summary: This project displays a running sushi animation on a VGA screen. It outputs VGA signals and requires a TinyVGA PMOD for connection. The design is a simple demo with minimal documentation, and no silicon test results are provided. It is intended for visual demonstration.

ttcad25a/tt_um_synth_simple_mm.summary: This is a simple monophonic synthesizer with PWM left and right output channels. It uses five input pins for note enable signals and eight switches to select sounds or notes, producing PWM outputs on uo[0] and uo[1]. External hardware includes five IR modules to generate notes, eight switches to choose sounds or notes, and two low-pass filters to produce left/right audio signals. The design is a basic synth whose documentation is very brief.
ttcad25a/tt_um_synth_simple_mm.review_notes: Removed sensor-interface which overstates the IR note inputs; summary aligned with the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tappu_tobias1012.summary: This project implements the Tappu CPU, an 8-bit processor inspired by the esoteric language BF. It includes a ROM memory that turns the outputs on and off. The design is written in Chisel. It can be tested by watching the outputs blink.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tappu_tobias1012.review_notes: Proposed summary invented PTAT, microrobotics and other content not present in the source; tags replaced with CPU, esoteric, Chisel and ROM.

ttcad25a/tt_um_test_commit.summary: This project is a first test for basic IP blocks such as a PTAT temperature sensor, oscillator, decoder, command checker and driver, intended for microrobotics applications. It is an analog design with two analog pins and spans a 1x2 tile area. The documentation is very thin, so the exact capabilities and usage cannot be fully determined. It appears to be a test chip for evaluating these IP blocks.
ttcad25a/tt_um_test_commit.review_notes: Removed robotics tag as the design is a test chip of IP blocks, not a robotics controller; added analog, oscillator, decoder, driver, temperature-sensor and incomplete.

ttcad25a/tt_um_thexeno_rgbw_controller.summary: The RGBW Color Processor generates PWM control signals for RGBW LEDs based on color index, intensity, and white level, or acts as a direct SPI-to-four-channel PWM converter in bypass mode. It is an SPI slave in mode 0 that receives an 8-byte command, and it can produce hue, tint, and intensity from a color index when in color wheel mode. Testing is typically done with a MicroPython script on the Tiny Tapeout demoboard, connecting LEDs to the PWM outputs while respecting the 4 mA current limit. No silicon test results are provided, but the design is well documented and supports both RP2040-based and STM32-based test setups.
ttcad25a/tt_um_thexeno_rgbw_controller.review_notes: rgb-led implies an addressable LED interface; the design only drives external LEDs via PWM, so driver is more accurate.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tiny_pll.summary: Tiny PLL is a 4-channel fractional-N frequency synthesizer that generates four independent clock outputs based on control register settings. It is configured through a simple CSR interface using data and address inputs, and it includes an ADC to monitor the tuning voltage of channel 0. Silicon testing showed that the PLL blocks work and produce the expected outputs, but the ADC output was stuck high, indicating a fault. The design is notable for integrating multiple PLL channels and an ADC on a tiny tapeout tile, though the ADC issue limits its usefulness for monitoring.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tiny_pll.review_notes: Removed analog (digital Verilog design, no analog pins); clock-generator already present in proposed tags, so no add needed beyond confirming it.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tiny_shader_mole99.summary: Tiny Shader is a programmable shader unit that executes a 10-instruction shader per pixel to generate images and animations, output via VGA at 640x480 with an internal resolution of 64x48. It includes an SPI interface for loading new shaders and setting a user register. Testing requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally an SPI controller. Silicon testing confirmed all features work, including custom shader upload and animation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tmkong_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer reads three digital rotary encoders to control the brightness of three PWM outputs, intended for driving RGB LEDs. It debounces the encoder inputs and includes a debug mode where the internal encoder values are output on the bidirectional pins when the debug input is set to 0, 1, or 2. The design is tested by twisting each encoder and observing the corresponding LED brightness change. External hardware consists of three digital encoders connected to the first six inputs, and the project is noted as the creator's first ASIC design.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tmkong_rgb_mixer.review_notes: rgb-led overstates the interface; the design only provides PWM LED drive outputs.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_diff_rx.summary: This is a test module for a differential input receiver, implemented in analog circuitry. It accepts differential clock and data inputs, along with a bias current and a bias select signal, and deserializes the data to 16 parallel outputs. The author reports that silicon testing successfully deserialized data up to 600 Mbit/s with a 500 mV single-ended swing (1 V differential). The documentation is minimal, with 'FIXME' placeholders for how it works, how to test, and external hardware.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_diff_rx.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested because the only report is an author self-report, not independent silicon validation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_ff_yolo_test.summary: This is a test structure for a flip-flop implemented in the SKY130 process, intended as an analog characterization vehicle. It is not designed for the standard demo board but requires a dedicated test platform with FPGA hardware to drive control signals with precise timing. The documentation is minimal, stating only that design data should be consulted and that no test procedure has been written yet. The exact testing platform is still to be determined.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_ff_yolo_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator and standard-cell tags; added insufficient-doc and corrected the summary to match the sparse documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_rf_yolo_test.summary: This project contains test structures for a future register file macro, implemented in the SKY130 process. It is not intended for the standard demo board but requires a dedicated test platform with FPGA hardware to drive control signals with precise timing. The documentation is minimal, stating only that design data should be consulted and that no test procedure has been written yet. The exact testing platform is still to be determined.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros modified to remove the LVT implant from the bitcell. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

ttcad25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo.summary: This design is a demo entry for the TT08 demo competition, implemented in Verilog. It outputs VGA video and audio signals, using the Tiny VGA and TT Audio pinouts. To use it, a TinyVGA Pmod and an audio Pmod are required on the demo board. The documentation is incomplete, with a TODO for the 'How it works' section, but the test procedure is described.

ttcad25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo_deluxe.summary: Sequential Shadows Deluxe is an extended version of the TT08 demo competition entry, adding a shadow beneath the logo and credits, with support for both TinyVGA and Digilent Pmod VGA pinouts. It requires a VGA PMOD and an audio PMOD, and it includes the same controls as the original for pausing, stepping frames, and disabling bass or drums. The design was tested on hardware by the author and confirmed to work similarly to the simulation. Documentation refers to the original version for details, and the deluxe version offers additional visual tweaks.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tommythorn_maxbw.summary: This design is an asynchronous multiplier that emits the sequence r = x^2 + x for x = 0, 1, 2, ... using a four-phase bundled-data handshake. Internally it uses 26-bit precision but folds the result down to 15 output bits with r ^ (r >> 15). It is tested by tying ack to req for free-running operation and observing the outputs, optionally with a logic analyzer or RP2040. The author notes that timing analysis is still in progress and the inserted delays are likely oversized.

ttcad25a/tt_um_top.summary: Flame demo displays a flame animation on a VGA monitor and plays simple 1-bit PWM audio. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and either Mike's audio PMOD or a basic RC filter for sound, and it runs at a 25 MHz clock with a reset pulse. Silicon testing by two independent testers confirmed that both audio and video work as expected, with good use of color and dithering. The design is a compact demoscene-style demo suitable for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition.

ttcad25a/tt_um_torurstrom_async_lock.summary: This design implements an asynchronous locking unit that accepts eight request signals and provides eight grant signals, ensuring that only one grant is active at a time. It functions as a mutual exclusion arbiter for asynchronous systems. The documentation is brief and does not describe the arbitration policy or testing methodology. No external hardware is specified.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tt08_aicd_playground.summary: AICD Playground is a mixed-signal test project for the analog IC design course at Graz University of Technology. It integrates a digital 8-bit controller with analog IPs including level shifters, an R2R DAC, and a comparator, forming a simple SAR-ADC. The design is configured via SPI to load memory with a program, and then the CPU executes it to perform analog-to-digital conversion. No external hardware is necessary for basic operation.
