ttcad25a/tt_um_tt08_wirecube.summary: Wirecube is a demo for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition that displays a rotating wireframe cube on a VGA screen. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and operates at a clock frequency of 50.35 MHz. Inputs allow toggling background and cube colors, as well as speed. The documentation is sparse and will be updated after the competition, but the design is functional as a visual demo.
ttcad25a/tt_um_tt08_wirecube.review_notes: Added multi-tile; summary is supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_tt_tinyQV.summary: This is a RISC-V SoC based on TinyQV, implementing the RV32EC instruction set with additional extensions. It uses QSPI flash for program storage and QSPI PSRAM for data memory, and includes peripherals such as UART, SPI, and PWM. The design is intended to be used with a QSPI Pmod containing flash and RAM, and can drive an ST7789 LCD display via SPI. Testing requires loading an image into flash and following a specific reset sequence, typically handled by MicroPython scripts on the demo board's RP2040.

ttcad25a/tt_um_uart_bgdtanasa.summary: ttUART is a UART repeater that mirrors received serial data back out on the transmit line. It exposes rx_data_in, rx_data_ready, rx_sample_clk, tx_data_out and tx_data_done pins and can be used like a regular UART. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief, giving only the repeater behavior and pin functions.

ttcad25a/tt_um_ultra_tiny_cpu.summary: UltraTiny-CPU is a minimal 8-bit CPU with an accumulator, a B register, a program counter and a 16-byte internal instruction memory. It is programmed through a load mode where ui[7] selects loading, ui[3:0] supplies the address and uio[7:0] supplies the byte, then runs from address 0 with results visible on the accumulator output uo[7:0]. No external hardware is strictly required, though a logic analyzer or LED display can be attached to watch the accumulator. The design is notable for fitting a complete fetch-decode-execute loop and small instruction set into a single tile.

ttcad25a/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.summary: This project implements a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that steps up the input voltage to approximately 3.65V, with the output divided by two available on an analog pin. The design uses diodes and capacitors clocked at 2 MHz, but the output is limited by the analog pin voltage constraints (VDDIO/VDDA). Silicon testing by the author shows that the charge pump works but produces much lower voltage than simulation: at 30 MHz, the output peaks at 1.9V instead of the expected 3.6V. The design is a simple power conversion circuit intended for evaluation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttcad25a/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.summary: UW ASIC - Optimized Dino is described as a Dino game compressed into only two tiles. The documentation consists entirely of placeholders, so the actual controls, video output format and testing method are not stated. The pin names are generic and give no further detail about the interface. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.
ttcad25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.review_notes: Removed game tag since only the title hints at a game and no gameplay is documented; kept insufficient-doc and verilog.

ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_cbtest.summary: This design generates VGA output to display patterns similar to Ishihara plates used for color blindness testing. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA display, and works out of the box without any configuration. The project is for experimental purposes only and is not an approved medical test. No silicon test results are provided.
ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_cbtest.review_notes: Removed biomedical (explicitly not a medical test) and added image-processing and pmod.

ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.summary: Glyph Mode is a standalone VGA demo submitted for the VGA Demoscene competition. It generates a display and allows palette selection via two input pins, choosing between green, red, blue, or pride color schemes. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA monitor, and operates at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, including palette changes, and it also functions at higher clock speeds.
ttcad25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.review_notes: Removed text tag; the source does not describe text rendering.

ttcad25a/tt_um_virantha_enigma.summary: This is a silicon implementation of an Enigma I cipher machine with a limited three-wire plugboard and a 52-bit key length. It takes 5-bit data and 3-bit command inputs, returns data on the bidirectional pins with a ready signal, and drives the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is needed because it uses the PCB's built-in display. The design is notable for implementing a historical rotor cipher machine in Amaranth on a single tile.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wakki_0123_Raw_Transistor.summary: The Raw_Transistors project provides direct access to raw NMOS and PMOS transistors for performance evaluation. The circuit includes three MOSFETs (two NMOS and one PMOS) with separate gate, source, and drain connections brought out to analog pins. Testing requires a source-measure unit to apply bias voltages and measure currents. Silicon measurements on a TT08 sample confirmed that the transistors work as designed, making it useful for transistor characterization.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wakki_0123_Raw_Transistor.review_notes: Removed unsupported instrumentation tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

ttcad25a/tt_um_whynot.summary: This design is a single-tile demo that combines VGA video and audio outputs, created quickly during coffee breaks. It uses a rotozoom effect and plays an attempt at music, with VGA output via a Pmod and audio via an Audio Pmod. Silicon tests confirm that both audio and video work as expected, and testers noted the presence of a Doomguy image, rotozoom, and a bit of E1M1 music, all in one tile. The design operates at 25 MHz and also works at 32 MHz.
ttcad25a/tt_um_whynot.review_notes: Added silicon-tested and retro tags supported by the test reports and Doom/E1M1 references.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.summary: This design is a test circuit for DDR throughput and flip-flop aperture, implemented in Verilog. It generates a 2x clock by detecting edges on the input clock and its complement, with varying pulse widths controlled by inverter chains. The outputs capture data on these pulses and on a normal flip-flop, allowing comparison. Testing requires an Analog Discovery 3 or similar equipment to drive and observe the signals.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.summary: This design is an octal ALU that executes binary operations on two octal numbers encoded in an 8-bit instruction and outputs the result to a 7-segment display. The instruction includes operation code bits and two operands, supporting operations such as addition, XOR, AND, and OR. It is used by setting the instruction on the input pins and viewing the result on the 7-segment display; an overflow during addition illuminates the decimal point. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires only the 7-segment display on the TT08 PCB.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added dip-switch interface tag based on the documented test procedure.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_407852791999030273.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit ALU implemented in Wokwi, featuring a shift register, two registers, and an arithmetic unit capable of addition and subtraction. It uses a bus for data transfer, with control pins to load registers, enable outputs, and select operations; external LEDs display the result in binary. The design is intended for educational purposes, with detailed documentation explaining its operation and testing procedure. Silicon testing confirmed that loading registers and addition work correctly, including a counting example.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.summary: Traffic-light-sequence implements a simple traffic light state sequence from red through red-yellow, green and yellow back to red. Two input pins select the state and three output pins drive the corresponding lights. It is a Wokwi project with no tiles. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any external hardware beyond the implied LEDs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.review_notes: Removed industrial and education tags not supported by the source; kept fsm, sequencer, wokwi, led.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.summary: The Logic Test project is a simple design intended to verify basic logic functionality. It has eight input pins and two output pins, but the documentation provides no details on the logic implemented or how the outputs are derived. The design is likely a template or placeholder for testing purposes. There is insufficient documentation to determine its exact behavior or use.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.review_notes: Removed factory-test and education; factory-test is not supported and education is not stated.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.summary: The Abacus Lock is a digital combination lock that activates a servo when a specific sequence of switches is entered. It displays the current combination status in binary on an LED bar. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires external hardware including LEDs, an LED bar, a servo, and an Arduino Nano. It was sponsored by The MITRE Corporation and MIT/LL Beaverworks Summer Institute.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.review_notes: Removed security (combination lock, not a security design) and added dip-switch and led-matrix.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_408237988946759681.summary: This project implements a counter that increments from 0 to 99 when a button is pressed, displaying the count on a 7-segment display. Two LEDs indicate whether the current count is even or odd. The design includes modules for button debouncing, counting, and display driving, and is intended for use with the Wokwi simulator. External hardware such as a 7-segment display and LEDs are required.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422192563267712001.summary: Padlock is a digital lock design implemented in Wokwi that stores a 7-bit secret code and indicates locked or unlocked status on a 7-segment display. The user sets the code via input pins and toggles a set pin to store it; entering the correct code unlocks the safe until reset. The design is tested by setting the clock to free-running mode and following a sequence of input changes. No external hardware is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422192563267712001.review_notes: Removed game tag; the design is a security lock, not a game.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957657550394369.summary: This is a full adder with inputs A, B, and Cin, and outputs S and Cout. It is tested using a provided truth table. An LED is used as external hardware to indicate the output. The documentation is concise and clear.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957657550394369.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added combinational, which the full adder clearly is.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957918936350721.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ripple carry adder using four full adders, with the first carry-in tied to ground. It adds two 4-bit numbers and outputs a 5-bit result. It is tested by setting inputs A0-A3 and B0-B3 and observing outputs S0-S3 and C_OUT. External hardware includes LEDs for outputs and switches for inputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957918936350721.review_notes: education tag removed: no teaching intent stated in the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957954050029569.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ripple carry adder without carry-in, taking two 4-bit inputs A and B and producing a 5-bit sum output. It is used by applying logic levels to the eight input pins and observing the five output pins, for example with a scope. External hardware can include LEDs with series resistors on the outputs and switches on the inputs to make testing easier. The design is a simple arithmetic block built in Wokwi, and the documentation is brief but sufficient to describe its function.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422957954050029569.review_notes: Removed alu and education tags unsupported by source; added combinational.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422958894385882113.summary: This is an unmodified Tiny Tapeout Wokwi template with two input pins and one output pin, and its documentation still contains placeholder text. No actual logic function is described beyond the template structure. It is intended as a starting point for a user to fill in their own design and test instructions. Because the documentation is essentially empty, no specific behavior or external hardware can be determined.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422959954857061377.summary: This design is a small combinational circuit made of NOT gates and an AND gate, with eight inputs and eight outputs. It is tested by flipping input switches until the outputs show a pattern that looks like the digit 8. The author is unsure what external hardware is needed. It appears to be a beginner Wokwi exercise, and the documentation is very thin about the exact logic mapping.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422959954857061377.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source never states a teaching or learning purpose.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422959974126748673.summary: This project accepts an 8-bit input code and displays the letter A on a 7-segment display when the correct secret code is entered. It is tested by trying different input combinations to guess the secret code. No external hardware is required according to the documentation. The design is a simple Wokwi workshop exercise, and the documentation does not reveal the secret code or the exact comparison logic.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422959974126748673.review_notes: Removed decoder and comparator tags not supported by the source text.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960054456096769.summary: This design takes a 3-bit input value and displays it on a 7-segment display through seven segment output pins. It is tested by applying different 3-bit input values and checking that the corresponding digit appears. A 7-segment display is the required external hardware. The project is a straightforward Wokwi exercise in binary-to-seven-segment decoding.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960054456096769.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added display for the 7-segment output.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960078645704705.summary: This Verilog design echoes a predefined text string onto a 16x2 character LCD using a 4-bit data interface with RS and E control signals. It is used by connecting an LCD1602 module according to the pinout and supplying a clock on the input pin. The only external hardware needed is the 16x2 character LCD. The project implements a small LCD text controller, though the documentation is very brief.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960078645704705.review_notes: Removed clock-generator contradicted by the clock input pin; kept lcd and text, trimmed display tag and speculative summary claim.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960080008854529.summary: This design displays symbols on a 7-segment LED display based on an 8-bit input binary word, and it outputs the letter n only when the input equals 0b00010101. It is tested by trying different input words and verifying that outputs 0, 1, 2, 4, and 5 are high only for that specific input. External hardware includes eight input switches and a 7-segment LED display. The project is a simple Wokwi exercise in binary pattern detection and seven-segment output, with clear but limited documentation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960080008854529.review_notes: Removed unsupported sequence-detector and education tags.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960085743520769.summary: This project is described as an adder with three input pins and two output pins, but the documentation says it works by magic and gives no real explanation. It is tested simply by using it, with switches and LED displays listed as external hardware. No details are provided about the bit width, encoding, or internal logic of the adder. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual behavior beyond the title.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960130190575617.summary: This design combines four basic building blocks: an inverter, an AND gate, an OR gate, and an Earle latch with an enable signal, mapped across several input and output pins. It is tested by exercising every input combination for the NOT, AND, and OR gates and by checking that the latch holds both a 0 and a 1. No external addons are required. The project is a Wokwi exercise in fundamental digital logic, and the documentation describes the intended connections clearly.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960174616660993.summary: This Wokwi design displays a mirrored '3' (or 'M') on a 7-segment display when inputs IN0, IN2, IN4, and IN6 are set high. An LED also lights to indicate the correct combination. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs on the Tiny Tapeout tile, but only the specified inputs matter for the intended behaviour. The design is a simple introductory project, and the documentation is very brief.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960174616660993.review_notes: Removed decoder as unsupported; adjusted summary to match the source without adding purpose claims.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960332734617601.summary: This Wokwi project checks an input code entered on switches and displays the number 4 when the code 267 is matched. The inputs are provided via IN0 through IN6, and the output drives a display to show the number. The design is a simple combinational code-matching demonstration with no external hardware beyond the display. It has minimal documentation, but the intended function is clear.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960332734617601.review_notes: Removed unsupported security and decoder tags; corrected summary to avoid invented binary encoding details.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960491546730497.summary: This Wokwi design combines AND, NOT, and flip-flop logic gates to connect inputs IN0-IN3 to outputs OUT0-OUT2. The exact function is not precisely described beyond 'AND and NOT and FlipFlop logic gates', and the test method is simply observing LEDs. The project uses four inputs and three outputs; no external hardware other than LED indicators is mentioned. The documentation is very thin, making detailed assessment difficult.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422960491546730497.review_notes: Removed combinational since flip-flops make it sequential; added insufficient-doc for the sparse documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422961309631153153.summary: This Wokwi design continually outputs the letter 'A' on a 7-segment display unless any input is active, in which case the display changes. It uses a clock at 10000 Hz and a logic circuit to drive the display. The test involves running the clock and observing the output while toggling inputs. No external hardware beyond the display and input switches is required.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422961309631153153.review_notes: Removed logic-gate and text tags; the design is a 7-segment letter display.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962760920307713.summary: This Wokwi project implements a standard 4-bit adder using AND, XOR, and OR gates, with a 5-bit output to handle overflow. The inputs are arranged as element-wise pairs: IN0 and IN1 are the LSBs of the two numbers, IN2 and IN3 are the next bits, and so on. The design can be tested by performing 4-bit additions on paper and comparing with the circuit's outputs. No external hardware is required beyond the inputs and outputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962760920307713.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a simple adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962904571040769.summary: This Wokwi design sets all outputs high when inputs IN0, IN1, IN2, and IN3 are high; otherwise, the outputs are low. The description claims that 'power goes in, power maybe comes out?' and that no testing is needed. The project is extremely simple and lacks detailed documentation. It uses 8 inputs and 8 outputs, but the logic only involves four inputs.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962904571040769.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate and combinational tags; added insufficient-doc.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962914561876993.summary: This Wokwi design connects inputs to outputs through a couple of logic gates, with no specific function described. The documentation states that there is nothing to test and no external hardware is used. It appears to be a trivial passthrough or simple gate arrangement with minimal documentation. The design likely serves as a basic exercise in using the Wokwi editor.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962914561876993.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the source gives no functional detail beyond a trivial gate connection.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962959838345217.summary: This Wokwi project implements a 4-bit adder that outputs a 5-bit sum. Two 4-bit numbers are input via IN0-IN3 and IN4-IN6 (with IN7 possibly unused), and the result is presented on OUT0-OUT4. Testing involves setting input switches to form two numbers and verifying the binary sum on the outputs. No external hardware is required beyond LEDs or other indicators.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962959838345217.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a simple adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964381148718081.summary: This Wokwi project is completely non-functional; the documentation states that it does not work and cannot be tested. All pins are labeled N/A, and no external hardware is used. It appears to be an empty or unfinished design, possibly a placeholder or failed experiment. There is no discernible function or purpose.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964381148718081.review_notes: Replaced template with placeholder because the source describes a non-functional empty design, not a starter template.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964384478997505.summary: This Wokwi design implements a NAND gate with a NOT gate on one input, using inputs IN2 and IN3 and output OUT3. The documented truth table specifies that output is high except when both inputs are high (for the NAND function after inversion). Testing can be done with LEDs or other indicators. The design is a simple logic gate demonstration with clear documentation.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964384478997505.review_notes: Removed led tag because LEDs are only suggested as external test indicators, not part of the design.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964754310747137.summary: This project is described as a test to try fabricating a chip with some special function other than simple logic. The documentation is extremely thin and does not specify what the logic actually does or how it should behave. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, but no external hardware is required according to the description. The design appears to be a learning exercise rather than a complete, documented circuit.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964754310747137.review_notes: Removed template tag as source describes a logic test, not a template; added logic-gate.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422965035809389569.summary: The project is titled '3 Bit Adder' and is intended to add two 3-bit numbers, producing a sum and carry. The documentation consists only of the placeholder word 'dup' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections, so no actual implementation details are provided. It uses six inputs and four outputs, which is consistent with a 3-bit adder with carry-in and carry-out. No external hardware is required, but the lack of documentation makes it impossible to verify the design's functionality.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422965035809389569.review_notes: Removed alu and template tags that are not supported by the source.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968416190311425.summary: This design implements an 8-to-3 encoder that, according to the description, displays the letter 'U' on a 7-segment display when a specific 8-port switch code is set. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, with the outputs presumably driving the segments of the display. The documentation is minimal and does not explain the encoding scheme or the exact switch pattern required. External hardware includes an 8-port switch and a 7-segment display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968416190311425.review_notes: Removed encoder tag due to unclear implementation; added 7-segment tag for the display.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968696249282561.summary: The project is titled 'Simple NAND 2' and is described as a work in progress with documentation that will follow later. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections contain placeholder text, so the actual functionality is unknown. It has eight inputs and three outputs, which might suggest a simple logic gate implementation, but this is not confirmed. The external hardware list includes an LED display, a flux compensator, and a quantum computer, which appears to be a joke and not a serious requirement.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968696249282561.review_notes: Removed template tag as there is no evidence of boilerplate; incomplete tag already covers the work-in-progress nature.

ttcad25a/tt_um_wrapper.summary: This design implements a six-digit seven-segment clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds. Two active-high pushbuttons increment hours and minutes for setting the time, and the decimal points blink once per second. It requires a 32768 Hz clock, a six-digit common-anode display, and six PMOS/PNP digit-enable transistors. The outputs include active-low segment drives and multiplexed digit enables, and the design is intended for breadboard or custom PCB assembly.
ttcad25a/tt_um_wrapper.review_notes: Removed clock-generator, oscillator, and rtc tags because the design consumes an external clock and is a display clock, not an oscillator or RTC; added counter.

ttcad25a/tt_um_xor_encryption.summary: This design provides an SPI interface that converts serial input into 8-bit parallel output on the uo pins. The documentation states that an SPI interface is used, but does not describe the SPI mode, bit order, or register map. Testing requires an external SPI master such as an RP2040 board, and no other external hardware is specified. The documentation is thin and leaves key implementation details undefined.
ttcad25a/tt_um_xor_encryption.review_notes: Removed gpio tag as pins are generic and no GPIO-specific evidence exists.

ttcad25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_f.summary: This design implements an adder with separate flow control for each argument and the result, using one of several selectable pipeline register or buffer modules. It is a solution to an RTL job interview question described by Yuri Panchul and is used in the educational systemverilog-homework and basics-graphics-music repositories. The design includes a self-checking testbench and can be manually tested with buttons and LEDs to cover back-to-back data, argument starvation, and backpressure. It is an educational design demonstrating different flow control strategies at the RTL level.
ttcad25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_f.review_notes: Replaced unsupported FIFO tag with supported silicon-tested tag based on documentation.

ttcad25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_schoolriscv_.summary: This project is a minimalistic SoC featuring the schoolRISCV educational CPU and a ROM containing a program that computes Fibonacci numbers. The CPU was designed for introductory Verilog and FPGA classes and is based on a textbook. The design outputs the CPU register a0 and program counter bits for observation, along with test pass/fail signals. It requires only LEDs as external hardware.

ttcad25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_sea_battle_v.summary: Sea Battle is a VGA game with sprites where the player controls a torpedo using left and right keys to hit a moving target. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout Demoscene competition and is part of a graphics and music examples repository. The design requires a VGA display and buttons, and has been tested on silicon where it works as an interactive graphics game. There is no self-checking testbench, and the game resets after each round.
ttcad25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_sea_battle_v.review_notes: Replaced verilog with systemverilog and added silicon-tested and button.

ttcad25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttcad25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttcad25a/tt_um_zec_square1.summary: SQUARE-1 is a VGA and audio demo that displays munching squares on video and generates audio based on the logistic map. It requires a VGA display and audio output hardware, such as the Tiny VGA and TT Audio Pmods. Silicon tests show that the video works, but audio may require a manual reset and was not consistently heard. The design is notable for combining visual and audio demonstrations in a single project.
ttcad25a/tt_um_zec_square1.review_notes: Added silicon-tested per working test report; tags otherwise supported.

ttcad25a/tt_um_zedulo_spitest1.summary: This project is an SPI device that provides a GPIO and memory interface. It uses dedicated pins for SPI MOSI, clock and chip select, with MISO, debug, system clock mirror and status outputs. Testing is done with an external USB-to-SPI adapter such as an MCP2210 board, and no other external hardware is required. The documentation refers to a readme file that is not included here, so the register map and protocol details remain unspecified.
ttcad25a/tt_um_zedulo_spitest1.review_notes: Removed gpio and memory tags that lack support in the thin documentation; added verilog impl tag.

ttcad25a/tt_um_zerotoasic_logo_screensav.summary: This design displays a bouncing Zero to ASIC logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo or use a solid color, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.
ttcad25a/tt_um_zerotoasic_logo_screensav.review_notes: silicon-art mislabels a VGA screensaver; demoscene better matches the visual demo intent.

ttcad25a/tt_um_zhouzhouthezhou_adder.summary: This design adds two 4-bit numbers and displays the sum on a seven-segment display. Inputs are set using DIP switches on the upper and lower nibbles, and an always block maps the sum to display segments. If the sum cannot be shown on the display, a dot is shown instead, and overflow is not handled. The design is a straightforward arithmetic demonstration with no external hardware beyond the switches and display.
ttcad25a/tt_um_zhouzhouthezhou_adder.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added combinational.

ttcad25a/tt_um_zoom_zoom.summary: Zoom Zoom is a custom CPU with an external memory bus and hardware accelerators for SHA-3 and CORDIC. It includes UART communication and a parallel memory interface. The design is tested by loading a binary program into memory, resetting the chip, and checking memory writes. External hardware such as an SPI RAM chip or an MCU emulator is required for the custom protocol.
ttcad25a/tt_um_zoom_zoom.review_notes: Removed uart (custom parallel bus, not UART) and added sha-3, coprocessor, and multi-tile.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set, with 28-bit addresses and 24-bit program addresses. It executes code from QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, sharing QSPI lines between them. The SoC includes a UART and SPI controller, and is intended to be used with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display. Silicon testing showed the core works and runs MicroPython and benchmarks, but UART RX has a bug that was worked around in software.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray-casting graphics engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, rendering textured walls with flat floor and ceiling by racing the beam. The player point of view is controlled over SPI, and an optional external QSPI ROM can supply textures instead of the internally generated ones. It needs a Tiny VGA PMOD on the dedicated outputs, an SPI host for control, and a clock around 25.175 MHz for standard 640x480 VGA. Silicon reports say it works without the glitches of the earlier TT04 version, including external SPI textures, though a clock hack was needed and the SPI peripherals still need full testing.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_dinogame.summary: This project implements an endless-runner game similar to the Chrome Dino game, rendered on a VGA monitor. The game uses four input buttons for jump, halt, debug, and mode control, and outputs VGA signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works well and is playable, though some testers noted occasional screen tearing at higher speeds. The documentation is minimal, consisting mainly of a brief description and pinout, but the test reports provide evidence of functionality.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_dinogame.review_notes: Removed redundant video tag; added button and retro tags supported by the pin names and game description.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv4.summary: This project implements a 4-bit combinational multiplier and divider unit that supports both signed and unsigned operations. The multiplier uses a ripple carry array, while the divider uses a restoring array algorithm. It has error indicators for division overflow and divide-by-zero. The design was created in Logisim and exported to Verilog, and silicon tests confirm it works.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This factory test module is designed to verify all I/O pins of an ASIC and has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. Mode selection is controlled by rst_n and sel signals, with the counter incrementing every clock cycle and resetting when rst_n is low. The design is written in Verilog and occupies a single tile. It is intended for manufacturing test and requires no external hardware beyond the ASIC itself.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_flappy_vga_cutout1.summary: This project is a clone of the Flappy Bird game, rendered on a 640x480 VGA display with a single button input for flapping. The game state is updated each frame, and the score is output in binary on the bidirectional pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a debounced active-low button, and a VGA adapter compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works and is playable, though several testers found it challenging.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit consisting of an 8x8 grid of identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop, and a buffer, with each tile individually rotatable and mirrorable via configuration. Configuration and state are managed through a scan chain, and a loop breaker mechanism helps debug combinational loops. The design supports loading and dumping state, single-stepping, and free running, and it has been tested on silicon with a provided test suite. It is notable for being a port of a larger FPGA design to TinyTapeout with significant area optimization.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag because the design occupies only one tile.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, plus UART over the demo board USB. It is a full Linux-capable SoC implemented in Verilog on a 8x2 tile Tiny Tapeout chip.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Removed redundant microcontroller tag and corrected the summary to avoid implying built-in flash or an onboard UART bridge.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs the sound wave on uio_out[1:0]. A 100kHz clock is provided on the clk pin, and a brief reset on rst_n starts playback. A piezo speaker connected across uio_out[1:0] is required for audible output.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommyt.summary: This design is a 12-hour clock rendered on a 640x480 VGA display using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, where three triangle hands indicate the time and twelve dots aid readability. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 31.5 MHz clock, reset, and hour and minute advance buttons. Silicon test reports confirm it works out of the box with a Tiny VGA Pmod, with testers noting the hands move correctly and the time can be set by holding the buttons. The design is notable for its triangle-based rendering approach and includes a Rust software model for reference.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommyt.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design only consumes an external clock; added silicon-tested and button based on the test reports and pinout.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_pad_test.summary: This design provides control logic for test pads on the north side of the TTGF0p1 die, allowing configuration bits to be set and read back. It uses a config-bit index and toggle signals to select and modify configuration bits, with outputs reflecting pad inputs and the selected config bit value. The design is intended for silicon testing and does not require external hardware beyond the chip's pads. The documentation is sparse and focuses on pin functions rather than a full description.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_pad_test.review_notes: Removed scan-chain and asic as unsupported in favor of factory-test, characterization, and insufficient-doc.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_psychogenic_neptuneproport.summary: This design is a guitar tuner that counts rising edges of an input pulse over a fixed sampling period and compares the count to frequencies of interest for standard guitar tuning, covering notes from about 80 to 400 Hz. It supports multiple clock configurations via three input bits and can drive either a dual or single 7-segment display, with the dot indicating an exact match in single mode. The raw pulse count is output on the bidirectional pins, and testing requires feeding a variable frequency signal and observing the closest note on the display. A silicon test report confirms it works, showing the closest note for a variable frequency input.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square wave tone generators, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with 10 shapes. It is controlled via an 8-bit multiplexed data/address bus and produces audio through either an 8-bit digital output for an external DAC or a PWM output for analog filtering. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to hear the audio. Silicon test reports indicate it works well, with users successfully playing chiptunes and using the 128 divider mode.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Removed dac (external only) and added silicon-tested and retro.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_robojan_top.summary: Tiny Breakout is a single-player Breakout game in Verilog that outputs a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. The game is controlled by three buttons (left, right, action) and includes an SPI interface for reading the game state and writing commands to modify it. The design uses a VGA timing module, painter modules for graphics, and a shift register to store the 13x16 block grid efficiently. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC made from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_robojan_top.review_notes: Removed r2r-dac (external hardware only) and added silicon-tested and speaker.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This design implements a simple VGA pong-style game with paddles controlled by four input pins. It outputs VGA signals on the bidirectional and output pins and supports two different VGA PMOD pinouts selected by an input, with the recommended Tiny VGA pinout. The game has no scoring and the ball only moves horizontally, so it is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete game. Silicon tests report that pong works, though one tester had to adjust monitor centering and another could not get a proper display on a CRT.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported gamepad tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_top_mole99.summary: This design produces an 800x600 60 Hz SVGA output with a background and a single 12x12 sprite, rendered internally at 100x75 so each sprite pixel is 8x8 screen pixels. The sprite is initialized with a pixelated Tiny Tapeout logo that moves around the screen, and an SPI receiver accepts commands to replace sprite data, change colors, set the background and control the sprite position. It can run at either a 40 MHz or 10 MHz pixel clock selected by a configuration bit, and it needs an external Tiny VGA PMOD for display. Silicon tests report that the logo bounces around and the SPI interface works, with some glitching when moving the sprite.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_top_mole99.review_notes: Removed vga (SVGA over Pmod, not VGA) and added silicon-tested and pmod based on pins and test reports.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This design implements a Simon Says memory game where the player must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors and tones. The sequence is shown on four LEDs with corresponding tones on a speaker, and the player responds using four buttons. A two-digit seven-segment display shows the current level, and the game restarts after a mistake. It requires external hardware such as the Simon Says Pmod or discrete buttons, LEDs, a speaker, and a seven-segment display, and a Wokwi simulation is available.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed memory type tag; added canonical game, 7-segment, led, speaker, wokwi, pmod, verilog and button tags.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB to Serial bridge using the USB CDC protocol, allowing a computer to communicate with the chip as a virtual serial port. It uses a 48 MHz clock and connects to USB D+ and D- pins, requiring a 1.5k ohm pull-up resistor on D+ for device detection. Data received from the USB host appears on the rx output pins, and data can be transmitted by setting the tx input pins and asserting tx_valid. A silicon test report confirms both RX and TX work as expected, and the design is based on an open-source USB serial core.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_uwuifier.summary: This design operates on a UART signal and transforms the text into 'uwu' speak. It interfaces via UART at 115200 baud with a 6 MHz clock, using dedicated receive and transmit pins. It is intended to be connected inline with a UART transceiver to modify data in real time. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester using a serial terminal to send data and receiving the uwuified version back.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_uwuifier.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttgf0p1/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.summary: This design displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display based on a 6-bit binary value entered on DIP switches. It drives the display one segment at a time, so a high clock rate is needed to see the full character. The character set covers a-z plus space, underscore, hyphen, period, exclamation mark and quote. Silicon tests report it working, and it is notable as a simple character generator with a documented mapping table.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.review_notes: Removed text (7-segment output only) and added silicon-tested per test reports.

ttgf0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.summary: This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display. It uses a modulo-12 counter to select which character to display and has logic to light the appropriate segments. It is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by running the clock to scroll text or using pins to manually select characters. Silicon test reports confirm the design is working on fabricated hardware.
ttgf0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.review_notes: Corrected tags to match the modulo-12 counter and silicon-tested status, and removed the false no-report claim from the summary.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_BLE_RX.summary: This design is a Bluetooth Low Energy digital baseband receiver for the SCuM single-chip micro-mote platform, taking I/Q samples and performing GFSK matched filtering, clock and data recovery, preamble detection and packet decoding with de-whitening and CRC checking. It is tested by connecting the SCuM RF front-end I/Q outputs, configuring it to receive BLE packets, and observing decoded data through the Tiny Tapeout output interface with a Digital Discovery and computer. External hardware includes the SCuM chip, a Digital Discovery for probing and a computer for serial communication and logging. The project is a large 3x4-tile SystemVerilog wireless receiver with detailed processing-stage documentation.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_BLE_RX.review_notes: Removed rf because the RF front-end is external; added demodulator, crc, systemverilog and communication which are directly supported by the source.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_MATTHIAS_M_PAL_TOP_WRAPPER.summary: This design is a simple programmable array logic device whose AND/OR matrix is configured by shifting a bitstream into an internal shift register. It is tested by clocking in a configuration bitstream from a microcontroller, then applying inputs through switches and observing the resulting boolean functions on LEDs connected to the outputs. No external hardware is strictly required, though switches and LEDs make the logic visible. The design is parametric in the Verilog sources and was originally written by Matthias Musch and included in TTGF180 by Ken, making it an educational programmable-logic block.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RV32EC RISC-V SoC that executes code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with peripherals including UART, SPI, gamepad, PWM, CORDIC and others contributed by the Tiny Tapeout community. It is used by loading a program image into flash and following a specific reset and clocking sequence, with MicroPython scripts on the RP2040 demo board handling the setup. External hardware includes a QSPI PMOD with flash and RAM, a UART connection to the demo board, and optional buttons on the GPIO inputs. Silicon testers have confirmed MicroPython boots and runs at up to 59 MHz, though some peripherals have issues at high clock speeds, and the CORDIC core only converges within about ±99.9 degrees.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.review_notes: Removed microcontroller as redundant with soc; added silicon-tested based on working test reports.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_SophusAndreassen_dogbattle.summary: Dog Battle Game is a VGA display engine that renders four animated colored boxes bouncing around a 640x480 screen with a simple physics simulation including friction, elastic collisions and wall bouncing. It runs continuously at 60 FPS on power-up and requires only a VGA monitor connected to the output pins, with no other external hardware or input needed. The design is a small 1x1 tile Verilog project that outputs 2-bit-per-channel RGB plus HS and VS sync signals. No silicon test report is provided, so the actual hardware behaviour is not documented.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_nyancat.summary: This design displays the classic Nyan Cat animation on a VGA monitor with accompanying music. It uses a 2x2 Bayer dithering matrix for color rendition and generates sound from a MIDI file using square waves with exponential decay envelopes, a low-pass filter, and a sigma-delta DAC. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for audio. Silicon tests confirm it works, and it was originally intended for one tile but expanded to two.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray casting engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D that renders textured walls, optional doors and flat floor and ceiling by racing the beam, with player point-of-view and effect registers controlled over a single SPI interface. It is used by supplying a 21-31.5 MHz clock, attaching a Tiny VGA PMOD, and optionally driving the SPI interface or using the inc_px and inc_py inputs for a demo without an SPI host. External hardware includes a Tiny VGA PMOD, optional SPI controller and optional external QSPI ROM for textures, with a pin selecting between Leo Moser and Digilent QSPI PMODs. The design is an experimental GF180 port of earlier TT07 and TTCAD25a versions, and the documentation notes that testing instructions are still to be completed.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_vgaringosc.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator using manually instantiated inverter cells. The ring oscillator or an external clock drives a counter that counts up to 3000. A VGA sync generator uses the upper bits of the counter to produce colored bars on a VGA display. Silicon tests confirmed VGA output and a ring oscillator frequency of about 78 MHz.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_vgaringosc.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ring oscillator VGA visualization.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_calonso88_spi_i2c_reg_bank.summary: This design implements a register bank that can be accessed through either an SPI or an I2C serial interface, with a digital input selecting which interface is active. It is used by writing and reading registers over the selected bus, and the first register is documented as controlling LEDs on the demo board. External hardware may include 2k2 pull-up resistors on the I2C SDA and SCL lines, and testers have used a Bus Pirate and a Pico with internal pull-ups to exercise both interfaces. Silicon tests confirmed read and write access over SPI and I2C, including multi-byte transfers and cross-interface access to the same registers.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_digital_clock_example.summary: This is a digital desk clock that keeps hours, minutes and seconds and drives a six-digit 7-segment display through a MAX7219 over SPI because there are not enough output pins to drive the segments directly. The time is set with hours_set and minutes_set inputs, with a fast/slow select input controlling the increment rate, and pressing both set inputs clears the seconds. It requires a 5 MHz clock, a 32.768 kHz reference clock on the refclk pin, and a MAX7219 7-segment display connected to the bidirectional PMOD. The design is a rehardening of a test design from Skywater and IHP processes for GF180, and no silicon test report is included.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_digital_clock_example.review_notes: Removed clock-generator, counter and timer as they mischaracterize the design; added max7219 and rtc which are directly supported.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_bad_synchronizer.summary: This project is a GF180 implementation of the bad synchronizer example from Dally and Harting, which passes a counter value between two clock domains through multiple register stages to demonstrate synchronization failures. It is used by aligning and then separating the two clocks and observing bit errors on the stage outputs, with an input selecting binary or Gray code counting. External hardware is a way to generate a clock, and the design exposes stage1, stage2 and stage3 outputs plus a skew signal. The documentation is intentionally brief and describes the design as working badly, since the point is to illustrate a known bad synchronization practice.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ddr_throughput_tes.summary: This is a test structure that captures data on both edges of a clock using pulse generators of varying widths, with outputs for each width and a normal flop. It is intended to explore DDR throughput and flop aperture using Analog Discovery 3 hardware. The documentation is minimal and self-deprecating, stating the design is probably bad. It is a timing characterization experiment rather than a functional block.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ddr_throughput_tes.review_notes: Adjusted tags to characterization and edge-detector; removed unsupported clock-generator, flip-flop and instrumentation tags.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_loopback.summary: This is a GF180 loopback tile with input skew measurement that counts seconds and displays a value on a 7-segment output while exposing counter bits and compare bits on the pins. It is used by clocking the project and varying the timing between clock and data to examine flip-flop capture reliability. External hardware is a skewable clock and data source, and the design is based on an earlier TT05 loopback-with-skew project ported to GF180MCU. The documentation is minimal and no silicon test report is provided, so the measured behaviour is not documented.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_loopback.review_notes: Removed unsupported communication, education and clock-generator tags; added clock-domain-crossing, 7-segment, counter and verilog.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ringosc_5inv.summary: This design is a five-inverter ring oscillator with an enable input and a set of divided-down outputs ranging from divide-by-1 up to divide-by-32768. It is used by releasing reset, setting the ring enable input high, and measuring the frequency at the various outputs. External hardware is a frequency counter, and the design is a small 1x1 tile with no other interfaces. No silicon test report is provided, so the actual oscillation frequency on silicon is not documented.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ringosc_5inv.review_notes: Replaced arithmetic 'divider'/'counter' tags with 'clock-divider', which matches the documented divide-by-N outputs.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_essen.summary: This is a 2x2 multiply-and-accumulate systolic array for signed 8-bit values with design-for-test infrastructure including a JTAG interface. It is used by feeding data through the data_i inputs with valid and mode controls and reading results from the result_o outputs, while the JTAG port allows scan testing of the internal logic. No external hardware beyond a JTAG controller and signal sources is described, and the design occupies a 1x2 tile area. A silicon tester only performed a basic JTAG test and confirmed the correct IDCODE was returned, so the arithmetic functionality has not been fully verified on silicon.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_essen.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag; added silicon-tested based on the working JTAG test report.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_flummer_ltc.summary: This design generates Linear Timecode (LTC) for audio and video synchronisation, using counters to track time and frame count and serialising 80-bit biphase mark coded frames. It is driven by a 12 MHz clock and starts counting from 00:00:00:00 after reset, with the frame rate selected by two input pins for 24, 25, or 30 fps. The LTC output appears on a bidirectional pin and can be fed to an audio PMOD for levels usable by audio equipment, or connected directly to a logic analyser. The 29.97 fps mode is documented as not implemented, and the project is a small single-tile Verilog design.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_flummer_ltc.review_notes: Removed synchronizer (not a CDC block) and added signal-generator for the LTC waveform output.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an external signal by counting pulses over 100 ms periods and displays the result on a 128x32 SSD1306 OLED display using an emulated 7-segment format. It requires an external 1 MHz clock, a PMOD OLED display, and the signal to be measured connected to the input pin. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and uses SPI to communicate with the OLED. No silicon test results are provided, so the actual performance is not documented.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_gf0p2_faust_top.summary: The project compiles a Faust soft-clipper function into a fixed-point hardware datapath using a multi-stage MLIR compilation flow. The design demonstrates the use of the open-source Faust audio circuit compiler for generating silicon-ready RTL. The output is an 8-bit digital signal intended for a DAC or R-2R ladder for line-level audio. The design is verified with a cocotb testbench.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_gf0p2_faust_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported factory-test and gpio tags; added dac, fixed-point, and r2r-dac based on the documented output path.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.summary: Asicle v2 is a hardware implementation of the Wordle word-guessing game, rewritten for Tiny Tapeout after an earlier version on the Google-Skywater shuttle. It uses a QSPI Pmod for external flash to store the word list and font bitmaps, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output, and a Gamepad Pmod or direct input pins for controls. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and requires flashing a data file to the QSPI Pmod before play. It fits a complete game into a 2x2 tile area by moving data off-chip, and includes debug features for showing or re-rolling the solution.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; added retro for the Wordle-style game; trimmed unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_cells.summary: This project instantiates one copy of each standard cell from the GF180mcu 7-track library. It multiplexes the project I/O pins so that the functional behaviour of each cell can be verified. The 210 cell outputs are arranged into 27 pages of 8 pins, selected by ui_in[4:0]. The selected page's outputs appear on uo_out.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_cells.review_notes: Replaced incorrect reconfigurable/FPGA/scan-chain/cocotb tags with standard-cell, multiplexer and characterization tags.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit built from identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop and a buffer, that can be individually rotated or mirrored according to configuration. It is a port of the original ROTFPGA from Caravel to TinyTapeout, reduced from 24x24 to 8x8 tiles with 8 inputs and 8 outputs. Configuration and reset use a routing-efficient scan chain, and tiles are written as hand-optimized gate-level Verilog with configuration stored in latches. The test suite sets up two configurations and runs upload, download, single-step, propagation and loop-breaker tests.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a VGA/SPI video tool with no basis in the source; replaced with fabric-related tags.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.summary: This project is a video mode tester that allows experimenting with different VGA timing parameters. It provides a TinyVGA output and an SPI interface for configuring horizontal and vertical visible pixels, front porch, sync pulse, and back porch registers. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to the Tiny Tapeout board. It supports setting the pixel clock to 25 MHz to produce a 640x480 @ 60 Hz test pattern.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.review_notes: Tags and summary were about a RISC-V SoC, but the source is a VGA timing parameter tester.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_javibajocero_top.summary: This project is a UART responder that listens for the ASCII string 'MARCO' and replies with '\n\rPOLO!\n\r' after a 10 microsecond delay. It also drives a single WS2812b LED that blips from red to green upon detection. The design is implemented in Verilog and includes debug outputs for baud ticks and UART status. Silicon testing confirmed the UART reply but the LED behavior was not observed.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_javibajocero_top.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the UART responder and WS2812b LED driver.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_kbeckmann_flame.summary: Flame demo displays a flame animation on a VGA monitor and plays simple 1-bit PWM audio. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and either Mike's audio PMOD or a basic RC filter for sound, and it runs at a 25 MHz clock with a reset pulse. Silicon testing by two independent testers confirmed that both audio and video work as expected, with good use of color and dithering. The design is a compact demoscene-style demo suitable for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_kercrafter_leds_racer.summary: LEDs Racer is a multiplayer game where up to four players press arcade buttons to race their LED segment toward a center circle on a WS2812B LED ring. The design drives the LED data line and provides per-player ready-to-play indicators and a frame update signal. It requires external arcade buttons with pull-down resistors and a WS2812B LED ring. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the game and its hardware needs.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This project is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA processor capable of booting Linux. It includes 16 MiB of external SPI flash, 16 MiB of external PSRAM, a UART peripheral, and a SPI peripheral. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs at 16 MHz. Silicon test reports confirm it works, with the author booting uLinux at 34 MHz and a tester verifying operation at 30 MHz.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the RISC-V SoC documentation and silicon test status.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_lisa.summary: This project is an 8-bit microcontroller SOC featuring a custom LISA CPU core and 128 bytes of DFFRAM. It provides SPI, UART, and I2C interfaces, along with general-purpose I/O ports. The design is implemented in Verilog and includes a C-based toolchain and Python debugger for programming and debugging. It is intended as a complete microcontroller platform with on-chip memory and multiple communication peripherals.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_lisa.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original tags and summary were unrelated to the microcontroller design.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_mmorri22_cse_30342.summary: This project is an example final project for a digital integrated circuits course, implementing an advanced finite-state machine in SystemVerilog. The FSM acts as a 'memory calculator' that performs various arithmetic and logic operations on 128-bit inputs a and b, using the previous result. It includes eight internal states with self-feedback loops and return edges, meeting specific course requirements. The design is intended for educational purposes and includes a testbench for verification.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_mmorri22_cse_30342.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original tags and summary were unrelated to the FSM example.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_mmorri22_lockpick_game.summary: This is a SystemVerilog example of a lockpick game for classroom use on Tiny Tapeout, featuring pipelined input/output of two 256-bit values through the 8-bit pins using an enable signal. A testbench is included to verify the design, and the output can be observed on the conventional 8-bit LED and an output_valid signal. The project is intended as a teaching example for future Tiny Tapeout classroom projects. No external hardware beyond the on-board LED is required.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_multi_bit_puf_wrapper.summary: This is a physical unclonable function (PUF) based on the difference between two registers, comprising an array of one-bit PUF cells addressed by a 4-bit input. The PUF outputs 8 bits at a time, selected by the address, and the output is 0 in the reset condition. No external hardware is required. The design is notable for its use of register mismatch as a source of entropy, but documentation is very limited.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_noritsuna_CAN_CTRL.summary: This design implements a transmit-only CAN controller intended to send GPS data. It accepts an 8-bit data bus, a 4-bit address, clock and reset inputs, and drives CAN_TX plus a TXING status output. Testing used an Arty Z7 running the design, a ZYBO Z7 transmitting dummy GPS data, a Raspberry Pi as the CAN destination, and an Analog Discovery 3 for the clock. External hardware requires a GPS data receiver and a mechanism to feed that data into the chip.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_proppy_megabytebeat.summary: This chip generates bytebeat music by evaluating five fixed bytebeat formulas and emitting PWM audio on several output pins. Four 4-bit parameter buses (a, b, c, d) select the values used in the formulas, and the outputs can be connected to speakers or the TinyTapeout Audio PMOD. Testing involves connecting a speaker to a chosen output pin and adjusting the parameter pins with binary rotary switches. External hardware needed is 16-position rotary switches and speakers or the TT Audio PMOD, with out7 requiring the audio PMOD.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_proppy_megabytebeat.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp/synthesizer tags and added sound-generator and speaker tags supported by the bytebeat PWM audio description.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the Texas Instruments SN76489 programmable sound generator, providing three square-wave tone channels, a noise channel with white and periodic modes, and 16 attenuation levels. It is programmed through an 8-bit data bus with a write-enable strobe, and outputs either an 8-bit digital audio bus or a PWM audio output, with individual channel outputs also exposed. Testing is done by writing register commands from a microcontroller and listening to the resulting audio, and the design includes a regression test suite against original chip behavior. External hardware includes a DAC or RC filter, amplifier and speaker, plus a microcontroller to send commands; the design is fully digital and omits the original analog op-amp and some control pins.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_rejunity_vga_logo.summary: This design displays a large 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo over VGA using time-based dithering to extend the apparent color range. It drives the standard TinyVGA PMOD pinout with two bits per color channel plus HSync and VSync, and runs from a 25.175 MHz clock. It is used simply by connecting a VGA monitor through the TinyVGA PMOD and powering the chip. Silicon test reports confirm it works on multiple boards, including at 32 MHz, with testers noting the dithering makes the image slightly fuzzy but yields an impressive color range.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.summary: This is an eight-part audio-visual megademo that outputs VGA graphics through the TinyVGA PMOD and PWM audio on the bidirectional pins. It runs at 25.175 MHz and is used by connecting a VGA monitor and speakers or the TT Audio PMOD. Silicon test reports confirm both VGA and audio work on multiple boards, with testers reporting it also runs at 32 MHz and even 66 MHz though monitors may not sync that fast. The documentation is thin, describing the design only as a compressed VGA logo, so the internal demo structure is not documented.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.review_notes: Removed music tag as redundant and added silicon-tested based on working test reports.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_schoeberl_wildcat.summary: Wildcat is an educational three-stage RISC-V core written in Chisel, taped out with a minimal assembler program that counts up and displays the value on a 7-segment display. It exposes eight input pins, eight bidirectional pins and eight output pins, and requires no external hardware beyond the demo board display. Testing consists of letting it run and observing the 7-segment display counting from 0 to F. A silicon test report confirms the counting works, though the tester's PMOD was active low so the segments appeared inverted.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_simple_riscv.summary: This is a simple single-stage RISC-V CPU based on a university lecture, loading 32-bit instructions four bytes at a time over an 8-bit input bus. It exposes the instruction byte inputs, a reset and instruction-memory write-enable on the bidirectional pins, and the ALU output byte on the outputs. Testing is done with a testbench containing simple instructions to verify calculations are correct. The documentation notes the chip is not being shipped at this time, and no silicon results are available.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_spi_cpu_top.summary: This is a 4-bit CPU that loads and runs programs from the SPI flash RAM on the QSPI PMOD. It takes two 4-bit data inputs, drives SPI chip select, MOSI, MISO and clock on the bidirectional pins, and exposes an 8-bit output register plus a CPU_VALID signal. Programs are loaded using a RAM flasher application, after which the CPU is reset to run. External hardware required is the RAM flasher and the QSPI PMOD, and the documentation is otherwise brief.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_spi_cpu_top.review_notes: Added qspi tag for the QSPI Pmod flash RAM interface; risc-v was not added because the source does not state an ISA.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_thezoq2_quickscope.summary: Quickscope is a small logic analyzer that samples eight input pins and the bidirectional pins and streams the captured values over UART. It triggers when ui[0] goes high and sends data at 115200 baud on uo[0], where a host client converts it into a VCD file viewable in Surfer. Testing requires connecting a UART adapter and the signals to be analyzed. The documentation refers to an external blog post for details, so the on-chip implementation is not described in the project text.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB CDC device that bridges USB to a UART interface at a fixed 115200 baud. It uses usb_p and usb_n for the USB differential pair, dp_pu_o for the 1.5k pull-up, and RX and TX for the UART side, with a configured status output. It is based on tinyfpga_bx_usbserial and enumerates with vendor_id 1209 and product_id 5454. External hardware needed is a USB breakout board and a 1.5k ohm resistor, and silicon test reports confirm successful enumeration, loopback and external UART communication.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag because the provided silicon status is working with tester reports.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttgf0p2/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.review_notes: Removed image-processing tag; the design is a logo screensaver, not an image-processing algorithm.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_wokwi_392873974467527681.summary: This Wokwi design sequentially displays the characters of the text "PILIPINASLASALLE" on a 7-segment display, one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. It includes a manual mode where the four BCD input pins select one of 16 predefined characters. The project is intended to be tested with a low-frequency clock (e.g., 1 Hz) and an external 7-segment display. Silicon tests show it working correctly on a demoboard.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_wokwi_392873974467527681.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_wokwi_442081253563458561.summary: This Wokwi project combines a simple snake game (TinySnake) with a design called PRISM, though the documentation does not describe what PRISM does. The snake game speed is controlled by the eight input pins, with larger values producing slower movement, and the game state is shown on a 7-segment display.
