The design requires only the on-board 7-segment display and no other external hardware. The documentation is thin and lacks details about the PRISM portion and how the two designs interact.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_wokwi_442081253563458561.review_notes: Removed redundant game tag and added display for the 7-segment output.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_wokwi_445338187869298689.summary: This project implements a 4-channel PWM generator with programmable frequency, duty cycle, and phase offset for channels 2-4. It uses an 8-bit input bus to load control registers, with a 7-segment display showing the current register address, and outputs PWM signals on four bidirectional pins. The design is built using the Wokwi simulator and is intended for educational purposes. It has been tested on fabricated silicon.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_zacky1972_PVTMonitorSuite.summary: PVTMonitorSuite is a fully digital, modular suite for measuring gate delays, flip-flop timings, and clock skew under varying process, voltage, and temperature conditions. It uses ring oscillators and flip-flop-based measurement circuits to quantify timing characteristics, with high-speed counters converting delays into digital values. External equipment including a frequency measurement device, a precise 50 MHz signal source, and a target clock generator are required. The design avoids GF180MCU standard cells and passes all Tiny Tapeout checks.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_zacky1972_PVTMonitorSuite.review_notes: Removed clock-domain-crossing (no synchronizer evidence) and added characterization and time-to-digital-converter tags supported by the text.

ttgf0p2/tt_um_zedtc1_top.summary: Zedulo TestChip1 integrates UART and SPI IP blocks to convert UART data into SPI transfers and echo the SPI response back over UART. Bytes sent to the UART RX pin are transmitted out via SPI, and data received from SPI MISO is echoed on the UART TX pin. Testing requires a TTL-232 to UART interface and observing SPI activity on the SPI pins. The documentation is minimal, referring to a README that is not included.
ttgf0p2/tt_um_zedtc1_top.review_notes: Added systemverilog tag; uart, spi and communication were already supported.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported display tag and added button for the documented direction inputs.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_74hct00.summary: This project is an open-source silicon realization of a 74HCT00 quad 2-input NAND gate on the GlobalFoundries gf180mcuD process at 3.3V. Each gate uses a skewed-inverter/NOR2/output-buffer chain to achieve TTL-compatible input thresholds and ±4mA drive, with outputs routed to analog pins for direct measurement. Gate 1's A input is brought out on an analog pin to allow characterization of the HCT input window without digital pad interference. Testing involves applying power, verifying the NAND truth table, and performing a DC ramp to check the input thresholds.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_74hct00.review_notes: Removed verilog tag because the design is full-custom analog with no HDL; added mixed-signal because it uses both analog and digital pins.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_AbAdA_2048.summary: This design implements a colorful version of the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game. It outputs a VGA video signal and accepts directional inputs from a keyboard or game controller to move the tiles. The design requires a VGA display and an input device, and a VGA playground link is provided for simulation. The author reports uploading it successfully to the TT FPGA with a game pmod.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_AbAdA_2048.review_notes: Removed fpga tag because the source only mentions FPGA as the author's test platform, not the design target.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_LPCAS_TTGF0P3_TP1.summary: This is an analog folded cascode operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) with an NMOS input pair. It has four analog pins: VINN, VINP, VBIAS, and VOUT. The design is a transistor-level analog block, but the documentation provides only a one-line description and pin names, with no details on biasing, performance, or testing. Therefore, it is not possible to describe its operation or external requirements beyond the pin functions.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_LPCAS_TTGF0P3_TP1.review_notes: Removed instrumentation tag because no measurement application is stated in the source.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set plus the Zcb and Zicond extensions, with 28-bit addresses, 24-bit program addresses, and hardcoded gp and tp values. Instructions are read using QSPI from flash, and a QSPI PSRAM is used for memory, with the QSPI clock and data lines shared between flash and RAM so only one can be accessed at a time. Code can only be executed from flash, while data can be read from flash and RAM and written to RAM, and many peripherals are contributed by the Tiny Tapeout community. This version also includes Matt Venn's R2R DAC as an additional peripheral, and the design is intended to be used with a QSPI PMOD and the RP2040 on the demo board.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.review_notes: Replaced unrelated analog/VCO tags with tags supported by the RISC-V SoC documentation and pins.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_a1k0n_nyancat.summary: This design displays the classic Nyan Cat animation on a VGA monitor with accompanying music. It uses a 2x2 Bayer dithering matrix for color rendition and generates sound from a MIDI file using square waves with exponential decay envelopes, a low-pass filter, and a sigma-delta DAC. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for audio. Silicon tests confirm it works, and it was originally intended for one tile but expanded to two.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_gf_analog.summary: This is an analog VCO experiment using a current-starved ring oscillator. It consists of five current-starved inverter stages in a ring, followed by a buffer pair, with the output available on an analog pin and a divided digital copy on the bidirectional pins. For an input voltage in the range 0.55V to 3.3V, the oscillator output is expected to be a square wave roughly in the range of 2MHz to 400MHz. Testing requires a precision variable voltage source and an oscilloscope.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_gf_analog.review_notes: Replaced incorrect factory-test/characterization/current-mirror/power-management tags with VCO, ring-oscillator, analog, and full-custom.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: This project provides test structures for GF180MCU analog support, consisting of a couple of large current mirror loads. A reference current is input on iref, multiplied internally by about 50x, and drawn from a selected power rail via enable pins. Sense wires are routed out to measure both the voltage drop of the power rails and the voltage raise of the VGND rail. Testing requires providing a test current to iref, toggling the appropriate enable pin, and using a programmable current source and precision multimeter.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_analog_factory_test.review_notes: Replaced unrelated Ethernet/counter/communication/timer/FPGA tags with analog current-mirror factory-test tags.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_coldbrew.summary: This design counts upward and broadcasts the counter value over 100Mbps Ethernet once per second. It reuses the Teapot Ethernet accelerator wrapper for full-duplex communication over a CAT-3/5 cable. The design sends an application packet with ethertype 0x88b5 autonomously every second. Testing requires an Ethernet 100BASE-T Pmod connector with a LAN8720A PHY and 50MHz oscillator.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_coldbrew.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the Ethernet counter design.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_combined.summary: This is a Verilog design that renders a waving Philippine flag as a VGA screensaver. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout with RGB and sync signals to drive a VGA display. The design also shows 'PILIPINAS' text in a 7-segment style at the bottom of the screen. Testing simply involves connecting a VGA monitor and observing the flag animation.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_combined.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated analog tags with correct VGA/graphics tags based on the actual pins and description.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_cw_testbuffer.summary: This project is an analog test buffer that buffers a voltage signal and drives an off-chip probe. It has an input pin, a bias pin, and an output pin. Testing involves biasing the amplifier with a 5uA current from the bias pin, applying a test signal to the input pin, and measuring the buffered signal at the output pin. External hardware such as an oscilloscope and function generator, or a voltage source and multimeter, is required.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_cw_testbuffer.review_notes: Replaced incorrect SRAM/memory/register-file/sequential-logic tags with analog buffer tags.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_essen.summary: This project implements a 256x8 SRAM for testing, though only the top 128 entries are addressable. It has 6 address bits, 8 write data bits, and 8 read data bits, with a gwen signal that must be de-asserted to write and otherwise puts the SRAM in read mode. The SRAM is entirely cleared on reset, and incoming data, write enable, and address are flopped once before the SRAM, with outgoing data flopped once before reaching the uo_out pins. No external hardware is required, and testing follows the pin functions described above.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_essen.review_notes: Replaced incorrect FPGA/LUT/reconfigurable/education/cocotb/bit-serial tags with SRAM and memory tags.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_fabulous_gf_0p3.summary: Tiny FABulous FPGA is a small FPGA fabric with 64 LUT4+FF logic cells, configurable via a bitbang interface, and designed for use with Yosys and nextpnr. It provides 26 I/O buffers, global buffers, and a system reset, and can implement simple Tiny Tapeout designs directly. The bitstream is uploaded while reset is applied, and no external hardware is required. The design is notable for being a fully open-source FPGA fabric on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_fabulous_gf_0p3_3v3.summary: This project implements a tiny FABulous FPGA fabric with 64 LUT4+FF logic cells arranged in a 6x4 tile grid, of which 4x2 are LUT4x8_ha tiles. The fabric includes a vertical carry-chain for fast additions up to 15 bits and supports up to four clock domains via global buffers. User designs are synthesized with Yosys and placed and routed with nextpnr, then loaded via a bitbang interface using the ui pins while reset is asserted. The I/Os mimic the Tiny Tapeout interface, allowing direct implementation of simple Tiny Tapeout designs on the FPGA, and no external hardware is required.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_gf_r2r_dac.summary: This is an 8-bit R-2R digital-to-analog converter implemented in analog circuitry. It can be driven externally by digital inputs or by an on-chip digitally generated sine waveform generator. The analog output is available on a single analog pin, and an oscilloscope is required to measure the output voltage. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no detailed testing procedure.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_gf_r2r_dac.review_notes: Removed signal-generator tag because the design is a DAC, not a signal generator.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_gojimmypi_ttgfa_UART_FSM_T.summary: This design implements a ring-oscillator-based true random number generator (TRNG) and physical unclonable function (PUF) entropy source, controlled via UART or SPI. It includes memory-mapped registers for configuration and readback of raw entropy samples, with status outputs and a UART transmit line. The project is intended for exploring hardware entropy sources for cryptographic applications, and can be tested using a Tiny Tapeout demoboard or an external UART adapter. The documentation provides detailed usage instructions and references to NIST standards.

This is an experimental analog version of the Hardware Entropy Explorer, adding six analog pins for external stimulus, DAC output, comparator input, monitor outputs, and a passive probe structure. It includes a ring-oscillator-based TRNG and PUF entropy source controlled via UART or SPI, with memory-mapped registers for configuration and readback. The analog features enable experiments with RC circuits, touch sensing, leakage, and PUF-style measurements, but the design is not a precision analog macro and requires external equipment for full validation. Testing can be done via the Tiny Tapeout demoboard or an external UART adapter.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_htfab_momcap.summary: This project implements a simple interdigitated metal-oxide-metal capacitor that fills a 1x2 analog tile. It provides two active terminals and two dummy terminals for parasitic control, with an estimated capacitance of around 85 pF from magic extraction. The capacitor is intended for measurement using test equipment such as a function generator and oscilloscope or a VNA. The design is a passive test structure with no active circuitry.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This project is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA processor capable of booting Linux. It includes 16 MiB of external SPI flash, 16 MiB of external PSRAM, a UART peripheral, and a SPI peripheral. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs at 16 MHz. Silicon test reports confirm it works, with the author booting uLinux at 34 MHz and a tester verifying operation at 30 MHz.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the RISC-V SoC documentation and silicon test status.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_kiterai_current_dac.summary: This is a simple 4-bit current-output digital-to-analog converter. The digital input is provided on four input pins, and the analog output current is sunk from a single analog pin. A resistive load connected to the analog output is required to observe the current. The documentation is very brief, providing only a one-line description and basic testing instructions.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_mattvenn_signal_generator.summary: This design generates two square waves: channel 0 with independently programmable high and low times, and channel 1 as a phase-shifted replica with a programmable delay. It is controlled over SPI by an external master such as an RP2350, which writes configuration registers; an encoder can also be used for fast-scan adjustments. The outputs are intended to be observed on an oscilloscope and can drive an SR latch for metastability experiments by bringing the two edges arbitrarily close. The design is notable for its specific focus on metastability exploration and its use of a Digilent PModEnc for interactive control.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_mattvenn_signal_generator.review_notes: Removed phase-detector and synchronizer as unsupported; replaced encoder with rotary-encoder; signal-generator was already present.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_mcml_vco.summary: This project is an MCML (MOS Current Mode Logic) voltage-controlled oscillator. It has six analog pins for tail bias and differential clock outputs. The documentation is essentially a placeholder, with no explanation of how the circuit works or how to test it. External hardware requirements are not specified.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_odgrip_polywave.summary: PolyWave is a mixed-signal four-channel waveform source with a digital engine driving four 16-bit R-2R DACs. The digital engine includes four 20-bit phase accumulators, a shared 16-bit LFSR noise source, a 4-bit sequencer, and DAC sample registers, and can run autonomously or accept direct byte writes. The analog outputs are on four pins, and the design uses the Tiny Tapeout custom GDS path with prebuilt layout files. Testing requires a clock/reset source, digital control signals, and an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe the outputs.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This design is a ring oscillator built from hand-drawn SkullFET transistors, producing a ~120 MHz square wave, followed by an 8-bit ripple divider that provides divided outputs from /2 to /256. The raw oscillation is buffered to an analog pin, and the divided outputs are on digital pins. Post-layout simulation confirms rail-to-rail oscillation and clean divider taps, with the buffer preventing load pulling. An oscilloscope is the only external hardware needed to observe the outputs.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_rahulbhagwat_gf180_bandgap.summary: This project implements a simple bandgap reference that outputs a stable voltage over a temperature range of -40°C to 125°C, with about 1% variation in simulation. It lacks supply noise rejection and trimming, making it a basic design for providing a stable reference. Testing requires applying 3.3V to the analog supply and measuring the output voltage over temperature using a bench power supply, multimeter, thermocouple, and temperature chamber. The documentation includes a simulation graph showing the typical output voltage range.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_tnt_gf_555.summary: This project is an analog re-implementation of the classic 555 timer IC on GF180mcu, with internal circuitry that differs from a CMOS 555 but is intended to behave identically. It exposes threshold, trigger, reset, control, output and discharge pins plus on-chip oscillator discharge and output pins. It is tested by recreating typical 555 datasheet circuits with external resistors and capacitors and observing the output on an oscilloscope. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog recreation of a well-known part rather than a digital design.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_tnt_gf_vco.summary: This is an analog four-stage differential delay voltage-controlled oscillator that uses a comparator tapping two stages to produce four single-ended quadrature outputs at 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Its nominal target frequency is 240 MHz with an expected tuning range of roughly 120 MHz to 500 MHz, controlled by an analog control voltage. Testing requires a programmable precision voltage source and an oscilloscope to observe oscillation. The design is notable for providing quadrature phases from a compact analog VCO suitable for clock generation or PLL use.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_tnt_gf_vco.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag not supported by the source.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB CDC device that bridges USB to a UART interface at a fixed 115200 baud. It uses usb_p and usb_n for the USB differential pair, dp_pu_o for the 1.5k pull-up, and RX and TX for the UART side, with a configured status output. It is based on tinyfpga_bx_usbserial and enumerates with vendor_id 1209 and product_id 5454. External hardware needed is a USB breakout board and a 1.5k ohm resistor, and silicon test reports confirm successful enumeration, loopback and external UART communication.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag because the provided silicon status is working with tester reports.

ttgf0p3/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.
ttgf0p3/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.review_notes: Removed image-processing tag; the design is a logo screensaver, not an image-processing algorithm.

ttgf26a/tt_um_8bit_risc_cpu.summary: This is an 8-bit RISC CPU with an ALU, registers, and data memory, designed to execute 16-bit instructions provided externally. The instruction bits are mapped to the input pins, and the CPU's 8-bit output is presented on the output pins. The design is implemented in Verilog and runs on a 5 MHz clock. No documentation on testing or external hardware is provided, and silicon results are not mentioned.

ttgf26a/tt_um_8bitcustomcomputer.summary: The SAP 8 Bit Computer is a processor implementing a 16-instruction, 8-bit ISA inspired by SAP architectures, with support for memory access, immediate operations, arithmetic/logic, control flow, and basic I/O. It operates at a very low clock of 10 Hz, making its state visible on LEDs. Testing requires DIP switches or buttons for program entry, LEDs for output observation, and optionally a logic analyzer or 7-segment display. No external hardware is strictly required, but these aids are recommended for easier testing. The design is notable for its simplicity and educational value, emulating early computer architectures.
ttgf26a/tt_um_8bitcustomcomputer.review_notes: Removed unsupported gpio and education tags; added ALU, instruction-decoder, and register-file implied by the ISA.

ttgf26a/tt_um_AlvaroRub_ringcounter.summary: This project is a 16-bit one-hot ring counter that sequentially activates its outputs at the clock rate, with a single high bit shifting through 16 outputs. The first 8 outputs are on dedicated output pins, and the next 8 are on bidirectional pins configured as outputs. It requires only a clock source and reset button, with LEDs for visual feedback; the Tiny Tapeout demo board provides these. The design is simple and useful for educational demonstrations of shift registers and one-hot encoding. No silicon test results are provided.
ttgf26a/tt_um_AlvaroRub_ringcounter.review_notes: Removed redundant counter tag and added led because the source explicitly uses LEDs for output visualization.

ttgf26a/tt_um_algofoogle_dottee.summary: DOTTEE is a demoscene demo that generates VGA graphics and audio, racing the beam to produce a 640x480 60fps output with music synthesized via a 1-bit sigma-delta DAC. It renders an array of colored circles using distance calculations and constructs a 'DOTTEE' logo with a Tiny Tapeout-inspired 'TT'. The demo loops after 4096 frames and includes a noise generator for percussive sounds. It requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD for output, and is notable for its efficient 1-tile implementation and participation in the Tiny Tapeout Demoscene Competition.

ttgf26a/tt_um_algofoogle_ttgf26a_vco.summary: This mixed-signal project features a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO) implemented as a current-starved ring oscillator, with its control voltage set by a 9-bit DAC. The VCO output drives a 5-bit counter and clock divider stages, providing divided outputs. It operates without an external clock and is tested by applying power and varying the 9-bit DAC input to observe frequency changes on the outputs, with an oscilloscope recommended for monitoring. The design combines an analog oscillator with a standard-cell digital block.
ttgf26a/tt_um_algofoogle_ttgf26a_vco.review_notes: Added 'standard-cell' (explicitly stated) and removed the unsupported 'notable for wide frequency range' claim from the summary.

ttgf26a/tt_um_apa102_ws2812_squidgeefish.summary: This design converts an SPI-style APA102 LED protocol stream into a single-line WS2812 output. It is hard-coded for seven LEDs, waits for a 32-bit low start condition, shifts in the pixel data, and forwards it to the WS2812 output until a stop condition is recognized. It ignores the APA102 intensity byte and also emits a continuous UART output of "Arglius Barglius" at approximately 115200 baud. Testing requires an SPI driver and a string of at least seven WS2812 LEDs, and no silicon results are reported.
ttgf26a/tt_um_apa102_ws2812_squidgeefish.review_notes: Tags were unrelated (wokwi/logic-gate/template/incomplete); replaced with the actual APA102-to-WS2812 translator tags and summary.

ttgf26a/tt_um_arty3_mac_engine.summary: This design is a quantized INT8 multiply-accumulate (MAC) engine with bias, activation, and quantizer post-processing, intended as a co-processor for neural-network inference on a microcontroller. It is controlled via a 4-wire SPI slave interface and provides status outputs including idle, busy, result-valid, and accumulator overflow. Testing requires an SPI master host, and optional logic analyzer; no other external hardware is needed. The chip is self-contained and notable for its integrated post-processing pipeline, but it has no silicon test results reported.
ttgf26a/tt_um_arty3_mac_engine.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'neural-network' tag; the rest of the proposed tags are supported.

ttgf26a/tt_um_bgao43.summary: The Tiny TPU Systolic Array is a small matrix multiplication accelerator based on a systolic array of processing elements, each performing multiply-accumulate operations. It is controlled via SPI, with results sent back over MISO. The design can be tested using a cocotb testbench that drives SPI commands and observes serial output, and no external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout pins. The source does not provide silicon test results.
ttgf26a/tt_um_bgao43.review_notes: Removed tpu tag because the source describes a systolic-array matrix accelerator, not a tensor processing unit; added cocotb tag and removed the unsupported 'potential for neural network acceleration' claim.

ttgf26a/tt_um_bioimpedance.summary: This design is a digital bioimpedance demodulator that processes a 1-bit sigma-delta ADC input through eight cascaded I/Q stages, each halving the clock frequency, to produce 128 bits of I and Q data. The results are stored in a register and can be read either via a UART transmitter at 9600 baud on uio[0] or through a 16-to-1 multiplexer selected by ui[1:4] and output on uo[0:7]. It requires an external 1-bit signal source, such as a sigma-delta ADC, and a USB-UART adapter for serial readout. The design is notable for its very low resource implementation of bioimpedance analysis in GF180 technology, though no silicon test results are provided.

ttgf26a/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttgf26a/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttgf26a/tt_um_danielpenas42.summary: This project displays a bouncing ball on a 640x480 VGA screen, with position and velocity controlled via SPI commands. The SPI receiver decodes one-byte commands where the upper two bits select the parameter and the lower six bits provide the value, with velocity clamped to -10 to 10 and position updated every six video frames. It is tested using a cocotb testbench that sends SPI commands and checks movement, clamping, reset, and edge rebound behavior. The design requires a TinyVGA-style PMOD for output and an SPI master for command input, and it is notable for its simple physics engine and live pixel rendering without a framebuffer.

ttgf26a/tt_um_dino7.summary: Dino-7 is a minimalist endless runner game inspired by the Chrome Dinosaur game, rendered on a single 7-segment display. It uses a finite state machine with idle, run, jump, hit, and score-display states, pseudo-random obstacle generation via a 32-bit LFSR, a hardware difficulty selector, and a retained high score. The game is controlled by a jump button on ui[0] and a reset button on ui[1], with optional switches for difficulty and LFSR seed selection. It requires a common-cathode 7-segment display and push buttons, and is notable for fitting a complete game into a single tile with a high-score memory.

ttgf26a/tt_um_divadnauj_GB_serv_soc_wb.summary: This project implements a custom system-on-chip using the SERV processor core under the RV32e instruction set. It provides GPIO inputs and outputs, a UART interface for serial communication, and SPI/QSPI interfaces for external flash and RAM memory. The design requires an external SPI Flash/RAM memory module, such as the QPMOD, and a USB-to-serial converter to interact with the system. It is notable for being a compact RISC-V SoC that fits within a 3x2 tile area and has been proven with external QSPI memory hardware.
ttgf26a/tt_um_divadnauj_GB_serv_soc_wb.review_notes: Removed microcontroller tag because the design is explicitly a SoC using the SERV CPU, not a microcontroller-style integrated design.

ttgf26a/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttgf26a/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttgf26a/tt_um_fer_logo_music_vga.summary: This project displays a FER logo on a VGA screen and plays music, with the logo bouncing and its direction controllable via four buttons. The VGA output uses the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout, and audio is output on uio[0]. It requires a VGA monitor connected to the VGA PMOD and uses inputs 2-5 for left, right, up, and down control. The documentation is very thin, providing only a one-line description and basic pin information, so details about the music generation and logo animation are limited.
ttgf26a/tt_um_fer_logo_music_vga.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added demoscene tag for the logo/music showcase.

ttgf26a/tt_um_fhw_appel_spiPWMio.summary: This module provides a PWM generator on output pin 7 and a PWM reader on input pin 7, with the generator duty cycle set by input pins [6:0] and the reader output reflected on output pins [6:0]. The PWM period is assumed to be 20 ms with duty cycle adjustable between 1 ms and 2 ms. An SPI interface allows configuration and read/write operations when enabled, and the design can be tested by looping back the generated PWM signal to the input. It requires a development kit and optionally an oscilloscope and signal generator for testing, and is notable for combining PWM input and output with SPI configurability.
ttgf26a/tt_um_fhw_appel_spiPWMio.review_notes: Removed 'servo' and 'motor-control' as the source never describes servo or motor control.

ttgf26a/tt_um_gen1_digital_companion_til.summary: This project is a digital companion tile for a future local memristive AI chip, implementing the digital control contract around a symbolic memristive update without real memristors. It loads target and current values, runs a bounded write-verify loop, emits pulse_up or pulse_down events, and finishes with verify_ok or fault based on an attempt budget. The design is tested with cocotb scenarios and Yosys formal contract checks, and no external hardware is required for logic testing. It is notable for its symbolic approach to memristive control and the inclusion of formal verification for the public output contract.

ttgf26a/tt_um_gojimmypi_ttgf_UART_FSM_TR.summary: This project is a UART/SPI-controlled ASIC lab for exploring true-random number generation and PUF-style hardware entropy sources, using a bank of ring oscillators as the entropy source. A host can send ASCII commands over UART to configure internal registers, control the oscillator network, and read back raw entropy samples, with status and data also available over SPI. It requires an external UART adapter for interaction, and the design is intended for cryptographic and security applications. It is notable for providing a hands-on platform for evaluating hardware entropy sources, though no silicon test results are included.
ttgf26a/tt_um_gojimmypi_ttgf_UART_FSM_TR.review_notes: Removed education (not explicitly a teaching design) and added verilog.

ttgf26a/tt_um_grace_spi_led_driver.summary: This chip is an SPI-controlled 8-channel LED driver with a 16-register file, where eight BRIGHT registers set the PWM brightness of eight LED outputs. Each SPI transaction is 16 bits, with the first byte selecting a register address and direction and the second byte carrying data, and the PWM uses a shared 8-bit counter with a prescaler for flicker-free refresh. It is tested through a recommended bring-up sequence that verifies SPI communication, address decoding, read/write loopback, read-only protection, enable control, and LED output. The design requires a Pmod 8LD with eight discrete LEDs connected to the output Pmod header, and is notable for its robust SPI interface with synchronizers and a clear register map.

ttgf26a/tt_um_happyhop_deadcast2.summary: This project renders a 16x16 smiley sprite bouncing around a 640x480 VGA screen, with each pixel computed live from the beam position and ball coordinates without a framebuffer. The smiley blinks every approximately two seconds and its eyes shift toward the direction of motion. It is tested by plugging the TT VGA PMOD into the output PMOD and connecting a 640x480 at 60 Hz monitor, with no input controls. The design is notable for its live pixel computation and simple animation, requiring only the VGA PMOD and a compatible monitor.

ttgf26a/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.summary: This project is a video mode tester that allows experimenting with different VGA timing parameters. It provides a TinyVGA output and an SPI interface for configuring horizontal and vertical visible pixels, front porch, sync pulse, and back porch registers. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to the Tiny Tapeout board. It supports setting the pixel clock to 25 MHz to produce a 640x480 @ 60 Hz test pattern.
ttgf26a/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.review_notes: Tags and summary were about a RISC-V SoC, but the source is a VGA timing parameter tester.

ttgf26a/tt_um_hydrocomms.summary: This design implements a digital binary FSK modem for underwater acoustic communication in the 46-56 kHz band, using 48 kHz for mark and 54 kHz for space. It transmits and receives framed data with preamble, sync word, payload, and CRC-8, generating samples via a numerically controlled oscillator and decoding with parallel Goertzel filters. The chip interfaces through SPI for configuration and data transfer, and provides several debug outputs for monitoring. Notable limitations include half-duplex operation and lack of symbol-timing recovery, which may require multiple frames for initial synchronization.

ttgf26a/tt_um_joannec34_teenytpu.summary: TeenyTPU is a 2x2 INT8 systolic array TPU designed for matrix multiplication operations. It features a 2x2 grid of Processing Elements that perform matrix multiplication on INT8 data, producing 16-bit partial sums. The design includes an SPI slave bridge for communication with an external host, supporting opcodes for loading weights, activations, and reading results. It requires an external SPI master connected to the designated pins for testing and operation.
ttgf26a/tt_um_joannec34_teenytpu.review_notes: Replaced incorrect CPU/esoteric/memory/education tags with TPU, systolic-array, machine-learning, edge-ai, and clock-domain-crossing tags; corrected summary to match the actual TPU design.

ttgf26a/tt_um_joseph_bf.summary: This design is a multicycle CPU that executes programs written in the BF (Brainfuck) language. It has no on-chip RAM; both program and data tape reside in an external SPI RAM emulated by an RP2040 running spi-ram-emu. The CPU uses an on-chip SPI master to access memory, performing at least one SPI transaction per instruction. It is tested with cocotb and requires an external RP2040 for memory, making it suitable for educational purposes.

ttgf26a/tt_um_jpigdon_gps_accelerator_to.summary: This is a GNSS accelerator that implements acquisition and tracking for GPS L1 signals, including Gold code generation, NCO for frequency correction, and early/mid/late tracking. It interfaces with a MAX2769 or MAX2771 front-end via SPI for configuration and receives quantized I/Q samples. The design provides SPI slave registers for control and readback, and an interrupt output for frame timing or acquisition events. It requires a custom hardware setup with a GNSS front-end and an RP2040 for software interaction, and testing may be limited due to hardware availability.

ttgf26a/tt_um_kluterirv_rv32e_core.summary: This design is a minimal RV32E microcontroller SoC with a UART program loader, internal instruction memory, GPIO, and configurable 7-segment output. It can boot from internal memory or load a program via UART, and it supports a demo program that drives seven-segment displays. The core includes 16 registers and supports a subset of RISC-V instructions. It requires an external USB-UART adapter for loading programs and can drive a 7-segment display directly.
ttgf26a/tt_um_kluterirv_rv32e_core.review_notes: Removed education and sram tags; added bootloader, 7-segment, gpio, uart, risc-v, soc, microcontroller.

ttgf26a/tt_um_line_follower_arvaloez.summary: This is a controller for an 8-sensor line-following robot car. It reads digital signals from an IR sensor array, computes a tracking error using a weighted method, and generates PWM signals for two DC motors to correct the trajectory. Four configuration pins allow tuning of the correction magnitude for more aggressive or smoother turns. The design requires external hardware including an 8-channel IR sensor array, analog comparators, dual DC motors, an H-bridge driver, and configuration switches.

ttgf26a/tt_um_logoUACJ_MOGA.summary: This project is a VGA screensaver that displays a bouncing logo with the text UACJ and A.M.G on a 640x480 @ 60 Hz screen. It is based on a DVD screensaver design and includes modules for VGA sync generation and bitmap ROM. The logo moves around the screen and changes color upon hitting edges. It requires a VGA display and a VGA PMOD or breakout board with a resistor DAC for connection.
ttgf26a/tt_um_logoUACJ_MOGA.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'graphics' and 'display' tags; the rest of the proposed tags are supported.

ttgf26a/tt_um_machinelearning.summary: This design implements a small two-layer neural network with 4 hidden neurons that predicts digits 0-9 from 7-segment display patterns. It takes the 7 segment inputs and outputs a 4-bit prediction. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no details on training, accuracy, or testing. It likely requires no external hardware beyond input switches and output LEDs for verification.
ttgf26a/tt_um_machinelearning.review_notes: Removed perceptron (multi-layer network, not single perceptron); added edge-ai for embedded inference.

ttgf26a/tt_um_main.summary: This is a simple Pong game with VGA-style output, supporting two players and an auto mode. The documentation is essentially a work-in-progress placeholder with no details on how it works or how to test it. It likely requires a VGA display and buttons for player input, but this is inferred from the pin names. The design is not sufficiently documented to provide a complete summary.
ttgf26a/tt_um_main.review_notes: Added incomplete for WIP documentation and removed redundant video/display tags.

ttgf26a/tt_um_maqsudbek_dyadic_pwm.summary: This is a digital PWM generator with selectable resolution (5-9 bits), dyadic modulation, and dithering modes. It produces complementary high-side and low-side outputs with dead-time, plus a sync clock. The design is configured via a register file written over the pins, and it defaults to 8-bit normal PWM after reset. It is intended for power electronics applications such as buck converters or class-D stages, and requires no external hardware for bench testing.

ttgf26a/tt_um_mattvenn_signal_generator.summary: This design generates two square waves: channel 0 with independently programmable high and low times, and channel 1 as a phase-shifted replica with a programmable delay. It is controlled over SPI by an external master such as an RP2350, which writes configuration registers; an encoder can also be used for fast-scan adjustments. The outputs are intended to be observed on an oscilloscope and can drive an SR latch for metastability experiments by bringing the two edges arbitrarily close. The design is notable for its specific focus on metastability exploration and its use of a Digilent PModEnc for interactive control.
ttgf26a/tt_um_mattvenn_signal_generator.review_notes: Removed phase-detector and synchronizer as unsupported; replaced encoder with rotary-encoder; signal-generator was already present.

ttgf26a/tt_um_memory_game_top.summary: This project implements a number-based memory game where the player must remember and submit sequences of numbers. It uses input switches for starting the game and submitting answers, with LED outputs to display game state and feedback. The documentation is very thin, providing only a one-line description and pin names, so the exact gameplay mechanics and display method are not fully specified. It appears to be a simple demonstration project with no external hardware required beyond the PCB board's switches and LEDs.
ttgf26a/tt_um_memory_game_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported dip-switch and education tags; added insufficient-doc to match the very thin documentation.

ttgf26a/tt_um_mgj_bist8.summary: BIST-8 implements a built-in self-test architecture for an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder, including a 12-bit LFSR pattern generator, a 16-bit MISR response compactor, fault injection, and a 4-state FSM controller. In normal mode it acts as a standard adder; in BIST mode it runs 4095 test vectors and compares the MISR signature against a golden value of 0xCF77. A fault injection input forces a stuck-at-0 fault on bit 3 of the adder output, producing a faulty signature of 0x927F to demonstrate detection. The design is notable for its complete self-test capability and clear documentation of expected signatures.

ttgf26a/tt_um_microlane_demo.summary: This project scrolls the text "hardened using python" across a 7-segment display. It is a demo for the microlane hardening flow and is intended to be run with a slow clock such as 5 Hz. No external hardware is required beyond the display itself. The documentation is brief and does not explain the microlane flow or the hardening results.
ttgf26a/tt_um_microlane_demo.review_notes: Added ascii tag for the text-scrolling behaviour; summary unchanged.

ttgf26a/tt_um_ohuettenhofer_tiny_qsim.summary: This design simulates a universal one-qubit quantum computer, executing operations such as reset, X/Y/Z/H/S/T gates, and measurement. Amplitudes are stored as 8-bit fixed-point numbers, and an LFSR provides pseudorandom numbers for measurement. The operation is selected via three input pins, and a start signal triggers execution; measurement results appear on an output pin, and a done signal indicates completion. The design is notable for bringing quantum computing concepts to a tiny digital chip, though it is limited to a single qubit.
ttgf26a/tt_um_ohuettenhofer_tiny_qsim.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; source does not mention teaching or learning intent.

ttgf26a/tt_um_peg_top.summary: This project implements a 2x2 systolic processing-element grid for CNN inference, controlled entirely over UART from a host PC. The host sends 3-byte packets to drive activations and weights, and receives 2-byte partial-sum results. It is tested using a Python host script that runs nine test cases matching the simulation testbench. The design requires a USB-to-UART adapter and a host PC, and is notable for its compact systolic architecture and UART-based control.

ttgf26a/tt_um_pixel_processor.summary: The Tiny Pixel Processor is a custom processor designed to procedurally generate graphics, outputting a 640x480 VGA signal with an internal resolution of 64x48 pixels. It features a 16-bit custom instruction set and 8 registers, and can be programmed via UART using a provided Python script. The default configuration runs a simple program that generates a procedural pattern, which can be displayed on a VGA monitor using the tiny-vga board. The design is notable for its application-specific architecture and the ability to upload new programs over UART.

ttgf26a/tt_um_prem_pipeline_test.summary: This project implements a compact 32-bit RISC-V processor with a five-stage pipeline (IF, ID, EX, MEM, WB). It includes two UART interfaces (one for bootloading, one for general communication), an SPI master interface, and GPIO pins. The design is intended for hardware deployment and can be tested via simulation and on an FPGA or ASIC. It is notable for being a zero-to-ASIC demo project, showcasing a complete RISC-V core with standard peripherals.

ttgf26a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttgf26a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttgf26a/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_decod.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttgf26a/tt_um_rgb_mixer.summary: This design implements an RGB mixer that uses two push buttons (inc and dec) and a 2-position dip switch to select one of three PWM outputs. The selected output's pulse width is increased or decreased by the buttons, allowing control of the brightness of each RGB LED color. It requires external push buttons, a dip switch, an RGB LED, and resistors for pull-up configurations. The design is a custom implementation of the Z2A course's RGB mixer, intended for educational purposes.

ttgf26a/tt_um_roberto_tiny_radar_tile.summary: BioPulse Tile processes an 8-bit radar or biosignal sample stream to detect breathing cycles, classify breathing patterns (normal, fast, slow, irregular, apnea), and detect heartbeats, all using digital logic without a CPU. It includes a demo mode with synthetic patterns, and streams metrics over UART. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench and can be used with external radar or biosignal front-ends. It is notable for its comprehensive vital-sign monitoring capabilities in a tiny digital tile.
ttgf26a/tt_um_roberto_tiny_radar_tile.review_notes: Added cocotb tag because the source explicitly mentions a cocotb testbench.

ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_ring_osc_gf.summary: This design is a GF180mcuD port of a ring-oscillator PVT sensor featuring five gatable ring oscillators with different stage counts, a 16-bit frequency counter, auto gate timer, prescaler, XOR jitter TRNG, per-RO health history, differential beat-frequency mode, and frequency-bounds health monitor. It supports both parallel and SPI control modes, with a register file for configuration and readout. The design is intended for cross-foundry PVT characterization and includes a cocotb test suite. It is notable for its comprehensive on-chip characterization features and the inclusion of GF-specific health-history registers.
ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_ring_osc_gf.review_notes: Added cocotb, clock-domain-crossing, synchronizer, process-experiment and verilog tags supported by the source; summary unchanged.

ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_rsd_char_gf.summary: This design is a standalone characterization platform for a single external resistive-switching device such as an RRAM, memristor, or phase-change cell. It drives an 8-bit DAC rail and reads back an 8-bit ADC rail, with four SPI-selectable modes: DC sweep with on-chip histogram and min/max tracking, pulse endurance with read-verify and fail-index latching, retention with periodic reads, and free-running mode. The design is implemented in mixed-signal style and is intended for silicon characterization of the external device. It requires an external resistive-switching device and an SPI host to control the modes and read results.

ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_stoch_stdp_pair_g.summary: This design implements an 8-bit saturating leaky-integrate-and-fire neuron with a stochastic firing mode, an 8-entry sigmoid LUT, an 8-bit Galois LFSR, programmable refractory and leak, and homeostatic theta adaptation. It also includes an STDP controller with 8-bit pre and post spike traces, exponential-shift decay, an anti-Hebbian polarity bit, and optional reward-gated learning. All registers are programmable through a shared 8-bit SPI mode-0 slave, and the design emits spike, weight-update, theta, Bayesian confidence, learning-direction and busy outputs. It is written in Verilog and requires only an external SPI host and a spike-train source.
ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_stoch_stdp_pair_g.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated memristor/characterization tags with the actual spiking-neuron, LFSR, LUT and SPI features.

ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_xbar_ctrl_gf.summary: This design is a device-agnostic peripheral controller for 8x8 memristive crossbar arrays, supporting READ, SET, RESET, FORMING, and sweep modes. It is programmed through a Mode-0 SPI slave and drives row/column enables, pulse outputs, and a 4-bit DAC code. The design includes a 16-bit pulse counter, a sticky compliance-history register, and a last-ADC-in-sweep snapshot. It is written in Verilog and verified with a cocotb test suite.
ttgf26a/tt_um_santhosh_xbar_ctrl_gf.review_notes: Tags and summary were entirely wrong, describing a TPU instead of a memristive crossbar controller.

ttgf26a/tt_um_systolic_array.summary: This is a 2x2 multiply-and-accumulate systolic array for signed 8-bit values with design-for-test infrastructure including a JTAG interface. It is used by feeding data through the data_i inputs with valid and mode controls and reading results from the result_o outputs, while the JTAG port allows scan testing of the internal logic. No external hardware beyond a JTAG controller and signal sources is described, and the design occupies a 1x2 tile area. A silicon tester only performed a basic JTAG test and confirmed the correct IDCODE was returned, so the arithmetic functionality has not been fully verified on silicon.
ttgf26a/tt_um_systolic_array.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag; added silicon-tested based on the working JTAG test report.

ttgf26a/tt_um_systolic_mac_2x2.summary: This design implements a 2x2 output-stationary systolic array that computes signed 4-bit matrix multiplication and produces 8-bit results. Each processing element is a bit-serial multiply-accumulate unit, and the array uses input skew registers to align data across the grid. An FSM sequences the computation through IDLE, COMPUTE, DRAIN and READ states, and an output serializer streams the four accumulator results one per cycle. The design is written in Verilog and is loaded and started through the Tiny Tapeout input pins.
ttgf26a/tt_um_systolic_mac_2x2.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated Setun/Amaranth tags with the actual systolic-array, multiplier, MAC, bit-serial and FSM features.

ttgf26a/tt_um_top.summary: This design implements a custom SPI module to interface with RHD2164 neural amplifier chips and transfer selected channel data to an MCU via SPI. It also includes a register bank accessible either by SPI or a scanchain/shift register. The design can be tested with an FPGA using RHD2164 and MCU-SPI emulators, or connected directly to an RHD2164 chip and MCU. No silicon test results are documented.
ttgf26a/tt_um_top.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match SPI bridge and neural amplifier interface.

ttgf26a/tt_um_tpu.summary: This project is an AI chip inspired by Google's TPU that multiplies 8-bit floating-point valued matrices. It tiles in 2x2 to fit on the chip's tiny area, so performance is degraded compared to regular chips. The chip's I/O bandwidth is intended to be fully utilized and saturated. Testing uses cocotb and pyuvm, and external hardware connects the Tiny Tapeout PCB to a personal computer via USB.
ttgf26a/tt_um_tpu.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the TPU-inspired fp8 matrix multiplier description instead of an unrelated RISC-V core.

ttgf26a/tt_um_ttmul.summary: This design is a serial balanced-ternary integer multiplier that takes two 8-bit signed operands and produces a 16-bit signed product. Internally it converts the binary operands to balanced ternary, multiplies them with a serial ternary shift-and-add core, and converts the product back to binary. It is implemented in Amaranth and uses a bit-serial protocol with strobes for loading operands, starting the multiply, and reading the result. A cocotb test exercises the protocol and corner cases, and no external hardware is required.
ttgf26a/tt_um_ttmul.review_notes: Replaced unrelated biomedical/SPI/mixed-signal tags with the actual balanced-ternary multiplier described in the source.

ttgf26a/tt_um_uacj.summary: This design displays a bouncing DVD logo on VGA with color change on wall hits, speed control, invert, and flip options. It is implemented in Verilog and matches the Tiny VGA pinout. Configuration inputs select tile, color, invert, slow, flip, checker, scanline, and glitch modes. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout ASIC shuttle and requires no external control beyond the configuration pins.
ttgf26a/tt_um_uacj.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated neural-network tags with VGA/graphics tags supported by the pins and description.

ttgf26a/tt_um_uacj_bouncing_DVD_screensa.summary: This design implements a DVD-style bouncing logo on a VGA monitor, using a 128x40 bitmap that displays UACJ IIT. It includes a VGA sync generator, bouncing logic with position registers, a bitmap ROM for the logo, a color palette, an RGB output multiplexer with scanline and glitch effects, and a VHS-style corruption engine. The design is written in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout ASIC shuttle. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout for video output and needs no external hardware beyond a VGA display.
ttgf26a/tt_um_uacj_bouncing_DVD_screensa.review_notes: Replaced unrelated UART/FSM tags and summary with the VGA DVD screensaver graphics design described in the source.

ttgf26a/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.

It is written in SystemVerilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. All pin assignments are currently TBD, and the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are placeholders. ttgf26a/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.

ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_451184391728659457.summary: This design implements a simple sprinkler controller whose output depends on four input conditions: rain, water supply, soil moisture and time of day. The sprinkler is enabled only when the water supply is sufficient and the soil is dry within the watering period, with the logic documented as a truth table in the README. It is tested by toggling inputs A through D and observing two LEDs that indicate the sprinkler state and water supply. No external hardware is required, and it is a beginner-level Wokwi logic exercise.

The documentation consists only of template prompts. No pins, test procedure, or external hardware are specified. It cannot be determined what the design does or how it is used.
ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_465736691688630273.review_notes: Removed unsupported workshop/education tags and added insufficient-doc to match the very thin documentation.

ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_465737290543084545.summary: This project is a Tiny Tapeout template with no functional description beyond 'My first project'. The documentation consists only of template prompts. No pins, test procedure, or external hardware are specified. It cannot be determined what the design does or how it is used.
ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_465737290543084545.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational purpose.

ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_465737601403996161.summary: Tiny Number Simon is a Simon-style digital memory game implemented in Wokwi. It uses eight active-high buttons as number inputs and a common-cathode 7-segment display to show the sequence and score. The game requires a slow or manually stepped clock and an active-low reset, with no microcontroller or external memory needed. The design is notable for its simple state-machine implementation and clear test procedure.
ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_465737601403996161.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; kept the rest.

ttgf26a/tt_um_wokwi_467219410242853889.summary: This project is a test design for a segment display, with minimal documentation stating 'this is just test'. It has eight input pins and eight output pins, but no functional description or test procedure. No external hardware is required. The design is not aimed at specific criteria and appears to be a placeholder.

ttgf26a/tt_um_xoroshiro64plus_v2.summary: This design implements a lightweight xoroshiro64+ random number generator with ring oscillator noise injection to provide entropy. It maintains two 32-bit states, generates a 32-bit random word per enabled clock cycle, and serializes it out with a valid pulse. The design can be seeded through an 8-bit interface and requires an external 1-bit ring oscillator noise source. It is notable for combining a PRNG with true randomness from an RO.

ttgf26b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.
ttgf26b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported display tag and added button for the documented direction inputs.

ttgf26b/tt_um_4b_accumulator_cpu.summary: This is a minimal 4-bit accumulator-driven CPU implemented in Verilog. It fetches instructions from an internal ROM, decodes them, and performs ALU operations (ADD, SUB, AND, OR) on the accumulator with an immediate value. The design has eight input pins for data and opcode, and eight output pins for data and ALU results. It uses a clock to advance the program counter through the instruction sequence.
ttgf26b/tt_um_4b_accumulator_cpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and last sentence claimed an intended educational purpose not present in the source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_60hz_load.summary: This ASIC implements a 60 Hz grid-forming reference using a CORDIC-locked sine wave generator and a linear dump-load controller for micro-inverters. It includes PWM modulators for driving an H-bridge and dump FET, with ADC sampling for AC and DC voltage feedback. The design requires substantial external hardware including a grid-tied solar system, H-bridge, transformer, rectifier, and dump load. It is notable for its complex control loops and power electronics application.
ttgf26b/tt_um_60hz_load.review_notes: Removed filter-analog and mixed-signal tags not supported by the digital Verilog source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_Alanduan21_triad01_top.summary: Triad01 is a clocked failsafe arbitration block for autonomous drone control paths, evaluating RC and FC health signals to select PRIMARY, FALLBACK, or SAFE_HOLD. It drives a 50 Hz PWM output and includes a scan chain for counter observability and lightweight LBIST for post-silicon diagnosis. The design supports four operating modes: normal, PWM-test, scan, and LBIST. It is notable for its built-in test features and safety-critical application.
ttgf26b/tt_um_Alanduan21_triad01_top.review_notes: Removed 'motor-control' and 'watchdog' as unsupported by the source; the design is an arbitration block with PWM output and built-in test features.

ttgf26b/tt_um_Arctic0.summary: Arctic0 is a 16-bit multi-cycle CPU that executes programs from an external SPI NOR flash and uses SPI SRAM for data storage. It includes UART transmit and receive for serial communication, GPIO for general-purpose I/O, and a register dump feature. The design requires external SPI flash, SPI SRAM, and a USB-serial adapter for operation. It is notable for its comprehensive test suite covering ISA, memory boundaries, and FPGA bring-up.

ttgf26b/tt_um_BastiBudde_i2c_slave_senso.summary: This project implements an I2C slave that emulates a real-world sensor. It exposes two register banks of eight 8-bit registers each, with Block A writable and Block B read-only and driven by an internal LFSR. The slave operates at Standard, Fast and Fast Mode Plus bus speeds with a 25 MHz system clock. It is a reusable template that was verified on an FPGA with an ESP32-C6 acting as I2C master.
ttgf26b/tt_um_BastiBudde_i2c_slave_senso.review_notes: Replaced incorrect cipher/crypto/logic-gate tags with i2c, lfsr, sensor-interface, template, register-file and fpga tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_JCT_PoC.summary: This project is a naive and very simple implementation of a stream cipher demonstration. It contains two internal 8-bit registers, data_mem and key_mem, which store the input data and encryption key. The output is generated by XORing the stored data and key values, with uio_in[0] triggering register updates on a rising edge and uio_in[1] selecting which register is loaded. The bidirectional pins are configured as inputs only and are never driven by the design.
ttgf26b/tt_um_JCT_PoC.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated washing machine controller; replaced with tags and summary matching the stream cipher source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_Kieckenwama_Traffic_LIGHT_.summary: This project is a digital traffic light controller implemented as a finite state machine in Verilog. It cycles through red, yellow, and green phases for main road, side road, and pedestrian lights. An internal timer controls the duration of each phase. The design outputs signals to drive eight LEDs.
ttgf26b/tt_um_Kieckenwama_Traffic_LIGHT_.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the traffic light FSM design.

ttgf26b/tt_um_KimLuu02_WashingMachine_FS.summary: The washing machine controller is a modular digital system implemented in Verilog using a finite-state machine. It simulates a simplified washing process and automatically progresses through stages such as filling, washing, rinsing, and spinning. If the door is closed, the start button can be pressed, and the washing duration can be changed using a lever. Outputs include water valve, wash motor, spin motor, and a done LED, with a button for start and levers for mode select and door closed.
ttgf26b/tt_um_KimLuu02_WashingMachine_FS.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated image-processing/DSP design; replaced with tags and summary matching the washing machine FSM source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_LukeSilva_cartrip.summary: This project is a VGA demo intended to show a car trip scene. It provides RGB and sync outputs compatible with the Tiny VGA pinout. The documentation is very thin and states the design has not been written yet. External hardware required is a VGA PMod.
ttgf26b/tt_um_LukeSilva_cartrip.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary described an RGB PWM controller, but the source is a VGA demo with no PWM or LED control mentioned.

ttgf26b/tt_um_PWM.summary: This project is a PWM generator with configurable period and duty cycle via 8-bit input pins. It uses a two-process finite-state machine structure consisting of an 8-bit counter and an 8-bit comparator, with the period set on ui_in and the duty cycle set on uio_in. The module continuously increments the counter and compares it against the duty cycle configuration to drive uo_out[0] HIGH or LOW, with asynchronous reset and synchronous enable. An LED or PMOD LED module can be connected to uo_out[0] to observe brightness scaling with duty cycle.
ttgf26b/tt_um_PWM.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated cocotb template test design; replaced with tags and summary matching the PWM generator source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_PaulineKreis_PWM_Analyser.summary: This design analyses an input PWM signal to measure its duty cycle and frequency, displaying the results on a 4-digit 7-segment display. A mode switch toggles between duty cycle and frequency display, and the frequency counter handles 1-9999 kHz with error messages for out-of-range or faulty signals. It requires an external 7-segment display and a PWM signal source. The design is useful for characterizing PWM signals in real-time.

ttgf26b/tt_um_Vincent2405_adder_tree.summary: This project implements a multiplierless shift-add tree for image convolution using binary signed-digit (BSD) arithmetic. It reads eight 8-bit values into registers and computes a weighted sum with shifts, outputting a 26-bit result in BSD format multiplexed over 8 output pins. Control signals on bidirectional pins manage register writing and output chunk selection. It is a specialized arithmetic unit for efficient convolution.

ttgf26b/tt_um_aidenkoch4.summary: This is a three-channel RGB PWM controller that generates independent PWM signals for red, green, and blue LEDs based on stored brightness values. It includes a programmable clock divider to adjust the PWM frequency range. The design is intended to drive RGB LEDs or external driver stages, requiring current-limiting resistors for direct LED connection. It was tested using cocotb and Icarus Verilog simulation.

ttgf26b/tt_um_alu.summary: This project implements an 8-bit arithmetic logic unit with two internal registers and a multiplexed output that can show either the 8-bit result or the carry flag. It supports eleven operations selected by a 4-bit opcode, including addition, subtraction, bitwise logic, shifts, and negation. The design is intended to be driven by an external microcontroller or Raspberry Pi, which loads operands, selects the operation, and reads the result. It is a straightforward educational ALU with no on-chip test features, and it requires external hardware for control and observation.
ttgf26b/tt_um_alu.review_notes: Removed instruction-decoder and logic-gate tags because the source describes an ALU opcode decoder and bitwise ALU operations, not instruction decoding or basic logic gates.

ttgf26b/tt_um_antimatter15_pdm_vad.summary: This design computes a voice activity score from a 1-bit PDM microphone stream by counting pulse density over windows and combining magnitude, change, and three spectral probes. It accumulates a smoothed score that increases with speech-like energy and decays for quiet input, outputting an 8-bit value once per frame. The circuit is self-contained and requires only a PDM clock and data input, with no external hardware beyond the microphone. It is a compact, tile-friendly estimator that avoids a full FFT and leaves the bidirectional pins unused.
ttgf26b/tt_um_antimatter15_pdm_vad.review_notes: Removed scoreboard and sensor-interface tags because the output is an activity score and the input is PDM data, not a generic sensor interface.

ttgf26b/tt_um_arrakeen_spsram_direct.summary: This is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins for use as a standalone memory. It performs synchronous read and write operations on the rising clock edge, with a write-through behavior where the output reflects the written data during a write. The design is implemented in full-custom layout for 3.3V using standard design rules, not SRAM-specific rules. Testing involves applying addresses, data, and write-enable signals to verify read-back of stored values.

ttgf26b/tt_um_arrakeen_spsram_direct_5v.summary: This is a 5V-compatible version of a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It operates synchronously with read and write operations on the clock edge, including write-through behavior. The design is full-custom and also compatible with 3.3V. Testing is done by performing writes and reads to verify data retention.
ttgf26b/tt_um_arrakeen_spsram_direct_5v.review_notes: Removed level-shifter tag; no level-shifting circuit is documented.

ttgf26b/tt_um_arrakeen_spsram_direct_sra.summary: This design is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins, implemented in full-custom layout for 3.3V using SRAM-specific design rules for the bit cell. It performs synchronous read and write operations on the rising clock edge, with write-through behavior. The block is intended to be used as a standalone memory, and testing involves verifying read and write functionality. The use of SRAM design rules distinguishes it from other variants.

ttgf26b/tt_um_aswarby_mac.summary: This is a weight-stationary signed INT8 multiply-accumulate engine that computes a 32-bit saturating accumulator from a stationary weight and a stream of activation bytes. It uses a 4-stage pipeline to meet timing at 50 MHz on a 180 nm process, with a simple strobe-based handshake and byte-serial readout of the accumulator. The design is intended as a compute primitive for quantized neural network inference and includes a cocotb test suite with a golden model. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout demo board.

ttgf26b/tt_um_brisq.summary: This project implements BRISQ, an approximate IEEE-754 single-precision inverse square root unit. It receives one 32-bit FP32 operand over an 8-bit byte-serial input bus, performs one Newton-Raphson refinement using a Quake-style integer seed, and returns a 32-bit FP32 result over an 8-bit byte-serial output bus. The datapath uses a truncated positive-magnitude FP32-style multiplier and a parametric subtractor, with a default precision of 11 high fraction bits, and is explicitly not a fully rounded IEEE-754 FPU. The design is verified with a self-checking cocotb RTL vector test and a sweep test, and requires no external hardware.
ttgf26b/tt_um_brisq.review_notes: Replaced incorrect LFSR/PRNG/crypto tags with tags matching the FP32 approximate inverse square root design.

ttgf26b/tt_um_cambridge_nlfsr.summary: This project implements a 16-bit non-linear feedback shift register with two selectable non-linear feedback functions for cryptographic pseudo-random number generation. The mode select input switches between a high algebraic degree function and a chaotic variant, with the 16-bit state output on dedicated and bidirectional pins. It is seeded with 0xACE1 and requires only a clock and reset to operate, making it self-contained for testing with a logic analyzer. The design is intended for cryptographic primitives and demonstrates programmable non-linear feedback.

ttgf26b/tt_um_cherny_xor_8bi.summary: This design outputs the bitwise XOR of the 8-bit input with a previously configured 8-bit value. Configuration is done by holding a control pin high for at least two clock cycles while the desired value is on the input. After configuration, the output continuously reflects the XOR of the current input and the stored value. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any additional features or testing details.
ttgf26b/tt_um_cherny_xor_8bi.review_notes: Replaced register-file with combinational, which better matches the XOR logic.

ttgf26b/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttgf26b/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttgf26b/tt_um_coffeepot.summary: This is an unmanaged 3-port 100 Mbps Ethernet switch implemented in Verilog, using RMII interfaces to connect to external PHYs. It performs cut-through switching between the three ports, with two ports on dedicated pins and one on bidirectional pins. The design requires external Ethernet PHY hardware, such as LAN8720A modules, and a 50 MHz oscillator. It is a complex networking design that fits in a 2x2 tile area and is intended for hardware testing with real network traffic.
ttgf26b/tt_um_coffeepot.review_notes: Removed multi-tile; 2x2 tiles is a single tile group, not multiple tiles.

ttgf26b/tt_um_comp8.summary: This project is an 8-bit comparator that compares two input values and indicates whether they are equal, greater, or less than each other. It is implemented as a purely combinational circuit in Verilog, requiring no clock or sequential logic. The inputs can be driven by switches or FPGA pins, and the output is presented on the output pins. The design can be verified through simulation or on Tiny Tapeout hardware.

ttgf26b/tt_um_configurable_pwm.summary: This project is a run-time configurable PWM generator with dynamic controls for period, duty cycle, and output polarity. It includes input safety clamps that enforce a minimum period of three clock cycles and prevent duty cycle overflow. The design outputs both the primary PWM signal and its complementary inverted signal, and disabling the module forces both outputs to zero. It can be tested using DIP switches, LEDs, or an oscilloscope on the output PMOD pins.
ttgf26b/tt_um_configurable_pwm.review_notes: Removed unsupported power-management, clock-divider, gpio, and education tags; added signal-generator; corrected summary to match the documented PWM functionality.

ttgf26b/tt_um_connerdaehler_boop.summary: This project is a video and graphics generator that outputs a continuous pixel stream for display. It is verified using a cocotb-based Python testbench that reconstructs full images from the output. The design includes logic gates and counters to generate the video signal. It can be connected to a VGA or other display interface for visual output.

ttgf26b/tt_um_cwru_cpu.summary: This project is an educational single-cycle RISC-V processor implemented in Verilog. It executes a Fibonacci sequence using RISC-V assembly and displays the result on a seven-segment display. The design is intended as pedagogical material for CWRU computer engineering students learning computer architecture. No external hardware is needed to run the ASIC.
ttgf26b/tt_um_cwru_cpu.review_notes: Removed counter tag; the design is a RISC-V CPU running Fibonacci, not a simple counter.

ttgf26b/tt_um_d5smith_mfa.summary: This project is a music synthesizer that generates audio tones using an LFSR-based noise source and an NCO for pitch control. It outputs audio through a PWM or DAC interface. The design includes a synthesizer core and can be used for chiptune-style music generation. External speakers or audio amplifiers can be connected to the output.

ttgf26b/tt_um_detronyx_arith_lab.summary: This tile combines a byte adder, an 8x8 multiplier, and a reciprocal-ROM divider behind a small register-loaded interface with four task slots and command, mode, and bank selection pins. It is verified with a cocotb testbench and implemented as an ASIC. The design supports basic arithmetic operations and can be used for educational or computational purposes.
