The GF180MCU AS 3.3 V hardening flow uses a project SDC with explicit I/O delay, clock uncertainty/transition, fanout, transition, and capacitance constraints.
ttgf26b/tt_um_detronyx_arith_lab.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file tag; added alu, multiplier, adder, divider, cocotb and asic tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_detronyx_uart_trace_exerci.summary: This project is a UART-based pattern generator that uses an LFSR and counter to produce test patterns. It is designed for factory testing and communication applications. The design includes a UART interface for external communication. It can be used to generate deterministic patterns for testing other hardware.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ecc_accelerator.summary: This project is a simplified ECC scalar multiplication accelerator implemented in Verilog for ASIC implementation. It accepts two 8-bit operands through Tiny Tapeout GPIO pins and performs arithmetic similar to ECC point processing by adding the operands and generating a scaled output. The architecture includes an input interface, arithmetic processing block, scalar multiplication logic, and output interface. It is optimized for the SKY130 process using the OpenLane physical design flow.
ttgf26b/tt_um_ecc_accelerator.review_notes: Corrected ECC meaning from error correction to elliptic curve cryptography and removed unsupported ALU/multiplier/register-file tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ecc_processor.summary: This project is an ECC accelerator that performs error correction using cryptographic algorithms. It includes an ALU, multiplier, and register file for computation. The design can be tested entirely using Tiny Tapeout simulation, gate-level simulation, or FPGA-based verification environments. It is intended for hardware acceleration of error correction tasks.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ecc_scalar_mult.summary: This project is an ECC accelerator with error correction capabilities, implemented with an ALU, multiplier, and register file. The documentation is brief and reports no silicon results. It can be tested using simulation or FPGA-based verification. The design is intended for hardware acceleration of error correction tasks.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ecdsa_verify.summary: This design is a simplified ECDSA digital signature verification module intended for firmware authentication in automotive V2X systems. The documentation describes the intended security purpose but does not specify the elliptic curve, key sizes, or internal datapath, and the pin names are generic. The module is designed to verify the authenticity and integrity of firmware before execution inside automotive electronic systems. The documentation does not provide silicon test results or detailed implementation specifics.
ttgf26b/tt_um_ecdsa_verify.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; added rsa for the ECDSA public-key verification and insufficient-doc for the sparse implementation detail.

ttgf26b/tt_um_egurapha_chacha20.summary: This is a hardware implementation of the ChaCha20 stream cipher as specified in RFC 8439, with a 256-bit key, 96-bit nonce and 32-bit block counter. A host loads the key, nonce and counter and issues GEN to emit raw keystream or CRYPT to XOR data with the keystream for encryption or decryption. The core runs 20 rounds through four parallel quarter-round units and streams results one 32-bit word at a time. A runtime MODE pin selects between a UART 8N1 interface and a synchronous parallel byte bus, and no external hardware is required.
ttgf26b/tt_um_egurapha_chacha20.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated game; corrected to the ChaCha20 cipher core.

ttgf26b/tt_um_elemental_harmony.summary: This design is a silicon-based 4x4 strategy game called Elemental Harmony, where players compete against a logic engine to score points by matching elemental patterns. It uses an internal 16-bit occupancy register and a finite state machine to coordinate turns between a human player and an internal logic engine. The engine uses a linear feedback shift register to search for empty tiles and calculates scores based on adjacent pattern matches using a combinational adder tree. The design includes a tri-state error reporting system that streams board occupancy and fill-count back to the interface for move retry.
ttgf26b/tt_um_elemental_harmony.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented Elemental Harmony game.

ttgf26b/tt_um_elvtide01_7SegmentDice.summary: This project is a six-sided electronic dice with a seven-segment display output. Pressing a trigger button starts a counter that rapidly counts and then slows down to simulate a rolling dice. After the counter stops, the display shows a random number between 1 and 6. The design is implemented in Verilog.
ttgf26b/tt_um_elvtide01_7SegmentDice.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the electronic dice design.

ttgf26b/tt_um_emiliopeju_lightscan.summary: This project implements a BISS-C master that acquires position from an absolute encoder and produces a pulse output to synchronize an external trigger with the acquisition. It includes an SPI register interface using CPOL=1 and CPHA=1 with an 8-bit command plus 32-bit data frame, where the top command bit selects read or write. Extra features include BISS-C delay compensation and spare UIO control via registers that can be synchronized with the trigger. Testing requires a BISS-C encoder connected through an RS422 transceiver and optionally an external instrument on the pulse output.
ttgf26b/tt_um_emiliopeju_lightscan.review_notes: Removed unsupported template/placeholder/wokwi/education tags and added SPI, sensor-interface, instrumentation and industrial tags matching the documented BISS-C encoder acquisition design.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ex_drosen766.summary: This project is a placeholder Verilog design with generic input, output, and bidirectional pins. The documentation does not describe any actual functionality beyond boilerplate text. No external hardware is specified. No silicon test results are documented.
ttgf26b/tt_um_ex_drosen766.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect placeholder/insufficient documentation.

ttgf26b/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttgf26b/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_fast_auth.summary: This design implements a hardware IP block that performs low-latency ECDSA verification for V2X communication. It authenticates digital signatures in under 1 ms, meeting IEEE 1609.2 automotive security requirements. The design is implemented in Verilog and is intended for automotive security applications.
ttgf26b/tt_um_fast_auth.review_notes: Removed incorrect tags and added tags based on the ECDSA verification and automotive context.

ttgf26b/tt_um_fhw_appel_spiPWMio.summary: This module provides a PWM generator on output pin 7 and a PWM reader on input pin 7, with the generator duty cycle set by input pins [6:0] and the reader output reflected on output pins [6:0]. The PWM period is assumed to be 20 ms with duty cycle adjustable between 1 ms and 2 ms. An SPI interface allows configuration and read/write operations when enabled, and the design can be tested by looping back the generated PWM signal to the input. It requires a development kit and optionally an oscilloscope and signal generator for testing, and is notable for combining PWM input and output with SPI configurability.
ttgf26b/tt_um_fhw_appel_spiPWMio.review_notes: Removed 'servo' and 'motor-control' as the source never describes servo or motor control.

ttgf26b/tt_um_franretfie_top.summary: This project generates two sinusoidal waveforms with a fixed 90-degree phase offset (I/Q signals) using Direct Digital Synthesis. The outputs are presented as Pulse Code Modulation via two first-order sigma-delta modulators. The DDS block can be prescaled by sending a prescaler value through the SPI port. The oscillator design is based on a published recursive sinusoid generation algorithm, and recommended external hardware includes a digital buffer and two RC filters.
ttgf26b/tt_um_franretfie_top.review_notes: Replaced unrelated LFSR/PRNG/counter/sequencer/shift-register tags with DDS, signal-generator, NCO, sigma-delta, SPI and audio tags supported by the documentation.

ttgf26b/tt_um_geeta_doddamani_lfsr.summary: This project implements a 4-bit maximum-length Linear Feedback Shift Register using the feedback polynomial x4+x+1 with taps at bit positions 3 and 0. On every rising clock edge the register shifts left by one position and a feedback bit computed as the XOR of bits 3 and 0 is inserted at the LSB. When the active-low reset is asserted the register loads the seed value 0x1, and the LFSR cycles through all 15 non-zero states before repeating. The 4-bit output appears on uo_out[3:0], the upper nibble is always zero, and no external hardware is required.
ttgf26b/tt_um_geeta_doddamani_lfsr.review_notes: Removed fabricated ML/automotive/security tags and corrected the summary to describe the documented 4-bit LFSR.

ttgf26b/tt_um_hardware_anomaly_detection.summary: This project implements a lightweight machine-learning-based hardware anomaly detection engine for V2X packet data. It serially ingests 64-bit packets, extracts velocity and heading features, and runs a MAC-based inference core with ReLU activation and threshold scoring. The 8-bit threat score is output on uo_out, with done and interrupt flags on uio pins. The design is written in Verilog and can be tested by feeding serial packets and monitoring the outputs.
ttgf26b/tt_um_hardware_anomaly_detection.review_notes: Removed incorrect crypto tag and added machine-learning/security/mac-unit/pipeline/uart/automotive/edge-ai tags with a corrected summary.

ttgf26b/tt_um_hasheddan_nni.summary: This design performs nearest neighbor interpolation demosaicing for RGGB Bayer color filter arrays. It receives pixel data over a UART serial interface and outputs the demosaiced result over UART. The project is implemented in Verilog and fits in a single Tiny Tapeout tile. The documentation is minimal, providing only the title, one-line description, and pin names, so details of the implementation and testing are not available.

ttgf26b/tt_um_i2c_master.summary: This project implements a simple I2C master controller that transmits one byte to a fixed slave address (0x50). When the START input is asserted, it serially sends an 8-bit data value over SDA while generating SCL, and it produces START and STOP conditions. The BUSY output indicates an active transfer, and DONE and ACK status outputs are also provided. Testing involves applying reset, placing an 8-bit value on ui_in, asserting START, and observing SCL and SDA activity with an I2C slave device, logic analyzer, or oscilloscope.
ttgf26b/tt_um_i2c_master.review_notes: Replaced unrelated combinational/lookup-table/education/cocotb tags with I2C, communication, FSM, and Verilog tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_jct_lea.summary: This design implements the LEA-128 block cipher using an iterative approach. It loads a 128-bit key and data block serially through an input handshake protocol, then performs encryption or decryption based on control signals, and outputs the result serially through an output handshake. The design is implemented in Verilog and occupies a 2x2 tile area. Testing uses a test vector sourced from Wikipedia, but no external hardware is mentioned.

ttgf26b/tt_um_jsabree11_fibonacci_checke.summary: This design checks whether an 8-bit input value is a Fibonacci number. It compares the input against the Fibonacci numbers that fit in 8 bits and sets an output high if a match is found. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. It is tested with a cocotb testbench that applies known Fibonacci and non-Fibonacci values.

ttgf26b/tt_um_jte_cordic.summary: This project computes the sine and cosine of an 8-bit input angle using an iterative 8-stage CORDIC algorithm in Q2.6 fixed-point format. The angle is provided on the input pins, and a start signal triggers the computation, with results available after about 11 clock cycles. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench that sweeps all 128 angles and checks against a golden model. External hardware is not required, but an optional 8-bit LED PMOD can be connected to view the cosine output.
ttgf26b/tt_um_jte_cordic.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'signal-generator' tag; the rest of the proposed tags are supported.

ttgf26b/tt_um_karthik_trng.summary: This design implements a true random number generator using a ring oscillator as the entropy source. The oscillating signal is sampled by a clock, and the sampled bits are checked by a health checker to detect repeated patterns. Post-processing improves randomness and generates the final random output bits. The project is tested in simulation using Icarus Verilog and GTKWave, but no silicon test results are provided.

ttgf26b/tt_um_layla_spike_detector.summary: This design implements an adaptive neural spike detector with an IIR bandpass filter (300-3000 Hz), a nonlinear energy operator (NEO), and an EWMA adaptive threshold. It processes 8-bit signed ADC samples and outputs a spike detection pulse along with a 7-bit timestamp. The threshold multiplier and refractory period are configurable via a 3-wire SPI interface. The design is intended as a digital backend for neural recording AFEs and is tested with a cocotb testbench; external hardware such as an ADC or microcontroller is recommended for real-world use.
ttgf26b/tt_um_layla_spike_detector.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network tag because the design is a spike detector, not an SNN; added instrumentation tag for its measurement role.

ttgf26b/tt_um_lif_snn.summary: This project implements a 4-neuron spiking neural network using the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire model. Each neuron integrates input current, leaks a fraction of its membrane potential, and fires a spike when the threshold is reached. The weight matrix is programmed serially via a shift register, and spike outputs are provided for each neuron. The design is tested by programming weights and observing spike outputs; no external hardware is required.

ttgf26b/tt_um_likitha_trng.summary: This design is a hardware entropy mixing circuit that generates randomized outputs using XOR feedback paths. It accepts an 8-bit entropy input and produces an 8-bit randomized output stream. The design is lightweight and requires no external hardware. However, the documentation is very thin, providing only a high-level description and no details on testing or implementation.
ttgf26b/tt_um_likitha_trng.review_notes: Removed trng and crypto; the XOR feedback design is a pseudo-random generator, not a true RNG or crypto core.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ljhahne_pong.summary: This project is a simple implementation of the classic video game Pong. It generates a VGA video signal through the Tiny VGA Pmod and accepts input from a Gamepad Pmod, allowing two players to control paddles. The design was developed and verified on the Analogue Pocket and in the VGA Playground, with testing done visually rather than with an automated testbench. External hardware required includes a Gamepad Pmod and a Tiny VGA Pmod.

ttgf26b/tt_um_mealycpp_ascon_sdmc_uart.summary: This design implements an ASCON AEAD cryptographic processor with a shared permutation core and a UART command interface. It supports ASCON-AEAD-128 encryption and decryption, and includes an on-die ring-oscillator entropy source with NIST SP 800-90B health tests and an ASCON Hash_DRBG for key and nonce generation. The design also integrates a debug pin for raw entropy characterization. It is notable for its reconfigurable implementation of the ASCON family standardized in NIST SP 800-232.

ttgf26b/tt_um_multi_protocol.summary: This design is a multi-protocol communication controller that supports UART, SPI, and I2C transmission modes from a single module. It is controlled via the Tiny Tapeout input and bidirectional pins. The design is compact and integrates all three protocols in one module. It is notable for its versatility in supporting multiple serial communication standards.

ttgf26b/tt_um_pattern_gen.summary: This Verilog design is a UART-programmable waveform and PWM generator. Samples sent over UART are stored in a 256-byte RAM and played back either as an 8-bit parallel DAC output or as eight independent PWM channels. The mode and load pins select operation, and the outputs carry the DAC data or PWM channels. The recommended pinout is TT Audio.
ttgf26b/tt_um_pattern_gen.review_notes: Removed unsupported nco/cordic/lookup-table/dsp; added uart, pwm, dac, memory, audio.

ttgf26b/tt_um_polytrig_core.summary: PolyTrig is a compact ASIC-oriented digital waveform synthesis core implemented in Verilog. It generates multiple waveform types including sine, cosine, tangent and cotangent approximations, triangle, sawtooth, square and rectified sine using LUT-based signal reconstruction. The architecture uses quarter-wave LUT optimization with symmetry and phase transformations, and supports NCO-style waveform generation. Waveform selection and runtime configuration are controlled through the TinyTapeout input interface, and a cocotb verification environment is included.
ttgf26b/tt_um_polytrig_core.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original invented PWM tremolo guitar-pedal functionality unsupported by source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_pqc_ntt_butterfly.summary: This project implements a hardware-accelerated Cooley-Tukey Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) butterfly core optimized for CRYSTALS-Kyber post-quantum cryptography with q = 3329. It performs fast modular addition and subtraction using specialized combinational subtraction matrix logic blocks without slow division operations. The design provides X_out and Y_out buses for the butterfly results, with A_in and B_in input buses and split bidirectional lines for B_in and Y_out. Testing is done by applying input arrays and twiddle factors, then driving clock transitions to observe the modular transformation outputs.
ttgf26b/tt_um_pqc_ntt_butterfly.review_notes: Proposed summary described an LFSR data masker that does not exist; corrected to the documented NTT butterfly core.

ttgf26b/tt_um_pschuetz_tremolo.summary: This project implements a digital tremolo modulation controller intended for guitar pedal applications, generating a PWM signal that can be converted to a smooth analog control signal with an RC filter. At its center is an 8-bit low frequency oscillator whose rate is set by the rate select inputs, feeding a waveform generator that produces saw up, saw down, square and triangle shapes. Depth logic controls the intensity of the tremolo effect, and the resulting modulation level is compared against a PWM counter to produce the output. The design is verified with Cocotb testbenches covering reset, enable, PWM generation, rate, waveform, depth and debug outputs, and requires external RC filtering, an op-amp buffer and analog tremolo staging.
ttgf26b/tt_um_pschuetz_tremolo.review_notes: Removed incorrect security/FSM tags and rewrote the summary to match the documented tremolo PWM controller.

ttgf26b/tt_um_push.summary: This project implements a Secure V2X Mini Demonstrator using an 8-bit Linear Feedback Shift Register. The design accepts an 8-bit plaintext input on ui_in and internally generates an 8-bit pseudo-random key stream with the LFSR. The plaintext is XORed with the key stream to produce masked output data on uo_out, with the LFSR updating on every rising clock edge. No external hardware is required, and testing involves applying input data, clocking the design and verifying that the output changes according to the XOR operation.
ttgf26b/tt_um_push.review_notes: Replaced unrelated arithmetic tags with LFSR, PRNG, crypto, security, communication and automotive tags supported by the V2X masking documentation.

ttgf26b/tt_um_pwm_cit.summary: This project implements a configurable 8-bit PWM generator that produces a variable duty cycle signal from an 8-bit input. An internal 8-bit counter increments on every clock cycle and is compared with the duty cycle value on ui_in, driving uo_out[0] high while the counter is below the input and low otherwise. Examples include ui_in = 64 for 25% duty cycle, 128 for 50% and 192 for 75%. No external hardware is required, and testing involves applying a clock, releasing reset and observing the PWM waveform on uo_out[0].
ttgf26b/tt_um_pwm_cit.review_notes: Removed fabricated TRNG/ring-oscillator/crypto/hash tags and corrected the summary to the documented 8-bit PWM generator.

ttgf26b/tt_um_raksha.summary: This design implements a lightweight secure packet authentication engine for V2X communication. An incoming 8-bit packet is XORed with a predefined secret key of 0xA5, and the outputs indicate authentication success or alert. It is implemented in Verilog and can be tested by applying clock and reset and supplying packet data. The design is intended for low-latency vehicular communication systems.
ttgf26b/tt_um_raksha.review_notes: Removed hash/cipher and added crypto/security/communication/automotive; summary now describes the XOR packet authentication.

ttgf26b/tt_um_rameshwar_door_lock.summary: This project implements a simple digital door lock system that verifies a 4-bit password against a stored value of 1010. If the entered password matches, an unlock signal is asserted; otherwise, an error signal is generated. The design consists of a password checker, a lock controller, and a top module, and can be tested with a provided testbench using iverilog. No external hardware is required.

ttgf26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttgf26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttgf26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_decod.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttgf26b/tt_um_reflex_s4.summary: This design is the decision and relay core of a robot-arm reflex system that forwards normal joint commands to a CAN bus via an external MCP2515 controller and, upon a danger trigger, blocks the normal stream and injects a reflex pose. It includes two SPI ports: a slave for host configuration and frame relay, and a master for driving the MCP2515. The reflex behavior is programmable through a rule table with priority and debounce, supporting actions such as freeze, home, and flinch. It requires external hardware including an MCP2515, a CAN transceiver, a DIP switch, and an FSR sensor connected to an FPGA XADC.
ttgf26b/tt_um_reflex_s4.review_notes: Removed motor-control, automotive, industrial and fsm tags not supported by the source; kept can-bus, spi, robotics and verilog.

ttgf26b/tt_um_ro_puf.summary: This project implements a programmable-length ring oscillator designed as a Physical Unclonable Function for hardware security. The inverter chain delay path can be dynamically configured using sel_mux_0, sel_mux_1, and n_inv, and the circuit oscillates at a device-specific frequency due to process variations in the GF180MCU process. An integrated control path monitors sample capture events and triggers telemetry when output is ready, with debug and valid outputs on the dedicated pins. Testing involves reset, challenge selection, enabling the oscillator, setting tx_ready to acquire data, and then disabling the oscillator to save power; an oscilloscope, logic analyzer, or PMOD-connected microcontroller/FPGA can be used for validation.
ttgf26b/tt_um_ro_puf.review_notes: Replaced incorrect LFSR/PRNG/shift-register tags with PUF, ring-oscillator, security, and related implementation tags.

ttgf26b/tt_um_sandy_venky.summary: This is an 8-bit linear-feedback shift register (LFSR) circuit implemented in Verilog, serving as a sequential pseudo-random number generator. The design has no documented inputs or control signals; it only provides eight output bits from the LFSR state. There is no documentation on how to use or test the design, and no external hardware is specified. The project appears to be a minimal demonstration of an LFSR, but the lack of documentation limits its practical application.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_aer_router_gf.summary: This design is a 4-input, 4-output asynchronous address-event-representation (AER) spike router implemented in GF180mcuD digital logic. It uses a 4-phase bundled-data REQ/ACK handshake, double-flop synchronised into a single clock domain, and routes events through a 16-entry routing table or bypasses them unchanged. Incoming events are queued in a 4-deep FIFO and emitted with another handshake. It requires external AER-compliant sources and sinks, and is programmable via SPI.
ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_aer_router_gf.review_notes: Removed unsupported spiking-neural-network tag; the design is an AER router, not an SNN.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_cim_bist_gf.summary: This design is a compute-in-memory (CIM) peripheral featuring an 8x8 1-bit cell array with built-in self-test (BIST) and a 64-bit sticky fault map. It performs a 16-bit dot-product accumulation over user-programmable row activations, configurable via SPI. The BIST supports march, checkerboard, and diagonal patterns, and an external trigger can start the test. It requires an SPI master for programming and reading results, and provides status outputs such as busy, done, and fault flags.
ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_cim_bist_gf.review_notes: Removed 'neural-network' and 'mac-unit' tags not supported by the CIM peripheral description.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_neuro_puf_gf.summary: This design is a digital physical unclonable function (PUF) that uses eight distinct-tap maximal-length 10-bit LFSRs as virtual ring oscillators. A 6-bit challenge selects a pair of LFSRs, and an arbiter compares their popcounts over a programmable window to produce a response bit. 64 challenges accumulate into a 64-bit response, which can be XORed with a host-loaded memristor vector for dual-entropy mode. It is SPI-programmable and requires no external hardware, though an SPI master is needed for configuration.
ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_neuro_puf_gf.review_notes: Removed prng tag; the LFSRs are used as PUF entropy sources, not as a pseudo-random number generator.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_snn_wta_gf.summary: This design is a 4-neuron digital spiking neural network (SNN) inference engine with hard winner-take-all lateral inhibition. Each neuron accumulates a MAC of its bias, input currents, and synaptic weights, with programmable threshold, leak, and refractory parameters. It is SPI-configurable and provides spike outputs, winner ID, and status flags. It requires an SPI master for programming and an input pattern generator, with optional oscilloscope for spike capture.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_spike_codec_gf.summary: This design is a neuromorphic spike codec that combines three encoders (rate, latency, delta) and three symmetric decoders (rate, latency, delta) in a single SPI-programmable block. The encoders convert values to spike trains using methods such as LFSR-based rate coding, time-to-first-spike, and delta modulation, while the decoders reconstruct values from spike trains. It operates on a shared window counter and provides status flags and an IRQ output. It requires an SPI master for configuration and a spike source for decoding, and can be paired with an SNN inference core.
ttgf26b/tt_um_santhosh_spike_codec_gf.review_notes: Removed sigma-delta and communication tags not supported by the design; added silicon-tested based on the author's working report.

ttgf26b/tt_um_santosh_aes_sbox.summary: This project implements an AES S-Box accelerator in Verilog, providing a combinational lookup table that maps an 8-bit input to its AES substitution value. The design uses the 8-bit input pins and 8-bit output pins, with no clocked logic required. It is fully self-contained and requires no external hardware, making it easy to test by applying input values and observing the corresponding outputs. The design demonstrates a hardware implementation of a cryptographic primitive widely used in secure communication systems.

ttgf26b/tt_um_smerity_mandelbrot.summary: This design is an interactive fixed-point Mandelbrot renderer that iterates z = z² + c in Q4.28 format and outputs the iteration count for each pixel. It uses a single sequential bit-serial shift-add multiplier shared across three products per iteration to reduce area. The host sends view packets containing the top-left corner, step size, and maximum iterations, and the chip outputs a pixel stream with valid, frame start, and line end strobes. It requires an RP2040 or similar microcontroller to bridge the parallel bus to USB for display, and a host viewer to compute view packets.
ttgf26b/tt_um_smerity_mandelbrot.review_notes: Removed video and fpga tags not supported by the pins or design target; added image-processing, cocotb and sequential-logic.

ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_config_reg.summary: This design implements an 8-bit unidirectional SPI configuration register intended for external configuration of future analog/mixed-signal designs. It consists of a shift register and an output latch, shifting in data MSB-first on MOSI when chip select is low, and updating the parallel output when chip select goes high. An active-high asynchronous clear resets the register to a default value of 0xAA. The design is tested by writing to the register via SPI and observing the parallel output pins.
ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_config_reg.review_notes: Removed analog/mixed-signal and register-file tags; the design is a single digital SPI shift register, not an analog or multi-register block.

ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_cpu_top.summary: This project implements a compact 4-bit microcoded CPU that fetches and executes instructions from an external SPI RAM, such as a 23LC512 chip or an RP2040 emulating it. The CPU uses the SPI Pmod interface for program storage and provides an 8-bit output register plus a CPU_VALID signal. It is designed for the TinyTapeout GF180MCU platform and verified using cocotb with Icarus Verilog. The design requires external SPI RAM hardware for operation.
ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_cpu_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'memory' tag and added 'qspi' for the SPI Pmod program-storage interface.

ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_master.summary: This design implements an 8-bit SPI master controller using Verilog. The master accepts 8-bit parallel data and, when started, shifts it out via MOSI while generating SCLK and CS signals, with a DONE signal indicating completion. The design includes a finite state machine with IDLE, LOAD, TRANSFER, and DONE states, and a shift register for serial transmission. Testing involves applying reset, loading data, asserting START, and observing the SPI signals.
ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_master.review_notes: Corrected summary to match the source, which describes only an SPI master controller, not a full-duplex master-slave system.

ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_slave.summary: This design implements a standard 4-wire SPI slave peripheral with an internal 8-byte register file, targeting the GlobalFoundries 180nm platform. It uses a synchronous FSM to decode SPI transactions on SCLK, MOSI, and CS_N, supporting read and write commands with a 1-byte command phase followed by a 1-byte data phase. Register 0's content is continuously driven to the output pins for real-time monitoring. Testing involves sending SPI commands to write data and verifying the output pins update accordingly.
ttgf26b/tt_um_spi_slave.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'industry-grade' claim from summary; source describes a standard SPI slave.

ttgf26b/tt_um_teapot.summary: This project is a network-connected accelerator wrapper that interfaces with a custom bfloat16 multiplier via a 100Mbps Ethernet PHY. It uses a LAN8720A PHY and a 50MHz oscillator on an Ethernet Pmod, and responds to application packets with EtherType 0x88b5. Testing requires connecting the ASIC to a local network and running a provided packet sender/receiver tool. The documentation is incomplete (how-it-works is TODO), but the testing procedure and external hardware are described.
ttgf26b/tt_um_teapot.review_notes: Removed floating-point tag because the design is a wrapper around a bfloat16 multiplier, not a floating-point unit; added incomplete tag due to TODO documentation.

ttgf26b/tt_um_uart_soc.summary: This design implements a UART receiver that samples serial data on ui_in[0], shifting in bits and after 7 bits transferring the data to an output register and asserting a done signal. The received data appears on uo_out[6:0], and the design includes a verified output and status LED. Testing involves sending serial data and observing the output and done signal. The documentation does not describe any hash comparison or signature verification logic, despite the title and pin names suggesting one.
ttgf26b/tt_um_uart_soc.review_notes: Added incomplete tag and corrected summary to avoid claiming an undescribed hash comparison module.

ttgf26b/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttgf26b/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttgf26b/tt_um_v2x_warning.summary: This project implements a simple vehicle-to-vehicle (V2X) collision warning system in Verilog. It takes 4-bit inputs representing two vehicles and outputs a collision warning signal. The documentation is very thin, stating only that the module should be placed in both cars and they should communicate. No details are provided on the communication protocol, testing procedure, or external hardware beyond a generic PCB.
ttgf26b/tt_um_v2x_warning.review_notes: Removed 'communication' because no data communication protocol is documented.

ttgf26b/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing Wafer.space logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo across the screen or to use a solid color instead of the gradient. An optional Gamepad Pmod allows starting/pausing the bounce and changing the direction or position of the logo. Silicon tests confirm it works, with testers noting that it runs at up to 32 MHz and that gamepad interaction functions correctly.
ttgf26b/tt_um_waferspace_vga_screensaver.review_notes: Removed image-processing tag; the design is a logo screensaver, not an image-processing algorithm.

ttgf26b/tt_um_wnn.summary: This project implements an 8-bit Weightless Neural Network (WNN) for pattern recognition using pattern matching. It takes an 8-bit input and produces a pattern match result along with individual bit comparison outputs. The documentation is minimal, describing only that the circuit processes inputs and generates outputs according to designed functionality, with no details on the neural network architecture or training. Testing involves applying inputs and observing outputs, and no external hardware is required.

ttgf26b/tt_um_wokwi_466666882406199297.summary: This project is a binary-to-hexadecimal decoder that drives a seven-segment LED display, taking a 4-bit input (A-D) and outputting the corresponding hexadecimal digit (0-9, A-F). It was designed in Wokwi using combinational logic, with color-coded truth tables and K-maps for clarity. Testing involves toggling the inputs to change the displayed character. No external hardware is required.
ttgf26b/tt_um_wokwi_466666882406199297.review_notes: Removed education tag; the documentation describes a personal decoder project with no stated teaching purpose.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_MichaelBell_nanoV.summary: This is a minimal RV32E bit-serial processor that uses an external SPI RAM for both instructions and data, with the SPI RAM and UART connected to the bidirectional pins. It has no caches and runs at roughly clock speed divided by 32, with registers x3 and x4 hardcoded for cheap access to RAM and peripherals, and no support for ebreak or interrupts. The eight inputs and eight outputs are general-purpose GPIO, and the outputs can also drive a 7-segment display; the UART runs at clock speed divided by 128 with simple status bits and no FIFOs. Silicon testing by the author confirmed the design works, and programs can be built with the nanoV-sdk and tested against an SPI RAM or an RP2040-based emulator.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray-casting graphics engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, rendering textured walls with flat floor and ceiling by racing the beam. The player point of view is controlled over SPI, and an optional external QSPI ROM can supply textures instead of the internally generated ones. It needs a Tiny VGA PMOD on the dedicated outputs, an SPI host for control, and a clock around 25.175 MHz for standard 640x480 VGA. Silicon reports say it works without the glitches of the earlier TT04 version, including external SPI textures, though a clock hack was needed and the SPI peripherals still need full testing.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_dinogame.summary: This project implements an endless-runner game similar to the Chrome Dino game, rendered on a VGA monitor. The game uses four input buttons for jump, halt, debug, and mode control, and outputs VGA signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works well and is playable, though some testers noted occasional screen tearing at higher speeds. The documentation is minimal, consisting mainly of a brief description and pinout, but the test reports provide evidence of functionality.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_dinogame.review_notes: Removed redundant video tag; added button and retro tags supported by the pin names and game description.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv4.summary: This project implements a 4-bit combinational multiplier and divider unit that supports both signed and unsigned operations. The multiplier uses a ripple carry array, while the divider uses a restoring array algorithm. It has error indicators for division overflow and divide-by-zero. The design was created in Logisim and exported to Verilog, and silicon tests confirm it works.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This factory test module is designed to verify all I/O pins of an ASIC and has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. Mode selection is controlled by rst_n and sel signals, with the counter incrementing every clock cycle and resetting when rst_n is low. The design is written in Verilog and occupies a single tile. It is intended for manufacturing test and requires no external hardware beyond the ASIC itself.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_flappy_vga_cutout1.summary: This project is a clone of the Flappy Bird game, rendered on a 640x480 VGA display with a single button input for flapping. The game state is updated each frame, and the score is output in binary on the bidirectional pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a debounced active-low button, and a VGA adapter compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works and is playable, though several testers found it challenging.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit consisting of an 8x8 grid of identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop, and a buffer, with each tile individually rotatable and mirrorable via configuration. Configuration and state are managed through a scan chain, and a loop breaker mechanism helps debug combinational loops. The design supports loading and dumping state, single-stepping, and free running, and it has been tested on silicon with a provided test suite. It is notable for being a port of a larger FPGA design to TinyTapeout with significant area optimization.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag because the design occupies only one tile.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a RISC-V SoC called KianV uLinux that can boot a small Linux system, implemented in Verilog across an 8x2 tile area. It provides a UART interface, SPI connections for flash and PSRAM, and several LED outputs, with one bidirectional pin held always high. The design is notable for being a full Linux-capable RISC-V ASIC on a Tiny Tapeout shuttle. External hardware includes SPI flash and PSRAM memories, and the documentation is limited to pin names without detailed usage instructions.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Removed memory tag since the design only exposes SPI pins to external memories rather than implementing one.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog and outputs the sound wave on uio_out[1:0]. A 100kHz clock is provided on the clk pin, and a brief reset on rst_n starts playback. A piezo speaker connected across uio_out[1:0] is required for audible output.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommy.summary: This design is a 12-hour clock rendered on a 640x480 VGA display using a race-the-beam triangle renderer, where three triangle hands indicate the time and twelve dots aid readability. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 31.5 MHz clock, reset, and hour and minute advance buttons. Silicon test reports confirm it works out of the box with a Tiny VGA Pmod, with testers noting the hands move correctly and the time can be set by holding the buttons. The design is notable for its triangle-based rendering approach and includes a Rust software model for reference.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommy.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design only consumes an external clock; added silicon-tested and button based on the test reports and pinout.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_psychogenic_neptunepropor.summary: This design is a guitar tuner that counts rising edges of an input pulse over a fixed sampling period and compares the count to frequencies of interest for standard guitar tuning, covering notes from about 80 to 400 Hz. It supports multiple clock configurations via three input bits and can drive either a dual or single 7-segment display, with the dot indicating an exact match in single mode. The raw pulse count is output on the bidirectional pins, and testing requires feeding a variable frequency signal and observing the closest note on the display. A silicon test report confirms it works, showing the closest note for a variable frequency input.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square wave tone generators, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with 10 shapes. It is controlled via an 8-bit multiplexed data/address bus and produces audio through either an 8-bit digital output for an external DAC or a PWM output for analog filtering. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to hear the audio. Silicon test reports indicate it works well, with users successfully playing chiptunes and using the 128 divider mode.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Removed dac (external only) and added silicon-tested and retro.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_robojan_top.summary: Tiny Breakout is a single-player Breakout game in Verilog that outputs a 2-bit-per-channel VGA video signal and a sound output. The game is controlled by three buttons (left, right, action) and includes an SPI interface for reading the game state and writing commands to modify it. The design uses a VGA timing module, painter modules for graphics, and a shift register to store the 13x16 block grid efficiently. It requires a VGA monitor, a VGA DAC made from 2-bit R2R resistor networks, and external buttons; the author reports that the silicon works.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_robojan_top.review_notes: Removed r2r-dac (external hardware only) and added silicon-tested and speaker.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This design implements a simple VGA pong-style game with paddles controlled by four input pins. It outputs VGA signals on the bidirectional and output pins and supports two different VGA PMOD pinouts selected by an input, with the recommended Tiny VGA pinout. The game has no scoring and the ball only moves horizontally, so it is a minimal demonstration rather than a complete game. Silicon tests report that pong works, though one tester had to adjust monitor centering and another could not get a proper display on a CRT.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported gamepad tag and added silicon-tested based on test reports.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_top_mole99.summary: This design produces an 800x600 60 Hz SVGA output with a background and a single 12x12 sprite, rendered internally at 100x75 so each sprite pixel is 8x8 screen pixels. The sprite is initialized with a pixelated Tiny Tapeout logo that moves around the screen, and an SPI receiver accepts commands to replace sprite data, change colors, set the background and control the sprite position. It can run at either a 40 MHz or 10 MHz pixel clock selected by a configuration bit, and it needs an external Tiny VGA PMOD for display. Silicon tests report that the logo bounces around and the SPI interface works, with some glitching when moving the sprite.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_top_mole99.review_notes: Removed vga (SVGA over Pmod, not VGA) and added silicon-tested and pmod based on pins and test reports.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This design implements a Simon Says memory game where the player must repeat an ever-growing sequence of colors and tones. The sequence is shown on four LEDs with corresponding tones on a speaker, and the player responds using four buttons. A two-digit seven-segment display shows the current level, and the game restarts after a mistake. It requires external hardware such as the Simon Says Pmod or discrete buttons, LEDs, a speaker, and a seven-segment display, and a Wokwi simulation is available.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed memory type tag; added canonical game, 7-segment, led, speaker, wokwi, pmod, verilog and button tags.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB to Serial bridge using the USB CDC protocol, allowing a computer to communicate with the chip as a virtual serial port. It uses a 48 MHz clock and connects to USB D+ and D- pins, requiring a 1.5k ohm pull-up resistor on D+ for device detection. Data received from the USB host appears on the rx output pins, and data can be transmitted by setting the tx input pins and asserting tx_valid. A silicon test report confirms both RX and TX work as expected, and the design is based on an open-source USB serial core.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_uwuifier.summary: This design operates on a UART signal and transforms the text into 'uwu' speak. It interfaces via UART at 115200 baud with a 6 MHz clock, using dedicated receive and transmit pins. It is intended to be connected inline with a UART transceiver to modify data in real time. Silicon testing confirmed it works, with a tester using a serial terminal to send data and receiving the uwuified version back.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_uwuifier.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttihp0p1/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.summary: This design displays a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display based on a 6-bit binary value entered on DIP switches. It drives the display one segment at a time, so a high clock rate is needed to see the full character. The character set covers a-z plus space, underscore, hyphen, period, exclamation mark and quote. Silicon tests report it working, and it is notable as a simple character generator with a documented mapping table.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_380408823952452609.review_notes: Removed text (7-segment output only) and added silicon-tested per test reports.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.summary: This circuit outputs the string 'tiny tapeout' to a 7-segment display. It uses a modulo-12 counter to select which character to display and has logic to light the appropriate segments. It is implemented in Wokwi and can be tested by running the clock to scroll text or using pins to manually select characters. Silicon test reports confirm the design is working on fabricated hardware.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397140982440144897.review_notes: Corrected tags to match the modulo-12 counter and silicon-tested status, and removed the false no-report claim from the summary.

ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397142450561071105.summary: This circuit is a padlock that lets you set a code for a safe using pins 2 to 4 and pin 7. Pin 1 resets the safe, and the clock button is used to enter the code. The seven-segment display shows "L" for locked when pin 1 is on and the clock button is pressed. A partial silicon test report notes errors where the saved code inverts each clock cycle and the third code bit is ignored, so some invalid codes are accepted.
ttihp0p1/tt_um_wokwi_397142450561071105.review_notes: Replaced invented game/debouncer/edge-detector tags and summary with the actual padlock functionality and partial silicon status.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display. Players use four directional buttons to slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid, merging tiles to reach 2048. The design includes modern and retro color themes and a debug mode for unit testing. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and has been tested on silicon, where it works as expected.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Added retro and silicon-tested tags; removed unsupported removal of puzzle tag.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.summary: This design plays Pachelbel's Canon while displaying synchronized visuals on a VGA screen. It uses a PWM output for audio and requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a Tiny Audio Pmod. Silicon testing showed it works, though one tester noted the audio was out of sync until manually reset. The design is a demonstration of audio and video capabilities on Tiny Tapeout.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_canon.review_notes: Removed generic graphics tag; added silicon-tested and verilog tags supported by the silicon reports and language.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_mandelbrot.summary: This design computes the Mandelbrot fractal in real time while racing the VGA beam, using one iteration per clock cycle and a maximum depth of 16 iterations. It outputs a 720x480 VGA signal through a Tiny VGA Pmod, with the fractal rendered at 180x480 pixels using 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic and approximated multipliers. The image position and zoom are configured through the input and bidirectional pins, with control values written during vsync. It is notable for fitting a real-time fractal renderer into a 2x2 tile area at 100 MHz.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.summary: This design reads run-length encoded video data from a QSPI flash memory and outputs it to a 640x480 VGA display, suitable for playing the Bad Apple music video. It requires external QSPI and VGA PMODs, and the SPI read latency is configurable via input pins. The design operates at 25.175 MHz and was successfully tested on silicon, playing Bad Apple, though there were minor issues with short back-to-back runs that the author believes are fixed in a later version. The documentation notes the flash must support the h6B Fast Read Quad Output command with 8 dummy cycles.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.review_notes: Removed 'memory' and 'demoscene' as unsupported; added 'silicon-tested' to match the working silicon report.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set with Zcb and Zicond extensions, using QSPI flash for program storage and QSPI PSRAM for data memory. It includes a UART and an SPI controller intended for driving an ST7789 LCD, and is designed to work with a QSPI Pmod containing flash and RAM. Testing requires loading an image into flash and following a specific reset and clocking sequence, with MicroPython scripts on the RP2040 handling the setup. Silicon tests confirmed it runs CoreMark and MicroPython at 64 MHz with latency 1 or 2, and up to 100 MHz with latency 2.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.review_notes: Removed memory (external RAM) and added silicon-tested, qspi, lcd, rp2040 supported by the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_NicklausThompson_SkyKing.summary: This design displays a static image of a plane flying into the sunset with a text overlay that types out character by character. It also includes demos for oscilloscope XY display PMODs, which can be selected via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for the main demo and additional PMODs for the XY demos. The text animation may complete before the VGA monitor recognizes the signal, so viewing in a VGA playground is recommended.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_QIF_8bit.summary: This is an 8-bit digital QIF (quadratic integrate-and-fire) circuit that spikes when the input is positive and resets when the signal exceeds a predetermined value. It accepts an 8-bit two's complement positive number on inputs B0 through B7 and outputs spike signals on AS0 and S1 through S7. The documentation is very thin, consisting only of a brief description and a note about external hardware. It is unclear from the provided text how the threshold is set or what the output encoding represents.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_QIF_8bit.review_notes: Removed non-canonical 'qif' tag and added insufficient-doc; summary kept as-is since it is supported.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.summary: This is a standalone VGA and sound demo that loops after about 25 seconds, developed for a 48 MHz clock and using a non-standard 1220-pixel horizontal VGA mode with RGB222 dithered output. It generates sound through a 16-bit sigma-delta DAC on one pin from an internal three-channel synthesizer with triangle, noise, and square waves. The graphics include a procedurally rendered plane, a starfield from an LFSR, and a TT08 logo, with a soundtrack based on a riff from a demoscene track. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and either a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or a simple RC filter for sound, and silicon tests confirm it works as expected.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag to match the working silicon test reports.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_nyancat.summary: This design displays the classic Nyan Cat animation on a VGA monitor with accompanying music. It uses a 2x2 Bayer dithering matrix for color rendition and generates sound from a MIDI file using square waves with exponential decay envelopes, a low-pass filter, and a sigma-delta DAC. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video, and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for audio. Silicon tests confirm it works, and it was originally intended for one tile but expanded to two.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.summary: This project renders a 3D torus (donut) on a VGA display using a raymarching technique with a CORDIC unit to calculate distances. It runs at a non-standard 1220x480 resolution and uses spatial and temporal dithering to improve appearance despite low horizontal resolution. It requires a 48 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output. Silicon tests show it works but may have minor glitches at 48 MHz; running at 45 MHz avoids them.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_a1k0n_vgadonut.review_notes: Added silicon-tested: the source reports working silicon results from testers and the author.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This is a framebuffer-less VGA ray casting engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D, rendering textured walls with flat-colored floor and ceiling while racing the beam. The player point of view is controlled via SPI, and an optional external QSPI memory can supply textures instead of internally generated ones. It outputs standard 640x480 VGA at 25.175 MHz and includes debug and demo modes, though the documentation notes that testing details are still to be confirmed. It is a resubmission of a previous Tiny Tapeout design and lacks doors, sprites, or other game elements.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_tinyvga_fun_wr.summary: This design is the digital block from a larger VGA project, packaged with a simple sequencer loop and dithering to simulate 8-bit color output on the 2-bit Tiny VGA Pmod. It runs standalone by plugging into a VGA monitor and resetting, with manual mode and bit-depth selection available by overriding the sequencer. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 25 MHz clock, and silicon tests by the author confirm it works as expected. The design is a 1x1 tile implementation intended for the Tiny Tapeout shuttle.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_fun_wrappe.summary: This is the same digital VGA block as the Tiny VGA version but targeting the Digilent PmodVGA with 4 bits per color channel, including a simple sequencer loop and dithering. It runs standalone when connected to a VGA monitor and reset, with manual mode and bit-depth selection possible by overriding the sequencer. It requires a Digilent PmodVGA and a 25 MHz clock, and the author's silicon test confirms it works as expected. The documentation notes that another version of this design on the same shuttle targets the Tiny VGA Pmod.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_autosel.summary: This prototype reads a 16-bit design ID from an I2C EEPROM and uses it to select the corresponding Tiny Tapeout project by driving control signals for the multiplexer. It also prints the read value over UART at 115200 baud for debugging. It requires an external 1 kbit or 2 kbit I2C EEPROM such as a 24C01 or 24C02 with 10k pull-up resistors on SCL and SDA. The design is intended for automatic project selection in Tiny Tapeout and is documented with specific expected behavior for the control outputs.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_autosel.review_notes: Removed rom and multiplexer tags that misdescribe the design; added rp2040 for the demo-board context.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.summary: The design implements a two-player Pong game that uses two NES controllers for input and outputs a VGA video signal.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.review_notes: Removed gpio tag because the bidirectional pins are dedicated to NES controller signals.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_calonso88_74181.summary: This design replicates the 74181 4-bit slice ALU twice to form an 8-bit ALU that performs arithmetic and logical operations on 8-bit words. It includes an SPI slave peripheral supporting all four SPI modes with eight configurable read/write registers and eight read-only status registers, and a multiplexer maps internal signals to a 7-segment display for debug. It is controlled from an RP2040 SPI1 master on GPIOs 24 to 27, and no external hardware is required. Silicon tests by the author confirmed read and write operations of all registers across all four SPI modes.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_calonso88_74181.review_notes: Removed 7-segment because no 7-segment interface pins exist; added silicon-tested and rp2040 from the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_calonso88_rsa.summary: This is an 8-bit RSA encryption and decryption coprocessor that implements modular exponentiation through Montgomery modular multiplication. It uses an SPI slave peripheral with all four SPI modes, eight configurable 8-bit registers, and eight status registers, controlled from an RP2040 SPI1 master. The documentation provides a detailed key generation example and test procedure, and no external hardware is required. Silicon tests by the author confirmed register read and write operations across all SPI modes, with a self-checking test verifying encrypted output against predicted values.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_calonso88_rsa.review_notes: Removed cipher because RSA is asymmetric, and added silicon-tested and rp2040 based on the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_ccattuto_conway.summary: This design simulates Conway's Game of Life on a 32x16 grid with periodic boundary conditions. The simulation state is output over UART as ANSI terminal characters and over VGA using a TinyVGA PMOD. Control is via single characters received over UART: space to start/stop, '0' to randomize, and '1' to single-step. The initial state is generated by an LFSR, and the design is notable for providing both serial and video outputs on a small tile.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_cejmu.summary: This design bundles four educational modules selected by an internal multiplexer: a vending machine state machine, a coin acceptor decoder, a 24-bit ripple carry adder, and a 24-bit carry lookahead adder. The adders are tested by feeding 24-bit operands in 8-bit chunks and reading the 25-bit result in 8-bit chunks. An oscilloscope can be used to measure the difference in execution speed between the two adder types. The coin acceptor decoder is designed for the HX-916 model.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_cejmu.review_notes: Removed multiplexer tag as it is an internal selection mechanism, not a primary design feature.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_cfib_demo.summary: This demoscene competition entry generates a pseudo-random soundtrack via PWM and displays a waveform on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA Pmod on uo_out and Mike's audio Pmod on uio_out[7]. The design is written in Verilog and runs from a 50 MHz clock with asynchronous reset. A silicon test report confirms the design is working.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_cfib_demo.review_notes: Removed waveform-generator (not a general waveform generator) and added silicon-tested per the working test report.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_crispy_vga.summary: Crispy VGA takes a standard Tiny Tapeout VGA signal as input and adds a programmable amount of random noise to the video and audio signals before passing them to the output. The uio_in[0] through uio_in[4] inputs individually toggle noise on the hsync, B, G, R, and vsync signals. The uio_in[5] input sets the noise level applied to the R, G, and B wires to high or low, and the uio_in[0:5] inputs set successively increasing noise levels on the audio signal. Testing requires plugging an existing Tiny Tapeout VGA project into the input, connecting the output to a VGA monitor, and selecting the control bits for the desired noise level.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_crispy_vga.review_notes: Summary expanded to four sentences covering the documented noise controls and test setup.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_demosiine_sda.summary: DemoSiine is a demoscene-style audio-visual project that generates a 640x480 VGA video signal and a looping ~28 second audio track. The video output includes dynamic wavy sine layers and a rainbowy overlay, with user controls to enable/disable layers, pause the animation, and toggle styles. The audio engine drives a frequency synthesizer to produce the soundtrack. It requires external hardware: a TinyVGA PMOD for video output, a TT Audio PMOD for audio output, and switches for input control.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_demosiine_sda.review_notes: Removed button (inputs are switches); added pmod, music, and video to match the PMOD hardware and audio/video outputs.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_devinatkin_pulse_width_co.summary: This design is a pulse width counter that measures the time high, time low, and period of an input square wave. It is accessible over a UART interface for reading the measured values. The design can be tested by feeding in a PWM signal and observing the output changes. No external hardware is required for the project to function.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_devinatkin_pulse_width_co.review_notes: Replaced incorrect clock/display tags with UART and counter tags based on the pulse width counter description.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_digital_clock_example.summary: This design is a simple digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes and seconds in 24-hour format. It shifts data over SPI to a MAX7219 to drive 7-segment displays. The time can be set using the hours_set and minutes_set inputs, with fast or slow increment rates. It requires a 5 MHz clock and a 32.768 kHz reference clock.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_digital_clock_example.review_notes: Removed unsupported education/CDC/synchronizer tags; added rtc, counter, spi, max7219 and 7-segment tags.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_bad_synchronizer.summary: This design is an example of a bad synchronizer based on Figure 29.3 from Dally & Harting. It exposes stage1, stage2, and stage3 signals along with a skew output for observing bit errors. Testing involves aligning and then separating the clocks to look for errors. The design is written in Verilog and requires an external clock source.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_bad_synchronizer.review_notes: Tags described an arithmetic divider; corrected to synchronizer/CDC example tags.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_loopback.summary: This design is a loopback tile with input skew measurement based on a previous project but for IHP30. It counts up to 10, one second at a time, and uses flip-flops to capture data. The design is intended to be tested by clocking the project and modifying timing to examine flip-flop capture reliability. It is written in Verilog and requires a skewable clock and data source.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_loopback.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary incorrectly describe an I2C Pmod communication interface, while the source describes a loopback tile with skew measurement.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8.summary: This design is an 8-bit signed/unsigned multiply and divide unit. It uses latches to capture two 8-bit inputs through a multiplexed interface and provides immediate or registered results. The divider reports overflow and divide-by-zero errors, while multiplier mode mutes error bits. The design is written in SpinalHDL and can be tested with an RP2040 and Python REPL.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_muldiv8.review_notes: Tags described a CPU with register file/ROM; corrected to multiplier/divider unit tags.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ringosc_5inv.summary: This design is a ring oscillator built from five inverters. It is enabled by setting ui[0] to 1. The outputs provide the oscillator signal divided by various factors from 1 to 32768. A frequency counter is required as external hardware to measure the output frequency.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_ringosc_5inv.review_notes: Corrected tags to reflect the ring oscillator and frequency divider outputs; removed unrelated demoscene and video tags.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.summary: This is an I2C bit error rate tester implemented in SpinalHDL. It is an I2C peripheral that implements an 8-bit ALU over I2C to allow pattern testing and read back accumulated results. It supports open-drain or push-pull modes and various clocking configurations set at power-on reset. The design is intended to be driven by an RP2040 controller and outputs results to a 7-segment display.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dlmiles_tt05_i2c_bert.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated process characterization structure; corrected to the documented I2C BERT.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_dvxf_dj8v.summary: DJ8 is an 8-bit CPU implemented in Verilog with a parallel Flash/RAM interface. It features an 8 x 8-bit register file, 3-4 cycles per instruction, a 15-bit external address bus, and an 8-bit external data bus. A built-in 256-byte demo ROM provides two demos selected by DIP switches at reset. It can connect to parallel flash or RAM and run at full speed without serialization overhead.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_dvxf_dj8v.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated restoring array divider; corrected to the documented DJ8 CPU.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_edwintorok.summary: This project is a demoscene competition entry written in HardCaml that outputs VGA video and PWM audio. Its pins match the Tiny VGA and TT Audio pinouts, with uo[0..7] carrying RGB, vsync and hsync and uio[7] providing a PWM output. A test mode input is provided on ui[0], and the design runs from a 25.25 MHz clock. A silicon tester reports it works as expected when tested with the Tiny VGA PMOD using default settings.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_edwintorok.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary invented a process-characterization test structure that the source does not describe.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module designed to verify all I/O pins of the ASIC. It operates in three modes: mirroring the dedicated inputs to the outputs, mirroring the bidirectional pins to the outputs, or outputting an 8-bit counter on both the outputs and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by the rst_n and sel pins. It requires no external hardware and is used during chip bring-up to confirm pin functionality.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed gpio because the design is a factory test module, not a general purpose IO interface.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_favoritohjs_scroller.summary: This design generates a scrolling pixelated cityscape video signal for VGA output. The terrain layers are produced using an LFSR to create deterministic randomness. It requires a Tiny VGA carrier board and a 25.18 MHz clock to display video. Silicon testing confirmed it works and produces a Tetris-like scrolling display.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_favoritohjs_scroller.review_notes: Removed demoscene tag; the source does not describe a demoscene-style showcase.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_fountaincoder_top_V2.summary: This is a multi-use dot product accelerator that can compute vector dot products, minimums, and maximums of data lists. It is a 4-bit system that loads data via index and data pins and produces a 12-bit result after at least 16 clock cycles. It is intended to be used as a coprocessor driven by an RP2040 for vector calculations. The design was tested using Verilator simulation, focusing on numerical stability.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_fountaincoder_top_V2.review_notes: Removed mac-unit and bit-serial tags because the source only documents 4-bit load/run operation and 16-cycle latency, not a MAC unit or one-bit serial path.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an input signal and displays the result on a dual seven-segment display. It debounces the input, counts transitions over a configurable period, and divides the count by ten for display. The period can be set via input pins to match the clock frequency for accurate measurements. It requires a dual seven-segment PMOD and a frequency source, and includes a debug mode for monitoring internal state.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_froith_goldcrest.summary: Goldcrest RISC-V is a microcoded RISC-V processor based on the SUBLEQ architecture. It interfaces with external SPI ROM and RAM, a UART, and GPIO pins, and supports three additional SPI devices. The design is intended to run at 20 MHz and requires external SPI memory chips and a UART connection. Testing has not yet been performed, so no silicon results are available.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_froith_goldcrest.review_notes: Removed unsupported coprocessor tag and added incomplete because testing is not yet possible.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_gray_sobel.summary: This project implements grayscale conversion and Sobel filtering for edge detection in images. Pixels are sent via SPI, and the processing mode is selected through input pins, with options for bypass, grayscale, Sobel, or combined grayscale and Sobel. An internal LFSR can generate test pixels. The design requires an external SPI master, such as a Raspberry Pi, to send and receive data.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_gray_sobel.review_notes: Removed edge-detector tag; it is ambiguous for image processing.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_hpretl_minilogix.summary: Minilogix is a configurable 8-bit input, 8-bit output logic block with optional internal feedback, intended to function like an FPGA logic element. It is loaded serially via dedicated pins and can be used for various logic functions once configuration software is available. Testing involves loading the logic block and applying digital inputs to verify the output. It requires only a way to set digital inputs and observe outputs.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_hpretl_spi.summary: This design implements a simple serial 16-bit register file with SPI-like interface and magic cookie detection. It also includes a 16-bit sigma-delta modulator of 1st or 2nd order and a sine generator based on a lookup table. The sine generator can be selected to drive the input of the DAC. The design is intended for testing the flow and can be tested by loading the shift register, checking the magic cookie detection, and monitoring the DAC output with an external RC lowpass filter.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_hpretl_spi.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the source; corrected to reflect the SPI test design.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.summary: This is a demoscene project that displays a bouncing capsule with background and text on a VGA output, accompanied by PDM audio. It includes input switches to pause, reset, mute, hide elements, lock colors, and disable re-orientation. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD (or compatible) for output. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition and runs at 25 MHz.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.review_notes: Removed speaker tag: PDM audio on uio pins is a digital audio output, not a driven speaker stage.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_cells.summary: This design is a multiplexer that allows selection of different IHP standard cells for testing. It uses page bits to select among cells and input bits to drive them, with outputs reflecting the selected cell's behavior. The documentation is minimal, with 'to be filled later' for how it works and how to test. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected, with manual testing of the mux and standard cells.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_cells.review_notes: Removed factory-test (no factory self-test described); added silicon-tested based on the working report.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_latch_test.summary: This is a latch test design that verifies the proper technology mapping of $_DLATCH_N_ and $_DLATCH_P_ cells. It provides a P latch and an N latch with enable and data inputs, and outputs to observe their behavior. The P latch is transparent when its enable is high, and the N latch when its enable is low. Silicon testing by both the author and an external tester confirmed correct operation.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_latch_test.review_notes: Removed characterization and added silicon-tested to match the working silicon reports.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_pg_1x1.summary: This project is a placeholder for a power-gated test design that was intended as preliminary work for supporting power-gated designs on later IHP shuttles. The documentation states that the pins and behavior are to be filled in later, and the author's silicon report confirms that the power gating experiments did not end up on the shuttle. No functional design was implemented, so there is nothing to test or use. The project is notable only as a reserved but unused slot.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_pg_1x2.summary: This project is a placeholder for a power gating test design on the IHP shuttle. Its documentation states that the how-it-works and how-to-test sections were to be filled later, and the author's silicon report confirms the power gating experiments did not end up on the shuttle.
