The pins are labeled TODO, and no functional logic was implemented. It was reserved as preliminary work toward supporting power gated designs on later IHP shuttles.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_pg_1x2.review_notes: Source describes a placeholder power-gating experiment; removed invented hardware tags and replaced with placeholder, incomplete, insufficient-doc, and power-gating.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: This project is a reconfigurable logic circuit built from identical rotatable tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop and a buffer. It is a port of the original ROTFPGA from Caravel to TinyTapeout, reduced to an 8x8 tile fabric with 8 inputs and 8 outputs. Configuration and reset use a scan chain, and the design was rewritten as hand-optimized gate-level Verilog. The author's silicon test report states that it works as expected.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Removed unsupported power-gating and latch tags; added fpga, reconfigurable, scan-chain, multi-tile, silicon-tested and gate-level based on the source and silicon report.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2_ff.summary: This project is a reconfigurable logic circuit built from identical rotatable tiles, arranged as a 1x2 tile design. It is a minor modification of ROTFPGA v2a that simulates latches using flip-flops and combines some inputs to make room for two extra inputs, serving as a control group for latch testing on IHP. The design includes scan chain input and output pins plus configuration and loop-breaker controls, and its test suite replaces each original clock tick with 50 latch clocks, a latch-and-flip-flop clock, and 50 more latch clocks. A silicon test report from the author states it works as expected, with no external hardware required.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2_ff.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated radio modulator; replaced with the documented reconfigurable FPGA-like fabric and its silicon-tested status.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.summary: This project is a 1-bit AM software-defined radio pipeline written in Verilog. It uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC frontend, oversampled and decimated 4096 times to gain extra precision. The core includes an SPI interface for setting demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs demodulated audio via PWM. The design spans 3x2 Tiny Tapeout tiles and is based on a Hackaday project by Alberto Garlassi.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.review_notes: Removed risc-v, cpu, soc, uart, qspi, and memory tags as unsupported; added radio, rf, dsp, spi, adc, demodulator, nco, audio, pwm, and multi-tile tags based on the source documentation.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_jayjaywong12.summary: This is a 4-bit vector multiplication engine that multiplies two vectors of up to 32 elements and accumulates the result into an 8-bit output. It is programmed via a register interface using read/write opcodes and a run command, and it operates in two clock cycles. The design is intended to be controlled by an RP2040 and requires no other external hardware. Silicon tests show it works, though timing adjustments were needed.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_jayjaywong12.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu/dsp tags and added mac-unit, rp2040, and silicon-tested based on the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_joerdsonsilva_modem.summary: This Verilog multimode modem performs digital modulation and demodulation using ASK, FSK, and PSK schemes. It uses a 10 MHz clock to generate digitized sinusoidal signals internally, and two selection inputs choose the modulation scheme. The modulated signal appears on mod_out pins and the recovered data appears on demod_out. Testing requires applying a 10 MHz clock, a reset pulse, and using selection inputs 01, 10, or 11 for ASK, FSK, or PSK respectively.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_joerdsonsilva_modem.review_notes: Replaced incorrect PUF/security draft tags with tags matching the documented multimode modem.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_kbeckmann_flame.summary: Flame demo displays a flame animation on a VGA monitor and plays simple 1-bit PWM audio. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and either Mike's audio PMOD or a basic RC filter for sound, and it runs at a 25 MHz clock with a reset pulse. Silicon testing by two independent testers confirmed that both audio and video work as expected, with good use of color and dithering. The design is a compact demoscene-style demo suitable for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.summary: This project is a baremetal RISC-V RV32E SoC based on the KianV architecture. It includes a UART, QSPI memory controller for flash and PSRAM, a generic SPI interface, and a sigma-delta emulator for audio playback. The CPU starts executing instructions from NOR flash at a 1 MiB offset. The design requires a PMOD flash and PSRAM module for operation.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the RISC-V SoC with UART, SPI, QSPI, and audio.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_meiniKi_ttihp_fazyrv_exot.summary: FazyRV-ExoTiny is a minimal System-on-Chip based on the FazyRV RISC-V core that uses external QSPI ROM and RAM for program storage and data memory. It converts Wishbone bus accesses into QSPI transfers, enabling continuous mode for the ROM to reduce latency, and supports Quad Mode for the RAM. The design requires external QSPI flash and RAM chips, such as the W25Q128JV and APS6404L-3SQR, and careful reset synchronization; its implementation is near the edge of timing convergence.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_multi_bit_puf_wrapper.summary: This project implements a one-bit PUF based on a difference of two registers. It contains an array of one-bit PUF cells addressed by addr to read out OUT_BITS PUF bits. The output is zero in the reset condition. The documentation is sparse and does not describe the implementation in detail.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_multi_bit_puf_wrapper.review_notes: Removed unsupported PRNG, register-file, and crypto tags; summary now reflects the documented PUF array.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommy.summary: This Verilog design is a 12-hour clock rendered as triangles using a race-the-beam triangle renderer. A state machine incrementally rasterizes three triangles from their edge equations while generating VGA timing, and each frame updates the second, minute, and hour hands from lookup tables. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a TinyVGA adapter and VGA monitor to view. Input pins advance the minute and hour hands, and the silicon-tested clock was confirmed to run on time and respond to adjustments.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_no_time_for_squares_tommy.review_notes: Replaced incorrect PUF/security draft tags with tags matching the documented and silicon-tested VGA clock.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_oled_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an external signal by counting pulses over 100 ms periods and displays the result on a 128x32 SSD1306 OLED display using an emulated 7-segment format. It requires an external 1 MHz clock, a PMOD OLED display, and the signal to be measured connected to the input pin. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and uses SPI to communicate with the OLED. No silicon test results are provided, so the actual performance is not documented.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_one_bit_puf_wrapper.summary: This project implements a one-bit PUF based on a difference of two registers. It is written in Verilog and has a start signal input and a single PUF output. The output is 0 in the reset condition. The documentation is sparse and does not describe the implementation in detail.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_one_bit_puf_wrapper.review_notes: Removed incomplete tag and added Verilog; summary corrected to match the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_phansel_laplace_lut.summary: This design is a read-only memory that stores ASCII encodings of LaTeX code for a few dozen Laplace transforms, generated by a Python script from the LaTeX source. The user selects a transform index on the lower six input pins, toggles reset, then asserts the character output enable to clock out the transform characters one at a time. The left-hand side output shows the transformed function F(s) and the right-hand side output shows the original function f(t), padded with spaces when lengths differ. External switches or jumpers are needed to set the input address and enable signals, and LEDs on the outputs help observe the characters.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_phansel_laplace_lut.review_notes: Removed lookup-table tag as the design is a ROM, not a lookup-table logic block; trimmed unsupported verification claim from summary.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_pulse_generator.summary: This is a simple TTL pulse generator that produces one of sixteen pre-programmed pulse sequences selected by a 4-bit input. The selected sequence appears on a single TTL output pin, and the design is intended to be tested by setting the sequence select pins and observing the output. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself, though the documentation does not describe the sequences or their timing. The documentation is very thin, providing only the basic function and pin usage.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_pulse_generator.review_notes: Removed counter: the source describes sequence selection through pre-programmed patterns, not a counter.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.summary: This design implements an iterative multiply-and-accumulate (MAC) unit intended for machine learning accelerators. It performs a 7x8-bit multiplication and adds a third operand provided on the bidirectional pins, with the result output on uo_out. The design uses a reset to latch the first operand and then accepts the second operand each clock cycle. Testing is described as complex, with full instructions to be added later, and it requires a CPU to supply input data.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.review_notes: Removed alu, dsp, and neural-network as unsupported by the source, which describes a MAC unit for ML accelerators.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_ravenslofty_chess.summary: This is a chess move generator implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a 256-bit chessboard and a 64-bit square-enable mask to compute attacks and arbitrate the most promising move. The design is intended to be driven by an external RP2040 microprocessor, as the chip lacks the space to run the full game logic. It is tested using a provided test suite.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_ravenslofty_chess.review_notes: Removed fsm (not described) and added rp2040 and arbiter which are supported by the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_colorbars.summary: This design generates a VGA test pattern resembling NTSC color bars, with optional station ID display, scrolling ID, and scrolling bars. It is configured through input pins for showing the ID, using a custom ID, scrolling the ID, and scrolling the bars, and it outputs RGB and sync signals on the Tiny VGA pinout. A TinyVGA PMOD is required to connect to a VGA monitor, and the colors are explicitly not accurate to real NTSC color bars. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester noted the clock must be manually set to 25 MHz in the commander app.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large selection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to show the first flag, move to the next or previous flag, or select a flag by index. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a monitor. The design is extensible by adding new flag modules and updating the index, as described in the documentation. No silicon test reports are provided, but the documentation is clear about usage and configuration.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed overly generic video tag and added pmod tag supported by external hardware.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This is a Verilog replica of the AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, providing three square-wave tone channels, a white noise generator, and an envelope generator with ten shapes. It is programmed through a multiplexed data/address bus with bus control pins, and it outputs digital 8-bit audio as well as PWM signals for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are needed to hear the audio, and the design includes a configurable clock divider to match different clock frequencies. The project is notable for its thorough test suite and goal of hardware preservation, fitting on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Removed dac since conversion is external; added sound-generator and retro for the classic PSG replica.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This design is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square-wave tone channels, a noise generator with white and periodic modes, and 16 levels of attenuation per channel. It is controlled via an 8-bit data bus with a write-enable pin, and it provides digital 8-bit audio output plus PWM outputs for each channel and a master audio output. External hardware such as a DAC, RC filter, amplifier, and speaker are required to produce sound, and the design includes a configurable clock divider. The project emphasizes hardware preservation and includes a comprehensive test suite, fitting on a single tile.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.review_notes: Removed dac tag because the chip does not include a DAC, and added chiptune for the classic PSG replica.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_vga_logo.summary: This design displays a 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor, using compressed data and dithered colors to fit into a single tile. It generates standard VGA signals including red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for operation, and it has been tested successfully by a silicon tester who confirmed the video works as expected. Notable features include the large resolution crammed into a small area and the use of dithering for color effects.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.summary: This design is an audio/visual demo that generates VGA video and PWM audio outputs, forming an 8-part megademo. It uses eight PWM audio pins and standard VGA pins for red, green, blue, and sync signals. The demo requires external hardware: a VGA PMOD and audio output hardware. Silicon tests report that both audio and video work as expected, and one tester described it as a very nice demo with polished graphics and audio.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.summary: This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer input, returning the orbit length and an indicator of the maximum value reached. The input number is uploaded byte-by-byte into a 144-bit register via an address bus, and the computation is started with a pin; the busy indicator is polled until completion, after which the results are read back in 16-bit chunks. The design is intended for brute-force searching of path records, and the documentation explains the state machine and I/O protocol in detail. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.review_notes: Removed alu and register-file tags not supported by the source; added fsm, verilog and esoteric.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_silice.summary: This is a demoscene demo for Tiny Tapeout that generates both VGA video and audio, using the Tiny VGA and audio PMODs. It is written in Silice and can be simulated on an ECPIX5 with a VGA PMOD and an I2S audio PMOD, or the audio can run on an ULX3S using its DAC. The author reports that the design works as expected when tested with the PMODs. The design is part of a demoscene competition and combines video and audio in a small area.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_silice.review_notes: Removed verilog (Silice source) and added silicon-tested based on the working test report.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_simon_cipher.summary: This is a bit-serial implementation of the SIMON-128 lightweight block cipher, trading throughput for a compact area dominated by flip-flops and multiplexers. A 2-bit control word on ui[7:6] selects idle, plaintext load, key load, or encrypt, with serial data entering on ui[0] and ciphertext emerging on uo[0] over 128 consecutive clock cycles, flagged by a valid bit on uo[7]. The design is verified through a testbench containing example test vectors, and no external hardware is required. The documentation notes a limitation in the key-loading process and includes a debug bit to verify key register loading.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_snow.summary: This is a demoscene demo for Tiny Tapeout that produces a VGA video effect and audio, using the Tiny VGA and audio PMODs. It is written in Silice and is intended to be run by plugging in the PMODs, with a silicon test report confirming it works as expected with the Tiny VGA PMOD. The documentation is extremely sparse, providing only a one-line description and a rhetorical question, so little is known about the specific visual or audio content. The design is notable for being part of a demoscene competition and for fitting on a single tile.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_snow.review_notes: Removed verilog because the source language is Silice.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.summary: This design implements a stochastic multiplier, adder and self-multiplier using serial bit streams, with an LFSR-based stochastic number generator and a digital quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron as an application. Numbers are entered as two repeating 9-bit serial streams and results are read out serially on separate output pins. Testing requires an ADALM2000 to generate and capture the serial streams. The documentation is largely a reference list with images, so the exact internal architecture is only partly described.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo with an animated color gradient on a VGA monitor at 640x480 resolution. It uses the TinyVGA PMOD for video output and provides two configuration inputs: one to tile the logo across the screen and another to use a solid color instead of the gradient. Silicon testing confirmed that the design works correctly in default, tiled, and solid color modes at standard VGA clock and even up to 32 MHz. The design is a simple graphics demo with no external components beyond the VGA PMOD.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.review_notes: Added silicon-tested because the source reports working silicon test results.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_toivoh_demo_deluxe.summary: Sequential Shadows Deluxe is an extended version of the TT08 demo competition entry, adding a shadow beneath the logo and credits, with support for both TinyVGA and Digilent Pmod VGA pinouts. It requires a VGA PMOD and an audio PMOD, and it includes the same controls as the original for pausing, stepping frames, and disabling bass or drums. The design was tested on hardware by the author and confirmed to work similarly to the simulation. Documentation refers to the original version for details, and the deluxe version offers additional visual tweaks.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_toivoh_retro_console.summary: This design is an 8½ bit retro console with sprite and tile graphics plus a synthesizer. The PPU generates a stream of pixels for VGA output based on tile graphics, map, sprite data, and palette registers. The synth context-switches between voices at 96 kHz to produce audio samples. Testing requires an RP2040 RAM emulator and a VGA Pmod, with sound output left to the RP2040.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_toivoh_retro_console.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated UART transmitter summary and tags with retro console, VGA, graphics, sprite, audio, synthesizer, RP2040, and Pmod tags based on the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_tomkeddie_a.summary: This is a simple VGA tennis game where four input pins move the left and right paddles and additional inputs reset the score and select the ball speed. It outputs VGA signals through a Pmod, with a pin option selecting between mole99 and Digilent VGA pinouts. The design needs a VGA Pmod and a monitor plus buttons to play. The documentation is brief and does not describe the internal game logic in detail.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_tomkeddie_b.summary: This design is a simple UART transmitter that continuously sends a fixed set of strings on four separate output pins. The clock input is used directly to set the baud rate, so applying a 115200 Hz clock yields 115200 baud. It is tested by connecting one of the outputs to an asynchronous serial receiver. No external hardware beyond a serial port is required, and the documentation is very short.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_tommythorn_maxbw.summary: This design is an asynchronous multiplier that emits the sequence r = x^2 + x for x = 0, 1, 2, ... using a four-phase bundled-data handshake. Internally it uses 26-bit precision but folds the result down to 15 output bits with r ^ (r >> 15). It is tested by tying ack to req for free-running operation and observing the outputs, optionally with a logic analyzer or RP2040. The author notes that timing analysis is still in progress and the inserted delays are likely oversized.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_top_mole99.summary: This SystemVerilog design produces an 800x600 60 Hz SVGA output with a background and a single 12x12 sprite, internally rendered at 100x75 and scaled up. An SPI receiver accepts commands to replace sprite data, change colors, set the background and move the sprite, with the Tiny Tapeout logo shown by default. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod for output and an SPI master for configuration. The design is deliberately limited to one sprite, as the name suggests.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_top_mole99.review_notes: The vga tag is inaccurate because the source describes SVGA 800x600 output, not VGA.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.summary: This is a configurable ring oscillator built from up to 3853 inverters, with taps at chain lengths of 1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 21, 51, 101, 201, 501, 1001, 2001, 3001 and 3853. The ring is enabled by connecting one of the tap outputs back to the ring_in input, and the resulting frequency is measured externally. A scope or logic analyzer is needed to measure the output frequency and the delay between different points in the chain. The design is intended for characterizing inverter delay and oscillator behavior on the process.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.review_notes: The logic-gate, standard-cell, and instrumentation tags are not well supported; characterization and process-experiment better describe the purpose.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_silife_max.summary: This project is a silicon implementation of Conway's Game of Life on an 8x32 grid, with optional output to a MAX7219 LED dot matrix. It supports both manual mode, where the grid is loaded row by row, and a demo mode that cycles through pre-defined patterns. The game advances one generation per clock cycle when enabled, or every 0.4 seconds in demo mode with a 10 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it works well with the LED matrix, though a delay before animation starts was noted, and one tester reported issues with demo patterns progressing.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_spell.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF, with 256 bytes of program memory, a 32-byte stack and 32 bytes of data memory. Programs and internal registers are loaded and inspected through a serial shift-register interface controlled by run, step, load, dump and register-select pins. It also exposes eight bidirectional and eight output-only pins as I/O ports. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable for implementing a complete esoteric language interpreter in hardware.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_spell.review_notes: Removed unsupported security tag and added cpu, stack-machine, esoteric, and shift-register which are directly supported.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_sram_test.summary: This design is a controller and test harness for a foundry-provided 1024x8 SRAM macro, allowing single-byte reads and writes through 10 address lines, 8 data lines and a write-enable. The lower six address bits are direct inputs while the upper four are held in an address bank register selected by bank_sel. It is tested by writing and reading back values across addresses, and silicon testing passed with all values at a few addresses and random values over 2M cycles. No external hardware is needed.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_urish_sram_test.review_notes: Added silicon-tested based on the reported successful silicon test.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_vc32_cpu.summary: This project implements a 16-bit RISC-V CPU with a memory management unit in Verilog. It uses an external RAM system for program and data storage, with separate buses for read data, address/data, and control signals. Testing requires that external RAM be connected, as the CPU cannot run standalone. The design is noted as a CPU plus MMU, but the documentation is brief and gives few details beyond the pin names and the need for external RAM.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_vc32_cpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added multi-tile because the design occupies 6x2 tiles.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttihp0p2/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.summary: Glyph Mode is a standalone VGA demo submitted for the VGA Demoscene competition. It generates a display and allows palette selection via two input pins, choosing between green, red, blue, or pride color schemes. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA monitor, and operates at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, including palette changes, and it also functions at higher clock speeds.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.review_notes: Removed text tag; the source does not describe text rendering.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_wokwi_392873974467527681.summary: This design drives a 7-segment display to show the text PILIPINASLASALLE one character per clock cycle, with the decimal point toggling each cycle. It also has a manual mode where a 4-bit BCD input selects which character to display. It is based on a Wokwi project and requires an external 7-segment display. Silicon tests confirm it works in default mode, and a second tester verified both modes, noting that a slow clock is needed and the demoboard clock button is poorly debounced.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.summary: This is a test structure that captures data on both edges of a clock using pulse generators of varying widths, with outputs for each width and a normal flop. It is intended to explore DDR throughput and flop aperture using Analog Discovery 3 hardware. The documentation is minimal and self-deprecating, stating the design is probably bad. It is a timing characterization experiment rather than a functional block.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.review_notes: Adjusted tags to characterization and edge-detector; removed unsupported clock-generator, flip-flop and instrumentation tags.

ttihp0p2/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttihp0p2/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_NicklausThompson_555_1x1.summary: This project provides a single high-speed comparator built with SiGe NPN heterojunction bipolar transistors. It compares two analog inputs and outputs a mostly-digital signal, with an enable pin controlling the comparator. Testing involves setting the enable high, applying analog signals between 0.0 V and 1.2 V to the inputs, and observing the output. No external hardware is required, and the documentation notes that there is no power gating, so the comparator should be disabled when not in use.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_NicklausThompson_555_1x1.review_notes: Removed power-gating because the source explicitly states no power gating is implemented; added comparator-analog for the analog comparator function.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.summary: This is a standalone VGA and sound demo that loops after about 25 seconds, developed for a 48 MHz clock and using a non-standard 1220-pixel horizontal VGA mode with RGB222 dithered output. It generates sound through a 16-bit sigma-delta DAC on one pin from an internal three-channel synthesizer with triangle, noise, and square waves. The graphics include a procedurally rendered plane, a starfield from an LFSR, and a TT08 logo, with a soundtrack based on a riff from a demoscene track. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and either a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or a simple RC filter for sound, and silicon tests confirm it works as expected.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_a1k0n_demo.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag to match the working silicon test reports.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_antonalog.summary: This design contains a rough 24-bit VGA DAC with a digital control block for testing different modes. It outputs analog RGB signals on ua pins and digital sync and blanking signals, and includes various test patterns selectable via input mode pins. Silicon test reports indicate that some patterns are fine, some are distorted, and the VGA screen occasionally loses sync, but the analog output looked good in scope shots. It requires a VGA monitor and likely a Tiny VGA PMOD for connection.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_antonalog.review_notes: Removed silicon-tested (status is partial) and instrumentation; added mixed-signal for the analog DAC plus digital control block.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_fun_vga_clock.summary: This design is a VGA clock demo that shows a bouncing ball animation over an adaptation of Matt Venn's VGA clock. It produces 640x480 60Hz VGA timing with RGB222 colour outputs compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Inputs allow adjusting hours, minutes, and seconds, and selecting between Tiny VGA and Matt's VGA Clock PMODs. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a VGA monitor, and the appropriate PMOD, and the seconds timer assumes an exact 25.000 MHz clock.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_fun_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed clock-generator/counter/game as unsupported; added rtc, pmod, and video based on the documented clock and VGA PMOD functionality.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_ro_worker.summary: This design includes a simple digital counter that can be driven by either an external clock or an internal ring oscillator. Data is loaded through a shift interface, and the counter runs as fast as possible to produce a result that can be read back. Testing involves selecting the internal clock, loading a starting value and cycle count, and observing that the output is the starting value plus the counter value. An oscilloscope is recommended to measure the actual speed, and the ring oscillator frequency divided by 16 is expected to be between 12.5 MHz and 25 MHz.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_algofoogle_ro_worker.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and instrumentation as unsupported; added shift-register because the documented load/readback interface is a shift register.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_arud4172_ROOTS_vga.summary: This design displays a bouncing ROOTS logo with a kaleidoscope background and an animated colour gradient on a VGA monitor. It is configured through input pins, though the documentation does not specify what each input controls. The design requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD for connection. It is a visual demo with no other external hardware requirements.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_arud4172_ROOTS_vga.review_notes: Removed generic display/art tags and added demoscene and silicon-art to match the visual showcase nature of the design.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_bleeptrack_prism.summary: This design is a visual demo that shows a hypnotic prism floating in a starry night on a VGA monitor. It has no control inputs and simply runs when connected to a VGA display. The design requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD interface. The documentation is minimal and provides no additional details about the implementation or testing.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_calonso88_spi_test.summary: This design implements an SPI peripheral with eight read/write 8-bit registers and eight read-only 8-bit status registers, derived from the tt07_alu_74181 project. It is tested by connecting an RP2040 SPI master to the SPI pins and using MicroPython code to write and read registers, with the first register also driving a 7-segment display. The design improves on the original by using a single buffer counter and adding high-impedance control for MISO when chip select is high. No external hardware is required beyond the RP2040 and the 7-segment display.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_calonso88_spi_test.review_notes: Removed rp2040 because the RP2040 is only an external test host, not a designed-for interface.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_colorful_stripes.summary: This is an analog design intended to generate colorful stripes when viewed under a microscope. It is tested by viewing the chip under a microscope or smartphone camera. The design has essentially no documentation beyond the one-line description and a single unconnected input pin. It is notable only as a simple optical experiment.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_digital_clock_example.summary: This design implements a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format. It uses SPI to drive a MAX7219 7-segment display driver because there are not enough output pins to directly control six 7-segment displays. The time can be set using dedicated buttons for hours and minutes, with a fast/slow adjustment mode and a 12-hour mode option. The design requires an external MAX7219 module and a 32.768 kHz reference clock for accurate timekeeping.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_digital_clock_example.review_notes: Removed rtc and clock-generator tags that are not supported by the source.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_htfab_r2r_dac.summary: This project implements a basic 8-bit R-2R resistor ladder DAC using 25 identical resistors plus two dummies. It is tested by applying a binary input on ui_in[7:0] and measuring the analog output voltage on ua[0] with a multimeter, ADC, or oscilloscope. Silicon test reports indicate it is working, though the tester noted a discontinuity on the MSB and imperfect grounding. It requires external measurement equipment to observe the output.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_htfab_yadge.summary: This is a remix of Uri's Colorful Stripes experiment, intended to generate a colorful pattern when viewed under a microscope. It is tested by viewing the chip under a microscope or smartphone camera. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the one-line description and a single unconnected input pin. It is notable only as a variant of an existing optical experiment.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_ihp_logo_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing IHP logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo, use a solid color, or use a white background, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_lfsr_stevej.summary: This project implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register that produces a pseudo-random sequence. It is used by reading the output pins, which change on each clock cycle, and can be seeded by setting the write enable pin high while providing a seed on the input pins. No external hardware is needed other than a way to read the output pins. The design is a straightforward LFSR implementation with no notable limitations mentioned.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_lfsr_stevej.review_notes: Summary is accurate; no tag changes needed.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_rte_eink_driver.summary: This is a Verilog driver for the Adafruit 2.13-inch e-ink display, which uses the SSD1680 chipset. It generates eight simple patterns in real time and sends them via SPI, with a special mode to copy SRAM contents to the display. It requires the specific e-ink display and a bundle of jumper wires to connect to the PMOD. The design is notable for its low memory overhead and ability to put the display into deep sleep while retaining the image.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_sathworld_spi_pwm_periphe.summary: This design is an SPI-connected PWM generator with eight outputs, featuring two independent generators and four total PWM channels. The documentation is essentially empty, with no explanation of how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware is needed. The pin names indicate SPI communication and PWM outputs, but no further details are provided. It is not possible to describe the design's operation or testing from the available information.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_sathworld_spi_pwm_periphe.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc; removed signal-generator as redundant with pwm.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_strau0106_simple_viii.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit CPU architecture implemented in SystemVerilog. It interfaces with external QSPI flash and RAM memories through dedicated chip select and data pins. The design is intended to be a minimal CPU, but the documentation is very sparse, providing only the title and pin names without detailed operation or testing instructions. No silicon test results are available.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_urish_dickson_pump.summary: This project implements a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that boosts voltage. It is tested by applying a 2 MHz clock signal to the clk input and measuring the output voltage on ua[0], which should rise to approximately 3.2 V. No external hardware is specified beyond a clock source and a voltage measurement device. The design is a simple analog voltage booster with minimal documentation.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_urish_dickson_pump.review_notes: Removed power-management tag; the design is a charge pump, not a power management application.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttihp0p3/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttihp0p3/tt_um_zerotoasic_logo_screensav.summary: This design displays a bouncing Zero to ASIC logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo or use a solid color, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.
ttihp0p3/tt_um_zerotoasic_logo_screensav.review_notes: silicon-art mislabels a VGA screensaver; demoscene better matches the visual demo intent.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported display tag and added button for the documented direction inputs.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_MichaelBell_photo_frame.summary: This design reads RGB332 pixel data from a QSPI flash memory and displays it on a VGA screen, with configurable timing and latency. It is used by flashing an image to QSPI flash, setting configuration registers via a shift register interface, and enabling the display. External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod and a Tiny VGA Pmod. The design supports up to 720p and 1024x768 resolutions and allows switching between multiple images stored in flash.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_MichaelBell_photo_frame.review_notes: Removed 'memory' tag because the design uses external QSPI flash rather than implementing a memory block.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_SotaSoC.summary: SotaSoC is a RISC-V 32-bit embedded system-on-chip with an RV32IC core and peripherals including SPI, I2C, UART, PWM, and GPIO. It is used by connecting a QSPI Pmod for program storage and optionally other peripherals like an ST7789 LCD, with software support for FreeRTOS and bare-metal. External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod, LEDs, and an optional SPI LCD. The design is notable for its configurability and support for FPGA prototyping, but no silicon test results are provided.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_SotaSoC.review_notes: Removed pwm tag as it is an output tag not matching the SoC's primary interface; added missing interface and type tags supported by pins and text.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_YannGuidon_TinyScanChain.summary: This project is a low-footprint scan chain designed for the iHP PDK / SG13CMOS5L process. It uses a single chain with a rate of one bit per byte and a granularity of 4 steps but only 3 actual data bits, with clock pulses in bursts of 8. The scan chain includes control signals SC_RESET, SC_CLK, SC_GET, SC_SET, SC_DIN, and SC_DOUT, plus extra input and output pins. It is intended to be hooked up to a microcontroller or CPU for testing.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_YannGuidon_TinyScanChain.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented scan chain design.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.summary: This project is a framebuffer-less VGA ray casting game engine inspired by Wolfenstein 3D. It renders textured walls, flat-colored floor and ceiling, and optional doors. The player's point of view and visual effects are controlled via an SPI interface. It supports internally generated or external QSPI textures.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_algofoogle_raybox_zero.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe an ALU with registers and 7-segment display, but the source describes a VGA ray casting game demo.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_algofoogle_vgaringosc.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator built from manually instantiated inverter cells, which can optionally drive a counter whose value is displayed as vertical colour bars on a VGA monitor. The user selects the number of inverter stages via input pins and can also choose an external clock or a VGA mode. A Tiny VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor are required for visual output, and the oscillator output is also available on bidirectional pins for measurement. The project targets oscillator frequencies from about 20 MHz up to 855 MHz and is a resubmission of an earlier design to a different PDK.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_algofoogle_vgaringosc.review_notes: Corrected the implementation tags: manual inverter instantiation is full-custom, not transistor-level or standard-cell.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_calonso88_spi_i2c_reg_ban.summary: This Verilog project implements a register bank that can be accessed through either SPI or I2C, with the interface selected by a digital input pin. The SPI interface uses standard cpol, cpha, cs_n, clk, mosi, and miso signals, while the I2C interface uses sda and scl with a configurable 3-bit address. Writing to the first register is intended to control LEDs on the demo board, and the remaining outputs are spare. External pull-up resistors may be needed on the I2C lines depending on the host, and the documentation notes that this is to be checked later.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_chatelao_fp8_multiplier.summary: This Verilog design is a streaming multiply-accumulate unit supporting the OCP MXFP8 microscaling formats, including E4M3 and E5M2, with hardware-accelerated shared scaling for AI inference. It receives two 8-bit data streams on the input and bidirectional pins and produces an 8-bit output stream. A Tiny Tapeout DevKit with a provided MicroPython driver can be used for quick prototyping, while a Sipeed Tang Nano 4K with an FPGA bitstream and Cortex-M3 testbench is available for high-speed testing. The design is notable for implementing a compact floating-point MAC core for sub-8-bit AI workloads.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_digital_clock_example.summary: This design implements a digital desk clock that displays hours, minutes, and seconds in 24-hour format. It uses SPI to drive a MAX7219 7-segment display driver because there are not enough output pins to directly control six 7-segment displays. The time can be set using dedicated buttons for hours and minutes, with a fast/slow adjustment mode and a 12-hour mode option. The design requires an external MAX7219 module and a 32.768 kHz reference clock for accurate timekeeping.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_digital_clock_example.review_notes: Removed rtc and clock-generator tags that are not supported by the source.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_essen.summary: This design performs bfloat16 multiplication. It accepts two values as four bytes over four cycles with a valid signal and produces the result byte-wise along with valid and early-valid indicators. No external hardware is required and testing is not documented beyond informal notes. It is a very fast but little-documented bfloat16 multiplier.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_essen.review_notes: Removed unsupported pipeline and insufficient-doc tags, added multiplier/floating-point/bit-serial/sequential-logic, and rewrote the summary to match the thin source.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_float_synth_nikleberg.summary: This design implements an 8-bit floating-point multiplier in the E4M3 format, computing y = a * b with a latency of six clock cycles. It takes two 8-bit inputs from the UI and UIO pins and outputs the 8-bit result, which can be observed on a seven-segment display, though the display is not easily interpretable. The design is a demonstration of synthesizing the VHDL-2008 IEEE.float_pkg for a multiplier that truncates toward zero and saturates on overflow. It has a default clock of 50 MHz and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout demo board and optionally a PMOD or TT Commander for input.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_float_synth_nikleberg.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; retained floating-point, multiplier, pipeline, 7-segment supported by detailed documentation.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_flummer_ltc.summary: This project generates Linear Timecode (LTC) for audio and video synchronization, using counters to track time and frame count and emitting 80-bit biphase-mark-coded frames on a single pin. It adds I2C control for setting timecode and user bits, with framerate, drop-frame, color-frame, and background-format flags on ui[2..7], and debug outputs including a seven-segment framerate display. It is designed to work with the Tiny Tapeout Audio PMOD for line-level output, and I2C requires pull-ups and a host such as a Bus Pirate. This is a v2 revision of a design previously taped out on several shuttles, and the documentation is detailed about wiring and testing.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_flummer_ltc.review_notes: Removed modulator (timecode generator, not a general modulator); added timer and instrumentation.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_glyph_mode_hd.summary: This design is a standalone VGA demo that produces a Matrix-like digital rain animation on a VGA monitor. It supports four different VGA timing modes, selectable via input pins, and allows the user to choose between different colour palettes. The circuit requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, and it must be clocked at or near 25.175 MHz for the default mode. It is notable for being a visual demo with programmable display options and no external processing requirements.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.summary: Asicle v2 is a hardware implementation of the Wordle word-guessing game, rewritten for Tiny Tapeout after an earlier version on the Google-Skywater shuttle. It uses a QSPI Pmod for external flash to store the word list and font bitmaps, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output, and a Gamepad Pmod or direct input pins for controls. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and requires flashing a data file to the QSPI Pmod before play. It fits a complete game into a 2x2 tile area by moving data off-chip, and includes debug features for showing or re-rolling the solution.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; added retro for the Wordle-style game; trimmed unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.summary: ROTFPGA v2 is a reconfigurable logic circuit built from identical tiles, each containing a NAND gate, a D flip-flop and a buffer, that can be individually rotated or mirrored according to configuration. It is a port of the original ROTFPGA from Caravel to TinyTapeout, reduced from 24x24 to 8x8 tiles with 8 inputs and 8 outputs. Configuration and reset use a routing-efficient scan chain, and tiles are written as hand-optimized gate-level Verilog with configuration stored in latches. The test suite sets up two configurations and runs upload, download, single-step, propagation and loop-breaker tests.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_htfab_rotfpga2.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a VGA/SPI video tool with no basis in the source; replaced with fabric-related tags.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_lisa.summary: The LISA 8-bit microcontroller is a complete system-on-chip with 128 bytes of flop-based RAM, designed to run programs assembled or compiled by a custom toolchain. It includes multiple communication interfaces such as UART, SPI, and I2C, and its pins are multiplexed to support various functions, including autobaud detection and division. The design is tested using a C-based assembler, linker, and C compiler, along with a Python debugger that can program flash memory, control the core, and read back data. The toolchain is still a work in progress, with the C compiler not fully functional and lacking floating-point support, but the assembler and linker are operational.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_lisa.review_notes: Summary and tags are supported; no changes required.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_lledoux_bf16_diminished_k.summary: This design provides a streaming byte-fed accumulator generated from an MLIR for-loop pattern, implementing a specialized S3FDP accumulator for bfloat16 multiplication and addition. It is part of a toolflow that detects loop patterns and emits optimized arithmetic circuits instead of generic floating-point datapaths. The design has a byte-wide input and output interface and requires no external hardware. It is notable for being generated automatically from MLIR and for its use of the Kulisch accumulator architecture.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_lledoux_bf16_diminished_k.review_notes: Removed alu because the source describes a specialized MLIR-generated accumulator, not a general ALU; added systemverilog and multi-tile from the stated language and tile count.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_lledoux_s3fdp_seqcomb.summary: This design implements a streaming byte-fed IEEE754 per-operation sequential and combinational accumulation core, generated from an MLIR for-loop pattern. The MLIR flow detects a loop with multiplication and addition and emits a specialized S3FDP accumulator, avoiding generic floating-point logic. The design has a byte-wide input and output interface and requires no external hardware. It is notable for being automatically generated from MLIR and for its use of the S3FDP architecture.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_lledoux_s3fdp_seqcomb.review_notes: Removed unsupported ALU tag and added mac-unit and systemverilog tags supported by the multiply-accumulate core and language.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_microlane_demo.summary: This project scrolls the text "hardened using python" across a 7-segment display. It is a demo for the microlane hardening flow and is intended to be run with a slow clock such as 5 Hz. No external hardware is required beyond the display itself. The documentation is brief and does not explain the microlane flow or the hardening results.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_microlane_demo.review_notes: Added ascii tag for the text-scrolling behaviour; summary unchanged.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_miniMAC.summary: The miniMAC_5L is a 16-bit scrambler/framer/error detector designed for the IHP SG2CMOS5L PDK, intended for high-speed serial communication. It encodes and decodes 18-bit words using a gPEAC and Hammer18 scheme, with a pipelined architecture that processes 9-bit half-words and has a latency of five cycles, plus an additional three cycles in loopback mode. The circuit can operate in encode, decode, or loopback mode, with control signals for data enable and output enable, and it provides error and zero flags. It requires custom external hardware for full testing and is notable for its use of a specialized PDK and its ability to chain multiple chips.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_miniMAC.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects errors, and added crc for the Hammer18 scrambler.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_nicklausthompson_twi_moni.summary: This design is a Two-Wire Interface (I2C) bus monitor that passively captures I2C frames and outputs the captured data over a UART at 115200 baud. It does not act as an I2C slave; instead, it shifts in the bus data and formats it into three bytes per frame: the address and read/write bit, the data byte, and the acknowledge bits. The monitor requires an external UART-to-USB adapter to view the output on a PC. It runs at 50 MHz and cannot currently capture repeated I2C frames, but it has been tested on an FPGA.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_pakesson_glitcher.summary: This design is a fault injection pulse generator with configurable parameters, controllable over UART. It implements a state machine with idle, target reset, delay, pulse active, and pulse spacing phases, and provides outputs for pulse, target reset, busy, armed, and a combined pulse-or-reset signal. The trigger input is synchronized and active high, with a minimum trigger-to-pulse latency of 60-80 ns. External hardware such as a MOSFET, analog switch, or ChipSHOUTER is required to perform voltage or electromagnetic fault injection.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_prism_lite.summary: This design is a programmable finite state machine (FSM) that can be configured via a bitstream called a 'chroma' generated by a custom Yosys fork. The FSM has 7 inputs, 8 outputs, and a UART interface, along with an SPI interface for loading the configuration. To use it, the user defines an FSM in Verilog, generates a chroma bitstream using the provided tools, and loads it into the device via UART or SPI. The project is notable for its use of a custom open-source toolchain and for enabling rapid prototyping of custom FSM-based controllers.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_prism_lite.review_notes: Added spi: the pinout exposes spi_miso, spi_cs_n, spi_clk and spi_mosi.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_silicon_strummer.summary: Silicon Strummer turns a VGA monitor into a playable guitar fretboard with an 8x6 grid of notes. The user moves a cursor with four buttons and holds a fifth button to output a square wave tone at the selected note's frequency. The design uses a counter to generate the tone and is tested by connecting a VGA monitor and audio output. It is notable for combining real-time graphics and audio on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_snake_game.summary: This design implements the classic Snake game, where the player controls a snake to eat food and grow while avoiding collisions with walls and itself. The game state is displayed on a VGA monitor, and the player uses four directional buttons plus optional pause and restart buttons. It provides a PWM audio output and exposes game state signals such as failure, success, eat, and tick for external hardware like a scoreboard. The design requires a VGA PMOD, optional audio PMOD, and buttons, and is notable for being a complete game implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_snake_game.review_notes: Removed pmod tag since detected pinouts are Tiny VGA and TT Audio, not a Pmod interface; added scoreboard as the source explicitly mentions it.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_spongent88.summary: This chip is a hardware accelerator for the Spongent-88/80/8 lightweight hash function, intended as the cryptographic primitive for Winternitz One-Time Signatures (W-OTS), a post-quantum secure signature scheme. It communicates through the standard Tiny Tapeout pin interface with data input, data output, busy, out_valid, and address/strobe signals. No external hardware is required, but for W-OTS use, a host microcontroller handles key generation, storage, and protocol logic. The design is notable for providing a compact hardware implementation of a hash function suitable for post-quantum cryptography.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_tinymoa_ihp0p4_16x16.summary: This project implements a 16x16 digital compute-in-memory (DCIM) array core. It provides an array that can be written to and executed, with results read out via dedicated pins. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets an experimental IHP SG13G2 CMOS5L shuttle. Documentation is in progress, so the full testing procedure and external hardware requirements are not described.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_tinymoa_ihp0p4_16x16.review_notes: Replaced unsupported CPU/ALU/register-file/education tags with memory, accelerator, and incomplete.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_tinymoa_ihp0p4_8x8.summary: TinyMOA-IHP0P4-8x8 is an 8x8 digital compute-in-memory core implemented in Verilog on an experimental IHP SG13G2 CMOS5L shuttle. It exposes 8 data input bits, write-enable, execute, read-next and accumulator-clear controls, along with column-select and done outputs. Results are read out on 8 output pins, with the top two marked as zero. Documentation and testing details are still in progress.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_tinymoa_ihp0p4_8x8.review_notes: Proposed UART/communication/cocotb tags and summary were unrelated to the compute-in-memory source.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_toivoh_demo.summary: This project is a Tiny Tapeout demo competition entry that generates VGA video and audio output. It includes a logo, star field, floating point unit, synthesizer, and sequencer. The video output is VGA 640x480 at 60 Hz, clocked at 50.4 MHz with two clock cycles per pixel. It is tested using a TinyVGA Pmod and an audio Pmod.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_toivoh_demo.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the VGA/audio demo description.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_rings.summary: This project generates a mesmerizing VGA display of hypnotic concentric rings that expand or contract from the center of the screen. It is designed as a demoscene-style visual effect for the Tiny Tapeout platform. The design takes speed and direction inputs and outputs RGB222 VGA signals with VSync and HSync. Testing requires connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, then applying power and releasing reset.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_rings.review_notes: Removed unsupported accelerator/alu/pipeline tags and corrected the summary, which described hardware not present in the source.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB CDC device that bridges USB to a UART interface at a fixed 115200 baud. It uses usb_p and usb_n for the USB differential pair, dp_pu_o for the 1.5k pull-up, and RX and TX for the UART side, with a configured status output. It is based on tinyfpga_bx_usbserial and enumerates with vendor_id 1209 and product_id 5454. External hardware needed is a USB breakout board and a 1.5k ohm resistor, and silicon test reports confirm successful enumeration, loopback and external UART communication.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag because the provided silicon status is working with tester reports.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttihp0p4/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_dlhq.summary: This design is a high-density shift register using standard cells for deep digital delays. It is implemented in Verilog and uses transparent latches with an 8-phase clock to store bits, with support for 4-bit Johnson counter outputs and an LFSR. The outputs include shift-register data, Johnson counter state, LFSR period and bit, and internal pulse signals. Test instructions cover clock/reset selection and observing the delayed output after 502 clock cycles.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_dlhq.review_notes: Replaced unsupported tags with accurate LFSR/Johnson/delay-line/gate-level/standard-cell tags and rewrote the summary to match the full design description.

ttihp0p4/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_rs.summary: This project implements a high-density shift register using latch-based storage and an 8-phase clock. It uses four latches to store three bits per stage and eight parallel lanes to preserve throughput while relaxing timing. A Johnson counter generates the staggered pulses, and an optional LFSR mode provides observability. The design targets the IHP SG13G2 process and demonstrates a compact alternative to conventional DFF-based shift registers.
ttihp0p4/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_rs.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the documented shift-register design.

ttihp25a/tt_um_09eksdee.summary: This project has no functional description and its purpose is unknown. The documentation states the author does not know how it works or how to test it. The pin names are generic input and output labels. It is an incomplete or placeholder submission.
ttihp25a/tt_um_09eksdee.review_notes: Added placeholder tag to better characterize the submission.

ttihp25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.summary: This design recreates the Crossy Road game on an ASIC, where a chicken crosses roads while avoiding cars. It is controlled by a move button and outputs VGA video to a display. External hardware needed includes a debounced button and a 25 MHz clock. The project is a complete game implementation in Verilog.
ttihp25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.review_notes: Added retro tag for the arcade-style game recreation; removed unsupported 'notable' claim from summary.

ttihp25a/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunt.summary: This design implements a fixed zero-delay delay-and-sum beamformer that accepts up to 16 PDM digital microphones and produces an I2S audio output. It requires an external clock generator to supply a 3.072 MHz bit clock and 48 kHz LR clock, plus 16 digital microphones and an I2S receiver such as a Raspberry Pi. The documentation is largely placeholder text, so the internal signal processing and configuration details cannot be verified from the provided material. The pin names and external hardware list are the main evidence for its function.
ttihp25a/tt_um_16_mic_beamformer_arghunt.review_notes: Removed clock-generator because the design receives clocks rather than generating them.

ttihp25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttihp25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttihp25a/tt_um_4_bit_ALU.summary: This is a simple Verilog ALU that uses a push button to switch between addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division operations. It expects switches for inputs and LEDs for outputs as external hardware. The documentation does not explain the pin mapping or how the operation selection works in detail, and the testing instructions are absent. It appears to be a basic educational arithmetic design with limited documentation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_4_bit_ALU.review_notes: Removed calculator tag because no numeric display or keypad is documented.

ttihp25a/tt_um_4x4_array_multiplier_NuKo.summary: This Verilog design implements a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned numbers and outputs their 8-bit product. It uses a structural approach with full adders and AND gates, and is intended to be tested with switches for inputs and LEDs for outputs on the TinyTapeout demo board. The project appears to be a student lab exercise, with the description noting it is based on a previous lab. Testing involves setting switches and verifying the LED output matches the expected product.
ttihp25a/tt_um_4x4_array_multiplier_NuKo.review_notes: Removed alu because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttihp25a/tt_um_4x4multiplier.summary: This design is a 4x4 combinational multiplier that takes two 4-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit product using layers of full adders. It is tested by placing inputs in a Python test script and comparing the output to the expected multiplication result. No external hardware is required. The documentation describes the structural approach and test method clearly, though it is a straightforward arithmetic block.
ttihp25a/tt_um_4x4multiplier.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the source does not describe an educational purpose.

ttihp25a/tt_um_A_6_array_multiplier.summary: This project is a 4x4 structural array multiplier implemented in Verilog, with inputs q and m and output p. The documentation consists only of the title, pin names, and a note that no external hardware is needed, with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The design is presumably a standard array multiplier based on the title and pin names. The lack of documentation makes it difficult to confirm any further details.
ttihp25a/tt_um_A_6_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed education because the course code alone does not document an educational purpose; added insufficient-doc.

ttihp25a/tt_um_B_14_array_multiplier.summary: This design is a 4-bit array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers using AND gates and full adders to produce an 8-bit product. It is tested by applying two 4-bit inputs and checking the 8-bit output against the expected product. No external hardware is required. The documentation explains the structural array approach and includes a diagram.
ttihp25a/tt_um_B_14_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and trimmed the final sentence to avoid an unsupported quality claim.

ttihp25a/tt_um_C6_array_multiplier.summary: This project implements a 4x4 array multiplier in Verilog using a structural design with partial products and 4-bit adders. It takes two 4-bit inputs (m and q) and outputs an 8-bit product (p). The design includes internal wires for partial products and intermediate sums, and was tested with a provided Verilog testbench. No external hardware is required. The documentation describes the circuit structure and testing approach.

ttihp25a/tt_um_C8_array_mult.summary: This project is a 4-bit multiplier that takes two 4-bit numbers and produces an 8-bit product by computing partial products and summing them. It was tested with a test bench that applies various input pairs and checks the output against expected multiplication results. No external hardware is needed. The documentation describes the partial-product method and testing approach, though the pin list shows only four output pins despite the 8-bit product description.
ttihp25a/tt_um_C8_array_mult.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added 8-bit tag for the documented 8-bit product; summary kept but sentence 4 matches source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_CLA8.summary: This project implements an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder in Verilog, designed for fast addition by computing carry bits in parallel using propagate and generate signals. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit sum, ignoring carry out. The design is fully combinational and was tested with all possible pairs of integers from 0 to 255, resulting in 25536 test cases. No external hardware is needed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_CLA8.review_notes: Removed alu and education because the source only supports a combinational adder and does not claim educational intent.

ttihp25a/tt_um_C_1_4bit_multiplier.summary: This is a 4-bit multiplier that accepts two unsigned 4-bit integers m and q and calculates their 8-bit product p. It is tested by providing several input pairs and verifying that the output equals the product of the two numbers. No external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the basic function and test method.
ttihp25a/tt_um_C_1_4bit_multiplier.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added 8-bit tag for the documented 8-bit product.

ttihp25a/tt_um_CarrySelect8bit.summary: This project implements an 8-bit carry-select adder in Verilog, using two ripple carry adders with different carry inputs and a multiplexer to select the correct sum. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces an 8-bit sum, ignoring carry out. The design was tested with all possible input combinations. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_CarrySelect8bit.review_notes: Removed alu and education because the source only supports a combinational adder and does not claim educational intent.

ttihp25a/tt_um_Coline3003_spect_top.summary: This project is a digital readout for a two-channel time-frequency spectrogram extractor, part of a MEMS-based acoustic emission sensor interface. It processes 7-bit thermometer-coded inputs per channel, decodes them to 3-bit BCD, and performs event-based sampling at 1 MHz for 200 us, storing data in a double buffer for serial readout. The design includes an RTC for timestamping and a state machine for control. It is an early work-in-progress test implementation and requires external analog front-end and a logic analyzer for debugging.
ttihp25a/tt_um_Coline3003_spect_top.review_notes: Removed rtc because the design only uses an RTC clock input, and added incomplete because the source calls it work-in-progress.

ttihp25a/tt_um_Coline3003_top.summary: This project is a 15-channel pulse counter designed for acoustic emission detection, counting short digital pulses on each channel and periodically outputting the counts serially.
