More complete testing requires an external board with SRAM and address latches attached to the user PMOD connectors, and that memory board is noted as still pending design. The design is documented in an accompanying PDF and occupies a 1x2 tile area.

ttihp25a/tt_um_gxrii_spi_sevenseg.summary: This is a small SPI slave that receives 6-bit messages and drives the 7-segment display on the Tiny Tapeout carrier board. The first two bits of each message form a command that turns the decimal point on or off, and the remaining four bits select the digit to display; malformed commands turn the decimal point on with the rest of the display blank. The SPI signals SCLK, SS and MOSI are mapped to the clock and two input pins, and the seven segments plus decimal point appear on the eight outputs. It requires the carrier board's seven-segment display and a microcontroller to act as SPI master.

ttihp25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.summary: This is a 16-bit CPU based on the HACK architecture, featuring an ALU, three registers (A, D, PC), and two SPI modules for memory and debug communication. It uses SPI to fetch instructions and data from an external SPI RAM, and a separate SPI debug interface allows reading internal registers. The design requires an external SPI RAM (e.g., 23XX512) and a microcontroller with SPI for debugging. It is notable for fitting a CPU into a single tile and using serial memory access due to pin limitations.
ttihp25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.review_notes: Removed risc-v tag because the HACK architecture is not RISC-V.

ttihp25a/tt_um_histogramming.summary: This project implements a histogramming unit, but the documentation is essentially empty, providing no details on its functionality, interface, or usage. The pin names are generic and do not indicate specific behavior. It is not possible to determine how the design works or how to test it from the available information.

ttihp25a/tt_um_hpdl1414_uart_atudoroi.summary: This design is a 115200 baud UART transceiver that stores received characters in a 16-byte buffer and asynchronously drives four HPDL-1414 alphanumeric LED display modules. When the buffer fills, existing characters shift left to make room, a blinking cursor shows the input position, and Ctrl-H performs a backspace for editing. Testing is done by connecting a computer or microcontroller at 115200 baud, sending ASCII characters, and observing them on the HPDL-1414 modules. It requires the external HPDL-1414 PMOD module and uses a 12 MHz clock.

ttihp25a/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.summary: This is a demoscene project that displays a bouncing capsule with background and text on a VGA output, accompanied by PDM audio. It includes input switches to pause, reset, mute, hide elements, lock colors, and disable re-orientation. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a TT Audio PMOD (or compatible) for output. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition and runs at 25 MHz.
ttihp25a/tt_um_htfab_bouncy_capsule.review_notes: Removed speaker tag: PDM audio on uio pins is a digital audio output, not a driven speaker stage.

ttihp25a/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

ttihp25a/tt_um_htfab_checkers.summary: This project recreates the classic Checkers demo from VGA Playground, with each of its five layers generated by a different Python-based HDL: Amaranth, MyHDL, PyCDE, PyRTL and PyMTL3. It outputs VGA signals on the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout at a 25.175 MHz clock, and the eight input pins can be toggled to change the main, sub, foreground and background colours. The only external hardware needed is the TinyVGA PMOD and a screen, and the design is notable for demonstrating several Python HDLs in a single chip. It is essentially a visual demonstration rather than a functional application.
ttihp25a/tt_um_htfab_checkers.review_notes: Removed amaranth/myhdl since only individual layers use them; added demoscene and retro for the classic demo recreation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_huffman_coder.summary: This ASIC compresses ASCII characters into Huffman codes using a lookup table, taking a 7-bit ASCII character on the input pins with a load strobe on ui[7]. After loading, a Valid_out signal indicates when the Huffman code and its bit length are available on the uo and uio pins. Communication requires an RP2040 or external microcontroller to send ASCII input and read the compressed output. The documentation is brief and does not describe the code table or the internal implementation beyond the lookup table.
ttihp25a/tt_um_huffman_coder.review_notes: Removed encoder; compression, lookup-table, ascii and verilog are all supported.

ttihp25a/tt_um_hybrid_adder.summary: This 8-bit hybrid adder combines a 4-bit Kogge-Stone adder with a 4-bit carry-lookahead adder to balance gate efficiency and latency. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and produces the sum on uo_out. Testing requires only applying 3.3V logic levels to the inputs and reading the outputs. The design is described as faster than an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder and more gate-efficient than an 8-bit carry-lookahead adder.
ttihp25a/tt_um_hybrid_adder.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source documents only an adder, not an ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_i2c_peripheral_stevej.summary: This design implements two I2C peripherals: a 32-bit FNV-1a hash unit and a leading-zero counter, plus two constant-byte generators. Bytes are written over I2C and results are read back, with each read resetting the hash. It is tested with an Arduino I2C master using known input/output pairs. The design packages small arithmetic and hashing functions behind a standard I2C Pmod interface.
ttihp25a/tt_um_i2c_peripheral_stevej.review_notes: Replaced popcount with counter; the source describes a leading-zero counter, not a population count.

ttihp25a/tt_um_i2c_regf.summary: This block is an asynchronous I2C slave that exposes a register file, intended to configure analog blocks on the same chip. An I2C master writes and reads words to the registers, and an LED is listed as external hardware for testing. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the register map or address. The design is notable for providing a reusable configuration interface for analog circuitry.

ttihp25a/tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.summary: This design converts 8-bit I2S/PDM microphone input into PWM output, with eight PDM microphone channels and a beamformed PCM output. Pin names indicate a bit clock, LR clock, microphone clock, per-microphone PCM outputs, and a 5-bit delay select for beamforming. The documentation is essentially placeholder text, so the actual signal processing and configuration are not described. External hardware needed includes microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver.
ttihp25a/tt_um_i2s_to_pwm_arghunter.review_notes: Removed iir-filter and delay-line because neither is supported by the source documentation or pin names.

ttihp25a/tt_um_idann.summary: This design implements a forward pass for a simple artificial neural network with 4 input neurons, 8 hidden neurons, and 1 output neuron, and also computes the mean squared error loss. It accepts a 4-bit input on ui_in[3:0] and uses ui_in[7] to start the computation, with the result and state available on the output pins. External hardware consists of switches to set the input value and a button or switch to trigger the forward pass. The design is intended for inference and loss calculation, and can be simulated by modifying the test script.
ttihp25a/tt_um_idann.review_notes: Replaced accelerator with edge-ai to match the small embedded ANN inference design.

ttihp25a/tt_um_iitbbs.summary: This project is titled as a dual-mode washing machine controller with a LiPSi microprocessor and a standalone controller selected by pin configuration. The documentation body states 'Not meant for submission' and provides no functional details, test procedure, or external hardware information. Pin names are generic and add no technical detail. As a result, the design cannot be properly evaluated from the available source.
ttihp25a/tt_um_iitbbs.review_notes: Conflicting title vs. 'not meant for submission' body; needs a second opinion on whether this is a real washing-machine controller or a placeholder.

ttihp25a/tt_um_instrumented_ring_oscilla.summary: This instrumented ring oscillator allows selection of the number of stages and initial state via input pins, and outputs 16 phases for observation. It is intended for studying the decay or persistence of high-frequency modes, not as a reliable clock source. Testing involves connecting a logic analyzer or oscilloscope to the outputs, configuring the stage count and seed, then enabling the oscillator and observing whether it stabilizes to the longest period or retains high-frequency modes. External hardware such as a logic analyzer or multi-channel oscilloscope is recommended for capturing the phase outputs.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.summary: This project is a 1-bit AM software-defined radio pipeline written in Verilog. It uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC frontend, oversampled and decimated 4096 times to gain extra precision. The core includes an SPI interface for setting demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs demodulated audio via PWM. The design spans 3x2 Tiny Tapeout tiles and is based on a Hackaday project by Alberto Garlassi.
ttihp25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.review_notes: Removed risc-v, cpu, soc, uart, qspi, and memory tags as unsupported; added radio, rf, dsp, spi, adc, demodulator, nco, audio, pwm, and multi-tile tags based on the source documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.summary: This is a software-defined radio core for AM reception that uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC and performs digital bandpass filtering and envelope detection. It is configured via a SPI interface to set the demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs a PWM signal representing the demodulated audio. External hardware includes a comparator, resistor bias network, RC network, SPI microcontroller, and an RF amplifier. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile size, trading off selectivity compared to a previous larger implementation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.review_notes: Removed comparator/adc (external components, not on-chip); added pwm and rf tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jayjaywong12.summary: This is a 4-bit vector multiplication engine that multiplies two vectors of up to 32 elements and accumulates the result into an 8-bit output. It is programmed via a register interface using read/write opcodes and a run command, and it operates in two clock cycles. The design is intended to be controlled by an RP2040 and requires no other external hardware. Silicon tests show it works, though timing adjustments were needed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_jayjaywong12.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu/dsp tags and added mac-unit, rp2040, and silicon-tested based on the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jmack2201.summary: This design displays a bouncing sprite with multiple background options on a VGA output, with sprite ROM, background control registers, and audio ROM configured via SPI. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and an audio Pmod for sound output. The design is controlled by SPI to set the background, sprite image, and sound effects. It is a hardware sprite engine suitable for simple demos.
ttihp25a/tt_um_jmack2201.review_notes: Removed unsupported game/framebuffer tags and added pmod and demoscene based on the documented external hardware and demo purpose.

ttihp25a/tt_um_johshoff_metaballs.summary: This design attempts to render metaballs on a VGA display. It outputs RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Silicon tests show partial functionality: one ball moves as expected, but the other exhibits erratic behavior, and results vary across chips. The documentation is minimal and the design is described as rushed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_johshoff_metaballs.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added 'silicon-tested' to match the reported silicon status.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jp_cd101_saw.summary: This is a digital saw-wave synthesizer with a programmable pulse generator, ADSR amplitude modulation, a one-pole IIR filter, and a first-order delta-sigma audio output. Parameters are set over an SPI slave interface, and a trigger input starts and stops notes; a VST/CLAP plugin generates the SPI commands. It is an educational design that deliberately mirrors the audio pipeline structurally in hardware, and it requires an external lowpass filter, button Pmod, audio Pmod, and SPI master. Testing uses a cocotb testbench that writes audio to a file and compares against a golden reference.

ttihp25a/tt_um_juarez_jimenez.summary: This design implements a linear feedback shift register with synaptic neuron-inspired behavior, where bit transitions generate excitatory or inhibitory signals that modify the feedback path. It accepts an 8-bit seed on the input pins and produces an 8-bit pseudo-random output sequence on uo_out. Testing involves providing a clock and reset, setting the seed, and observing the output sequence over multiple cycles. No external hardware is required, and the design allows customizable seed values to vary the output sequence.

ttihp25a/tt_um_jun1okamura_test0.summary: This design drives a 7-segment display from a counter whose period is either fixed or pseudo-random, selected by an input pin. A second input chooses between a hexadecimal sequence and a fixed text string, and the low 8 bits of a 24-bit counter are exposed on the bidirectional pins. It is tested on the Tiny Tapeout evaluation board by observing the display and changing the two select inputs. The design is notable mainly as a simple display and LFSR demonstration.
ttihp25a/tt_um_jun1okamura_test0.review_notes: Removed lfsr (source only says pseudo-random value) and added bcd for the binary-to-decimal display conversion.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kailinsley.summary: This project implements a dynamic threshold leaky integrate-and-fire model that simulates a spiking biological neuron. The documentation is essentially placeholder text and does not describe how the model works or how to test it. The pin names suggest eight inputs and eight outputs, but their functions are not explained. No external hardware is mentioned, and the design cannot be evaluated from the available information.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kailinsley.review_notes: Replaced insufficient-doc with incomplete because the documentation is placeholder text rather than sparse.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kapilan_alarm.summary: This project implements a simple alarm clock with configurable alarm hours and minutes. It uses internal counters for hours and minutes, and asserts an alarm output when the current time matches the alarm setting. The design was sponsored by MITRE and MIT/LL Beaverworks Summer Institute, and includes a testbench for simulation. It uses both dedicated and bidirectional pins to accommodate all inputs and outputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kapilan_alarm.review_notes: Removed industrial, clock-generator and education tags unsupported by the source; added timer.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kashmaster_carryskip.summary: This 8-bit carry-skip adder uses two 4-bit sections with skip logic to reduce carry propagation delay compared to a ripple-carry adder. It takes two 8-bit operands on ui_in and uio_in and outputs the registered sum on uo_out after each rising clock edge. Testing can be done by applying input values and verifying the output against expected sums, either manually or with a testbench. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kashmaster_carryskip.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source documents only an adder, not an ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.summary: This design is a 4-bit ALU slice intended for use in minicomputer or microcomputer CPUs. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 3-bit function code, and produces a 4-bit result along with carry, equal, and zero flags. The design was tested using an Altera FPGA. It provides basic arithmetic and logic functions.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.review_notes: Removed adc, cpu, and education tags not supported by the source; added alu, retro, and fpga.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kch_cd101.summary: This is a digital synthesizer with a programmable pulse-wave generator, ADSR amplitude modulation, a one-pole IIR filter, and a first-order delta-sigma audio output. It is controlled through an SPI slave interface and a trigger input, with a VST/CLAP plugin available to generate SPI commands from a DAW. The design is educational and intentionally maps the audio pipeline directly into hardware, requiring an external lowpass filter, button Pmod, audio Pmod, and SPI master. Testing uses a cocotb testbench that captures audio to a file and compares against a golden reference.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kentrane_tinyspectrum.summary: This is a small square-wave tone generator that produces 16 notes across 4 octaves with an optional tremolo effect. Note and octave are selected by input pins, an enable pin gates the tone, and seven outputs drive LEDs as a simple visualizer while the audio comes from the eighth output. It requires an external RC low-pass filter, a DC blocking capacitor, and a speaker or headphones, and the documentation suggests it could be controlled from a Pi Pico or a small keyboard. The documentation is informal and notes that the project was completed under time pressure.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kentrane_tinyspectrum.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; softened the control sentence to match the source's speculative wording.

ttihp25a/tt_um_keszocze_ssmcl.summary: This design is a 3-bit unsigned multiplier that trades speed for area by streaming operands and results over multiple clock cycles. A start signal begins the operation, the product appears after 18 cycles, and a valid output indicates when the result is ready. It can be driven from the Tiny Tapeout motherboard web interface or with input/output Pmods. The design is notable for its explicit multi-cycle streaming behavior.
ttihp25a/tt_um_keszocze_ssmcl.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu, fsm and education tags and speculative educational wording.

ttihp25a/tt_um_kev_ma_matmult222.summary: This design multiplies two 2-bit 2x2 matrices, accepting matrix A on the standard input pins and matrix B on the bidirectional pins, and outputting the result matrix C on the standard output pins. Each matrix element is 2 bits, and the pin mapping is explicitly documented. Testing requires pulling pins high or low to set the input matrices and reading the output pins for the product. No external hardware is needed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_kev_ma_matmult222.review_notes: Removed accelerator and alu as unsupported; added combinational for the purely combinational matrix multiply.

ttihp25a/tt_um_koggestone_adder8.summary: This project implements an 8-bit Kogge-Stone adder in Verilog. It takes two 8-bit inputs and produces their sum, but lacks a carry-out so sums above 255 are not representable. The design is intended as a class exercise and includes a testbench that iterates through all input combinations, skipping cases where overflow would occur. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
ttihp25a/tt_um_koggestone_adder8.review_notes: Removed alu (single adder only); added workshop for the class context.

ttihp25a/tt_um_larva.summary: This project is a RISC-V CPU (LaRVa) with a serial port, JTAG interface, and a few other peripherals, but it requires external memory. An included bootloader allows programs loaded through the serial port to execute, and JTAG provides an additional debug path. A simple test is to connect a serial port at 8-bit, no parity, 115200 bps and send an 'L', expecting the bootloader to reply with another 'L'. More complete testing needs an external board with SRAM memory and address latches attached to the Pmod ports, and the JTAG port can also be used.
ttihp25a/tt_um_larva.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm/sram tags, added gpio and education, and rephrased the summary from source-supported facts.

ttihp25a/tt_um_led_cipher.summary: This design implements a nibble-serial version of the LED block cipher, which encrypts a 64-bit plaintext block using a 128-bit key. Data is loaded and unloaded serially through the 8 input and 8 output pins, with control signals for loading key and plaintext, starting encryption, and reading ciphertext. The design is intended to be controlled by external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi, and test vectors are provided for verification. Notable features include a compact implementation that reuses datapath logic across nibbles, at the cost of higher latency (2045 cycles for encryption).

ttihp25a/tt_um_led_jellyant.summary: This design simply turns on one output pin, as described in its minimal documentation. It has no inputs and only eight output pins, all labeled A[0] through A[7]. The testing instructions state that no action is needed, and no external hardware is required. The project is a minimal LED test with essentially no functionality beyond driving an output high.
ttihp25a/tt_um_led_jellyant.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and gpio tags; added insufficient-doc given the very thin documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_led_matrix_ayla_lin.summary: This project drives a 32x8 LED matrix using a MAX7219/7221 controller via SPI. It displays an animation that alternates between a beaver logo and the letters 'BWSI', with bitmaps stored in an internal ROM. The design is intended to be tested on an FPGA connected to a breadboard, requiring external hardware including the LED matrix, the MAX7219/7221 chip, and a 5V power source. The SPI interface handles both configuration and bitmap data transmission.

ttihp25a/tt_um_levenshtein.summary: This design implements a fuzzy search engine based on the bit-vector Levenshtein distance algorithm. It finds the closest matching word in a dictionary stored in external QSPI PSRAM, communicating with the host via SPI. The design requires a specific QSPI PSRAM PMOD that supports quad-mode operations and runs at half the clock speed of the chip. It is notable for being a hardware implementation of a string matching algorithm, with a provided client tool for testing.
ttihp25a/tt_um_levenshtein.review_notes: Removed memory tag because the design only interfaces to external PSRAM rather than implementing memory.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lfsr_stevej.summary: This project implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) that generates a pseudo-random sequence. It accepts an 8-bit seed value and a write-enable signal to load the seed, and outputs the current LFSR state on eight output pins. The design is simple and requires no external hardware beyond reading the output pins. It can be used as a basic pseudo-random number generator.

ttihp25a/tt_um_liaf.summary: This project simulates a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit input current and updates an internal state variable, producing a spike output when the state exceeds a threshold. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed usage or testing instructions. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_liaf.review_notes: Tags were already correct; no changes needed.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lif1.summary: This project implements a spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) circuit in Verilog. It detects pre- and post-synaptic spikes, measures the time difference between them, and adjusts a synaptic weight using an exponential trace model. The design is still under development and testing is incomplete. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_lif1.review_notes: Removed machine-learning; STDP is neuromorphic only.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_ZB.summary: This project implements a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current on ui_in and outputs an 8-bit state variable on uo_out, with a spike signal on uio[7]. The documentation is very sparse, providing only a brief description and no detailed testing procedure or external hardware requirements. It is labelled as a tutorial, but the lack of documentation makes it difficult to assess its completeness or correctness.
ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_ZB.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added incomplete for 'do something' test instruction; spiking-neural-network was both proposed and canonical.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_clarencechan28.summary: This project implements a single-layer perceptron in Verilog. It takes 8 bits of input and 8 bits of weights, and classifies the input into one of two classes based on a weighted sum and threshold. The design is tested using a Python script that initializes inputs and expected outputs, and then runs a makefile-based test. No external hardware is required.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_network_MR.summary: This project implements a small spiking neural network based on the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model. It consists of three input neurons that receive 5-bit input currents, and one output neuron that integrates weighted spikes from the input neurons. The design can be tested in simulation or on an FPGA, with LEDs and switches for input and output. It is suitable for basic pattern recognition or response simulations.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_tk.summary: This project implements eight leaky integrate-and-fire neurons connected in a ring topology, with configurable base current, coupling strength, and one of five firing patterns (independent, wave, synchronous, clustered, burst). Inputs are split across ui_in for pattern select and base current scaling, and uio_in for coupling strength, while spike outputs appear on uo_out and the first neuron's membrane potential on uio_out. Testing involves applying reset and enable, selecting a pattern and current, and monitoring the spike outputs for the expected propagation or synchronization behavior. No external hardware is needed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_lif_tk.review_notes: Removed oscillator and synchronizer tags unsupported by the source; dropped unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lifn.summary: This design is a simple leaky integrate-and-fire neuron implemented in Verilog that integrates an 8-bit input current into a membrane potential, leaks it over time, and fires a spike when a threshold is reached before resetting. The input current is applied on ui_in, the membrane state is exposed on uo_out, and the spike appears on uio[7]. The testing section only says 'Do something', so no concrete test procedure is documented. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is too thin to describe the implementation details beyond the general LIF behavior.

ttihp25a/tt_um_log_afpm.summary: This design is a 16-bit floating-point multiplier that uses logarithmic approximation to reduce hardware complexity and power consumption. It has 8 input pins for operand A, 8 bidirectional pins for operand B, and 8 output pins for the product, with the pins time-multiplexed to handle 16-bit values. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of the algorithm or testing procedure. Notable aspects include the use of approximation for efficiency, but without further documentation, its accuracy and limitations are unclear.
ttihp25a/tt_um_log_afpm.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; no DSP application is described, only a floating-point multiplier.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lrc_stevej.summary: This design computes a running longitudinal redundancy check (LRC) over a stream of bytes, updating the code each time a new byte is presented on the input pins. A byte is supplied on ui_in and the current LRC is read from uo_out, with the running value resetting when the chip is reset. No external hardware is needed, and the design is a straightforward checksum generator. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the function and basic usage.
ttihp25a/tt_um_lrc_stevej.review_notes: Removed crc since the design is an LRC, not a CRC.

ttihp25a/tt_um_lsnn_hschweig.summary: This project implements a leaky spiking neural network (LSNN) neuron with a 12-bit membrane potential, configurable decay, adaptive threshold with optional learning, a three-cycle refractory period, and a 7-bit spike counter. Input current is applied on ui_in, the membrane potential and refractory indicator are output on uo_out, and the spike plus spike counter appear on uio_out, with learning enabled via uio_in[0]. Testing covers reset behavior, basic spiking, learning mode, and spike-count verification entirely through digital I/O. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_lsnn_hschweig.review_notes: Removed redundant neural-network tag and unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttihp25a/tt_um_luke_clock.summary: This design is a VGA-based binary clock implemented in Chisel that displays hours, minutes, and seconds as a matrix of binary squares. It accepts switches to select the time clock source and display mode, and plus/minus buttons to set the time. The VGA output shows the binary time representation, updating every second. External hardware includes a TT VGA PMOD, buttons, switches, and optionally a real-time clock for precision timekeeping.
ttihp25a/tt_um_luke_clock.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated multiplier project; corrected to match the VGA binary clock source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_m4rthaswur1d.summary: This design is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned inputs and produces an 8-bit product. It uses full adders to sum partial products, as described in the documentation. The design is intended to be tested with a testbench of varying input values, and no external hardware is required. It is a straightforward educational example of a digital multiplier.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mac.summary: This project implements a Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) unit using a Dadda multiplier and a Kogge-Stone adder. The design includes pipeline registers and an accumulator, and is intended for digital signal processing tasks such as filtering and convolution. A testbench is provided to simulate input scenarios and observe the output behavior. The clock is specified as 100 Hz, which is unusually low and may be a documentation error.
ttihp25a/tt_um_mac.review_notes: Removed dsp tag since the design is a MAC building block rather than a DSP algorithm; no silicon-tested claim since there are no test reports.

ttihp25a/tt_um_matrix_mult.summary: This design multiplies a 2x2 matrix by a 2x1 vector, with 2-bit elements, producing a 2-element output vector. Matrix elements are supplied on ui_in, the input vector on uio_in, and the output vector is split across uo_out and uio_out. The documentation is inconsistent: the 'How it works' section describes treating inputs as current injection into a LIF neuron, which does not match the title or pin descriptions, and the test section only says 'Test it'. External hardware is listed as 'Possibly', and the documentation is too thin and contradictory to describe the design reliably.
ttihp25a/tt_um_matrix_mult.review_notes: Escalated because the source is contradictory about whether this is a matrix-vector multiplier or a LIF neuron circuit.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.summary: This design debounces inputs from three rotary encoders and generates PWM signals to control LED brightness. It is intended for use with external digital encoders connected to the first six inputs. The project is a demo for the Zero to ASIC course. Testing involves twisting the encoders and observing the LED brightness changes.
ttihp25a/tt_um_mattvenn_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed unsupported rgb-led and education tags; added rotary-encoder and driver tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mattvenn_spi_test.summary: This is an SPI test design based on the tt07_alu_74181 project, as stated in the documentation. It includes SPI signals (MISO, MOSI, clock, chip select) and inputs for CPOL and CPHA, but the documentation provides no further details on functionality or testing. The design is likely a test for SPI communication, but its exact behavior is unclear from the available information. No external hardware is required according to the description.
ttihp25a/tt_um_mattvenn_spi_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported communication tag and added insufficient-doc to match very thin documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_meriac_play_tune.summary: This design plays the Super Mario theme tune through a piezo speaker connected to the bidirectional pins in a differential PWM configuration. It requires an external piezo speaker or the Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod. The design also copies the input pins to the output pins for testing purposes. It operates with a 100 kHz clock and is intended for audio output.

ttihp25a/tt_um_michaelmcculloch_alu.summary: This project implements a 6-bit input ALU that selects an operation based on a 4-bit RISC-V opcode and produces an 8-bit output. Inputs A and B are provided through the bidirectional pins and the dedicated input pins, while the opcode is set on the remaining input pins. Testing involves applying input values and opcodes and observing the output, optionally with LEDs connected for visual feedback. The design is a straightforward iterative ALU with no external hardware required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_michaelmcculloch_alu.review_notes: Removed risc-v tag because the design is an ALU using RISC-V-style opcodes, not a RISC-V core.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mikegoelzer_7segmentbyte.summary: This design drives a two-digit 7-segment display to show the hexadecimal representation of an 8-bit input byte. The byte is latched on a rising clock edge when the write enable signal is high, and the display is continuously driven with segment outputs and a digit select signal. Testing requires connecting a 7-segment display and manipulating the input and write enable pins to verify latching and display updates. The project uses a simple interface with a standard 7-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_mikegoelzer_7segmentbyte.review_notes: Removed driver (no driver stage); added pmod for the linked Pmod SSD display; reworded final sentence to avoid unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttihp25a/tt_um_monishvr_fifo.summary: This project implements a synchronous FIFO with a 4-bit data width. It has inputs for write and read control, 4-bit data input, and outputs for full, empty, and 4-bit data output. The documentation mentions that it is based on a debouncing mechanism, but the testing procedure is listed as 'TBA' and no external hardware is required. The design is a basic first-in-first-out memory buffer.
ttihp25a/tt_um_monishvr_fifo.review_notes: Removed redundant memory tag and added debouncer, which is explicitly mentioned in the documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_moody_mimosa.summary: This project implements a Tamagotchi-like artificial creature called Mimosa, which reacts to external stimuli such as tickling, playing, talking, feeding, and temperature changes. It outputs emotional states like sleeping, eating, playing, smiling, babbling, kicking legs, doing nothing, and crying, and includes SPI and UART interfaces for debugging. The design is supported by extensive simulation, FPGA prototyping, and a microcontroller-based logger for debugging. Notable aspects include its complex behavioral model inspired by biological processes and its use of multiple subprojects for testing and emulation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_moody_mimosa.review_notes: Removed game tag because the design is a Tamagotchi-like creature rather than an interactive game implementation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mp_lif_schor.summary: This project implements a mixed-precision leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that can compute either one neuron with a 24-bit membrane value and 8-bit weights or two neurons with 12-bit membrane values and 4-bit weights. It has 4 input pins for weights, a ready output, and two spike outputs for upper and lower neurons. The documentation is minimal, with testing instructions stating to apply weights and observe spikes, and no external hardware is required. The design is notable for its mixed-precision approach, but further details are lacking.

ttihp25a/tt_um_mroblesh.summary: This project implements an 8-bit frequency encoder and decoder for a 1-bit frequency channel, with a selector pin to choose between encoding and decoding modes. The documentation also mentions that it treats an 8-bit input voltage as a current injection to a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, but the connection between the two functions is unclear. Testing instructions are minimal, stating only 'Do something', and no external hardware is specified. The design appears to be a mixed-signal or neuromorphic experiment with incomplete documentation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_mroblesh.review_notes: Removed encoder/decoder tags because they do not match the canonical meanings; added neuromorphic and spiking-neural-network tags based on the LIF neuron description.

ttihp25a/tt_um_multiplier_tt09.summary: This design implements a 4x4 array multiplier in Verilog, taking two 4-bit inputs and producing an 8-bit product using partial products and full adders. The documentation explains the column-wise addition of partial products and suggests testing by applying binary values and comparing against known products. Testing can be done via a Python test script or by modifying the Verilog to expose internal signals such as partial products and carries. No external hardware is required, and the project appears to be an educational exercise in digital arithmetic.
ttihp25a/tt_um_multiplier_tt09.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the source does not explicitly state an educational purpose.

ttihp25a/tt_um_multiplier_tt10.summary: This is an 8-bit unsigned binary multiplier implemented in SystemVerilog, with two 8-bit inputs and a 16-bit product split across outputs. The documentation is brief, stating that inputs are given through ui_in and uio_in and the product appears on uo_out and uio_out. No details are provided about the internal Vedic algorithm or testing methodology beyond basic pin usage. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_multiplier_tt10.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and overly harsh insufficient-doc tags; fixed summary to mention Vedic.

ttihp25a/tt_um_murmann_group.summary: This Verilog design implements a decimation filter for both incremental and regular delta-sigma modulators, reducing oversampled data while preserving signal accuracy. For incremental modulators the output updates after accumulating 16 input samples, while for regular modulators the output update is controlled by the reset signal. The filter provides a 16-bit decimated output and is clocked at 50 MHz. No silicon test reports are included, but the design targets ADC signal processing by converting a high oversampled data rate into a lower downsampled rate.
ttihp25a/tt_um_murmann_group.review_notes: Summary corrected: the regular-modulator mode is described in the source as internal timing controlled by the reset signal, not an internal reset signal, and the unsupported claim that testing details are not provided was dropped.

ttihp25a/tt_um_my_elevator.summary: This project simulates an elevator control system that displays floor numbers on a 7-segment display based on switch inputs. The user selects a floor using the board switches, and the display increments or decrements according to the elevator's state (moving up, moving down, or idle). Testing involves using the switches to select floors and observing the display, which requires an external LED display. The design is a simple state machine demonstration with no additional hardware beyond the display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_my_elevator.review_notes: Removed industrial (no industrial application stated); added fsm for the elevator state machine.

ttihp25a/tt_um_neural_navigators.summary: This design implements a neural network accelerator for MNIST handwriting prediction in Verilog. It uses a 4x2 tile area and runs at 10 MHz, with all pins labeled generically as ui, uio, and uo. The documentation is essentially absent, providing only the title and one-line description, so no details on architecture, usage, or testing are available. The project is notable for targeting a neural network ASIC but lacks sufficient documentation to verify its functionality.
ttihp25a/tt_um_neural_navigators.review_notes: Removed asic tag not supported by source and added insufficient-doc for very thin documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_nithishreddykvs.summary: This Verilog module generates a PWM signal with an adjustable duty cycle controlled by two debounced buttons, using a 50 MHz input clock. The duty cycle can be increased or decreased in 10% steps from 0% to 90%, producing a PWM output. Testing can be done in simulation or on an FPGA, with buttons connected to the inputs and an oscilloscope or LED on the output to verify the waveform. External hardware includes two push buttons, a clock source, a reset, and a device such as an LED or motor to use the PWM signal.
ttihp25a/tt_um_nithishreddykvs.review_notes: Removed clock-generator which is contradicted by pins; kept verilog and corrected summary wording to match source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_nomuwill.summary: This project implements a 16-bit Izhikevich neuron model in Verilog, which simulates spiking neuron dynamics using 16-bit arithmetic. It accepts an 8-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit state variable along with a spike signal. Testing is done via a supplied testbench that checks reset behavior, sub-threshold non-spiking, and supra-threshold spiking conditions. The design is notable for its efficient implementation of a biologically plausible neuron model, with no external hardware required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_nomuwill.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag; the design is a spiking neuron model, not a DSP block.

ttihp25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.summary: This Verilog design generates a VGA demo that displays a virtual 7-segment LED display with decimal point, controlled by 8-bit input. It also has a demo mode that counts down from 9 to 0 and toggles the decimal bit, but the reset for this mode is flawed. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD for output and runs at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm the basic display and user input work, but the demo mode does not reset correctly.
ttihp25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.review_notes: Removed 7-segment/display since the seven-segment display is only virtual on VGA; added silicon-tested per test reports.

ttihp25a/tt_um_nyan.summary: This design plays the Nyan Cat animation and music on infinite repeat. It outputs VGA video signals and a PWM audio signal, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD and Mike's audio PMOD for full functionality. The design runs at 25 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon, with testers reporting that it delighted children. It is a simple, self-contained demo with no inputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_nyan.review_notes: Added silicon-tested and speaker tags to reflect the confirmed silicon status and audio output hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_obriensp_jtag.summary: This project implements a JTAG Test Access Port with boundary scan support, wrapping an inner design that drives a seven-segment display from either an internal 4-bit counter or an external 4-bit value. The TAP supports standard instructions including IDCODE, SAMPLE/PRELOAD, EXTEST, INTEST, CLAMP, and BYPASS, and a BSDL file is provided for testing with tools like UrJTAG. The design requires a JTAG adapter connected to specific bidirectional pins. Notable features include the integration of boundary scan for testing both the inner project and external pins.

ttihp25a/tt_um_ole_moller_priority_encod.summary: This Verilog design implements an 8-bit priority encoder that converts the highest-priority set bit into a decimal digit displayed on a 7-segment display. If no bits are set, a decimal point is shown instead of a digit. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware beyond the 7-segment display and input switches. It is a simple project for demonstrating priority encoding and 7-segment decoding.
ttihp25a/tt_um_ole_moller_priority_encod.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

ttihp25a/tt_um_patater_demokit.summary: This Verilog design outputs a waggling 6-bit rainbow demo on VGA, with effects controlled by input pins. Inputs enable dual mode (horizontal flip per scanline) and horizontal waves, with offsets controlling wave speeds. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and runs at 25.175 MHz. The design can be tested in a VGA playground or with hardware, and an incomplete cocotb testbench is provided.

ttihp25a/tt_um_pdm_correlator_arghunter.summary: This chip performs cross- or auto-correlation on up to eight PDM microphone inputs by XORing pairs of bitstreams and summing the results, with lower sums indicating higher correlation. It outputs PCM data for each microphone and a beamformed PCM output, with delay selection controlled via bidirectional pins. The design requires external PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an SPI port for configuration. The documentation is sparse and contains placeholder text, but the core function and pinout are described.
ttihp25a/tt_um_pdm_correlator_arghunter.review_notes: Removed unsupported tag and added correct ones based on source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_pdm_pitch_filter_arghunte.summary: This project implements a moving average filter and decimator for PDM microphone input, intended to filter out a specific frequency and its harmonics by averaging over a period where the sine wave's energy sums to zero. It outputs PCM data for each microphone plus a beamformed PCM output, with filter and decimator parameters set via an SPI port. The design requires external PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an SPI interface. The documentation contains placeholder text and testing instructions that are still in progress.
ttihp25a/tt_um_pdm_pitch_filter_arghunte.review_notes: Filter is a moving average/IIR style not a FIR; testing section is explicitly unfinished.

ttihp25a/tt_um_perceptron_mtchun.summary: This project implements a perceptron neuron in Verilog that is intended to function as a NAND gate, with 8-bit input and output buses for current and state variables. The documentation consists entirely of placeholders, providing no explanation of how the perceptron works, how it is trained, or how to test it. No external hardware is listed. Due to the lack of documentation, the design's functionality and usage cannot be determined from the provided information.

ttihp25a/tt_um_pid_controller.summary: This design implements a hardware PID controller in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit setpoint and an 8-bit feedback signal as inputs and produces an 8-bit control signal output. The controller uses proportional, integral, and derivative terms to adjust the output based on the error between setpoint and feedback, but it only outputs positive values, making it suitable for systems that naturally tend in one direction, such as heating. The design is intended for simulation testing and can be deployed with sensors and actuators for real-world control applications.
ttihp25a/tt_um_pid_controller.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm tag; summary is supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_prefix8.summary: This project presents an 8-bit prefix network-based high-speed adder that was automatically designed using a large language model to achieve a trade-off between power, performance, and area. The design uses specialized modules for carry and sum generation, and it is tested by exhaustively applying all 8-bit input combinations and verifying the sum against expected results. No external hardware is required. The notable aspect is the use of an LLM to generate a novel prefix network for the adder.
ttihp25a/tt_um_prefix8.review_notes: Removed alu and machine-learning; the design is a dedicated adder and the LLM was only a design aid.

ttihp25a/tt_um_program_counter_top_level.summary: This project implements a synchronous 4-bit counter with control signals for counting, loading, and output enable. The counter increments on each clock cycle when the count enable is asserted, can load a 4-bit value when the load enable is asserted, and can be disabled to put the output in high-impedance. It includes a reset that clears the counter to zero. The design is tested by observing the output on dedicated pins while manipulating the control signals to verify counting, pausing, loading, and output disabling.

ttihp25a/tt_um_project_tt09.summary: This project implements a basic leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in SystemVerilog. It integrates input current by addition and leaks by dividing by two at each time step, with an enable pin advancing time roughly once per second when clocked at about 50 MHz. The neuron fires a spike when the integrated value exceeds a threshold, and it includes a timeout to prevent constant output from overstimulation. Testing involves manually setting input switches to provide current and observing spike output on LEDs, with a dedicated LED indicating time steps.

ttihp25a/tt_um_project_tt10.summary: This is a simple 8-bit shift register that shifts left on each clock cycle and outputs the current value, with new data loaded when a specific bidirectional pin is high. The clock is specified as 1 Hz, making it suitable for visual observation of the shifting bits. Testing involves setting an 8-bit input, asserting the load pin, and watching the output shift. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_project_tt10.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and register-file tags; summary's educational claim was not supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_purdue_socet_uart.summary: This project is a general-purpose UART with FIFO buffers, developed by Purdue's SoCET team. It supports standard UART signals (rx, tx, cts, rts) and includes FIFO buffers for both transmit and receive paths. The design allows configuration of baud rate and operation mode (idle, transmit, receive, buffer clear) through control pins. It can be tested by connecting to another UART or a USB-to-serial adapter, and it provides error and buffer status flags.
ttihp25a/tt_um_purdue_socet_uart.review_notes: Removed driver tag as the UART is a communication interface, not a generic driver output stage.

ttihp25a/tt_um_pwm_top.summary: This design is a versatile PWM generator with adjustable frequency and duty cycle. It takes a 6-bit divisor input to set the frequency by dividing the clock, and two control inputs to increase or decrease the duty cycle by 10% steps. The PWM output can be used to drive RGB LEDs, servomotors, and other devices, but external power is recommended for the driven device. The design is intended to be tested by applying a clock, setting the divisor, and adjusting the duty cycle while observing the PWM output.

ttihp25a/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.summary: This design is a 16-bit counter with count enable and multiplier enable inputs. It accepts 3-bit operands m_a and m_b for the multiplier. The counter outputs its lower 8 bits on uo and upper 8 bits on the bidirectional pins. The documentation is extremely thin, describing it only as "like a 16-bit counter" and providing no details on the multiplier functionality or testing.
ttihp25a/tt_um_pyamnihc_dummy_counter.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source only supports counter and multiplier functionality.

ttihp25a/tt_um_quarren42_demoscene_top.summary: This Verilog design displays a parody of the 'graphic design is my passion' meme with bouncing shapes on a VGA monitor. It has no inputs and outputs standard VGA signals, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon. It is a simple graphics demo with no interactive elements.

ttihp25a/tt_um_ran_DanielZhu.summary: This SystemVerilog design generates a random number from 0 to F when a button is pressed, using an inverter ring as the entropy source. It outputs the result on its output pins, intended for a 2-digit LED display. The design runs at 50 MHz and requires external hardware for the button and display. The documentation is very thin, with pin names all labeled '1', so the exact interface is unclear.
ttihp25a/tt_um_ran_DanielZhu.review_notes: Removed game (not an interactive game) and added insufficient-doc for the very thin documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_colorbars.summary: This design generates a VGA test pattern resembling NTSC color bars, with optional station ID display, scrolling ID, and scrolling bars. It is configured through input pins for showing the ID, using a custom ID, scrolling the ID, and scrolling the bars, and it outputs RGB and sync signals on the Tiny VGA pinout. A TinyVGA PMOD is required to connect to a VGA monitor, and the colors are explicitly not accurate to real NTSC color bars. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester noted the clock must be manually set to 25 MHz in the commander app.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_styler.summary: The Styler chip manipulates 16x16 character glyph bitmaps based on text mode attributes such as bold, faint, italic, underline, and blink. It has registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and it interfaces via 8 bidirectional data pins and several control inputs. The typical use involves writing a scanline number, reading back a logical scanline, and then manipulating bitmap halves to apply visual effects. The chip is intended as part of a larger text mode video display hardware system, and testing is covered by provided test scripts.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_tt09ball_scree.summary: This design generates a 640x480 VGA signal displaying a bouncing DVD-style logo with an animated color gradient. Two inputs control the behavior: ui_in[0] tiles the logo across the screen, and ui_in[1] switches to a solid color instead of the gradient. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor via a TinyVGA Pmod and observing the animation. The design is notable for being a compact VGA screensaver implementation that fits on a single tile and requires the TinyVGA Pmod as external hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large selection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to show the first flag, move to the next or previous flag, or select a flag by index. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and requires a TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a monitor. The design is extensible by adding new flag modules and updating the index, as described in the documentation. No silicon test reports are provided, but the documentation is clear about usage and configuration.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed overly generic video tag and added pmod tag supported by external hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_exp.summary: This design is a configurable VGA signal generator that allows full control over display timings, sync polarities, and test patterns. It can be programmed via a register interface using ui_in and uio pins to set parameters such as visible width, porches, and sync widths, and it includes 32 test patterns like checkerboards, grids, and color bars. Testing involves connecting a VGA monitor through a TinyVGA Pmod and using the inputs to select patterns or modify timing registers. The design is notable for its flexibility in experimenting with VGA signal generation, requiring only the TinyVGA Pmod as external hardware.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_exp.review_notes: Removed 'education' because the source only says experimentation, not teaching or learning.

ttihp25a/tt_um_reemashivva_fifo.summary: The design implements an asynchronous FIFO that buffers data between two clock domains with independent read and write clocks. It uses Gray-coded pointers and synchronization logic to prevent metastability, with full and empty flags indicating when the FIFO cannot accept or provide data. The documentation describes how to test by setting write and read enables and observing the flags and data outputs, but the pin list provided in the documentation does not match the actual pin names given in the project metadata. External hardware is minimal, likely just a way to drive the inputs and observe the outputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_reemashivva_fifo.review_notes: Removed generic memory tag; added fifo, asynchronous, clock-domain-crossing, synchronizer, gray-code, and verilog based on source evidence.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.summary: This design is a replica of the Atari 2600 video game console system-on-chip, implemented in Verilog. It accepts joystick inputs, switches, and a reset signal, and outputs VGA video and PWM audio, with QSPI pins for external memory. It is tested by connecting a TinyVGA Pmod, Tiny Audio Pmod, and a VGA display, then playing games. The design is notable for being a complete recreation of a classic console on a Tiny Tapeout tile, requiring external hardware for video, audio, and game storage.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.review_notes: Removed cpu because the source does not document an implemented processor core.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.summary: This Verilog implementation is a replica of the classic AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a 3-voice PSG chip from General Instrument. It provides three square-wave tone generators, a white noise generator using a 17-bit LFSR, an envelope generator with 10 shapes, and 16 volume levels, controlled through 14 registers. The design outputs digital 8-bit audio and a PWM pseudo-analog audio signal, and can be configured with an external clock divider. It is intended for hardware preservation and educational purposes, with a test suite for regression testing against the original chip behavior.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_ay8913.review_notes: Replaced incorrect neural-network/machine-learning/decoder tags with sound-generator, music, audio, pwm, lfsr, verilog, retro, and dac based on the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_decoder.summary: This design unpacks ternary, quinary, and septenary packed weights, converting them from a compressed format of 1.6 to 2.6 bits per parameter into an unpacked representation. It takes 8 bits of packed weight data on the input pins and outputs the unpacked values on both the output and bidirectional pins, with a control input to select between ternary and septenary modes. Testing requires providing packed weights on the input Pmods, and external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi Pico is needed to supply the data. The design is notable for its application in neural network quantization, but the documentation is minimal and lacks detailed usage instructions.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_e2m0_x_i8_matmul.summary: This design implements a systolic array for matrix multiplication using reduced-precision packed weights of 2.6 bits per parameter (septenary and quinary formats) and INT8 activations. It accepts packed weights on the input pins and activations on the bidirectional pins, and outputs the multiplication results on the output pins, with a strobe enable pin to start receiving results. Testing requires an external processor such as an RP2040 to feed weights and activations and to fetch the results. The design is notable for its use of compressed weights to reduce memory footprint in neural network acceleration, but it requires external hardware for operation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_e2m0_x_i8_matmul.review_notes: Removed fixed-point tag unsupported by source; added rp2040 since the source names it as required external hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_sn76489.summary: This design is a Verilog replica of the SN76489 programmable sound generator, featuring three square wave tone generators and one noise generator with white and periodic noise types. It is programmed via an 8-bit data bus and provides both digital 8-bit audio and PWM audio outputs, with separate channel outputs for external mixing. Testing involves sending register write commands and observing the audio output, which can be connected to a DAC, RC filter, or amplifier. The design is notable for its faithful reproduction of the original chip's behavior, thorough test suite, and educational documentation, requiring external hardware such as a microcontroller and audio output circuitry.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_ternary_dot.summary: This project computes a dot product between a binary vector A and a ternary vector B, with ternary weights and 1-bit activations, targeting on-chip neural network inference. The inputs are eight binary elements of A and serial ternary elements of B, and the dot product result is provided on eight output pins. Testing is done via the Commander app to set inputs and weights, with no additional hardware required. The documentation is very brief, only stating the basic function and test method.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_ternary_dot.review_notes: Removed multiplier; added mac-unit and accelerator to reflect the actual dot-product datapath.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_vga_logo.summary: This design displays a 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor, using compressed data and dithered colors to fit into a single tile. It generates standard VGA signals including red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for operation, and it has been tested successfully by a silicon tester who confirmed the video works as expected. Notable features include the large resolution crammed into a small area and the use of dithering for color effects.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_vga_test01.summary: This design is an audio/visual demo that generates VGA video and PWM audio outputs, forming an 8-part megademo. It uses eight PWM audio pins and standard VGA pins for red, green, blue, and sync signals. The demo requires external hardware: a VGA PMOD and audio output hardware. Silicon tests report that both audio and video work as expected, and one tester described it as a very nice demo with polished graphics and audio.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rejunity_z80.summary: This project is an open-source silicon implementation of the Zilog Z80 8-bit CPU, based on the TV80 Verilog core. It aims to be a pin-compatible replacement for the classic Z80, which has reached end-of-life. The design has been tested on silicon and successfully runs demos such as 'Hello World' and the Z80 instruction set exerciser. It requires external hardware like a bus demultiplexer, memory, and an 8-bit computer such as a ZX Spectrum, or can be tested with the RP2040 on the TinyTapeout test PCB.

ttihp25a/tt_um_resfuzzy.summary: This project implements a fuzzy logic system that estimates a risk value based on rainfall and soil moisture inputs. It uses triangular membership functions to evaluate inputs as low, medium, or high, and applies three fuzzy rules to compute a weighted average risk output. The design requires external hardware: eight switches for sensor inputs, one switch for sensor selection, and an 8-bit LED display for the risk output. Testing involves feeding different sensor data and verifying the expected risk levels (high, low, medium).

ttihp25a/tt_um_ring_divider.summary: This design implements a ring oscillator operating in the GHz range, followed by a divider to produce a lower-frequency output in the 20 MHz range. It includes test and debug modes to verify divider functionality at low frequencies, and can be disabled via an enable signal. Testing requires an oscilloscope, power supply, and function generator, as described in the documentation. Silicon verification results are not provided.

ttihp25a/tt_um_riscv_mini.summary: This design is a compact 8-bit RISC-V processor core that uses a customized compressed instruction set (RVC) with 16-bit instructions to fit Tiny Tapeout constraints. It includes a control unit, an 8-register file, an ALU, and a single-cycle datapath, and it executes R-Type, I-Type, L-Type, S-Type, and B-Type instructions. Testing is done by setting the instruction on the input pins and clocking once to receive the result on the output pins, with different instruction types producing different outputs. The design is a compact RISC-V core optimized for area, but it lacks detailed documentation on its instruction encoding and limitations.
ttihp25a/tt_um_riscv_mini.review_notes: Removed education tag not supported by the source; adjusted summary wording.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rkarl_Spiral.summary: This design generates an Archimedean spiral pattern for VGA display, with adjustable foreground/background colors and animation speed via input pins. It requires an external PMOD VGA adapter and optionally switches for control. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a short description and basic testing instructions.

ttihp25a/tt_um_ronikant_jeremykam_tinyre.summary: This design provides three types of registers for a basic 8-bit CPU: a general-purpose register, a memory address register, and an instruction register. The registers are selected using two control pins (uio[6] and uio[7]), and data can be written to or read from the selected register via the input and output pins. Testing involves selecting a register and verifying that data is stored and retrieved correctly. The design is notable for being a simple building block for CPU designs, but it has minimal documentation and requires external control logic to be useful.
ttihp25a/tt_um_ronikant_jeremykam_tinyre.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the register-file and cpu tags are supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_roy1707018.summary: This design combines a ring-oscillator-based true random number generator with an ASCON S-box cryptographic substitution block. Sixteen ring oscillators are split into two banks controlled by ui_in bits 0 and 1, and a 64-bit shift register captures their outputs, with bits 2-4 selecting which 8-bit slice is presented. The S-box is enabled by ui_in bit 7 and takes bits 2-6 as its 5-bit input, and the final uo_out is the bitwise XOR of the TRNG and S-box results. It was verified only in simulation with a testbench driving various input values, and no external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_roy1707018.review_notes: Removed prng tag since the design is explicitly a TRNG, not a PRNG.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rte_sine_synth.summary: The project implements a monophonic keyboard synthesizer with one octave of notes, generating sine waves using an efficient delta-step method. The 8-bit output is provided directly and also via a PWM generator for audio output, intended for use with Mike Bell's audio PMOD. Testing involves attaching the input PMOD to a row of buttons for playing notes. No silicon test results are mentioned.

ttihp25a/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.summary: This design computes the Collatz sequence for a large integer input, returning the orbit length and an indicator of the maximum value reached. The input number is uploaded byte-by-byte into a 144-bit register via an address bus, and the computation is started with a pin; the busy indicator is polled until completion, after which the results are read back in 16-bit chunks. The design is intended for brute-force searching of path records, and the documentation explains the state machine and I/O protocol in detail. No external hardware is required beyond the chip itself.
ttihp25a/tt_um_rtfb_collatz.review_notes: Removed alu and register-file tags not supported by the source; added fsm, verilog and esoteric.

ttihp25a/tt_um_samkho_two_channel_square.summary: This design generates two independent square waves using 8-bit reloadable countdown timers, with periods proportional to the input values plus one. It also provides a 2-bit sum output of the two square waves. The design is tested by applying arbitrary 8-bit values to the inputs and probing the outputs with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer. External hardware is not required, but the intended use is to drive speakers via resistor dividers and an amplifier.
ttihp25a/tt_um_samkho_two_channel_square.review_notes: Removed oscillator and retro tags not supported by the source; added sound-generator for the speaker-driving tone generation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_samuelm_pwm_generator.summary: This design is a PWM generator with configurable period (12-bit) and duty cycle (7-bit, 1%-99% coverage). It contains two 12-bit registers for duty and period, selected via a sel signal and written when wr_en is high. Testing involves connecting the output to an oscilloscope to verify frequency and duty cycle. External hardware includes a microcontroller or pattern generator to set the inputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_samuelm_pwm_generator.review_notes: register-file tag removed: design has only two configuration registers, not a register file.

ttihp25a/tt_um_save_buffer_hash_table.summary: This design implements a hash table with eight slots, 4-bit keys, and 4-bit values, supporting lookup, insert, and delete operations. Commands are issued via CMD and GO signals, with status and output value provided on output pins. The table handles collisions using linear probing and buffers inputs during operation. Testing involves setting keys, values, and commands, then observing status and output. No external hardware is required beyond input switches and output displays.

ttihp25a/tt_um_schoeberl_test.summary: This is a test project created to explore the Chisel hardware construction language. It has 8 inputs, 8 bidirectional pins, and 8 outputs, but the documentation does not describe any specific functionality beyond being a test. The project includes a ChiselTest that can be run with sbt test. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable only as a learning exercise.
ttihp25a/tt_um_schoeberl_test.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; source explicitly says it is just a Chisel test project.

ttihp25a/tt_um_schoeberl_wildcat.summary: Wildcat is a 3-stage RISC-V CPU implementation written in Chisel. The documentation is extremely sparse, with only a one-line description and a 'TBD' for testing, and the pin names are generic. It may require external flash and RAM PMODs for operation according to the pin description. No further details on functionality, testing, or silicon results are provided.

ttihp25a/tt_um_sebastienparadis_hamming_.summary: This project implements a (7,4) Hamming encoder and decoder with a shared input bus, where the mode is selected by the most significant input bit. In encode mode, it takes a 4-bit input and produces a 7-bit encoded output; in decode mode, it takes a 7-bit input and outputs the corrected 7-bit codeword. Testing involves applying known data and verifying the encoded output, then flipping one bit in the encoded input to confirm error correction. No external hardware is specified, and the design is a straightforward implementation of a classic error-correcting code.

ttihp25a/tt_um_secA_11_nyancar_alanz23.summary: This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It uses AND gates and full adders arranged in a grid, as described in the documentation. Testing involves applying two 4-bit inputs and reading the 8-bit product. The design is educational, likely from a class (ECE 2204), and requires no external hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_secA_group5_array_multipl.summary: This project is a 4x4 array multiplier that takes two 4-bit unsigned numbers and outputs their 8-bit product. It is built from 12 full adders and 16 AND gates, following a structural array multiplier architecture. Testing is done by applying two 4-bit inputs via the ui_in pins and reading the product on the uo_out pins. No external hardware is required, and the design is a typical class project for learning digital arithmetic.
ttihp25a/tt_um_secA_group5_array_multipl.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_secB_15_array_multiplier.summary: This is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit binary numbers to produce an 8-bit result. It generates 16 partial products using AND gates and sums them with full adders. The design is tested by applying various 4-bit inputs in a simulation environment and verifying the product. No external hardware is needed, and the project is a standard educational implementation of an array multiplier.
ttihp25a/tt_um_secB_15_array_multiplier.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_secd_8_array_mult.summary: This project implements a 4-bit array multiplier that computes the product of two 4-bit unsigned numbers, outputting an 8-bit result. It uses partial product generation with AND gates and summation with full adders. Testing is done by applying an 8-bit input representing two 4-bit numbers and checking the 8-bit output. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward educational example of a structural multiplier.
ttihp25a/tt_um_secd_8_array_mult.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_section_d_group_fifteen_a.summary: This is a 4x4 array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit unsigned binary numbers to produce an 8-bit product. It is implemented structurally using logic gates and 1-bit full adders, following a partial product and addition approach. The design can be tested via an automatic testbench or by building the circuit from provided schematics. No external hardware is used, and the project is a class assignment for a digital logic course.
ttihp25a/tt_um_section_d_group_fifteen_a.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a dedicated multiplier, not a general ALU.

ttihp25a/tt_um_senolgulgonul.summary: This design displays the letters of 'SEnOLGULGONUL' on a 7-segment display using an internal three-gate oscillator. It requires external resistors and a capacitor to complete the oscillator circuit, and the outputs connect directly to a 7-segment display. Testing involves connecting the external components and observing the letters on the display. The project is notable for using a simple gate-based oscillator to drive a text display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_senolgulgonul.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator tag; the source specifies a three-gate oscillator.

ttihp25a/tt_um_shifter.summary: This project implements a shifter that outputs the result of shifting the 8-bit input right by the number of positions specified on the 8-bit bidirectional input. The design is tested by setting switches on the inputs and observing the shifted value on LEDs connected to the outputs. No external hardware beyond switches and LEDs is required. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic operation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_shifter.review_notes: Removed barrel-shifter and education tags as unsupported by the minimal documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.summary: This project implements a basic calculator supporting addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division on positive integers. It scans a 4x4 matrix keypad through the ROW and COL pins and drives a 3-digit seven-segment display via the sseg outputs, with E_1 through E_3 likely acting as digit enables. Testing is done by entering operands through the keypad and checking that the display shows the expected result. External hardware required is a 4x4 matrix keypad and a 3-digit seven-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.review_notes: Removed alu and decoder tags not supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_sign_addsub.summary: This is a 4-bit signed adder-subtractor built from multiplexers, half adders, and full adders. Two 4-bit operands a and b are supplied on ui_in, and the two sign bits on uio select one of four operations: A+B, -A+B, A-B, or -A-B, with the 4-bit result on uo and sign outputs on uio. The design was verified in QuestaSim using an extensive testbench covering the operation modes. No external hardware is needed.
ttihp25a/tt_um_sign_addsub.review_notes: Removed alu (only add/subtract, no logic ops) and added systemverilog and combinational tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_silice.summary: Warp is a demoscene demo that generates audio and video output, intended for use with VGA and audio PMODs. It can be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio also runs on an ULX3S. The documentation is minimal and uncertain, with statements like 'Maybe it works?'. External hardware includes VGA and audio PMODs, and the design is written in Silice.

ttihp25a/tt_um_simon_cipher.summary: This is a bit-serial implementation of the SIMON-128 lightweight block cipher, trading throughput for a compact area dominated by flip-flops and multiplexers. A 2-bit control word on ui[7:6] selects idle, plaintext load, key load, or encrypt, with serial data entering on ui[0] and ciphertext emerging on uo[0] over 128 consecutive clock cycles, flagged by a valid bit on uo[7]. The design is verified through a testbench containing example test vectors, and no external hardware is required. The documentation notes a limitation in the key-loading process and includes a debug bit to verify key register loading.

ttihp25a/tt_um_snn_with_delays_paolaunis.summary: This design implements a spiking neural network with 18 programmable digital LIF neurons and 144 synapses arranged in three fully connected layers.
