It is configured via an SPI interface to set neuron thresholds, decay rates, refractory periods, and synaptic weights and delays. Input spikes are applied to the first layer, and output spikes or membrane potentials can be read back through SPI. The project is notable for being generated by ChatGPT and for its use of programmable delays, though no silicon test results are provided.
ttihp25a/tt_um_snn_with_delays_paolaunis.review_notes: Removed delay-line; the delays are synaptic delays within the SNN, not a delay-line circuit.

ttihp25a/tt_um_space_invaders_game.summary: This is a Verilog implementation of the classic Space Invaders game. The player controls a ship using three input buttons to move left, move right, and shoot, with the game state output on eight pins. It is intended to be played using the TinyTapeout Commander app, which maps keyboard inputs to the ASIC pins, and tested with the TinyTapeout VGA Playground. No external hardware is required beyond the standard TinyTapeout setup, and no silicon test results are mentioned.
ttihp25a/tt_um_space_invaders_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported vga and gpio tags; added button and multi-tile.

ttihp25a/tt_um_spacewar.summary: This project is a scaled-down Spacewar-style design with VGA output, based on the VGA playground controller example. It accepts a SNES gamepad for input and outputs VGA signals, and the pinout also accommodates an audio PMOD. The design was left incomplete when work stopped at the Efabless shutdown, so it only allows moving a square on the screen rather than being a full game. It is configured for the demoscene competition and requires external VGA and gamepad hardware.
ttihp25a/tt_um_spacewar.review_notes: Removed game tag because the source states it is not a complete game; kept incomplete, retro, demoscene, vga, gamepad.

ttihp25a/tt_um_spi_pwm_djuara.summary: This design is an SPI-controlled PWM generator with eight bidirectional IO pins. It contains eight registers accessible via two different SPI interfaces (clocked and sampled) to configure PWM on-time and cycle, as well as IO direction and values. The design includes test modes for SPI reads/writes, PWM output, external PWM control, and bidirectional IO. It requires an external SPI master for configuration and testing.

ttihp25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.summary: This design implements a stochastic-computing multiplier, adder, and self-multiplier that operate on serial bitstreams. Two 9-bit repeating input streams enter on ui[0] and ui[1], and the multiplier, adder, and self-multiplier results appear as serial outputs on uo[0], uo[1], and uo[2], with uo[3] resetting the clock counter; the self-multiplier uses only the first stream. Testing involves feeding the repeating streams and reading the resulting 9-bit serial outputs. The documentation consists mainly of images with little explanatory text, and an ADALM2000 is listed as external hardware.
ttihp25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.review_notes: Removed dsp; added verilog to match the stated language.

ttihp25a/tt_um_stochastic_integrator_tt9.summary: This design implements a stochastic integrator using Euler's method in the stochastic computing domain. It takes two serial inputs and produces multiple serial outputs representing different integrator configurations. The design is based on published research and uses LFSRs for stochastic number generation. Testing involves setting the inputs to constant high and low to observe the integration behavior, and external hardware such as an ADALM2000 may be used for signal generation and analysis.

ttihp25a/tt_um_strau0106_simple_viii.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit CPU architecture implemented in SystemVerilog. It interfaces with external QSPI flash and RAM memories through dedicated chip select and data pins. The design is intended to be a minimal CPU, but the documentation is very sparse, providing only the title and pin names without detailed operation or testing instructions. No silicon test results are available.

ttihp25a/tt_um_subtile_factory_test.summary: This is a factory test module for Tiny Tapeout subtiles, designed to verify all available I/O. It has three modes controlled by reset and clock signals: mirroring inputs to outputs, inverting inputs to outputs, or driving outputs low. The design is implemented in a single line of Verilog and is used to test the connectivity of subtile pins on an ASIC. It is a simple utility with no external hardware requirements.
ttihp25a/tt_um_subtile_factory_test.review_notes: Removed gpio and logic-gate: the design is a factory test structure, not a GPIO interface or logic gate.

ttihp25a/tt_um_supermic_arghunter.summary: This design is an 8-channel customizable beamforming signal processor for audio applications. It accepts PDM microphone inputs and outputs PCM audio, with delay selection via pins. The documentation is extremely thin, consisting of placeholder text, so the exact functionality and testing procedure are unclear. External hardware includes PDM microphones, a clock generator, and an I2S receiver.
ttihp25a/tt_um_supermic_arghunter.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc because pin documentation and purpose are present; added i2s from the clock pins and external-hardware note.

ttihp25a/tt_um_sushi_demo.summary: This project displays a running sushi animation on a VGA screen. It outputs VGA signals and requires a TinyVGA PMOD for connection. The design is a simple demo with minimal documentation, and no silicon test results are provided. It is intended for visual demonstration.

ttihp25a/tt_um_synth_simple_mm.summary: This is a simple monophonic synthesizer with PWM left and right output channels. It uses five input pins for note enable signals and eight switches to select sounds or notes, producing PWM outputs on uo[0] and uo[1]. External hardware includes five IR modules to generate notes, eight switches to choose sounds or notes, and two low-pass filters to produce left/right audio signals. The design is a basic synth whose documentation is very brief.
ttihp25a/tt_um_synth_simple_mm.review_notes: Removed sensor-interface which overstates the IR note inputs; summary aligned with the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_systolicLif.summary: This project implements a systolic array model of leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons in Verilog. The design uses weight-stationary multiply-accumulate (MAC) units with bypass logic to prevent overstimulation of the LIF neurons. The user input ui_in drives the MAC inputs, and the output bits indicate the LIF state and spike events. The design has not been tested on silicon.
ttihp25a/tt_um_systolicLif.review_notes: Removed unsupported SPI tag and added systolic-array and mac-unit tags; summary corrected to match the actual LIF/MAC design.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tappu_tobias1012.summary: Tappu is an 8-bit CPU inspired by the esoteric language BF, implemented in Chisel. It includes a ROM that causes all outputs to blink, and the design is intended to be observed by watching the output blink. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no detailed usage or testing instructions. No external hardware is required beyond power and observation of the outputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tappu_tobias1012.review_notes: Removed led; the source only says outputs blink, not that LEDs are driven.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tetrap_triggerer.summary: This module captures timestamps of rising edges on input triggers, referenced to an internal 24-bit counter with a period of about 30 ms. It provides a data-ready signal and allows reading the captured timestamp via a clocked serial interface. The design is intended for capturing events and may benefit from a signal generator for testing. The documentation notes that it was tested manually only once in simulation, indicating limited verification.

ttihp25a/tt_um_thexeno_rgbw_controller.summary: The RGBW Color Processor generates PWM control signals for RGBW LEDs based on color index, intensity, and white level, or acts as a direct SPI-to-four-channel PWM converter in bypass mode. It is an SPI slave in mode 0 that receives an 8-byte command, and it can produce hue, tint, and intensity from a color index when in color wheel mode. Testing is typically done with a MicroPython script on the Tiny Tapeout demoboard, connecting LEDs to the PWM outputs while respecting the 4 mA current limit. No silicon test results are provided, but the design is well documented and supports both RP2040-based and STM32-based test setups.
ttihp25a/tt_um_thexeno_rgbw_controller.review_notes: rgb-led implies an addressable LED interface; the design only drives external LEDs via PWM, so driver is more accurate.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tiny_shader_mole99.summary: Tiny Shader is a programmable shader unit that executes a 10-instruction shader per pixel to generate images and animations, output via VGA at 640x480 with an internal resolution of 64x48. It includes an SPI interface for loading new shaders and setting a user register. Testing requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally an SPI controller. Silicon testing confirmed all features work, including custom shader upload and animation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout.summary: This design is a ternary matrix multiplication processor. It loads weights into an internal register array and performs matrix multiplication using a pipelined architecture. The module can continuously accept new input vectors while completing previous computations. Outputs are produced as 8-bit integers representing the matrix multiplication result.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout.review_notes: Removed incorrect neural network tags and added accelerator, verilog, and pipeline tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout_csa.summary: This project is a ternary matrix multiplication processor using carry-save adders, written in Verilog. It loads weights into an internal register array and multiplies input vectors by those weights, summing the products to produce 8-bit integer outputs. The datapath is pipelined so it can accept new input vectors while computing on previous ones, producing continuous results. Testing is done by driving the inputs from an external MCU such as a Raspberry Pi over GPIO, and no silicon test reports are available.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tiny_ternary_tapeout_csa.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a spiking neural network that does not appear anywhere in the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tinysynth.summary: This design is a tiny square wave oscillator that accepts MIDI commands. It receives MIDI commands over UART and generates a corresponding square wave signal using PWM. The design is written in Chisel. External hardware includes a Pmod AMP2 connected to the PMOD connector.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tinysynth.review_notes: Removed incorrect neural network tags and added music, pwm, uart, sound-generator, and chisel tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tmkong_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer reads three digital rotary encoders to control the brightness of three PWM outputs, intended for driving RGB LEDs. It debounces the encoder inputs and includes a debug mode where the internal encoder values are output on the bidirectional pins when the debug input is set to 0, 1, or 2. The design is tested by twisting each encoder and observing the corresponding LED brightness change. External hardware consists of three digital encoders connected to the first six inputs, and the project is noted as the creator's first ASIC design.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tmkong_rgb_mixer.review_notes: rgb-led overstates the interface; the design only provides PWM LED drive outputs.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tobimckellar_top.summary: This design is a basic PWM controller that generates a pulse-width modulated output on uo[7] when enabled by ui[7]. The six-bit input ui[5:0] sets the duty cycle in manual mode, or the frequency of an internally generated triangular reference when ui[6] is high, producing a breathing effect. It is tested by enabling the output and observing the PWM signal on uo[7] while flipping the input switches. No external hardware is required, though an LED and resistor are suggested for visual feedback.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tobimckellar_top.review_notes: Removed signal-generator (PWM only); added led per the stated LED-control purpose.

ttihp25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo_deluxe.summary: Sequential Shadows Deluxe is a demo competition entry for TT08 that generates VGA video and audio, featuring visual effects and music. It requires a TinVGA or Pmod VGA for video output and Mike's audio Pmod for sound, with pinout selection via an input. The demo includes flashing lights by default, which can be disabled via inputs. The design is notable for its integration of video and audio in a single submission.
ttihp25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo_deluxe.review_notes: Removed unsupported audio-synthesis style tags; added music and pmod based on documented demo content and Pmod pinout.

ttihp25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo_tt08.summary: Sequential Shadows is a demoscene demo that combines a ray caster, synthesizer, music sequencer, and audio visualizer to produce a real-time audiovisual experience. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and Mike's audio PMOD for sound, and it includes controls for pausing, stepping frames, and disabling bass or drums. The design was developed for the TT08 demo competition and was tested on hardware by both the author and an independent tester, who confirmed it works as simulated. The demo is best viewed with the monitor rotated 90 degrees and includes flashing lights by default.

ttihp25a/tt_um_toivoh_demo_tt10.summary: Orion Iron Ion is a TT10 demo competition entry that produces VGA video and audio, including a logo, star field, floating-point unit for graphics, and a synthesizer. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod and Mike's audio Pmod for full functionality. The demo starts automatically after reset and was verified working on silicon by the author. The design is notable for its use of a floating-point unit in a demo context.

ttihp25a/tt_um_toivoh_pio_ram_emu_exampl.summary: This design demonstrates the use of a PIO-based RAM emulator on the RP2040 to store a 320x480 2-bit-per-pixel frame buffer and continuously output a 640x480 VGA signal. The logic computes a Julia fractal and writes it to the frame buffer, with user input via buttons to adjust parameters. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for VGA output and the RAM emulator running on the RP2040, and includes helper modules and a simulation model for testing. The design serves as an example for using the RAM emulator and includes test infrastructure.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tommythorn_cgates.summary: Cgates tests two different implementations of Muller's C-gate: one using a latch and one using combinatorial logic, and also builds rings of various lengths from these gates. The design allows observation of the C-gate outputs and ring transitions, with testing requiring an oscilloscope for the ring outputs. It is a variant of a previous design and serves as an experiment in asynchronous logic elements. The documentation provides clear instructions for basic testing.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tommythorn_cgates.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator because the source describes C-gate rings and transitions, not oscillator circuits.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tommythorn_maxbw.summary: This design is an asynchronous multiplier that emits the sequence r = x^2 + x for x = 0, 1, 2, ... using a four-phase bundled-data handshake. Internally it uses 26-bit precision but folds the result down to 15 output bits with r ^ (r >> 15). It is tested by tying ack to req for free-running operation and observing the outputs, optionally with a logic analyzer or RP2040. The author notes that timing analysis is still in progress and the inserted delays are likely oversized.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tommythorn_workshop.summary: This is a workshop demo design with a UART receiver on ui[0], a UART transmitter on uo[0], and a PDM output on uo[1]. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is magic and suggesting connecting the TX pin to a terminal. No external hardware is listed, and the design appears to be a workshop example. Due to the lack of detail, its exact functionality cannot be determined.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tommythorn_workshop.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added incomplete due to very thin documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_toniklippeo.summary: toni_clk_gen generates multiple clock signals by dividing the input frequency. It provides two divided clock outputs, but the documentation does not specify the division ratios or intended application. The testing procedure is unknown, and external hardware such as a clock generator is suggested. The design appears to be a simple clock divider experiment with minimal documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_top.summary: Flame demo displays a flame animation on a VGA monitor and plays simple 1-bit PWM audio. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD for video and either Mike's audio PMOD or a basic RC filter for sound, and it runs at a 25 MHz clock with a reset pulse. Silicon testing by two independent testers confirmed that both audio and video work as expected, with good use of color and dithering. The design is a compact demoscene-style demo suitable for the Tiny Tapeout demo competition.

ttihp25a/tt_um_torurstrom_async_lock.summary: This design implements an asynchronous locking unit that accepts eight request signals and provides eight grant signals, ensuring that only one grant is active at a time. It functions as a mutual exclusion arbiter for asynchronous systems. The documentation is brief and does not describe the arbitration policy or testing methodology. No external hardware is specified.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tt08_wirecube.summary: Wirecube is a demo for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition that displays a rotating wireframe cube on a VGA screen. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and operates at a clock frequency of 50.35 MHz. Inputs allow toggling background and cube colors, as well as speed. The documentation is sparse and will be updated after the competition, but the design is functional as a visual demo.
ttihp25a/tt_um_tt08_wirecube.review_notes: Added multi-tile; summary is supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_tt09_array_multiplier.summary: This design implements a 4x4 array multiplier using structural logic, taking two 4-bit inputs and producing an 8-bit product. It uses full adders to sum partial products along diagonals. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. The documentation includes diagrams and a GitHub link, but the testing procedure is simply to apply inputs and observe the output.

ttihp25a/tt_um_two_lif_stdp.summary: This design implements two leaky integrate-and-fire neurons connected by a synapse with spike-timing-dependent plasticity, using 8-bit fixed-point arithmetic. The first neuron receives an 8-bit input current on ui, the second neuron's state is driven out on uo, and spike outputs plus the 6-bit synapse weight appear on the bidirectional pins. It is tested by applying current patterns and observing spike timing and weight changes, a process that can be automated with cocotb or optionally observed with a logic analyzer or signal generator. The project is notable for putting a small plastic spiking neural network on a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttihp25a/tt_um_two_lif_stdp.review_notes: Added cocotb supplement to corrected summary and tag; no tag removals needed.

ttihp25a/tt_um_uart_bgdtanasa.summary: ttUART is a UART repeater that mirrors received serial data back out on the transmit line. It exposes rx_data_in, rx_data_ready, rx_sample_clk, tx_data_out and tx_data_done pins and can be used like a regular UART. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief, giving only the repeater behavior and pin functions.

ttihp25a/tt_um_uart_mvm.summary: This design performs matrix-vector multiplication, receiving the matrix and vector via UART and outputting the result via UART. Internally, it uses AXI-Stream to pass data between the UART modules and the multiplication core. The design is tested with a provided testbench using iverilog. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_uart_mvm.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; the source describes matrix-vector multiplication, not digital signal processing.

ttihp25a/tt_um_uart_mvm_sys.summary: This design performs matrix-vector multiplication, receiving the matrix and vector via UART and outputting the result via UART. Internally, it uses AXI-Stream to pass data between the UART modules and the multiplication core. The design is tested with a provided testbench using iverilog. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_uart_mvm_sys.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; the source describes matrix-vector multiplication, not digital signal processing.

ttihp25a/tt_um_udxs.summary: This design implements a basic perceptron with a ReLU activation layer, using a single-cycle multiply-accumulation unit. It takes four signed 4-bit weights and four signed 4-bit inputs, and outputs a 16-bit ReLU result. The design is tested by providing weight-input pairs cycle-by-cycle and sampling the output, then resetting for a new invocation. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25a/tt_um_udxs.review_notes: Added verilog and machine-learning tags that were clearly supported but missing.

ttihp25a/tt_um_ultra_tiny_cpu.summary: UltraTiny-CPU is a minimal 8-bit CPU with an accumulator, a B register, a program counter and a 16-byte internal instruction memory. It is programmed through a load mode where ui[7] selects loading, ui[3:0] supplies the address and uio[7:0] supplies the byte, then runs from address 0 with results visible on the accumulator output uo[7:0]. No external hardware is strictly required, though a logic analyzer or LED display can be attached to watch the accumulator. The design is notable for fitting a complete fetch-decode-execute loop and small instruction set into a single tile.

ttihp25a/tt_um_underserved.summary: This is a RISC-V based system that boots by accessing an SPI flash over the SPI bus, configuring it in XIP mode and executing instructions from it. It exposes four GPIO pins that can be used to output data, for example as a bitbanged UART. The design is written in Verilog and targets a 2x2 tile area. Testing uses a testbench containing an SPI flash model preloaded with a program in Verilog Hex format, and the project can be run locally with FuseSoC.
ttihp25a/tt_um_underserved.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an Enigma cipher in Amaranth, which does not match the RISC-V SoC source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator with up to 3853 inverter stages. By connecting one of the output pins to the ring_in input or enabling internal loopback, a ring of a specific length is formed, and the output frequency can be measured. External hardware such as an oscilloscope or logic analyzer is required to measure the frequency and delay between different points in the chain. The design is notable for its large number of stages and the ability to select from many tap points.
ttihp25a/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag; the design is an inverter-chain ring oscillator, not a logic gate implementation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttihp25a/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.summary: UW ASIC - Optimized Dino is described as a Dino game compressed into only two tiles. The documentation consists entirely of placeholders, so the actual controls, video output format and testing method are not stated. The pin names are generic and give no further detail about the interface. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.
ttihp25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.review_notes: Removed game tag since only the title hints at a game and no gameplay is documented; kept insufficient-doc and verilog.

ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_cbtest.summary: This design generates VGA output to display patterns similar to Ishihara plates used for color blindness testing. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA display, and works out of the box without any configuration. The project is for experimental purposes only and is not an approved medical test. No silicon test results are provided.
ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_cbtest.review_notes: Removed biomedical (explicitly not a medical test) and added image-processing and pmod.

ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.summary: Glyph Mode is a standalone VGA demo submitted for the VGA Demoscene competition. It generates a display and allows palette selection via two input pins, choosing between green, red, blue, or pride color schemes. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a VGA monitor, and operates at 25.175 MHz. Silicon tests confirm it works, including palette changes, and it also functions at higher clock speeds.
ttihp25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.review_notes: Removed text tag; the source does not describe text rendering.

ttihp25a/tt_um_virantha_enigma.summary: This is a silicon implementation of an Enigma I cipher machine with a limited three-wire plugboard and a 52-bit key length. It takes 5-bit data and 3-bit command inputs, returns data on the bidirectional pins with a ready signal, and drives the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is needed because it uses the PCB's built-in display. The design is notable for implementing a historical rotor cipher machine in Amaranth on a single tile.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wallento_4bit_toycpu.summary: This is a 4-bit toy CPU based on a design from a German textbook, featuring a 4-bit accumulator and 4-bit instructions with 4-bit operands. It uses external memory and requires a testbed to drive the pins, including a microcontroller program to handle the clock, reset, and tristate data bus. The internal 19-bit state can be scanned out for debugging and visualization. The design is intended as an educational tool to transition from digital design to microprocessors.

ttihp25a/tt_um_warp.summary: This is a demo design that generates VGA video and audio output, intended for the Tiny Tapeout demoscene competition. It requires external VGA and audio PMODs to be plugged into the board for testing. The design can also be simulated on an ECPIX5 FPGA with appropriate PMODs, and the audio portion can run on an ULX3S using its DAC. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed technical information about the implementation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_warp.review_notes: Removed pmod (external hardware, not a design interface) and added fpga and music tags supported by the documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_whynot.summary: This design is a single-tile demo that combines VGA video and audio outputs, created quickly during coffee breaks. It uses a rotozoom effect and plays an attempt at music, with VGA output via a Pmod and audio via an Audio Pmod. Silicon tests confirm that both audio and video work as expected, and testers noted the presence of a Doomguy image, rotozoom, and a bit of E1M1 music, all in one tile. The design operates at 25 MHz and also works at 32 MHz.
ttihp25a/tt_um_whynot.review_notes: Added silicon-tested and retro tags supported by the test reports and Doom/E1M1 references.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.summary: This is a test structure that captures data on both edges of a clock using pulse generators of varying widths, with outputs for each width and a normal flop. It is intended to explore DDR throughput and flop aperture using Analog Discovery 3 hardware. The documentation is minimal and self-deprecating, stating the design is probably bad. It is a timing characterization experiment rather than a functional block.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_407306064811090945.review_notes: Adjusted tags to characterization and edge-detector; removed unsupported clock-generator, flip-flop and instrumentation tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.summary: This design is an octal ALU that executes binary operations on two octal numbers encoded in an 8-bit instruction and outputs the result to a 7-segment display. The instruction includes operation code bits and two operands, supporting operations such as addition, XOR, AND, and OR. It is used by setting the instruction on the input pins and viewing the result on the 7-segment display; an overflow during addition illuminates the decimal point. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires only the 7-segment display on the TT08 PCB.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_407760296956596225.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added dip-switch interface tag based on the documented test procedure.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_407852791999030273.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit ALU implemented in Wokwi, featuring a shift register, two registers, and an arithmetic unit capable of addition and subtraction. It uses a bus for data transfer, with control pins to load registers, enable outputs, and select operations; external LEDs display the result in binary. The design is intended for educational purposes, with detailed documentation explaining its operation and testing procedure. Silicon testing confirmed that loading registers and addition work correctly, including a counting example.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.summary: Traffic-light-sequence implements a simple traffic light state sequence from red through red-yellow, green and yellow back to red. Two input pins select the state and three output pins drive the corresponding lights. It is a Wokwi project with no tiles. The documentation is minimal and does not describe any external hardware beyond the implied LEDs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408118380088342529.review_notes: Removed industrial and education tags not supported by the source; kept fsm, sequencer, wokwi, led.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.summary: The Logic Test project is a simple design intended to verify basic logic functionality. It has eight input pins and two output pins, but the documentation provides no details on the logic implemented or how the outputs are derived. The design is likely a template or placeholder for testing purposes. There is insufficient documentation to determine its exact behavior or use.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408216451206371329.review_notes: Removed factory-test and education; factory-test is not supported and education is not stated.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.summary: The Abacus Lock is a digital combination lock that activates a servo when a specific sequence of switches is entered. It displays the current combination status in binary on an LED bar. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires external hardware including LEDs, an LED bar, a servo, and an Arduino Nano. It was sponsored by The MITRE Corporation and MIT/LL Beaverworks Summer Institute.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_408231820749720577.review_notes: Removed security (combination lock, not a security design) and added dip-switch and led-matrix.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_411379488132926465.summary: This project is a union of projects done in a class, as indicated by its title and description. It has 8 input pins and 7 output pins, and requires external hardware such as 7-segment displays and LEDs. The documentation is very sparse, providing only pin names and a list of external hardware, with no explanation of functionality or how to test it. Therefore, it is difficult to determine what the design actually does beyond being an educational exercise.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_411379488132926465.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc tag because documentation is very thin and lacks functional description.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_411783629732984833.summary: This design is a binary counter built from D flip-flops, with additional logic gate examples on the bidirectional pins. It is intended to be tested by connecting a 1 Hz oscillator to the clock pin and observing the output on LEDs, which count from 0 to 15 and roll over. External hardware includes a 555 timer for the oscillator, DIP switches or pushbuttons for input, and LEDs with resistors for output. The project is a first-time Tiny Tapeout submission.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_411783629732984833.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added dip-switch and button tags supported by the documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_412367067047460865.summary: This project is a simple single gate design created for workshop validation. It has two input pins and one output pin, and requires external hardware such as an LED display and input switches for testing. The documentation is extremely minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and a note to look at the Wokwi project. It appears to be a basic test design with little original functionality.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_412367067047460865.review_notes: Replaced unsupported template tag with workshop based on the explicit workshop validation description.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_412635532198550529.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU trainer that executes opcodes fed via input pins, with an 8-bit accumulator and four 8-bit working registers. It supports arithmetic and logical operations, shifts, and provides carry and zero flags. The design is tested by providing a 10 kHz clock, loading opcodes and immediate data, and observing results on a 7-segment display or via output pins. It is intended as an educational tool for learning CPU operation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413385294512575489.summary: This design consists of a string of inverters intended to function as a delay line or ring oscillator, with an XOR gate on the bidirectional pins that could be used as a mixer. The outputs are derived from the inputs according to a specific logic function: OUT1 = IN3 ? (IN0 & IN1) : IN2, and OUT0 and OUT2 are the inverse of OUT1. Testing requires basic DC logic signals on the input pins, and no specific external hardware is needed beyond switches or digital inputs. The documentation is brief and the design appears to be an experiment.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386973689694209.summary: This project counts the number of input switches that are turned on, providing the count on its output pins. It is tested by simply flipping the switches and observing the output. No external hardware is required. The design is a straightforward circuit created in Wokwi.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386973689694209.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and speculative learning-exercise wording.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386988538584065.summary: This Wokwi project implements a simple combinational logic circuit that converts the ASCII binary representation of the letter 'A' (0x37) to the letter 'V' (0x56). The design is described as 'basic (broken) logic', suggesting it may not function correctly. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and a test procedure. No external hardware is specified.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386988538584065.review_notes: Removed unsupported 7-segment, education, and template tags; added wokwi, logic-gate, and incomplete; corrected summary to remove invented DIP switch and 7-segment display.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386991502909441.summary: This design displays the contents of a register map on a charlieplexed 8x7 LED display and can generate waveforms for PWM, UART, and WS2812 in response to a trigger. A SPI serial connection is used to set values in the register map, with CS active low, SPI mode 0, and MSB first. Auxiliary functions such as LFSR, PWM, frequency counting, and ultrasonic distance sensing are implemented as space and time permit. Testing uses SPI to read and write registers and observe the LEDs or serial response, with a charlieplexed 7x8 LED display as external hardware.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413386991502909441.review_notes: Removed unsupported ws2812/led/uart interface tags and corrected the summary, which had invented a WS2812 driver as the main function.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.summary: This Wokwi project uses simple logic gates to display the letter 'P' on a 7-segment display when the 8-bit input equals 0x46. The design requires external hardware including a breadboard, 1.8V power supply, connector wires, an 8-position DIP switch, and a 7-segment display. The documentation describes the basic function and test procedure, noting that with all inputs at 0x00 the display shows the inverse of the P pattern. The design is a simple combinational logic demonstration.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and template tags and added combinational; summary otherwise matches the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387014781302785.summary: This Wokwi project displays the letter L on a seven-segment display when the input bits 00101111 are entered on IN0 through IN7. The display only appears while the Step button is pressed, and releasing it clears the display. The documentation is minimal, describing only the basic function and test procedure. The design requires external hardware including a DIP switch, a push button, and a seven-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387014781302785.review_notes: Corrected the summary's wrong bit pattern and letter, and replaced unsupported logic-gate/template tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387015959903233.summary: This Wokwi project implements the 'secret code' exercise from the TinyTapeout workshop. If the correct code 10101010 is set on IN0 through IN7, the design outputs 10001100 on OUT0 through OUT7 to display the letter 'r' on a 7-segment display. Any other input outputs 00000000. External hardware includes a DIP switch for inputs and a 7-segment display for outputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387015959903233.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated shift-register/led/clock-generator/template tags with wokwi, 7-segment, dip-switch, education, workshop, comparator, and sequential-logic.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387032609197057.summary: This design connects a bunch of AND gates together to make a really big AND gate. ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387064715554817.summary: This Wokwi project drives a string of D flip-flops so that LED segments illuminate in a circle. External hardware includes a clock, a button and a 7-seg LED.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387064715554817.review_notes: Removed logic-gate/template; design is a flip-flop ring driving LED segments.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387065339458561.summary: This design converts an SPI-style APA102 LED protocol stream into a single-line WS2812 output. It is hard-coded for seven LEDs, waits for a 32-bit low start condition, shifts in the pixel data, and forwards it to the WS2812 output until a stop condition is recognized. It ignores the APA102 intensity byte and also emits a continuous UART output of "Arglius Barglius" at approximately 115200 baud. Testing requires an SPI driver and a string of at least seven WS2812 LEDs, and no silicon results are reported.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_413387065339458561.review_notes: Tags were unrelated (wokwi/logic-gate/template/incomplete); replaced with the actual APA102-to-WS2812 translator tags and summary.

The documentation explains the pin functions and configuration; it is a Wokwi design with no tiles, no measured silicon results, and no external hardware specified. The frequency is described as 1/(5*inverter cell delay) for the ring oscillator case.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962760920307713.summary: This Wokwi project implements a standard 4-bit adder using AND, XOR, and OR gates, with a 5-bit output to handle overflow. The inputs are arranged as element-wise pairs: IN0 and IN1 are the LSBs of the two numbers, IN2 and IN3 are the next bits, and so on. The design can be tested by performing 4-bit additions on paper and comparing with the circuit's outputs. No external hardware is required beyond the inputs and outputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962760920307713.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a simple adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962904571040769.summary: This Wokwi design sets all outputs high when inputs IN0, IN1, IN2, and IN3 are high; otherwise, the outputs are low. The description claims that 'power goes in, power maybe comes out?' and that no testing is needed. The project is extremely simple and lacks detailed documentation. It uses 8 inputs and 8 outputs, but the logic only involves four inputs.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962904571040769.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate and combinational tags; added insufficient-doc.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962914561876993.summary: This Wokwi design connects inputs to outputs through a couple of logic gates, with no specific function described. The documentation states that there is nothing to test and no external hardware is used. It appears to be a trivial passthrough or simple gate arrangement with minimal documentation. The design likely serves as a basic exercise in using the Wokwi editor.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962914561876993.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc because the source gives no functional detail beyond a trivial gate connection.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962959838345217.summary: This Wokwi project implements a 4-bit adder that outputs a 5-bit sum. Two 4-bit numbers are input via IN0-IN3 and IN4-IN6 (with IN7 possibly unused), and the result is presented on OUT0-OUT4. Testing involves setting input switches to form two numbers and verifying the binary sum on the outputs. No external hardware is required beyond LEDs or other indicators.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422962959838345217.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is a simple adder, not an arithmetic logic unit.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964381148718081.summary: This Wokwi project is completely non-functional; the documentation states that it does not work and cannot be tested. All pins are labeled N/A, and no external hardware is used. It appears to be an empty or unfinished design, possibly a placeholder or failed experiment. There is no discernible function or purpose.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964381148718081.review_notes: Replaced template with placeholder because the source describes a non-functional empty design, not a starter template.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964384478997505.summary: This Wokwi design implements a NAND gate with a NOT gate on one input, using inputs IN2 and IN3 and output OUT3. The documented truth table specifies that output is high except when both inputs are high (for the NAND function after inversion). Testing can be done with LEDs or other indicators. The design is a simple logic gate demonstration with clear documentation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964384478997505.review_notes: Removed led tag because LEDs are only suggested as external test indicators, not part of the design.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964754310747137.summary: This project is described as a test to try fabricating a chip with some special function other than simple logic. The documentation is extremely thin and does not specify what the logic actually does or how it should behave. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, but no external hardware is required according to the description. The design appears to be a learning exercise rather than a complete, documented circuit.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422964754310747137.review_notes: Removed template tag as source describes a logic test, not a template; added logic-gate.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422965035809389569.summary: The project is titled '3 Bit Adder' and is intended to add two 3-bit numbers, producing a sum and carry. The documentation consists only of the placeholder word 'dup' for both the how-it-works and how-to-test sections, so no actual implementation details are provided. It uses six inputs and four outputs, which is consistent with a 3-bit adder with carry-in and carry-out. No external hardware is required, but the lack of documentation makes it impossible to verify the design's functionality.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422965035809389569.review_notes: Removed alu and template tags that are not supported by the source.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968416190311425.summary: This design implements an 8-to-3 encoder that, according to the description, displays the letter 'U' on a 7-segment display when a specific 8-port switch code is set. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, with the outputs presumably driving the segments of the display. The documentation is minimal and does not explain the encoding scheme or the exact switch pattern required. External hardware includes an 8-port switch and a 7-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968416190311425.review_notes: Removed encoder tag due to unclear implementation; added 7-segment tag for the display.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968696249282561.summary: The project is titled 'Simple NAND 2' and is described as a work in progress with documentation that will follow later. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections contain placeholder text, so the actual functionality is unknown. It has eight inputs and three outputs, which might suggest a simple logic gate implementation, but this is not confirmed. The external hardware list includes an LED display, a flux compensator, and a quantum computer, which appears to be a joke and not a serious requirement.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_422968696249282561.review_notes: Removed template tag as there is no evidence of boilerplate; incomplete tag already covers the work-in-progress nature.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498066535550977.summary: This design sums eight input signals, treating them as the numbers 1 through 10, and displays the last digit of the sum on a 7-segment display. It uses eight inputs and eight outputs, with the outputs connected to the segments of the display. The project is intended as a simple test or educational example, and it requires an external 7-segment display to show the result. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498066535550977.review_notes: Removed calculator tag because the design is a simple sum-and-display, not a calculator with keypad/switch input and numeric display.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498096996685825.summary: The project is titled 'nothing-yet' and has no actual design implemented. The documentation explicitly states that there is no design yet and that the how-to-test section is a placeholder. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, but no functionality is described. No external hardware is required, and the project appears to be an empty template.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498138683883521.summary: This project is a counter that counts to 4, as indicated by its title and one-line description. It divides the frequency of an input clock to produce an output signal that drives an LED. The design has a single output pin labeled 'Signal_to_led' and no inputs, suggesting it uses an internal clock or the clock is provided elsewhere. The documentation is very sparse, and the external hardware section is left as a template placeholder.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498138683883521.review_notes: Removed counter and clock-divider because the source does not clearly document those functions.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498175661927425.summary: This design displays a simple snake pattern on a 7-segment display, advancing with each clock cycle. It was created during a Wokwi workshop and requires an external 7-segment indicator, with the decimal point unused. The design lacks reset logic, so the initial state is unpredictable, and it has no debounce, meaning a physical button clock source will not work reliably. It uses one input for the clock and eight outputs for the display segments.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498175661927425.review_notes: Removed clock-generator: the project takes a clock input rather than generating one.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498176219770881.summary: This sequential circuit spells out the phrase 'tinytapeoutrocks' symbol by symbol on a 7-segment display, advancing on each clock edge. It is designed to run at 2 Hz or in manual clock mode, where pressing a button cycles through the 16 symbols. The eight outputs must be connected to the display segments in the classic order, and no external hardware is needed beyond the display. The project is notable for its simple, self-contained operation and clear documentation.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498176219770881.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and clock-generator tags; added text and sequential-logic tags supported by the description.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498190842166273.summary: This design acts as a secret code detector: it turns on output 1 when inputs 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8 are all active. It uses eight inputs and one output, which can drive an LED to indicate the correct combination. The documentation is very thin but sufficient to understand the basic function, and no test procedure is provided beyond checking the output. External hardware needed includes an 8-input device (such as switches) and an output LED.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498190842166273.review_notes: Removed the unsupported logic-gate tag and corrected the summary's overclaim about documentation and test details.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498200554080257.summary: This is a simple design created during the TinyTapeout workshop. It has eight inputs and eight outputs, but the documentation does not describe any specific function. The design is likely intended as a learning exercise or template. No external hardware or testing procedure is mentioned.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498200554080257.review_notes: Removed template (not supported by source) and added insufficient-doc for the sparse documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498241932991489.summary: This project implements a flip-flop with set, reset, and enable inputs. The outputs provide both the stored value and its complement. To test it, the inputs should be pulled high via resistors and then momentarily grounded using buttons to change state. External hardware includes four resistors, two LEDs, and two buttons.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498323071819777.summary: This is a simple test project described as just experimenting a bit. It has two inputs and three outputs, but the documentation states that twiddling the inputs causes something arbitrary to happen at the outputs. No specific function or external hardware is described. The design is not intended for any particular application.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498323071819777.review_notes: Replaced template with placeholder; the source is a generic placeholder submission.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498338463870977.summary: This design is a 4-bit serial-in parallel-out shift register with an output enable. Data is shifted in on the clock edge, and the parallel outputs are only active when the output enable is high. It can be tested by providing a clock and data input, and observing the outputs with LEDs. External hardware requires four LEDs for the outputs.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498675799185409.summary: This project creates configurable spinning animations on a 7-segment display. The animation mode and direction are selected via an 8-pin DIP switch, and the decimal point can show the clock pulse. It requires a 7-segment display, DIP switch, reset switch, and clock input for testing. The design supports multiple animation patterns including large and small circle spinners and a figure-8 spinner.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498675799185409.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator tag and replaced the unsupported 'notable' sentence with documented animation modes.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425498910144429057.summary: This project implements a D flip-flop with clock and data inputs, and both Q and Q' outputs. It can be tested manually by connecting a clock signal and a button to the data input, and observing the outputs with LEDs. External hardware includes a clock source, a button, and two LEDs. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand the basic function.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425499372555997185.summary: This design is a 4-bit synchronous counter with a fully decoded hex output for a 7-segment display. It uses 29 2-input NAND gates for decoding, based on a minimized design from Kim Oyhus. The counter has an active-high enable and asynchronous reset, and counts on the positive clock edge. It requires no external hardware beyond the standard demo board.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425499738293047297.summary: This project displays numbers 1 through 8 on a 7-segment display based on which of eight switches is turned on. The decimal point is connected to the clock to visualize its operation. It is tested by simply toggling the input switches. External hardware required is a 7-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425499738293047297.review_notes: Replaced dip-switch with button because the source refers to input buttons/switches rather than DIP switches.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425500385593779201.summary: This design blinks the number 7 on a 7-segment display using a single AND gate. The blinking is activated by a high signal on input 6. It is tested by turning on switch 7. External hardware includes a 7-segment display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425500385593779201.review_notes: Removed 'oscillator' as the design is just an AND gate; the oscillator is external/implied, not implemented.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425501309236263937.summary: This project consists of some logic gates intended for mask production testing. The documentation explicitly states it should not be used at all. It has four inputs and four outputs, and testing would involve connecting LEDs to the outputs. The design is not meant for any functional application.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wokwi_425501309236263937.review_notes: Removed factory-test because the source only mentions mask production testing, not a factory self-test structure; added incomplete for the very thin, explicitly unusable design.

ttihp25a/tt_um_wrapper.summary: This design implements a six-digit seven-segment clock displaying hours, minutes and seconds. Two active-high pushbuttons increment hours and minutes for setting the time, and the decimal points blink once per second. It requires a 32768 Hz clock, a six-digit common-anode display, and six PMOS/PNP digit-enable transistors. The outputs include active-low segment drives and multiplexed digit enables, and the design is intended for breadboard or custom PCB assembly.
ttihp25a/tt_um_wrapper.review_notes: Removed clock-generator, oscillator, and rtc tags because the design consumes an external clock and is a display clock, not an oscillator or RTC; added counter.

ttihp25a/tt_um_xor_encryption.summary: This design provides an SPI interface that converts serial input into 8-bit parallel output on the uo pins. The documentation states that an SPI interface is used, but does not describe the SPI mode, bit order, or register map. Testing requires an external SPI master such as an RP2040 board, and no other external hardware is specified. The documentation is thin and leaves key implementation details undefined.
ttihp25a/tt_um_xor_encryption.review_notes: Removed gpio tag as pins are generic and no GPIO-specific evidence exists.

ttihp25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_f.summary: This design implements an adder with separate flow control for each argument and the result, using one of several selectable pipeline register or buffer modules. It is a solution to an RTL job interview question described by Yuri Panchul and is used in the educational systemverilog-homework and basics-graphics-music repositories. The design includes a self-checking testbench and can be manually tested with buttons and LEDs to cover back-to-back data, argument starvation, and backpressure. It is an educational design demonstrating different flow control strategies at the RTL level.
ttihp25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_adder_with_f.review_notes: Replaced unsupported FIFO tag with supported silicon-tested tag based on documentation.

ttihp25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_schoolriscv_.summary: This project is a minimalistic SoC featuring the schoolRISCV educational CPU and a ROM containing a program that computes Fibonacci numbers. The CPU was designed for introductory Verilog and FPGA classes and is based on a textbook. The design outputs the CPU register a0 and program counter bits for observation, along with test pass/fail signals. It requires only LEDs as external hardware.

ttihp25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_sea_battle_v.summary: Sea Battle is a VGA game with sprites where the player controls a torpedo using left and right keys to hit a moving target. It was created for the Tiny Tapeout Demoscene competition and is part of a graphics and music examples repository. The design requires a VGA display and buttons, and has been tested on silicon where it works as an interactive graphics game. There is no self-checking testbench, and the game resets after each round.
ttihp25a/tt_um_yuri_panchul_sea_battle_v.review_notes: Replaced verilog with systemverilog and added silicon-tested and button.

ttihp25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttihp25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttihp25a/tt_um_zec_square1.summary: SQUARE-1 is a VGA and audio demo that displays munching squares on video and generates audio based on the logistic map. It requires a VGA display and audio output hardware, such as the Tiny VGA and TT Audio Pmods. Silicon tests show that the video works, but audio may require a manual reset and was not consistently heard. The design is notable for combining visual and audio demonstrations in a single project.
ttihp25a/tt_um_zec_square1.review_notes: Added silicon-tested per working test report; tags otherwise supported.

ttihp25a/tt_um_zedulo_spitest1.summary: This project is an SPI device that provides a GPIO and memory interface. It uses dedicated pins for SPI MOSI, clock and chip select, with MISO, debug, system clock mirror and status outputs. Testing is done with an external USB-to-SPI adapter such as an MCP2210 board, and no other external hardware is required. The documentation refers to a readme file that is not included here, so the register map and protocol details remain unspecified.
ttihp25a/tt_um_zedulo_spitest1.review_notes: Removed gpio and memory tags that lack support in the thin documentation; added verilog impl tag.

ttihp25a/tt_um_zhouzhouthezhou_adder.summary: This design adds two 4-bit numbers and displays the sum on a seven-segment display. Inputs are set using DIP switches on the upper and lower nibbles, and an always block maps the sum to display segments. If the sum cannot be shown on the display, a dot is shown instead, and overflow is not handled. The design is a straightforward arithmetic demonstration with no external hardware beyond the switches and display.
ttihp25a/tt_um_zhouzhouthezhou_adder.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added combinational.

ttihp25a/tt_um_znah_vga_ca.summary: This design generates a VGA signal that displays 1D elementary cellular automata. It is used by plugging it into a VGA PMOD and a display. External hardware required is a VGA PMOD. The project is notable for its creative visual output and is implemented in Verilog.
ttihp25a/tt_um_znah_vga_ca.review_notes: Removed unsupported signal-generator tag; added vga, cellular-automaton, video, display, and verilog tags.

ttihp25a/tt_um_zoom_zoom.summary: Zoom Zoom is a custom CPU with an external memory bus and hardware accelerators for SHA-3 and CORDIC. It includes UART communication and a parallel memory interface. The design is tested by loading a binary program into memory, resetting the chip, and checking memory writes. External hardware such as an SPI RAM chip or an MCU emulator is required for the custom protocol.
ttihp25a/tt_um_zoom_zoom.review_notes: Removed uart (custom parallel bus, not UART) and added sha-3, coprocessor, and multi-tile.

ttihp25b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttihp25b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttihp25b/tt_um_Xelef2000.summary: This project implements a true random number generator using three ring oscillators of different lengths (6, 12, and 24 inverters) whose outputs are XORed to produce a chaotic bitstream. A Von Neumann corrector debiases the stream, and 32-bit random numbers are output via UART at 9600 baud. The raw oscillator outputs are also available on pins for monitoring. A UART-to-USB adapter is required to view the generated numbers.
ttihp25b/tt_um_Xelef2000.review_notes: Removed prng, crypto, cpu; added uart interface tag supported by pin and text.

ttihp25b/tt_um_abhinav8prasad_dds.summary: This is an 8-bit direct digital synthesizer (DDS) that generates a digitized sine wave with user-defined frequency. The frequency is set by an 8-bit phase increment loaded via input pins, and the output is an 8-bit amplitude sample updated every clock cycle. An external R-2R ladder DAC is required to convert the digital output to an analog sine wave. The design is based on standard DDS principles and can produce frequencies up to about 33 MHz at a 66 MHz clock.

ttihp25b/tt_um_alif_dual_unileak.summary: This project implements a hardware-optimized Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog, designed for area efficiency while maintaining biological realism. It includes a serial interface for loading parameters and provides outputs for membrane voltage and spike events. The design can be used with DIP switches for stimulus and LEDs or a 7-segment display for monitoring. No external hardware is required for basic operation.
ttihp25b/tt_um_alif_dual_unileak.review_notes: Removed uart tag; the serial interface is not a UART. Added verilog and spiking-neural-network.

ttihp25b/tt_um_alif_single_dualleak.summary: This project implements a hardware-optimized Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog, designed for area efficiency while maintaining biological realism. It accepts two 3-bit channel inputs and provides a 7-bit membrane voltage output plus a spike output. Configuration parameters are loaded serially via a load mode and serial data pin. The design is intended for educational or research use in spiking neural networks, and requires only simple external hardware such as switches, LEDs, or a 7-segment display for interaction.
ttihp25b/tt_um_alif_single_dualleak.review_notes: Removed uart tag because the serial configuration uses dedicated LOAD_MODE/SERIAL_DATA pins rather than a UART interface.

ttihp25b/tt_um_anujic.summary: This Morse Code Trainer is an interactive learning game that displays letters on a 7-segment display and challenges users to input the correct Morse code pattern using a switch. It provides immediate feedback and progresses through the English alphabet. The design can be tested in simulation or on hardware. It requires a 7-segment display and a switch for user input.
ttihp25b/tt_um_anujic.review_notes: Swapped button for dip-switch because the source specifies a switch input.

ttihp25b/tt_um_bleeptrack_prism.summary: This design is a visual demo that shows a hypnotic prism floating in a starry night on a VGA monitor. It has no control inputs and simply runs when connected to a VGA display. The design requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD interface. The documentation is minimal and provides no additional details about the implementation or testing.

ttihp25b/tt_um_blptrk_weaving01.summary: This tile is an experimental silicon art tile that plays with the idea of crossing traditional crafts like weaving with the weaving-like work of entangled transistor lines. It has no functional purpose and is meant to be appreciated visually after decapping the chip. No testing is required or possible. The artwork will be unveiled when decapping the chip.

ttihp25b/tt_um_blptrk_weaving02.summary: This tile is an experimental silicon art piece that plays with the idea of crossing traditional crafts like weaving with the weaving-like work of entangled transistor lines. It is written in Verilog and has a single dummy output pin. There is no test procedure; the artwork is meant to be seen by decapping the chip. No external hardware is required.
ttihp25b/tt_um_blptrk_weaving02.review_notes: Replaced unrelated ADC/DAC tags with art and silicon-art, and corrected the language tag to Verilog.

ttihp25b/tt_um_blptrk_weaving03.summary: This tile is an experimental silicon art tile that plays with the idea of crossing traditional crafts like weaving with the weaving-like work of entangled transistor lines. It has no functional purpose and is meant to be appreciated visually after decapping the chip. No testing is required or possible. The artwork will be unveiled when decapping the chip.

ttihp25b/tt_um_blptrk_weaving04.summary: This tile is an experimental silicon art tile that plays with the idea of crossing traditional crafts like weaving with the weaving-like work of entangled transistor lines. It has no functional purpose and is meant to be appreciated visually after decapping the chip. No testing is required or possible. The artwork will be unveiled when decapping the chip.

ttihp25b/tt_um_cedrichirschi_sar.summary: This project implements a simple SAR ADC controller designed to work with external analog circuitry. It outputs an 8-bit DAC control signal and accepts a comparator input to perform successive approximation. The design requires an external R-2R ladder network and a comparator to function. It has no end-of-conversion signal, and the start input must be toggled to initiate conversions.

ttihp25b/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttihp25b/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttihp25b/tt_um_dpi_adexp.summary: This project implements an Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire (AdExp) neuron in Verilog, consisting of a neuron core and a parameter loader. It supports loading parameters via a nibble interface and provides a spike output and debug values. The design is self-contained and requires no external components. Testing involves loading parameters to induce spiking and observing the spike output within a set time limit.

ttihp25b/tt_um_ds_comp_adc.summary: This project explores a delta-sigma ADC implemented digitally using flip-flops as quantizers and switched-capacitor lines for reference and measurement. It outputs pulse-density modulated signals and filtered 13-bit values, with a difference output representing the ADC code. The design requires external capacitors, resistors, and a current source/sink for operation. It aims to evaluate PVT effects and mismatch on ADC linearity, with an effective resolution of 11 bits.
ttihp25b/tt_um_ds_comp_adc.review_notes: Removed characterization: the documentation frames this as an exploratory delta-sigma ADC feasibility study, not a process/device characterization structure.

ttihp25b/tt_um_dumbrv_yliu_hashed.summary: This project is a simple RISC-V processor supporting the RV32E base instruction set plus Zicond and Zbs extensions. It uses two independent SPI memory interfaces for instruction and data storage, and provides 8 GPIO inputs and 8 GPIO outputs. The processor begins execution from address 0x0 and requires external SPI ROM and RAM for operation. A test program is provided that records GPIO inputs and outputs them after a delay to verify functionality.

ttihp25b/tt_um_emmk_riscv.summary: This project implements a simple 32-bit RISC-V processor core with 8 general-purpose registers. It includes a boot select input, UART receive and transmit pins, and eight bidirectional GPIO pins. The design is intended to be tested over the demo board USB UART, but no test has been implemented yet. External hardware includes a boot mode selector, a UART interface, and GPIO connections.

ttihp25b/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttihp25b/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttihp25b/tt_um_gamepad_pmod_demo.summary: This project reads input from a Gamepad PMOD and displays the pressed buttons as green symbols on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout and a 25.175 MHz clock, and is intended to be run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board with both PMODs attached. After reset, pressing a gamepad button causes its corresponding symbol to appear on screen. It is a demonstration of combining the Gamepad and Tiny VGA PMODs, derived from the VGA Playground, and needs both external PMOD boards to operate.

ttihp25b/tt_um_htfab_yadge.summary: This is a remix of Uri's Colorful Stripes experiment, intended to generate a colorful pattern when viewed under a microscope. It is tested by viewing the chip under a microscope or smartphone camera. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the one-line description and a single unconnected input pin. It is notable only as a variant of an existing optical experiment.

ttihp25b/tt_um_ihp_logo_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing IHP logo on a 640x480 VGA screen with an animated color gradient. It is configured via input pins to tile the logo, use a solid color, or use a white background, and an optional Gamepad Pmod allows pausing and changing direction. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is notable for its use of the TinyVGA standard and interactive controls.

ttihp25b/tt_um_iz_neuron.summary: This project is an implementation of the Izhikevich neuron model in Verilog. It accepts an 8-bit input current and outputs an 8-bit state variable. The documentation is essentially placeholder text, providing no meaningful explanation of how the design works, how to test it, or what external hardware is required. As a result, little can be said about its functionality or usage.

ttihp25b/tt_um_izh_neuron_lite.summary: This project implements a hardware-optimized Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) neuron in Verilog, designed for area efficiency while maintaining biological realism. It includes a serial interface for loading parameters and provides outputs for membrane voltage and spike events. The design can be used with DIP switches for stimulus and LEDs or a 7-segment display for monitoring. No external hardware is required for basic operation.

ttihp25b/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, plus UART over the demo board USB. It is a full Linux-capable SoC implemented in Verilog on a 8x2 tile Tiny Tapeout chip.

ttihp25b/tt_um_nefelimet_updown_cntr.summary: This project is a 3-bit up/down counter with reset, enable, load, and up/down control signals. When reset is low the output is zero, when load is low the input data is loaded, and when count enable is high the counter increments or decrements on each positive clock edge. It is written in Verilog and provides three data output bits. Testing uses a 7-segment display and driver with resistors to confirm counting.

It provides four output pins with the fundamental frequency and divided versions (divide-by-2, 4, and 8). The oscillator is expected to run at approximately 148.6 MHz based on simulation. Testing requires an oscilloscope connected to one of the output pins.

It has two input pins and one output pin, but the documentation does not describe any specific functionality. The testing instructions are vague, and the external hardware section is left as a placeholder. The design serves as a starting point for new users.

ttihp25b/tt_um_pqn.summary: This project implements a PQN model in Verilog that can generate Class 1 and Class 2 neuron firing patterns, selectable via a mode pin. It accepts a 12-bit input current and outputs a 16-bit membrane potential. The design was verified against Julia simulations using provided test vectors, with outputs updated every 180 clock cycles. External hardware requires only a PCB board for testing.

ttihp25b/tt_um_pwm_block.summary: This project is a PWM module controlled via an SPI interface. It provides three PWM outputs and several status pins indicating non-zero register values. The SPI interface allows programming of counter and duty cycle registers, and override pins enable direct PWM testing. External hardware includes an SPI master and a way to observe the PWM signals.

It accepts joystick inputs, switches, and a reset signal, and outputs VGA video and PWM audio, with QSPI pins for external memory. It is tested by connecting a TinyVGA Pmod, Tiny Audio Pmod, and a VGA display, then playing games. The design is notable for being a complete recreation of a classic console on a Tiny Tapeout tile, requiring external hardware for video, audio, and game storage.

It accepts an 8-bit input packet shifted in on the input pins and outputs a 4-bit digit plus a 7-bit confidence score. A /WE input pauses the design, and an external MCU is needed to provide input data and read out results. The documentation is sparse and the test procedure is still marked TO DO, with no silicon results reported.

It accepts a 16-bit instruction and outputs an 8-bit result, with different instruction types producing specific outputs. Testing involves setting the instruction and clocking once to receive the result, as R-Type/I-Type/L-Type output 0, S-Type outputs the register value, and B-Type outputs the branch-taken flag.

Testing requires connecting external memory, loading a program, and providing a clock. The design is notable for its detailed documentation and custom instruction set.

It can display eight built-in patterns selected by input pins, and also supports copying SRAM contents to the display. The driver initializes the display, sends image data, and puts it into deep sleep to retain the image. External hardware includes the e-ink display and jumper wires to connect it to the PMOD.

ttihp25b/tt_um_tt_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is an early version of the Tiny Tapeout collaborative competition Risc-V SoC, using a small RV32EC CPU with the Zcb and Zicond extensions. It uses 28-bit addresses, 24-bit program addresses, and reads instructions over QSPI from Flash while using QSPI PSRAM for memory. Because QSPI clock and data lines are shared, flash and RAM cannot be accessed simultaneously, and code can only execute from flash. It is intended for use with a QSPI PMOD carrying 16MB flash and two 8MB RAMs, with RP2040 MicroPython scripts handling reset and flash programming.

ttihp25b/tt_um_wokwi_434917320361309185.summary: This design is an 8-bit pseudo-random number generator built from four Fibonacci maximum-length LFSRs of 9, 10, 11 and 13 bits, whose outputs are XOR-combined. The chip clock is divided by 14 cascaded divide-by-two stages, giving a total division of 16384, so a 10 kHz clock yields about 0.61 Hz for the LFSRs. The eight random bits appear on the eight output pins and can be observed with a 7-segment LED display, an oscilloscope or a logic analyzer. A 7-segment LED display is recommended as external hardware, and the design is notable for using relatively prime LFSR lengths to reduce correlation.

ttihp25b/tt_um_wokwi_434918300941464577.review_notes: Replaced unsupported logic-gate/multiplexer tags with combinational and insufficient-doc; corrected the summary's claim that documentation is clear.

ttihp25b/tt_um_wokwi_434918311072808961.summary: This project is a Wokwi design with eight inputs and eight outputs, and it mentions using a seven-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is very poor: 'How it works' says 'i DONT NOW', and testing is described as 'KLICK THE BOTTOM'. The title 'GG' and description 'not much' provide no further clarity. The design's actual function is unknown due to the lack of documentation.
