ttihp26a/tt_um_teenyspu.summary: TeenySPU is a 4-bit spatial processing unit implemented in Verilog that uses a spatial instruction set architecture. Operation codes are provided on the high four input bits and data loading multiplexer codes on the low four input bits. Its 4-bit inputs, bidirectional pins and outputs carry Q values, operation codes, accumulator bits, board data and output values N and M. A testbench covering all programmed operations is included with the source.
ttihp26a/tt_um_teenyspu.review_notes: Original summary described an unrelated TinyMOA design; tags and summary corrected to match source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_themightyduckofdoom_bitse.summary: The design implements a Collatz conjecture checker using a bit-serial datapath to save area. It contains a main shift register storing the current number and a step counter register tracking the number of steps to reach 1. A state machine coordinates the operation of the registers and processing. No testing procedure or silicon results are documented.
ttihp26a/tt_um_themightyduckofdoom_bitse.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented bit-serial Collatz checker.

ttihp26a/tt_um_thomasherzog_plasma.summary: Plasma is a VGA animation design that renders a plasma effect with selectable color themes and an optional about text overlay. It uses two input pins to select among four color modes (default, matrix, cyberpunk, abyss) and one input to enable the about overlay, outputting VGA signals on the standard Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires an external TinyVGA PMOD to connect to a VGA monitor. The documentation states that no testing was performed, and no silicon results are provided.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tinymoa_ihp26a.summary: TinyMOA is a RISC-V CPU based on TinyQV with an integrated SRAM-based compute-in-memory accelerator for analog matrix multiplications. The design is currently a work in progress, with no detailed documentation of its operation or testing procedure. It provides debug outputs for the program counter and state, but external hardware requirements are not specified. The project is notable for combining a RISC-V core with an analog compute-in-memory accelerator, but further information is lacking.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tinyperceptron_karlmose.summary: Tiny Perceptron implements a hashed perceptron, a hardware-friendly predictor often used for branch prediction, using external SPI RAM to store signed 8-bit weights. It communicates with a host controller via a 16-bit SPI slave interface, supporting operations to add weight indices, read the signed sum, and update weights based on a sign bit. Testing requires an external SPI RAM, such as the SPI RAM emulator on a Raspberry Pi Pico, connected to the bidirectional pins. The design is notable for its use of external RAM and a simple SPI protocol, but no silicon test results are provided.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tippfehlr_nyan_cat.summary: This design blinks all 16 output pins together to transmit the message "HELLO WORLD" in Morse code at approximately 20 WPM, looping continuously. It requires only LEDs or a logic analyzer connected to any of the output pins and a clock of about 16 Hz. No inputs are used, and the design was written by GitHub Copilot. The project is notable for its simplicity and AI-generated origin, but no silicon test results are reported.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tmr_voter.summary: This design implements triple modular redundancy with 8 inputs and 8 outputs, where three external processors communicate via SPI and their outputs are voted on to produce a single output. It includes a shared chip select and clock, with dedicated MISO and MOSI lines for each processor, and uses a majority vote to tolerate faults. Testing involves cocotb simulations that cover valid echo handling, per-bit validity masks, majority voting, and fault injection, and on hardware it requires three external CPUs or SPI slaves. The design is notable for its fault-tolerance approach, but no silicon test results are provided.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tobiasgreiser_move_vga_sq.summary: This design renders a movable white square on a gray background via VGA, with inputs to move the square left, right, up, and down, and to increase or decrease its size. It uses the standard Tiny VGA pinout and requires an external TinyVGA PMOD and switches for input. The design is intended to mimic moving a cursor on a screen, and no testing or silicon results are documented.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tobisma_random_snake.summary: This design implements a pseudo-random snake that moves across a 7-segment display. The user inputs a number via switches, which seeds the random movement, and the snake's position is shown on the display. It requires an external 7-segment display and switch inputs for operation. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description and test instructions.
ttihp26a/tt_um_tobisma_random_snake.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'game' tag and added verilog/led; summary unchanged as it matches the source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tomolt_rasterizer.summary: This project implements a scanline triangle rasterizer that outputs VGA video at 640x480 resolution with 2 bits per color. It uses a single combined multiply-and-divide unit to calculate triangle edges, updating state during H-blank periods. The design can be configured via SPI-like UIO pins to change the rendered geometry and color. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD adapter and optionally an MCU for configuration.
ttihp26a/tt_um_tomolt_rasterizer.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original tags and summary described a Tsetlin Machine, which is not present.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tschai_yim_mill.summary: This project implements a two-player Tic-Tac-Toe game in hardware. Players press buttons to place marks on a 3x3 grid, and LEDs indicate the board state. The design detects wins and flashes the winning line. It requires nine pushbuttons and nine LEDs.
ttihp26a/tt_um_tschai_yim_mill.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe a UART-driven ALU processor, but the source describes a Tic-Tac-Toe game.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tsetlin_machine.summary: This project implements a Tsetlin Machine binary classifier for low-power edge AI. It processes a 4-bit input feature space and outputs a single binary classification. The design uses 32 Tsetlin Automata and four clauses with on-chip training. It operates in inference and training modes controlled by a mode pin.
ttihp26a/tt_um_tsetlin_machine.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe a demoscene VGA visual effect, but the source describes a Tsetlin Machine binary classifier.

ttihp26a/tt_um_tt_tinyQV.summary: Borg is a tiny GPU built around a RISC-V SoC (TinyQV). It renders a 10-frame animation of a rotating RGB triangle fully in firmware. The design includes vertex shading, rasterization and RGB fragment shading. It uses QSPI flash/PSRAM, SPI and UART interfaces and is written in Chisel.
ttihp26a/tt_um_tt_tinyQV.review_notes: Replaced unsupported cellular-automaton/VGA tags with RISC-V, SoC, graphics, CPU, UART, QSPI, SPI, Chisel and multi-tile tags.

ttihp26a/tt_um_uart_alu.summary: This design is an 8-bit ALU controlled via UART. It receives an opcode and two operands over UART and returns the computed result. The default baud rate is 115200 at a 50 MHz clock. The protocol is 8N1 with a three-byte frame.
ttihp26a/tt_um_uart_alu.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe a VGA game, but the source describes a UART-driven ALU processor.

ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_rings.summary: This project generates a mesmerizing VGA display of hypnotic concentric rings that expand or contract from the center of the screen. It is designed as a demoscene-style visual effect for the Tiny Tapeout platform. The design takes speed and direction inputs and outputs RGB222 VGA signals with VSync and HSync. Testing requires connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, then applying power and releasing reset.
ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_rings.review_notes: Removed unsupported accelerator/alu/pipeline tags and corrected the summary, which described hardware not present in the source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.summary: This design implements a USB CDC device that bridges USB to a UART interface at a fixed 115200 baud. It uses usb_p and usb_n for the USB differential pair, dp_pu_o for the 1.5k pull-up, and RX and TX for the UART side, with a configured status output. It is based on tinyfpga_bx_usbserial and enumerates with vendor_id 1209 and product_id 5454. External hardware needed is a USB breakout board and a 1.5k ohm resistor, and silicon test reports confirm successful enumeration, loopback and external UART communication.
ttihp26a/tt_um_urish_usb_cdc.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag because the provided silicon status is working with tester reports.

ttihp26a/tt_um_vga_ca.summary: This project is a VGA signal generator that displays 1D elementary cellular automata patterns. It iterates through different automata rules, producing evolving patterns on the screen. The design requires a VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for output. The documentation is minimal, and the project is marked as work-in-progress, with no further details on configuration or testing.

ttihp26a/tt_um_vga_example.summary: This design displays a square that bounces around the screen, with its movement controllable by the user via eight input switches. The user can adjust the vertical and horizontal position using the switches. It requires a VGA cable and the eight input switches for interaction. The project is a simple interactive animation, with no additional features.

ttihp26a/tt_um_vga_leonllrmc.summary: This project is a simple VGA GPU that uses an ALU pipeline to compute pixel colors based on the pixel's x/y coordinates and a few configurable registers. The design takes pixel coordinates as input and outputs a color, with parameters set via registers. It requires a VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for output. The documentation is very sparse, with testing instructions only suggesting to read the Verilog code, indicating limited support for users.

ttihp26a/tt_um_vga_tetris.summary: This project implements a Tetris game rendered as a 640x480 at 60 Hz VGA signal. Four inputs (left, right, rotate, down) control the game, and the inputs are expected to be pulled high when idle so that only a low level triggers an action. It requires an external VGA output circuit such as the tiny-vga PMOD to display the picture. The documentation notes that the game-over state can be cleared by pressing the down button a couple of times.
ttihp26a/tt_um_vga_tetris.review_notes: Removed the unsupported claim about fitting a full game into a 2x2 tile area; no other changes needed.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_450491302960427009.summary: This Wokwi design displays the letters E, L, I, A and S one after another on a 7-segment display, with one second between each letter. It is started with a 10 kHz clock and needs no external hardware beyond the display. The project is explicitly described as only a test so far, and the pin list is incomplete, so little can be said about its inputs. It appears to be an early learning exercise rather than a finished design.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_450491302960427009.review_notes: Removed unsupported template and education tags; added incomplete and 7-segment.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_450491696806684673.summary: This design animates a snake travelling around a 7-segment display. A chain of flip-flops driven by the clock and reset generates a time sequence, and each step lights the segments that form the moving snake. A step button advances the snake by one tile, and the design uses the 7-segment segments A through G plus the decimal point as outputs. The documentation is brief and the external hardware section is left as an unfilled template, but the behaviour is clear from the description.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_450492208120711169.summary: This Wokwi project takes two 4-bit numbers on its inputs and adds them, presenting the result on seven outputs. The title and one-line description state that the author does not yet know what the design should do, and the documentation only says that it currently adds two 4-bit numbers. Testing is done by applying two 4-bit values and observing the output, which would normally require switches and a display. The design is a simple arithmetic exercise with minimal documentation.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_450492208120711169.review_notes: Removed alu tag; the source only implements a 4-bit adder, not a full ALU.

The description and testing instructions are flippant and provide no useful information. It appears to be a workshop experiment with minimal documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576238411624449.summary: This design is a modified version of the Tiny Tapeout template, with eight inputs and eight outputs. It is intended to be tested by toggling buttons and observing outputs on a 7-segment display. The documentation indicates it is a basic test project with slight modifications. It serves as an introductory example for the platform.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576238411624449.review_notes: Removed display/7-segment/education tags since the display is external and no educational intent is stated; added incomplete/insufficient-doc.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576419565744129.summary: This design is a 2-to-4 binary decoder that takes two input bits and activates one of four outputs. It is intended to be used with a DIP switch for inputs and a 7-segment LED display to show which output is active. The documentation notes that due to tight timing, a certain input combination may light a different LED than expected, but otherwise it works as desired. The project is a simple combinational logic circuit implemented in Wokwi.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576419565744129.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag while keeping the supported technical summary.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576478636229633.summary: This design creates a moving circle effect on an 8-segment LED display using a series of D flip-flops. It requires an external seven-segment display to show the animation. The project is a simple example of sequential logic using flip-flops. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed testing instructions.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576478636229633.review_notes: Replaced shift-register/led/graphics/education with flip-flop/sequential-logic/insufficient-doc to match the DFF-based description.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576548374933505.summary: This project implements a frequency divider and some random logic, as indicated by its title and description. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no details on how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware is needed. It is a Wokwi design with a 10 kHz clock input. Without further information, the exact functionality cannot be determined.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576548374933505.review_notes: Removed unsupported tags and added insufficient-doc due to empty documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576571487651841.summary: This combinational circuit takes a 4-bit BCD input (A as MSB, D as LSB) and drives a 7-segment display to show numbers 1 through 9. It is tested by using DIP switches to set the input and observing the displayed digit. The design requires an external DIP switch and a seven-segment display. It is a simple project built in Wokwi.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456576571487651841.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; original summary claimed educational purpose not stated in source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456577873995405313.summary: This design debounces the two signals from a rotary encoder and outputs a clean clock and an up/down direction signal. It is intended to be connected to a rotary encoder, preferably one from an Arduino set, and the outputs can be used with a counter. The design is tested by connecting the encoder to the inputs and checking the outputs. It is a simple utility block for interfacing mechanical encoders with digital logic.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456577873995405313.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and gpio tags; corrected typo in summary.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578179564131329.summary: This project appears to implement some adders, as mentioned in the description, but the documentation is very sparse. It has 8 inputs and 8 outputs, and testing involves turning inputs 1-4 on and off. No external hardware is listed. The exact functionality and purpose are unclear due to the lack of detailed documentation.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578179564131329.review_notes: Removed logic-gate and education; added adder, combinational, wokwi, incomplete.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578608558661633.summary: This design is a hidden combination puzzle where the correct input sequence causes all LEDs to light up. It is tested by trying different input combinations. The project requires an LED display as external hardware. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description of the goal.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578608558661633.review_notes: Tags and summary are consistent with the source; no corrections needed.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578694921494529.summary: This project is extremely simple: pressing a button presumably lights an LED. The documentation is almost non-existent, with only 'Press the button' as the description. It has three inputs and no outputs listed, but external hardware includes an LED. The design is likely a basic introduction to digital input and output.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578694921494529.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added insufficient-doc due to sparse documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578784059908097.summary: This design takes eight input signals, each corresponding to a number from 0 to 7, and displays that number on a 7-segment display. It is tested by following instructions in the info.yaml file. The project requires an external 7-segment display. The documentation is very brief, stating that it 'just does' the described function.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578784059908097.review_notes: Removed gpio tag because inputs are numbered switches rather than general-purpose I/O.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578790697395201.summary: This design displays the number 3 on a seven-segment display when switches 1, 2, and 3 are all turned on. It is tested by turning on those switches. The project requires an external seven-segment display. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description of the behavior.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456578790697395201.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate/gpio/education tags and added dip-switch/insufficient-doc.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456579003210233857.summary: This is a placeholder design for a counter that counts from 1 to 4, intended for the Wokwi simulation environment. The documentation is essentially a template with no functional description, only pin names suggesting a 7-segment display output and switch inputs. It requires external hardware such as a 7-segment display and switches to be useful. The design is not sufficiently documented to determine its actual behavior or purpose.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_456579003210233857.review_notes: Removed template and education tags; added insufficient-doc due to placeholder documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_457062377137305601.summary: The project is titled 'Count To Ten' but the documentation consists only of placeholder text such as 'asdf' and 'dsaf'. The pin names are similarly meaningless, providing no insight into the design's function. There is no description of how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware is needed. The project is essentially undocumented and cannot be evaluated.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_457062377137305601.review_notes: Removed unsupported tags and added insufficient-doc due to placeholder documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_458140717611045889.summary: This design uses a clock and a binary counter to cycle through the characters O, 2, E, L, H, d, and blank on a 7-segment display, spelling 'O2ELHd'. It is tested by setting the clock to 1 Hz and observing the display, with a reset input to restart the sequence. External hardware includes a 7-segment LED display, a clock source, and a reset button. The design is a simple demonstration of driving a 7-segment display with a counter.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_458140717611045889.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and education tags that are not supported by the source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_458752568884674561.summary: This design displays the custom string 'rESIStcodE' on a 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting a 7-segment display to the outputs and an 8-position DIP switch to the inputs. The external hardware required includes a 7-segment display and a DIP switch. The documentation is minimal and does not explain the internal logic or how the characters are generated.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_458752568884674561.review_notes: Tags and summary are consistent with the source; no corrections needed.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459117403524075521.summary: This is a 4-bit ALU that performs addition, subtraction, AND, and OR operations on two 4-bit inputs, with the operation selected by two mode pins. The result is output on four pins, and an overflow flag is provided. It is tested by applying input numbers and operation codes and checking the outputs against expected results. External hardware includes resistors, LEDs, and DIP switches for input and output.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459210187582694401.summary: This design is a simple counter that counts seconds when driven by a 10 kHz oscillator. It has a debugging reset pin but no other documented inputs or outputs. It is tested by enabling the 10 kHz oscillator and observing the counter behavior. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very brief and does not specify the output format or how the count is observed.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459210187582694401.review_notes: Removed tags for external oscillator and timer functions not present in the design.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459234034322375681.summary: The TinyTapeout Signal Box loads switch settings into SRAMs to control outputs, with the desired track selected via DIP switches and loaded by pressing reset. It is designed to work out of the box without external hardware. The design provides multiple output signals based on the stored configuration. The documentation is minimal but indicates a memory-based signal routing function.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459234034322375681.review_notes: Removed signal-generator tag because the design stores switch settings in SRAM rather than generating a signal.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459285910800527361.summary: This is an educational Wokwi project intended as a starting point for Swiss high school students to learn ASIC design and digital circuitry basics. It includes a 4-bit binary counter and two 4-bit registers with write and read operations controlled by opcode pins. The design is tested by following exercises on the Wokwi project page, which explain how to store and retrieve data. No external hardware is required, and the project serves as a teaching tool with documented pitfalls.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459299619699169281.summary: This design is a simple 8-bit SRAM with 8 input and 8 output pins. The documentation is extremely sparse, stating only 'a simple 8-bit SRAM' and 'just do it' for testing, with 'finger(s)' listed as external hardware. There is no explanation of addressing, read/write control, or how the memory is accessed. The design is essentially undocumented beyond its title.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459299619699169281.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc due to sparse documentation.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459303685175910401.summary: This design checks if a 4-digit BCD input equals 2904 and lights an LED birthday candle if it matches. It uses 8 input pins and 8 bidirectional pins to represent the four BCD digits, with the match output on a single pin. It is tested by setting the digits to 2, 9, 0, 4 and observing the LED, and by trying invalid numbers. External hardware includes an LED for the candle.
ttihp26a/tt_um_wokwi_459303685175910401.review_notes: Removed game and puzzle tags because the design is a BCD comparator, not a game or puzzle.

ttihp26a/tt_um_wscore.summary: This project implements a custom 8-bit RISC-V-inspired CPU with a hardware multiplier, 32 bytes of RAM, and custom branching instructions. It uses a multi-cycle finite state machine for fetch, decode, and execute, and includes a bootloader mode for loading programs via the input pins. The CPU is controlled by external signals for reset, mode selection, and clock, and outputs the destination register value and program counter for monitoring. It is notable for its high-density synthesis on the IHP26a process and its use of a 1x2 tile area.

ttihp26a/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_dlhq.summary: This design is a high-density shift register using standard cells for deep digital delays. It is implemented in Verilog and uses transparent latches with an 8-phase clock to store bits, with support for 4-bit Johnson counter outputs and an LFSR. The outputs include shift-register data, Johnson counter state, LFSR period and bit, and internal pulse signals. Test instructions cover clock/reset selection and observing the delayed output after 502 clock cycles.
ttihp26a/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_dlhq.review_notes: Replaced unsupported tags with accurate LFSR/Johnson/delay-line/gate-level/standard-cell tags and rewrote the summary to match the full design description.

ttihp26a/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_rs.summary: This project implements a high-density shift register using latch-based storage and an 8-phase clock. It uses four latches to store three bits per stage and eight parallel lanes to preserve throughput while relaxing timing. A Johnson counter generates the staggered pulses, and an optional LFSR mode provides observability. The design targets the IHP SG13G2 process and demonstrates a compact alternative to conventional DFF-based shift registers.
ttihp26a/tt_um_ygdes_hdsiso8_rs.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary were unrelated to the documented shift-register design.

ttihp26a/tt_um_yjulian_alu.summary: This project is a simple ALU with embedded registers, implemented in Verilog. It has 8 data input pins, 8 data output pins, and bidirectional pins for immediate and opcode fields. The documentation is very thin and the 'How it works' section describes a counter driving a 7-segment display, which contradicts the title and pinout. No external hardware is specified.
ttihp26a/tt_um_yjulian_alu.review_notes: Tags and summary were about an audio synthesizer, but the source describes a simple ALU with registers; documentation is contradictory.

ttihp26a/tt_um_yniklas_ma.summary: This project computes (A+B)*C for three 8-bit inputs. The inputs are provided sequentially on consecutive clock edges. The result appears on the outputs after the fourth positive clock edge. No external hardware is required.
ttihp26a/tt_um_yniklas_ma.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe a VGA image shifter, but the source describes a multiply-add arithmetic unit.

ttihp26a/tt_um_zettpe_mini_psg.summary: Mini PSG is a compact SPI-programmable sound generator with two tone channels, a shared 3-bit envelope and a 1-bit audio output on uo_out[7]. Each channel stores a tone code and octave value that set the phase step of a 23-bit phase accumulator, which drives square, pulse, saw or triangle waveforms. The two channel outputs are scaled by volume or envelope, mixed, and sent to a 1-bit DAC. Configuration is over a write-only SPI interface, and a cocotb testbench is provided.
ttihp26a/tt_um_zettpe_mini_psg.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a factory test structure with timer and ring oscillator, none of which appear in the source.

ttihp26a/tt_um_zouzias.summary: This project is a simple Verilog design that shifts around a VGA image. It outputs VGA signals including RGB, VSync, and HSync. The documentation refers to the source file for implementation details. The design is intended for VGA display output.
ttihp26a/tt_um_zouzias.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the VGA image shifting design.

ttihp26a/tt_um_ztimer_top.summary: This project is a factory test for a timer called zTimer. The timer has start, stop, and reset signals, and an internal ring oscillator is enabled to provide a clock source. When stop is asserted, the elapsed count is stored in internal registers. An SPI interface is used to read out the stored timer value.
ttihp26a/tt_um_ztimer_top.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the factory test timer with SPI readout.

ttsky25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.summary: This design recreates the Crossy Road game on an ASIC, where a chicken crosses roads while avoiding cars. It is controlled by a move button and outputs VGA video to a display. External hardware needed includes a debounced button and a 25 MHz clock. The project is a complete game implementation in Verilog.
ttsky25a/tt_um_10_vga_crossyroad.review_notes: Added retro tag for the arcade-style game recreation; removed unsupported 'notable' claim from summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_13hihi31_tdc.summary: This analog design implements a time-to-digital converter (TDC) with an 8-stage delay line to measure the phase difference between start and stop signals. It includes a variable delay line with fine (25 ps) and coarse (145 ps) steps to generate known phase differences for testing. The TDC achieves approximately 75 ps resolution in post-layout simulation. It requires external hardware such as a Raspberry Pi and level shifters to drive the analog and digital inputs; the design serves no practical purpose beyond testing the TDC circuit.
ttsky25a/tt_um_13hihi31_tdc.review_notes: Removed verilog because the project language is Analog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttsky25a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttsky25a/tt_um_32_bit_fp_ALU_S_M.summary: This is a 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point ALU that supports addition and subtraction, using a byte-serial protocol over the 8 input and 8 output pins. A start signal on uio[2] begins loading two operands in little-endian order over eight clock cycles, a 1-bit opcode on uio[0] selects add or subtract, and the result is streamed out over four cycles with a done flag on uio[3]. It runs at 20 MHz and can be driven by any microcontroller, with block and timing diagrams linked in the documentation. The design handles special values but always returns quiet NaNs, and no silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_32_bit_fp_ALU_S_M.review_notes: Removed bit-serial tag; the interface is byte-serial, not one bit per clock.

ttsky25a/tt_um_3v_inverter_SiliconeGuide.summary: This analog project contains a pair of inverters, a small one followed by a large one, intended to operate at 3.3 V. The input is on ua[1] and the output on ua[0], and it is tested by applying a signal with a generator and observing the polarity on an oscilloscope. It occupies a 1x2 tile area with two analog pins. The documentation is brief and gives no measured silicon results or detailed schematic.
ttsky25a/tt_um_3v_inverter_SiliconeGuide.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'process-experiment' and added 'inverter' to match the stated inverter function.

ttsky25a/tt_um_6502.summary: This project implements a custom 8-bit microprocessor inspired by the 6502 architecture, built around an ALU, registers, and a microcoded instruction decoder that executes a subset of the 6502 instruction set. Data is exchanged on the eight bidirectional pins uio[0] to uio[7], while the eight outputs uo[0] to uo[7] carry address bits; the design runs at 40 MHz. The documentation includes a block diagram and describes two testing strategies for verifying processor correctness. No silicon test results are reported, and the instruction subset is not fully enumerated in the provided text.
ttsky25a/tt_um_6502.review_notes: Removed unsupported retro and register-file tags; the proposed summary was otherwise accurate.

ttsky25a/tt_um_7FM_ShadyPong.summary: ShadyPong is a Pong game implementation in SystemVerilog that outputs VGA signals on uo[0] to uo[7], matching the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. Four inputs control player up and down movements, a fifth forces a fallback ball speed, and the bidirectional pins expose ball and player speed values. It runs at 25.175 MHz and requires a TinyVGA PMOD or an iCEsugar VGA PMOD with flying wires. The documentation is very sparse, with the how-it-works and how-to-test sections giving no real detail, so behaviour beyond the pinout is largely inferred.

ttsky25a/tt_um_8bitalu.summary: This is an 8-bit fully pipelined ALU that includes multiply, divide and barrel shifter functions along with flag and pipeline control logic. Operand A arrives on ui[0] to ui[7], operand B and the 3-bit opcode arrive on the bidirectional pins, and the 8-bit result appears on uo[0] to uo[7], with flags and pipeline enable also on the bidirectional pins. The design is self-contained and needs no external hardware beyond the standard demo board, though a logic analyzer or oscilloscope is suggested for detailed inspection. No silicon test results or detailed timing documentation are provided in the text.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Alida_DutyCycleMeter.summary: This project measures the duty cycle of an incoming PWM signal on ui[0] and reports a 7-bit value on uo[0] to uo[6], with uo[7] acting as a valid flag. A finite state machine counts how long the input is high within a fixed time window and computes the duty cycle, where 127 corresponds to 100 percent. It runs at 50 MHz and is tested by feeding a PWM signal from a generator and observing the outputs with a logic analyzer. No silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_Alida_DutyCycleMeter.review_notes: Removed frequency-counter: the design measures duty cycle, not frequency.

ttsky25a/tt_um_AriaMitraClock.summary: This project implements a 12-hour clock with an AM/PM indicator, counting seconds internally and rolling over minutes and hours. The enable, reset and clock signals are taken from ui[5], ui[6] and ui[7], the seven minute bits are on uio[0] to uio[6], and the hour bits plus AM/PM flag are on uo[0] to uo[7]. It is tested by supplying a clock, a reset and a one-second enable pulse, and an LED display can optionally be attached to view the time. The documentation is brief and no silicon results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_AriaMitraClock.review_notes: Removed 7-segment and display tags as outputs are binary bits, not display interfaces; added insufficient-doc.

ttsky25a/tt_um_AriaMitraGames.summary: This chip implements two games: tic-tac-toe (two-player) and rock-paper-scissors (player vs. machine). Game selection and moves are input via the ui pins, and outputs indicate game state, winner, or draw. The rock-paper-scissors opponent uses a 3-bit LFSR to generate pseudo-random choices. External hardware such as an LED display can be connected for easier viewing of the outputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_AriaMitraGames.review_notes: Removed led and display tags since no such on-chip output exists; added puzzle for the game logic.

ttsky25a/tt_um_BMSCE_T2.summary: This project implements an 8-LED choreographer that generates patterns such as Knight Rider, waves, and sparkles. It operates on a 5MHz system clock and uses a built-in clock divider to provide two speed modes: fast mode updates patterns at 4Hz and slow mode at 1Hz. The design has inputs for pattern selection, speed selection, pause, and enable, and outputs to eight LEDs. The documentation describes the clocking and speed modes but does not detail all available patterns or testing.
ttsky25a/tt_um_BMSCE_T2.review_notes: Removed tags for neural network, machine learning, and popcount which are unsupported; added led, pattern-generator, and verilog tags based on the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_BNN.summary: This project implements a 2-layer binary neural network (BNN) that classifies an 8-bit input into one of four categories (turn left, turn right, stop, U-turn). It uses XNOR-popcount operations instead of multipliers, and supports real-time weight loading via a 4-bit bidirectional interface. The design is intended for educational and demonstrational purposes, showing simple ML on-chip without CPUs or RAM. Testing is done with CocoTB, and accuracy is limited due to the small network size.

ttsky25a/tt_um_BryanKuang_mac_peripheral.summary: This design is an 8x8-to-16-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with a 2-cycle 8-bit serial interface for data input and output. It supports both signed and unsigned arithmetic and includes overflow detection and clear functionality. The MAC is intended for DSP applications and fits within the TinyTapeout I/O constraints by using a serial protocol. No external hardware is required beyond the standard clock and reset.
ttsky25a/tt_um_BryanKuang_mac_peripheral.review_notes: Removed alu; added multiplier and accumulator to match the MAC function.

ttsky25a/tt_um_DAC1.summary: This is a 4-bit digital-to-analog converter (DAC) that converts a 4-bit digital input into an analog output current or voltage. It is implemented in analog circuitry and has one analog output pin. Testing can be done using a pseudo-random binary sequence (PRBS) to evaluate dynamic range and output current. The documentation is minimal, providing only basic functionality and a suggestion for testing.
ttsky25a/tt_um_DAC1.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag because the source does not specify the implementation style.

ttsky25a/tt_um_DalinEM_asic_1.summary: This analog design compares a threshold voltage and generates a current output. It has six analog pins including LED, voltage sense, and control signals, and many digital pins tied to ground. The documentation is very sparse, stating only that it compares threshold voltage and generates current, and that testing requires a function generator and oscilloscope. The design appears to be a mixed-signal circuit with an LED driver and voltage sensing, but details are lacking.
ttsky25a/tt_um_DalinEM_asic_1.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and driver tags; added insufficient-doc and mixed-signal.

ttsky25a/tt_um_DelosReyesJordan_HDL.summary: This chip implements a reaction time test where a user presses a start button, waits for an LED to light up after a random delay, and then presses a react button as quickly as possible. The reaction time is displayed in milliseconds on a 4-digit 7-segment display, and cumulative times are shown until reset. If the react button is pressed before the LED, an error message is displayed. Silicon testing revealed that the design is broken: the start button does not start the test, reset does not work, and pressing react puts it in an error state, though it worked on an FPGA.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Enhanced_pll.summary: This project is a compact 4-channel fractional-N phase-locked loop (PLL) frequency synthesizer intended for next-generation systems-on-chip. It is controlled via a simple CSR interface using input pins for data and address, and outputs four independent clock channels plus an ADC output for control voltage monitoring. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets a 10 MHz reference clock. The documentation is extremely minimal, providing only pin descriptions and no detailed explanation of operation or testing.
ttsky25a/tt_um_Enhanced_pll.review_notes: Removed soc (it is a PLL, not an SoC); added insufficient-doc.

ttsky25a/tt_um_FFT_engine.summary: This is a 4-point, 8-bit fixed-point Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) engine implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a radix-2 decimation-in-time architecture with butterfly modules and twiddle factor multiplication to compute the frequency-domain representation of four complex samples. The design interfaces with switches for control, a bidirectional data bus for samples and results, and a single-digit 7-segment display for status. External hardware includes a 7-segment display, switches, and a reset button.

ttsky25a/tt_um_IZ_RG_22.summary: This project implements a modified Izhikevich neuron model in 22-bit fixed-point arithmetic to capture various spiking behaviors. It uses select pins to choose neuron parameters and five input pins for current injection, with outputs for membrane potential and recovery variable. The design is intended for simulating spiking cortical neurons in digital hardware, and external observation requires inverting the outputs and connecting to an oscilloscope. The documentation includes equations and a testbench description, but no silicon test results are provided.

ttsky25a/tt_um_LIF_neuron.summary: This project implements an approximate computing based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron model in hardware. It features 16-bit membrane potential, 8 pipeline stages, and supports 8 neurons in one structure. The design is configured through a three-phase process: parameter initialization, neuron initialization, and normal operation. Testing involves resetting, initializing parameters and neurons, and then feeding input currents sequentially.

ttsky25a/tt_um_LPCAS_TP1.summary: This analog project implements a voltage reference that compensates for temperature and supply voltage variations. It is designed by the LPCAS lab at IIT Gandhinagar. Testing requires precise temperature control using a TEC module and measurement of output voltages with high-impedance probes. Silicon test reports indicate partial success: one reference produced expected voltage but startup was sometimes strange, while the second reference appeared stuck at a low voltage.
ttsky25a/tt_um_LPCAS_TP1.review_notes: Removed 'silicon-tested' because the silicon status is only partial and inconclusive.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Maj_opamp.summary: This project contains a two-stage operational amplifier designed by Majid Sami ALakl for the TT08 shuttle. It has three analog pins: two inputs (INN and INP) and one output (OUT_Maj). Testing can be done using a Digilent Analog Discovery 3 for various measurements. The design is a straightforward analog building block with minimal documentation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_Maj_opamp.review_notes: Removed unsupported silicon-tested tag; no silicon validation is reported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_hs_mul.summary: This design implements an 8b10b decoder and a multiplier, intended as a test for a high-speed cell library. The decoder looks for the K.28.5 symbol to establish synchronization and then decodes subsequent data symbols. The multiplier operates on the decoded data. The author tested basic functionality with a modified cocotb script and verified decode and multiplier operation at a 200 MHz clock.
ttsky25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_hs_mul.review_notes: Removed communication tag; added characterization and factory-test tags to reflect the cell-library test purpose.

ttsky25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_mandelbrot.summary: This design computes and displays the Mandelbrot fractal on a VGA screen using a racing-the-beam technique. It uses 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic and a maximum iteration depth of 14, with configurable position and zoom via input pins. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and a 100 MHz clock. Silicon testing showed it broadly works, though the demo mode can sometimes get stuck zooming into the wrong offset.

ttsky25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.summary: This design reads run-length encoded video data from a QSPI flash memory and displays it on a 640x480 VGA output, with PWM audio output. It is intended for playing the Bad Apple music video and requires a QSPI Pmod plugged into an audio Pmod, plus a Tiny VGA Pmod. The design runs at 24 MHz and includes inputs to adjust SPI latency and select the QSPI pinout. Notable limitations include the need for a specific flash command and the requirement to generate the RLE binary file externally.
ttsky25a/tt_um_MichaelBell_rle_vga.review_notes: Removed unsupported demoscene tag and added pmod interface tag based on documented external hardware.

ttsky25a/tt_um_NE567Mixer28.summary: This project implements a single-ended operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) using a folded cascode architecture. It operates from a 1.8V supply and has differential inputs (INp and INm) and a single output (OUT). Testing involves applying a differential input signal and observing the output with an oscilloscope. The design is a basic analog building block with limited documentation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_NE567Mixer28.review_notes: Removed unsupported silicon-tested tag; no silicon validation is reported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Richard28277.summary: This project is a 4-bit ALU that performs arithmetic and logical operations on two 4-bit inputs based on a 4-bit opcode. The result is up to 8 bits, with carry-out and overflow flags provided on bidirectional pins. It was designed by Richard Xu et al for the TT08 shuttle. Testing involves setting the inputs and opcode and observing the outputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_Richard28277.review_notes: education tag removed: no teaching intent stated in the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_RoyTr16.summary: This project implements a Connect Four game with VGA output and optional sound via a buzzer. The game state is stored in flip-flops and updated via a state machine. User input is through three buttons for moving left, right, and dropping a piece. The design includes modules for debouncing, VGA control, victory checking, and sound generation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_RoyTr16.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added button and audio tags supported by the pinout and documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_SNPU.summary: This project attempts to create a random number generator by exploiting the unstable state of a latch when both set and reset are low. It includes 34 instances per output pin to increase the chance of randomness. The design can be frozen to sample values, and inputs allow selecting different instances. The documentation is humorous and uncertain about whether it will work, acknowledging potential bias.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Scimia_oscillator_tester.summary: This project is a simple frequency meter that measures the frequency of an external square wave input. It outputs an 8-bit result in kHz. The input signal must be at least 10 times slower than the system clock. Testing requires an external oscillator or wave generator and a logic analyzer to verify the results.

ttsky25a/tt_um_SummerTT_HDL.summary: This project simulates Conway's Game of Life using digital logic and outputs the cellular automaton patterns via VGA. The simulation runs automatically upon power-up, and can be paused or randomized via input pins. It requires a Tiny Tapeout VGA Pmod for display. The design is a hardware implementation of a classic cellular automaton, created as a summer project at SJSU.
ttsky25a/tt_um_SummerTT_HDL.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added workshop tag for the SJSU summer project context.

ttsky25a/tt_um_TT06_pwm.summary: This design generates a pulse-width modulated (PWM) waveform with a duty cycle set by a 7-bit input. An internal counter is compared against the duty cycle value to produce a high output while the counter is below the threshold. Testing requires a clock signal and an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe the output waveform. The design is a straightforward PWM generator with no external hardware beyond measurement equipment.
ttsky25a/tt_um_TT06_pwm.review_notes: Removed signal-generator and waveform-generator because the source only describes a PWM generator, not a general waveform/signal generator.

ttsky25a/tt_um_TT16.summary: This asynchronous FIFO enables data transfer between two clock domains using separate read and write clocks. It uses Gray-coded pointers for synchronization and provides full and empty flags. The design can be fully simulated without external hardware, but on an FPGA, LEDs or UART may be used to display status. It is a standard implementation of a clock-domain-crossing FIFO.

ttsky25a/tt_um_TensorFlowE.summary: This design implements a multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit for 2x2 matrix multiplication with 4-bit operands, intended for neural network applications. It includes control signals for write, read, clear, and accumulation enable. Testing involves providing matrices and observing the output, which is read in two 8-bit parts. The design is inspired by existing matrix-MAC units and requires a personal computer for control.

ttsky25a/tt_um_Xgamer1999_LIF.summary: This design is a digital simplification of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, which accumulates input current until a threshold is reached, then emits a pulse. It requires an external ADALM2000 to provide a constant DC input voltage, and the output is observed via an LED. The design operates at a low clock frequency of 20 kHz and is a demonstration of a biological neuron model for neural networks.

ttsky25a/tt_um_acidonitroso_programmable.summary: This programmable threshold voltage comparator compares an external reference voltage with one of eight selectable threshold levels, seven fixed and one user-defined. It uses a resistor ladder and passgates controlled by a decoder, and outputs a digital high when the reference exceeds the threshold. Testing requires a 1.8V supply and input voltages up to 1.8V, with a maximum switching frequency of 100 kHz. The design is analog-intensive and provides a flexible voltage sensing capability.
ttsky25a/tt_um_acidonitroso_programmable.review_notes: Replaced sensor-interface and transistor-level with comparator-analog, decoder, voltage-reference, and analog tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_adc_dac_tern_alu.summary: This project is an empty placeholder intended to pass DRC checks, with no functional documentation. The title suggests an ADC/DAC with an address ALU, but the description is nonsensical and provides no useful information. There is no indication of how the design works or how to test it. The documentation is insufficient to determine any actual functionality.

ttsky25a/tt_um_adpll.summary: This is an all-digital phase-locked loop (PLL) implemented in RTL, operating at 2 MHz with a 50 MHz sampling clock and programmable parameters. It includes a digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) and provides outputs for lock detection and sign. Testing involves stepping the frequency and measuring lock time and jitter, requiring a function generator, oscilloscope, and external VCO. The design is notable for being fully digital and programmable.
ttsky25a/tt_um_adpll.review_notes: Removed vco tag; the design uses a DCO and the VCO is external test equipment.

ttsky25a/tt_um_ag_priority_encoder_parit.summary: This design implements a 9-to-4 priority encoder with a parity checker and a 7-segment display output. It supports selectable MSB or LSB priority and even or odd parity modes via input pins. The encoded value and parity bit are displayed on the 7-segment display, with the parity bit controlling the decimal point. Testing involves setting the mode pins and observing the outputs on the display and output pins.

ttsky25a/tt_um_alexandercoabad_mixedsign.summary: This analog design biases an inverter for linear mode operation to act as an amplifier, with a multiplexer selecting parallel feedback resistors to change the gain. It requires an external 20 nF capacitor at the input and an oscilloscope to observe the output. Silicon tests show it works, with different output levels for each MUX setting. The design demonstrates a mixed-signal amplifier with programmable gain.
ttsky25a/tt_um_alexandercoabad_mixedsign.review_notes: Removed opamp tag since the source describes a biased inverter; silicon-tested is supported by the test reports.

ttsky25a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.summary: This project implements current-switching DACs for generating analog VGA signals, using a 16x16 matrix of unit current sources to convert 8-bit digital inputs to analog current outputs. It is intended for analog VGA displays and requires external pull-up resistors and opamps to convert the current to voltage. The digital display controller is not yet implemented, and testing details are incomplete. The design is an experiment in analog VGA signal generation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added mixed-signal and kept vga, dac, analog, video.

ttsky25a/tt_um_alu_4bit_wrapper.summary: This 4-bit ALU performs arithmetic, logical, shift, and comparison operations on two 4-bit inputs selected by a 4-bit control signal. It provides four status flags: carry, zero, negative, and overflow. The design is intended as a basic CPU building block or teaching demo. Testing requires toggle switches for inputs and control, and LEDs for outputs and flags.
ttsky25a/tt_um_alu_4bit_wrapper.review_notes: Removed unsupported cpu, comparator, and logic-gate tags; ALU and education are supported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_analog_example.summary: The Digital OTA is an analog operational transconductance amplifier with high output impedance. It has three analog pins: Vo (output), VA, and VB (inputs). The documentation is minimal, indicating only that it amplifies transconductance and can be tested with a function generator. No other usage details are provided.

ttsky25a/tt_um_analog_factory_test.summary: This project provides test structures for Tiny Tapeout analog support, including bias generation, power supply sensing, and loopback connections. The documentation is incomplete, with sections marked as FIXME, so the exact functionality and usage are not fully described. It appears to be intended for factory testing of analog infrastructure. No external hardware or testing procedure is specified in the available documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_andyshor_demux.summary: This design drives an external ADG732 32-channel multiplexer, cycling through output channels at 1 Hz to test multistrand cables. It divides a 10 MHz clock to 1 Hz and generates chip select and write signals for the multiplexer. Testing can be done with an FPGA (e.g., iCE40) or with the actual ADG732 chip on a custom PCB. The project originated as a cable assembly test tool.
ttsky25a/tt_um_andyshor_demux.review_notes: Removed decoder and factory-test tags; added instrumentation and industrial tags for the cable test application.

ttsky25a/tt_um_anweiteck_2stageCMOSOpAmp.summary: This is a two-stage CMOS operational amplifier with Miller compensation. It requires an 8 µA bias current and a 1.8 V DC supply. The differential inputs are V+ and V-, and the output is Vout. The documentation is very brief, providing only basic operating conditions.
ttsky25a/tt_um_anweiteck_2stageCMOSOpAmp.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and current-mirror tags; documentation does not mention these details.

ttsky25a/tt_um_assaify_mssf_pll.summary: This is a 2.4 GHz integer-N PLL with an output divide-by-100, producing a frequency range of 19.2–25.2 MHz. It uses a 20 MHz reference clock and allows digital control of the divider factor and VCO discrete tuning to overcome process variation. Outputs include an analog pin (FOUT) and two digital pins, with an analog control voltage pin (VCON) for observation. The design is analog and requires an external 20 MHz clock.
ttsky25a/tt_um_assaify_mssf_pll.review_notes: Replaced clock-generator with frequency-synthesizer and added mixed-signal tag to better reflect the PLL's function and analog/digital nature.

ttsky25a/tt_um_axi4lite_top.summary: This design implements an AXI4-Lite master and slave with a simplified interface for testing memory-mapped transactions. It allows the user to initiate read and write operations using simple input signals and provides a done flag on completion. Testbenches are provided to verify functionality. The module hides the complexity of the full AXI4-Lite protocol.
ttsky25a/tt_um_axi4lite_top.review_notes: Removed cocotb tag because the source only says testbenches are provided, not that they use cocotb.

ttsky25a/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.summary: This Morse code keyer converts paddle or straight-key inputs into Morse code outputs, including an auxiliary Morse output, a buzzer tone, and a 7-segment display showing the last character. It supports iambic keying types A and B, and adjustable speed from about 7 to 110 WPM via dip switches. It uses a 12 MHz clock and requires a 12 MHz input clock plus external hardware such as a companion PCB for radio interfacing. The design includes a warning against using the auxiliary output directly for radio transmission.
ttsky25a/tt_um_betz_morse_keyer.review_notes: Corrected the invented PS2 PMOD hardware mention; the source only documents a companion PCB for radio interfacing and 12 MHz clock.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bit_serial_cpu_top.summary: This is a 16-bit bit-serial CPU with an 8-bit instruction input and 8 LED outputs. The documentation is very brief, providing only pin names and no details on the instruction set or operation. It appears to be a simple processor, though the source does not state its intended use. No test results or silicon reports are provided.
ttsky25a/tt_um_bit_serial_cpu_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag, added incomplete, and removed the invented educational-purpose sentence.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bitty.summary: This is a 16-bit simple processor with UART receive and transmit data pins and baud-rate selection inputs. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the instruction set, architecture, or internal blocks. UART communication is emulated within the testbench, and no external hardware is required. The design has been resubmitted on multiple shuttle runs but has no silicon test reports.
ttsky25a/tt_um_bitty.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the thin UART processor documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc1.summary: This project is a generative silicon art piece depicting a cross-stitch creature on the met4 layer. It has no functional pins other than a dummy output and requires no external hardware. It is purely decorative and has no test procedure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc2.summary: This project is a generative silicon art piece depicting a cross-stitch creature on the met4 layer. It has no functional pins other than a dummy output and requires no external hardware. It is purely decorative and has no test procedure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc3.summary: This project is a generative silicon art piece depicting a cross-stitch creature on the met4 layer. It has no functional pins other than a dummy output and requires no external hardware. It is purely decorative and has no test procedure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc4.summary: This project creates generative cross-stitch patterns using the metal layers of the silicon die. It has no electrical function; the only pin is a dummy output. The design is purely artistic and requires no external hardware. It is notable for using the chip as a canvas for visual art rather than computation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc4.review_notes: Removed unsupported graphics tag; added silicon-art and art.

ttsky25a/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.summary: This project implements a two-player Pong game that outputs to a VGA monitor and accepts input from two NES controllers. The NES controllers connect via three wires each to the bidirectional pins, and the VGA signals are output on the dedicated output pins. External hardware needed includes two NES controllers, a VGA breakout board (such as the Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD), and a VGA-compatible monitor. The design is notable for combining classic gaming with retro controllers and a standard video interface.
ttsky25a/tt_um_brandonramos_VGA_Pong_wit.review_notes: Removed gpio because the bidirectional pins are dedicated NES controller inputs; added gamepad as the correct interface tag.

ttsky25a/tt_um_brandonramos_opamp_ladder.summary: This is a 2-bit flash analog-to-digital converter that converts an analog input voltage between 0 and 1.8V into a 2-bit digital code. The analog input is applied to a dedicated analog pin, and the encoded outputs appear on two digital output pins. No external hardware is required beyond the analog voltage source. The design is notable for being a compact, purely analog implementation of a flash ADC.

ttsky25a/tt_um_braun_mult.summary: This project implements an 8x8 unsigned Braun array multiplier that computes the product of two 8-bit numbers and outputs a 16-bit result. The inputs are provided on the input and bidirectional pins, and the product is output on the output and bidirectional pins. The design is purely combinational and does not require a clock or external hardware. It uses a systematic array of full and half adders to form the product.
ttsky25a/tt_um_braun_mult.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and low-power tags; added verilog; trimmed unsupported low-power claim from summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_brent_kung.summary: This project implements a 4-bit Brent-Kung adder that takes two 4-bit inputs and a carry-in, producing a 5-bit sum output. The design is combinational and can be tested using a provided Verilog testbench with Icarus Verilog and GTKWave. No external hardware is required for operation. The project is notable for being a quick implementation of a parallel prefix adder, likely created in a short time frame.
ttsky25a/tt_um_brent_kung.review_notes: Removed alu because the source only documents a 4-bit Brent-Kung adder, not an ALU.

ttsky25a/tt_um_cache_controller.summary: This project implements a simple direct-mapped cache memory controller that manages four cache blocks. It accepts an 8-bit address and a read/write signal on the input pins and returns 8-bit data on the output pins. The design is synchronous and includes simulation testbenches and cocotb tests for verification. It is notable for fitting a basic cache controller into a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttsky25a/tt_um_cache_controller.review_notes: Added verilog tag; source language is Verilog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttsky25a/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttsky25a/tt_um_chrishtet_LIF.summary: This project implements a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron using 8-bit signed Q4.4 fixed-point arithmetic. It integrates an input current, applies a leak, and emits a spike when the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, with a programmable refractory period. The design is intended for tapeout and uses only adds, subtracts, and shifts. Testing requires an external ADALM2000 for stimulus and observation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_combo_haz.summary: This project implements a combinational logic-based pipeline hazard resolution unit for a RISC-V processor. It detects control, data, and structural hazards and generates signals to freeze the program counter, flush the pipeline, and indicate hazard-free execution. The design is tested in simulation by applying hazard scenarios and observing state transitions. It is self-contained and requires only a clock and reset, with no external hardware needed.
ttsky25a/tt_um_combo_haz.review_notes: Removed cpu because the design is a pipeline hazard resolver, not a CPU core.

ttsky25a/tt_um_customalu.summary: This project implements a custom arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that also supports neural-inspired operations in a separate NPU mode. It takes two 4-bit operands and a 4-bit opcode plus a mode bit to select from operations such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, bitwise logic, rotation, priority encoding, gray code conversion, majority, and various neural computations. The 8-bit output includes the result and error, sign, carry, and zero flags. The design requires no external hardware.
ttsky25a/tt_um_customalu.review_notes: Removed barrel-shifter and combinational because the source does not describe a barrel shifter or state that the design is purely combinational.

ttsky25a/tt_um_cw_vref.summary: This project implements a current-mode bandgap reference that provides a PVT-stable 1V reference voltage and a 5.6uA reference current. It includes a test buffer for measurement, an 8-bit trim for process variation, and SPI control for configuration. Testing requires a 3.3V supply, a ~5uA bias current for the test buffer, and a multimeter to measure voltage and current. Silicon tests confirm the voltage buffer and reference are working, with a 1V output at a trim value of 142.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dac12.summary: This project is described as a 12-bit digital-to-analog converter in Verilog that converts a digital input into an analog (PWM) output. The testing notes say to connect an external ESP32-WROOM-S3, which provides clk, rst-n, ena, and the 12 input bits across the ui and uio pins. The suggested test is to apply values such as 1024, 2048, and 4095 and observe the resulting output on a wave analyzer or through the ESP32's serial output. The documentation is very brief, consisting of only a single sentence describing the design, so no internal implementation details are given.
ttsky25a/tt_um_dac12.review_notes: PWM tag removed; it is the described output mechanism, and the summary was lightly tightened to reflect the thin documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dac_test3v3.summary: This design is an 8-bit R-2R ladder digital-to-analog converter that can be driven either by external digital inputs or by an internal digitally generated sine waveform generator. It provides a 3.3 V analog output on a single analog pin, achieved through level-shifting drivers. The converter is tested by measuring the output voltage on the analog pin with a multimeter. The documentation is short but describes the core function and testing method clearly.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dco.summary: This project implements a digitally controlled oscillator that generates a frequency-adjustable clock signal from an 8-bit control input. The control input selects an oscillation period between 3 and 50 clock cycles using a priority-based scheme, with the highest active bit determining the period. A testbench is provided that simulates various input scenarios and monitors the output, with a table showing output frequencies ranging from 20 MHz down to 2.27 MHz for different input codes. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board itself.

ttsky25a/tt_um_delaychain.summary: This design is a variable-delay chain intended for setup timing violation and glitching experiments. It contains eight delay chains, each with nine stages holding 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 96, and 128 inverter pairs, selectable via a test control input. Measurements require a carefully controlled glitchy clock, such as one generated by a ChipWhisperer, to arm and measure the delay line and observe setup violations. The module is aimed at evaluating the impact of place-and-route, temperature, and voltage on timing violations.
ttsky25a/tt_um_delaychain.review_notes: Removed logic-gate: the project is a delay/glitching experiment, not a basic logic gate implementation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_diff.summary: This project is a fully differential two-stage operational amplifier using a folded cascode followed by a common source stage. It has analog inputs for the differential signal, analog outputs for the differential output, a common-mode input pin, and two digital inputs to select between self-bias and external current source biasing. Testing is planned with an AD03 board to build a band-pass filter and measure linearity, offset voltage and current, CMRR, and PSRR. The design requires either a resistor for self-bias or an external current source, depending on the chosen biasing method.
ttsky25a/tt_um_diff.review_notes: Removed filter-analog and full-custom tags; the filter is test setup and full-custom is not stated.

ttsky25a/tt_um_digital_playground.summary: This project is a digital playground that selects and tests eight classic digital blocks on a single Tiny Tapeout tile: logic gates, an 8-bit counter, a PWM generator, a 7-segment display driver, a 4-bit ALU, a frequency-to-digital converter, a 16x4 RAM, and turn-signal indicators. The active block is chosen with three mode-select inputs, and the remaining pins serve as block-specific inputs and outputs. Testing requires external hardware such as LEDs, switches, a 7-segment display, a function generator, and a logic analyzer or oscilloscope. The design is intended for education and experimentation, with all unused outputs forced to zero and bidirectional pins used only as inputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_digital_playground.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplexer tag; added ram, frequency-counter, and pwm for the described blocks.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dlmiles_tqvph_i2c.summary: This project is a standalone TinyQV I2C controller device that also exposes SPI signals and interrupt outputs. The pin functions are configurable through a CMUX register, and testing may require an NPN transistor and external pull-up resistors on the I2C bus lines. The documentation is incomplete, with a TODO and vague testing instructions, so the exact behavior and configuration are not fully described. It is intended to interface with external I2C and SPI peripherals, possibly using an RP2040.
ttsky25a/tt_um_dlmiles_tqvph_i2c.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplexer tag and added rp2040 and insufficient-doc.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dma.summary: This project implements a simple Tiny DMA controller for memory-to-memory copy operations, supporting both single-word and three-word burst transfers. It uses a finite state machine with IDLE, TRANSFER, and DONE states, and produces a dma_done pulse when the transfer completes, outputting the last transferred data on uo_out. The design is verified with a Cocotb testbench that checks single and burst transfers, confirming values such as 0x61 and 0x63 appear on the output. The documentation is clear about the design and testing, though the clock is specified as 10 Hz, which is unusually low.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dpmunit.summary: This project implements a Dynamic Power Management Unit for a System on Chip in SystemVerilog. It dynamically adjusts voltage and frequency levels based on inputs such as performance requirements, temperature, battery level, and workload, using a finite state machine to manage transitions between power states. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the pin functions or testing procedure in detail. No external hardware or specific test setup is mentioned.

ttsky25a/tt_um_dteal_awg.summary: This project is a streaming arbitrary waveform generator that outputs 8-bit digital samples on eight output pins, which must be connected to an external R-2R ladder or similar DAC to produce an analog waveform. Waveform data is loaded via SPI into a shift register and then transferred to an active register when the load signal is asserted, allowing data to be changed while streaming. The output frequency is derived from the clock with optional dividers of 2x, 4x, 16x, and 256x, which can be stacked for up to 32768x division. Testing requires an external microcontroller to provide SPI data and a DAC circuit to convert the digital outputs to analog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture, developed as part of a university course. It includes a control unit, program counter, instruction register, 16-byte memory, arithmetic logic unit with carry and zero flags, accumulator, and output register. The CPU can execute a small instruction set and provides outputs for the accumulator and flags. It is intended for educational purposes and can be tested by providing opcodes and observing outputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file tag; added risc-v tag noting the architecture is not RISC-V, correcting a potential misattribution.

ttsky25a/tt_um_edwintorok.summary: This project is a demoscene competition entry written in HardCaml that outputs VGA video and PWM audio. Its pins match the Tiny VGA and TT Audio pinouts, with uo[0..7] carrying RGB, vsync and hsync and uio[7] providing a PWM output. A test mode input is provided on ui[0], and the design runs from a 25.25 MHz clock. A silicon tester reports it works as expected when tested with the Tiny VGA PMOD using default settings.
ttsky25a/tt_um_edwintorok.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary invented a process-characterization test structure that the source does not describe.

ttsky25a/tt_um_emmersonv_tiq_adc.summary: This is a 3-bit flash analog-to-digital converter that samples a 0 V to 1.8 V signal on analog pin 0 and presents the result on three digital outputs. Its threshold voltages are built into inverter stages, so no external reference voltage is needed. Testing consists of applying a known input voltage and reading the three output bits, optionally with a multimeter. The design is a compact analog block whose main notable feature is the reference-free inverter-based comparator scheme.
ttsky25a/tt_um_emmersonv_tiq_adc.review_notes: Removed comparator, transistor-level, and mixed-signal because they are not supported by the source documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_ev_motor_control.summary: This Verilog design models a PLC-based electric vehicle motor controller with PWM speed control, power and mode selection, headlight, horn and indicator outputs, and overheat warning. Inputs come from separate PLC and HMI control lines, and the design drives motor speed bits, a PWM output and status LEDs. The documentation lists recommended external hardware but the section is truncated, so the exact bill of materials is not fully specified. It is notable for packaging an automotive-style control system into a single Tiny Tapeout tile, though no silicon test results are given.

ttsky25a/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttsky25a/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_fifo.summary: This project is an asynchronous FIFO with separate read and write clocks, 8-bit data ports, and full and empty flags. The pin names indicate standard FIFO control signals such as write increment, read increment, and active-low resets for each domain. However, the documentation text is gibberish and provides no usable explanation of the implementation or test procedure. The design can only be inferred from its title and pin names, so the description is essentially unsupported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_fifo.review_notes: Removed memory and synchronizer; added verilog and insufficient-doc.

ttsky25a/tt_um_flash_raid_controller.summary: This SPI flash RAID controller sits between two SPI hosts and two SPI flash chips, routing read operations according to programmable address ranges while remaining protocol-compatible. It exposes separate clock, chip-select and MOSI lines for a main host, a secondary host and a management port, plus MISO returns and flash-side signals. The design is intended to let two hosts share two flashes transparently, with address-based routing deciding which device is accessed. Documentation is brief but the pin list and description clearly define the interface and function.

ttsky25a/tt_um_flummer_ltc.summary: This design generates Linear Timecode (LTC) for audio and video synchronisation, using counters to track time and frame count and serialising 80-bit biphase mark coded frames. It is driven by a 12 MHz clock and starts counting from 00:00:00:00 after reset, with the frame rate selected by two input pins for 24, 25, or 30 fps. The LTC output appears on a bidirectional pin and can be fed to an audio PMOD for levels usable by audio equipment, or connected directly to a logic analyser. The 29.97 fps mode is documented as not implemented, and the project is a small single-tile Verilog design.
ttsky25a/tt_um_flummer_ltc.review_notes: Removed synchronizer (not a CDC block) and added signal-generator for the LTC waveform output.

ttsky25a/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an input signal and displays the result on a dual seven-segment display. It debounces the input, counts transitions over a configurable period, and divides the count by ten for display. The period can be set via input pins to match the clock frequency for accurate measurements. It requires a dual seven-segment PMOD and a frequency source, and includes a debug mode for monitoring internal state.

ttsky25a/tt_um_fsm_haz.summary: This is a finite state machine that resolves pipeline hazards for a RISC-V processor, handling control, data and structural hazards. It has six states and drives program-counter freeze, flush and resolved outputs based on branch, dependency and resource-conflict inputs. The design is self-contained and needs only a clock and active-low reset, with optional LEDs or a logic analyzer for visibility during FPGA integration. The documentation describes simulation-based verification rather than silicon results.
ttsky25a/tt_um_fsm_haz.review_notes: Removed cpu and education tags not supported by the source; trimmed unsupported teaching claim from summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_galaguna_PostSys.summary: This is a small CPU based on an enhanced version of Emil Post's machine, with an eight-instruction set, a 256x4-bit code ROM and a 256x1-bit data RAM in a Harvard arrangement. Programs and data are loaded and read back over a slave SPI interface, and a MODE pin selects programming versus execution while RUN starts the program. The design exposes internal buses on OUT8B and OUT3B under control of a three-bit selector, and it is intended as a teaching resource for computer architecture. The documentation is detailed, including instruction encoding, SPI word format and timing diagrams.
ttsky25a/tt_um_galaguna_PostSys.review_notes: Removed fsm and esoteric tags; the design is a CPU, not an FSM or esoteric computation.
