ttsky25a/tt_um_gamepad_pmod_demo.summary: This project reads input from a Gamepad PMOD and displays the pressed buttons as green symbols on a VGA monitor. It uses the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout and a 25.175 MHz clock, and is intended to be run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board with both PMODs attached. After reset, pressing a gamepad button causes its corresponding symbol to appear on screen. It is a demonstration of combining the Gamepad and Tiny VGA PMODs, derived from the VGA Playground, and needs both external PMOD boards to operate.

ttsky25a/tt_um_gray_sobel.summary: This SystemVerilog design performs grayscale conversion and Sobel edge detection on pixel data streamed in over SPI. A two-bit select input chooses bypass, grayscale, Sobel, or grayscale-plus-Sobel processing, and an enable pin gates the Sobel stage. An internal LFSR can generate test pixels instead of external data, and the processed result appears on a single output pin. The design needs an SPI-capable host such as a Raspberry Pi to feed pixels, and the documentation explains the pin mapping and processing modes.
ttsky25a/tt_um_gray_sobel.review_notes: Removed dsp because the source describes image processing rather than general digital signal processing.

ttsky25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.summary: This is a 16-bit CPU based on the HACK architecture, containing D and A registers, a program counter, an ALU with 18 operations, and SPI master logic. Because the chip lacks on-chip memory, instructions and data are fetched from an external SPI RAM one 16-bit word at a time, and a second SPI port provides debug access to the D register, A register, program counter and FSM state. The design targets a Microchip 23XX512 SPI RAM and a microcontroller for debugging, and it matches the SPI Pmod pinout. It is notable for fitting a working CPU into a single tile by serializing memory access.
ttsky25a/tt_um_hack_cpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added cpu, alu, spi, memory, and fsm tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_htfab_split_flops.summary: This project is an experiment in using two-phase nonoverlapping clocks to make a design immune to hold violations, implemented by patching the flip-flops of Simon's Caterpillar into pairs of latches. It adds a scan chain through every flip-flop for debugging and disables static timing analysis by marking all paths as false paths. The design drives a seven-segment display, LEDs and a speaker, and requires a Simon Says PMOD plus two 50 kHz clocks with 25 percent duty cycle at 0 and 180 degrees. Silicon testing by the author reports it works as intended, with a bring-up script provided for the two-phase clock setup.
ttsky25a/tt_um_htfab_split_flops.review_notes: clock-generator removed (design consumes clocks, does not generate them); silicon-tested added per working report.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.summary: This project is a 1-bit AM software-defined radio pipeline written in Verilog. It uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC frontend, oversampled and decimated 4096 times to gain extra precision. The core includes an SPI interface for setting demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs demodulated audio via PWM. The design spans 3x2 Tiny Tapeout tiles and is based on a Hackaday project by Alberto Garlassi.
ttsky25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_1bitam.review_notes: Removed risc-v, cpu, soc, uart, qspi, and memory tags as unsupported; added radio, rf, dsp, spi, adc, demodulator, nco, audio, pwm, and multi-tile tags based on the source documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.summary: This is a software-defined radio core for AM reception that uses an external comparator as a 1-bit ADC and performs digital bandpass filtering and envelope detection. It is configured via a SPI interface to set the demodulation frequency and gain, and outputs a PWM signal representing the demodulated audio. External hardware includes a comparator, resistor bias network, RC network, SPI microcontroller, and an RF amplifier. The design is notable for its compact 1x2 tile size, trading off selectivity compared to a previous larger implementation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_jamesrosssharp_tiny1bitam.review_notes: Removed comparator/adc (external components, not on-chip); added pwm and rf tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_javibajocero_top.summary: This design is a UART receiver that watches for the ASCII string MARCO and, upon detecting it, replies with a carriage-return and newline wrapped POLO! and toggles a WS2812B LED from red to green. It runs at 50 MHz with 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity and one stop bit, and exposes debug signals for the baud ticks, transmit trigger and busy flag. Testing requires a USB-to-TTL adapter and a WS2812B LED, and the author reports it was verified on an FPGA. It is a small, self-contained demonstration of UART plus addressable-LED driving.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jnw_wulffern.summary: This analog block contains two temperature sensors designed by NTNU students in the TFE4188 Advanced Integrated Circuits course. One sensor outputs a PWM signal whose period varies with temperature, while the other emits a single pulse whose duration is inversely proportional to temperature when its reset input is toggled. Testing requires an external clock and monitoring of the output pins with appropriate measurement equipment. The design is notable as a student coursework project with limited published documentation beyond the brief testing instructions.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jonathan_thing_vga.summary: This Verilog design reads RLE-encoded video and audio data from an external flash memory, decodes it, and outputs 8-bit VGA colour signals plus PWM audio. It continues playback until a stop signal resets it to the beginning. Testing is done with a cocotb testbench that consumes a data.bin file and produces an output.bin log of every pixel, which can be converted for visual inspection. A custom PCB is required to handle the VGA output, PWM audio, and external memory connections.
ttsky25a/tt_um_jonathan_thing_vga.review_notes: Removed spi and decoder tags not explicitly supported; trimmed unsupported SPI claim from summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jonnor_pdm_microphone.summary: This Verilog peripheral generates a bit clock for a PDM microphone and decodes the returned density signal into PCM words. It is configured through parameters for clock period and enable, and connects to the microphone via clock and data pins. Silicon testing with an MP34DT01-M breakout succeeded, capturing five seconds of audio while clocked from an RP2350 SPI interface. The design is notable for having a verified working silicon test report.

ttsky25a/tt_um_jyblue1001_pll.summary: This analog PLL targets a 2.4 GHz output frequency and includes a bandgap reference circuit for its charge pump. It is tested by applying a 20 MHz, 1.8 Vpp reference signal and monitoring the output frequency with a multimeter, expecting convergence within about 3 microseconds. The designer notes doubt that the output will reach exactly 2.4 GHz and suggests increasing the input frequency if needed. External hardware required includes a signal generator and a multimeter.

ttsky25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.summary: This Verilog design implements a 4-bit ALU slice intended for mini and microcomputer CPUs, supporting ADD, AND, OR, XOR, pass-through, and shift operations selected by a 3-bit function code. It provides carry in/out, complement, zero, and negative-zero flags, and was tested on an Intel/Altera FPGA. The design is controlled entirely through its input pins and requires no external hardware beyond the FPGA used for verification. It is a straightforward educational ALU block with clear function and pin documentation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_kb2ghz_xalu.review_notes: Removed unsupported cpu, logic-gate, retro, and fpga tags; ALU and verilog are supported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, plus UART over the demo board USB. It is a full Linux-capable SoC implemented in Verilog on a 8x2 tile Tiny Tapeout chip.
ttsky25a/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Removed redundant microcontroller tag and corrected the summary to avoid implying built-in flash or an onboard UART bridge.

ttsky25a/tt_um_kishorenetheti_tt16_mips.summary: This Verilog design is a complete 8-bit MIPS single-cycle processor supporting eight instruction types covering arithmetic, logical, memory, and jump operations. The program counter bits are exposed on bidirectional pins and the ALU result on the outputs, while all dedicated inputs are unused. No documentation is provided beyond the pin list and one-line description, so the instruction encoding and memory interface are not described. The design appears to be an educational processor implementation with no test or usage instructions given.
ttsky25a/tt_um_kishorenetheti_tt16_mips.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc because the description and pins adequately identify the design; added MIPS/single-cycle/8-bit tags supported by the title and description.

ttsky25a/tt_um_krisjdev_manchester_baby.summary: This Verilog design is a modern implementation of the Manchester Baby, the first stored-program computer, with an 8-bit data path and control signals for the PTP interface. It exposes data in and out, stop lamp, RAM read/write, and debug controls, and can be driven from a microcontroller such as the official devkit or a Raspberry Pi Pico. A serial mode reduces the number of required GPIO pins. The design is notable as a historical reimplementation intended for education and demonstration.

ttsky25a/tt_um_lcd_controller_Andres078.summary: This Verilog design controls a 16x2 HD44780-compatible LCD in 4-bit data mode and displays a hardcoded funny message. It requires a 50 MHz clock and an active-low reset, and its pins are named to match the LCD signals for direct wiring. After reset is released the message should appear on the screen. The only external hardware needed is the 16x2 LCD module itself.

ttsky25a/tt_um_led_matrix_driver.summary: This Verilog design is a write-only SPI peripheral that drives WS2812B RGB LED matrices or strips, latching each 3-byte GRB frame to the next LED in sequence. It operates with SPI mode 0 at 1 MHz and supports roughly 300 Hz refresh for an 8x8 matrix. Testing involves connecting a Pi Pico as SPI master and running an example MicroPython script, with optional status LEDs for debugging. Up to 64 LEDs have been tested, and the design requires an external WS2812B matrix or strip plus an SPI master.

ttsky25a/tt_um_lfsr_stevej.summary: This Verilog design implements an 8-bit linear feedback shift register that produces a new pseudo-random value on each read. A seed can be loaded by placing a value on the input pins and pulsing the write-enable pin, or the register can be reset with the chip reset. Testing consists of reading the output pins repeatedly and confirming that each value differs from the last. The design is a simple, self-contained PRNG block requiring no external hardware.

ttsky25a/tt_um_librelane3_test.summary: This is a factory test module hardened with LibreLane 3.0.0.dev38. It provides three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. The mode is selected by rst_n and sel signals. It is used to verify the connectivity and functionality of all I/O pins on the ASIC.
ttsky25a/tt_um_librelane3_test.review_notes: Removed asic because the source describes a factory test module rather than an ASIC implementation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_limpix31_r0.summary: This design measures human reaction time with microsecond precision using a VGA monitor and a single button. It displays a green screen after a random delay, and the user must press the button as quickly as possible; pressing too early results in a red screen. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and a pulled-up button connected to ui[0]. It is an ASIC adaptation of the r0 project, optimized for area, and includes an LFSR debug block that appears as noise when idle.
ttsky25a/tt_um_limpix31_r0.review_notes: Removed 'game' tag because the source describes a reaction-time measurement instrument, not a game.

ttsky25a/tt_um_log_afpm.summary: This design is a 16-bit floating-point multiplier that uses logarithmic approximation to reduce hardware complexity and power consumption. It has 8 input pins for operand A, 8 bidirectional pins for operand B, and 8 output pins for the product, with the pins time-multiplexed to handle 16-bit values. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a one-line description and pin names, with no detailed explanation of the algorithm or testing procedure. Notable aspects include the use of approximation for efficiency, but without further documentation, its accuracy and limitations are unclear.
ttsky25a/tt_um_log_afpm.review_notes: Removed dsp tag; no DSP application is described, only a floating-point multiplier.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mac.summary: This project implements a Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) unit using a Dadda multiplier and a Kogge-Stone adder for high-performance digital signal processing. It performs multiplication and accumulation operations, essential for filtering and convolution. The design is verified through a provided testbench that simulates various input scenarios. No external hardware is required beyond standard clock and reset signals.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mac.review_notes: Removed alu because the design is a MAC unit rather than an arithmetic logic unit.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mac_spst_tiny.summary: This design is an 8-bit Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) unit with a specialized SPST adder for efficient addition. It multiplies two 8-bit inputs to produce a 16-bit product, which is accumulated in an internal register. The lower 8 bits are continuously output, while the upper 8 bits are available on a bidirectional bus that can be externally overridden. It is optimized for Tiny Tapeout's limited IO and minimal area, and can be tested with simulation testbenches or Cocotb.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mac_spst_tiny.review_notes: Removed alu because the design is a MAC unit; added cocotb because the documentation mentions Cocotb tests.

ttsky25a/tt_um_markgarnold_pdp8.summary: This is a bit-serial implementation of a subset of the PDP-8 computer, adapted from a textbook example and using one-hot state encoding generated by VITO. It emulates instructions such as AND, TAD, ISZ, DCA, JMP, and microinstructions, with a reduced memory of 128 words accessed serially. The design requires an external serial memory emulation, typically via a Python testbench, and includes wait states to accommodate cocotb testing. It is an educational project demonstrating computer architecture and hardware design.
ttsky25a/tt_um_markgarnold_pdp8.review_notes: Removed fsm tag; the design is a CPU with an internal state machine, not an FSM-centric design.

ttsky25a/tt_um_marxkar_jtag.summary: This project implements a JTAG TAP controller compliant with IEEE 1149.1, supporting bypass, IDCODE, and boundary scan register instructions. It manages shifting, capturing, and updating of instruction and data registers via TDI, TMS, and TCLK. The TDO output reflects the serial data shifted out of the selected register. It is intended for testing and debugging of digital circuits.
ttsky25a/tt_um_marxkar_jtag.review_notes: Removed scan-chain tag because the design is a JTAG TAP controller, not a scan-chain test structure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_matrag_chirp_top.summary: This design accepts a byte from a UART input and produces a chirp waveform as an 8-bit parallel output, using LoRa-style modulation with a bandwidth of 125 kHz and spreading factor 8. It requires a UART transmitter, a 10 MHz clock source, and a digital signal analyzer for testing. The chirp is output on uo[7:0], and a done signal is available on uio[0]. The design is intended for generating chirp signals for communication or testing purposes.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.summary: This analog design contains two ring oscillators, one built from 18 inverters and a NAND enable gate targeting roughly 600 MHz, and one from 36 inverters targeting roughly 300 MHz, each followed by a two-stage driver to drive the analog pads. Ring 1 is enabled via ui[0] and observed on uo[0], while ring 2 is enabled via ui[1] and observed on uo[1]. Testing requires an oscilloscope to measure the attenuated analog output, and the documentation notes that the 300 MHz oscillator had a missing contact in TT08 and was fixed for TT09. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog oscillator experiment with known silicon issues.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.review_notes: Removed incorrect clock-generator tag and added silicon-tested tag per documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.summary: This design is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) with a 3.3V output, driven either externally or by an internal sine waveform generator. Silicon tests confirm a smooth sine wave over the full 3.3V range, with a slight nonlinearity at the mid-code transition. It requires an external multimeter to measure the output voltage. The design uses level shifting drivers to achieve the 3.3V output.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.review_notes: Removed transistor-level, which is not supported by the R2R ladder description; silicon-tested was already correctly applied.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mattvenn_spi_test.summary: This is an SPI test design based on the tt07_alu_74181 project, featuring two read/write 8-bit registers and two read-only status registers. The first read/write register drives a 7-segment display. It is tested using an RP2040's SPI master, with example code provided to write and read registers. No external hardware is required beyond the RP2040 and the demoboard.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mbikovitsky_audio_player.summary: This design plays raw unsigned 8-bit PCM audio samples from an attached SPI flash chip through DACs connected to analog pins ua[0] and ua[1]. It requires an SPI flash configured for 24-bit addressing and audio amplifiers connected to the analog outputs. The design supports play/pause control and mode selection via input pins. It is notable for integrating analog output with digital SPI flash reading.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mbikovitsky_audio_player.review_notes: Removed memory and qspi tags not supported by the source; added speaker for the analog audio outputs.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mbist.summary: This project implements a Built-In Self-Test (BIST) mechanism for an 8-bit by 16-word internal SRAM. It uses a finite state machine to write a test pattern to all addresses and then read back and compare the values, setting a fail flag on mismatch and a done flag upon completion. The test pattern is provided on ui_in[3:0], and the start signal initiates the process. It is intended for memory integrity verification and can be tested with a Cocotb testbench.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mcs4_cpu.summary: This project implements the Intel MCS-4 4004 CPU in Verilog, intended for use in a replica of the 141-PF calculator. The design can be configured in three ways: as an internal CPU within an FPGA, as an FPGA-based CPU connected to external MCS-4 system components, or as a standalone chip connected to an FPGA-based MCS-4 system. The chip requires external ROM and RAM to function as a complete system, and the documentation describes a debug system using an FPGA and a RISC-V subsystem for chip selection. The design runs at 750 kHz and exposes data, sync and chip-select pins for the MCS-4 bus.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mcs4_cpu.review_notes: Removed memory tag (external only); added retro and calculator.

ttsky25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.summary: This project implements a generic synchronous FIFO buffer with a single clock domain. It buffers data from an 8-bit input to an 8-bit output, with write and read enable signals and full/empty flags. The design is intended as an experimental microtile container. Testing involves writing data until full and reading until empty.
ttsky25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag because the project uses only one tile.

ttsky25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container_gro.summary: This design implements a maze game where the player can walk around and see adjacent walls on a 7-segment display. It uses the first four inputs to move up, down, left, or right. No external hardware is required beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout PCB. The documentation is minimal and does not provide details on the maze layout or game mechanics.
ttsky25a/tt_um_micro_tiles_container_gro.review_notes: Removed multi-tile because the project is 1x1 tiles.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mikael.summary: This project is a Tiny Tapeout test run with eight inputs and eight outputs. The documentation states only that it works by trial and error and was tested with APyTypes. No detailed functional description is provided. The exact behavior of the design is unclear from the available documentation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mikael.review_notes: Removed unsupported FSM, sequential-logic, and education tags; added insufficient-doc.

ttsky25a/tt_um_minirisc.summary: This project implements a simple MiniRISC processor using an FSM-based control unit. It fetches instructions from the ui_in pins and steps through fetch, decode, execute and write-back phases, with an accumulator register holding intermediate results and uo_out reflecting the ACC value or operation result. The design is intended to demonstrate a minimal RISC-like processor synthesized for Tiny Tapeout and verified through simulation and hardware testing. A cocotb testbench is provided for verification.
ttsky25a/tt_um_minirisc.review_notes: Replaced unrelated analog tags and summary with content supported by the documented MiniRISC-FSM design.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mod6_counter.summary: This project implements a 3-bit Mod-6 synchronous counter. The counter increments on every rising edge of the clock and wraps from 5 back to 0, with the value output on uo_out[2:0] and higher bits tied to 0. An active-low asynchronous reset clears the counter to 0. It can be tested with the provided cocotb or Verilog testbenches.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mod6_counter.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated 8-bit processor; corrected to the Mod-6 counter actually documented.

ttsky25a/tt_um_mosbius.summary: This project implements a mini MOSbius analog chip in a 3x2 Tiny Tapeout slot. It contains programmable NMOS and PMOS transistors, differential pairs, OTAs, and current sources. Six buses with transmission gates allow interconnection of the blocks, programmed by a shift register. Silicon tests confirmed working inverter, differential amplifier, ring oscillator, and current source configurations.
ttsky25a/tt_um_mosbius.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the analog MOSbius design.

ttsky25a/tt_um_murmann_group.summary: This Verilog design implements a decimation filter for both incremental and regular delta-sigma modulators, reducing oversampled data while preserving signal accuracy. For incremental modulators the output updates after accumulating 16 input samples, while for regular modulators the output update is controlled by the reset signal. The filter provides a 16-bit decimated output and is clocked at 50 MHz. No silicon test reports are included, but the design targets ADC signal processing by converting a high oversampled data rate into a lower downsampled rate.
ttsky25a/tt_um_murmann_group.review_notes: Summary corrected: the regular-modulator mode is described in the source as internal timing controlled by the reset signal, not an internal reset signal, and the unsupported claim that testing details are not provided was dropped.

ttsky25a/tt_um_myprocessor.summary: This project is an 8-bit custom processor designed in Verilog. It includes a program counter, control unit, ALU, and register file. The processor fetches instructions, decodes them, performs operations via the ALU, and stores results synchronized with the clock. Testing is done using a cocotb testbench in the test folder.
ttsky25a/tt_um_myprocessor.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to accurately describe the custom processor.

ttsky25a/tt_um_nitelich_conway.summary: This project implements Conway's Game of Life with VGA output and GPIO controls for field manipulation and randomization. It uses a 2x2 tile area and outputs VGA color, HSync and VSync signals on uo_out. Inputs on ui and uio handle stepping, holding, selection movement, target state setting and randomization. The design is written in Verilog and no silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_nitelich_conway.review_notes: Proposed summary invented 7-segment inputs and demoscene/retro purposes; corrected to the documented Game of Life with VGA and GPIO controls.

ttsky25a/tt_um_nitelich_riscyjr.summary: This project is RISCY Jr., an original scratch-built 8-bit MCU design. It provides SPI RAM access, a UART with optional hardware flow control, general purpose I/O, PWM outputs, a PSRNG and a CPU activity indicator. It is implemented in Verilog and uses the SPI Pmod and UART Pmod pinouts. Testing requires an RP2040 running SPI RAM emulation and a UART connection.
ttsky25a/tt_um_nitelich_riscyjr.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary were generic and did not reflect the documented MCU, SPI RAM, UART and PWM features.

ttsky25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.summary: This project adds retro graphics to existing Tiny Tapeout projects by using their 7-segment display outputs as input and rendering them to a VGA display. It outputs a 640x480 @ 60 FPS VGA signal through the Tiny VGA pinout. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires the TinyVGA PMOD. Silicon tests report it working, showing a default "HELLO 3OrLd" message and responding to other ui_in inputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_nvious_graphics.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary were generic and missed the VGA demoscene purpose and silicon-tested status.

ttsky25a/tt_um_openfpga22.summary: This project is a small 2x2 OpenFPGA fabric containing 4 configurable logic blocks, 8 I/O blocks, 9 switch boxes and 12 connection boxes. A Verilog design is compiled into a bitstream that configures the routing and logic resources to implement the intended circuit. It is implemented in Verilog and spans a 3x2 tile area. Testing involves loading the bitstream, driving inputs through the I/O blocks and observing outputs in simulation or with lab equipment.
ttsky25a/tt_um_openfpga22.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary were generic and did not describe the OpenFPGA fabric documented in the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_openram_top.summary: This is a testchip containing a 16x32 single-port OpenRAM SRAM macro that uses two-phase clocking to avoid hold violations. It includes a scan chain for testing and supports byte write masking via the bidirectional pins. The design operates at clock frequencies up to 250 MHz and is controlled through dedicated inputs for clocks, chip select, write enable, and scan signals. No external hardware is required, but a scan chain tester may be used to verify functionality.
ttsky25a/tt_um_openram_top.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (clocks are inputs, not generated) and insufficient-doc (documentation is adequate).

ttsky25a/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This design is a stylish ring oscillator built from 21 SkullFET inverters, generating a square wave with a simulated frequency of about 169.2 MHz. It is tested by connecting an oscilloscope to one of the divided outputs, as the full-speed outputs are too fast for GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond an oscilloscope. Notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and the inclusion of frequency dividers for observability.
ttsky25a/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Removed the overbroad clock-generator tag; simulation frequency kept as stated in the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_pchri03_levenshtein.summary: A fuzzy search engine that finds the best matching word in a dictionary using the bit-vector Levenshtein distance algorithm. It communicates with a host via SPI and requires an external QSPI PSRAM module to store the dictionary. Silicon testing confirmed it works but encountered a pinout mismatch with the v3 demo board, forcing a software SPI implementation limited to 500 kHz. The design is based on a 2003 paper by Heikki Hyyrö and is intended for applications needing approximate string matching.

ttsky25a/tt_um_pe_simonbju.summary: A simple processing element (PE) implemented in VHDL that takes two 4-bit inputs and a 3-bit operation selector to produce a 4-bit result. The documentation is minimal, only stating to 'send in data' for testing. The exact operations or architecture are not described, so its capabilities are unclear. The design occupies one tile and uses the standard 8-input, 8-output pin configuration.
ttsky25a/tt_um_pe_simonbju.review_notes: Removed unsupported instruction-decoder and gate-level tags; added accelerator.

ttsky25a/tt_um_plc_prg.summary: Implements a simple PLC-style programmable logic controller in Verilog that reads eight digital inputs and drives eight digital outputs based on programmed control rules. It mimics the scan cycle of a PLC: read inputs, execute logic, update outputs. The design can be used with switches and LEDs for testing, and optional external hardware includes buttons and relays. It is a combinational or sequential design depending on configuration and is intended for prototyping small automation tasks.
ttsky25a/tt_um_plc_prg.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm and combinational tags; added verilog and industrial tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_program_counter_top_level.summary: This project implements a synchronous 4-bit counter with control signals for counting, loading, and output enable. The counter increments on each clock cycle when the count enable is asserted, can load a 4-bit value when the load enable is asserted, and can be disabled to put the output in high-impedance. It includes a reset that clears the counter to zero. The design is tested by observing the output on dedicated pins while manipulating the control signals to verify counting, pausing, loading, and output disabling.

ttsky25a/tt_um_pwen.summary: A pulse width encoder that generates a digital pulse of programmable width based on a 4-bit input and control signals. An FSM coordinates the pulse generation across idle, counting, and done states. The design is fully synchronous and includes a testbench for simulation. It has no mandatory external hardware and can be used in larger digital systems.
ttsky25a/tt_um_pwen.review_notes: Removed incorrect 'pwm' tag; the design is a one-shot programmable-width pulse encoder, not a duty-cycle PWM generator.

ttsky25a/tt_um_quarren42_demoscene_top.summary: This Verilog design displays a parody of the 'graphic design is my passion' meme with bouncing shapes on a VGA monitor. It has no inputs and outputs standard VGA signals, requiring a TinyVGA PMOD. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and has been tested successfully on silicon. It is a simple graphics demo with no interactive elements.

ttsky25a/tt_um_r2r_dac.summary: A 4-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter that converts a 4-bit input signal to an analog output voltage. The design is implemented in analog and has one analog output pin. It requires an external signal source (e.g., ADALM2000 in digital mode) to provide the 4-bit input. The documentation is very brief, describing it as similar to an example design.
ttsky25a/tt_um_r2r_dac.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal, full-custom and insufficient-doc: the source documents a purely analog R2R DAC with an adequate test procedure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rburt16_bias_generator.summary: A test chip for evaluating mismatch in a simple CMOS beta multiplier current source. It contains 16 identical cells (eight oriented one way and eight rotated 90 degrees) whose outputs are combined into a single analog output. Individual cells can be disabled via digital inputs. Silicon measurements show an output current mean of 0.7uA with a standard deviation of 0.1uA, and no statistical difference due to orientation. External precision current measurement equipment is required.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rburt16_bias_generator.review_notes: Removed voltage-reference: the circuit is a current source, not a voltage reference.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rburt16_opamp_3stage.summary: This project is a test chip for a 3-stage PMOS operational amplifier. It provides three analog pins: an output, an inverting input, and a non-inverting input. The documentation is minimal, indicating it is primarily a test vehicle for the amplifier topology. No silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rburt16_opamp_3stage.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added incomplete for thin test-chip documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_colorbars.summary: This design generates a VGA test pattern resembling NTSC color bars, with optional station ID display, scrolling ID, and scrolling bars. It is configured through input pins for showing the ID, using a custom ID, scrolling the ID, and scrolling the bars, and it outputs RGB and sync signals on the Tiny VGA pinout. A TinyVGA PMOD is required to connect to a VGA monitor, and the colors are explicitly not accurate to real NTSC color bars. Silicon test reports indicate it works, though one tester noted the clock must be manually set to 25 MHz in the commander app.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_dipped.summary: Converts between binary, binary-coded decimal (BCD), and densely packed decimal (DPD) formats for values from 0 to 999. The design supports read and write operations via dedicated control pins and bidirectional data pins. It includes a Python test script that verifies conversions in all directions. External hardware is optional, as the design can be used with any input and output devices.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_dipped.review_notes: Removed encoder and lookup-table tags not supported by the source; added bcd, combinational and verilog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: An ALU for the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND, OR, XOR, interleave, and select. It features two 32-bit registers and supports reading and writing bytes via address and selector pins. The design is intended for educational and novelty purposes, with extensive documentation and test cases. It can be used without external hardware, though a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file and multiplexer tags; added alu, esoteric, education, and verilog tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_styler.summary: The Styler chip manipulates 16x16 character glyph bitmaps based on text mode attributes such as bold, faint, italic, underline, and blink. It has registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and it interfaces via 8 bidirectional data pins and several control inputs. The typical use involves writing a scanline number, reading back a logical scanline, and then manipulating bitmap halves to apply visual effects. The chip is intended as part of a larger text mode video display hardware system, and testing is covered by provided test scripts.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_tt09ball_gdsar.summary: This design drives a seven-segment display from an 8-byte ROM containing the characters '9', blank, 'C', 'I', 'Г', 'П', 'O', blank, which spell out a message as part of a GDS artwork. An octal counter cycles through the ROM addresses automatically, but the counter can be bypassed by setting ui_in[3] high and providing a 3-bit address on ui_in[2:0]. Testing involves pulsing the clock to advance the display or manually selecting addresses to verify the ROM contents. The design is notable for being a carrier for the 'THE STRONGEST' GDS art and requires an external seven-segment display or chip decapping tools to observe the output.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_tt09ball_scree.summary: A VGA screensaver that displays a bouncing logo with an animated color gradient, similar to the classic DVD screensaver. It supports a tiling mode and solid color mode via input pins, and can optionally be controlled with a Gamepad Pmod. The design outputs VGA signals for a 640x480 display and requires a TinyVGA Pmod for connection to a monitor. It is a fun visual demo with minimal external hardware.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large collection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to select the flag by index or step through them. It is used by connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and using the input pins to change the displayed flag. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. Silicon testing confirmed that flag switching works, though the index-based selection via uio was not tested.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added pmod, video, and silicon-tested tags supported by documentation and silicon status.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_exp.summary: This design is a configurable VGA signal generator that allows full control over display timings, sync polarities, and test patterns. It can be programmed via a register interface using ui_in and uio pins to set parameters such as visible width, porches, and sync widths, and it includes 32 test patterns like checkerboards, grids, and color bars. Testing involves connecting a VGA monitor through a TinyVGA Pmod and using the inputs to select patterns or modify timing registers. The design is notable for its flexibility in experimenting with VGA signal generation, requiring only the TinyVGA Pmod as external hardware.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_timing_exp.review_notes: Removed 'education' because the source only says experimentation, not teaching or learning.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebelmike_incrementer.summary: This is a 16-bit counter built from standard cell flip-flops and custom half adder cells, designed in Magic. It increments when the enable input is high and resets when rst_n is low. The design is tested by providing a clock and observing the count on the output pins. Silicon tests show it works correctly up to 198 MHz, with errors in the top bit at 200 MHz.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebelmike_incrementer.review_notes: Removed transistor-level (standard cells used) and added silicon-tested and sequential-logic.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rebelmike_register.summary: This project implements a test of a manually placed circulating register intended for TinyQV's register file. It provides two 32-bit registers that constantly cycle, with a 4-bit wide interface for writing and two read ports for reading. The design is tested by writing data over 8 cycles and reading it over 4 cycles. It is notable for being a manually placed test structure for a register file.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rebelmike_register.review_notes: Removed risc-v tag because the source only references TinyQV's register file, not a RISC-V processor.

ttsky25a/tt_um_regfield.summary: This design is a register field made of 8 chains of 64 flip-flops, intended for studying the effects of electromagnetic pulses on initialized flip-flops. It is used by loading a pattern, injecting an EM pulse with external equipment like a Chipshouter, and scanning out the pattern to observe changes. The design requires external hardware for EM pulse injection. It is notable as a test structure for glitching experiments rather than a functional module.
ttsky25a/tt_um_regfield.review_notes: Removed register-file; added side-channel for EM glitching study.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.summary: This design is a replica of the Atari 2600 video game console system-on-chip, implemented in Verilog. It accepts joystick inputs, switches, and a reset signal, and outputs VGA video and PWM audio, with QSPI pins for external memory. It is tested by connecting a TinyVGA Pmod, Tiny Audio Pmod, and a VGA display, then playing games. The design is notable for being a complete recreation of a classic console on a Tiny Tapeout tile, requiring external hardware for video, audio, and game storage.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rejunity_atari2600.review_notes: Removed cpu because the source does not document an implemented processor core.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rejunity_lgn_mnist.summary: This project is an experiment with Deep Differential Logic Networks for classifying hand-written MNIST digits at 16x16 pixels. It accepts an 8-bit input packet shifted in on the input pins and outputs a 4-bit digit plus a 7-bit confidence score. A /WE input pauses the design, and an external MCU is needed to provide input data and read out results. The documentation is sparse and the test procedure is still marked TO DO, with no silicon results reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_rejunity_lgn_mnist.review_notes: Removed unsupported perceptron and UART tags; added image-processing and insufficient-doc, and corrected the summary to match the actual pins and sparse documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_resfuzzy.summary: This project implements a fuzzy logic system that estimates risk based on rainfall and soil moisture inputs. It uses triangular membership functions and three fuzzy rules to compute a weighted average risk value. The design is tested by providing sensor data via switches and observing the risk value on LEDs. It requires external switches and LEDs for input and output.
ttsky25a/tt_um_resfuzzy.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp tag and added instrumentation for the sensor-based risk measurement.

ttsky25a/tt_um_richardgonzalez_ped_traff.summary: This is a simulation of a pedestrian traffic light controller that toggles between green and red lights with a countdown. It is tested by observing the output pins, where the lights swap after the countdown resets. No external hardware is required, but LEDs can be connected for visualization. The design is a simple state machine with a countdown timer.
ttsky25a/tt_um_richardgonzalez_ped_traff.review_notes: Removed industrial tag; added fsm and led tags supported by the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_robot_controller_top_modu.summary: This is an experimental controller for an autonomous robot, enabling sensor communication and path tracking. It interfaces with a gyro via I2C and a proximity sensor via UART, and controls motors with PWM and direction signals. The design is tested by connecting the specified sensors and enabling the robot. It requires external gyro and proximity sensors, as well as motor drivers.
ttsky25a/tt_um_robot_controller_top_modu.review_notes: Removed sensor-interface; added servo for the motor PWM/direction outputs.

ttsky25a/tt_um_rom_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing 64x64 Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen, with options to tile or double the logo size. It can be controlled with a gamepad to start/pause and change direction. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally a Gamepad PMOD. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected, including tile, double, and gamepad modes.

ttsky25a/tt_um_romless_cordic_engine.summary: This is a ROM-less CORDIC engine that computes sine and cosine of an input angle using 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic. It interfaces via SPI to receive four 16-bit inputs and returns three 16-bit outputs. The design is tested with an SPI master, such as an RP2040, and achieves high accuracy. It is notable for avoiding ROM by generating micro-rotation angles with Taylor series approximation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_romless_cordic_engine.review_notes: Added silicon-tested tag based on the working silicon test report.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sc_bipolar_qif_neuron.summary: This design models a Quadratic Integrate and Fire (QIF) neuron using stochastic computing in bipolar format. It uses an LFSR to generate random bitstreams and implements the neuron equation with XNOR, MUX, and up/down counter. The design is tested by setting a 9-bit input value and observing the neuron's current value on the outputs. It requires an oscilloscope to view the output.
ttsky25a/tt_um_sc_bipolar_qif_neuron.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network and neural-network tags; the design is a single stochastic-computing neuron model.

ttsky25a/tt_um_semaforo.summary: This project implements a finite state machine (FSM) combined with a counter to simulate a traffic light controller for two perpendicular streets. It was developed as part of the Digital Systems course at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The design supports normal mode with priority for Street A and a parade mode where Street B stays green indefinitely. It requires external LEDs and push-buttons for testing and can be simulated using cocotb.
ttsky25a/tt_um_semaforo.review_notes: Removed industrial tag; the design is an educational traffic light controller.

ttsky25a/tt_um_serdes.summary: This design implements a serial data pipeline that combines SERDES, a 4-tap FIR filter, and XOR encryption. It deserializes 8-bit words from a serial input, filters and encrypts them, then serializes the result. The design includes a done pulse to indicate completion of each byte transmission. It requires no external hardware and can be tested with a logic analyzer or LEDs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_serdes.review_notes: Added verilog and serial tags supported by the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sha256_processor_dvirdc.summary: This project is a fully synthesizable, stream-oriented SHA-256 implementation that processes a byte stream and outputs a 256-bit digest. It consists of a compression core, a ROM for constants, a byte-stream front-end, and a GPIO wrapper with a skid buffer. The design uses a simple handshake interface and requires no special peripherals. It is notable for its efficient implementation and Tiny Tapeout compatibility.

ttsky25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.summary: This project implements a basic calculator supporting addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division on positive integers. It scans a 4x4 matrix keypad through the ROW and COL pins and drives a 3-digit seven-segment display via the sseg outputs, with E_1 through E_3 likely acting as digit enables. Testing is done by entering operands through the keypad and checking that the display shows the expected result. External hardware required is a 4x4 matrix keypad and a 3-digit seven-segment display.
ttsky25a/tt_um_shuangyu_top.review_notes: Removed alu and decoder tags not supported by the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_simonsays.summary: This project implements a modified version of the Simon Says game using digital logic and memory elements to store a pseudo-random sequence of colors. It interfaces with external buttons and LEDs for gameplay. A Raspberry Pi is used to send an 8-bit seed and read a 2-bit state debug signal. The design requires six push buttons and four LEDs.
ttsky25a/tt_um_simonsays.review_notes: Removed rp2040 because the external controller is a Raspberry Pi, not an RP2040.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sjsu.summary: This is a simple VGA demo that displays a bitmap and allows color inversion via an input pin. It outputs standard VGA signals including RGB and sync. The design was tested on VGA playground and requires a VGA PMOD for external connection. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to understand its function.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sjsu_vga_music.summary: This project displays an animated dance of navy-blue and yellow figures synchronized with the San Jose State Fight Song for the first 15 seconds. It outputs VGA signals and audio through a sound PMOD. The design requires a VGA monitor and speaker connected via appropriate PMODs. The documentation is brief but indicates the intended behavior.
ttsky25a/tt_um_sjsu_vga_music.review_notes: Removed audio tag because no audio output pins or audio generation details are documented; added vga, graphics, music, and pmod based on the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sky1.summary: This project is an 8-bit basic ALU unit with 8-bit instructions. It uses separate instruction address and data buses, with a write enable signal. The documentation is extremely thin, providing no details on operation or testing beyond vague statements. It appears to be a simple design but lacks sufficient information for thorough understanding.
ttsky25a/tt_um_sky1.review_notes: Removed unsupported memory and education tags; added instruction-decoder based on instruction bus pins.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sleepwell.summary: This design generates a bouncing ball pattern with an SJSU-themed backdrop on a VGA display. It automatically starts upon power-up and requires a Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD. The documentation is minimal, stating that details will be explained later, but the basic functionality is clear from the description and pins.

ttsky25a/tt_um_snn.summary: This project implements a spiking neural network with STDP and reward-based learning. It consists of 8 layers, each with 2 neurons, and weights are loaded from memory. The design accepts 32 4-bit weights and 2 input values to execute. The documentation is brief but provides enough to understand the basic operation and testing procedure.
ttsky25a/tt_um_snn.review_notes: Removed edge-ai since no embedded inference target is stated; memory tag is already supported by the weight-loading description.

ttsky25a/tt_um_snn_core.summary: This project implements an adaptive leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neuron core for edge AI. It features a 12-bit membrane potential with configurable decay, adaptive threshold, and a 3-cycle refractory period. The design outputs the membrane potential, spike, and spike count. It includes learning mode control and is intended for edge AI applications.
ttsky25a/tt_um_snn_core.review_notes: Adjusted summary to avoid unsupported low-power performance claim.

ttsky25a/tt_um_sortaALUAriaMitra.summary: This is a 4-bit ALU implemented in Verilog that performs addition, subtraction, negation, multiplication, and bitwise AND, OR and XOR. Two 4-bit operands are supplied on the eight input pins, and the operation is selected by driving the corresponding bidirectional pin high. The 4-bit result appears on the upper four output pins, while the lower four output pins carry the upper half of the multiplication result. The documentation is brief and does not describe timing, testing or any silicon results.

ttsky25a/tt_um_spacewar.summary: Spacewar is a scaled-down version of the classic Spacewar game written in Verilog, targeting VGA video output and audio. It reads a SNES-style gamepad over a clocked serial interface and also provides a PWM audio output and XY scope outputs. The pinout matches the Tiny VGA, TT Audio and Gamepad PMOD conventions, so external VGA, audio, SNES controller and scope hardware are required. The documentation is thin: testing is listed as 'Cocotb coming soon' and no silicon results are reported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_spi2ws2811x16.summary: This VHDL design translates an SPI stream into eight parallel WS2811 LED strip output channels. A microcontroller drives CS and COPI at roughly 14 MHz, sending interleaved RGB bytes for the eight strips followed by eight null bytes to keep the clock and chip select active. Each of the eight output pins then emits a WS2811 frame for its strip, and the design is flexible about SPI timing. An IceStick was used for testing, and the documentation gives a clear frame format example.

ttsky25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.summary: This Verilog design implements a stochastic multiplier, adder and self-multiplier that operate on serial probability-coded bit streams. Binary-weighted two's-complement inputs are converted to stochastic streams, combined, and converted back to a serial binary-weighted output. Two serial input pins feed the computation and four output pins carry the multiply, add, self-multiply and counter-reset signals. Testing requires an ADALM2000 and Python to generate and analyse the serial streams, and no silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25a/tt_um_stochastic_addmultiply_CL.review_notes: Summary corrected to match the stated no-reports silicon status, and tags adjusted to remove the unsupported ALU while keeping the adder.

ttsky25a/tt_um_stochastic_integrator_tt9.summary: This Verilog project uses stochastic computing to implement an integrator based on Euler's definition of integration in the unipolar probability domain. Two serial input pins accept stochastic bit streams, and eight output pins expose several sequential, system and test integrator outputs. The suggested test is to hold one input high and the other low and observe the resulting equations on the outputs. An ADALM2000 is listed as the external hardware, and the documentation gives only a brief description of the internal structure.
ttsky25a/tt_um_stochastic_integrator_tt9.review_notes: Removed dsp and physics as unsupported; kept stochastic-computing and verilog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_stopwatchtop.summary: This Verilog design is a digital stopwatch that counts seconds and minutes and displays them on a multiplexed 4-digit 7-segment display. A clock divider produces a 1 Hz enable from the Tiny Tapeout clock, and start and stop are controlled by two input pins. The segment and decimal-point lines are on the eight output pins, while the four digit-select lines are on the bidirectional pins. It needs a common-anode 7-segment display connected externally, and the documentation describes simulation and hardware testing clearly.
ttsky25a/tt_um_stopwatchtop.review_notes: Removed education tag, which the source does not support.

ttsky25a/tt_um_stress_sensor.summary: This Verilog design monitors three input signals and asserts an alarm output when all three are active within the same time window of about six seconds at 100 MHz. The three sensor inputs are on the lower input pins and the single response output is on the first output pin. External sensors, buttons or similar sources drive the inputs, and the output can be connected to an LED, display or sounder. The documentation is very short and gives no detail on the timing logic or any test results.
ttsky25a/tt_um_stress_sensor.review_notes: Removed fsm because the source does not describe a finite state machine; the other tags and summary are supported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_subdiduntil2_mixed_signal.summary: This is a mixed-signal two-class classifier built from analog Gaussian circuits, with both analog and digital inputs. Four digital input pins act as DAC controls, one analog pin supplies a reference voltage, and two analog output pins provide the class currents. Testing involves sweeping the digital DAC inputs and the analog reference while observing the output currents with an oscilloscope or multimeter. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the classifier's accuracy or any measured silicon behaviour.

ttsky25a/tt_um_swangust.summary: This SystemVerilog design is a fully combinational adder for 8-bit posit numbers with zero exponent bits. It decodes the two posit operands into fixed-point values and scale factors, aligns and adds them, then re-encodes the rounded result back into posit format. Operand A is supplied on the input pins, operand B on the bidirectional pins, and the sum appears on the output pins. The design was exhaustively verified in simulation against a software reference before fabrication, and post-silicon testing is planned with a microcontroller or DIP switches.

ttsky25a/tt_um_swangust2.summary: This SystemVerilog design is a fully combinational multiplier for 8-bit posit numbers with zero exponent bits. It decodes the two posit operands into fixed-point values and scale factors, aligns and multiplies them, then re-encodes the rounded product back into posit format. Operand A is supplied on the input pins, operand B on the bidirectional pins, and the product appears on the output pins. The design was exhausted in simulation against a software reference before fabrication, with the description mistakenly referring to a sum rather than a product.
ttsky25a/tt_um_swangust2.review_notes: Corrected the summary because the original invented post-silicon testing; the source only mentions planned testing, not actual silicon test status.

ttsky25a/tt_um_swangust3.summary: This design implements an <8,0> posit division circuit, accepting two 8-bit posit inputs via ui and uio and outputting the 8-bit quotient on uo. Pre-fabrication testing compared simulated outputs against a software-generated table for all possible input pairs, and post-fabrication testing requires supplying input posit values and observing the quotient on the output pins. External hardware such as a microcontroller or DIP switches is needed to drive the input pins. The design is notable for supporting the posit number format, an alternative to IEEE floating point.
ttsky25a/tt_um_swangust3.review_notes: Removed unsupported floating-point/alu/decoder/encoder/combinational tags; added divider, fixed-point, and systemverilog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tc503_countdown_timer.summary: This design implements a countdown timer that uses three rotary encoders to adjust seven-segment display values and PWM brightness. It includes debouncing logic and a control pin to enable a minute-based countdown, and it requires a 16 MHz clock oscillator. To use it, external hardware including a PMOD, three seven-segment LED displays, and three digital encoders must be connected to the appropriate pins. The design was created as a term project for the Zero to ASIC course, and its functionality is straightforward but relies on external components for interaction.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tc503_countdown_timer.review_notes: Removed education: the source only identifies it as a term project, not as teaching or learning material.

ttsky25a/tt_um_td4.summary: This project is a 4-bit toy CPU called TD4, based on the book 'CPUの創り方', and it includes an on-chip 8-bit by 16-word ROM for program storage. It operates in three modes: Load, Read, and Execution, selectable via two input pins, with pin functions varying by mode. Testing is done via a provided makefile, and external hardware such as LEDs or an Arduino is suggested for reading or writing data. The design is notable for being a learning tool and originated from a project supervised at Security Camp 2025 in Japan.
ttsky25a/tt_um_td4.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tdctest_container.summary: This is an experimental microtile container that places ring oscillators in a separate tile to add power stress. It has 8 digital inputs, 8 digital outputs, and 2 select pins, but the documentation states that there is nothing to test and it serves as an experimental basis. The design is a Verilog module clocked at 20 MHz. No external hardware or specific testing procedure is described.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tdctest_container.review_notes: Removed unsupported TDC and multi-tile tags; added incomplete since the design is explicitly an untested experimental basis.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tgrillz_sixSidedDie.summary: This design simulates a six-sided die by using an 8-bit LFSR to generate pseudo-random numbers between 1 and 6, outputting the result on a seven-segment display. A dipswitch input triggers the dice roll, and the design outputs zero when the switch is off. It uses on-board dipswitches and a seven-segment display for interaction, requiring no additional external hardware. The design is a simple game-like utility, with the limitation that the LFSR state locks on the first clock cycle after the switch is turned on, which may cause unexpected behavior at startup.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tgrillz_sixSidedDie.review_notes: Removed button tag since the only input is a dipswitch.

ttsky25a/tt_um_thexeno_rgbw_controller.summary: This design is an RGBW color processor that converts SPI commands into four PWM channels for driving LEDs, with a color wheel mode that generates hue, tint, and intensity from a color index. It operates as an SPI slave in Mode 0 and can also directly map RGBW values to PWM outputs in bypass mode. Testing is typically done with a MicroPython script on the Tiny Tapeout demoboard, and external hardware consists of four LEDs connected to the output pins with current-limiting to avoid exceeding 4 mA per pin. The design is notable for its flexibility in controlling RGBW LEDs and its provision of test outputs for debugging, but it requires careful handling of output current.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tiny_pll.summary: Tiny PLL is a 4-channel fractional-N frequency synthesizer that generates four independent clock outputs based on control register settings. It is configured through a simple CSR interface using data and address inputs, and it includes an ADC to monitor the tuning voltage of channel 0. Silicon testing showed that the PLL blocks work and produce the expected outputs, but the ADC output was stuck high, indicating a fault. The design is notable for integrating multiple PLL channels and an ADC on a tiny tapeout tile, though the ADC issue limits its usefulness for monitoring.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tiny_pll.review_notes: Removed analog (digital Verilog design, no analog pins); clock-generator already present in proposed tags, so no add needed beyond confirming it.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor with an animated color gradient, supporting tiling and solid color options via input pins. It can be controlled with a Gamepad Pmod to start, pause, and change the bouncing direction or move the logo. External hardware includes a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod. The design is a simple graphical demo, notable for its use of the VGA interface and gamepad input, but it has no complex functionality beyond the screensaver behavior.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_mosbius.summary: This project is an alternative layout for Andrew Kang's mini-MOSbius, a reconfigurable analog array intended for building and experimenting with MOS circuits, adapted for SKY130 on Tiny Tapeout. It includes analog switches controlled by a serial bitstream, with digital logic for configuration, and it requires external hardware to generate the bitstream and to interface with the analog pins depending on the circuit being built. Silicon test reports indicate that the configuration shift registers work and that various circuits functioned properly. The design is notable for bringing the MOSbius educational concept to a Tiny Tapeout-compatible form, though the software suite for generating configuration bitstreams is not yet written.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rf_test.summary: This project is a test structure for a future register file macro, implemented as an SRAM with one write port and two read ports. It is not designed for use with the demo board but instead requires a dedicated test platform, ideally using FPGA hardware to drive control signals with precise timing. Silicon test reports from the author indicate that the memory works correctly, with tens of thousands of random read/write cycles passing, but timing characterization is incomplete due to limitations of the RP2040 controller. The design is notable as a successful early test of a memory macro, though further testing is needed.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rf_test.review_notes: Removed analog, characterization, and fpga; added sram, register-file, memory, and silicon-tested.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros modified to remove the LVT implant from the bitcell. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_nolvt_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.summary: This project is a test structure for prototype ROM macros. Registers are placed in front of the ROM macros to send addresses and capture data at controlled intervals. The design supports multiple testing modes selected by clock and reset signals. The author reports successful silicon testing with 10 ns propagation time and notes that an FPGA would be needed for more precise timing characterization.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tnt_rom_test.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ROM test structure.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tobi_mckellar_top.summary: This design implements a capacitive touch sensor that measures changes in the capacitive time constant when a finger is applied to a touch pad. It uses a simple external circuit with a large pull-up resistor and a capacitive pad, and it outputs button signals on uo pins while also providing pass-through buttons. Silicon test reports from the author show that the capacitive touch portion mostly works, but required a stronger pull-up resistor (15k instead of 100k) due to pulldowns in the RP2350, and it was tested at clock frequencies of 1, 10, and 24 MHz. The pass-through buttons also work as expected.

ttsky25a/tt_um_toivoh_pwl_synth.summary: This design is a 4-channel chiptune synthesizer that uses a 12-13 bit ALU with a barrel shifter, a latch-based register file, and a 64-cycle program to calculate each sample, outputting PWM audio signals. It requires external hardware to convert the PWM outputs to audio, such as Mike's audio Pmod for mono or a resistive divider and capacitor for stereo, and it is controlled via register writes through a command interface. Example test code and functions are provided for playing notes and configuring waveforms. Silicon test reports indicate that the design works after adapting the test scripts, and care must be taken to avoid damaging audio equipment with high output voltages.
ttsky25a/tt_um_toivoh_pwl_synth.review_notes: Removed unsupported claim about compact implementation from summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_top_layer.summary: The documentation describes a factory test module that mirrors input pins to outputs, mirrors bidirectional pins to outputs, or outputs a counter depending on control signals. However, the project title and pin labels indicate a spike detection and classification system with four parallel detectors, which is not described. The actual functionality is ambiguous due to this contradiction. No external hardware or test procedure for the spike system is described.
ttsky25a/tt_um_top_layer.review_notes: Escalated because the source documentation contradicts the project title and pin labels.

ttsky25a/tt_um_torurstrom_async_lock.summary: This design implements an asynchronous locking unit that accepts eight request signals and provides eight grant signals, ensuring that only one grant is active at a time. It functions as a mutual exclusion arbiter for asynchronous systems. The documentation is brief and does not describe the arbitration policy or testing methodology. No external hardware is specified.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tpu.summary: This is a Tiny Tapeout Tensor Processing Unit that multiplies two 2x2 matrices of signed 8-bit elements to produce signed 16-bit results using a systolic array of four multiply-accumulate processing elements. It is controlled through an external microcontroller that sends input matrices sequentially in row-major order and receives outputs in the same order, with control signals LOAD_EN, TRANSPOSE, and ACTIVATION, and a DONE output. The design includes memory registers for the input matrices, a control unit, and a feeder module to schedule data flow. It achieves over 99.8 million operations per second when streamed and requires an external clock and coordination via the chip interface.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported dsp, neural-network, and gpio tags; machine-learning is already supported by the TPU inspiration.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tqv_peripheral_harness.summary: This design is a rotary encoder peripheral that reads up to four incremental encoders and stores their position values in a register. The encoder A and B signals are connected to the eight input pins, and the stored values are accessed via an SPI slave interface on the bidirectional pins. The design is tested by connecting encoders and using firmware to read the values, and it requires external rotary encoders with pull-up or pull-down resistors if not already present on the encoder board. It operates at a 64 MHz clock and is intended as a simple peripheral for microcontroller systems.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tqv_peripheral_harness.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart, gpio and sensor-interface tags; SPI and rotary-encoder are the correct interface tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_trivium_stream_processor.summary: This design implements a lightweight Trivium stream cipher variant using three 64-bit shift registers to generate a keystream that is XORed with input data for encryption and decryption. It uses 8-bit data and control inputs via the input and bidirectional pins, and outputs an 8-bit stream on the output pins. The design is fully self-contained and is tested only in simulation using Verilog or Cocotb testbenches, with no external hardware required. It is a compact hardware implementation of a cryptographic primitive suitable for Tiny Tapeout.
ttsky25a/tt_um_trivium_stream_processor.review_notes: Removed trng tag: the design is a deterministic stream cipher, not a true random number generator.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tt_tinyQV.summary: This is a crowdsourced RISC-V SoC named TinyQV 'Asteroids' that integrates a small RV32EC CPU with QSPI flash and PSRAM memory and various community-contributed peripherals. It runs code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with UART for communication and GPIO for interrupts. The design requires external QSPI flash and PSRAM modules (such as the QSPI Pmod) and is programmed using a custom toolchain and SDK. Silicon tests confirm it can run MicroPython and Coremark at 64 MHz, and various peripherals like PWM, VGA graphics, and 7-segment drivers have been verified working.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tt_tinyQVb.summary: This is a crowdsourced RISC-V SoC named TinyQV 'Berzerk' that integrates a small RV32EC CPU with QSPI flash and PSRAM memory and various community-contributed peripherals. It runs code from external QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with UART for communication and GPIO for interrupts. The design requires external QSPI flash and PSRAM modules (such as the QSPI Pmod) and is programmed using a custom toolchain and SDK. Silicon tests confirm it can run MicroPython and Coremark at 64 MHz, and peripherals like a frequency synthesizer have been partially tested.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tv_b_gone.summary: This project is a TV-B-Gone device that sends infrared codes to turn off many European TVs, either in a continuous loop or once per button press. It uses an external IR LED connected through a transistor for higher current, and status LEDs indicate active and failure states. The design requires an 8 MHz clock, which can be generated by an RPi Pico, and an optional start button. Silicon tests show it successfully turned off a TV, but it needed a manual reset and the start signal is active low, requiring a pull-up.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tv_b_gone.review_notes: Removed modulator and oscillator tags not supported by the source; added silicon-tested, rp2040 and ir tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tv_b_gone_rom.summary: This is a ROM macro variant of the TV-B-Gone-EU project that sends infrared codes to turn off many European TVs, either in a continuous loop or once per button press. Like the original, it uses an external IR LED with a transistor and status LEDs, and requires an 8 MHz clock. The design uses a ROM macro for code storage, which may reduce logic usage. Silicon tests confirm it works, generating good-looking IR codes, and it also needed a reset to start.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tv_b_gone_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported modulator/gpio tags and added silicon-tested and rp2040 based on the documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_tx_fsm.summary: This design is an error-correcting FIFO buffer that uses SECDED error correction and ARQ retransmission to provide reliable data transmission. It buffers 4-bit data and supports normal, corrupted, and retransmission modes through error mode selection, generating ACK and NACK signals for handshaking. The design is verified using Cocotb testbenches that cover normal transmission, error injection, retransmission, and sequential reads. It runs at a very low clock of 10 Hz and is notable for integrating lightweight error correction into a small FIFO buffer.
ttsky25a/tt_um_tx_fsm.review_notes: Removed shift-register tag; the source describes FIFO buffering, not a shift register.

ttsky25a/tt_um_uart.summary: This is a UART controller with configurable baud rate, separate transmit and receive FIFOs, and interrupt generation for various events. It uses input pins for control signals like transmit enable and data loading, bidirectional pins for serial data and FIFO status/interrupt outputs, and output pins for received data. The design includes a mode for loopback or external serial communication and is intended to interface with a microcontroller or processor. It operates at a 50 MHz clock and provides a full-featured serial communication peripheral.
ttsky25a/tt_um_uart.review_notes: Removed gpio and added pmod to match the detected UART Pmod pinout.

ttsky25a/tt_um_uart_spi.summary: This design integrates a UART and an SPI communication block into a single Tiny Tapeout tile, with pins arranged so both can operate simultaneously. A loopback input connects the input register directly to the output register, so serial output echoes serial input when loopback is asserted, which simplifies testing without external devices. The UART exposes start, valid, and ready signals, while the SPI exposes chip select, start, sclk, and separate slave receive and transmit starts. The documentation describes the top-level wrapper and submodules but gives no silicon test results or measured behavior.

ttsky25a/tt_um_upalermo_simple_analog_ci.summary: This is a simple NMOS current mirror implemented as an analog block occupying a 1x2 tile area with a single analog pin. The stated purpose is to exercise the full custom analog flow, including xschem schematic entry, ngspice simulation, SKY130 PDK usage, Magic layout, DRC/LVS, and GitHub submission, as preparation for future tapeouts. Testing consists of applying a voltage to the output pin and sweeping it while measuring current to plot an IV curve. The documentation is brief and reports no measured silicon results.
ttsky25a/tt_um_upalermo_simple_analog_ci.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal (no digital content) and education (learning intent is personal, not a teaching design).

ttsky25a/tt_um_updown_counter.summary: This project implements an 8-bit up/down counter in Verilog that increments or decrements between 0 and 255 depending on the up_down control input. Counting only occurs on the rising edge of the clock when the enable input is high, and an active-low reset clears the counter to zero. The current value is presented on the eight output pins, which can optionally drive LEDs, a logic analyzer, or a display module. The documentation is straightforward and includes simulation instructions, but no silicon test results are reported.

ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.summary: This is a 3-stage Dickson charge pump that boosts the input voltage to approximately 9.6 V, with the output divided by two and available on the analog pin ua[0]. It requires a 2 MHz clock signal to operate. In the TT09 shuttle, the analog pin voltage is limited to VDDIO/VDDA, so the output is divided by three instead. The design is tested by applying a clock and measuring the divided output voltage.
ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_charge_pump.review_notes: Removed clock-generator (clock is an input, not generated); charge-pump already present.

ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.summary: This design implements a configurable ring oscillator with up to 3853 inverter stages. By connecting one of the output pins to the ring_in input or enabling internal loopback, a ring of a specific length is formed, and the output frequency can be measured. External hardware such as an oscilloscope or logic analyzer is required to measure the frequency and delay between different points in the chain. The design is notable for its large number of stages and the ability to select from many tap points.
ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_giant_ringosc.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag; the design is an inverter-chain ring oscillator, not a logic gate implementation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttsky25a/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.summary: UW ASIC - Optimized Dino is described as a Dino game compressed into only two tiles. The documentation consists entirely of placeholders, so the actual controls, video output format and testing method are not stated. The pin names are generic and give no further detail about the interface. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.
