ttsky25a/tt_um_uwasic_dinogame.review_notes: Removed game tag since only the title hints at a game and no gameplay is documented; kept insufficient-doc and verilog.

ttsky25a/tt_um_vedic_4x4.summary: This design implements a 4x4 Vedic multiplier based on the Urdhva Tiryagbhyam sutra, hierarchically composing four 2x2 Vedic multipliers to produce an 8-bit product from two 4-bit inputs. The eight input pins carry the two operands and the eight output pins carry the product. Testing is done with a cocotb testbench run through make in the test directory, which sets inputs and checks outputs with assertions. The documentation is short and gives no silicon test results or hardware requirements beyond simulation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_vedic_4x4.review_notes: Removed alu (multiplier is not an ALU) and education (no teaching intent stated).

ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_example.summary: The documentation describes a PRBS31 generator built from a 31-bit Fibonacci LFSR with feedback from registers 30 and 27, whose output is taken off-chip and fed back for analysis. The pin list matches the Tiny VGA pinout and the design is clocked at 25.175 MHz, but the described PRBS behavior does not match the VGA pin functions. A silicon test report from a tester states that it is a bouncing ball demo that appears to work as intended while the documentation seems unrelated. The mismatch between the documentation and the observed silicon behavior makes the design's actual function unclear.
ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_example.review_notes: Title/description and tester report describe a VGA bouncing ball demo while the documentation describes a PRBS31 LFSR, so the source is contradictory.

ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.summary: This is a standalone VGA demo that renders a Matrix-style digital rain animation using glyphs, with four selectable VGA timing modes and two palette selection pins. It requires the TinyVGA PMOD and a pixel clock near 25.175 MHz for the default mode, with higher resolutions requiring correspondingly higher clocks and mode pin settings. Silicon test reports from both the author and an independent tester confirm that the video modes, color palettes, mode inputs, and reset all work, including 1024x768 at 60 to 70 Hz. The design is notable for being verified across multiple resolutions on real hardware.
ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'text' tag and added 'silicon-tested' to match the working silicon reports.

ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_hello_world.summary: This project drives a VGA monitor to display a Hello World message with changing colors, using the standard Tiny VGA pinout at 25.175 MHz. The only external hardware named is the TinyVGA PMOD, and the design is a single 1x1 tile implemented in Verilog. The documentation is thin, giving just the display purpose and a testing instruction to connect a VGA monitor. No implementation details or silicon test results are provided.
ttsky25a/tt_um_vga_hello_world.review_notes: Removed audio because the pinout and documentation do not define any audio interface; re-added vga/text as supported canonical tags.

ttsky25a/tt_um_virantha_enigma.summary: This is a silicon implementation of an Enigma I cipher machine with a limited three-wire plugboard and a 52-bit key length. It takes 5-bit data and 3-bit command inputs, returns data on the bidirectional pins with a ready signal, and drives the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is needed because it uses the PCB's built-in display. The design is notable for implementing a historical rotor cipher machine in Amaranth on a single tile.

ttsky25a/tt_um_voting_machine.summary: This design implements a 4-bit digital voting machine that records votes for up to four candidates, counts them, and displays the winner in one-hot form along with debug vote totals. Voters select a candidate with a one-hot button and confirm, and a two-bit mode input selects voting, counting, reset, or test behavior. The outputs provide the one-hot winner, a voting-complete flag, and a three-bit debug value equal to the total vote count modulo eight. The documentation is clear about the mode table and testing procedure but reports no silicon test results.

ttsky25a/tt_um_weighted_majority.summary: This project implements a weighted majority voter and trend detector that observes a stream of binary input bits over a configurable sliding window, weighting more recent bits more heavily. The weighted sum is compared against upper and lower thresholds with hysteresis, so the output holds its state between thresholds and only changes on sustained input trends, acting as a debouncer and noise filter. It is fully digital and synchronous, requiring no external hardware beyond an optional LED or logic analyzer on the output, and can be simulated with the provided Verilog testbench or cocotb test. The documentation is detailed but reports no silicon test results.

ttsky25a/tt_um_will_keen_solitaire.summary: This design simulates a peg solitaire board using English rules, accepting the x and y coordinates of a peg to move plus a two-bit direction, and outputting the remaining piece count and a game-over flag. Invalid moves, such as coordinates outside the grid or positions without a peg, leave the board state unchanged. The game is clocked at 1000 Hz and the goal is to reduce the board to a single remaining piece. The documentation describes the starting board layout and testing approach but reports no silicon test results.
ttsky25a/tt_um_will_keen_solitaire.review_notes: Removed education (no teaching intent) and fsm (no state machine described).

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_412635532198550529.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU trainer with an accumulator, four working registers, and an ALU supporting add, subtract, logic, and shift operations. It is controlled by feeding opcodes and immediate data through the ui pins and toggling load and execute inputs, with results shown on a 7-segment display or as binary. The design requires a 10 kHz clock and a 7-segment display for output. Silicon testing confirmed operation from 10 kHz to 50 MHz, though a known bug in the subtract-with-borrow instruction adds the carry flag instead of subtracting it.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_412635532198550529.review_notes: Removed education (no teaching intent stated); added silicon-tested to match the working silicon report.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_414120207283716097.summary: This Wokwi project implements a full adder using three input switches for A, B, and Carry-in. The outputs drive LEDs to show the sum and carry-out. It is an educational example of combinational arithmetic logic. The design is simple and intended for learning digital logic.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_414123795172381697.summary: TinySnake is a simple game where a three-segment snake moves around a 7-segment display, with direction randomized by an LFSR. The speed is set via the ui input pins, and the snake's position is stored in three 3-bit registers. It requires only the on-board 7-segment display and a 10 kHz clock. A limitation is that changing from a slower to a faster speed may cause a delay because the speed comparison uses an equality check rather than greater-than-or-equal.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_414123795172381697.review_notes: Removed game (source describes a display demo, not an interactive game); snake-game retained.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_438920793944579073.summary: This design bundles several digital structures: a 4-bit counter, positive and negative edge trigger circuits, an LFSR for pseudo-random sequences, and multiple pulse counters with trigger circuits. It is tested by connecting external inputs and observing outputs on the uo and uio pins. The documentation is brief and does not specify external hardware requirements beyond basic input/output connections. The project appears to be an educational collection of common digital building blocks.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_440004235377529857.summary: This is a 4-bit adder built from four full adder stages, with the sum latched by D flip-flops on each clock rising edge. The carry-out is not latched and is available directly as an output. It is tested by applying two 4-bit numbers via the ui pins using the dip switch and observing the sum on the uo pins, with a 1 Hz clock. External hardware needed is just LEDs to display the result.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_440004235377529857.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added dip-switch and led interfaces that are explicitly documented.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441378095886546945.summary: This sequential circuit uses D flip-flops to display the name 'Andre' on a 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting the outputs to a common-cathode 7-segment display and providing a 1 Hz clock. The design requires only the 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the internal state machine or character sequence in detail.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441382314812372993.summary: This circuit performs 4-bit addition or subtraction based on a control pin: low for addition, high for subtraction using two's complement. The binary result is output on the uo pins and can be converted to decimal via an external BCD-to-7-segment decoder for display. It is tested by providing two 4-bit numbers and toggling the control pin. The design requires a 7-segment display and decoder for easy reading of the result.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441382314812372993.review_notes: Removed education and bcd tags because the BCD decoder is external and no educational intent is stated.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441564414591667201.summary: This is a parity detector that controls an LED output based on the number of active switch inputs. The documentation describes it as turning off the parity LED when an odd number of switches are on, built from six XOR gates, and tested by toggling the switches. No external hardware beyond the switches and LED is required. The documentation is very brief and does not include a schematic or detailed explanation.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441564414591667201.review_notes: Removed education as unsupported; rewrote the first sentence to avoid a parity ambiguity between the title and the body.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441835796137492481.summary: This design implements an 8-bit binary counter and shift register using D or RS flip-flops, selectable via control inputs. It can operate as a ripple counter or a serial shift register, with outputs shown on LEDs. Testing involves providing a clock, reset, and control signals to select the mode and flip-flop type. External hardware needed is basic LEDs and switches.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_441835796137492481.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the rest of the description matches the source.

ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_442131619043064833.summary: This is a BCD to 7-segment encoder that converts a 4-bit BCD input into segment drive signals for a 7-segment display. It includes additional gates to control the decimal point. The design is tested by applying BCD values to the ui pins and observing the segment outputs on the uo pins. It requires a 7-segment display for visual output.
ttsky25a/tt_um_wokwi_442131619043064833.review_notes: Removed education and incorrect decoder tag; also dropped the unsupported common-cathode claim from the summary.

ttsky25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttsky25a/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttsky25b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This project implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game in Verilog with VGA video output and optional SNES-compatible gamepad input. Players move tiles using the ui_in buttons or a Gamepad Pmod, and the design includes a start animation, two color themes, and a unit test mode with debug pins. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod for display and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. The design is notable for fitting a complete graphical game with input handling and debug support into a 2x2 tile area.
ttsky25b/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag; added button and pmod supported by pins and text.

ttsky25b/tt_um_6502_chip_select.summary: This design is a chip selector for Ben Eater's breadboard 6502 computer. It takes the high address bits and clock, and generates active-low or active-high chip select signals for ROM, RAM, VIA, UART, and SID. It is intended to be used with the actual breadboard computer or with an LED bar graph for testing. The design is a simple combinational decoder with no internal state, and its behavior is documented with a truth table.
ttsky25b/tt_um_6502_chip_select.review_notes: Removed cpu because the project is a chip-select decoder, not a processor core.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.summary: This is a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder implemented in Verilog. It takes two 4-bit operands and a carry input, and produces a 4-bit sum and a carry output. The design is purely combinational and can be used as a building block for larger adders. It was tested on an FPGA, and no external hardware is required.
ttsky25b/tt_um_Electom_cla_4bits.review_notes: Removed alu tag because the design is an adder, not an ALU.

ttsky25b/tt_um_FG_TOP_Dominik_Brandstett.summary: This project implements an 8-bit function generator targeting the AD5330 parallel DAC. It includes a write-only register interface to select a constant signal, a sine wave, or programmable trapezoid/pulse waveforms with adjustable amplitude, offset, phase, and timing. The design is controlled via input pins and provides DAC control signals and 8-bit data outputs. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pin list and a one-line description, so detailed operation and testing are not described.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Jsilicon.summary: Jsilicon is a dual-mode 8-bit CPU/ALU core with manual and automatic (ROM) modes. In manual mode, it acts as an ALU controlled by external opcode and operand inputs, with results shown on output pins and transmitted via UART. In CPU mode, it executes a built-in program from ROM, streaming results to outputs and UART. The design includes a UART transmitter and is intended for educational or embedded use.
ttsky25b/tt_um_Jsilicon.review_notes: Removed fsm as unsupported; the core is a CPU/ALU with ROM program execution.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Lukasseirl.summary: This project is a two-player scoreboard controlled by two pushbuttons. It counts points for each player, with short presses incrementing and long presses decrementing the score. The scores are displayed on two 7-segment displays that alternate between showing 'P1' or 'P2' and the respective score. The design includes debounce logic and was tested with testbenches.
ttsky25b/tt_um_Lukasseirl.review_notes: Removed 'game' tag because the design is a scoreboard accessory, not a game implementation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Max00Ker_Traffic_Light.summary: This is a digital traffic light controller with pedestrian request handling and MAX7219 display interface. It controls car and pedestrian lights with precise timing, button debouncing, and a countdown displayed on LED matrices. The design includes an FSM, clock divider, MAX7219 driver, and SPI master, and was validated in simulation and Wokwi. It requires external LEDs, pushbuttons, and MAX7219 modules.
ttsky25b/tt_um_Max00Ker_Traffic_Light.review_notes: Removed 'industrial' tag because a traffic light controller is not an industrial control application.

ttsky25b/tt_um_MichaelBell_tinyQV.summary: TinyQV is a small RISC-V SoC implementing the RV32EC instruction set with Zcb and Zicond extensions, using QSPI flash for program storage and QSPI PSRAM for data memory. It includes a UART and SPI controller, and is intended to be used with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display and game controller. The QSPI clock and data lines are shared between the flash and the RAM, so only one can be accessed simultaneously. Data can be read from flash and RAM, and written to RAM.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Onchip_BandGap.summary: This is an analog bandgap voltage reference based on a Beta amplifier topology with a folded cascode OTA. It provides a typical output voltage of approximately 1.23 V. The circuit includes a buffer for one output node and requires an external DC voltage source for testing. Silicon measurements showed a Vref of 1.26 V, close to the expected value.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Onchip_VCOx2.summary: This project contains two identical 11-stage ring oscillator voltage-controlled oscillators. Each oscillator uses current-starved inverters controlled by an external voltage and a reset input to start or stop oscillation. Silicon tests showed both oscillators working, starting at around 45 mV input. External hardware includes a voltage source and oscilloscope.

ttsky25b/tt_um_PWM.summary: This design is a PWM generator that produces a pulse-width modulated signal with a duty cycle resolution of 12.5%. It uses a 5-bit counter and a comparator, with the duty cycle selected by a 3-bit speed input. The output frequency is the clock frequency divided by 32. It requires external pull-down resistors, switches, and an oscilloscope for testing.

ttsky25b/tt_um_PseudoSM_ASIC.summary: This project is an 8-bit pseudo-softmax accelerator for neural networks, implementing a reduced softmax activation function. It takes 8-bit data inputs and produces 8-bit outputs, with selection signals for configuration. The design was tested by comparing the post-synthesis netlist with the RTL using random inputs, but no external hardware is required. The documentation notes that behavioral testing is complex due to the nature of softmax inputs.
ttsky25b/tt_um_PseudoSM_ASIC.review_notes: Removed unsupported fpga tag; other tags and summary are supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_Sai222777.summary: This design implements a two-channel XOR stream cipher using programmable Galois LFSRs that can be configured for 32, 16, 8, or 4-bit operation. It provides separate transmit and receive channels, each with enable pins, to encrypt plaintext and decrypt ciphertext bitstreams. A 130-bit serial shift register allows dynamic loading of the LFSR configuration at runtime, with read-back capability for verification. The design includes debug outputs and heartbeat signals.
ttsky25b/tt_um_Sai222777.review_notes: Removed shift-register tag (only a config mechanism) and dropped the unsupported educational/experimental intent claim from the summary.

ttsky25b/tt_um_TinyWhisper.summary: Tiny Whisper is a mixed-signal chip that implements a transmitter for the WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter) protocol in the 3-30 MHz shortwave band. It integrates a digital core containing a CORDIC, a delta-sigma modulator, and local oscillator generation, along with an analog IQ modulator. The design requires external hardware such as an SPI master, UART-to-USB breakout board, and an RF power amplifier with filters and antenna for testing. Documentation is currently incomplete, with references to an external GitHub repository for details.

ttsky25b/tt_um_VHDL_FSM.summary: This project implements a Moore finite state machine for a vending machine controller, handling coin insertion, product selection, and change dispensing. It uses a small datapath for credit tracking and selection, with debounced inputs for coin and buttons. Outputs include dispense and change signals, along with a 4-bit product number, intended to drive LEDs. The design is a simple educational example of an FSM with spaced pulse outputs.
ttsky25b/tt_um_VHDL_FSM.review_notes: Removed debouncer (not implemented in design) and added education.

ttsky25b/tt_um_VHDL_PWM_DEMUX.summary: This design is a 10-bit PWM generator with a configuration demultiplexer and double-buffering mechanism. It uses three shadow registers for set, clear, and reload values, which are written via a shared bus and committed simultaneously to update the PWM output. The PWM frequency and duty cycle are determined by the reload, set, and clear values, allowing flexible waveform generation. The design includes reset gating and is intended for applications requiring precise PWM control.
ttsky25b/tt_um_VHDL_PWM_DEMUX.review_notes: Removed decoder tag; the demux is register write selection, not decoding.

ttsky25b/tt_um_ag2048_tiny_calculator.summary: Tiny Calculator is a calculator chip with built-in I/O drivers, implemented in SystemVerilog. It provides arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and supports input from buttons and output via serial and control signals. The pin names indicate connections for a keypad and a seven-segment or LCD display. Documentation is minimal, so the exact usage and external hardware requirements are not fully described.
ttsky25b/tt_um_ag2048_tiny_calculator.review_notes: Removed unsupported keypad/display interface tags and added button and 7-segment based on pin evidence.

ttsky25b/tt_um_alexlowl_myTTproject.summary: This project implements a Knight Rider-style LED chaser with PWM brightness control, where the speed and pause functionality are adjustable via three debounced buttons. It drives an 8-LED bargraph or individual LEDs, with outputs cycling in a chasing pattern. The design includes debouncing for the pause, faster, and slower buttons, and operates from a 50 kHz clock. External hardware includes push buttons, a reset button, and a bargraph or 8 LEDs.

ttsky25b/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.summary: This project implements three current-switching DACs for generating analog VGA display signals, using a 16x16 matrix of unit current sources to convert 8-bit digital inputs to analog current sinks. It includes a digital controller that generates VGA control signals and test patterns, and supports both digital RGB222 output via the TinyVGA PMOD and analog outputs requiring external pull-up resistors and opamp circuits. The design is an experiment in analog VGA signal generation, with documentation referencing a previous version for test modes. External hardware includes a VGA display, optional PMOD, and opamp circuits for current-to-voltage conversion.
ttsky25b/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag and added mixed-signal and pmod based on the documented analog/digital mix and PMOD usage.

ttsky25b/tt_um_arko.summary: The project titled 'Arko' has no meaningful documentation; the description and test instructions are placeholder text. The pin names are generic (in0-in7, io0-io7, out0-out7), suggesting a simple I/O design, but the actual functionality is unknown. No external hardware or testing details are provided. The design cannot be evaluated due to insufficient information.
ttsky25b/tt_um_arko.review_notes: Removed unsupported placeholder and gpio tags; kept insufficient-doc and verilog.

ttsky25b/tt_um_attention_top.summary: This design implements a transformer attention engine that computes a dot product over four terms from sequential 8-bit Q0.7 samples and outputs exp(mac/2) in UQ3.6 format. It uses a credit-based handshake interface for input and output, processing four pairs of samples to produce a 9-bit result. The module is always ready for input and signals output validity, requiring acknowledgment from the master. It is intended for neural network or machine learning acceleration, though external hardware details are not specified.
ttsky25b/tt_um_attention_top.review_notes: Removed pipeline (no pipelined datapath described); added dsp and fixed-point.

ttsky25b/tt_um_axc1271_tinypong.summary: Tiny Pong is a VGA display driver for a single-player Pong game, designed to output 640x480 video with 2-bit color per channel. It uses two buttons for paddle up and down control, and generates VGA HSYNC, VSYNC, and RGB signals. The chip is intended as a demo project for the Hacker Fab club at Case Western Reserve University, requiring a VGA monitor and a way to program the chip. The design is a fun and educational example of a simple game on an ASIC.
ttsky25b/tt_um_axc1271_tinypong.review_notes: Removed generic 'display' tag; added 'education' since the source explicitly frames it as a club demo/learning project.

ttsky25b/tt_um_b2nch_DreiMann_top.summary: DreiMann implements a dice-based party game where two button presses simulate rolling two dice and the result is shown on a seven-segment display. The display encodes doubles as the number 1-6, a 1-and-2 combination as all segments lit, a single 3 as the three horizontal lines, and any other combination as the middle line only. It needs two push buttons on inputs 0 and 1, an optional switch on input 2 to select common anode or common cathode, and a seven-segment display wired to the eight outputs. The design is a straightforward Verilog game with no reported silicon results and is intended to be played socially rather than tested automatically.

ttsky25b/tt_um_baud_rate_cdr.summary: This design is a baud-rate clock and data recovery circuit for PAM4 signals, using a Mueller-Muller phase detector, a proportional-integral loop filter, and a digitally controlled oscillator. It accepts an 8-bit data input and produces recovered sample outputs X[4:7], status bits S[0:2], and a Sample_en strobe on the outputs. The documentation consists only of the title, pin names, and a one-line description, so the exact interface timing and configuration are not explained. No test procedure, external hardware, or silicon results are given, leaving the design's operation largely inferred from the pin names.
ttsky25b/tt_um_baud_rate_cdr.review_notes: Removed dsp: the CDR is link communication circuitry, not signal-processing design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bleeptrack_nn1.summary: Negative Nature #1 is a generative Voronoi pattern placed on the met4 layer as silicon artwork rather than a functional circuit. It has a single dummy output pin and no inputs, and the documentation states that it is meant only to be looked at. No external hardware is required and there is no test procedure beyond visual inspection. The project is notable as a decorative layout experiment rather than a logic design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bleeptrack_nn2.summary: Negative Nature #2 is a generative Voronoi pattern placed on the met4 layer as silicon artwork rather than a functional circuit. It has a single dummy output pin and no inputs, and the documentation states that it is meant only to be looked at. No external hardware is required and there is no test procedure beyond visual inspection. The project is notable as a decorative layout experiment rather than a logic design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bleeptrack_nn3.summary: Negative Nature #3 is a generative Voronoi pattern placed on the met4 layer as silicon artwork rather than a functional circuit. It has a single dummy output pin and no inputs, and the documentation states that it is meant only to be looked at. No external hardware is required and there is no test procedure beyond visual inspection. The project is notable as a decorative layout experiment rather than a logic design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bleeptrack_nn4.summary: Negative Nature #4 is a generative Voronoi pattern placed on the met4 layer as silicon artwork rather than a functional circuit. It has a single dummy output pin and no inputs, and the documentation states that it is meant only to be looked at. No external hardware is required and there is no test procedure beyond visual inspection. The project is notable as a decorative layout experiment rather than a logic design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bmellor_lightsout.summary: Lights-Out is a puzzle game implemented with a 3x3 multiplexed LED matrix and three row buttons. The design drives three LED row outputs, three column outputs, and a DONE signal, while reading three button inputs for the rows. It requires an external breakout board, for which the repository link is provided, to connect the LEDs and buttons. The documentation is brief and gives no test results or detailed gameplay description beyond the title and pin names.

ttsky25b/tt_um_bouncing_squares.summary: Bouncing squares renders five moving squares as a screensaver-style animation on a VGA output. It uses the standard Tiny VGA pinout with two bits each for red, green, and blue plus horizontal and vertical sync, and runs from a 25.175 MHz pixel clock. The only external hardware needed is an older VGA monitor, and testing consists of plugging the board into a VGA port. The documentation is minimal, describing the design only as a screensaver with five squares.

ttsky25b/tt_um_brainfck_asic.summary: The Brainf*ck ASIC is a hardware interpreter for the Brainf*ck language that stores its tape in external SPI RAM and communicates with a host over a two-wire serial link. It accepts encoded instruction bits and validity on its inputs, drives SPI chip select, MOSI, MISO, and clock on the bidirectional pins, and exposes transmit, interrupt, and inspection signals on the outputs. Testing requires the Tiny Tapeout I/O board with an RP2040 or RP2350 running SPI RAM emulation firmware, plus a protoboard and wiring, and programs are converted from Brainf*ck source with a provided Python script. The design is notable for offloading bracket handling to an interrupt-driven MCU collaboration and for using external memory rather than on-chip storage.

ttsky25b/tt_um_camdenmil_sky25b.summary: OctoPWM is an eight-channel PWM driver controlled over SPI, with each channel having a 10-bit compare threshold and a shared configurable clock divider. It accepts 16-bit SPI transactions with a write address and value, uses active-low chip select and enable pins, and outputs eight PWM signals plus a divided clock output. The design targets a 10 MHz clock, matches the Tiny Tapeout audio pinout, and needs no external hardware beyond the SPI host. The author notes it was made in one night with no prior HDL experience and that the testbench is lacking, so correct operation is hoped for rather than fully verified.

ttsky25b/tt_um_cejmu_wspr.summary: This design encodes amateur radio WSPR messages from a callsign, locator and power level into 162 symbols and generates corresponding sine and cosine PWM outputs for 4-FSK transmission. It is configured over a 115200 baud UART using a provided Python script, and a start_transmission input triggers the symbol sequence. The PWM outputs require external low-pass filtering, and the I/Q signals are intended to work with the TinyWhisper analog project on the same shuttle. Silicon testing confirmed that UART configuration and transmission start work and that 25% duty cycle local oscillator and PWM data appear on the outputs, though the RF output itself was not validated.
ttsky25b/tt_um_cejmu_wspr.review_notes: Removed unsupported cordic tag and added rf, which is clearly supported by the WSPR radio transmission purpose.

ttsky25b/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttsky25b/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttsky25b/tt_um_chrimenz_tinyturing.summary: This project implements a Turing machine with a configurable state transition table on a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It supports manual and automatic modes, tape initialization, wrap and loop options, and bank selection, with status and tape contents shown on external LED and 7-segment displays. Control is via DIP switches and pushbuttons for clock and reset, allowing step-by-step configuration and execution. The design requires external LED PMODs, a 7-segment display, and switches for full use.
ttsky25b/tt_um_chrimenz_tinyturing.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

ttsky25b/tt_um_classic_vga_clock.summary: This design renders an analog-style clock on a VGA monitor, using a CORDIC algorithm to compute hand angles and pixel positions. It includes an alarm function that compares a set alarm time to the current time and outputs a 3.15 kHz square wave pulsed at 1 Hz for a buzzer. Time and alarm settings are adjusted via five external pushbuttons, and the VGA output follows the standard Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD pinout. The design requires a 31.5 MHz clock and external pushbuttons with pulldown resistors, and the alarm output needs an external driver for a buzzer.
ttsky25b/tt_um_classic_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed 'clock-generator' (misleading for a timepiece) and added 'rtc' for the real-time clock function.

ttsky25b/tt_um_counter_isaharp.summary: This is a 4-bit saturating counter with a seven-segment display output, written in VHDL. The counting direction is controlled by input pin 0, and the counter saturates at 15 when counting up and at 0 when counting down. The seven-segment output is active-low with the decimal point as the most significant bit. Testing requires an external clock and a seven-segment display; no other external hardware is specified.

ttsky25b/tt_um_cpu_fabianp1704.summary: This project implements a minimal 8-bit CPU with a simple datapath and two finite-state machines. It accepts serial input data through the ui_in pins and provides an 8-bit output along with carry, zero, overflow, and negative flags. A start signal triggers serial input, and multiplexer select lines control internal routing. No external hardware is required for operation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_cpu_fabianp1704.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed beyond confirming the CPU/FSM/Verilog tags.

ttsky25b/tt_um_devmonk_ay8913.summary: This Verilog implementation is a replica of the classic AY-3-8913 programmable sound generator, a 3-voice PSG chip from General Instrument. It provides three square-wave tone generators, a white noise generator using a 17-bit LFSR, an envelope generator with 10 shapes, and 16 volume levels, controlled through 14 registers. The design outputs digital 8-bit audio and a PWM pseudo-analog audio signal, and can be configured with an external clock divider. It is intended for hardware preservation and educational purposes, with a test suite for regression testing against the original chip behavior.
ttsky25b/tt_um_devmonk_ay8913.review_notes: Replaced incorrect neural-network/machine-learning/decoder tags with sound-generator, music, audio, pwm, lfsr, verilog, retro, and dac based on the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_df_top.summary: This design is a third-order digital FIR filter with an 8-bit architecture, configurable cutoff frequency, and selectable low-pass or high-pass behavior. It accepts 8-bit data input and provides 8-bit filtered output, with configuration pins for weight selection, filter type, and enable. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pinout and a one-line description, so details of the filter coefficients and testing procedure are not available.

ttsky25b/tt_um_dip_switch_game_TobiasPfa.summary: This is a logic game where the player must convert a decimal number shown on a seven-segment display into its binary equivalent using eight DIP switches before a timer expires. The design uses a 1 kHz clock and provides seven-segment display outputs for the decimal number and game status. Input is via the eight DIP switches, and the game logic includes a timer to create pressure. No external hardware beyond the DIP switches and a seven-segment display is required.

ttsky25b/tt_um_dlmiles_dffram32x8_2r1w.summary: This project implements a 32x8 dual-port-read single-port-write RAM using D-type flip-flops, described by the author as a 'really bad implementation' due to its inefficiency. The RAM has two read ports (A and B) and one write port (A), with configurable features such as read buffering, write-through policy, and page selection via configuration bits latched on reset release. It is intended to be tested with standard Tiny Tapeout hardware and an RP2040, and a MicroPython interface is planned. The design is notable for its use of flip-flops instead of dedicated RAM blocks and its flexible read/write policies.
ttsky25b/tt_um_dlmiles_dffram32x8_2r1w.review_notes: Removed register-file (it is a RAM array, not a register file) and added sram as the canonical memory-block tag.

ttsky25b/tt_um_dumb_turing_yliu_hashed.summary: This design implements a Turing machine in Turing's original mathematical construction, using external SPI ROM and RAM for the transition table and tape. It supports 128 states and an alphabet size of 256, with separate SPI interfaces for state and tape memory. The design is difficult to test because it requires preloading the external memory devices with data before execution. It requires one 512Kbit ROM and one 512Kbit RAM, and the ROM can be emulated by the on-board RP2040.
ttsky25b/tt_um_dumb_turing_yliu_hashed.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'fsm' tag; added 'rp2040' and 'pmod' from the documented external hardware and detected pinout.

ttsky25b/tt_um_dyno.summary: This is a test project synthesized with Dyno-SV, a new open-source synthesis tool, to gate level using the SkyWater 130nm standard cell library. The design finds the indices of the first, second, and third set bits in an 8-bit input word and outputs their positions along with valid flags. It also includes a counter and configuration bits to select registered or combinational input and output paths. The project serves as a validation of the Dyno-SV synthesis flow and requires no external hardware.

ttsky25b/tt_um_eestevez3_SAR_ADC.summary: This project implements an 8-bit successive-approximation-register (SAR) ADC in an analog process, converting an analog input voltage to an 8-bit digital output. It includes a sample-and-hold circuit, a comparator, and a digital SAR logic block, with enable and calibration inputs for the comparator. The design currently lacks full rail-to-rail detection without precise timing and accurately converts only above approximately 0.8V; it requires two clock signals, one for the digital logic and a slower one for sampling. External hardware such as a signal generator and oscilloscope is needed for testing.
ttsky25b/tt_um_eestevez3_SAR_ADC.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal because the source does not explicitly claim a mixed analog/digital design; added comparator-analog for the described analog comparator.

ttsky25b/tt_um_emilian_opamp_3v3.summary: This analog design combines a simple opamp powered at 3.3V with a DRAM cell and an 8-bit R2R DAC. The opamp inputs are shared with the DRAM bit lines, and digital control pins select write and read operations. The 3.3V output is achieved with level shifting drivers, and the design is intended to be tested by measuring the output voltage on analog pin 0 with a multimeter. The documentation is brief and does not explain the DRAM cell operation or the exact role of the bias control pins.
ttsky25b/tt_um_emilian_opamp_3v3.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and instrumentation tags; added mixed-signal for the analog/digital combination.

ttsky25b/tt_um_endecoder_workfefra.summary: The EnDecoder encrypts or decrypts a 4-bit code using a 4-bit key, with the mode selected by an input pin. A done output pulses when the operation completes, and the result appears on a 4-bit output. Testing involves feeding a code and key in encrypt mode, then feeding the result back in decrypt mode to recover the original code. No external hardware is required, but the documentation does not specify the encryption algorithm.
ttsky25b/tt_um_endecoder_workfefra.review_notes: Removed fsm tag not supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_enjimneering_tts_top.summary: TinyTapeStation is a retro gaming console that plays a single pre-loaded game called Gnome Knight, controlled with an NES or SNES gamepad. It outputs 640x480 VGA video and analog audio, and supports standard retro controller layouts with simple remapping. The design requires a gamepad PMOD or direct NES controller wiring, a VGA monitor, and speakers or an amplifier. A silicon test report notes that the game starts up and characters move, though the tester did not have a SNES controller.
ttsky25b/tt_um_enjimneering_tts_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported pwm tag and added silicon-tested and sound-generator based on the documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_essen.summary: This project implements the Blake2s hashing algorithm in Verilog with C firmware support, including secret key support and block streaming. It exposes an 8-bit data input, command and valid handshake signals, and an 8-bit hash output with a valid flag. The documentation is essentially absent beyond the pin names and one-line description, so the exact usage and testing procedure are unclear. The design is notable for being a hardware implementation of a modern cryptographic hash.

ttsky25b/tt_um_evm.summary: The Electronic Voting Machine counts votes for three candidates, with each candidate having a dedicated input button. When the vote_over signal is asserted, voting stops and the results for all three candidates are output as 6-bit binary values. A reset signal clears all counts for a new session. The design is tested with a testbench that simulates button presses and dumps waveforms, but no external hardware is specified.
ttsky25b/tt_um_evm.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag and added button interface based on documented candidate buttons.

ttsky25b/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttsky25b/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttsky25b/tt_um_felixzhou_spi_slave_ctrl.summary: This is a simple SPI slave controller for reading and writing internal registers. It uses standard SPI signals (NCS, CLK, MOSI, MISO) and also provides a FIFO output serial line. The system clock must be at least four times faster than the SPI clock. Testing requires an external SPI controller connected to the SPI pins, and the documentation includes timing diagrams for read and write transactions.

ttsky25b/tt_um_femto.summary: This is a femtoRV RISC-V implementation that uses external SPI flash and SPI RAM for program and data storage. It provides UART communication for debug messages and an LED output. To use it, an external flash memory must be programmed with the desired application, and a USB-serial dongle is needed for communication. The design is notable for being a compact RISC-V core on a tiny tapeout tile.
ttsky25b/tt_um_femto.review_notes: Source is sparse and contains typos; 'fpga' added cautiously as the femtoRV core is an FPGA-origin design, but the documentation does not explicitly state an FPGA port.

ttsky25b/tt_um_fkd_xorshift.summary: This is an 8-bit VHDL implementation of the XORShift random number generator, based on Tzarc's algorithm. It uses the previous output and a counter of generated numbers to produce a new 8-bit output. Testing involves comparing the output with a known-good software implementation by manually clocking the circuit. The design is a straightforward PRNG with no external hardware requirements.

ttsky25b/tt_um_flappy_vga_cutout1.summary: This project is a clone of the Flappy Bird game, rendered on a 640x480 VGA display with a single button input for flapping. The game state is updated each frame, and the score is output in binary on the bidirectional pins. It requires a 25 MHz clock, a debounced active-low button, and a VGA adapter compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. Multiple silicon test reports confirm that the design works and is playable, though several testers found it challenging.

ttsky25b/tt_um_four_bit_cpu_top_level.summary: This is a small custom 4-bit CPU with 16 instructions and 16x4-bit storage. It includes a RX pin, four input pins, four output pins, instruction register outputs, and state signals for program, fetch, decode, and execute phases. The documentation is extremely thin, consisting only of placeholder text like 'TESTETSet' and 'TESTSEt', so the operation and testing procedure cannot be determined. External hardware is mentioned but not specified.
ttsky25b/tt_um_four_bit_cpu_top_level.review_notes: Removed fsm tag not clearly evidenced, added insufficient-doc, and kept the CPU vs risc-v distinction since no RISC-V claim is made.

ttsky25b/tt_um_hammal_fir_filter.summary: This is a 5-tap FIR filter implemented in VHDL that computes a filtered output from the last five input samples. Filter coefficients can be loaded serially over five clock cycles and updated with a load signal. The design requires no external hardware and is tested by feeding coefficients and then applying input samples while observing the filtered output. The documentation provides a clear explanation of the filter operation and testing method.

ttsky25b/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.summary: Asicle v2 is a hardware implementation of the Wordle word-guessing game, rewritten for Tiny Tapeout after an earlier version on the Google-Skywater shuttle. It uses a QSPI Pmod for external flash to store the word list and font bitmaps, a Tiny VGA Pmod for video output, and a Gamepad Pmod or direct input pins for controls. The design runs at 25.175 MHz and requires flashing a data file to the QSPI Pmod before play. It fits a complete game into a 2x2 tile area by moving data off-chip, and includes debug features for showing or re-rolling the solution.
ttsky25b/tt_um_htfab_asicle2.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag; added retro for the Wordle-style game; trimmed unsupported 'notable' claim.

ttsky25b/tt_um_ieeeuoftasic_simproc.summary: SimProc is an 8-bit processor that can be programmed and read back via UART using 3-byte packets. It has a UART receive input, a UART transmit output, and flags for halt and done. The baud rate is set by driving the bidirectional pins UIO7-UIO0. External hardware needed is a USB-to-UART converter or any UART device.
ttsky25b/tt_um_ieeeuoftasic_simproc.review_notes: Added microcontroller tag for the programmable 8-bit processor with UART and memory.

ttsky25b/tt_um_instrumented_ring_oscilla.summary: This project is an instrumented ring oscillator with a selectable number of stages and a configurable initial state, intended for studying high-frequency modes rather than as a reliable clock source. It provides 16 phase outputs and uses a shift-register-like interface to seed the oscillator state. The design is controlled via input pins for enable, hold, stage selection, and seed data. Silicon tests confirmed functionality, though the slowest configuration runs near 50 MHz, requiring a spectrum analyzer and H-field probe for verification.
ttsky25b/tt_um_instrumented_ring_oscilla.review_notes: Removed unsupported phase-detector and prng tags; added silicon-tested and instrumentation based on source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_jakedrew_qei.summary: The QEI (Quadrature Encoder Interface) decodes A/B quadrature signals into a 15-bit up/down count and a direction flag. It synchronizes the inputs to the clock and outputs the count across the output and bidirectional pins. The design can be tested with an encoder connected directly for single-ended signals or via an RS-422 receiver for differential signals. It is a compact, straightforward implementation with clear documentation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_jakedrew_qei.review_notes: Removed 'encoder' tag as the design only decodes quadrature signals.

ttsky25b/tt_um_julke_gussinatorn2.summary: JulkeGussinatorn 2.0 is a Morse code entry and encryption/decryption device implemented in VHDL. Users input short and long Morse signals via buttons, lock in letters, and can encrypt or decrypt the stored message. An LED output displays the Morse code saved on the device. The documentation is minimal and the description is terse, but the basic functionality is clear from the pin names and text.
ttsky25b/tt_um_julke_gussinatorn2.review_notes: Removed text (LED Morse output is not textual display); added button for the six pushbutton inputs.

ttsky25b/tt_um_kercrafter_leds_racer.summary: LEDs Racer is a multiplayer game where up to four players press arcade buttons to race their LED segment toward a center circle on a WS2812B LED ring. The design drives the LED data line and provides per-player ready-to-play indicators and a frame update signal. It requires external arcade buttons with pull-down resistors and a WS2812B LED ring. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the game and its hardware needs.

ttsky25b/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.summary: This is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA SoC capable of booting Linux, featuring external SPI flash and PSRAM, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. It is tested by building a system image and loading it into the SPI flash, then running at 30 MHz (max tested 34.5 MHz). External hardware includes a QSPI Pmod for flash and PSRAM, plus UART over the demo board USB. It is a full Linux-capable SoC implemented in Verilog on a 8x2 tile Tiny Tapeout chip.
ttsky25b/tt_um_kianV_rv32ima_uLinux_SoC.review_notes: Removed redundant microcontroller tag and corrected the summary to avoid implying built-in flash or an onboard UART bridge.

ttsky25b/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.summary: This project is a baremetal RISC-V RV32E SoC based on the KianV architecture. It includes a UART, QSPI memory controller for flash and PSRAM, a generic SPI interface, and a sigma-delta emulator for audio playback. The CPU starts executing instructions from NOR flash at a 1 MiB offset. The design requires a PMOD flash and PSRAM module for operation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_kianv_bare_metal.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the RISC-V SoC with UART, SPI, QSPI, and audio.

ttsky25b/tt_um_kianv_rv32_regfile.summary: KianV uLinux RISC-V regfile edition is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA processor capable of booting Linux, featuring a 32x32 register file macro. It includes external SPI flash and PSRAM interfaces, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. The system runs at 30 MHz and requires a QSPI Pmod for external memory. Silicon tests showed partial functionality: it could not boot Linux due to an impedance mismatch when integrating the register file, though the register file itself works.
ttsky25b/tt_um_kianv_rv32_regfile.review_notes: Removed memory tag because memory is external; added silicon-tested, qspi, and pmod based on silicon reports and external hardware.

ttsky25b/tt_um_libokuohai_asap_cpu_v1.summary: ASAP CPU v1 is a minimal SAP-1 inspired CPU with an 8-bit data path and 4-bit address space, running a built-in Fibonacci program. It outputs the current value in BCD to a multiplexed 7-segment display and provides a heartbeat signal. The design requires three common-cathode 7-segment displays and current-limiting resistors. It is an educational project influenced by Ben Eater and others, with clear documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_lime_cic_filter.summary: lime_cic_filter implements first-order and second-order Cascaded Integrator-Comb (CIC) filters for processing sigma-delta modulator bitstreams. It provides 16-bit output and includes debug selection inputs. The design requires no external hardware and is intended for digital signal processing applications. The documentation is partly AI-generated and lacks a detailed test plan, but the core functionality is described.
ttsky25b/tt_um_lime_cic_filter.review_notes: Removed fir-filter because the design is a CIC filter, not FIR; added filter-analog as the closest canonical filter tag and systemverilog for the language.

ttsky25b/tt_um_lukasdragoste_vga_pattern.summary: VGA Pattern Generator produces colorful geometric patterns on a VGA monitor at 640x480 @ 60 Hz. It uses a 25 MHz pixel clock and generates patterns procedurally from pixel coordinates, with input switches selecting between modes and palettes. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD adapter and a VGA monitor. Silicon tests confirmed working patterns that change with input toggles.
ttsky25b/tt_um_lukasdragoste_vga_pattern.review_notes: Added 'silicon-tested' to match the provided silicon test reports.

ttsky25b/tt_um_markr_transientshaper.summary: This design implements a real-time audio transient shaper that independently controls the attack and sustain portions of an audio signal using dual envelope followers. It processes 6-bit digital audio input and produces 8-bit digital audio output, with control pins for attack and sustain amounts. The design operates entirely in the digital domain and requires external ADCs, DACs, and analog filters for practical audio use. It is a compact DSP block for audio effects, notable for its envelope modulation technique.
ttsky25b/tt_um_markr_transientshaper.review_notes: Removed DAC/ADC/signal-generator/filter-analog tags because those functions are only external supporting hardware, not implemented on chip.

ttsky25b/tt_um_mastermind.summary: This project recreates the classic Mastermind game where players guess a secret combination of colors. It uses a random number generator to set the secret code and compares guesses to provide feedback on correct and half-correct positions. The game supports up to 16 turns and outputs hints via pins intended for seven-segment displays. It is a VHDL implementation of a puzzle game, best experienced with external displays.
ttsky25b/tt_um_mastermind.review_notes: Removed unsupported button/led/fsm tags and added dip-switch for the switch-based guess inputs.

ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.summary: This analog design contains two ring oscillators, one built from 18 inverters and a NAND enable gate targeting roughly 600 MHz, and one from 36 inverters targeting roughly 300 MHz, each followed by a two-stage driver to drive the analog pads. Ring 1 is enabled via ui[0] and observed on uo[0], while ring 2 is enabled via ui[1] and observed on uo[1]. Testing requires an oscilloscope to measure the attenuated analog output, and the documentation notes that the 300 MHz oscillator had a missing contact in TT08 and was fixed for TT09. The design is notable for being a transistor-level analog oscillator experiment with known silicon issues.
ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_analog_ring_osc.review_notes: Removed incorrect clock-generator tag and added silicon-tested tag per documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.summary: This design is an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter (DAC) with a 3.3V output, driven either externally or by an internal sine waveform generator. Silicon tests confirm a smooth sine wave over the full 3.3V range, with a slight nonlinearity at the mid-code transition. It requires an external multimeter to measure the output voltage. The design uses level shifting drivers to achieve the 3.3V output.
ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.review_notes: Removed transistor-level, which is not supported by the R2R ladder description; silicon-tested was already correctly applied.

ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_relax_osc.summary: This is an analog relaxation oscillator designed to produce a ~2 MHz signal, with an inverter providing a full-swing square wave output. The analog output is on one pin and the digital square wave on another. Silicon tests show it oscillates at around 1 MHz, but the frequency is highly sensitive to loading on the analog pin, and a 10k pulldown must be removed for oscillation. The author notes that loading the analog output can stop oscillation due to the lack of a buffer.
ttsky25b/tt_um_mattvenn_relax_osc.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added silicon-tested per the working test report.

ttsky25b/tt_um_morse.summary: This design implements a Morse code transmitter and receiver using two finite state machines to encode and decode Morse sequences for alphabets and digits. It accepts button inputs for dots, dashes, and spaces, and outputs decoded ASCII characters. The design is intended for testing with an FPGA board and a 16x2 LCD for display. It is a straightforward educational project for learning Morse code and FSM design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_morse.review_notes: Removed lcd tag since the LCD is external test hardware, not an implemented interface; added fpga tag for the listed FPGA board.

ttsky25b/tt_um_morse_it.summary: This project translates Morse code input from push buttons into ASCII characters. It provides an 8-bit ASCII output on pins uo[0] through uo[7], which can be shown on LEDs. A button supplies the input, and the documentation is minimal. It leaves the implementation and testing details largely undescribed.
ttsky25b/tt_um_morse_it.review_notes: Thin documentation; communication and fsm tags unsupported, and LED is external rather than a dedicated LED output.

ttsky25b/tt_um_morse_w_serial.summary: This design is a Morse code transmitter and receiver with an additional serial receive input, implemented with two finite state machines. It encodes button inputs into Morse and decodes Morse sequences into ASCII characters. The design is intended for use with an FPGA board and a 16x2 LCD for output display. It is similar to a previous project but includes a serial RX pin for external Morse input.
ttsky25b/tt_um_morse_w_serial.review_notes: Removed lcd and uart tags; LCD is only external hardware and RX_CW is not a UART.

ttsky25b/tt_um_mosbius.summary: This project implements a mini MOSbius analog chip in a 3x2 Tiny Tapeout slot. It contains programmable NMOS and PMOS transistors, differential pairs, OTAs, and current sources. Six buses with transmission gates allow interconnection of the blocks, programmed by a shift register. Silicon tests confirmed working inverter, differential amplifier, ring oscillator, and current source configurations.
ttsky25b/tt_um_mosbius.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the analog MOSbius design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_nco.summary: This numerically controlled oscillator generates various waveforms including sine, cosine, triangular, square, and specialized shapes like Gaussian chirplet and ECG. It uses a phase accumulator and waveform lookup ROM to produce an 8-bit digital output, which can be converted to analog via an external R-2R ladder DAC. The design is tested in simulation or on hardware with an oscilloscope to observe the generated waveforms. It is a versatile DDS core for signal generation applications.
ttsky25b/tt_um_nco.review_notes: Removed dac tag; the DAC is external hardware, not implemented on-chip.

ttsky25b/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This design is a stylish ring oscillator built from 21 SkullFET inverters, generating a square wave with a simulated frequency of about 169.2 MHz. It is tested by connecting an oscilloscope to one of the divided outputs, as the full-speed outputs are too fast for GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond an oscilloscope. Notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and the inclusion of frequency dividers for observability.
ttsky25b/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Removed the overbroad clock-generator tag; simulation frequency kept as stated in the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_pantelis300_nco.summary: This project implements a numerically controlled oscillator with linear-interpolated sine output. It uses an 8-bit frequency control input and produces an 8-bit DAC output, with a 16-bit phase accumulator and sine ROM with interpolation. The design is a basic block for direct digital synthesis and requires an external 8-bit DAC and oscilloscope for testing. It is a compact and efficient NCO suitable for generating sine waves with controlled frequency.

ttsky25b/tt_um_patrick_lin_git_mcht_trx.summary: This chip performs Manchester encoding and decoding, converting between parallel 8-bit data and serial bitstreams. It includes a built-in 5x PLL and supports bidirectional operation controlled by a direction pin, with additional features like BIST mode and debug outputs. The design requires two clock inputs (25MHz and 100MHz) and uses bidirectional pins for data. Silicon testing confirmed functionality, with successful loopback tests using an external CPLD.
ttsky25b/tt_um_patrick_lin_git_mcht_trx.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart and clock-generator tags; added pll, bist, systemverilog, silicon-tested.

ttsky25b/tt_um_pommarkus_i2c_slave.summary: This project is a write-only I2C slave with address 0x8E, featuring three control registers and eight data registers. It supports direct passthrough mode and a stepper mode that sequentially activates outputs based on a programmable counter. The design requires an external I2C master, switches for inputs, and LEDs or a seven-segment display for outputs. It is a configurable I2C peripheral for controlling external devices.
ttsky25b/tt_um_pommarkus_i2c_slave.review_notes: Removed unsupported SPI, stepper-motor, button, and 7-segment tags; added gpio and sequencer to match the documented passthrough and stepper behavior.

ttsky25b/tt_um_pongsagon_tinygpu_v2.summary: This design is a standalone GPU that performs transformation, lighting, and rasterization to render 3D models from QSPI flash memory. It outputs VGA signals with 4-bit color and supports double buffering and z-buffering, achieving 6.5 fps for 1K triangles at 320x240 resolution. It interfaces with a gamepad for interactive control and uses QSPI RAM for frame buffers. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected, making it a notable compact 3D graphics accelerator.

ttsky25b/tt_um_project.summary: This project is a silicon design evolution experiment that gradually modifies the Tiny Tapeout template to perform more tasks. It uses an 8-bit input bus and an 8-bit output bus, with no external hardware required. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it is a gradual evolution and that testing methods are yet to be determined. There is no clear description of the specific functions or tasks implemented.

ttsky25b/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.summary: This design implements a bytebeat formula in hardware, generating 8-bit PCM audio samples from four 4-bit parameters. It accepts parameters via input and bidirectional pins and outputs the PCM sample on the output pins. The design is written in XLS and can be easily modified to change the formula. It requires an external 8-bit parallel DAC to convert the digital samples to analog audio.
ttsky25b/tt_um_proppy_bytebeat.review_notes: Removed unsupported pipeline tag; added insufficient-doc because documentation is very thin despite the formula being present.

ttsky25b/tt_um_proppy_megabytebeat.summary: This project is a compilation of bytebeat formulas that generate PWM audio signals on multiple output pins. It takes four 4-bit parameters and produces different bytebeat tunes on pins 0, 3, and 7, with other pins unused. The design is written in XLS and can be regenerated with modified formulas. It requires external rotary switches for parameter adjustment and speakers or a TinyTapeout Audio PMOD to hear the output.
ttsky25b/tt_um_proppy_megabytebeat.review_notes: Removed pipeline as unsupported; the design is a bytebeat PWM audio generator.

ttsky25b/tt_um_pwm_led_top.summary: This design uses two buttons to adjust the brightness of an LED dot on a 7-segment display. The current brightness level is shown as a number on the display. It requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout board's built-in buttons and display. The project is a simple demonstration of PWM-based LED dimming with user input.
ttsky25b/tt_um_pwm_led_top.review_notes: Removed counter as unsupported; the design is a button-controlled PWM LED dimmer.

ttsky25b/tt_um_quick_cpu.summary: This is a simple 8-bit CPU inspired by Ben Eater's design and the game Turing Complete, created in a four-hour sprint before the submission deadline. It has an 8-bit input bus and an 8-bit output bus, with no bidirectional pins used. Testing requires an RP2040 or RP2350 on a test board acting as a memory controller to run programs. The documentation is sparse and does not detail the instruction set or architecture.
ttsky25b/tt_um_quick_cpu.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc since the documentation does describe the design and test approach.

ttsky25b/tt_um_ragnar_lucasnilsson954.summary: This is a calculator that accepts two 4-bit operands and an operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division) via input pins, and outputs an 8-bit result. A strobe signal indicates when a button is pressed. Division rounds upwards, and zero is not supported as an operand. It requires an external hexadecimal keypad for input and displays to show the result.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rc_servo_motor_xy_ea.summary: This design is a two-channel RC servo pulse generator that produces standard 20 ms PWM frames with pulse widths between 1.0 ms and 2.0 ms based on two asynchronous comparator inputs. It uses a 50 MHz clock and has active-low reset and enable signals. The outputs are PWM signals for X and Y axes. Testing involves driving the comparator inputs with digital levels and observing the PWM outputs on a scope or in simulation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_rc_servo_motor_xy_ea.review_notes: Removed 'comparator' tag because the design processes comparator inputs rather than implementing a comparator.

ttsky25b/tt_um_react_test_saksh156.summary: This project is a simple reaction test game implemented in VHDL. It has one input pin and one output pin, but the documentation does not describe how the game works or how to interact with it. The description states only that it works and to send in data. There is no information on external hardware or testing procedures.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_arrow_board.summary: This design displays animated arrow signs for traffic control using 25 LEDs arranged in a specific pattern. It supports 16 selectable patterns with options for flashing and sequential animation, controlled by input pins. The outputs drive the LEDs directly, and the design includes a lamp test and active-low control. It requires an external array of 25 LEDs connected to the output and bidirectional pins.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large collection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to select the flag by index or step through them. It is used by connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and using the input pins to change the displayed flag. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. Silicon testing confirmed that flag switching works, though the index-based selection via uio was not tested.
ttsky25b/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added pmod, video, and silicon-tested tags supported by documentation and silicon status.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rebelmike_femtorv.summary: This is a modified FemtoRV RISC-V SoC that uses a register file from tnt and a QSPI controller from TinyQV. It executes code from QSPI flash and uses QSPI PSRAM for data memory, with shared clock and data lines. The SoC includes a UART and an SPI controller, and is intended to work with a QSPI PMOD containing flash and RAM, as well as an ST7789 LCD display. Silicon testing showed it works perfectly, even at 80 MHz, and a minimal MicroPython binary was run on it.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rejunity_vga_playground.summary: This project is a playground for (S)VGA experiments implemented in Verilog. It drives a VGA or SVGA monitor through the standard Tiny VGA pinout, with the eight outputs carrying the two-bit RGB colour signals plus horizontal and vertical sync. Testing simply means running it with a VGA PMOD and a monitor attached. The documentation is very thin, giving no detail on what the experiments actually display or how they are configured.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rejunity_ym2413_ika_opll.summary: This design is a Verilog implementation of the YM2413, the OPL-series FM synthesis audio chip, based on the IKA OPLL core. It accepts an 8-bit data bus plus register latch, chip select and write strobes, and produces audio either as an 8-bit parallel DAC output or as a PWM signal on a bidirectional pin. The chip is intended for music synthesis and can be used with external audio hardware. The design is notable for recreating a classic FM synthesis chip in a small form factor.

ttsky25b/tt_um_relax.summary: This project is an analog relaxation oscillator with two analog capacitor pins, two enable inputs, and complementary outputs Q and Qn. The oscillation frequency is changed by varying the values of the capacitors. It is tested using an oscilloscope and requires no external hardware. The documentation is very thin, providing only a brief description of the frequency behavior.
ttsky25b/tt_um_relax.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated op-amp/SKY130 summary with the documented relaxation oscillator; removed unsupported tags.

ttsky25b/tt_um_reservoir.summary: This project implements a neural network accelerator for machine learning inference, designed as an ASIC. It is intended for edge AI applications, providing hardware acceleration for neural network computations. The design is notable for its neuromorphic-inspired architecture, potentially mimicking brain-inspired computing. The project is implemented as an ASIC, targeting efficient inference in embedded systems.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rh_bf_top.summary: TinyBF is a complete hardware implementation of a Brainfuck interpreter in Verilog, fitting within a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It is a fully functional CPU with integrated UART I/O that executes a hardcoded demonstration program in ROM. The design provides UART transmit and receive pins plus debug outputs for the program counter, data pointer, and cell values. Because the program is hardcoded in ROM, it serves as a demonstration platform rather than a general-purpose Brainfuck interpreter.
ttsky25b/tt_um_rh_bf_top.review_notes: Corrected language tag and replaced communication with CPU/esoteric/ROM tags matching the Brainfuck interpreter description.

ttsky25b/tt_um_ring_osc3.summary: This project implements a multistage ring oscillator with externally-selectable length, enable, and a counter. The oscillator length is selected via tap inputs, and eight outputs provide the oscillator/counter outputs. The design is written in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. Documentation is very thin, but the title and pin names clearly indicate a ring oscillator with counter functionality.
ttsky25b/tt_um_ring_osc3.review_notes: Corrected erroneous CPU/esoteric/UART/ROM tags to match ring oscillator and counter design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_rom_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing 64x64 Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen, with options to tile or double the logo size. It can be controlled with a gamepad to start/pause and change direction. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally a Gamepad PMOD. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected, including tile, double, and gamepad modes.

ttsky25b/tt_um_s_grundner.summary: This project implements a polyphonic MIDI synthesizer that decodes MIDI note messages and generates square waves for up to four voices. Each voice is routed to a separate output pin so the signals can be mixed externally, and each oscillator responds to a different MIDI channel to simplify voice allocation. A PWM output encodes the number of currently active voices and can be low-pass filtered to control the gain of the mixed output. The design is written in SystemVerilog and can drive a speaker through an external driver circuit.
ttsky25b/tt_um_s_grundner.review_notes: Replaced unrelated oscillator/counter/LFSR tags with the actual MIDI synthesizer, music, audio and PWM features.

ttsky25b/tt_um_se_opamps.summary: This project is a low-power single-ended two-stage operational amplifier implemented in the SKY130 PDK. It is intended to function as a non-inverting unity-gain buffer for low-frequency analog signals from 1 to 10 kHz. Three digital input pins enable one of three different op-amp submissions on the chip. The design uses two analog inputs for a differential signal and one analog output for the single-ended result.
ttsky25b/tt_um_se_opamps.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an audio synthesizer, which is not supported by the analog op-amp source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_sergejsumnovs_spi_slave.summary: This VHDL design is an SPI slave component with an 8-bit address and data interface, a 21-register map, GPIO, an LFSR with serial output, and a timer with PWM and edge capture. It communicates over the SPI bus, allowing external controllers to read and write registers. The design includes GPIO for general-purpose I/O and an LFSR for pseudo-random bit generation. The timer provides PWM output and edge capture functionality.

ttsky25b/tt_um_seven_segment_animations.summary: This project is a counter with seven-segment display output, designed for educational purposes. It uses buttons for input and displays the count on a seven-segment display. The design is a simple counter circuit, likely for learning digital logic. It is notable for its educational value and use of seven-segment displays.

ttsky25b/tt_um_seven_segment_games.summary: This project implements three selectable minigames that take button input and display output on a 7-segment display. The design is written in Verilog and runs at 10 MHz. Testing is done by pressing different buttons to play the games. External hardware required includes eight buttons and a 7-segment display.

ttsky25b/tt_um_sky25a_nurirfansyah_nauta.summary: This is a Nauta operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) with 2-bit digital trimming for tuning. It is an analog design implemented at the transistor level, based on the Nauta OTA circuit with digital trim as described in referenced literature. The design is intended for analog signal processing applications. External hardware includes a power supply and measurement equipment for characterization.

ttsky25b/tt_um_sleepy_module.summary: Sleepy Chip is a dual-mode digital audio synthesizer featuring a 3-waveform oscillator with streaming capability and a delta-sigma DAC output. The design is controlled via SPI and includes a gate input, hardware reset, and outputs for DAC, gate LED, oscillator run, and sync. It is written in VHDL and requires a 4.8 MHz clock and an external speaker to play the music. The synthesizer supports multiple waveforms and streaming mode for continuous audio generation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_strasti.summary: This is an 8-bit arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that performs arithmetic and bitwise operations on integer binary numbers. It uses a state machine to read two 8-bit inputs (A and B) via the 8 digital input pins, with operation control and status output over the bidirectional pins. The ALU is implemented in Verilog and is suitable for educational purposes. The documentation does not specify external hardware, and the test procedure is marked as TODO.
ttsky25b/tt_um_strasti.review_notes: Removed the invented external hardware claim; the source only says the test explanation is TODO.

ttsky25b/tt_um_synth_magmusson.summary: This project is a hardcoded squarewave synth sequencer that plays a specific progression, with the tempo adjustable via two inputs. It is written in VHDL and runs from a 4.8 MHz clock. The output drives a speaker, which is required external hardware for the music to play. It is plug and play: connect a speaker and set the clock to 4.8 MHz and it should work.
ttsky25b/tt_um_synth_magmusson.review_notes: Tags and summary were entirely wrong (ADC instead of sequencer); replaced with documented music/sequencer functionality.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tadc_its.summary: This project is a time-domain comparator-based analog-to-digital converter. It uses analog inputs VCM, VIN, and VIP, with an enable input and a 9-bit data output plus a clock output. The documentation is very thin and provides no test procedure or external hardware details. No silicon results are reported.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tadc_its.review_notes: Tags claimed characterization/process-experiment/standard-cell without support; corrected to ADC/comparator/analog and insufficient-doc.
