ttsky25b/tt_um_technology_characterizati.summary: This project is a first attempt at characterizing the SKY130 technology and performing aging experiments. All input and output pins are currently unused, and the how-it-works and how-to-test sections are placeholders. The design is written in VHDL and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. The documentation is incomplete, with details to be updated later.
ttsky25b/tt_um_technology_characterizati.review_notes: Corrected erroneous game/LFSR/Verilog tags to match SKY130 characterization project.

ttsky25b/tt_um_timba307_LEDSpinner.summary: This project is a roulette-style LED spinner on a seven-segment display with variable speeds. The wheel spins continuously and its speed is set by four input bits, while a stop input triggers a pseudo-random LFSR-chosen stopping position. Users make guesses on the bidirectional pins, and a correct guess lights the decimal point on the display. The design is implemented in Verilog and tested with per-module testbenches and gtkwave.
ttsky25b/tt_um_timba307_LEDSpinner.review_notes: Removed unsupported ALU/register-file/logic-gate tags; added game, 7-segment, LFSR, PRNG and clock-divider tags supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tiny_4bit_alu.summary: This project implements a 4-bit ALU with an integrated 8x4-bit register file. It supports arithmetic and logical operations as well as register-file access, with outputs containing the result and flags. The design is written in Verilog and can be tested using DIP switches and LEDs. No external hardware is required, though a microcontroller board can be used for more comfortable testing.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tiny_4bit_alu.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated tags with supported ALU, register-file, Verilog, DIP-switch, and LED tags; summary rewritten to match the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tiny_hardware_authenticat.summary: This project is a self-contained hardware authentication engine that generates, stores and verifies a 4-digit (16-bit) one-time password using a 16-bit LFSR and an FSM. The FSM controls authentication, retry and timeout operations, and the result is shown on seven-segment displays as unlocked, locked or expired. It is tested by latching an OTP, entering four digits with user_in and user_latch, and observing the displayed result. The design is implemented in Verilog and is described as lightweight and Tiny Tapeout friendly, with observable outputs on FPGA using LEDs and seven-segment displays.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tiny_hardware_authenticat.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added lfsr, fsm, security and 7-segment supported by the documentation and pins.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tiny_shader_v2_mole99.summary: Tiny Shader v2 implements a fragment shader unit that executes a 16-instruction program per pixel to generate images and animations without a framebuffer. It outputs VGA at 640x480 (internal 80x60) and includes an SPI interface for loading new shader programs. The design is controlled via pins for pause, double instruction, half resolution, and frame/line advance. The project mimics GPU shading units and is notable for its on-the-fly color generation and SPI programmability.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tinyflash.summary: This is a 3-bit flash ADC that uses seven comparators and a resistor ladder to convert an analog input voltage (0-1V) into binary and thermometer-coded digital outputs. The design is implemented with analog comparators and a resistor ladder, providing a direct conversion without a clock. It is intended for educational purposes to demonstrate flash ADC operation. The project is notable for its simple analog-to-digital conversion approach.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tinytapeout_logo_screensa.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen at 640x480 resolution, with options for tiling and solid color. It can be controlled with an optional gamepad to pause, change direction, or move the logo. The design requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for interaction. Silicon testing confirmed it works, showing the bouncing logo as intended.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tinytone.summary: tt-tinytone is a PWM-based tone generator designed to drive a piezo buzzer. It produces a PWM signal on output pin sound_o. The design is controlled through the Tiny Tapeout interface and can generate tones. It is a compact implementation of audio synthesis.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tinytone.review_notes: Removed unsupported DAC tag and corrected summary to match the PWM tone generator description.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tnt_mosbius.summary: This project is an alternative layout for Andrew Kang's mini-MOSbius, a reconfigurable analog array intended for building and experimenting with MOS circuits, adapted for SKY130 on Tiny Tapeout. It includes analog switches controlled by a serial bitstream, with digital logic for configuration, and it requires external hardware to generate the bitstream and to interface with the analog pins depending on the circuit being built. Silicon test reports indicate that the configuration shift registers work and that various circuits functioned properly. The design is notable for bringing the MOSbius educational concept to a Tiny Tapeout-compatible form, though the software suite for generating configuration bitstreams is not yet written.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tnt_rf_test.summary: This project is a test structure for a future register file macro, implemented as an SRAM with one write port and two read ports. It is not designed for use with the demo board but instead requires a dedicated test platform, ideally using FPGA hardware to drive control signals with precise timing. Silicon test reports from the author indicate that the memory works correctly, with tens of thousands of random read/write cycles passing, but timing characterization is incomplete due to limitations of the RP2040 controller. The design is notable as a successful early test of a memory macro, though further testing is needed.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tnt_rf_test.review_notes: Removed analog, characterization, and fpga; added sram, register-file, memory, and silicon-tested.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tnt_rf_validation.summary: This project is a validation design for a register file macro. It includes control signals for capture, compare, and feedback selection to test the register file. The documentation describes functional testing with a demo board and advanced timing measurements using a scope and FPGA. No test procedure has been written yet.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tnt_rf_validation.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the register file validation design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_toivoh_delta_sigma.summary: This project implements a 16-bit noise-shaping delta-sigma DAC with a single digital output pin. It uses a pulse width modulator to create the digital output signal. The design can be driven with sample data or a built-in triangle wave generator for testing. The output can be low-pass filtered and converted to audio using an external audio Pmod.
ttsky25b/tt_um_toivoh_delta_sigma.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary are unrelated to the source documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_top_axis_uart.summary: This project bridges a parallel AXI-Stream interface with a serial UART communication protocol. Data is received from an AXI master, stored in an 8-byte synchronous FIFO, then serialized and transmitted over UART at 115200 baud. A loopback UART receiver is integrated to validate data integrity, and the design operates at 50 MHz. No external hardware is necessary to verify core functionality because the project is fully testable on-chip using the internal UART loopback.
ttsky25b/tt_um_top_axis_uart.review_notes: Replaced tags and summary that described an unrelated PWM/temperature design with the actual AXI-Stream/UART/FIFO design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_top_general.summary: This project implements two independent PWM channels with complementary outputs, where duty cycle and edge- or center-aligned mode are configured via SPI. It also repurposes unused output pins as simple gate-level logic test signals based on two test inputs, allowing validation of silicon gates. An internal divided clock is routed to an output pin for slower visual debugging. The design is purely digital and has been reported working on silicon.
ttsky25b/tt_um_top_general.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original tags and summary described a ring oscillator, which is not present.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tt05_analog_test.summary: This project implements a 3-bit R-2R DAC together with a ring oscillator, based on an analog design by Harald Pretl and Jakob Ratschenberger for Tiny Tapeout 5. The DAC output voltage is nominally 1.8 V divided by 8 times the 3-bit input value, and the ring oscillator provides a rail-to-rail clock output at about 500 kHz. It is tested by applying digital bits to inputs 0-2 and measuring the analog output with a voltmeter or oscilloscope. The design is an analog mixed-signal circuit with a nominal 1.8 V supply.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tt05_analog_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported voltage-reference tag; added ring-oscillator, oscillator and mixed-signal based on the documented ring oscillator and DAC.

ttsky25b/tt_um_tv_b_gone_rom.summary: This project drives IR LEDs to send a series of TV power-off codes for European protocols. It can send the codes once when triggered by a button or continuously in a loop. The design stores the codes in ROM macros to reduce area. External IR LEDs and a driving transistor are required.
ttsky25b/tt_um_tv_b_gone_rom.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary describe a temperature sensor PWM-to-UART design, but the source describes an IR TV-B-Gone remote control.

ttsky25b/tt_um_uart_temp_sens.summary: The PWM signal is generated by the temperature sensor, and this module counts the number of clock cycles during which the PWM signal remains LOW. The design operates at 50 MHz and converts the PWM low time into a value transmitted over UART. The result is sent over a UART interface at 115200 baud for external monitoring. The transmitted value is displayed in hexadecimal on a serial terminal.
ttsky25b/tt_um_uart_temp_sens.review_notes: Removed unsupported instrumentation tag; added counter and corrected the summary to match the documented PWM-to-UART behavior.

ttsky25b/tt_um_unclegravity_7seg_counter.summary: This design is a decimal counter that increments from 0 to 9 once per second and drives a 7-segment display. A 4-bit counter wraps at 9, and combinational logic decodes the value into segment patterns on outputs uo[0] through uo[6], with uo[7] as the decimal point. The design expects a 1 Hz clock input, configured via clock_hz: 1 in info.yaml. It is a simple educational example of counter and decoder logic.

ttsky25b/tt_um_underserved.summary: This project implements a minimal 32-bit RISC-V processor core (RV32I) using the bit-serial SERV architecture, processing one bit per clock cycle. It is optimized for area efficiency in ASIC implementation. The core connects to external SPI flash memory for program storage and can drive optional LEDs on GPIO pins. It is implemented in Verilog.
ttsky25b/tt_um_underserved.review_notes: Summary corrected to remove unsupported FPGA/BGM and Tiny Tapeout claims.

ttsky25b/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttsky25b/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_urish_spell.summary: SPELL is a hardware implementation of a minimal stack-based programming language created for The Skull CTF. It executes a cryptic program stored in volatile program memory, using a stack machine architecture with a shift register for serial access. The design provides 256 bytes of program memory, 32 bytes of stack memory, and 32 bytes of data memory, with 8 bidirectional pins and up to 8 output-only pins. Silicon test reports confirm the design works, with successful communication and demo program execution at 10 MHz and overclocking tests up to 156 MHz.
ttsky25b/tt_um_urish_spell.review_notes: Removed unsupported uart and security tags; added stack-machine and silicon-tested; corrected summary to match silicon status and remove invented external hardware claim.

ttsky25b/tt_um_verilog_meetup_template_p.summary: This project receives sound level data from an INMP441 microphone and runs sound recognition on it. It displays the recognized note on a 7-segment display of a TM1638-based interface module. It also draws color patterns on a VGA screen using the Tiny VGA interface. The design is written in SystemVerilog and was prepared as a test for the Verilog Meetup variant of the Tiny Tapeout Verilog Project Template.
ttsky25b/tt_um_verilog_meetup_template_p.review_notes: Replaced unsupported FSM/counter/clock-generator tags with tags supported by the pinout and description.

ttsky25b/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttsky25b/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttsky25b/tt_um_vga_projekt_ed_nkpng.summary: This project is a VGA color test image generator implemented in Verilog. Two FSM modules, two synchronous counters, and timing constants from the 640x480 VGA standard form a driver that generates output for the three color channels. It is tested by connecting VGA-compatible external hardware, powering on, and connecting a VGA device. The required external hardware is the TinyVGA Pmod.
ttsky25b/tt_um_vga_projekt_ed_nkpng.review_notes: Tags and summary described an unrelated ALU; replaced with the documented VGA test image design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_vhdl_ALU_top.summary: This project is a 6-bit signed two's-complement ALU implemented in VHDL. It samples inputs A, B, and a 4-bit opcode on a rising clock edge and registers the result, ZERO, and OVF flags with one cycle of latency. The ALU supports 16 operations including arithmetic, logic, shifts, and signed comparison. It requires an external clock source and a reset button for the active-low rst_n signal.
ttsky25b/tt_um_vhdl_ALU_top.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a clock/display circuit, but the source is a 6-bit VHDL ALU.

ttsky25b/tt_um_willwhang.summary: This design is a simple wall clock that uses the mains AC signal as its timebase. It counts the 50 Hz or 60 Hz input and drives a seven-segment display for the time. The design includes inputs for setting the time and selecting 12-hour or 24-hour display. The documentation is very thin, so the exact implementation cannot be fully determined.
ttsky25b/tt_um_willwhang.review_notes: Removed unsupported wokwi and decoder tags; added rtc, counter, 7-segment, display, and insufficient-doc based on the documented wall-clock design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.summary: This Wokwi project uses simple logic gates to display the letter 'P' on a 7-segment display when the 8-bit input equals 0x46. The design requires external hardware including a breadboard, 1.8V power supply, connector wires, an 8-position DIP switch, and a 7-segment display. The documentation describes the basic function and test procedure, noting that with all inputs at 0x00 the display shows the inverse of the P pattern. The design is a simple combinational logic demonstration.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_413387009513254913.review_notes: Removed unsupported education and template tags and added combinational; summary otherwise matches the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442976058838162433.summary: This Wokwi project is titled 7segCounter, suggesting a counter for a 7-segment display. The documentation, however, is placeholder text: the how-it-works section says 'TODO', the test section says 'TEST', and the external hardware section says 'LOL'. There is no description of the counter width, display decoding, or operation. The design therefore cannot be described beyond its title.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442976058838162433.review_notes: Source is a placeholder skeleton; the summary invented a 2-bit counter and display decoding without evidence.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977436543634433.summary: This project is a simple 2-bit counter that displays its current value on a 7-segment display. It is implemented in Wokwi. The counter advances when the clock is toggled. It is a minimal educational counter design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977436543634433.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register and ring-counter tags; summary invented Verilog and educational intent.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977452121292801.summary: This project is a shift register that runs along the outer ring of a seven-segment display. Setting the IN_SHR input high adds a bit to the shift register. Setting the INV_RING input high inverts the display. The documentation is minimal, with testing described only as 'edit'.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977452121292801.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented shift register rather than a template/decoder.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977456053457921.summary: This project uses seven lever inputs and a reset button to display a number on a 7-segment LED. Switching one of the levers from 1 to 7 shows the corresponding number, while the reset button clears the display. If more than one lever is activated, nothing happens. The design is implemented in Wokwi and uses digital inputs and outputs.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977456053457921.review_notes: Replaced VGA/video tags with 7-segment display tags and rewrote the summary to match the documented lever-to-display behavior.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977463421808641.summary: This design displays the letter P on a seven-segment display when a correct secret code is entered on the input switches. It is a first Tiny Tapeout chip built in Wokwi, with four input pins and four output pins. Testing is done by trying different DIP switch positions to find the code. The documentation deliberately withholds the code logic, so the exact behaviour cannot be verified from the text.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977465750697985.summary: This design uses a button input to turn on four outputs one after another, and additional presses to turn them off again. It requires external hardware to generate current, a button, and a way to display the outputs. The submission is explicitly labelled a broken counter, so its intended behaviour is unclear. It was created using the Wokwi simulator.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977465750697985.review_notes: Design is documented as a broken counter with unspecified output hardware; replaced counter/fsm/led tags with placeholder/incomplete/button and kept summary within three sentences plus Wokwi note.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977476137901057.summary: This design checks eight switches arranged in pairs and lights a seven-segment display with a zero only when exactly one pair is on. Testing is done by manually flipping switches in the Wokwi online project, and the seven-segment display from the template is the only external hardware.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977476137901057.review_notes: Removed comparator and logic-gate tags and added interface/output tags supported by the pins and text.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977476963131393.summary: This project is a Wokwi design containing random gates placed during a workshop. It includes a flip-flop with input FF_in and outputs FF_q and FF_qb, as well as a ring oscillator with ring_enable and ring_out pins. The documentation states that it does not do anything useful yet. Testing is described as powering on and hoping for the best, with a microswitch for input and an oscilloscope for output.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977476963131393.review_notes: Proposed summary was not four sentences and the tags did not match the random-gate workshop design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977490552687617.summary: This Wokwi project is a simple 2-input logic circuit with three outputs. Inputs 1 and 2 control the outputs, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is very thin and does not specify the exact logic function. It is implemented in Wokwi.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977490552687617.review_notes: Removed unsupported template, education and gpio tags; added insufficient-doc and rewrote summary to match sparse source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977493563151361.summary: This project is a 7-segment decoder built in Wokwi. It takes switch inputs S0 to S6 and each switch turns on a corresponding segment of the display. The design drives a 7-segment display as external hardware. The documentation is very thin, consisting of only a brief description and test instructions.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977493563151361.review_notes: Corrected tags to decoder/7-segment and added insufficient-doc; summary rewritten to match the sparse source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977495241922561.summary: This project is a test design for the Wokwi platform. It provides eight inputs and eight outputs but does not describe any specific logic function. The documentation states it is only a test for Wokwi. No external hardware or silicon test results are documented.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977495241922561.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect placeholder Wokwi test design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977503814034433.summary: This design implements basic logic gates including AND, OR, and NOT. The gates are connected so that pressing buttons changes the lights. The project was created in Wokwi. The documentation does not specify any external hardware.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977503814034433.review_notes: Replaced unsupported tags with logic-gate, wokwi, button, and led based on the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977509323262977.summary: This design combines two 4-bit registers, a full adder, and a full subtractor, with the output selected by a multiplexer. Inputs 0-3 provide the data in binary, input 4 selects which register to write, and input 7 chooses between addition and subtraction. The design is built in Wokwi and requires no external hardware, though LEDs and switches are useful for observing and setting the output. The documentation describes the operation and test procedure.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977509323262977.review_notes: Replaced unrelated LFSR/PRNG/arbiter tags and summary with the documented adder/subtractor design.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977515486800897.summary: This design combines a mutex arbiter, an inefficient C-gate, and an LFSR that drives a 4-bit pseudo-random output. The documentation does not specify any external hardware.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977531497515009.summary: This project implements a set of basic logic gates (AND, OR, NAND) on a Tiny Tapeout tile. It is built in Wokwi and takes eight input pins, producing outputs that reflect the gate operations. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of placeholder text, so the exact mapping of inputs to outputs is not fully described. It appears to be an educational or test design, but the lack of detail limits its usefulness.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977531497515009.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added incomplete due to placeholder-only documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977533467790337.summary: This design is a 4-bit binary counter that divides the input clock frequency. The text describes T flip-flops dividing the clock and four D flip-flops forming the counter, though the stated numbers are internally inconsistent. It is implemented in Wokwi and outputs the counter bits on pins uo[0] through uo[3]. The documentation is brief and does not specify external hardware or detailed testing steps.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977533467790337.review_notes: Source text conflicts with itself (11 flip-flops plus 4 D flip-flops vs a 4-bit counter) and contains template placeholders.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977534651634689.summary: This project combines AND, inverter, and XNOR gates to produce eight outputs based on eight button inputs. It is designed in Wokwi and tested interactively by pressing buttons and observing the outputs. The one-line description is only 'GDS' and the gate connections are described in a single short sentence. No external hardware is mentioned, and the external-hardware section is unfilled placeholder text.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977534651634689.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag, added button evidence and incomplete due to placeholder external-hardware text.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977548950021121.summary: This design implements AND, NAND, and OR gates that take two inputs and produce three outputs. It also includes a clock divider using 16 flip-flops, with outputs taken at the 12th and 16th stages. The project is built in Wokwi as a self-described test project. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text in the testing and external-hardware sections.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977548950021121.review_notes: Removed flip-flop as redundant with clock-divider evidence; added incomplete for placeholder sections.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977579441572865.summary: This project implements a Hamming (7,4) encoder and decoder with single-bit error correction. It uses eight input and output pins, with a mode selection pin to switch between encoding and decoding. In decode mode, it can correct single-bit errors and reports when a correction occurs. The design is built in Wokwi and is documented with pin descriptions and testing instructions.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977585335625729.summary: This is a test design with eight input and eight output pins, but the documentation is essentially empty, containing only the words 'test' and 'test it'. The functionality is not described, and no external hardware is mentioned. It appears to be a placeholder or minimal test project. Due to the lack of information, the design's purpose cannot be determined.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977603880750081.summary: This project displays the letter 'Y' on a 7-segment display when an 8-bit binary code (137 in decimal) is input. It uses eight input pins for the binary code and seven output pins to drive the segments. The design is built in Wokwi and requires an external 7-segment display connected to the outputs. The documentation explains the operation and testing procedure clearly.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977603880750081.review_notes: Removed decoder tag because the design is a fixed-value comparator, not a code-to-signal decoder.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_442977606409919489.summary: This project is titled 'Tiney Tapeout Test Gates' and claims to test logic gates and a clock divider. The documentation is filled with placeholder text ('123') and all pins are marked as 'not used'. There is no meaningful description of the design's functionality or how to test it. It appears to be an incomplete or abandoned project.

The project is built using the Wokwi simulator and serves as an educational example of basic logic gate operation. No external hardware is required beyond the simulator's input switches and output LEDs.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445265377104476161.review_notes: Summary is accurate; no tag changes needed.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445265826672030721.summary: This project implements several basic logic gates: two NOT gates, one OR gate, one XNOR gate, and one XOR gate, each connected to specific input pins. The outputs are routed to the output pins, and the design is intended to be tested by toggling the input switches and observing the corresponding outputs. The project is built using the Wokwi simulator and serves as an educational example of basic logic gate operation. No external hardware is required beyond the simulator's input switches and output LEDs.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445265925317879809.summary: This Wokwi project implements a small combinational logic block. NOT gates are connected to inputs a and b, an OR gate to inputs c and d, an XNOR gate to inputs e and f, and an XOR gate to inputs g and h. Its outputs on uo[0], uo[1], uo[5], uo[6] and uo[7] reflect these gate results. It is tested by setting the inputs and checking the outputs against expected combinations.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445265925317879809.review_notes: Original summary invented an unrelated 7-segment display project; corrected to match the documented logic gates.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445266058506969089.summary: This design displays the numbers 6, 7, or 8 based on the state of the first four switches. The logic is described in the pin descriptions, which specify the conditions for each number to appear. The project is built using the Wokwi simulator and is intended as a simple educational exercise. The documentation is thin but sufficient to understand the basic function.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445266058506969089.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary incorrectly describe a PWM generator and silicon testing, which are not supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445276353959823361.summary: This project counts in binary from 0 to 7 and converts the count into the segment outputs for a 7-segment display. The counter is reset by pulling pin 0 high and incremented by pulling the clock pin high, so the display advances by one on each button press. It is built using the Wokwi simulator and requires two buttons and a single 7-segment display as external hardware. No silicon test results are reported.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445276353959823361.review_notes: Replaced the fabricated PWM description with the actual counter-to-7-segment function and removed the false silicon-tested claim.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_445338187869298689.summary: This project implements a 4-channel PWM generator with programmable frequency, duty cycle, and phase offset for channels 2-4. It uses an 8-bit input bus to load control registers, with a 7-segment display showing the current register address, and outputs PWM signals on four bidirectional pins. The design is built using the Wokwi simulator and is intended for educational purposes. It has been tested on fabricated silicon.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446359782214875137.summary: This project celebrates a marriage covenant by displaying the letters JONANDANgIE on a seven-segment display. It has two modes of operation: dip switches can drive a single letter state, or a button can be used as a clock to cycle through the letters in order. It is built using the Wokwi simulator. The design is intended to be tested by pressing the clock button and reading the seven-segment display.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446359782214875137.review_notes: Removed unsupported PWM and silicon-tested tags and added art/button/dip-switch/text.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446362347802682369.summary: This project implements four dual-edge-triggered D flip-flops, each latching the D input to Q on either the rising or falling edge of its CLK input. The intended application is tamper detection, where sensors connected to the CLK inputs latch a logic-high D value when triggered. The Q and QN outputs are displayed on the 7-segment display, and asynchronous reset inputs are provided. It is built with Wokwi and requires no external hardware for testing.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446362347802682369.review_notes: Removed unsupported PWM and silicon-tested tags; added flip-flop, 7-segment, wokwi and security based on the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363696538901505.summary: This project implements an 8-player fastest finger game. It has eight input pins for player buttons and eight output pins for player indicators. The design is built using the Wokwi simulator. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the game logic in detail.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363696538901505.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the fastest finger game.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363696828310529.summary: This project implements a basic SR flip-flop with reset and set inputs and Q and ~Q outputs. It is built using the Wokwi simulator. Pulling input 1 high sets the flip-flop, and pulling input 0 high resets it. No external hardware is required.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363696828310529.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated tags with flip-flop, wokwi, and sequential-logic; summary rewritten to match the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363731295014913.summary: This design implements a binary-to-decimal decoder that converts an 8-bit binary value into signals for a 7-segment display. It uses simple AND and OR gates to produce the segment outputs, but the provided documentation only shows partial truth tables for a few inputs and outputs, making the full mapping unclear. The project is intended to drive a 7-segment display directly, with no external hardware required. Testing is described through truth tables, but the incomplete documentation limits verification of the complete design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363731295014913.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd tag; added decoder, 7-segment, logic-gate, wokwi and display.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363771447095297.summary: This project implements a tapped delay line using a chain of inverters and flip-flops, with eight tap outputs and a multiplexer to select which tap to observe. It is intended to measure the propagation delay between start and stop signals, serving as a characterization test for future projects. External hardware such as a signal generator and possibly an FPGA is suggested for testing. The design's main purpose is to evaluate timing characteristics, and no silicon results are provided.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363771447095297.review_notes: Removed logic-gate and clock-generator tags not supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363782054494209.summary: This design is a 4-bit Johnson counter that generates four offset square waves at one-quarter of the input clock frequency. It is built from four D flip-flops connected in a ring with the inverted output of the last stage fed back to the first. The outputs can be verified with a logic analyzer to observe the expected repeating pattern. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward sequential logic example.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363782054494209.review_notes: Replaced unsupported clock-generator and signal-generator tags with clock-divider.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363784753530881.summary: This project counts from 0 to 7 and displays the digit on a 7-segment LCD, incrementing every second. It converts a 3-bit binary value to the seven segment outputs using truth tables, sum-of-products, Boolean simplification, and Karnaugh mapping. The design is controlled by a clock switch and a reset button to start from zero. No external hardware is needed, and it is an exercise in combinational logic design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363784753530881.review_notes: Removed unsupported bcd and education tags; added decoder for the seven-segment conversion.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363829539267585.summary: This design outputs both the AND and NAND of two input signals, providing two separate outputs from the same inputs. It is a simple combinational logic block with no clock or sequential elements. Testing involves applying signals to the two inputs and observing the corresponding outputs. No external hardware is required.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363829539267585.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the unsupported claim that the project serves as a basic demonstration of logic gates.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363830909757441.summary: This design is a 2-bit to 7-segment display driver that converts a 2-bit binary input (0-3) into the corresponding segment outputs for a 7-segment display. The outputs map to segments a through g and the decimal point. It can be driven by any external signal source, and no specific external hardware is required. The project is described as a first Tiny Tapeout attempt.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363830909757441.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the unsupported claim that it provides an introduction to display decoding.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363833426340865.summary: This project is a Wokwi test design containing an AND gate whose output is connected to an LED. The documentation is very thin, stating only that there is an AND gate on input 1 and two connected to an LED. The testing instructions are simply 'I don't know,' and no external hardware is required. The design is a minimal logic gate demonstration.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363833426340865.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated sequencer/LFSR tags with logic-gate, led, and insufficient-doc based on the actual AND-gate documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363834407809025.summary: This design is a rhythm sequencer and randomizer that uses an 8-stage ring counter or LFSR to generate looping or pseudo-random patterns on eight outputs. It is controlled by three switches: one selects between looper and randomizer modes, another toggles to create a new loop, and a third clears the pattern or allows input of a custom rhythm. The outputs can drive external hardware via the Tiny Tapeout GPIO pins. Testing involves a specific sequence of switch operations to clear, start, and randomize the pattern.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363844132307969.summary: This project implements a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit numbers as inputs and produces their sum. The documentation is sparse, with no details on the output pins or the exact behavior, and the testing suggestion is to use a truth table. No external hardware is specified, and the description is tentative, indicating it is a work in progress. The design appears to be a basic arithmetic exercise.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363844132307969.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu tag; added incomplete for the tentative, output-less documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363880417243137.summary: This project is a placeholder with no functional description, only listing two inputs (A and B) and two outputs (S and C), which suggests a half-adder, but the documentation is entirely template text. No explanation of how it works or how to test it is provided. No external hardware is mentioned. The design is essentially undocumented and cannot be evaluated.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363880417243137.review_notes: Removed education tag not supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363928119066625.summary: This design uses combinational logic gates to decode dip switch settings into segment patterns for a seven-segment display. It is configured by setting the eight DIP switches, which select which segments to illuminate. The project requires an external LED display to show the segments. The documentation is minimal and does not provide a clear mapping of switch settings to segments, so the exact behavior is not fully specified.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363928119066625.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added 7-segment, decoder, logic-gate, dip-switch, display and wokwi.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363984157070337.summary: This design implements a simple AND gate logic function, with outputs labeled as 't1 and' and 't1 and 2'. It is intended to be run as-is, with no specific test procedure described. The external hardware requirement is unspecified, with the documentation stating it can be anything. The documentation is extremely thin, providing almost no detail about the design's purpose or operation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446363984157070337.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added insufficient-doc for the extremely thin documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364133350576129.summary: This design prints names (boris, dario, ivan, natasa) on a seven-segment display, with a period used as a separator. It was submitted as part of a Tiny Tapeout workshop at Supercon 25, but the testing procedure and external hardware are not yet documented. The design documentation notes a clock of 2 Hz. The documentation is incomplete, with placeholders for testing and hardware details.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364133350576129.review_notes: Removed education tag because workshop context alone does not support an education-domain claim.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364165240923137.summary: This project is described as having something to do with Meshtastic, but the documentation explicitly states that the author does not yet know what it will do. The pins are generically named as inputs and outputs, with no functional description. The external hardware is suggested to be a T-Echo, but this is uncertain. The documentation is essentially non-existent, providing no useful information about the design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364165240923137.review_notes: Removed communication tag since the design's purpose is explicitly unknown.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364777751946241.summary: This design converts a 4-bit binary input (0-9) into signals for a seven-segment display, driving segments A through G and the decimal point. It is tested by applying any binary number from 0 to 9 on the inputs. The project requires an external seven-segment display to show the decoded digits. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic function.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364777751946241.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the rest of the summary is supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364830841352193.summary: This design consists of 128 daisy-chained D flip-flops, with a single input and output, and several switches. The documentation describes the implementation as 'magic mixed with stuff' and the test procedure as doing 'all the right things in the right places and the right time', which is not informative. It requires two 'encabultors' (likely a misspelling of encabulators) as external hardware, but this is unclear. The documentation is too vague to determine the actual functionality or how to use it.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446364830841352193.review_notes: Removed shift-register tag not directly supported; added insufficient-doc for the vague documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446368563224770561.summary: This design implements a programmable logic function using a 4-input lookup table (LUT). The LUT is configured by presenting a truth table on inputs 4-7, and the function is evaluated with inputs on pins 0 and 1, producing the result on output 0. It requires no external hardware. The documentation is clear and sufficient to understand and test the design.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446368563224770561.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; the rest of the summary is supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446373432938861569.summary: This design displays the letter 'J' on a seven-segment display when dip switch 1 is active. It is tested by activating dip switch 1, and it requires an external LED display. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description of the function and test procedure.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446373432938861569.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; summary already matches the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446424200424416257.summary: This design implements a JK flip-flop. The clock is connected to input 1, J to input 0, and K to input 2, with outputs Q and Q-not on outputs 0 and 1. It is tested by applying appropriate signals to the inputs and observing the outputs. The design is created in Wokwi and the documentation is brief.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446424200424416257.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag because the project is a flip-flop, not a standalone gate.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446565876953355265.summary: This design converts a 3-bit binary input (0-7) into decimal digits displayed on a seven-segment display. It is tested by toggling the input switches B2, B1, B0 to select a binary number and observing the corresponding decimal digit on the output segments. The project requires an external seven-segment display. The documentation is clear and includes a truth table approach.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446565876953355265.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the unsupported claim that it is suitable for educational purposes.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446645853372820481.summary: This design is an 8-bit counter intended to behave like a TI CD4022B decade counter with eight outputs. It is driven by an external clock signal and an enable input, although the documentation notes that the enable does not actually work and the counter is always enabled. Testing requires a microcontroller such as an Arduino or ESP32 to generate the clock, and the outputs can drive the segments of a 7-segment LED display. The project is a first chip made in Wokwi, with the known enable bug being the main limitation.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446645853372820481.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not state an educational intent.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446847576277095425.summary: This design is an 8x8-bit multiplier that shifts two bytes in serially, MSB first, and presents the result as parallel data on the output pins. It is tested by supplying a clock and data signal to shift in the two operands, with the documentation giving a worked example of 53 times 77 equalling 4081. As of the documentation date only the least significant byte of the result appears on the outputs, and the author plans to add an output buffer and shift register. The project is a Wokwi-based arithmetic block with a clear but currently limited output interface.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446847576277095425.review_notes: Removed bit-serial: the multiplier datapath is parallel, only the operand loading is serial.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446907838117673985.summary: This design exposes basic logic functions including AND, NAND and OR, plus divided clock outputs at divide-by-16 and divide-by-12. The documentation claims that a coded DIP switch sequence should display an 'A.' on a connected 8-segment display, but the description is unclear and the title still says TBD. Testing requires connecting DIP switches to the input pins and an 8-segment LED cell to the outputs, along with a 5V supply. The documentation is thin and partly garbled, so the exact intended behaviour is difficult to confirm.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446907838117673985.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added insufficient-doc for the thin and garbled documentation.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446992736864284673.summary: This design is an 8-bit binary counter driven by an internal 1 Hz clock and a chain of D flip-flops, with each output intended to light an LED to show the binary count. It is tested simply by powering the chip and connecting up to eight LEDs, with resistors recommended to limit current. The documentation notes that the flip-flops may power up in an unknown state because the author could not implement a reset, so the LEDs may already be lit at boot. No external hardware beyond the LEDs is required.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_446992736864284673.review_notes: Removed clock-generator tag because the design consumes rather than generates a clock; the rest of the summary is supported by the source.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_447051835034957825.summary: This design implements a two-player Tic-Tac-Toe game using nine multiplexed common-cathode RGB LEDs and nine push-buttons. Pressing a button places a move in the corresponding cell, the logic evaluates the game state, and a separate RGB LED indicates the winner's colour when a winning combination is detected. Testing is done by wiring the Wokwi circuit with buttons, RGB LEDs and resistors and running the simulation at around 100 Hz or faster. The project is a complete interactive game on a single tile, with the main external requirement being the LED and button array.
ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_447051835034957825.review_notes: Summary is accurate; no tag changes needed.

ttsky25b/tt_um_wokwi_447138553926768641.summary: This design is a puzzle in which the user flips combinations of eight DIP switches to discover hidden numbers from 0 to 9, which are then shown on a 7-segment display. A valid combination lights the corresponding digit, while an invalid one shows nothing or lights the red decimal point, and combinations may be one to eight switches long. The documentation gives no testing procedure beyond saying there is no clue, and it expects the design to be used with the Tiny Tapeout PCB that carries the DIP switches and 7-segment display. The project is a small interactive fidget puzzle whose exact logic is intentionally undocumented.

ttsky25b/tt_um_yorimichi_kittscanner.summary: This design is a controller for K.I.T.T.-style scanner lights, with eight LED outputs and eight PWM outputs plus mode, speed, inversion and output-select inputs. It is used by setting the mode, speed, inversion and output-select pins, then raising the enable input to activate the LED scanning pattern and lowering it to stop. External hardware consists of eight LEDs and switches for configuration and triggering. The project is a Verilog LED animation controller with a documented pin table but only a placeholder image for the internal description.

ttsky25b/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
ttsky25b/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.review_notes: Removed generic asic tag; added rotary-encoder and silicon-tested based on pins and test report.

ttsky25b/tt_um_zerotoasic_logo_screensav.summary: This design drives a 640x480 VGA output showing a bouncing Zero to ASIC logo, with options for tiled mode and an animated colour gradient. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor and setting the tile and solid-colour inputs, and an optional Gamepad Pmod can start, pause and steer the logo. External hardware is the Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally the Gamepad Pmod. A silicon test report confirms it works after setting the clock, making it a verified VGA animation design.

ttsky26a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.
ttsky26a/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported display tag and added button for the documented direction inputs.

ttsky26a/tt_um_5482582_cat_vga.summary: This project currently displays a bouncing cat on VGA. It is planned to gain an SPI interface with time and an encrypted key for an ASIC to decrypt and reply with a TOTP code. The design outputs RGB222 VGA signals with VSync and HSync. There is no hardware yet, so testing instructions are not available.
ttsky26a/tt_um_5482582_cat_vga.review_notes: Summary was rewritten to match the bouncing cat and planned TOTP feature instead of an invented test pattern.

ttsky26a/tt_um_8_bit_cpu.summary: This project is an 8-bit CPU implemented in Verilog on a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It performs instructions such as arithmetic and load operations and outputs the result of each instruction on the eight output pins. A test script simulates the instruction register, allowing custom assembly programs to be loaded and tested. The design is a work in progress with features to be added as time and complexity allow.
ttsky26a/tt_um_8_bit_cpu.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a Blackjack game that does not match the 8-bit CPU source.

ttsky26a/tt_um_8b10.summary: This project is a test for an 8b10 serdes containing an 8b10 encoder and decoder. It accepts 9-bit symbols and outputs the encoded or decoded results after a number of clock cycles. The design uses a manual clock divided by 10 to generate internal clocks and supports an optional scrambler. Testing involves sending characters and verifying the received data matches the transmitted data.
ttsky26a/tt_um_8b10.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the 8b10 serdes test.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Acrazt05_titan_proccesing.summary: This project is a 16-bit computer based on the Nand2Tetris Hack architecture, with a CPU that fetches instructions via SPI from an off-chip memory module. The memory module, simulated on an RP2040, stores both ROM and RAM partitions. The design provides general-purpose I/O and is intended to run programs loaded into the RP2040's ROM section. It is a working implementation of the Hack computer with modifications for physical feasibility.
ttsky26a/tt_um_Acrazt05_titan_proccesing.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary; original tags and summary described a PLL test structure, which is not present.

ttsky26a/tt_um_AlephNaNsea_space_time_wa.summary: This project is a purely combinatorial generative VGA video synthesizer written in Verilog that renders procedural art at 640x480 and 60Hz. It uses a custom VGA sync engine and screen-space coordinates, relying on bitwise operations and triangle waves instead of RAM or DSP blocks, with a frame counter driving animation over time. A multiplexer selects one of six art engines based on input pins, with a strict priority where ui_in[4] overrides the lower inputs. Testing requires a 25.175 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA PMOD or equivalent resistor-ladder DAC connected to a 640x480 monitor, with DIP switches or buttons on ui_in[4:0] to change modes. No silicon test reports are available.
ttsky26a/tt_um_AlephNaNsea_space_time_wa.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a programmable sequencer and state machine, which the source does not contain.

ttsky26a/tt_um_AmitChen1415.summary: This project is a simplified Blackjack game implemented entirely in digital hardware. The core game logic, cards, rules and balance run as a finite-state machine, with a 16-bit LFSR used as a pseudo-random card generator. The player interacts using Hit, Stand, Double and Start push-buttons, and the internal state is visualized on a VGA blackjack table screen. All logic is fully synthesizable and fits into a single Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttsky26a/tt_um_AmitChen1415.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated counter/LED FPGA demo; replaced with tags and summary matching the documented Blackjack game.

ttsky26a/tt_um_BellaB05_Hearts.summary: This design generates a VGA video signal that animates columns of pink hearts transitioning on and off the screen. It is implemented in Verilog using the VGA Playground environment and is intended to be tested by running the simulation and observing the output. The design uses the Tiny VGA pinout to drive a VGA monitor. The project is a playful visual demonstration rather than a practical application.
ttsky26a/tt_um_BellaB05_Hearts.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'display' tag; corrected summary to state the Tiny VGA pinout rather than claiming a PMOD requirement.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Bingyao_FCOTA.summary: This analog tile integrates two independent circuits: a current-controlled ring oscillator VCO and a differential amplifier, sharing a single bias/control pin. It is implemented at the transistor level and requires external test equipment such as a DC supply, function generator, and oscilloscope or frequency counter. The design is intended for analog experimentation and characterization. No digital interface is used.

ttsky26a/tt_um_ChristmasTree_MaligayangP.summary: This project generates a VGA video signal showing a Christmas tree scene. It is implemented in Verilog and uses the Tiny VGA pinout. The design requires a VGA monitor connected to the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. Documentation is very thin, consisting only of the project name repeated.
ttsky26a/tt_um_ChristmasTree_MaligayangP.review_notes: Removed unsupported art tag and invented animation/hearts details; added insufficient-doc given very thin documentation.

ttsky26a/tt_um_IEEE_open_silicon_FOSSEE.summary: This tile integrates two independent analog designs in the SkyWater Sky130 130 nm PDK, sharing a single DC bias/control pin due to the 4-analog-pin Tiny Tapeout limit. One circuit is a current-controlled ring-oscillator VCO whose frequency appears on the digital output pin, and the other is a differential amplifier with input and output analog pins. Both circuits are permanently powered from VDD = 1.8 V and are tested through separate analog and digital pins. No external hardware is required beyond an Analog Discovery 3 or equivalent supply, function generator and oscilloscope or frequency counter.
ttsky26a/tt_um_IEEE_open_silicon_FOSSEE.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated digital LFSR; replaced with tags and summary matching the documented analog VCO and differential amplifier.

ttsky26a/tt_um_JAIMEPRYOR0_VGA_YAY.summary: This project is a VGA pattern generator based on a modified checkers example that bounces back and forth. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout to output RGB, HSync and VSync signals. The design is written in Verilog and runs at 25.175 MHz. It can be tested by compiling it in the VGA playground.
ttsky26a/tt_um_JAIMEPRYOR0_VGA_YAY.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplier/alu tags and added VGA/video/graphics/demoscene tags matching the actual design.

ttsky26a/tt_um_LFSR.summary: This project implements a 16-bit Configurable Galois LFSR designed for Tiny Tapeout SKY130. It supports configurable width (4/8/12/16-bit), primitive polynomial selection, nibble-serial seed loading, and provides the full 16-bit output. The design is written in Verilog and can be tested with standard digital inputs and outputs, for example driving an LED with the serial bit output or using a logic analyser for PRBS verification. It is a classic pseudo-random number generator circuit.
ttsky26a/tt_um_LFSR.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated PIO block; replaced with tags and summary matching the documented Galois LFSR. Note: 'configurable' is not in the canonical vocabulary, so it was omitted.

ttsky26a/tt_um_LH_TapeoutMultiplier.summary: This project implements an 8-bit signed Baugh-Wooley multiplier. The two input operands are provided through ui_in and uio_in, and the 16-bit product is split across uo_out and uio_out. The multiplier uses bitwise AND operations to generate partial products, which are summed using a tree reduction structure. A correction bit pattern is applied to handle two's complement signed multiplication.
ttsky26a/tt_um_LH_TapeoutMultiplier.review_notes: The proposed tags were unsupported by the source; corrected to reflect the documented multiplier design.

ttsky26a/tt_um_LinusSkucas_pio.summary: This project is a programmable IO block modelled after, but not compatible with, the RP2350's PIO. It is written in SystemVerilog and occupies a 3x2 tile area. The design exposes GPIO inputs and outputs along with load, external address and IO pins on the bidirectional lines. Documentation is very thin, with further explanation and testing details still to come.
ttsky26a/tt_um_LinusSkucas_pio.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a biomedical analog front-end that does not match the Tiny PIO source.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Melody_Generator_JLANordh.summary: This project is a stochastic music generator that uses two Markov chains to select note and duration on a pentatonic scale. It features a 16-bit LFSR entropy source, adjustable BPM, and selectable probability matrices. The logic control module uses two FSMs to model the Markov chains and drive a PWM generator. It is tested by connecting a buzzer PMOD and changing the seed and control inputs.
ttsky26a/tt_um_Melody_Generator_JLANordh.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the melody generator description.

ttsky26a/tt_um_NE567Mixer28.summary: This project implements an ECG front end for measuring electrocardiogram signals using a folded cascode based architecture. It has analog input pins INp and INm for the ECG signal, and output pins OUT and OUTDRL. The ref and Vref pins should be biased at 0.9V or connected to an offset compensation circuit. Testing involves connecting electrodes and observing the output with an oscilloscope.
ttsky26a/tt_um_NE567Mixer28.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the ECG front end description.

ttsky26a/tt_um_NguyenHuuHenry_vga_projec.summary: This project outputs a VGA signal displaying a moving logo from a bitmap. It is based on the VGA playground template and uses the Tiny VGA pinout. Testing is performed through a cocotb Python test file. The documentation does not specify any external hardware beyond a VGA display.
ttsky26a/tt_um_NguyenHuuHenry_vga_projec.review_notes: Removed framebuffer because the source only mentions a bitmap logo, not a framebuffer-based display.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Onchip_Folded_Cascode_N_w.summary: This is an analog folded cascode operational transconductance amplifier (OTA) with N-type input and on-chip bias. It operates from a 1.8V supply and provides a single-ended output. Testing requires applying input signals and measuring the output with an oscilloscope. The documentation is minimal, providing only basic specifications.
ttsky26a/tt_um_Onchip_Folded_Cascode_N_w.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; documentation is very thin but the analog/opamp tags are supported by the title and pins.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Rats2012_WobblyBits.summary: WobblyBits is a probabilistic computing chip containing six p-bits that fluctuate randomly, forming an Ising/Boltzmann machine. A 6x6 coupling matrix is loaded over SPI, and the network samples from the encoded probability distribution when the run pin is released. The p-bits are driven by a ring-oscillator true random number generator. The design is implemented in Verilog for the SKY130 process and fits in a 1x2 tile area.
ttsky26a/tt_um_Rats2012_WobblyBits.review_notes: Removed prng because the design uses a ring-oscillator TRNG, not a pseudo-random generator.

ttsky26a/tt_um_SimpleCounter.summary: This is an 8-bit counter with eight different counting modes. The mode is selected using three input pins, and the count value is displayed on eight LEDs. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires external LEDs for output. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the counting modes in detail.
ttsky26a/tt_um_SimpleCounter.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplexer and education tags.

ttsky26a/tt_um_TSARKA_TinyQV.summary: This project is a TinyQV RISC-V SoC with a Wishbone interconnect, integrating a UART16550 and GPIO peripherals. It exposes debug signals and supports QSPI flash/RAM interfaces. The design is implemented in Verilog and occupies a 6x2 tile area. Extensive testing is performed using cocotb and gate-level simulations, and external hardware such as a USB-UART bridge and QSPI memory can be connected for bring-up.

ttsky26a/tt_um_Terdoo_Osu.summary: This is a spiking pattern recognition core based on a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron that triggers an event when a target spike pattern is detected. It uses input switches to set the pattern and a signal generator to provide a 0.5Hz square wave. When the pattern matches, an output drives a MOSFET module to rotate a motor. The clock is deliberately set to 2 Hz to make internal processing observable, and the design is intended for educational demonstrations of robotic reflex responses.
ttsky26a/tt_um_Terdoo_Osu.review_notes: Removed machine-learning and education tags; added systemverilog and kept the supported spiking/motor/robotics tags.

ttsky26a/tt_um_TinyGPU_v3.summary: Tiniest GPU V3 is a standalone GPU with a programmable pixel shader. It outputs VGA video and interfaces with QSPI flash/PSRAM and a gamepad, including support for an SNES controller. The design is implemented in Verilog and occupies a 6x4 tile area. The documentation is incomplete, with testing instructions still being updated.
ttsky26a/tt_um_TinyGPU_v3.review_notes: Removed accelerator and added gpu, which is the explicit design type stated in the source.

ttsky26a/tt_um_adpll.summary: This is an all-digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL) that locks an internal ring oscillator to a 32.768 kHz crystal reference, synthesizing a 16.777216 MHz output clock (x512 multiplication). It provides lock indicator and phase error outputs. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires an external 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator module. Optional testing can be done with a frequency counter or logic analyzer.

ttsky26a/tt_um_advaittej_stopwatch.summary: This is an interactive 1Hz stopwatch with hardware debouncing, lap memory, alarm target, and 9600-baud UART RX/TX telemetry. It uses a 10 MHz clock and includes modules for debouncing, BCD counting, alarm comparison, and UART communication. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires external hardware such as a 7-segment display, push-buttons, DIP switches, and a USB-to-TTL serial cable for full testing. It was developed as part of the V-SPACE Demo.
ttsky26a/tt_um_advaittej_stopwatch.review_notes: Removed unsupported instrumentation tag; added pmod tag for the specified 7-segment PMOD.

ttsky26a/tt_um_aes_sbox.summary: This is a constant-time AES S-Box implementing both SubBytes (encrypt) and InvSubBytes (decrypt) operations per FIPS 197. The input byte is looked up in the standard AES substitution table via purely combinational logic, with registered output. The design is inherently constant-time in hardware and is part of the rtlforge project, which generates formally-verified cryptographic IP from Rust specifications. It requires no external hardware and can be exhaustively verified by iterating all 256 input values.

ttsky26a/tt_um_ahmed_nematallah_12_bit_a.summary: This is a 12-bit successive-approximation-register analog-to-digital converter implemented as an analog block. It samples an input on an analog pin and outputs the previous sample while starting the next conversion, with a comparator output and a VCO-related input also exposed. The documentation is very thin: it notes that the output bits may be active low and asks the user to check, and the external hardware section is left as an unfilled template. No silicon test results or detailed operating instructions are provided.
ttsky26a/tt_um_ahmed_nematallah_12_bit_a.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator tag and added insufficient-doc due to thin documentation.

ttsky26a/tt_um_alex_ha_192.summary: This design is an 8-bit by 8-bit multiplier that computes a 16-bit product internally and outputs it over two clock cycles. One operand is taken from the eight dedicated input pins and the other from the eight bidirectional pins, with the product bits driven on the outputs. The author notes that exhaustive testing of all 65536 input pairs is feasible at the current size, and that no external hardware is currently used, though a display might be added later. The documentation is brief and does not describe the two-cycle output sequencing in detail.
ttsky26a/tt_um_alex_ha_192.review_notes: Removed alu tag: source describes only a multiplier, not an ALU.

ttsky26a/tt_um_algofoogle_dottee.summary: This is a one-tile demoscene entry that generates animated graphics for a VGA monitor while racing the beam, using mathematical functions to produce the imagery. It also outputs mono audio on a bidirectional pin, and the whole sequence repeats after about 68 seconds. It needs a 25 MHz clock, a reset, a Tiny VGA PMOD for the display and a TT Audio PMOD for sound. The design is notable as a competition submission in the 1-tile category and relies on standard Tiny Tapeout VGA and audio pinouts.

ttsky26a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.summary: This project implements current-switching DACs for generating analog VGA signals, using a 16x16 matrix of unit current sources to convert 8-bit digital inputs to analog current outputs. It is intended for analog VGA displays and requires external pull-up resistors and opamps to convert the current to voltage. The digital display controller is not yet implemented, and testing details are incomplete. The design is an experiment in analog VGA signal generation.
ttsky26a/tt_um_algofoogle_vga_matrix_dac.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added mixed-signal and kept vga, dac, analog, video.

ttsky26a/tt_um_alu_bns.summary: This is a 6-bit multi-functional arithmetic logic unit that supports ripple-carry and carry-lookahead addition, multiplication, logic operations, shifts, popcount and comparison. Two 6-bit operands, a carry-in and a 3-bit opcode are supplied on the input and bidirectional pins, and an 8-bit result appears on the outputs. Testing is done by applying random input values and checking that the result matches the selected operation, with LEDs or a logic analyzer recommended to observe the outputs. The documentation lists the operation set only as empty bullet points, so the exact opcode mapping is not described.
ttsky26a/tt_um_alu_bns.review_notes: Removed barrel-shifter tag since only generic 'shifts' are documented.

ttsky26a/tt_um_analog_RO.summary: This analog block contains a dedicated 33-stage ring oscillator with a divide-by-32 stage expected to run near 15 MHz, plus a separate XOR-based true random number generator built from five distinct ring oscillators. Enable signals select the different ring oscillator configurations, and the oscillator outputs and TRNG output are brought out on analog and output pins. Testing consists of setting all enable signals high and observing the expected frequencies on the output pins, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is short but gives enough detail to understand the two main functions.
ttsky26a/tt_um_analog_RO.review_notes: Removed prng and logic-gate tags; the design is a TRNG and ring oscillator, not a PRNG or basic logic gate.

ttsky26a/tt_um_analog_atenfyr1.summary: This is a single-ended two-stage Miller-compensated operational transconductance amplifier with a self-biasing beta-multiplier current reference and configurable compensation, fabricated in SKY 130nm. The non-inverting and inverting inputs and the output are on analog pins, while two select pins configure the compensation and a beat output is provided. It is intended to be operated in feedback, for example as a unity-gain buffer by tying the inverting input to the output, from which the gain-bandwidth product can be estimated. The documentation is concise but clearly describes the circuit and a basic test configuration.
ttsky26a/tt_um_analog_atenfyr1.review_notes: Removed voltage-reference because the source only documents a current reference, not a reference voltage generator.

ttsky26a/tt_um_anweiteck_ldo.summary: This is a low-dropout linear regulator that accepts 1.2 V to 3 V on an analog input pin and produces a regulated 1 V output at up to 50 mA. A 0.6 V reference is applied on a separate analog pin, and the output appears on another analog pin. The documentation lists expected characteristics including 0.2 V dropout, 82 percent efficiency at 1.2 V input, 6.78 mV/V line regulation and 67 mV/A load regulation, along with schematic and layout images. Testing is simply a matter of connecting the input voltage and the 0.6 V reference and measuring the output.
ttsky26a/tt_um_anweiteck_ldo.review_notes: Removed transistor-level because the source does not document that the design is built from discrete transistors.

ttsky26a/tt_um_axi4lite2x2_top.summary: This design implements a dual-master, dual-slave AXI4-Lite interconnect that hides the AXI handshake behind a simplified interface. Start-write, start-read, address and write-data signals are driven from the input and bidirectional pins, and read data appears on the outputs, with a done indication. The top module instantiates an AXI4-Lite master and slave and drives the protocol signals internally when a transaction is started. Two testbenches are mentioned, but the provided documentation is truncated and does not describe the full test procedure or any silicon results.
ttsky26a/tt_um_axi4lite2x2_top.review_notes: Removed wishbone tag: design is AXI4-Lite, not Wishbone.

ttsky26a/tt_um_axi4lite_top.summary: This design implements an AXI4-Lite master and slave with a simplified interface for testing memory-mapped transactions. It allows the user to initiate read and write operations using simple input signals and provides a done flag on completion. Testbenches are provided to verify functionality. The module hides the complexity of the full AXI4-Lite protocol.
ttsky26a/tt_um_axi4lite_top.review_notes: Removed cocotb tag because the source only says testbenches are provided, not that they use cocotb.

ttsky26a/tt_um_bad_ode_plotter_vga.summary: This design plots the trajectory of a fixed system of two ordinary differential equations on a VGA display, using the coefficients a=0, b=-1, c=1, d=0. A reset transition from low to high starts the plotting, and cycling the reset restarts the trace from the beginning. It requires a 25 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to the output header. The author describes it as a very bad and very unstable plotter, and the documentation does not cover any silicon test results.

ttsky26a/tt_um_bch_code_15_7_2.summary: This is a hardware implementation of the BCH (15, 7) error-correcting code, which can correct up to two bit flips in a 7-bit message using an 8-bit checksum. It has two modes selected by the encode_enable pin: encoding produces the checksum from a clean message, and decoding recovers the original message from a corrupted message plus checksum. The datapath is pipelined into syndrome calculation, error location and Chien search stages, giving a three-cycle latency and one message per cycle throughput at 50 MHz. No external hardware is required, though LEDs may be used to visualize inputs and outputs.

ttsky26a/tt_um_bfcpu.summary: bfCPU implements a universal Turing machine as a superset of the Brainf*ck language. It is a 2x2 tile SystemVerilog design clocked at 10 MHz, with UART for serial communication and QSPI pins for memory access. The design is intended to be programmed and controlled via UART, though specific usage details are not provided. Documentation is limited to the title and pin names, so the exact instruction set and operation are not fully described.
ttsky26a/tt_um_bfcpu.review_notes: Removed fsm and education tags not supported by the very thin documentation.

ttsky26a/tt_um_bovi_cable_tester.summary: This design is an 8-wire DC continuity tester for Ethernet cables, driving each wire in turn and reporting per-wire pass/fail on eight LEDs. It requires a far-end shorting plug that ties all wires together and a near-end board with series resistors, pull-downs, and TVS diodes for protection. The chip continuously retests, allowing intermittent faults to be observed as flickering LEDs. It is a practical test tool rather than a data communication device, and its operation is well documented.

ttsky26a/tt_um_bubble_sort.summary: The IEEE Bubble Sort Engine is a hardware implementation of the bubble sort algorithm, accepting an 8-bit data stream and outputting sorted data. It uses a ready/valid handshake protocol with start, in_valid, in_last, out_ready, out_valid, and out_last signals. The design is a 1x1 tile with no external hardware required, as stated in the documentation. However, the documentation is minimal, providing only pin names and a brief description, so details of the sorting process and performance are not available.

ttsky26a/tt_um_c4m_spsram_direct.summary: TTSKY-SPSRAM-direct is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It provides address, write enable, data input, and data output signals, and performs read or write operations on each clock edge. The design is full custom and operates at 66 MHz, allowing it to be used as a standalone memory block. Testing involves writing data to an address and reading it back to verify functionality.
ttsky26a/tt_um_c4m_spsram_direct.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag as the source does not state discrete transistor construction.

ttsky26a/tt_um_canvas.summary: Tiny Canvas is a hardware drawing tool that mimics MS Paint, controlled by an SNES-compatible gamepad and outputting canvas coordinates and color data over I2C. It supports RGB color mixing, variable brush sizes, symmetry modes, and fill rectangle operations. The design requires a Gamepad PMOD and an SNES controller, and an I2C master device to render the canvas on a display. It is a 1x1 tile design that streams paint events in real-time to a host for a 256x256 canvas.
ttsky26a/tt_um_canvas.review_notes: Removed the display tag since rendering happens on the host, not on-chip.

ttsky26a/tt_um_catalinlazar_tinycore8.summary: TinyCore8 is an 8-bit programmable CPU with eight registers, a 4-bit program counter, and a simple accumulator-style instruction set. Programs are loaded serially through dedicated pins, and execution starts when the run signal is asserted. The CPU can perform ALU operations, branches, and I/O with a 4-bit input and 8-bit output. A smoke-test program is provided to demonstrate basic functionality.
ttsky26a/tt_um_catalinlazar_tinycore8.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not describe an educational purpose.

ttsky26a/tt_um_cfar_nobuzzer.summary: This project implements a Constant False Alarm Rate (CFAR) signal detection engine that processes a 14-bit ADC input and displays detection results on a 7-segment display. It uses an IIR running average to estimate the noise threshold and compares the input signal against a scaled threshold to detect targets. The design requires an external 14-bit signal source and a 7-segment display for visual feedback. It is a simplified version without a buzzer, optimized for area-constrained silicon.

ttsky26a/tt_um_chicagojones_sky26a_trng.summary: Sky26a Advanced TRNG is a true random number generator based on an 8-oscillator ring oscillator bank, with NIST health monitors and six chaotic whiteners. It provides random bytes via parallel output, UART, and SPI interfaces, and includes enable, auto mode, and tunable select pins. The design is a 2x2 tile and requires no external hardware beyond a standard Tiny Tapeout carrier board. It is intended for research-grade randomness generation with comprehensive characterization features.
