Two signal buffers route inputs through delay chains to verify path integrity. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external components such as a 7-segment decoder, LEDs, DIP switches, and a clock source for testing.
ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463666635153364993.review_notes: Removed driver because the buffer paths are delay-chain integrity checks, not a peripheral driver stage.

ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463698873100105729.summary: This project implements an 8-bit digital lock that compares an input pattern against a hard-coded master key (10110101) using a bit-matching architecture with inverters and an 8-input AND gate tree. When the correct pattern is entered via an external 8-bit DIP switch, a green LED lights up; otherwise, a red LED indicates failure. The design is purely combinational and requires only the DIP switch and two LEDs with resistors as external hardware. It is intended as an educational demonstration of pattern comparison and logic gates.

ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463706339714973697.summary: This project re-implements the 74181 4-bit ALU with inputs coming from programmable 2-bit and 4-bit registers to work within the pin constraints and demonstrate register operation. It deliberately avoids bidirectional pins and provides outputs for the ALU result, carry, and status flags. The design is educational, showing a step toward understanding basic CPU operation, and can be tested with simple external hardware like DIP switches and LEDs. The documentation notes that arbitrary external hardware can be used.

ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463711763041599489.summary: This project is an 8-bit UART transmitter that converts parallel ASCII data (characters 0x40 to 0x5F) into a standard UART frame using a parallel-in-serial-out shift register architecture. It uses D flip-flops and multiplexers to load data and then shift it out serially with start, stop, and idle bits. The design requires external DIP switches for input, a 7-segment display for debugging, status LEDs, and a logic analyzer or UART-to-USB converter to verify the serial output. It is implemented in Wokwi.
ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463711763041599489.review_notes: Removed education tag because the source does not describe an educational purpose.

ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463741407580251137.summary: This project is a 4-bit comparator that compares two 4-bit binary numbers A and B using logic gates to determine if A equals B, A is greater than B, or A is less than B. The result is displayed on a 7-segment display as the letters E, H, or L respectively. The design checks bits from MSB to LSB and uses OR logic to drive the display segments. It requires external switches for the inputs and a 7-segment display for output.
ttsky26a/tt_um_wokwi_463741407580251137.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the unsupported claim of educational intent from the summary.

ttsky26a/tt_um_xxsahanaxx_hwsec_glitch.summary: This project creates a hardware security glitch on a chip that can be detected using certain Trojan detection methods. It outputs VGA signals (R1, G1, B1, VSync, R0, G0, B0, HSync) and has inputs for speed and direction. The design is inspired by a Tiny Tapeout workshop and is intended for hardware security experimentation. Testing requires a main PCB that connects the chip to multiple peripherals and provides ports or jumpers for side-channel analysis.

ttsky26a/tt_um_yen.summary: This project implements an analog-controlled 8-pin multiplexer that selects among eight test circuits based on an input voltage from 0V to 1.8V, with thresholds every 200mV. The test circuits include various ring oscillators (3, 5, 7 inverters), frequency dividers using T flip-flops, and a resistor divider, allowing comprehensive testing of the design. The multiplexer uses only two analog pins: one for control voltage and one for the selected output. Testing requires a laboratory power supply, multimeter, and oscilloscope to measure frequencies and signal characteristics.

ttsky26a/tt_um_zed_analog.summary: This project contains two analog CMOS designs: three independent 2-input AND gates equivalent to the 7408, and an SR latch built from two cross-coupled NOR gates. The AND gates are constructed at the transistor level rather than from a digital library, while the latch sets, resets, or holds its state based on the s and r inputs. Testing the AND gates requires push buttons or DIP switches for inputs and LEDs on the outputs, whereas the latch needs no external hardware and can be verified by simulation or by observing q and qb. The design relies on the Tiny Tapeout padring for ESD protection and operates from the 1.8V VDPWR rail.
ttsky26a/tt_um_zed_analog.review_notes: Removed standard-cell tag as the source explicitly states transistor-level construction; logic-gate was already present in the proposed tags, so no add is needed.

ttsky26a/tt_um_zenith_tx26.summary: Zenith TX26 is a custom 16-bit CPU written in Verilog with eight registers, sixteen instructions, and a Harvard architecture separating instruction and data memory. It continuously computes the Fibonacci sequence and presents the current value in binary on its eight output pins. The design is tested by connecting eight LEDs to those outputs and watching the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, and so on. No external hardware beyond the optional LEDs is required, and the documentation is brief but sufficient to describe the architecture and use.

ttsky26b/tt_um_27jorge05_crc_fifo.summary: This design implements an IEEE 802.3 CRC-32 engine with polynomial 0xEDB88320, an 8-byte FIFO, and a one-bit-per-cycle serial processing path. It exposes a bidirectional register read interface with write, read, address, enable, and reset controls, plus an interrupt output, and it renders FIFO occupancy, FSM state, and all 32 CRC bits on a VGA display across two grid rows. A TinyVGA PMOD is required for the visual output, and a microcontroller such as an Arduino or RP2040 drives the input and bidirectional data buses. The project runs in a single clock domain at 25 MHz.
ttsky26b/tt_um_27jorge05_crc_fifo.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the design has a single CRC register and FIFO, not a multi-register file.

ttsky26b/tt_um_28add11_latchup.summary: This Verilog project generates a VGA scene of a grass field whose colors are chosen by a Fibonacci-based PRNG, with cloud height also driven by the random algorithm adapted from a rings demo. It outputs a Tiny VGA pinout and is used by connecting a TinyVGA PMOD and a monitor. The documentation is very short and does not describe the internal implementation beyond the PRNG and cloud adaptation. No silicon test results or additional hardware requirements are mentioned.

ttsky26b/tt_um_5tOTA.summary: This analog project implements a classic five-transistor operational transconductance amplifier with an NMOS differential pair, a PMOS active current mirror load, and a 5 microamp NMOS tail current source. The on-chip compensation capacitor is deliberately omitted to save area, so the dominant pole must be set externally with a 5 to 10 picofarad capacitor to ground for stability and a target 1.5 MHz bandwidth. Testing requires a 5 microamp bias current, a differential input with 0.9V common mode, and an oscilloscope or function generator for AC characterization. The design operates from the 1.8V VDPWR rail and is intended for off-chip loads with external compensation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_8_bit_cpu.summary: This project is an 8-bit CPU implemented in Verilog that performs arithmetic and load instructions and outputs the result of each instruction on eight output pins. It exposes an eight-bit input bus, a status pin, reset, clock, instruction enable, and four program counter bits on the bidirectional pins. Testing is done with a script that simulates the instruction register, waiting for the microcontroller to request a program counter value and returning the allocated instruction, allowing custom assembly programs to be swapped quickly. The documentation is a proposal-level description and does not detail the full instruction set or verified behavior.
ttsky26b/tt_um_8_bit_cpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported register-file and fsm tags; added verilog tag as the design is implemented in Verilog.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ALU_Porca.summary: This design is a configurable 8-bit ALU with registered inputs, eight arithmetic and logic operations, and eight configurable status flags. Inputs A and B arrive on the dedicated input pins, ALU control, register enable, and flag control come from the bidirectional pins, and the eight-bit result appears on the outputs with a status flag on a bidirectional pin. It requires synchronous operation with a toggling clock and an active-low reset pulse before use, and it is self-contained with no specialized external peripherals. The documentation describes the architecture as optimized for educational digital design and compact ASIC implementation, though the one-line description says 4-bit while the pins and title indicate 8-bit.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ALU_Porca.review_notes: Removed register-file tag because the source only describes registered inputs, not a register file.

ttsky26b/tt_um_AlephNaNsea_decentvgachip.summary: This Verilog project is a multi-application VGA graphics system that generates a 640x480 at 60Hz signal with all graphics computed combinatorially per pixel and no framebuffer or external memory. A mode multiplexer reads the input pins to select between a DLSU Animo shield with Galvantronix background, a cycling Hilbert curve of orders 1 to 5, and a maze game, with the maze taking priority when both select bits are high. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD, a VGA cable and monitor, and a DIP switch or button array on the input pins. The design fits in a single 1x1 tile and uses a 25.175 MHz pixel clock with frame counters driving the animations.

ttsky26b/tt_um_AlephNaNsea_space_time_wa.summary: This project is a purely combinatorial generative VGA video synthesizer written in Verilog that renders procedural art at 640x480 and 60Hz. It uses a custom VGA sync engine and screen-space coordinates, relying on bitwise operations and triangle waves instead of RAM or DSP blocks, with a frame counter driving animation over time. A multiplexer selects one of six art engines based on input pins, with a strict priority where ui_in[4] overrides the lower inputs. Testing requires a 25.175 MHz clock and a Tiny VGA PMOD or equivalent resistor-ladder DAC connected to a 640x480 monitor, with DIP switches or buttons on ui_in[4:0] to change modes. No silicon test reports are available.
ttsky26b/tt_um_AlephNaNsea_space_time_wa.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a programmable sequencer and state machine, which the source does not contain.

ttsky26b/tt_um_BFD100_Logic.summary: This Verilog design reads the five channels of a BFD1000 infrared line-follower sensor plus clip and near obstacle signals, and produces left and right motor enable and direction outputs according to a set of logic equations. It also accepts proportional and integral gain values and a select signal on the bidirectional pins, and can take a PWM input for speed control. The design is tested by connecting the sensor to the input pins and the motor drivers to the outputs, with simulations run on a Nexys4 FPGA using Vivado. External hardware includes the BFD1000 sensor and two motor drivers with LED indicators, and the documentation provides a full truth table and the derived logic equations.
ttsky26b/tt_um_BFD100_Logic.review_notes: Removed industrial tag as application is robotics/education, not industrial control.

ttsky26b/tt_um_BillNace_SumItUp.summary: This project is an instantiation of the SumItUp hardware thread from Don Thomas's textbook and CMU's 18-341 course, which accumulates a series of 8-bit values presented on the input pins. When go_l is asserted the thread begins adding subsequent values until the input equals zero, at which point done is asserted and the 8-bit sum appears on the outputs, with carry beyond eight bits discarded. No external hardware is required, and the author plans to write cocotb testbenches for verification. The design is a simple educational example of a hardware thread with a handshake interface.
ttsky26b/tt_um_BillNace_SumItUp.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm tag and added workshop for the course context.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Bio_SSG_.summary: This analog design generates a differential sinusoidal signal at approximately 25 kHz using a digital-to-analog converter and a low-pass filter. It is intended for bio-applications and requires external precision voltage references and an oscilloscope for testing. The design uses standard-cell-based analog techniques, including fully integrated capacitors and ultra-low-voltage OTAs. It operates from a 2.56 MHz clock and provides differential outputs on two analog pins.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Bio_SSG_.review_notes: Removed unsupported oscillator tag; added mixed-signal for the combined digital/analog signal path.

ttsky26b/tt_um_CFG_WDT.summary: This design implements a configurable 32-bit watchdog timer with optional password protection. It features a down-counter that generates a timeout event if not fed, and supports password modes to prevent accidental writes. The design is verified using Cocotb simulation, covering reset, enable, timeout, password, and feed functionality. It requires no external hardware and is intended for integration into larger systems.
ttsky26b/tt_um_CFG_WDT.review_notes: Removed 'security' tag as password protection alone does not constitute a hardware security design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_CNN4IC_sky.summary: This design is a hardware convolutional neural network accelerator that classifies 10x10 pixel images using two 5x5 kernels. It communicates over SPI to load image and weight data, trigger inference, and read results. The design includes a state machine that processes the image in fragments, performs multiply-accumulate operations, and uses max-pooling to produce a classification. It requires an external SPI master for control and data transfer.

ttsky26b/tt_um_DlynchR_spi_display.summary: This design implements an SPI slave that receives 8-bit data and displays it as a 2-digit hexadecimal value on a multiplexed 3-digit 7-segment display. It synchronizes SPI signals to the system clock and generates a receive valid pulse. The display controller time-multiplexes the digits at approximately 333 Hz. External hardware includes an SPI master and a common-anode 7-segment display.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Edward2005lol_Slot_Machin.summary: This design implements a slot machine game with three reels displaying four possible symbols on a VGA screen. The game starts with random flashing symbols, and pressing the start button initiates spinning that stops each reel sequentially. It requires a 25 MHz clock, two push buttons for start and reset, and a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to a VGA monitor. The design is a simple interactive game with no additional external components.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Edward2005lol_Slot_Machin.review_notes: Removed prng because the source does not describe a pseudo-random number generator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Floppy_LIGHT.summary: This design is a VGA-based mini-game inspired by Flappy Bird, where the player controls a logo that must avoid scrolling pipes. It includes features such as pause, hard mode, and score tracking, with controls mapped to input pins. The game outputs VGA signals to a TinyVGA PMOD and requires a VGA monitor or simulator. The design is implemented in Verilog and uses a bitmap ROM for the player sprite.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Floppy_LIGHT.review_notes: Removed button and rom tags (no button interface, ROM is internal detail); added pong for the arcade game style.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Halcy0nnnn.summary: This design displays the MMU Cybertron logo on a VGA screen. It provides inputs to tile the logo across the screen and enable color output. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. It is a simple visual display project with minimal documentation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Halcy0nnnn.review_notes: Removed unsupported button tag; the design has no button input.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Halcy0nnnn_1.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen. It includes inputs for tiling, color enable, color index selection, and vertical flipping. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. It is a simple visual display project with minimal documentation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Halcy0nnnn_1.review_notes: Removed unsupported button and silicon-art tags; added art for the decorative logo display.

ttsky26b/tt_um_IEEE_OpenSilicon_Submissi.summary: This design generates the IEEE logo bouncing around on a VGA screen, with the color changeable via a button. It is a submission to the Open Silicon 2026 workshop and requires a VGA display. The design is simple and uses no external hardware beyond a laptop to run and display the output. The documentation is minimal.
ttsky26b/tt_um_IEEE_OpenSilicon_Submissi.review_notes: Replaced silicon-art with art since the design is a VGA logo animation rather than a silicon layout artwork.

ttsky26b/tt_um_IEEE_perceptron.summary: This design implements a single artificial neuron (perceptron) in pure combinational logic. It takes four binary inputs, each multiplied by a 2-bit weight, sums them, and compares the result to a configurable threshold to produce a binary output. Weights and threshold are set via input pins, making it fully reconfigurable without re-synthesis. The design includes a cocotb testbench and requires no external hardware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_IEEE_perceptron.review_notes: Removed 'adder' as it is a sub-component rather than the primary design function; all other tags and summary are supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_KK_VGA01.summary: This design implements a motocross racing game for up to four players, each controlling a bike with a single button. It outputs a VGA signal to display the game track and uses bidirectional pins to select among four tracks and set game speed. The design is notable for supporting four simultaneous players with minimal controls and is based on an open-source project. It is implemented in Verilog.
ttsky26b/tt_um_KK_VGA01.review_notes: Removed incorrect wokwi tag; added game, vga, graphics and gpio tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_LAT.summary: The design displays either the Automation Laboratory logo or an author image through a VGA interface. Input pins select the image and control color. It outputs standard VGA red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync signals. The design is intended to be connected to a VGA monitor using a VGA PMOD board.
ttsky26b/tt_um_LAT.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect VGA image display rather than analog oscillator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Madd_CS_Ring_Osc.summary: This design implements a voltage controlled ring oscillator whose frequency can be adjusted by an external control voltage or by an internal 8-bit DAC. The DAC is enabled by holding the DAC_enable pin high. An additional output provides the oscillator signal divided by 64 for easier measurement. The design is intended to be tested by varying the control voltage or DAC bits and observing the output frequency.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Madd_CS_Ring_Osc.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the analog ring oscillator/DAC design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Medidor_Jitter.summary: This design is a high-precision digital jitter meter that characterizes signal integrity in high-speed digital systems up to 50 MHz. It measures the temporal displacement of a target signal relative to a reference clock using a 17-bit synchronous counter running at 50 MHz. The core includes an arithmetic unit, a register bank for maximum and minimum jitter and sample counts, a UART protocol FSM, and a hardware gate pin to pause and resume measurements. It requires an external microcontroller and USB-to-UART adapter to configure parameters and retrieve results.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Medidor_Jitter.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary describe an unrelated SPI multiplier/CORDIC design; corrected to the jitter meter.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Mitchell_s_Approximation_.summary: This design implements a multiplier-less EML gate using Mitchell's approximation for energy-efficient transcendental processing in ASICs. It includes an SPI interface for communication. The design is notable for its approximate computing approach to reduce power consumption.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Mitchell_s_Approximation_.review_notes: Removed unsupported tags and added tags based on the title and pin names.

ttsky26b/tt_um_NUPlace2.summary: This is the VAK FSM replacement for the VAK lab PCB board at Northwestern. It interfaces to an ADC through 12 data bits, end-of-conversion and conversion-start signals, and to SPI devices via spi_clk, MOSI and MISO. Chip selects for FRAM and LoRA, plus sensor and radio VCC enables, are provided on the outputs. It is written in SystemVerilog and will be tested locally, with no external hardware required at this time.
ttsky26b/tt_um_NUPlace2.review_notes: Proposed UART/LFSR/comparator tags and summary were unrelated to the SPI/ADC/radio FSM source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Nay0805_detector_de_patro.summary: This design receives an 8-bit serial data byte through a UART and stores it in a parallel register. An LFSR generates a pseudo-random 8-bit pattern, and a pattern detector compares the received byte with the generated pattern. If the values match, a match signal is activated on the output LEDs. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires no mandatory external hardware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Nay0805_detector_de_patro.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the UART, LFSR, and comparator described in the source; original tags and summary described an unrelated traffic light controller.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_Freq_Divider_Dig.summary: This design is a digital clock frequency divider that generates several divided clock signals from a user-selected M value. A counter counts to M-1 to enable a pulse, and a 7-bit counter then produces outputs divided by powers of two from 1/2 up to 1/128. The user selects the M module with switches on the dedicated inputs, and no external hardware is needed. The design is written in Verilog and is intended as a clock generation utility.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_Freq_Divider_Dig.review_notes: Replaced unrelated analog/voltage-reference tags and summary with the actual digital clock-divider function described by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_TrafficLight.summary: This design implements a traffic light controller as a finite state machine. It uses an instantiated clock frequency divider module for internal counting and timing. After the start input is set, the red light remains active for 30 seconds, then the green light for 20 seconds, with yellow transitions of 3 seconds. Three different color LEDs are optional external hardware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_TrafficLight.review_notes: Replaced unrelated oscillator/DAC tags and summary with the traffic-light FSM described in the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_Trimmed_BandGap.summary: This analog design implements a 1.2V CMOS bandgap voltage reference with a 3-bit resistor trimming network for PVT variation compensation. It uses a beta multiplier amplifier topology with a folded cascode OTA and provides two output nodes for measurement. Testing requires high-impedance measurement equipment to avoid loading the unbuffered outputs. The design is notable for its trimming capability and analog implementation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_adder_NM.summary: This project is a structural 4-bit ripple carry adder built from one half adder and three full adders, producing a 5-bit sum from two 4-bit unsigned inputs. The eight input pins carry operands A and B, and the five low output pins carry the sum and final carry-out, with the upper outputs tied low. It is purely combinational, with clock, reset and enable tied off internally to satisfy the synthesis flow. No external hardware is required beyond the demoboard switches and LEDs, and the documentation is clear and complete.
ttsky26b/tt_um_Onchip_adder_NM.review_notes: Removed alu because the block is a dedicated ripple carry adder rather than a general ALU.

ttsky26b/tt_um_RO_aging.summary: This is a 13-stage ring oscillator with an integrated 12-stage divider that scales the native frequency down by 4096 for off-chip measurement. It is intended for silicon aging studies, where elevated supply stress accelerates bias temperature instability and hot carrier injection, and the resulting frequency drop quantifies degradation. The analog pins expose the oscillator output plus header, footer, gate and drain sense/force nodes for the device under test. Testing needs a 1.8 V supply, a low-capacitance probe, an oscilloscope or frequency counter, and a way to drive the enable input.

ttsky26b/tt_um_RaphRaphyRofl_VerilogIEEE.summary: This design generates a VGA signal at 25.175 MHz showing the letters IEEE bouncing around the screen. It has no user controls and simply runs from the clock and reset, with the eight outputs wired to the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout. The only external hardware needed is a VGA PMOD and a compatible monitor. The documentation is very thin, noting only that the Verilog was produced with Gemini, so little can be said about the internal implementation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_RaphRaphyRofl_VerilogIEEE.review_notes: Removed demoscene tag not supported by the source; summary left unchanged.

ttsky26b/tt_um_Richard_Tarqui_contador_u.summary: This design combines a programmable countdown timer, a frequency meter with a one-second gate window, and a falling-edge pulse counter in a single tile. It is controlled over a 115200 baud 8N1 UART using ASCII commands such as setting an HH:MM:SS window and starting a measurement, and it returns telemetry frames on the transmit pin. An external signal source connects to the measurement input, and status pins indicate frame completion and active measurement. Testing requires a USB-to-UART bridge, a serial terminal and a signal or pulse generator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_STDCELL_LDO.summary: This is a low dropout voltage regulator that regulates its output using a reference voltage. The four analog pins provide the input, an output capacitor node, analog ground and the regulator output. Testing is described only as using a voltage source, with a power source and oscilloscope listed as external equipment. The documentation is extremely sparse, giving no information on dropout, load range, current capability or measured performance.
ttsky26b/tt_um_STDCELL_LDO.review_notes: Removed voltage-reference because the source only mentions using a reference voltage, not implementing one.

ttsky26b/tt_um_SollysLe_mac_8bits.summary: This design is an 8x8-to-16-bit multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with a 2-cycle 8-bit serial interface for data input and output. It supports both signed and unsigned arithmetic and includes overflow detection and clear functionality. The MAC is intended for DSP applications and fits within the TinyTapeout I/O constraints by using a serial protocol. No external hardware is required beyond the standard clock and reset.
ttsky26b/tt_um_SollysLe_mac_8bits.review_notes: Removed alu; added multiplier and accumulator to match the MAC function.

ttsky26b/tt_um_abhinavputhran_raycast.summary: This is a Wolfenstein-style raycaster that renders a 3D maze from a hardcoded 32x32 grid into a 640x480 VGA signal at 25 MHz, using one scanline per vertical scene column. Player position and angle are updated once per vsync, with direction stored as a 6-bit index into a 64-entry lookup table and wall height derived from a reciprocal lookup. Buttons on the inputs move and turn the player, a demo mode walks forward automatically, and two bits select the wall colour. It needs a VGA PMOD and a 640x480 monitor, and the bidirectional pins expose the angle index and debug position bits.

ttsky26b/tt_um_adithya_selvakumar_vco.summary: This is a current-controlled 4-stage differential ring VCO in SKY130 with buffered rail-to-rail outputs providing four quadrature phases at 45 degree spacing. Frequency is set by an external control current mirrored into the PFET loads and NFET tail sources of each stage, with a tuning range of roughly 200 kHz to 3 MHz. One analog pin takes the control current and another exposes the internal bias voltage for monitoring. Testing requires a current source or resistor network plus an oscilloscope or frequency counter, and the design is based on a published reference circuit.
ttsky26b/tt_um_adithya_selvakumar_vco.review_notes: Removed transistor-level because the source describes a standard analog VCO topology, not discrete-transistor construction.

ttsky26b/tt_um_advaittej_stopwatch.summary: This is an interactive 1Hz stopwatch with hardware debouncing, lap memory, alarm target, and 9600-baud UART RX/TX telemetry. It uses a 10 MHz clock and includes modules for debouncing, BCD counting, alarm comparison, and UART communication. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires external hardware such as a 7-segment display, push-buttons, DIP switches, and a USB-to-TTL serial cable for full testing. It was developed as part of the V-SPACE Demo.
ttsky26b/tt_um_advaittej_stopwatch.review_notes: Removed unsupported instrumentation tag; added pmod tag for the specified 7-segment PMOD.

ttsky26b/tt_um_advun.summary: This block compresses 8-bit trace data in a single clock cycle using four packet types: run-length encoding, delta run-length encoding, small signed delta, and raw. It was originally developed for an FPGA and is meant to reduce the memory needed to store high-rate signal traces before readout. Input data arrives on the eight input pins, and the outputs carry the compressed byte, a two-bit packet code and a save strobe that indicates whether the value should be stored. Testing is expected on a Basys3 FPGA board that supplies inputs and captures outputs, and the documentation notes that run-length modes emit no packets until interrupted or overflowing.

ttsky26b/tt_um_aelobo.summary: This design is a three-mode clock and timer that shows a clock, a date, or a Pomodoro countdown on an external MAX7219 8-digit 7-segment display driven over SPI. Four breadboard buttons enter and leave setup mode, cycle modes and fields, increment or decrement values, and start, pause or reset the Pomodoro. Eight LED outputs report the display mode, setup state, work and break phases, alarm, and selected field. It needs the MAX7219 display and buttons as external hardware, and the documentation is brief but consistent with the pin names.

ttsky26b/tt_um_akim_tinydma.summary: This is a two-channel byte DMA engine that moves data to and from an external SPI PSRAM device. Configuration bytes are loaded on the input pins with a valid strobe, a start pin triggers operation, and the SPI master pins connect to the memory. Status outputs report DMA activity, completion pulses per channel, pending configuration and configuration errors. It targets a QSPI PMOD with an APS6404 PSRAM used in single-bit SPI mode, and the documentation covers the pin mapping but not the internal architecture or measured throughput.
ttsky26b/tt_um_akim_tinydma.review_notes: Removed unsupported qspi tag and added systemverilog and multi-tile tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_alu7b.summary: This is a 7-bit ALU that accepts two operands serially, LSB first, on a single input pin and produces an 8-bit parallel result. The opcode is a stable 3-bit parallel input selecting ADD, AND, OR, XOR or SUB, and a Done pin pulses high for one clock cycle when the result is valid. It needs no external hardware for simulation; on a devkit, LEDs, buttons or a logic analyser can be used to observe results and protocol timing. The design is a straightforward IEEE-style student exercise with clear pin documentation but no reported silicon measurements.
ttsky26b/tt_um_alu7b.review_notes: Removed uart: the serial input is a custom bit-serial protocol, not UART framing.

ttsky26b/tt_um_alu8bit.summary: This 8-bit ALU loads two operands into internal registers A and B from an 8-bit data bus and executes arithmetic, logic and shift operations selected by a 3-bit opcode. Control signals on the bidirectional pins trigger loading and execution, and the result appears on the 8-bit output with zero and carry flags. The documentation gives a worked example of adding 7 and 5, and no external hardware is required beyond switches and LEDs on a demo board. It is a simple teaching-oriented design with no silicon test results reported.
ttsky26b/tt_um_alu8bit.review_notes: Removed register-file: only two operand registers are present, not a register file.

ttsky26b/tt_um_alu_7bits.summary: This project is a 7-bit arithmetic logic unit that works sequentially, taking serial input and producing parallel output. The pin names show a single serial data input, three opcode bits and a 7-bit data output with a Done signal, but there is no documentation of the instruction set or protocol. No external hardware or test procedure is described. The documentation is essentially limited to the title and pin list, so most details are inferred.
ttsky26b/tt_um_alu_7bits.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and corrected the output width to 7 bits per pin names.

ttsky26b/tt_um_amarjay.summary: mini_cpu is a minimal 8-bit accumulator-based processor with a compact custom instruction set stored in an internal ROM. It runs a fixed program that drives an 8-bit LED output in a Knight Rider-style scanner pattern, with optional input switches that are not required for basic operation. Testing consists of applying a slow clock, holding reset for at least ten cycles, then observing the LED outputs. The design is self-contained and emphasises small area and simple synchronous behaviour, but no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26b/tt_um_amarjay.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added led which is already present in the summary and pins.

ttsky26b/tt_um_amin_hong_ooo_cpu.summary: This is a small out-of-order CPU that includes an instruction queue, register alias table, reorder buffer and reservation stations. Instructions are fed in through the input pins and results are read from the output pins, with a testbench driving the design via io_in. No external hardware is needed because it runs entirely inside the Tiny Tapeout framework. The documentation is brief, giving only a pipeline outline and no measured results, so most architectural detail is inferred from the title and pin names.
ttsky26b/tt_um_amin_hong_ooo_cpu.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc tag because documentation is present and describes the pipeline.

ttsky26b/tt_um_analog_ota_v3_IEEE.summary: This analog block is a unity-gain buffer built from a two-stage Miller operational transconductance amplifier, together with a beta-multiplier reference and a startup circuit in the sky130 process. It is intended as the building block for a continuous-time Gm-C filter and is tested with a 3 pF load, square-wave pulses between 0.5 V and 1.0 V, DC sweeps and a 0 to 1.8 V supply ramp. External equipment includes a signal generator, 1.8 V supply, oscilloscope, 3 pF capacitor and multimeter, and the documentation warns that probe capacitance can degrade phase margin. Simulated figures such as 18.65 V/us slew rate and over 60 dB open-loop gain are quoted, but no measured silicon data are given.
ttsky26b/tt_um_analog_ota_v3_IEEE.review_notes: Removed bandgap (beta-multiplier, not bandgap) and transistor-level (no discrete transistor evidence); added voltage-reference and mixed-signal.

ttsky26b/tt_um_andriansyah_capless_ldo.summary: This is a capless low-dropout linear regulator with a 1.27 V output and a claimed 51.1 dB power-supply rejection ratio at 100 kHz. It is tested by sweeping the input voltage from 1.62 V to 1.98 V while monitoring the output. An oscilloscope and function generator are listed as the required external hardware. The documentation is very brief, consisting of a single sentence plus the test condition, so no load range, current capability or silicon measurements are described.

ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design1_top.summary: This design classifies water quality from eight digital sensor inputs by extracting peak, average and variation features and mapping them to clean, warning or unsafe states. It is simulated with cocotb and can be exercised in the lab by feeding a function generator through a comparator or ADC into the sensor pins. External hardware for lab testing includes a function generator and optionally a comparator or Arduino ADC interface. The approach uses electrical signal behaviour as a proxy for chemical water quality, and no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design1_top.review_notes: Removed dsp tag (no DSP algorithms) and added biomedical and instrumentation tags for the water-quality monitoring application.

ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design2_top.summary: This is a multi-mode digital signal processing unit that takes two 8-bit inputs and selects one of four operations from their low bits: FIR filtering, multiply-accumulate, edge detection or nonlinear compression. It keeps a previous output value so that some modes depend on past data, and the output updates every clock cycle. Testing is done with a cocotb testbench that cycles through all modes and produces a VCD waveform for inspection in GTKWave. No external hardware is required and no silicon measurements are reported.
ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design2_top.review_notes: Compression tag removed because the documented mode is nonlinear signal compression, not data compression; the summary otherwise matches the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design3_top.summary: This design implements a heat stress alert system that counts pulses on a single input pin, using pulse frequency as a proxy for temperature, and classifies the condition into safe, warm, high risk or critical. The state is continuously driven to four output pins and can be observed in simulation with a generated pulse stimulus. For real use, a signal generator can drive the input directly, or a temperature sensor can be connected through a microcontroller that converts readings to pulse frequency. The documentation is clear but brief, and no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26b/tt_um_arfanghani_design3_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'biomedical' tag; the rest of the proposed tags are supported.

ttsky26b/tt_um_array_mult_vga.summary: This design implements a structural 4x4 array multiplier using 12 full adders, producing an 8-bit product from two 4-bit inputs. It displays the multiplication as a decimal equation on a 640x480 VGA monitor via the Tiny VGA PMOD, along with the designers' initials and the Purdue Fort Wayne mascot. Inputs are provided through bare solder pads for direct cable connections. The project is notable for its educational visualization of a classic digital design and its use of VGA output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ascon_cxof_chain.summary: This is an ASCON-CXOF128 hash-chain hardware accelerator with a UART-framed protocol supporting single-shot and n-iteration chain modes. It communicates over UART at 115200 baud, 8-N-1, using framed commands with CRC16-CCITT and status responses. The design exposes done, busy, error, debug, heartbeat and receive-active signals on its outputs. Testing requires a UART host and involves sending PING, configuring registers, loading data, starting the hash, and reading the result.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ascon_cxof_chain.review_notes: Replaced incorrect RISC-V/QSPI/CPU/FPGA/GPIO/memory tags with crypto, hash, UART, accelerator, Verilog and CRC tags matching the ASCON accelerator documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_authQV.summary: This die is the memory-controller half of the authQV RISC-V system, containing a QSPI flash controller and an 8-phase parallel-bus bridge that exposes the memory-fetch interface to a companion FPGA. The actual RV32E CPU runs on the FPGA, and this chip only services flash reads for instruction fetch and read-only data loads. It requires a QSPI flash module and a companion FPGA running the CPU and block RAM. The design is notable for its split architecture and the use of a free-running 8-phase counter for synchronized communication.

ttsky26b/tt_um_auth_dmac.summary: This project implements an 8-bit DMA controller for transferring data between memory and I/O devices, structured as a finite state machine. The documentation provides a state-by-state explanation and a state diagram, but the provided excerpt does not include the full details. Testing is done via a cocotb-based Python testbench with Icarus Verilog. The design is notable for its DMA functionality in a small footprint.
ttsky26b/tt_um_auth_dmac.review_notes: Removed unsupported gpio tag and added cocotb tag for the stated testbench.

ttsky26b/tt_um_baby_cpu.summary: This design is a minimal 8-bit CPU with an accumulator architecture, featuring 16 bytes of program ROM and 16 bytes of data RAM. It executes one instruction per clock cycle and supports arithmetic, logic, memory, branching, and I/O instructions. The default program continuously reads external inputs, stores them in the accumulator, and outputs them to dedicated and bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required, but optional switches, LEDs, or a logic analyzer can be used for demonstration.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bad_apple.summary: This design generates a VGA animation that alternates between a U-shaped pattern and a spinning W, using combinational logic and a finite state machine. The U-state uses bullet-shaped areas to form a U that moves, while the W-state simulates a rotating plane using a lookup table for sin/cos values. The chip requires a VGA connection and is tested by uploading MicroPython code to a Raspberry Pi on the Tiny Tapeout board to set the clock and display the output. The project is notable for its creative visual effects within the constraints of the chip.
ttsky26b/tt_um_bad_apple.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added art tag for the decorative animation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bartu_kripto.summary: This design is a lightweight 64-bit symmetric encryption/decryption core that uses a 32-bit key to generate a keystream, which is then XORed with the data. It loads data and key bytes through dedicated input pins and control signals on the bidirectional pins, and outputs status or data on the output pins. The core performs encryption and decryption using the same operation, making it a simple demonstration of symmetric cryptography. No external hardware is required beyond the Tiny Tapeout interface.

ttsky26b/tt_um_basic8.summary: Basic8 is a minimal 8-bit CPU with 8 general-purpose registers, an ALU supporting arithmetic, logic, and shift operations, and branch and jump instructions. Instructions are 16 bits wide and are loaded in two cycles via the input pins, with the program counter output on the output pins to allow an external controller to feed instructions from a ROM. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench covering the full instruction set. No external hardware is required, as the CPU is driven entirely through the pins.

ttsky26b/tt_um_basic_na.summary: This design plays the Turkish National Anthem as a square-wave melody on a piezo buzzer connected to the output pin. It includes a start/restart button input and a loop mode input, and outputs a playing indicator LED and the current note address for debugging. External hardware includes a piezo buzzer or small speaker with a series resistor, and optionally an LED and push button. The project is notable for its specific cultural application and simple implementation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bfloat16.summary: This design is an SPI accelerator for continuous bfloat16 operations, supporting addition, subtraction, and multiplication on an accumulator. It uses a mode-0 SPI interface with 16-bit words, where the first word defines the operation and subsequent words are operands, with the accumulator value returned on MISO. The module is designed for a 50 MHz clock and recommends SPI clock frequencies up to 6.25 Mbps. It requires an external microcontroller with SPI, and an Arduino test program is provided.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bgr.summary: This project implements a bandgap voltage reference in the SkyWater 130nm process, producing an approximately 0.9V analog output on ua[0]. The design is written in Verilog but is an analog macro, with all digital inputs unused. It requires external measurement equipment to verify the reference voltage. The documentation is minimal, providing only the output voltage and pin assignment, so little else can be said about its implementation or performance.
ttsky26b/tt_um_bgr.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level and power-management tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_blackjack.summary: This design implements a complete Blackjack card game in Verilog for a 1x1 Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a finite state machine to manage game flow, an LFSR for card randomness, and outputs game status via LEDs and a 3-bit sum to a 7-segment display. The game is controlled by hit and stand buttons, with win/lose/push indicated by LEDs. External hardware needed includes a clock source, push buttons, LEDs, and a 7-segment display; button debouncing is optional.
ttsky26b/tt_um_blackjack.review_notes: Removed prng because the source only documents an LFSR for card generation; added puzzle for the card-game logic.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc2.summary: This project is a generative art piece that creates recursive rectangle patterns, described as 'silicon cross stitch', on a 2x2 tile canvas. It is written in Verilog and has a single dummy output pin, with no inputs or control interface. The design is purely visual and requires no external hardware; it is meant to be observed rather than tested. The documentation is very sparse, offering only a brief description and no technical details.
ttsky26b/tt_um_bleeptrack_cc2.review_notes: Removed pattern-generator (test-pattern meaning) and added multi-tile for the 2x2 canvas.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bn_lif_evan.summary: This design combines a Bernoulli stochastic multiplier, a conventional 4x4 unsigned multiplier, and a leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron on a single tile. The stochastic multiplier uses two LFSRs to generate random thresholds and estimates the product of two 4-bit probabilities over a window of cycles, while the conventional multiplier provides an exact product for comparison. The LIF neuron is a signed 8-bit integer model with configurable threshold, reset, and decay, and outputs a spike and membrane potential. The design is selected via two project select pins and requires no external hardware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_bn_lif_evan.review_notes: Removed alu, dsp, and neural-network; added multiplier, lfsr, prng, spiking-neural-network, stochastic-computing, and systemverilog to match the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_bytex64_wave_hi.summary: This design generates a VGA output showing a pseudo-3D sine wave ribbon animation and also produces simple music via an audio output pin. It requires a 25.175 MHz clock and external VGA and audio PMODs to view and hear the output. The documentation is incomplete, with a TODO note, but the pinout matches the Tiny VGA and TT Audio standards. The project is a light-hearted demo, as indicated by its description.
ttsky26b/tt_um_bytex64_wave_hi.review_notes: Added synthesizer tag to better capture the simple music generation feature.

ttsky26b/tt_um_c0d3d1_ldo.summary: This project is a low-dropout (LDO) linear regulator implemented in an analog process, capable of supplying 0.1 to 4 mA at an output voltage of 1.4 to 1.8V. It consists of a BJT bandgap reference, two op-amps, and a pass PMOS transistor, with an external reference current set by a 90k resistor. The output voltage is available on ua[0], and testing requires a multimeter. The documentation is brief but provides the essential information for basic operation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_c0d3d1_ldo.review_notes: Removed transistor-level: the design is an analog LDO built from a bandgap, op-amps and a pass PMOS, not a discrete-transistor implementation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_c4m_legacyspsram_direct.summary: This design is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It uses a legacy layout bit cell, which is larger than a thin-cell version, and is kept for historical reasons. The SRAM operates on a 66 MHz clock, with read and write operations controlled by a write-enable signal, and write-through behavior. Testing involves performing read and write operations and verifying data retention.
ttsky26b/tt_um_c4m_legacyspsram_direct.review_notes: Removed gpio tag because the interface is a dedicated SRAM port, not general purpose IO.

ttsky26b/tt_um_c4m_spsram_direct.summary: TTSKY-SPSRAM-direct is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins. It provides address, write enable, data input, and data output signals, and performs read or write operations on each clock edge. The design is full custom and operates at 66 MHz, allowing it to be used as a standalone memory block. Testing involves writing data to an address and reading it back to verify functionality.
ttsky26b/tt_um_c4m_spsram_direct.review_notes: Removed transistor-level tag as the source does not state discrete transistor construction.

ttsky26b/tt_um_c4m_spsram_direct_librela.summary: This design is a single-port SRAM block with 128 words of 8 bits, directly connected to the Tiny Tapeout tile pins, using the same SRAM block as TTSKY-SPSRAM-direct but with pin connections made via librelane. It operates on a 66 MHz clock and supports read and write operations with write-through behavior. The design is intended for use as a standalone SRAM block, and testing involves verifying read and write functionality. The use of librelane for pin connection is notable.

ttsky26b/tt_um_calebulboaca_calebchecker.summary: This project is a VGA-based checkers game with modified layer movements and colors, based on a VGA playground design. It outputs VGA signals on the standard Tiny VGA pinout and requires a 25.175 MHz clock. The design is meant to be viewed on a VGA monitor, and no external hardware beyond a VGA connection is specified. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text for external hardware, so details of gameplay or implementation are limited.

ttsky26b/tt_um_catalinlazar_adpll_125m_s.summary: This design implements a 127-stage coarse-tapped all-digital phase-locked loop (ADPLL) targeting 125 MHz in the SkyWater 130nm process. It features a structural digitally controlled oscillator (DCO) built from a 127-stage ring oscillator with coarse frequency tapping to switch between full and shortened loops. The feedback loop uses a synchronous digital divider, and the design includes pins for reference clock selection, reset, tap selection, and division ratio configuration. Testing involves applying reset, selecting the reference clock, configuring the tap and division settings, and monitoring the output clock and raw DCO clock.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ccollatz_SO.summary: This design computes the Collatz orbit for an 8-bit input, outputting the number of iterations to reach 1 and a busy status bit. It is controlled by a clock and active-low reset, with the input and iteration count presented on the ui and uio pins respectively. The circuit holds the final iteration count indefinitely after completion for inspection. No external hardware is required beyond switches for input, and the documentation is sufficient to understand its operation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_chaotic_rng.summary: This project implements a programmable chaotic random number generator based on a 3D double-scroll chaotic map. It uses three 32-bit state variables updated each clock cycle with arithmetic feedback and nonlinear functions, producing an 8-bit random output. The chaotic parameters are partially programmable via input pins, allowing configuration of the nonlinear function. No external hardware is required, and the design is documented with details on its internal state and programmability.
ttsky26b/tt_um_chaotic_rng.review_notes: Removed dsp and stochastic-computing; the source describes a chaotic-map RNG, not DSP or stochastic computing.

ttsky26b/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttsky26b/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttsky26b/tt_um_chronoINAAL.summary: This is a digital stopwatch implemented in Verilog with start/stop and lap functions. It displays hundredths of a second and seconds on a multiplexed 4-digit 7-segment display, using two buttons for control. The design requires external 7-segment displays and buttons to operate. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pinout and a one-line description, so detailed operation and testing procedures are not specified.

ttsky26b/tt_um_coffee_chip.summary: The Coffee Chip is a hardware-based color classifier for sorting coffee beans into unripe, optimal, and overripe categories. It interfaces with a TCS3200 color sensor to measure frequency signals and uses a digital state machine to classify the beans, indicating results via LEDs. The design supports optional UART calibration to update classification thresholds. External hardware includes the color sensor, LEDs, and optionally a UART bridge, and the documentation provides detailed testing steps.

ttsky26b/tt_um_cordic_ieee.summary: This design implements a CORDIC-based math processor that computes sine and cosine functions for a 16-bit fixed-point angle input. The angle is loaded serially in 4-bit chunks, and the result is output as a 16-bit fixed-point value, selectable between sine and cosine. No external hardware is required, and the testing procedure is clearly described, including fixed-point conversion steps. The design is notable for its use of the CORDIC algorithm to calculate trigonometric functions in hardware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_cordic_ieee.review_notes: Removed signal-generator and alu (unsupported); added fixed-point which is already described in the summary.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ctw_ldo.summary: This project is an analog Low Dropout Regulator designed in the SkyWater 130 nm process, targeting a 1.3 V output from a 1.5 V input with load currents up to 10 mA. It includes a current generator, error amplifier, push-pull composite power transistor, feedback network, and load circuit. Extensive pre-layout simulation results are provided for quiescent current, dropout voltage, load and line regulation, startup, transient response, PSRR, and open-loop gain. The design is notable for its detailed analog documentation and supply-independent current circuit, but silicon validation would require external test equipment such as a DC power supply, electronic load, and oscilloscope.

ttsky26b/tt_um_cycho.summary: This project is a simplified memory controller that simulates DRAM read/write behavior with request queuing, bank-row-column address decoding, and a fake memory. It services requests from a testbench CPU in order, using a bank table to track open rows, though the final design includes only one bank, two rows, and two columns to reduce area. The controller runs at 50 MHz and has a defined interface for read and write transactions. Testing was done with SystemVerilog testbenches and cocotb, and no external hardware is needed.
ttsky26b/tt_um_cycho.review_notes: Removed arbiter tag because the design only services queued requests in order and does not implement arbitration.

ttsky26b/tt_um_d_4_array_multiplier.summary: This design is a 4x4 structural array multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers using full adders and AND gates. It takes an 8-bit input that is split into two 4-bit operands and outputs the 8-bit product. The multiplier is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. The documentation describes the multiplication process and suggests testing with various input values, but does not provide detailed test results or silicon validation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_datdt_charizard.summary: This project displays a Charizard sprite with a flamethrower animation on a VGA monitor. It uses sprite ROM lookups, palette mapping, and state-based rendering logic to produce real-time animation at a 25.175 MHz clock. The design requires a VGA display and appropriate connections, with no other external hardware. The documentation notes that the original plan for a full evolution line was scaled back due to area constraints, and the final design uses a 1x2 tile area.
ttsky26b/tt_um_datdt_charizard.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'art' tag and added 'retro' and 'sprite' which are directly stated in the documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_datiuemm.summary: This design implements Memory Built-In Self-Test (MBIST) using the March C- algorithm and Hamming ECC (SECDED) for an 8x32 RAM, expanded to 8x40 for ECC. It provides status outputs for MBIST pass/fail, ECC error detection and correction, and RAM enable. The design is tested through functional checks and fault injection, with all test logic built-in. No external hardware is required, and the documentation details the algorithms and expected results.

ttsky26b/tt_um_db_PWM.summary: This project is a PWM generator that produces a signal with a duty cycle set by an 8-bit input. It uses a counter with a programmable maximum resolution, selected via three bidirectional pins, to determine the PWM frequency. A D flip-flop synchronizes the output to reduce glitches. The design requires external switches for the bit selector and operates at a 5 MHz clock, with testing described as straightforward.

ttsky26b/tt_um_dco.summary: The design is a digitally controlled oscillator that generates a frequency-adjustable clock signal based on an 8-bit control input. The control input selects an oscillation period from 3 to 50 clock cycles using a priority-based scheme, and the output toggles when a counter reaches the selected period. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware, but the documentation is limited to a basic testbench and frequency table. The oscillator is implemented with a counter and a clock divider, and unused outputs are tied low.

ttsky26b/tt_um_dean_foulds_ai_accelerato.summary: This project is a systolic binary neural network accelerator that performs inference for binary neural networks. Each neuron computes an XNOR dot product with a popcount tree and fires when the result plus a signed bias is non-negative. The compute engine processes one bit per clock cycle over eight cycles, reusing hardware to reduce silicon area. No external hardware is required, though a Raspberry Pi or Arduino can load weights and run inference via the pins.
ttsky26b/tt_um_dean_foulds_ai_accelerato.review_notes: Removed unsupported cocotb tag; added perceptron/popcount/verilog/edge-ai supported by the documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_devil_nyancat.summary: The design is a demoscene-style audio and video generator that produces visual and audio effects. It outputs VGA video signals and audio via a PWM or DAC output. External hardware includes a TinyVGA Pmod for video and a Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod or simple RC filter for sound. The design is notable for its retro computing aesthetic and real-time graphics generation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_digit_serial_divider.summary: The design is a fixed-point divider that computes division of fixed-point numbers. It uses a sequential algorithm and includes an ALU and finite state machine for control. The divider is implemented with a pipeline for throughput. External hardware may include a UART interface for data input and output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_digitalclock.summary: This project is a digital clock and date display implemented in Verilog. It supports 12h/24h modes, hour/minute adjustment, second sync, and a date mode for month/day/year. The output is a VGA signal matching the Tiny VGA pinout, intended for a VGA monitor. External hardware is a VGA display.
ttsky26b/tt_um_digitalclock.review_notes: Corrected tags: it is an RTC/VGA display, not a clock generator or timer.

ttsky26b/tt_um_dma_multi_channel.summary: This design is a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller with two independent channels for memory-to-memory data transfers. It supports single-word and burst transfers, programmable word widths, and error detection for boundary and address mismatch conditions. The controller is configured through input pins and reports completion and error flags on its outputs. Simulations are run with Cocotb to verify transfers in different modes and on both channels.
ttsky26b/tt_um_dma_multi_channel.review_notes: Added missing canonical tags for FSM and Verilog; corrected summary to match documented memory-to-memory operation rather than peripheral transfers.

ttsky26b/tt_um_dsp_top.summary: The design is a configurable 8-bit streaming DSP core that implements 4-tap FIR and IIR filtering with dynamic scaling and saturation protection. It processes an 8-bit digital input stream and outputs the filtered 8-bit result. The core is written in Verilog and runs at 50 MHz. Optional external hardware such as an ADC and DAC can be used for real-world signal processing.
ttsky26b/tt_um_dsp_top.review_notes: Removed audio/dac tags that describe optional external hardware rather than the design, and added fixed-point/filter tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_eml_gate.summary: The design is a math coprocessor that uses a shared multiplier and a hyperbolic CORDIC unit. It performs fixed-point arithmetic operations such as multiplication and trigonometric functions. The design is controlled via a SPI interface. External hardware may include a microcontroller to send commands and receive results.

ttsky26b/tt_um_enjimneering_bss_uart.summary: The design is a UART serial communication module. The documentation is extremely sparse, consisting only of the word UART for the description, how-to-test, and external hardware sections. It is written in Verilog and targets a Tiny Tapeout ASIC shuttle. The design is intended for serial communication, but no further implementation details are provided.
ttsky26b/tt_um_enjimneering_bss_uart.review_notes: Removed unsupported cocotb tag; added insufficient-doc because documentation is only the word UART.

ttsky26b/tt_um_enjimneering_spi_mem.summary: This design combines an SPI memory controller and a VGA timing core in Verilog. The SPI controller reads bytes from an external SPI RAM using command 0x03 with a 16-bit address, exposing busy and valid status. The VGA core generates 640x480 at 60 Hz timing with hsync, vsync, and 2-bit RGB output. A mode pin selects between raw SPI byte output and VGA timing output, and a cocotb test exercises the SPI path in simulation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_enjimneering_spi_mem.review_notes: Proposed tags claimed sparse documentation and incompleteness, contradicting the detailed source; replaced with SPI/VGA/memory tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_enrico_glr.summary: This design implements a two-player secret guessing game in which one player sets a 4-bit secret and the other has five rounds to guess it. Inputs set the secret, start the game, and submit guesses, while outputs report how many digits are correct in position and how many are correct but misplaced. It is a small design with no external hardware required beyond switches and LEDs for the inputs and outputs. The documentation is brief and contains typos, but the pin names and test steps are sufficient to understand the intended use.
ttsky26b/tt_um_enrico_glr.review_notes: Removed unsupported fsm and education tags; the design is a game but no FSM or educational intent is documented.

ttsky26b/tt_um_er_ring_osc.summary: This analog project is a seven-inverter ring oscillator intended to compare PEX simulation against measured silicon behavior. A chain of selectable dividers reduces the oscillator frequency by factors from 2 to 256, and the divided signal is routed to a digital output or, when enabled, to an analog pin through a buffer. Testing requires only setting the reset, enable, and select pins and observing the output, with no external hardware needed. The design is notable as a process and simulation-correlation experiment rather than a functional end product.
ttsky26b/tt_um_er_ring_osc.review_notes: Removed clock-generator and transistor-level tags that are not supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_eric_lcc.summary: This chip is the control core for a capacitive-discharge model rocket launch controller, managing capacitor charging, igniter continuity testing, current-controlled igniter drive, and a safety energy dump. It uses three PWM outputs to drive a flyback charger, a buck igniter driver, and a dump FET, with feedback from an external three-channel ADC over a serial interface. A built-in self-test runs a truncated system simulation after reset and reports pass or fail through the output pins. The design requires substantial external hardware including ADCs, power FETs, a transformer, a speaker, buttons, and LEDs, and is notable for implementing a complete safety-critical control system on a tiny tile.
ttsky26b/tt_um_eric_lcc.review_notes: Removed motor-control and industrial (rocket launch controller, not motor/industrial); added bist, pwm and adc.

ttsky26b/tt_um_erika24.summary: TinyFarm is a hardware farming game implemented in SystemVerilog that maintains four fields with crops that grow, can be watered, and are harvested to fulfill customer orders. Player inputs select mode, field, and crop and trigger actions, while a VGA output in RGB222 format displays the farm grid and game status. The design needs a Tiny VGA PMOD and a monitor to view the output, plus buttons or switches for the control inputs. It originated as a university final project and is notable for fitting a small game with inventory and order logic into a single tile pair.
ttsky26b/tt_um_erika24.review_notes: Removed fsm because no explicit finite state machine is documented; added workshop for the university final project origin.

ttsky26b/tt_um_fabulous_sky_26b.summary: This project implements a tiny FABulous FPGA fabric with 128 LUT4 plus flip-flop logic cells and a vertical carry chain for fast additions up to 15 bits. The I/Os resemble the Tiny Tapeout interface, allowing simple Tiny Tapeout designs to be mapped directly onto the fabric. User designs are synthesized with Yosys and implemented with nextpnr, and the bitstream is uploaded through a bitbang interface while reset is applied. The design is written in Verilog and includes cocotb tests, with no external hardware required.
ttsky26b/tt_um_fabulous_sky_26b.review_notes: Removed incorrect ASIC tag and added verilog and cocotb; summary now reflects the documented architecture.

ttsky26b/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttsky26b/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_fidel_makatia_digital_tap.summary: This project is a complete 8-bit accumulator-based microcontroller SoC with a 33-instruction ISA, a 32-word program ROM, 32 bytes of RAM shared with a hardware stack, a UART transmitter, a timer, and 8-bit GPIO. It runs a hardcoded demo program that counts on the GPIO outputs, calls a subroutine, sends a character over UART, reads the timer, and then halts. Testing involves applying reset and enable, then observing the GPIO outputs and the UART TX pin, optionally with LEDs and a USB-UART adapter connected. The design is notable for packing a full CPU with memory, stack, and peripherals into a small two-tile area.

ttsky26b/tt_um_flappy_vga_Akul18.summary: Flappy VGA is a simplified Flappy Bird-style game implemented entirely in digital logic, generating VGA timing and rendering a bird, moving pipes, ground, and background in real time. A physics module applies gravity and responds to a jump button, while collision detection ends the game when the bird hits a pipe or the ground. The design outputs 2-bit RGB with HSYNC and VSYNC and requires a Tiny VGA PMOD or resistor-DAC circuit plus a VGA monitor and two push buttons. It is notable for implementing a complete interactive game with sprite rendering and collision logic in a small tile area.
ttsky26b/tt_um_flappy_vga_Akul18.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'fsm' tag and added 'button' and 'sprite' based on explicit pin and rendering descriptions.

ttsky26b/tt_um_floating_bulk_test_2.summary: This analog test project is intended to measure punch-through current, with five analog pins exposed for connection to a multimeter. The documentation states the purpose and the required external hardware but does not explain the structure, biasing, or expected measurements of the test structure. A resistor is mentioned in the test instructions, and a multimeter is the stated external hardware. The design is a process/device characterisation structure rather than a functional circuit.
ttsky26b/tt_um_floating_bulk_test_2.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc since purpose is stated; added characterization and analog.

ttsky26b/tt_um_galois_lfsr16.summary: This design implements a 16-bit Galois LFSR random number generator with user-selectable shift direction and 32 different feedback polynomials, including standard CRC-16 polynomials and experimental tap patterns. Inputs select enable, direction, and polynomial, and the 16-bit state is exposed on the output and bidirectional pins for observation on LEDs. Testing requires only DIP switches and LEDs, with no external hardware needed. The design is notable for exposing a wide range of standard and experimental polynomials for comparison and educational use.

ttsky26b/tt_um_garage_project.summary: This project implements a finite state machine that controls an automatic garage door opener, handling open, close, and stop commands from a single button plus position and obstruction sensors. Outputs drive an up motor and a down motor, and an obstruction input causes the door to stop and reverse while closing. Testing can be done with two LEDs on the motor outputs or with an H-bridge and DC motor. The documentation is clear but brief, and the design is small and self-contained.
ttsky26b/tt_um_garage_project.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'industrial' and 'education' tags; added 'automotive' and 'button' based on application and pin evidence.

ttsky26b/tt_um_gen_onda.summary: This project implements a Direct Digital Synthesis waveform generator with a phase accumulator and a 16-entry lookup table, producing sine, sawtooth, square, triangle, and quadratic waveforms. Inputs select the waveform function, amplitude, and frequency control word, and an 8-bit digital output carries the generated samples. An external DAC and oscilloscope are required to view the analog waveform. The documentation includes the DDS frequency formula and test steps.
ttsky26b/tt_um_gen_onda.review_notes: Removed unsupported nco tag and trimmed an unsupported 'notable' claim from the summary.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ghtag_trinity_gf16.summary: TRI-1 Euler is a GF16 dot-product engine that computes a 4-element dot product using four parallel GF16 multipliers and a three-adder reduction tree. It is part of a larger Trinity TRI-NET family and is described as an e-engine SKU with support for multiple numeric formats, quantizers, and power modules. The default configuration computes dot4([1,2,3,4],[1,2,3,4]) = 30.0, observable as 0x47C0 on the output pins after reset. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is largely promotional and does not substantiate many of the claimed features.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ghtag_trinity_gf16.review_notes: Removed unsubstantiated neural-network, machine-learning and power-gating tags; kept only tags supported by the documented GF16 dot-product datapath.

ttsky26b/tt_um_gitragi_rng.summary: This design implements a 5-bit LFSR-based pseudo-random number generator with key-based logic locking, where an incorrect 2-bit key poisons the feedback path and drains the register to zero. A sampled value is reduced modulo a user-supplied maximum and displayed as the last decimal digit on a 7-segment display. The design requires an active-high 7-segment display, a clock source, and switches or buttons for the maximum value, key bits, and sample control. It is a compact demonstration of logic locking applied to an LFSR, with the locking mechanism being the notable feature.

ttsky26b/tt_um_gray_sobel.summary: This SystemVerilog design performs grayscale conversion, Sobel filtering, and thresholding on pixel data received over an SPI interface. Processing modes are selected via input pins, and an internal LFSR can optionally supply test pixels instead of external SPI data. The design requires an external SPI master such as a Raspberry Pi to send pixel data, and the processed result appears on a single output pin. The documentation is brief but includes a block diagram and pin-level usage details, though the thresholding and LFSR behavior are only lightly described.
ttsky26b/tt_um_gray_sobel.review_notes: Removed edge-detector: it denotes signal edge detection, not image edge detection.

ttsky26b/tt_um_gurtej_randhawa1_pulsemon.summary: PulseMon8 is an 8-bit pulse monitor that counts rising edges on an external signal sampled by the Tiny Tapeout clock, with edge detection, compare-match, freeze-on-match, and overflow status outputs. Counting is controlled by enable and clear inputs, and an 8-bit comparison value can be set to trigger match and freeze behavior. The design requires no custom external hardware and can be tested on a demoboard using switches, buttons, or a function generator, though mechanical buttons may bounce and produce spurious edges. The documentation is thorough and includes step-by-step test procedures for counting, comparison, freezing, and overflow.

ttsky26b/tt_um_hackin7_coprocessor.summary: The title and one-line description say this is an Advent of Code day-1 style position coprocessor implemented in Hardcaml with a byte-serial Tiny Tapeout wrapper, but the provided documentation instead describes a 640x480 VGA animation of a bouncing backpack mascot bitmap. The VGA output drives a TinyVGA PMOD, and input pins toggle tiling and palette rotation effects. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD or equivalent VGA DAC and a VGA monitor, and needs a ~25.175 MHz clock. There is a clear mismatch between the title and the documentation, so the actual function of the submitted design is ambiguous.
ttsky26b/tt_um_hackin7_coprocessor.review_notes: Title/description describe a Hardcaml coprocessor while the documentation describes a VGA mascot animation; source is contradictory.

ttsky26b/tt_um_hamming74.summary: This design implements a Hamming(7,4) error-correcting code system that can encode 4-bit data into a 7-bit codeword and decode a received codeword while detecting and correcting a single-bit error. A MODE input selects between encoding and decoding, and an error flag output indicates when a correctable error was detected. No external hardware is required beyond input switches and LEDs to observe the encoded or corrected output. The documentation is very short and does not describe the internal implementation or provide test vectors.

ttsky26b/tt_um_happy_birthday.summary: This design continuously transmits a looping serial bit stream and detects a hardcoded 9-bit birthday pattern within it, counting hits per second and displaying the count on two 7-segment digits. Transmission is enabled by an active-low input, and a valid pulse indicates when the hit count is updated each second. The design requires external 7-segment displays for the tens and units digits, and no other custom hardware. The documentation is detailed and includes step-by-step test instructions.
ttsky26b/tt_um_happy_birthday.review_notes: Added text output tag and removed the unsupported editorial sentence about limited configurability.

ttsky26b/tt_um_harveywong85_harveywilly.summary: This project is titled harveywilly and described only as a tiny tapeout demo, with pin names matching the Tiny VGA PMOD standard. The documentation consists of the phrases 'Ask Pat' and 'Use the code', providing no explanation of what the design does or how it works. The pinout suggests a VGA output design, but no functional details are given. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.
ttsky26b/tt_um_harveywong85_harveywilly.review_notes: Added verilog; removed redundant display tag.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ieee_opensilicon_bootcamp.summary: This project implements a number guessing game in hardware where a 4-bit LFSR generates a pseudo-random number between 1 and 15, and the user has three attempts to guess it. After each guess, outputs indicate whether the correct number is higher, lower, or correct, and the remaining attempts are shown. A new game is started by pulsing an input, and guesses are submitted by pulsing a verify input. No external hardware is required beyond LEDs or a logic analyzer, and the design originates from an IEEE OpenSilicon bootcamp.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ieee_pwd.summary: This design implements a 2-bit PWM generator using a free-running 2-bit counter, with the duty cycle selected by two reference input bits to produce 0%, 25%, 50%, or 75% output. The PWM output can drive an LED, an RC low-pass filter for analog voltage generation, or a motor driver. Two additional state input bits are connected internally but unused in the current logic. The documentation is clear and includes a duty-cycle table and test steps, and the design is a simple educational PWM example.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ik_0_ptat_bgr.summary: This analog block generates a reference voltage of about 1.2 V using a pseudo-PTAT current generator with enable-gated startup. It is used by applying a 1.8 V supply and asserting the appropriate enable pins (ui[6] and ui[3]) to obtain the reference on ua[0]. Testing requires voltage measurement equipment to measure the output and verify low temperature dependence. The design includes a startup circuit that can be toggled if the bandgap fails to start.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ik_0_ptat_bgr.review_notes: Removed temperature-sensor: the block outputs a voltage reference, not a temperature sensing interface.

ttsky26b/tt_um_iporre_rm121.summary: This design implements a two-player Pong game with score display, outputting a standard 640x480 VGA signal at 60 Hz. It is controlled by four buttons for paddle movement and requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for display. The game logic uses a finite state machine and procedural graphics generation without any microprocessor or external memory. The design is notable for its compact implementation and themed graphics inspired by The Legend of Zelda.

ttsky26b/tt_um_isalopez9_memory_game.summary: This chip implements a Simon Says memory game where a sequence is stored in RAM and the player must repeat it using two input buttons.
