It operates in two modes: programming mode to load the sequence via bidirectional pins, and game mode where the sequence is shown on LEDs and player input is checked. The design is tested with a Cocotb testbench that verifies programming, correct input, and error detection. External hardware such as switches and LEDs is suggested for manual testing.
ttsky26b/tt_um_isalopez9_memory_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'education' tag; added 'cocotb' and 'button' which are supported by the documentation and pins.

ttsky26b/tt_um_izh_neuron.summary: This analog circuit implements a compact spiking neuron that generates firing patterns based on five external bias and input controls. It is tested by tuning the analog inputs (IREFA, IREFB, BIASC, BIASD, and VCORE) and observing the output waveform on VOUT with an oscilloscope or DAQ. External hardware includes adjustable analog sources and a clean analog supply with decoupling. The design is a compact analog spiking neuron intended for neuromorphic use.
ttsky26b/tt_um_izh_neuron.review_notes: Replaced the unsupported 'notable for its small size' claim with the source's own 'compact' description.

ttsky26b/tt_um_jacob_kebaso_4bit_cpu.summary: Nibble is a minimalistic 4-bit accumulator CPU with a Harvard architecture designed for TinyTapeout. It executes a simple 16-instruction ISA over a 2-cycle fetch-execute pipeline. The CPU exposes instruction inputs, program counter outputs, accumulator and flag outputs, and a 4-bit input port. It is intended to be used with external program memory such as an RP2040 or EEPROM.
ttsky26b/tt_um_jacob_kebaso_4bit_cpu.review_notes: The proposed tags and summary described a PUF/ring-oscillator security primitive, which is not supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_jasonbrave_terre.summary: This design generates a VGA signal displaying the moving text 'Bonjour Terre!' on a monitor. It is created using the VGA playground with a logo template and requires only a VGA monitor for testing. The design is simple and serves as a demonstration of text animation on a VGA display. No external hardware beyond a monitor is needed.

ttsky26b/tt_um_jenny82121027_axi4lite.summary: This SystemVerilog design implements an AXI4-Lite slave with a read-only ID register and 32 general-purpose registers, providing a 16-bit readback path on the bidirectional pins. It is used by driving the address, write/read requests, and data through the input and bidirectional pins, with read data appearing on the outputs. No external hardware is required for basic operation, though a host controller is needed to exercise the AXI4-Lite interface. The design serves as a demonstration of integrating a standard bus protocol into a Tiny Tapeout project.

ttsky26b/tt_um_jonathanbytes_alu8_serial.summary: This 8-bit serial-in ALU processes two operands shifted in LSB-first and supports eight operations including ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, and NOT. It provides a parallel result and status flags (carry, zero, negative, overflow, done) after 16 clock cycles. Testing involves shifting in operands and reading the result and flags, and it can be interfaced with a microcontroller or manual switches. The design is notable for its serial interface, which reduces pin count while maintaining full ALU functionality.
ttsky26b/tt_um_jonathanbytes_alu8_serial.review_notes: Removed unsupported shift-register tag and added verilog tag based on stated language.

ttsky26b/tt_um_joo111emad_BGR.summary: This analog circuit provides a zero-temperature-coefficient (ZTAT) voltage reference, designed to be stable across temperature variations. It is tested by measuring the VREF pin at different temperatures, with the rate of change expected to be within 1.2 mV. External hardware includes a high-precision multimeter and an environmental chamber or thermal stream. The design is a simple bandgap reference, notable for its low temperature drift.

ttsky26b/tt_um_kazan_rqpu.summary: This design is a 4-bit processor inspired by reversible computing, featuring a 4-phase bus protocol and a 4x4 scratchpad RAM. It executes arithmetic, logic, shift, compare, and memory operations, with support for reversible operations like save and reverse using checkpoint metadata. Testing is done via cocotb, verifying phase progression, ALU operations, RAM access, and reverse functionality. No external hardware is required, but a host controller can drive the phase-aware transactions.
ttsky26b/tt_um_kazan_rqpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'fsm' tag; added 'cocotb' and 'reversible' which are directly supported by the documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_krisjdev_artwork.summary: This project is a silicon artwork featuring Hatsune Miku and Juno Teo Minh, implemented in Verilog. The documentation is essentially a template with no functional description, testing instructions, or external hardware details. It appears to be a decorative design rather than a functional circuit. As a result, its purpose and operation cannot be determined from the provided information.

ttsky26b/tt_um_krv8_ieee.summary: This project is a simple 8-bit, single-cycle processor with a RISC-V-style instruction set and an accumulator-based data path. It has no internal instruction memory; the 16-bit instruction is applied externally through the 8 input pins and 8 bidirectional pins. Testing requires driving those pins with switches, an MCU, or an FPGA, and the design is intended for educational use or small embedded control logic. The documentation notes that manual switch input is impractical, so an external microcontroller such as an ESP32 is recommended.
ttsky26b/tt_um_krv8_ieee.review_notes: Removed risc-v because the source only says RISC-V style, not RISC-V ISA; removed alu and instruction-decoder as they are not explicitly documented.

ttsky26b/tt_um_leongamboa_OpenSilicon_Su.summary: This design generates the IEEE logo bouncing around on a VGA screen, with the color changeable via a button. It is a submission to the Open Silicon 2026 workshop and requires a VGA display. The design is simple and uses no external hardware beyond a laptop to run and display the output. The documentation is minimal.
ttsky26b/tt_um_leongamboa_OpenSilicon_Su.review_notes: Replaced silicon-art with art since the design is a VGA logo animation rather than a silicon layout artwork.

ttsky26b/tt_um_leozqi_onetile.summary: This design implements Conway's Game of Life on a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It outputs a VGA video signal using the Tiny VGA pinout and runs at a 25.175 MHz clock. The project includes cocotb tests for verification and requires an external VGA screen to display the output. The documentation is very brief and does not describe the internal implementation or the initial pattern.
ttsky26b/tt_um_leozqi_onetile.review_notes: Removed game and display tags; game-of-life and cellular-automaton better describe the design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_lfearn_latchup.summary: This project generates a VGA display that shows a checkers pattern, based on a template from VGA playground. It uses the Tiny VGA pinout and was created during a workshop at Latchup. There is a test.py file in the test folder for verification, and an external VGA display is required to show the output. The documentation is minimal and does not specify any unique features.
ttsky26b/tt_um_lfearn_latchup.review_notes: Removed display and education because they are not supported by the source; added retro for the retro-style VGA checkers output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_llhtimlam_movingscreen.summary: This project displays a moving screen strip on a VGA monitor using the Tiny VGA pinout. It runs at a 25.175 MHz clock and is tested with CocoTB. The design requires an external TV screen and an FPGA for operation. The documentation is very sparse and does not explain the visual effect or the internal logic.
ttsky26b/tt_um_llhtimlam_movingscreen.review_notes: Removed fpga tag: FPGA is only external test hardware, not a target platform.

ttsky26b/tt_um_load_priority_controller.summary: This design is a 6-state finite state machine that manages power distribution across three prioritized loads based on undervoltage, medium-power, and high-power status flags. It includes a stability filter and staged load activation, with immediate de-escalation. Testing involves driving the flags and observing the enable outputs, and external hardware such as voltage comparators, MOSFET drivers, and LEDs is required to interface with real loads. The project is part of the IEEE Open-Silicon 2026 initiative and is implemented in pure digital logic without firmware.
ttsky26b/tt_um_load_priority_controller.review_notes: Removed arbiter and comparator tags that are not supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_lpf_ieee.summary: This project implements a moving average digital low-pass filter, which is a type of FIR filter with equal coefficients. It processes a 12-bit input and produces a 12-bit filtered output, using the input pins and bidirectional pins for data. An external MCU or FPGA is needed to provide input data and collect the output, which can be observed with a logic analyzer. The design is part of the IEEE Open-Silicon initiative and is documented with its mathematical basis.
ttsky26b/tt_um_lpf_ieee.review_notes: Removed the unsupported claim that implementation details are lacking; the source does not state this.

ttsky26b/tt_um_lstm_wakeword.summary: This project is an 8-bit quantized LSTM neural network accelerator for real-time wake word detection, specifically the word 'NYALA'. It accepts 7-bit signed audio features and a valid strobe, and outputs a trigger signal, confidence level, and busy flag. The design includes RTL and gate-level verification with cocotb, and it requires an external microphone and an RP2040 preprocessor for MFCC extraction. Notable features include a privacy-first smart home application and a fully digital inference pipeline.
ttsky26b/tt_um_lstm_wakeword.review_notes: Removed dsp; added audio, microphone, rp2040, cocotb, and verilog tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_lujji_ulogic_analyzer.summary: This project reads eight digital input pins and transmits their states over a UART interface at 1,000,000 baud. It outputs a serial transmit line and a clock output. To use it, an external UART receiver must be connected to the transmit pin. The design is described as a 'useless logic analyzer' and has minimal documentation, but it functions as a simple pin-state monitor.

ttsky26b/tt_um_magnetofield_ieee.summary: This project displays the Hackerspace Trójmiasto logo on a VGA monitor at 640x480 resolution. It includes a VGA timing generator and a bitmap ROM for the logo, with configurable color modes and animation such as bouncing or tiling. The design requires an external PMOD-to-VGA adapter to connect to a standard monitor. It is fully synthesizable for ASIC implementation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_magnetofield_ieee.review_notes: Removed silicon-art tag; the design is a VGA logo display, not an artistic silicon layout.

ttsky26b/tt_um_main_fsm_anbui_uci.summary: This project implements a finite state machine for a swarm microrobot drug delivery system, handling clot detection, communication, drug release, and motor control. It uses two inputs for local clot detection and nearby robot signals, and outputs drug release commands, transmission signals, and motor enables. The FSM has four states and includes a drug-available register that is cleared after release. No external hardware is required for the core logic, and the design is documented with a detailed test procedure.
ttsky26b/tt_um_main_fsm_anbui_uci.review_notes: Removed 'communication' as the TX/RX are simple flags, not a protocol; added 'sensor-interface' for the clot detection input.

ttsky26b/tt_um_maw_game.summary: MAW Bird Shooter is a single-player arcade game implemented in SystemVerilog that drives a 640x480 60 Hz VGA display directly from the chip. The player moves a crosshair with four directional buttons and fires up to ten shots at an animated bird, with hit/miss overlays, a shot counter, and win/lose screens. It requires a VGA monitor or TinyVGA PMOD, five momentary push-buttons, and five 10 kOhm pull-down resistors on the button inputs. The design is notable for fitting a complete game with sprite rendering, LFSR-driven enemy movement, and button conditioning into a 2x2 tile ASIC.
ttsky26b/tt_um_maw_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported silicon-tested tag, added pong domain tag, and corrected 'debouncing' to the documented button conditioning.

ttsky26b/tt_um_minmanrox_drone.summary: This project implements a simple quadcopter drone flight controller in SystemVerilog that converts four PWM control inputs (throttle, yaw, pitch, roll) into four motor PWM outputs. It mixes the inputs so throttle raises all motors together while yaw, pitch, and roll introduce differential adjustments, using a 20 ms PWM frame with 1 ms minimum and 2 ms maximum duty. The full system requires a radio receiver or control source, ESCs, and motors, with the author using an ELRS/CRSF receiver and a CRSF-to-PWM converter. The design is a straightforward hardware mixer without sensor feedback or stabilization, intended as a minimal flight controller.
ttsky26b/tt_um_minmanrox_drone.review_notes: Removed unsupported communication tag and added systemverilog to match the stated language.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ml_coprocessor.summary: The Kunal ML co-processor is a Verilog design that connects to an RP2040 over SPI to perform machine learning operations such as division and dot products. It uses Q8.8 signed fixed-point arithmetic and includes an SPI slave, an iterative 16-bit signed divider, and a command state machine with operand and weight registers. BUSY and DONE pins allow the host to poll operation status, though status can also be read via a READ_STAT command. No external components are required, and the design is notable for providing hardware acceleration for fixed-point ML primitives on a small ASIC.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ml_coprocessor.review_notes: Removed neural-network and multiplier tags; added fixed-point, divider, mac-unit, spi, rp2040, coprocessor, accelerator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_morse_code.summary: This SystemVerilog design translates Morse code entered via a push button into characters A-Z and displays the most recent two characters on seven-segment displays through a Digilent Pmod SSD. Timing rules distinguish dits (1 s hold), dahs (3 s hold), letter ends (3 s release), and word ends (7 s release), with an external LED blinking at 1 Hz to help the user keep time. It requires a tactile switch, an LED, and the Pmod SSD, and includes testbenches for the counting and translation modules. The project is a straightforward educational Morse decoder with no silicon test results reported.

ttsky26b/tt_um_mosbius.summary: This project implements a mini MOSbius analog chip in a 3x2 Tiny Tapeout slot. It contains programmable NMOS and PMOS transistors, differential pairs, OTAs, and current sources. Six buses with transmission gates allow interconnection of the blocks, programmed by a shift register. Silicon tests confirmed working inverter, differential amplifier, ring oscillator, and current source configurations.
ttsky26b/tt_um_mosbius.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the analog MOSbius design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_nezumi_tech_adc_sq_compar.summary: This Verilog project is an ultra-low-power controller for an energy harvesting system that evaluates two proprietary harvesting topologies (P and S) and switches to the one yielding more energy. It uses an external LTC2450 SPI ADC to measure capacitor voltages, outputs pulses to control external switches, and logs results over UART at 1200 baud. To fit within a Tiny Tapeout tile, it replaces hardware multipliers with a custom 17-cycle shift-and-add sequential multiplier and runs at 32.768 kHz to minimize power. The design requires external harvesting circuitry, a USB-to-UART adapter, and an RTC oscillator for standalone operation, and is intended for academic research.
ttsky26b/tt_um_nezumi_tech_adc_sq_compar.review_notes: Removed unsupported multiplier/fsm/sensor-interface tags and added cocotb, verilog, and the actual interface and power-related tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_nlanderso_morse_code.summary: This SystemVerilog design translates Morse code entered via a push button into characters A-Z and displays the most recent two characters on seven-segment displays through a Digilent Pmod SSD. Timing rules distinguish dits (1 s hold), dahs (3 s hold), letter ends (3 s release), and word ends (7 s release), with an external LED blinking at 1 Hz to help the user keep time. It requires a tactile switch, an LED, and the Pmod SSD, and includes testbenches for the counting and translation modules. This project appears to be a duplicate of another Morse code translator entry with identical documentation and no silicon test results.
ttsky26b/tt_um_nlanderso_morse_code.review_notes: Removed education and communication; added 7-segment, button, shift-register, pmod, led, and systemverilog tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_nn_3x3.summary: This Verilog design is a programmable sequential hardware neural network with a single layer of three neurons, each processing three inputs, using a shared multiply-accumulate unit to fit in one Tiny Tapeout tile. Weights, biases, and inputs can be loaded at runtime through a multiplexed memory-mapped interface on the bidirectional pins, and the design applies a ReLU activation after accumulation. No external hardware is required; a testbench or microcontroller can write parameters and trigger calculations over the bus. The design is notable for implementing a tiny tensor-processing-unit-like architecture with a single shared MAC engine.

ttsky26b/tt_um_noah_azz_demo.summary: My First TT Demo is a Verilog design that uses elementary bitwise logic to generate colorful graphics on a VGA display. It has no inputs and only VGA outputs, matching the Tiny VGA PMOD pinout, and requires a VGA monitor or compatible PMOD to view the output. The documentation is very thin, describing only that it produces subjectively cool colors through simple logic. There are no silicon test results or further details about the generated patterns.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ocd_charlieplex.summary: This Verilog project is a controller for an Adafruit Charlieplex LED array, supporting up to 8x7 (56) LEDs with the eight bidirectional pins. On reset it displays a brightness gradient, and a 9600-baud UART receive interface allows custom displays to be programmed by sending ASCII characters for brightness and pixel address. Because Charlieplex LEDs are addressed one at a time, brightness is controlled by on-time proportional to the desired level, making overall brightness depend on how many LEDs are lit. It requires an external Adafruit Charlieplex array and an FPGA implementation with a USB driver script is provided for testing.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ocpu.summary: OCPU is a PLL-based overclockable CPU implemented in Verilog that interfaces with an FPGA over an octal SPI (OSPI) bus for memory access. It exposes control signals such as page_done, page_loading, page_interrupt, is_halted, and data_req to coordinate with the FPGA, which acts as a memory and paging controller. The design is intended to be tested with an FPGA providing the OSPI memory and page management, and the PLL allows the CPU clock to be overclocked. The documentation is sparse, providing only pin names and no detailed description of the instruction set or architecture.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ocpu.review_notes: Source is ambiguous about memory architecture and pipeline details; escalated for second opinion.

ttsky26b/tt_um_okforth_ieee.summary: This design implements a SUBLEQ one-instruction-set computer (OISC) CPU in Verilog. It executes the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts one memory value from another and branches if the result is less than or equal to zero. The CPU requires an external RP2040 or similar microcontroller to act as 16-bit memory, communicating via read and write latches with byte-serial data transfer. The project is notable for demonstrating a minimal CPU architecture on a Tiny Tapeout tile, but it cannot function standalone without external memory hardware.

ttsky26b/tt_um_opensilicio_5g_rectifier.summary: This is a differential RF-DC rectifier designed in Sky130 for passive RFID and RF energy harvesting experiments. It converts an RF input signal into a DC output voltage, with three analog pins for the differential RF input and the rectified output. The design is implemented as an analog block and does not include digital control logic. No testing details or external hardware requirements are provided in the documentation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_opensilicio_5g_rectifier.review_notes: Removed unsupported transistor-level tag; added multi-tile for the 1x2 span.

ttsky26b/tt_um_oreoluwa_water_level.summary: This design is a 4-state finite-state machine that controls a water pump based on two binary level sensors, with an error flag for impossible sensor combinations. It is intended for fluid level detection and control, and can be tested by driving the sensor inputs and observing the pump output, error flag, and state outputs. External hardware includes two level sensors, a pump driver circuit (such as a relay or MOSFET), and optional LEDs for status indication. The project is part of the IEEE Open-silicon 2026 initiative and includes cocotb tests covering all state transitions.

ttsky26b/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This design is a stylish ring oscillator built from 21 SkullFET inverters, generating a square wave with a simulated frequency of about 169.2 MHz. It is tested by connecting an oscilloscope to one of the divided outputs, as the full-speed outputs are too fast for GPIO pins. No external hardware is required beyond an oscilloscope. Notable for its use of SkullFET transistors and the inclusion of frequency dividers for observability.
ttsky26b/tt_um_oscillating_bones.review_notes: Removed the overbroad clock-generator tag; simulation frequency kept as stated in the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pcs_link_lite.summary: This design implements a Physical Coding Sublayer (PCS) with 8b10b encoding and decoding, asynchronous clock domain crossing FIFOs, and a link training state machine for a half-duplex serial link. It operates between a 66 MHz link clock and a 10 MHz system clock, and can be tested using an RP2040 for functional validation or an FPGA for at-speed 66 MHz testing. External hardware for full validation includes a 3.3V FPGA and jumper wires, while basic functional tests can be done with just the demoboard. The design is notable for its compact implementation of a high-speed serial communication protocol on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttsky26b/tt_um_peterhan_ReactionGame.summary: This is a multiplayer reaction time game with VGA display output at 640x480 resolution, supporting Classic and Target Match modes for one or two players. It is controlled by push buttons and switches, and displays reaction times and winner information on a VGA monitor. External hardware includes a VGA monitor with a resistor DAC, momentary push buttons, and switches. The design is notable for being a complete game implementation on a Tiny Tapeout tile, using the Tiny VGA pinout.

ttsky26b/tt_um_petros.summary: This design is a pre-trained Binary Neural Network (BNN) for 8x8 MNIST digit classification, implemented in SystemVerilog. It serially loads a 64-bit image and outputs a 4-bit prediction (0-9) after processing, with a reported test accuracy of 70%. The network consists of 18 neurons and is combinational for minimal area, requiring no external hardware for operation. The project is notable for being a silicon-hardened neural network accelerator on a Tiny Tapeout tile, albeit with reduced accuracy due to area constraints.
ttsky26b/tt_um_petros.review_notes: Removed edge-ai: the source describes a fixed pre-trained BNN classifier, not an edge-AI targeted design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pfw_tpu.summary: This design implements a 2x2 systolic-array Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) that performs signed 8-bit matrix multiplication with 16-bit accumulation, optional fused transpose, and ReLU activation. It uses a pipelined streaming architecture that allows overlapping input and output operations, and is controlled via a simple handshake interface. External hardware such as a microcontroller or FPGA is needed to provide input data and read results, but no other external components are required. The project is notable for being a compact matrix multiplication accelerator on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pmendoza_ieee_tinyscan.summary: This design is a test module for learning about scan chains and Design for Testability (DFT) concepts. It contains two 4-bit universal shift registers, one of which can be configured to exhibit stuck-at faults via the ERR input, and both can be placed in scan mode for testing. The module can be used to practice scan chain operation and fault detection, and may require an FPGA or microcontroller to manipulate the inputs. The project is notable for being an educational tool for understanding scan chain testing and fault injection.
ttsky26b/tt_um_pmendoza_ieee_tinyscan.review_notes: Removed factory-test (not a factory self-test structure) and added verilog.

ttsky26b/tt_um_prathiba_finite_sbox.summary: This design implements a lightweight AES S-box using composite field arithmetic, performing the non-linear transformation required for 4-bit operations. It takes a 4-bit input and produces a 4-bit output, which can be verified against the standard AES S-box table. No external hardware is required for basic operation, as the S-box is a purely combinational logic block. The project is notable for its compact implementation of a cryptographic primitive on a Tiny Tapeout tile.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pree.summary: This is a mixed-signal design that implements a UART-programmable controller capable of selecting between different analog circuits such as inverters or MOSFET switches. It uses a UART interface for configuration and data transmission, with baud rate selection via input pins, and provides analog outputs on four pins. External hardware includes a voltage supply and an oscilloscope for observing the analog outputs. The project combines digital UART control with analog circuit selection on a Tiny Tapeout tile.
ttsky26b/tt_um_pree.review_notes: Removed logic-gate and instrumentation tags that were not supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pro_clk.summary: This project implements a programmable clock generator that produces output frequencies from 100 Hz to 900 kHz based on a 50 MHz input clock. The output frequency is selected by a 4-bit radix input (1-9) and a 2-bit scale input that sets the base frequency range. The design uses a precomputed division factor and an 18-bit counter to generate a 50% duty-cycle square wave, with glitch-free updates occurring only at half-period boundaries. No external hardware is required, and the output is available on a single pin for observation with an oscilloscope or logic analyzer.

ttsky26b/tt_um_processor_top.summary: TinyCrypto-8 is an 8-bit pipelined ALU with hardware cryptography support, featuring a 12-bit instruction set that includes arithmetic, logic, shift, and LFSR-based crypto operations. Instructions are loaded serially through three input pins, and the 8-bit accumulator result is output on eight pins. The design is verified with a testbench that exercises ALU operations, flag updates, and crypto functions, and it requires no external hardware for basic operation. It is intended for educational or integration purposes, with optional microcontroller-based testing.
ttsky26b/tt_um_processor_top.review_notes: Removed cpu and education tags because the source describes an ALU with an instruction set, not a CPU, and does not state an educational intent.

ttsky26b/tt_um_prog_clk_router.summary: This design is an 8-channel programmable clock router that generates divided clock signals from a 50 MHz system clock. Each output channel can be independently configured via a 3-bit address, 4-bit division value, and a write strobe to select one of 16 counter bits as the clock source. The outputs are directly observable with a logic analyzer or oscilloscope, and no external hardware is required. The design is a straightforward utility for clock management in digital systems.

ttsky26b/tt_um_puf.summary: This project implements a ring oscillator physical unclonable function (RO-PUF) using 16 toggle flip-flops driven by an LFSR to create unique oscillators. Eight 12-bit counter pairs measure frequency variations over a 1000-cycle window, and a three-state FSM manages the measurement cycle, producing a single-bit response and a done flag. The design requires no external hardware and outputs debug information on six pins. It is notable for exploiting silicon manufacturing variation for hardware security primitives.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pwm_4ch.summary: This project is a 4-channel PWM controller with SPI configuration, designed for half-bridge motor and LED driving. It includes configurable frequency, per-channel duty cycle and phase offset, dead-time insertion to prevent shoot-through, and fault protection that latches off outputs when the nFAULT input is asserted. The design requires an external SPI master and optionally a gate driver IC and power stage for motor control. It is notable for its comprehensive feature set and fault handling in a compact implementation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_pwm_4ch.review_notes: Removed robotics (no robotics control described); added driver and industrial for the half-bridge gate-drive and motor-control application.

ttsky26b/tt_um_pzhu2.summary: This project implements a hardware triangle rasterizer that renders filled triangles to a 256x256 viewport on a 640x480 VGA display. It uses the edge-equation method with incremental evaluation to avoid per-pixel multiplications, and triangles are loaded serially via an 8-bit input with a valid strobe. The design requires a VGA PMOD and monitor, and an external microcontroller to send triangle data. It is notable for its efficient hardware rasterization suitable for embedded graphics.
ttsky26b/tt_um_pzhu2.review_notes: Removed redundant 'display' tag; added 'pmod' and 'rasterizer' which are supported by the documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_quadpulse_pwm.summary: QuadPulse is a 4-channel PWM generator ASIC for servo and DC motor control, providing jitter-free PWM signals with 8-bit duty cycle resolution. It supports four frequency modes (50 Hz to 20 kHz) and accepts runtime duty cycle updates via a 3-wire SPI interface. A hardware emergency stop pin instantly forces all outputs to zero. The design is intended for robotic systems and requires external servos, motors, or LEDs for testing, along with an SPI master.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rahulbhagwat_brainamp_lna.summary: This is an AC-coupled low noise amplifier designed to amplify EEG signals for brain-computer interface applications. It takes differential inputs (EEG_IN and EEG_REF) and produces an amplified output for low-frequency signals (1-100 Hz). The design is analog and requires external electrodes for actual EEG measurement, though testing can be done with a signal generator. The documentation is brief and lacks detailed specifications such as gain, noise figure, or power consumption.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rajkamal_analog.summary: This project implements a configurable analog clock generation unit with a voltage-controlled MUX selecting between 3, 5, and 7-stage ring oscillators on the Sky130 process. The selection is based on a DC voltage applied to an analog input, with eight 200mV thresholds across the 0-1.8V range. Additional test structures include frequency dividers, a capacitor-loaded oscillator, and a resistor-ladder voltage reference. Testing requires a lab DC power supply and oscilloscope, and the design is notable for its analog configurability and inclusion of characterization structures.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rajkamal_analog.review_notes: Removed 'vco' as selection is via MUX not voltage control; added 'characterization' and 'voltage-reference' based on explicit test structures.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.summary: This design implements a 32-bit iterative multiply-accumulate (MAC) unit with a 7x8-bit multiplier, intended for tiny ML accelerators. A controller FSM manages partial sums and bias alignment across four training phases or one inference phase. The design is verified with cocotb tests comparing against a reference model, and it requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout carrier. It is notable for its iterative architecture suitable for resource-constrained AI applications.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rajum_iterativeMAC.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'dsp' tag; added 'cocotb' and 'edge-ai' which are supported by the documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ramp_adc.summary: This is a two-channel 8-bit single-slope ramp ADC built from analog blocks including a bias generator, linear ramp, 2:1 transmission-gate MUX, sample-and-hold, and a two-stage comparator. The selected input is compared against an on-chip ramp, and the 8-bit count at the first crossing is latched and presented on uo_out, with a sample-valid pulse on uio_out[0]. It needs an external clock around 4 MHz, a 0 to 1 V analog signal on ua[0] or ua[1], logic inputs for channel select and sample-and-hold bypass, and a logic analyzer or read-back on the digital outputs. The documentation is brief and does not report measured silicon results, so the actual reference value and temperature behavior are only expected rather than confirmed.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rcyaon.summary: This is a Brokaw bandgap voltage reference built with SKY130 PNP BJTs, using a PTAT current generator and a summing amplifier with OTA feedback to produce a stable reference near 1.2 V. The circuit includes a bias generator, a ramp generator, and a 2:1 analog MUX, with the output available on ua[0] and ua[1]. It requires an external clock and a 0 to 1 V analog input, and the digital output is read via uo_out. The documentation is brief and does not report measured silicon results, so the actual reference value and temperature behavior are only expected rather than confirmed.

ttsky26b/tt_um_reaction_game.summary: This project is a reaction-time game on a Simon Says board. Pressing the yellow button starts a random 2-5 second delay, after which a green LED and buzzer signal GO. The player presses the blue button as fast as possible, and the reaction time is shown on a 2-digit display. Early presses trigger an error state.
ttsky26b/tt_um_reaction_game.review_notes: Summary was rewritten to describe the documented reaction game instead of a generic random delay generator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large collection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to select the flag by index or step through them. It is used by connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and using the input pins to change the displayed flag. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. Silicon testing confirmed that flag switching works, though the index-based selection via uio was not tested.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added pmod, video, and silicon-tested tags supported by documentation and silicon status.

ttsky26b/tt_um_riscv_alu.summary: This design implements a 32-bit RISC-V rv32i arithmetic logic unit that is purely combinational. It supports ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR, SLL, SRL, SRA, SLT, and SLTU operations using a barrel shifter and comparison logic. The design was extracted from a complete rv32imsu RISC-V SoC implemented in Synopsys tools on the sky130A PDK at the University of Central Florida. It is implemented in Verilog and can be tested by setting operand and operation inputs and reading the result outputs.
ttsky26b/tt_um_riscv_alu.review_notes: Removed unsupported CPU, branch-predictor, and education tags; added combinational and multiplexer; corrected summary to describe the ALU rather than a CPU.

ttsky26b/tt_um_riscv_branch.summary: This is a RISC-V CPU core with a branch predictor, designed for educational purposes. It includes an ALU, comparator, and finite state machine control logic. The design is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform. It is intended to demonstrate advanced CPU features like branch prediction in a simple, learnable format.

ttsky26b/tt_um_riscv_gpu.summary: This is a 4x4 BitNet b1.58 matrix multiply accelerator controlled over SPI. It multiplies unsigned 8-bit activations by ternary {-1,0,+1} weights using a multiplier-free add/sub/skip datapath with two parallel compute lanes. The design is implemented in Verilog and uses 1x2 tiles. It is intended for edge AI inference, and the documentation describes the SPI command format and a 32-cycle compute latency.
ttsky26b/tt_um_riscv_gpu.review_notes: Removed unsupported systolic-array, multiplier and DSP tags; added SPI, MAC, multi-tile and edge-AI tags supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rom_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing 64x64 Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen, with options to tile or double the logo size. It can be controlled with a gamepad to start/pause and change direction. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally a Gamepad PMOD. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected, including tile, double, and gamepad modes.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ross_systolic.summary: This project is a 2x2 signed 4-bit systolic array matrix multiplier with 9-bit accumulators, overflow detection, sign reconstruction and a manual step mode. Data is loaded as an 8-bit byte with write-enable and start controls, and results are read out on 8 output bits. Status signals include busy, output-valid, 8-bit overflow, accumulator sign, manual clock and step mode. It is implemented in Verilog for Tiny Tapeout, though documentation is very thin.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ross_systolic.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described a VGA cellular automaton, which contradicts the matrix multiplier source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rule30_vga.summary: This project implements Wolfram Rule 30, a 1D cellular automaton, in hardware. It updates a 320-bit generation register each row and displays 480 generations on a VGA monitor using the Tiny VGA pinout. Two input pins select among four colour palettes. It produces the characteristic asymmetric triangular chaos pattern expanding from a centre seed.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rule30_vga.review_notes: Replaced unrelated accelerator/prng/demoscene tags with cellular-automaton and game-of-life; summary corrected to match the documented Rule 30 VGA implementation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rv32_vga.summary: This design is a Tiny Tapeout graphics demo built around a small 4x4 ternary systolic array and a VGA generator. The array computes one of several tiny matrix demos selected by ui_in[1:0], with positive outputs shown in green, negative in red, and zero in blue. The 16 output values are rendered directly as a fullscreen 4x4 heatmap on a 640x480 VGA output. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform with the standard VGA PMOD pin mapping.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rv32_vga.review_notes: Replaced unsupported pattern-generator tag with systolic-array/mac-unit/accelerator and corrected summary to match documented behavior.

ttsky26b/tt_um_rwnt_vgatest.summary: This project displays a moving checkered pattern on a VGA display. The code was pulled from VGA Playground and is implemented in Verilog. It outputs VGA signals through the Tiny VGA pinout. The documentation is very thin, providing only a brief description of the behavior.
ttsky26b/tt_um_rwnt_vgatest.review_notes: Removed fabricated esoteric/systolic-array/accelerator tags and added graphics/pattern-generator/insufficient-doc.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sandsim_Alden_G878.summary: SandSim is a SystemVerilog physics engine that simulates falling sand on a 36x48 binary grid, computing the next state for pairs of rows with a compute kernel. It outputs a 640x480-style VGA signal through the Tiny VGA pinout and stores data in external QSPI flash and RAM. Users drive any of the eight ui pins high to spawn a grain of sand at the top of the grid. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod and a TinyQSPI Pmod to operate.
ttsky26b/tt_um_sandsim_Alden_G878.review_notes: Removed cellular-automaton and display tags because the design is a falling-sand physics simulation with VGA output, not a cellular automaton or generic display.

ttsky26b/tt_um_scisneros29_BCR.summary: This project implements an 8-bit register bank with eight storage locations, addressed by separate 3-bit write and read pointers. Data is written when the write-enable signal is asserted and read back when the read-enable signal is asserted, with 8-bit data in and out on the dedicated pins. It is a simple design that needs no external hardware. The documentation is brief and does not describe any silicon test results or notable implementation details.
ttsky26b/tt_um_scisneros29_BCR.review_notes: Removed education: the source does not state any teaching or learning purpose.

ttsky26b/tt_um_seapanda0.summary: This is an 8-bit, 8-tap Finite Impulse Response filter with parallel 8-bit input and output buses, using Q1.7 fixed-point coefficients that can be generated with MATLAB or Scilab. It requires an external MCU for clock generation and coefficient loading, and is intended to interface with an ADC08100 and AD9708 converter on a companion PCB. The design was verified with FPGA testing before tapeout. The documentation notes that a supporting PCB is planned but does not report silicon measurements.
ttsky26b/tt_um_seapanda0.review_notes: Removed adc/dac tags because those converters are external, not on-chip.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sienahlee.summary: TINY_NN implements a two-layer fully-connected neural network in hardware that classifies whether a 4-bit (x, y) coordinate lies inside or outside a circle. Layer 0 is a 2-input, 6-neuron linear layer with ReLU activation, and layer 1 is a 6-input, 1-neuron linear layer, all using 4-bit signed fixed-point arithmetic with saturating multiply-accumulate. A 6-state FSM sequences the computation, and the result is read from the inside_circle output once valid goes high. It needs four switches, four push buttons and two LEDs, and the documentation does not state that it is a class or workshop project.
ttsky26b/tt_um_sienahlee.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the invented 'student class project' sentence; added button, led and dip-switch interface tags supported by the pin descriptions.

ttsky26b/tt_um_silicon_art_vga_screensav.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo with an animated color gradient on a 640x480 VGA screen, with the 128x128 monochrome bitmap stored in a custom NOR ROM macro. The ROM's transistor pattern doubles as silicon art, making the logo visible in the diffusion layer of the fabricated chip. Inputs allow tiling the logo, switching to a solid color, and optionally controlling bouncing with a Gamepad Pmod. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and an optional Gamepad Pmod.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sillylad_top.summary: This is a SystemVerilog implementation of the Snake game rendered over a 640x480 VGA interface, with an 8x8 tile gameboard and a rainbow-colored snake. The snake is stored in a 20-tile shift register, which caps its maximum length at 20 and the score at 99 due to limited BCD digit space. Five buttons control start and direction, and optional LEDs show current button presses. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod, a VGA monitor, and buttons or a joystick.
ttsky26b/tt_um_sillylad_top.review_notes: Adjusted tags: removed bcd and added button, but summary is unchanged and accurate.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sker.summary: This is a mini two-player Bomberman game implemented in SystemVerilog, where each player has up, down, left, right and bomb buttons. The game is displayed through a VGA interface using the standard Tiny Tapeout VGA pinout. Testing consists of connecting it to a VGA monitor and using the ten buttons. It requires a VGA Pmod, buttons, wires, resistors and a breadboard, and the documentation is otherwise very brief.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sky_pll.summary: This is a test tile for a Tiny Tapeout PLL covering roughly 50-250 MHz, combining Sky HS logic blocks with analog blocks including a five-stage VCO, charge pump and loop capacitors. The digital side includes a programmable 4-bit clock scaler, reset logic that asserts RESET_OUT_N after 16 stable clocks, and a phase detector driving the charge pump. Testing involves setting the divider pins, asserting and clearing reset, and observing the raw clock and divided outputs on an oscilloscope. It requires a scope to inspect the output signals and is explicitly a test structure rather than a functional product.

ttsky26b/tt_um_snk_pwm_uart.summary: This design is a UART-controlled seven-channel PWM generator that receives 8N1 serial commands on ui_in[0]. A two-byte command format selects a channel (0-6) and sets its duty cycle (0-255), with a shared 8-bit counter compared against each duty register to produce the PWM outputs. The UART transmitter returns 0xAA as an acknowledgment for every received byte, and an enable pin gates operation. It needs a USB-to-UART adapter or microcontroller and an oscilloscope or logic analyzer to observe the outputs.

ttsky26b/tt_um_snk_smart_io_hub.summary: This is a UART-controlled smart I/O hub built around a 64-channel PWM engine, with channels divided into banks of eight selected by ui_in[6:4]. UART commands can write duty cycles, set a prescaler, and load internal modulation registers, while the upper eight channels are driven by a phase counter, an LFSR-style pattern source and an add/multiply datapath. A status page can be shown on uio_out when ui_in[7] is asserted, and a sequencer enable and clear-registers input are provided. It requires a USB-to-UART adapter or microcontroller and an oscilloscope or logic analyzer, and the pinout matches the TT Audio recommendation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_snn_afib_detector.summary: This chip implements a spiking neural network reservoir computing core that detects atrial fibrillation and asystole from R-peak timing pulses. It uses eight LIF neurons with recurrent feedback and a readout stage that accumulates weighted spikes over fast and slow windows, requiring both windows to agree before raising an alarm. The design is configured by serially loading 33 bits of weights and is tested by applying synthetic R-peak pulses and observing the output flags and confidence score. Notable features include self-adapting neuron thresholds and a compact implementation in 959 logic cells, with no processor or software required.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sobel.summary: This design is a streaming Sobel edge detection accelerator for grayscale images, using line buffers and a 3x3 sliding window to compute horizontal and vertical gradients in real time. Pixels are streamed in one per clock cycle, and the edge strength is output as an 8-bit value. The design is verified using cocotb with a Python golden reference model across several test patterns. No external hardware is required for simulation, and physical testing can use a standard Tiny Tapeout demo PCB.

ttsky26b/tt_um_sqrt8_ieee.summary: This project implements an 8-bit square root calculator using the non-restoring algorithm, producing a Q4.4 fixed-point result. The user applies an 8-bit input via switches and pulses the start pin, then reads the 8-bit output on LEDs. The design operates at a 50 Hz clock and requires no special external hardware beyond the LEDs on the demo board. It is a straightforward arithmetic core with a simple start/done handshake.

ttsky26b/tt_um_systolic_array.summary: This design is a 3x3 systolic array with 4-bit inputs that performs matrix multiplication, using output-stationary dataflow. It includes SPI communication to load matrices A and B and to read out the resulting 3x3 matrix. The design is tested via a provided Makefile test, and manual testing requires driving SPI signals with a clock at most half the system clock. No external hardware is required beyond the SPI host.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tetrahedral_oscillator.summary: This project is a tetrahedral-style oscillator built from coupled CMOS inverter pairs with MIM capacitors as load elements, implemented in the SKY130 process. It provides four buffered observation outputs that oscillate around 12 MHz when powered from a 1.8 V supply. The design is tested by probing the outputs with a high-impedance oscilloscope or frequency counter, and no external passives or bias sources are needed. Post-layout extracted simulation was performed to verify oscillation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_tetrahedral_oscillator.review_notes: Removed ring-oscillator and full-custom; the source specifies a tetrahedral oscillator and semi-custom standard-cell layout.

ttsky26b/tt_um_the_siliconimist_chip1.summary: This is a simple hello-world design that counts from 0 to 9 once per second on a single 7-segment display. It uses a clock divider to generate a 1 Hz tick, a digit counter, and a combinational 7-segment decoder. The design is intended to run on the Tiny Tapeout demo board, using the onboard 7-segment display and reset button, and can also be simulated with a cocotb testbench. It is notable as the creators' first silicon design project, prototyped on Wokwi.

ttsky26b/tt_um_theandelope_checkers.summary: This project is a VGA display that shows a checkers pattern, using the Tiny VGA pinout with 2-bit color per channel and sync signals. The documentation is essentially placeholder text (lorem ipsum), so the exact functionality and testing procedure cannot be determined from the provided information. The design likely generates a checkerboard pattern on a VGA monitor. No external hardware details are given beyond the VGA connection implied by the pin names.
ttsky26b/tt_um_theandelope_checkers.review_notes: Removed unsupported pattern-generator; added verilog and insufficient-doc.

ttsky26b/tt_um_thorsten_shiftregister.summary: This design is a 40-bit shift register with a hardcoded secret number, forming a challenge where the output goes high only when the correct 40-bit sequence is shifted in. The user shifts bits in serially, one per clock cycle, and after 40 bits the output indicates whether the sequence matches. The register acts as a sliding window, so every new bit checks a new candidate. No external hardware is required beyond the clock, reset, and two input pins.

ttsky26b/tt_um_thunder.summary: This circuit implements a sequential rear-light controller inspired by the Ford Thunderbird, using a 2-bit counter and decoders to produce progressive left and right light patterns. The blinker input selects left, right, both, or neither sequence, and the outputs drive three LEDs per side. The design is tested by applying reset, setting blinker values, and observing the output progression over several clock cycles. It was created as part of the IEEE OpenSilicon Bootcamp and requires external LEDs for visual output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tile_growth_simulator_Noa.summary: This design is an interactive tile growth simulator for a 16x16 WS2812B LED matrix, where players place colored cells and then start a random growth process. It uses a 16-bit LFSR seeded by player cursor movements to drive the spreading of colors into empty neighbors until the grid is full. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench that runs three starting configurations and prints the grid state after each round. External hardware includes the 16x16 LED matrix and pushbuttons for input.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tiny3d_kevinqian11.summary: Tiny3D is a hardware 3D graphics pipeline that renders the vertices of a rotating cube to a VGA display. Six input pins select rotation directions for the cube around its axes, and a reset returns it to its initial orientation. It requires a Tiny Tapeout VGA Pmod and six buttons with pull-down resistors to drive the directional inputs. The design is notable for claiming to be the smallest 3D graphics engine, fitting a vertex pipeline into a 1x2 tile footprint.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tiny8_risclike.summary: This is an 8-bit CPU that loads 16-bit instructions over SPI into internal program memory and then executes them autonomously. A RUN input starts execution, while PROGRAM_LOADED, HALTED and RUN_ECHO pins report status, and the eight outputs expose the CPU result byte. The final stable version uses ten instruction slots and an enriched ISA, though the documentation does not list the instruction set. No external hardware beyond an SPI host is described.
ttsky26b/tt_um_tiny8_risclike.review_notes: Removed unsupported bootloader tag and added verilog tag based on stated language.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tiny_8bit_cpu.summary: This is a compact 8-bit teaching CPU with four general registers, a 24x8 data RAM, an 8-bit ALU and a 16-instruction ISA. Instructions are supplied externally on the eight input pins, with the destination register value on the outputs and PC, zero, carry and fetch-phase flags on the bidirectional pins for debugging. It is intended as an educational design, with unit tests for the ALU, control FSM, registers, memory and datapath, and it needs external memory to hold instructions. The design is configured for a 1x2 tile footprint and has no on-chip program ROM.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tinycgra.summary: tinyCGRA 2x2 is a 2x2 coarse-grained reconfigurable array where each processing element selects two of four neighbour inputs and applies a 2-bit ALU operation. Configuration is shifted in serially as a 24-bit bitstream, and a latched input byte is broadcast to the north and west edges while the output pins show one selected PE result or an XOR of all four. The repository also includes generic 3x3 and multi-context variants for area studies. It is tested through a Tiny Tapeout top regression and separate area-top regressions.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tnt_mosbius.summary: This project is an alternative layout for Andrew Kang's mini-MOSbius, a reconfigurable analog array intended for building and experimenting with MOS circuits, adapted for SKY130 on Tiny Tapeout. It includes analog switches controlled by a serial bitstream, with digital logic for configuration, and it requires external hardware to generate the bitstream and to interface with the analog pins depending on the circuit being built. Silicon test reports indicate that the configuration shift registers work and that various circuits functioned properly. The design is notable for bringing the MOSbius educational concept to a Tiny Tapeout-compatible form, though the software suite for generating configuration bitstreams is not yet written.

ttsky26b/tt_um_top.summary: This design computes the Henon map, a discrete-time chaotic dynamical system, in 10-bit signed Q2.8 fixed-point arithmetic. It serialises the resulting x and y samples as raw bit streams on separate output pins, each with its own enable and end-of-sequence flag, and asserts done_henon once the first valid sample is available. The documentation describes the three sub-blocks and the arithmetic format but the external hardware section is empty. It is a compact 1x1 implementation of a mathematical recurrence rather than a general-purpose processor.
ttsky26b/tt_um_top.review_notes: Removed unsupported signal-generator; added physics, fixed-point, verilog.

ttsky26b/tt_um_top_module_16_mips.summary: This is a complete 16-bit MIPS single-cycle processor that loads 16-bit instructions through the 8-bit Tiny Tapeout input pins. A mode pin selects load or run, address bits and a byte-select pin choose where each byte is written, and in run mode the ALU result is driven onto the outputs and upper bidirectional pins. The documentation consists mainly of pin descriptions, with no instruction set listing or test procedure. It is a 1x1 design that requires an external host to feed instruction bytes during load mode.
ttsky26b/tt_um_top_module_16_mips.review_notes: Removed bootloader tag: source describes pin-based instruction loading, not a bootloader.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tpu.summary: Mini TPU v2 is a 3x3 systolic array of processing elements that performs multiply-accumulate operations for matrix multiplication. Inputs and weights are fetched externally over SPI, and the eight-bit result is presented on the output pins. The design is a compact 1x1 accelerator built with IEEE funding, and the documentation is limited to the one-line description and pin names. No test procedure or external hardware details beyond the SPI host are given.
ttsky26b/tt_um_tpu.review_notes: Removed neural-network: only matrix-multiply systolic array behavior is documented, with no neural network inference described.

ttsky26b/tt_um_traffic_ctrl.summary: This design implements a seven-state Moore finite state machine controlling a two-road traffic intersection with N/S and E/W signals. Vehicle sensors on each road allow adaptive green-phase extension, and emergency-vehicle inputs on either axis trigger a hardware priority override. Outputs drive the green and yellow lamps for each road, an emergency-active flag, and three FSM state bits for 7-segment debug display. The documentation describes the state machine at a high level but does not detail the timing or override behaviour.
ttsky26b/tt_um_traffic_ctrl.review_notes: Swapped sensor-interface for automotive, which better matches the traffic-control application.

ttsky26b/tt_um_trinity_max_true.summary: TRI-1 Gamma is a 32-tile neuromorphic design combining eight cortical columns with leaky-integrate-and-fire dynamics and ternary MLP layers, a 20-PE GF16 mesh, and 24 supporting modules including ROMs, matrix multipliers, a Blake3 anchor and monitors. It includes a four-port die-to-die router for multi-chip spike propagation, and on reset it drives the canonical constant 0x47C0 onto the output pins. The design uses a custom GF16 format with shift-and-add mantissa multiplication, and no external hardware is required for single-die testing. The documentation is dense and uses unusual terminology, so the exact function of many blocks is hard to verify from the text alone.
ttsky26b/tt_um_trinity_max_true.review_notes: Removed spiking-neural-network and floating-point; added neural-network and soc to match the described architecture.

ttsky26b/tt_um_trinity_nano.summary: TRI-1 Phi is a single-tile design that computes a four-element dot product in a custom GF16 format using four parallel multipliers and a tree of adders. On reset it drives the canonical value 0x47C0, representing dot4(1,2,3,4) = 30.0, onto the output pins as a cross-die anchor shared with its sibling designs. It also includes a Lucas ROM, a hardware random number generator LFSR, a restraint controller and a friend-foe handshake, with input pins to select modes and probe the ROM. No external hardware is required, and the documentation is detailed but uses project-specific terminology.
ttsky26b/tt_um_trinity_nano.review_notes: Removed floating-point (GF16 is a custom format); added dsp and trng for the dot-product and HWRNG blocks.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tron_game.summary: This design implements a two-player Tron light-cycle game rendered over VGA at 640x480 resolution. Each player controls a light cycle using four directional buttons, and the trails are stored in circular buffers with collision detection against walls, trails, and head-on collisions. The game uses a 32x24 grid of 10x10 pixel cells, with procedural sprites and a blue checkerboard border. It requires a TinyVGA PMOD and eight pushbuttons, and is notable for its use of a multiply-by-reciprocal technique for pixel-to-grid mapping.
ttsky26b/tt_um_tron_game.review_notes: Removed fifo tag because the trail storage is a circular buffer, not a FIFO; added button and pmod interface tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_tt08_axis_fifo_fwft_bkeno.summary: This project implements an 8-bit depth-16 AXI4-Stream FIFO with First-Word Fall-Through (FWFT) using a register file instead of Block RAM. The register file allows combinational reads, so data falls through to the output on the same clock cycle without a read strobe, providing true zero-cycle latency. The FIFO manages AXI4-Stream handshaking with tvalid and tready signals and provides full and empty flags. It is tested by driving the AXI-Stream control signals and observing the data flow.
ttsky26b/tt_um_tt08_axis_fifo_fwft_bkeno.review_notes: Removed synchronizer (no CDC described) and added verilog.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ultrasage_danz.summary: This is a finite state machine that controls an irrigation pump based on soil moisture levels detected by two comparators. It has four states: IDLE, IRRIGATE, SATURATED, and INVALID, with the pump turned on only in the IRRIGATE state and an invalid flag asserted in the INVALID state. Testing involves connecting a moisture sensor and comparators to the inputs, a pump to the PUMP output, and checking state transitions for dry, mild, wet, and invalid moisture readings. External hardware includes a moisture sensor, two comparators, a relay-controlled pump, a clock source, and a power supply.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ultrasage_danz.review_notes: Replaced unrelated logic-gate/ring-oscillator/phase-detector/flip-flop/counter/standard-cell tags with FSM, industrial, Verilog, comparator-analog and relay tags matching the irrigation controller.

ttsky26b/tt_um_umitanik_matmul3x3.summary: This design is a 3x3 unsigned 4-bit matrix multiplier that computes C = A * B with 10-bit output. It uses a nibble-stream protocol to load the matrices serially due to limited I/O pins, and a finite state machine manages the loading, computation, and reading phases. The result is read as two bytes per element, and status pins indicate busy, done, and output valid. It requires an external host such as a microcontroller or FPGA to drive the protocol, and no analog components are needed.
ttsky26b/tt_um_umitanik_matmul3x3.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'alu' tag; the rest of the proposed tags are supported.

ttsky26b/tt_um_unified_error_detection.summary: This design is a combinational error detection engine that combines Hamming(12,8) encoding and CRC-8 checksum for 8-bit data protection. It uses pure XOR trees to provide zero-latency encoding, and a 4-to-1 multiplexer allows the 20-bit protected frame to be read in three 8-bit chunks. The design is tested by setting input data and toggling selection bits to read the segments. It requires an external controller to cycle through select states and reconstruct the frame.
ttsky26b/tt_um_unified_error_detection.review_notes: Removed parity tag because the source describes Hamming parity bits, not a standalone parity generator/checker.

ttsky26b/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttsky26b/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_usp_didactic.summary: This is a didactic testchip for teaching CMOS design, featuring five modules selected by a 3-bit MUX: a logic gate library, a ring oscillator with configurable divider, a phase-frequency detector, a D/T flip-flop study, and a 4-bit binary counter. The design includes always-live monitoring signals on bidirectional pins and is intended for hands-on experimentation with oscilloscopes, function generators, and push-buttons. It is notable for using explicit sky130 standard cell instantiations and for providing a range of frequencies from the ring oscillator for different measurement instruments. The chip is designed for educational purposes and includes detailed testing instructions for each module.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vga.summary: This project generates real-time VGA graphics using purely arithmetic logic, with no framebuffer or ROM. It cycles through four rendering modes (rings, plasma, interference, chaos) based on a frame counter, and every pixel is computed on-the-fly. The design requires a VGA monitor and a 25 MHz clock, and it automatically starts rendering and cycling through modes upon reset release. It is notable for its fully procedural approach and continuous animation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_vga.review_notes: Removed alu: the design performs arithmetic rendering but does not implement an ALU.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vga_ascii.summary: This design displays the sentence 'As above, so below' with a typewriter effect on a VGA monitor. It uses a standard 640x480 VGA timing generator and a state machine to manage the sequential animation, with a coordinate-based spatial hash to generate a flickering matrix of tiny green ASCII characters. The design requires a Tiny Tapeout VGA PMOD and a 25 MHz clock. It is notable for its text animation and pseudo-random character rendering.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vga_glyph_mode_clone.summary: This design displays 'PHILIPPINE IC DESIGN BOOTCAMP 2026!' in a Matrix-style display on a VGA monitor. It is based on the VGA Glyph mode by James Ross and includes palette selection and VGA mode bits. The design requires a VGA monitor and a 25 MHz clock. The documentation is minimal and refers to an external GitHub repository for details.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vga_sharc_demo.summary: This project generates a 640x480 VGA signal and renders a demo scene with three bouncing logos, a parallax checkerboard background, and optional ripple and color cycling effects. It uses a bitmap ROM for the logos and a palette for color mapping. The design is tested with a cocotb testbench and requires a VGA monitor. It is notable for its demo scene effects and per-frame physics.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vga_yusefkarim.summary: This project is a promotional VGA display for the RISC-V Ottawa group, based on the standard VGA demo from vga-playground.com. It drives a TinyVGA PMOD with 2-bit-per-channel colour and shows three text messages that bounce around the frame. The design uses a font ROM and stream ROM to fit in a 1×1 tile, with overlapping sprites highlighted in a strobe colour. It is intended as a promotional screen for the RISC-V Ottawa group.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vidishac2004_calc.summary: This project implements a calculator for a 4x4 matrix keypad in System Verilog. The keypad scanner drives the column lines and reads the row lines to detect key presses, buffering digits and storing operators. An ALU computes addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division, and the 8-bit result is presented on the dedicated output pins. An external 4x4 matrix keypad is required.
ttsky26b/tt_um_vidishac2004_calc.review_notes: Tags described a neural network accelerator unrelated to the keypad calculator source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_vmm_bnn.summary: This project is a 1-bit Vector-Matrix Multiplier coprocessor designed to accelerate Binary Neural Networks. It contains 8 physical neurons, each with an 8-bit weight shift register and a 10-bit accumulator, using XNOR gates for multiplication and a popcount adder tree for accumulation. The ASIC acts as a raw math engine without an internal state machine, while a host processor handles looping, routing, and layer management. It is intended to be driven by a host microcontroller or FPGA SoC.
ttsky26b/tt_um_vmm_bnn.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the documented BNN accelerator.

ttsky26b/tt_um_voltrare.summary: This project is a simple UART transmitter module written in Verilog. It transmits 8-bit parallel data presented on ui[7:0] at 115200 baud when the tx_send pin is asserted. The TX output pin carries the serial data, and tx_busy indicates transmission activity. No external hardware beyond a UART receiver is required.
ttsky26b/tt_um_voltrare.review_notes: Proposed tags described an unrelated subtractor/ALU design; replaced with UART transmitter tags.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wearlevel_controller.summary: This project is a hardware EEPROM wear-leveling controller implementing the Start-Gap algorithm with a 2-round Feistel address scrambler. It maintains an 8-entry logical-to-physical mapping table and 16-bit wear counters per physical block, triggering remaps when wear differences exceed a threshold. Additional features include Hamming(6,3) single-error correction, bad-block retirement, saturating wear counters, and an in-band telemetry port. The purely digital finite-state machine is written in Verilog and verified with a Cocotb testbench.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wearlevel_controller.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated adder/ALU design; replaced with tags and summary matching the wear-leveling controller source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_william_adc8.summary: This project is an enable-controlled 8-bit sigma-delta decimator ADC for 1-bit bitstreams. The incoming bitstream is sampled by the Tiny Tapeout clock and a 256-cycle decimator counts ones to produce a raw 8-bit code. Gain trim and signed offset trim are applied, with the calibrated result output on uo[7:0] and status bits {saturated, activity, busy, valid} on uio[7:4]. It is written in Verilog and verified with a cocotb testbench.
ttsky26b/tt_um_william_adc8.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated power supply design; replaced with tags and summary matching the sigma-delta ADC source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_william_pll.summary: This Verilog project models an enable-controlled PLL clock generator intended for smartcard timing experiments. It accepts a reference clock and provides configuration inputs for feedback divider ratio and charge pump gain, with outputs for the PLL clock, divided clocks, and lock status. The design is verified through cocotb simulation tests that check enable, disable, and lock behavior. No external hardware is required for RTL verification, and the design is notable for exposing internal PLL signals for monitoring.
ttsky26b/tt_um_william_pll.review_notes: Removed security tag as no security focus is described; added cocotb since the source explicitly mentions cocotb verification.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wlmoi_bcd_to_7segment.summary: This project is a BCD/HEX to 7-segment decoder that translates a 4-bit input into a seven-segment glyph pattern for 0-9, A, b, C, d, e, and F. It supports display enable, blank, lamp test, decimal point input, and an active-low mode for common-anode or common-cathode displays. Status outputs indicate valid digit, invalid digit, display on, and active-low mode echo. It is written in Verilog and verified with a cocotb regression plus a standalone Verilog check.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wlmoi_bcd_to_7segment.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated ROM/cipher design; replaced with tags and summary matching the 7-segment decoder source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458477197787547649.summary: This project is a full subtractor implemented in Wokwi. It takes three input values and produces two outputs: the result and the borrow. The design is purely combinational logic. External hardware consists of LEDs for observing the outputs.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458477197787547649.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated ADC/sigma-delta/FIR/FPGA tags with subtractor, combinational, wokwi, and led.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458489231265343489.summary: This project is a simple binary adder with inputs A, B, and carry-in, and outputs sum and carry-out. The truth table shows a full adder behavior for single-bit addition. It is implemented as combinational logic in the Wokwi simulator. The design is intended as an educational workshop example.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458489231265343489.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to reflect the adder design rather than BCD decoder.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458569964697822209.summary: This project is a 1-bit full adder that adds three binary inputs A, B, and Cin to produce Sum and Cout. It is built with XOR, AND, and OR gates implementing Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin and Cout = (A AND B) OR (Cin AND (A XOR B)). The design is combinational and can be cascaded to form multi-bit adders. It is implemented in Wokwi and tested with switches and LEDs.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458569964697822209.review_notes: Removed unsupported popcount tag; summary described a different circuit.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458951258752539649.summary: This is a small game where the player controls a child searching for a ball in a haunted house. Four directional buttons move the character, and an 'Eat' button plus a window action provide additional choices, with LED indicators showing life and ball status. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires two external LEDs for output. Testing involves following the game rules: turning on the life and ball lights, activating only one LED in each of six columns, and avoiding the cake.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_458951258752539649.review_notes: Removed education tag not supported by the source.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_460983138943099905.summary: This project is a trial logic block for a VGA data controller created for a Tiny Tapeout workshop. It takes two inputs and produces AND and NOR outputs, and is described as having a different clock configuration to test VGA output at various frame rates. The documentation is sparse: it does not explain the VGA interface, the clock settings, or how to connect external hardware, and the 'External hardware' section is left as a placeholder. The design appears to be a simple combinational logic experiment intended for workshop attendees, but its exact purpose and implementation cannot be fully determined from the provided text.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_460983138943099905.review_notes: Removed template and education; added vga and incomplete to match the stated VGA trial and sparse documentation.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461554799001985025.summary: This design implements a simple 3-input majority voting system, where the output goes high if any two or more of the three voter inputs are high. It is built in Wokwi. The circuit can be tested by connecting three switches to the inputs and an LED to the result output. External hardware includes an LED and switches or pushbuttons.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461554799001985025.review_notes: Removed arbiter and logic-gate tags because the design is a majority voter, not an arbiter or basic gate.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461620354455920641.summary: This is a 4-bit password security system that grants access for a correct code and triggers a persistent alarm for the trap code 1111. It uses combinational logic for comparison and an SR latch so that the alarm state remains active until a manual reset, demonstrating both combinational and sequential logic in hardware security. The design is implemented in Wokwi. To test it, DIP switches provide the 4-bit input, and LEDs (red and green) plus a buzzer indicate access granted or alarm states. External hardware includes an 8-position DIP switch, pushbuttons for step and reset, LEDs, a buzzer, and resistors.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461620354455920641.review_notes: Removed education tag; the source does not state an educational purpose.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461622504612675585.summary: This is a 4-digit passcode lock that unlocks only for the code 1010 and activates an alarm for 1111, with a wrong indicator for other codes. It is built from basic logic gates in Wokwi and is combinational, so outputs update directly with inputs. To test it, use DIP switches for the four inputs and observe three LEDs (unlock, wrong, alarm) and a buzzer. External hardware includes a DIP switch, three LEDs, and a buzzer. The design is intended for educational purposes and maps to Tiny Tapeout input/output blocks.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461622504612675585.review_notes: Removed security tag because it is a simple combinatorial lock, not a security-focused design.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461639934990157825.summary: This project implements a 4-bit digital lock that compares a 4-bit input against the fixed password 1010 using discrete logic gates. When the correct combination is entered, an output goes high to turn on a display showing 'U' for unlocked. An SR latch provides a permanent lock condition: entering 1111 triggers the latch and prevents any future unlocking, even with the correct password. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external switches, logic gates, a 7-segment display, and optionally an LED for debugging.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_461639934990157825.review_notes: Removed 7-segment interface tag since the display is external hardware, not an on-chip interface.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462089398612533249.summary: This is a puzzle circuit based on the 'Holidays' Tiny Tapeout example, modified to allow exactly two holiday choices (or an extra sunscreen option). It takes eight inputs and one bidirectional input, and outputs a single logic signal that is true for only specific input combinations. The design is implemented in Wokwi. Testing requires setting the inputs to the specified patterns to get a true output. External hardware is just one LED for output.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462089398612533249.review_notes: Removed logic-gate tag because implementation details are not specified in the source.
