ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462089659615737857.summary: This is a 'live or die' game where a trap is set using DIP switches and loaded into flip-flops, and another player tries to find the trap by pressing check. If the red LED turns on, the player is dead; otherwise, the 'ALIVE' output is indicated. The design is implemented in Wokwi. To test, place the trap with the DIP switch, load it, and then have another player press check. External hardware includes LEDs, a DIP switch, resistors, and pushbuttons. The documentation is very brief and does not detail the exact logic or input/output mapping.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462089659615737857.review_notes: Removed unsupported memory and education tags; flip-flop tag already covers storage.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462165147286899713.summary: This design is a simple UART transmitter that loads the text 'PSI Open IC 2026' into a shift register and clocks it out to the UART_TX pin. It uses a 100 Hz clock and has control inputs for output enable, reset, and input selection. To test, set RST_N low and provide a clock, then set RST_N high to start transmission; a UART receiver is needed to observe the output. External hardware includes a clock generator and a UART receiver.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462165147286899713.review_notes: Removed 'text' output tag: the design only serializes a fixed string over UART, with no text display/rendering output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462285560117329921.summary: This circuit converts a 4-bit binary-coded decimal (BCD) input (0-9) to 7-segment display outputs, similar to the 7448 IC but with the modification that a zero input always turns the display off. It is implemented in Wokwi. To test, connect four switches to the inputs and a common-cathode 7-segment display to the outputs, then apply valid BCD values from 0 to 9. External hardware includes 4 switches or a DIP switch, a common-cathode 7-segment display, and 7 resistors for protection.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462285560117329921.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'logic-gate' and 'education' tags; the design is a BCD-to-7-segment decoder.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462290658621740033.summary: This project implements a 3-bit magnitude comparator that takes two 3-bit unsigned integers A and B and displays the comparison result on a 7-segment display. The circuit uses XOR gates to detect differences and logic gates to determine greater than, equal, or less than, which are then encoded to drive the display segments. To test, set six switches for A and B, and the display shows the corresponding relationship. External hardware includes a common-cathode 7-segment display connected to the outputs.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462290658621740033.review_notes: Removed unsupported logic-gate tag and trimmed an unsupported educational claim from the summary.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462349004652630017.summary: This project implements a 2-bit reversible ALU using Toffoli, Fredkin, and Peres gates, with a security key that validates the mode selection. If the key is incorrect, the internal routing is flipped, causing the ALU to output a different operation than selected. The design preserves five input bits as garbage outputs to maintain bijective mapping, and it fits within a 1x1 tile. It is purely combinational and requires no external hardware beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout carrier board with switches and LEDs.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_462595774777167873.summary: This design is a universal bypass manager with hysteresis intended to protect lithium batteries by isolating them when fully charged and powering the device directly from the charger. It uses a combinational stage to monitor charger presence and battery limits, and an SR latch to implement hysteresis, preventing rapid charging cycles. The chip outputs charge and bypass signals that would drive external power MOSFETs or solid-state relays. It requires external sensors and power components for real-world use, such as voltage comparators and MOSFETs.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_463101366305871873.summary: The project is titled 'Tiny Laura L' and its one-line description states that setting the first four inputs to 1010 will display an 'L' on a 7-segment display. However, the documentation sections for how it works, how to test, and external hardware are all placeholder text, providing no actual details. Therefore, it is unclear how the design functions or what external hardware is needed. The project appears to be a simple display driver, but the lack of documentation prevents a full understanding.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_463557428446691329.summary: This is a 3-bit ALU that supports addition, subtraction, and multiplication, with a fourth mode that passes through switches, clock, and reset signals. The inputs are eight switches: six for two 3-bit operands and two for mode selection. The outputs are eight pins that can drive a 7-segment display, though the segments light up according to the binary output rather than decimal digits. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware beyond the standard board and a 7-segment display.
ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_463557428446691329.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added dip-switch tag based on the switch inputs.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_464171399090591745.summary: This design drives an 8-segment display based on two select inputs. When the selects are 00, it displays the letter 'K'; when 01, it displays 'A'; when 10 or 11, it shows an animated snake moving around the perimeter and through the middle bar. The animation is driven by a 3-bit counter clocked at 3 Hz. The design requires no external hardware beyond the standard board and display.

It uses three input pins (SC1, SC3, SC7) and seven output pins (RX0, RX1, RX3, RX4, RX5, RX7). It requires no external hardware beyond the development board. The design is notable for its puzzle-like interaction.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_464171612496799745.summary: This project implements a simple 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit inputs on ui[0:7] and produces a 5-bit sum on uo[0:4]. It is implemented in Wokwi. The design is purely combinational, with no clock or reset. Testing involves applying all pairs of 4-bit numbers and verifying the output sum, and no external hardware is required.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_464171864719209473.summary: This design is an 8-channel LED pattern sequencer that drives up to eight LEDs with various animation patterns. It supports enable, direction control, up to eight pattern modes, and four speed settings via clock dividers, all controlled by the input pins. The output is an 8-bit pattern that can directly drive LEDs or be used as logic signals. Testing is done by configuring the inputs and observing the LED patterns, and external LEDs are required to visualize the output.

ttsky26b/tt_um_wokwi_464178664603376641.summary: This design is described as a 16-bit counter but the documentation is minimal and unclear. It mentions clock dividers connected together and random elements, with inputs that select a multiplexer source and change a random seed. Outputs include a 4-bit counter output and a 6-bit random seed output. Testing requires a clock input and manipulation of the input pins to observe the outputs.

ttsky26b/tt_um_ww_charlieplex.summary: This project is a controller for an Adafruit Charlieplex LED array, supporting up to 56 LEDs (7x8). It includes an SPI slave interface for loading custom display data, with each byte representing the brightness of one LED. On reset, it displays a brightness gradient across the array. Testing involves connecting the eight signal pins to the LED array and optionally using SPI to update the display.
ttsky26b/tt_um_ww_charlieplex.review_notes: Removed unsupported 'pwm' and 'led' tags, added 'pmod' (explicitly mentioned), and dropped the unsupported efficiency claim from the summary.

ttsky26b/tt_um_xeniarose_sbox.summary: This project implements AES forward S-Box circuits using direct computation rather than lookup tables, and also includes the PRESENT cipher S-Box. It provides a memory-mapped interface with 6 address pins, a read/write mode pin, an I/O latch, and an 8-bit bidirectional data bus for accessing the S-Boxes. The design is used by following specific I/O sequences detailed in the test script. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable for avoiding lookup tables in the AES S-Box implementation.
ttsky26b/tt_um_xeniarose_sbox.review_notes: Removed unsupported combinational tag and added gpio to reflect the explicit pin-based I/O interface.

ttsky26b/tt_um_yfoong86_chasey.summary: Chasey is a maze game where the player controls a character to escape a ghost, rendered over VGA. It uses five active-high buttons for reset and directional movement, and outputs VGA color and sync signals through a Tiny VGA PMOD. The design is implemented in SystemVerilog and runs on a 25 MHz clock. Silicon test results are not provided, so correct operation on hardware is not confirmed.
ttsky26b/tt_um_yfoong86_chasey.review_notes: Removed the unsupported 640x480 resolution claim from the summary; all tags are supported.

ttsky26b/tt_um_youweiterrylu.summary: This project implements a Direct Memory Access (DMA) controller that processes transfer descriptors from a ring buffer, configured over SPI. It includes an SPI register interface, a ring manager, a descriptor fetcher and data mover, and an interrupt output for ring-empty and error conditions. The design is tested by connecting an external SPI master and writing configuration and descriptor tail pointer registers; internal activity is monitored via probe outputs. For this tapeout, an internal memory stub replaces an AXI4 master, and no external hardware beyond an SPI master is required. The design is notable for its autonomous descriptor processing and consolidated interrupt scheme.

ttsky26b/tt_um_zed_analog.summary: This project contains two analog CMOS designs: three independent 2-input AND gates equivalent to the 7408, and an SR latch built from two cross-coupled NOR gates. The AND gates are constructed at the transistor level rather than from a digital library, while the latch sets, resets, or holds its state based on the s and r inputs. Testing the AND gates requires push buttons or DIP switches for inputs and LEDs on the outputs, whereas the latch needs no external hardware and can be verified by simulation or by observing q and qb. The design relies on the Tiny Tapeout padring for ESD protection and operates from the 1.8V VDPWR rail.
ttsky26b/tt_um_zed_analog.review_notes: Removed standard-cell tag as the source explicitly states transistor-level construction; logic-gate was already present in the proposed tags, so no add is needed.

ttsky26b/tt_um_zlj8800_tiny_tapeout_v2.summary: This design displays a bouncing logo on a VGA monitor, using the standard Tiny VGA pinout for color and sync signals. It is a beginner project with minimal documentation, described only as 'v1 logo bouncing' with a test note of 'Test 123'. The implementation is in Verilog and requires a VGA monitor and a Tiny VGA PMOD for external connection. No silicon test results or detailed functionality are provided.
ttsky26b/tt_um_zlj8800_tiny_tapeout_v2.review_notes: Removed education and demoscene as unsupported; added insufficient-doc.

ttsky26c/tt_um_1DC_vga_dyoa.summary: This Verilog design drives a VGA display to show the text "DESIGN YOUR OWN CHIP" using the Tiny VGA pinout at a 25.175 MHz pixel clock. It outputs two bits each of red, green and blue along with horizontal and vertical sync on the eight outputs. It is used by connecting a VGA display through a Tiny VGA Pmod, with no other external hardware required. The project is a simple demonstration of generating a VGA signal from a Tiny Tapeout design.
ttsky26c/tt_um_1DC_vga_dyoa.review_notes: Removed text tag; VGA/video/display tags cover the output.

ttsky26c/tt_um_2048_vga_game.summary: This design implements the 2048 sliding tile puzzle game for VGA display, where players slide numbered tiles on a 4x4 grid to combine them and create a tile with the number 2048. The game is controlled via input pins or an optional SNES-compatible gamepad, and it includes two color themes and a unit test mode. The design requires a TinyVGA Pmod for video output and optionally a Gamepad Pmod for controller input. It supports debug commands via bidirectional pins when in unit test mode.
ttsky26c/tt_um_2048_vga_game.review_notes: Removed unsupported display tag and added button for the documented direction inputs.

ttsky26c/tt_um_Asaadkhex_6x6u.summary: This Verilog design implements a bidirectional 6x6 bussbar switch that can route any of six UART receive inputs to one or more of six UART transmit outputs, with each output connected to at most one input at a time. Configuration is loaded through a serial data-in pin and an 18-bit shift register, with a latch signal to apply the configuration and an active-low reset. It is tested by driving the configuration stream from an external microcontroller and connecting UART interfaces to the TXD and RXD pins. No external hardware beyond UART connections is required, making it a compact programmable serial routing block.

ttsky26c/tt_um_CCDmos3D.summary: This analog design is an 8-bit binary-search analog-to-digital converter intended to digitize analog pixel signals for a CCDmos3D pixel. It generates its own test input signal, feeds it through the ADC, converts the digital result back with a DAC, and outputs both the original and reconstructed signals on two analog pins for comparison. Testing requires a power source for the chip and an oscilloscope to verify that the two analog outputs match. The design is notable for including a self-test path that exercises the ADC and DAC together.
ttsky26c/tt_um_CCDmos3D.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal because the source describes only an analog ADC, and avoided adding silicon-tested since no silicon status is reported.

ttsky26c/tt_um_K_coder_9.summary: This Verilog design generates a PWM signal whose frequency and duty cycle are set by an 8-bit duty ratio input and speed and mode selection pins, intended to model the pulse control of a TENS device. It supports a continuous mode and a burst mode that gates pulses into a 200 ms on, 800 ms off envelope. Testing is done by holding reset, setting the duty ratio, selecting continuous or burst mode, and observing the output on an oscilloscope. The documentation explicitly warns that the design has not been reviewed for safety and must not be used to drive electrical impulses into skin.

ttsky26c/tt_um_LnL_SoC.summary: This Verilog project is a small system on chip containing a 16-bit microprocessor, a 32-word boot ROM, RAM, an 8-bit PWM, an 8-bit timer, a UART and an SPI interface, all memory-mapped for the CPU. After reset the boot ROM runs a program that reads the 8-bit input port, writes it to the 8-bit output port, and exercises the supported instructions and the SPI, timer and PWM blocks. It is tested by powering the chip and observing the parallel output on a 7-segment display or LEDs, with SPI data appearing on the MOSI and related pins. The documentation notes that external hardware such as a keypad and display is still to be decided.
ttsky26c/tt_um_LnL_SoC.review_notes: Removed education tag as the source does not indicate teaching intent; removed unsupported claim about teaching vehicle from summary.

ttsky26c/tt_um_Logy_FMAC.summary: This Verilog design is an 8-bit signed fused multiply-add unit that computes z = a*b + c with a 16-bit internal product and sum, outputting the low 8 bits of the result. It uses a two-phase streaming protocol in which a and b are captured on even cycles and c on odd cycles, producing one result every two cycles with no separate valid signal. It is verified with cocotb tests covering reset, corner cases, 2000 randomized triples against a Python reference, and back-to-back streaming, plus a plain Verilog self-checking testbench. No external hardware is required, and the design is notable for its compact streaming arithmetic datapath.
ttsky26c/tt_um_Logy_FMAC.review_notes: Removed alu and pipeline tags; added cocotb for the documented testbench.

ttsky26c/tt_um_Median_MAD.summary: This Verilog design is a zero-RAM streaming statistical co-processor that tracks a median and median absolute deviation baseline from an 8-bit input stream and classifies events using a temporal persistence engine. It outputs the tracked baseline on the eight outputs and an event code on three bidirectional pins, with a wake interrupt and debug and configuration pins. It is tested by applying an 8-bit signal and configuration pins, then injecting a one-cycle spike, a permanent baseline jump, a slow ramp, or a held value to obtain the corresponding glitch, shift, drift or stuck-sensor codes. The design is notable for distinguishing transient outliers from persistent baseline shifts without any memory buffers.
ttsky26c/tt_um_Median_MAD.review_notes: Removed machine-learning because the source describes statistical event classification, not ML hardware; added instrumentation for the sensor measurement/classification role.

ttsky26c/tt_um_SAR_ADC.summary: This is a custom analog test chip in SKY130 containing an LDO voltage regulator and a clocked dynamic comparator, occupying 2x2 Tiny Tapeout tiles with six analog connections. The LDO regulates an output near 1.0 V using an external reference, while the comparator evaluates differential inputs under the CLKB signal and exposes both outputs for characterization. Testing requires a Tiny Tapeout analog platform, current-limited supplies, a low-noise reference, programmable loads, a differential input source and clock generator, and low-capacitance probes for measurement. The documentation notes that the top-cell name tt_um_SAR_ADC does not imply a complete SAR ADC, and that several characterization details such as common-mode range and capacitor values are not fully specified.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ThomasCowieEngineering_LM.summary: This project implements a CPU that executes the Little Man Computer instruction set architecture. It interfaces with an external RAM module for program and data storage. The documentation is essentially a template with placeholder text, providing no details on how the CPU works, how to test it, or what external hardware is required. As a result, the design's capabilities and limitations cannot be assessed from the available information.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ThomasCowieEngineering_LM.review_notes: Removed insufficient-doc since documentation is marked present, though it is only a template.

ttsky26c/tt_um_TinyProcessor_naiyar_.summary: TinyProcessor is a 4-command UART-controlled processor that supports read, write, ALU operation, and ALU no-operand commands. It integrates a UART receiver and transmitter, a system controller, a register file, an ALU, and an asynchronous FIFO across two clock domains. The design is tested via a provided testbench, and it requires no external hardware beyond a UART connection. Notable features include parity and framing error outputs and the use of an asynchronous FIFO for clock domain crossing.

ttsky26c/tt_um_WaiMingLee888_nanov_1tile.summary: NanoV is a compact bit-serial RV32E RISC-V processor that executes base integer instructions over multiple clock cycles to reduce area. It uses external SPI RAM for instructions and data, and provides eight GPIO inputs and eight GPIO outputs that can also drive a seven-segment display. The design is tested with a self-checking program that exercises ALU operations, branches, jumps, memory access, and GPIO, writing success or failure codes to the output. Notable limitations include the absence of multiply, UART, traps, interrupts, and caches, making it a bare-metal processor rather than a full SoC.

ttsky26c/tt_um_adityarprasad_fft.summary: This project implements an adaptive-precision radix-2 FFT butterfly processing element that selects between 4-bit, 6-bit, and 8-bit precision based on a programmable error budget. It accepts two complex 8-bit inputs sequentially over an 8-bit interface and outputs the four result bytes sequentially. The design uses a time-multiplexed multiplier and a finite-state machine to control input capture, precision selection, multiplication, and output sequencing. It is verified through RTL simulation with directed tests covering precision selection, error budgets, and status signals, and requires no external hardware for the butterfly itself.

ttsky26c/tt_um_afra_123_ecc_memory.summary: This design is a runtime-reconfigurable memory that supports four error-control modes: off, parity, Hamming, and SECDED. It provides 8-bit data storage across 8 addresses, with mode selection via input pins and error status outputs. The memory encodes data on write and decodes on read, correcting single-bit errors in Hamming and SECDED modes and detecting double-bit errors in SECDED mode. It is tested using the standard Tiny Tapeout digital interface and requires no external hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_aialaqili_updown_counter.summary: This is a synchronous 4-bit up/down counter with enable and direction controls. The count value is output on four pins, and the counter wraps at both ends. It is tested with a cocotb testbench covering reset, count up, hold, count down, underflow wraparound, and a second reset. The design was built as a first Tiny Tapeout submission, intentionally kept simple to maximize the odds of a clean first tapeout, and requires no external hardware.
ttsky26c/tt_um_aialaqili_updown_counter.review_notes: Removed education tag: source describes a first tapeout, not a teaching/learning intent.

ttsky26c/tt_um_aka_regfile_ecc.summary: This project is an ECC-protected 32-bit register bank with four registers, controlled over a housekeeping SPI interface. Each 32-bit word is stored with 7 SEC-DED checkbits, allowing single-bit error correction and double-bit error detection on read. Error-injection masks enable flipping bits in stored data or checkbits to verify the ECC logic. The design is tested by sending SPI writes and reads, and it requires only a standard SPI controller connected to the pins.

ttsky26c/tt_um_akankaan_bf16_fma.summary: This project implements a single-rounded bfloat16 fused multiply-add (FMA) unit with a byte-serial I/O interface. It uses a six-stage pipeline to reduce the critical path delay, which is particularly useful because the limited I/O requires three clock cycles to load each set of operands. The design handles special values such as zero, infinity, and NaN, and rounds results using round-to-nearest, ties-to-even. It is intended for integration into larger systems and requires no external hardware beyond the Tiny Tapeout interface.
ttsky26c/tt_um_akankaan_bf16_fma.review_notes: Removed mac-unit; the source describes a fused multiply-add, not a multiply-accumulate unit.

ttsky26c/tt_um_algofoogle_ttsky26c_analo.summary: This project contains custom analog experiments in a 1x1 Tiny Tapeout tile, including a current-steering DAC and a 21-stage ring oscillator. The DAC acts as a current sink for the ring oscillator, allowing variable oscillation from about 8.7 MHz to 26 MHz. The design is tested by setting bias levels, sweeping DAC input codes, and measuring the oscillator output, ideally with an oscilloscope. It is notable for using custom layout in a standard digital tile and is based on a prior DAC submission.

ttsky26c/tt_um_amazing_sage_snn.summary: This project implements a two-neuron leaky integrate-and-fire spiking neural network accelerator on a single tile. It uses an 8-bit input bus for data and control signals to load inputs, write and read weights, perform neuron steps, and select the output neuron. The membrane potential and spike output are provided on the output pins. The design is functionally verified with a cocotb testbench and requires no external hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_andre_dpe.summary: This design is an FSM-driven dot product engine that reads input data on ui_in, controls a small register/memory bank, and performs multiply-accumulate operations. Control bits select idle, work, or debug modes, and status flags plus a debug selector expose internal state and results on the bidirectional and output pins. It is verified with a cocotb testbench that checks reset, state transitions, status changes, output values, and debug readback. No external hardware is required, and the project is presented as a learning-oriented Tiny Tapeout implementation.
ttsky26c/tt_um_andre_dpe.review_notes: Removed alu and multiplier: the source documents a MAC unit and FSM datapath, not an ALU or standalone multiplier.

ttsky26c/tt_um_arminkardovic_montenegro_.summary: Montenegro SecureKey combines a 64-bit challenge-response authentication engine with a melody player that renders phrases from a national anthem as square waves. The authentication engine loads eight challenge bytes over uio handshakes, runs a keyed nonlinear transform for 128 clocks, and streams back eight response bytes, while the music engine uses a 40-entry note ROM and programmable divider to drive an audio pin. A published known-answer vector and a cocotb suite cover reset, I/O directions, invalid frames, byte handshaking, and music start/stop. Audible playback needs a piezo element with a transistor driver stage, and the design is explicitly an educational proof of concept rather than a production secure element.

ttsky26c/tt_um_atx_phased_interferometer.summary: The Acoustic Interferometer samples two PDM microphones, mixes the 1-bit streams with a 20 kHz complex tone, averages over 2^16 samples, and uses a CORDIC in vectoring mode to compute the phase difference between channels. The resulting 7-bit signed angle is shown as a one-hot value on an LED bar and also transmitted over UART for debugging. It is intended to run with a dedicated PMOD PCB carrying the microphones and LEDs, and a phone speaker playing a 20 kHz tone is used to verify that the LED bar tracks the direction of arrival. The design is written in Chisel and is notable for combining PDM capture, complex mixing, and CORDIC phase detection on a 1x2 tile.

ttsky26c/tt_um_azara_cirom.summary: Azara CiROM is a mask-programmed ternary compute-in-ROM demonstrator that bakes +1/-1/0 weights into a 64x32 1T NOR array and senses a full row in a single strobe. A digital controller precharges bitlines, asserts a one-hot wordline, and pulses a shared strobe so single-ended StrongARM sense amplifiers compare each column's BLP/BLN lines against an external VREF, latching all 32 hits at once and streaming them out as bytes. Reading requires a mid-rail voltage source on ua[0], and ua[1]/ua[2] can be scoped to observe column-0 bitline discharge, which is slower because of probe capacitance. The analog front end is a hardened custom GDS while the read controller is standard digital logic, making this a mixed-signal compute-in-memory experiment.
ttsky26c/tt_um_azara_cirom.review_notes: Removed transistor-level because the design uses a 1T NOR array and custom GDS, not discrete transistors; added compute-in-memory as the core function.

ttsky26c/tt_um_baked_weights.summary: This is a character-level transformer language model with ternary weights baked into on-tile ROM. It streams int16 residuals in and int8 residuals out over a byte-wide handshake, one token per transaction. The chip performs transformer layers including RMSNorm, a minGRU mixer, and an MLP, while the host handles character tables and final sampling. The design is documented with a reference RP2350B host, test procedure, and debug status pins.
ttsky26c/tt_um_baked_weights.review_notes: The proposed summary was copied from a different project and used unsupported tags; replaced with corrected tags and summary matching the transformer ROM design.

ttsky26c/tt_um_bigmanraffa_clm.summary: Clementine is a 4-lane int8 SIMT GPU that is programmed and controlled over an SPI interface using the standard SPI Pmod pinout. Status outputs report when the sequencer has halted, whether any lane is active, instruction commit, and replay state, which together expose hardware divergence handling. The documentation is limited to the title, pin names, and a short description, so the instruction set, memory model, and test procedure are not described. It is notable for implementing SIMT execution with hardware divergence on a 2x2 tile area.

ttsky26c/tt_um_bruniliomuy_top.summary: Fir_Filter is an 11-coefficient fixed-point FIR filter that accepts an 8-bit digital audio signal on ui_in with a 4 kHz bandwidth and sends the filtered result out through a UART transmitter. Two select pins choose among four coefficient sets corresponding to high-pass, low-pass, band-pass, and all-pass responses. The documentation describes the filter types and selection pins but is thin on coefficient values, scaling, and the exact UART format. No external hardware is required, and the design is a straightforward DSP exercise on a 1x2 tile.
ttsky26c/tt_um_bruniliomuy_top.review_notes: Added uart tag because the design explicitly transmits the filtered signal over UART.

ttsky26c/tt_um_chip_rom.summary: This design implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip, including the shuttle name and commit hash. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display by holding reset low and toggling the clock, or by setting the address with DIP switches. The ROM is 8-bit wide and 256 bytes long. It is intended to provide chip information via ROM access and display.
ttsky26c/tt_um_chip_rom.review_notes: Removed unsupported counter and education tags; added rom, memory, 7-segment, and verilog; adjusted summary to remove educational claim.

ttsky26c/tt_um_colbywonn_poly_synth.summary: Poly Synth v1.0 is a three-voice polyphonic DDS synthesizer whose voices are configured over SPI with 35-bit frames carrying tuning words and waveform settings. Each voice has a 32-bit phase accumulator and a shaper that produces sawtooth, square with selectable PWM duty, or triangle, and the summed voices are converted to a 1-bit sigma-delta stream on the audio output pin. Hearing the output requires an external RC reconstruction filter and a DC-blocking capacitor, and an SPI controller such as the demo board's RP2040 drives the configuration. The design has no ADSR or other envelope shaping, so the author notes artifacts and plans to refine it in a future version.

ttsky26c/tt_um_costinemanuelv_gps_daily_.summary: GPS Daily Trigger generates a 50 ms pulse once per day at a UTC hour, minute, and second configured through a small parallel write interface. It receives 9600-baud NMEA data on UART_RX, parses and checksum-validates $GPRMC sentences, associates the decoded UTC timestamp with the next GPS_PPS rising edge, and asserts TRIG_OUT when the associated time matches the target. Status outputs report sentence validity, fix validity, configuration errors, PPS output, UTC/PPS lock, and whether a target is configured, and a cocotb testbench exercises the same protocol with faster simulation parameters. A 3.3 V GPS receiver providing $GPRMC sentences and a PPS signal is required, and the relationship between the receiver's RMC timestamp and PPS edge should be confirmed before fabrication.

ttsky26c/tt_um_cpu8.summary: CPU8 is a small 8-bit accumulator-based processor with a custom 8-bit instruction set, an ALU supporting arithmetic and logic operations, 8-bit RAM, conditional branches, HALT, and memory-mapped GPIO. Programs are uploaded through a UART interface using a simple protocol that writes instructions into instruction memory and then starts execution from address zero. The included cocotb testbench programs the CPU over the same UART interface and verifies reset, arithmetic, RAM access, GPIO, jumps, branches, and HALT. Basic operation needs no external hardware, though a USB-to-UART adapter or microcontroller is useful for physical programming.
ttsky26c/tt_um_cpu8.review_notes: Removed education tag: source presents a custom CPU, not an educational design.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ctw_spms.summary: This design is a programmable all-digital smart power-management and supervision ASIC. It monitors overcurrent, overtemperature and watchdog inputs, and controls four power rails and three loads, with an SPI interface for configuration and status. It can force shutdown externally and reports faults. The design is fully digital and requires no external analog components, though it is intended to supervise external power hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_darga_cirom.summary: This design reads a mask-programmed ternary compute-in-ROM array fully digitally and computes matrix-vector products on die. It uses a 64x32 1T NOR array with ternary weights, and a digital sampling scheme that replaces analog comparators. The tile includes an on-die ternary MAC that accumulates results in 12-bit accumulators. It is a controlled experiment comparing digital readout to an analog version on the same shuttle, and requires no external hardware beyond a host to stream activations and compare against a golden model.

ttsky26c/tt_um_dash_lucas_risc.summary: This is a 16-bit multicycle RISC CPU with 32x16 on-chip RAM. It is boot-loaded over a 2-pin serial link by the demo board RP2040, then runs standalone. The design includes observation pins for debugging. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text for how it works and how to test, so details of the instruction set and operation are not provided.
ttsky26c/tt_um_dash_lucas_risc.review_notes: RISC-V tag is not supported: source only says 'RISC', not RISC-V; removing it and flagging ambiguity.

ttsky26c/tt_um_davidbroughsmyth_ecg_sar1.summary: This design is a 12-bit ~500 SPS SAR ADC intended for heart monitoring, with decorative silicon art. It includes an analog front-end for ECG signals and a digital interface compatible with an SNN neuron tile. The ADC output is provided on a bus with a sample enable signal. It requires an external ECG front-end and can be tested with lab instruments or connected to a neural network tile.

ttsky26c/tt_um_diff_engine.summary: This design is a cubic polynomial sampler (difference engine) with an SPI request interface and step/dir output, written in DSLX and compiled with Google XLS. It samples a cubic polynomial using forward differences and outputs step and direction signals for a stepper motor driver. The design accepts 64-bit requests over SPI containing polynomial coefficients and sample count. It requires an SPI master and optionally a stepper driver, and can also be built for an FPGA board.
ttsky26c/tt_um_diff_engine.review_notes: Added pmod/fpga/fixed-point/dsp tags supported by the documentation; summary unchanged.

ttsky26c/tt_um_dilip951_cpu_systolic_arr.summary: This design is a 2x2 weight-stationary systolic multiply-accumulate array with configurable 4-bit/2-bit precision and zero-operand skip. Activations stream through the array while weights are preloaded, and partial sums are output alternately for each column. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware. It implements a systolic MAC datapath with operand isolation for zero-skip.
ttsky26c/tt_um_dilip951_cpu_systolic_arr.review_notes: Removed neural-network and machine-learning tags not supported by the source; added fixed-point for the integer MAC arithmetic.

ttsky26c/tt_um_dosci_500hz.summary: The design is a simple digital oscillator that outputs a 500 Hz waveform via UART at 115200 bps 8n1. It has an asynchronous reset and synchronous assertion. Internal communication between the oscillator and the TX115 transmitter is done via AXI4-Lite. The output can be sent to a PC via UART, and no external hardware is required.
ttsky26c/tt_um_dosci_500hz.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match digital oscillator with UART/AXI4-Lite.

ttsky26c/tt_um_dragonochi.summary: This design is a dragon-themed tamagotchi game rendered live to a VGA monitor. The player feeds, waters, sleeps, and plays with a virtual dragon, with mechanics based on variety of actions and a treasure chest gamble. It outputs VGA signals and game state on bidirectional pins, and requires a TinyVGA PMOD, a VGA monitor (rotated 90 degrees), and eight push buttons. The design is notable for its extensive cocotb test suite and visual sprite testing.

ttsky26c/tt_um_drewbabel_uart.summary: This design is a configurable, FIFO-buffered UART with an AMBA-APB register block, hardened to silicon on SkyWater SKY130. It supports 8N1 framing with optional parity, 16-deep FIFOs on transmit and receive, and runtime configuration via a serial CSR interface. The tile can self-test using an internal loopback, and for real links it requires a USB-to-serial adapter. The design is notable for its robust synchronization and error handling.

ttsky26c/tt_um_duzabf_2026_ow.summary: This design is a simple 8-bit counter that displays its value on a 7-segment display. The counter reset value is set by input switches, and the lower 4 bits are converted to a hexadecimal symbol. It is a work-in-progress Online Workshop 2026 project that is expected to be improved in the future. The design requires no external hardware beyond the display and switches.
ttsky26c/tt_um_duzabf_2026_ow.review_notes: Removed education (not stated), added incomplete (WIP per title and text).

ttsky26c/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.summary: This project is a basic 8-bit CPU based on the SAP-1 architecture, using a 6-stage counter and LUT for control sequencing. It includes a program counter, instruction register, 16-byte memory, MAR, 8-bit ripple-carry adder with flags, accumulator, B register, and output register, all connected via an 8-bit tri-state bus. The design is tested by providing opcode inputs and verifying that the correct output bits are asserted. Notable features include support for conditional operation using carry and zero flags, and the design originates from a simplified educational CPU model.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ece298a_8_bit_cpu_top.review_notes: Removed education tag (not stated in source); added memory tag for the 16-byte RAM.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ehofmannbr_pmodvga_06.summary: This project generates a 640x480 VGA display with moving color tiles. It outputs RGB222 video signals along with HSync and VSync, and is intended to be used with a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to a VGA monitor. Testing requires applying power and releasing reset after connecting the PMOD and monitor. The design is a straightforward demonstration of VGA output on the Tiny Tapeout platform, with no additional processing or external interfaces beyond the VGA connection.

ttsky26c/tt_um_fabulous_sky_26c.summary: This design implements a tiny FABulous FPGA fabric with 128 LUT4+FF logic cells arranged in an 8x4 tile grid, including carry chains and global buffers. The I/O mimics the Tiny Tapeout interface, allowing user designs to be synthesized with Yosys and nextpnr, then loaded via a bitbang interface using ui[0] and ui[1] while reset is held low. The bitstream is uploaded while rst_n is asserted, and after configuration, the user design runs on the fabric. This is a notable open-source FPGA fabric intended for use as a reconfigurable target for small digital designs, with no external hardware required.
ttsky26c/tt_um_fabulous_sky_26c.review_notes: Removed multi-tile tag as the 8x4 tile design is a single tile group; added fpga, reconfigurable, lookup-table, cocotb and verilog.

ttsky26c/tt_um_factory_test.summary: This design has been validated on fabricated silicon and works as expected. It is a factory test module that can test all the I/O pins of the ASIC. It has three modes: mirroring input pins to outputs, mirroring bidirectional pins to outputs, and outputting an 8-bit counter on both output and bidirectional pins. It is implemented in Verilog and targets the Tiny Tapeout platform.
ttsky26c/tt_um_factory_test.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and added factory-test, counter, and gpio tags.

ttsky26c/tt_um_fatigue_monitor.summary: This project implements a fatigue monitor that reads IR PPG samples from a MAX30102 sensor over I2C, detects heartbeat peaks, and tracks variability in pulse intervals. It includes a calibration phase to learn a personal baseline, after which it raises an alert when a sustained drop in variability occurs. The design requires a MAX30102 breakout connected to the I2C pins, external pull-ups, and optionally a transistor-driven buzzer or motor for the alert output. Debug pins provide visibility into sensor acquisition and beat detection, and the design has been characterized on real hardware, with bring-up notes emphasizing the importance of checking the I2C path first.

ttsky26c/tt_um_felixcheng_neural_core.summary: This is a pipelined 50 MHz byte-stream int8 multiply-accumulate engine with a single int32 accumulator, a streaming vector-MAC primitive, a wide-input mode, and a SPILL opcode for reading raw accumulator values. It also includes a MISR self-test and a serial debug interface, and is intended as a hardware target for a compiler/MLIR backend. The design is verified with a cocotb testbench that includes directed tests, randomized differential testing against a Python model, and an exhaustive test of the Booth multiplier. No external hardware is required; the host microcontroller drives the pins to feed instructions and operands and read results.

ttsky26c/tt_um_four_bit_nn_accel.summary: This project is a 4-bit neural network MAC accelerator with ReLU activation, supporting LOAD_BIAS, MAC, and ACTIVATE operations via a 2-bit opcode. It uses an 11-bit accumulator to prevent overflow and outputs a 4-bit quantized result after applying a right-shift and ReLU, clamped to [0,7]. Testing involves resetting the accumulator, loading a bias, performing MAC operations with 4-bit signed weights and features, and then activating to read the result. No external hardware is required, and the design is intended as a minimal building block for quantized neural network inference.
ttsky26c/tt_um_four_bit_nn_accel.review_notes: Removed instruction-decoder tag; the source describes an opcode-controlled MAC unit, not instruction decode logic.

ttsky26c/tt_um_foxworks_picorv32.summary: This project is a small RISC-V microcontroller based on the PicoRV32 core, executing in place from an external SPI flash with 128 bytes of on-chip SRAM, a UART, and an 8-bit GPIO port. It requires an SPI flash (or an RP2040 emulating one) connected to the uio pins and a USB-serial adapter for the UART console. The design boots a program from flash and can run example firmware like a bouncing LED or a self-test that reports over UART. Notable features include the execute-in-place architecture to save area, closed timing at 50 MHz but tested at 25 MHz, and the need for external flash and serial hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_fp16_mac.summary: This chip contains a floating-point adder for single-precision operands, along with an HDL counter connected to a seven-segment display. Inputs are provided via switches for test case selection, display nibble selection, reset, and direction control, and the result is shown on the seven-segment display. Testing involves setting the switches to pass different inputs and observing the output on the display. The design is generated entirely with MATLAB HDL Coder and does not use the bidirectional pins.
ttsky26c/tt_um_fp16_mac.review_notes: Removed calculator because the source describes an FP32 adder evaluation unit, not a keypad-driven arithmetic calculator.

ttsky26c/tt_um_fp8_fpu.summary: This project is an 8-bit floating-point unit in FP8 E4M3 format, implementing 18 operations including add, subtract, multiply, divide, square root, comparisons, and integer conversions, with support for five IEEE rounding modes. The core is a pipelined, elastic datapath with variable-latency divide and sqrt, and it uses a byte-stream interface with independent valid/ready handshakes to multiplex the wide internal datapath onto the limited Tiny Tapeout pins. The design has been exhaustively verified against a reference model for all 1,843,968 input combinations at both RTL and gate level. No external hardware is required; any host that can drive the handshake pins and data bus can operate the FPU.
ttsky26c/tt_um_fp8_fpu.review_notes: Removed alu (integer ALU, not FPU) and added fpga and divider based on explicit source statements.

ttsky26c/tt_um_frequency_counter.summary: This design measures the frequency of an input signal and displays the result on a dual seven-segment display. It debounces the input, counts transitions over a configurable period, and divides the count by ten for display. The period can be set via input pins to match the clock frequency for accurate measurements. It requires a dual seven-segment PMOD and a frequency source, and includes a debug mode for monitoring internal state.

ttsky26c/tt_um_fwilson12_mac.summary: This project is a single int8 multiply-accumulate unit that computes the dot product of two signed 8-bit vectors by time-multiplexing operands onto an 8-bit input port. It uses a two-state FSM to alternately capture an operand and then multiply-accumulate, and reads out a 24-bit accumulator over two clock cycles by using both the dedicated and bidirectional output pins. The design is a fundamental building block for neural network accelerators, and its operation is verified by feeding component pairs and reading the accumulated result, with overlapping output windows providing error checking. No external hardware is required, though a host must drive the inputs and read the outputs according to the phase timing.
ttsky26c/tt_um_fwilson12_mac.review_notes: Removed fixed-point (integer int8 MAC) and added mac-unit, neural-network, dsp which are directly supported.

ttsky26c/tt_um_galaguna_NanoSys_fit.summary: Nano-120 is a small CPU with a 120-instruction set intended as a teaching resource, where both code and data memory use generic RAM. A slave SPI block lets an external master load programs and inspect data before and after execution, with a MODE pin selecting programming or run and a RUN pin starting execution. The eight outputs expose selected internal buses under OUT_CTRL control, and eight bidirectional pins provide extra control, interrupt sources and SPI MISO. It is designed for foundry testing with minimal memory resources and includes only limited documentation of the ISA itself.
ttsky26c/tt_um_galaguna_NanoSys_fit.review_notes: Removed factory-test (design is a teaching CPU, not a self-test structure); added instruction-decoder, register-file and rp2040.

ttsky26c/tt_um_garnetkoebel_communotron.summary: Communotron is a prototype translator that listens on an I2C bus and emits the data portion of writes it receives as SPI traffic. It is a 1x1 design with an I2C address of 0x41, four SPI chip-select outputs, and SPI clock and data outputs, and it strips I2C ACK bits by stalling the SPI clock. Testing is done by connecting a 400 kHz clock, an I2C controller, and oscilloscope probes on the SPI lines, since the documentation describes no external hardware requirement beyond possible I2C bus drivers. The documentation is very thin, consisting of a short usage note rather than a specification.

ttsky26c/tt_um_gilangfajrul_sar_adc.summary: This 1x2 analog project is an 8-bit successive-approximation-register ADC with differential analog inputs vinp and vinn and an end-of-conversion flag. The eight digital outputs present the conversion result, and the documentation states only that an analog input is converted to an 8-bit digital value. No external hardware is listed beyond the placeholder text, and no test procedure, timing information, or reference details are given. The description is essentially a title and one line, so little can be said about its implementation or characterization.
ttsky26c/tt_um_gilangfajrul_sar_adc.review_notes: Removed mixed-signal and comparator tags not supported by the sparse source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_gina_env_monitor.summary: The Environmental Mapping Processor is a small digital ASIC that averages and thresholds temperature, humidity and pressure samples and also computes whether a position is within a Manhattan distance of a target location. It takes sensor type, sample validity, output selection, clear and mode signals on the inputs, an 8-bit sensor data word on the bidirectional pins, and returns an 8-bit result plus status. The chip has no sensors or radio of its own; a portable implementation would pair it with a BME280, a GNSS receiver, a low-power microcontroller, a memory LCD, microSD storage and a LiPo battery. Reset and enable sequences are the only test guidance given, and the spatial grid is defined by the external controller.
ttsky26c/tt_um_gina_env_monitor.review_notes: Removed dsp and edge-ai as unsupported by the environmental/spatial processing description; added instrumentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_group02_seethebeat.summary: SeeTheBeat is a real-time audio visualizer that calculates a 512-point radix-2 fixed-point FFT on chip and streams procedural pixels to a VGA output at 800x600. Because the FFT working buffer does not fit on chip, the sample memory lives in the demo board's RP2040/RP2350 and the chip exchanges data with it over a bus during each of the nine FFT stages; bin magnitude, log scaling, band summing and beat detection are left to firmware. With only a clock and a Tiny VGA Pmod the chip draws a built-in ramp visual state, which checks VGA timing, sync polarity, Pmod bit order and blanking. The design was verified block by block against a Python golden model with cocotb, and it avoids any multiplier or twiddle ROM by using a CORDIC rotator.
ttsky26c/tt_um_group02_seethebeat.review_notes: Removed unsupported pipeline tag; added rp2040 for the microcontroller pairing; trimmed unsupported 'notably' claim.

ttsky26c/tt_um_hariri4534_audioplayback.summary: This controller streams 8-bit PCM audio stored in an external QSPI flash device and reproduces it through a high-frequency PWM output on one of the dedicated and bidirectional pins. After reset it issues a software reset to put the flash into 1-bit mode, then reads data in 8-byte chunks using the Fast Read Quad I/O instruction and buffers them for playback. Two input pins select playback speed among 0.5x, 1x, 1.5x and 2x by repeating or skipping samples. It requires a W25Qxx-style QSPI flash and the Tiny Tapeout audio Pmod, and the clock is only 50 kHz.
ttsky26c/tt_um_hariri4534_audioplayback.review_notes: Removed memory because the flash is external and the controller does not contain an on-chip memory block.

ttsky26c/tt_um_haydenevans_top.summary: This design is a weight-stationary processing element that multiplies a stored int8 weight by an int8 activation, accumulates the product and applies bias and Leaky ReLU before saturating back to int8. It is controlled through an 8-bit time-multiplexed data bus and four control signals for loading weights, loading bias, accumulating and resetting, with output_valid and overflow status outputs. A three-stage pipeline separates the MAC, bias addition and activation so that each stage has a short critical path; the accumulator is saturated to int16 using a wider intermediate sum. It was prototyped on a Terasic MAX10 DE10-Lite and would be used as a building block for a larger array.
ttsky26c/tt_um_haydenevans_top.review_notes: Removed systolic-array tag; the design is a single processing element, not an array.

ttsky26c/tt_um_hdc_classifier.summary: The HDC Classifier is an 8-bit hyperdimensional computing classifier that compares an input vector against two class prototypes and selects the class with the smaller Hamming distance. Input data arrives on the eight input pins, while mode, class selection, valid and start controls are driven on the bidirectional pins and the six-bit distance, winner and done signals appear on the outputs. The workflow is to reset, present data and control signals, assert start, then read the winner and distance once done is high. No external hardware is required beyond the standard clock and reset, and the documentation is brief but sufficient for the interface.
ttsky26c/tt_um_hdc_classifier.review_notes: Removed perceptron (not a perceptron) and added machine-learning which is clearly supported.

ttsky26c/tt_um_htfab_caterpillar.summary: Simon's Caterpillar is a port of the Caterpillar Logic game to the Simon Says PMOD. The game has 20 levels where players deduce secret rules about color sequences. It uses a 7-segment display, LEDs, buttons, and a speaker for interaction. The design requires the Simon Says PMOD and runs at 50 kHz. Silicon testing by the author confirmed it works as expected.

ttsky26c/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.summary: This project is a video mode tester that allows experimenting with different VGA timing parameters. It provides a TinyVGA output and an SPI interface for configuring horizontal and vertical visible pixels, front porch, sync pulse, and back porch registers. The design is implemented in Verilog and requires a Tiny VGA PMOD connected to the Tiny Tapeout board. It supports setting the pixel clock to 25 MHz to produce a 640x480 @ 60 Hz test pattern.
ttsky26c/tt_um_htfab_vga_tester.review_notes: Tags and summary were about a RISC-V SoC, but the source is a VGA timing parameter tester.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ja_achtung_1x1.summary: JA Achtung Compact is a one-tile implementation of the two-player Achtung, die Kurve! game, where each player steers a head that leaves a permanent trail and loses on hitting a wall or any trail. The chip has no internal framebuffer: it uses an external APS6404L QSPI PSRAM as a 1-bit-per-pixel occupancy map, fetching bursts for 640x480 VGA during active video and using the vertical blanking interval for collision reads and trail writes. Input comes from the Tiny Tapeout Gamepad Pmod with SNES-style controllers, with shoulder buttons turning and start restarting, and player 2's trail uses a woven sub-pattern so the two monochrome trails differ. It needs the VGA, QSPI PSRAM and Gamepad Pmods plus a monitor, and the reset must be held for at least 150 us after PSRAM power-up.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ja_achtung_1x2.summary: JA Achtung Full is the larger 1x2 version of the two-player Achtung, die Kurve! game, with continuously rotating heads, trails that include periodic passable gaps, boost moves and a color-selection lobby. It stores a 640x480 framebuffer in external QSPI PSRAM packed four 2-bit pixels per byte, streaming 8-byte bursts for VGA and reusing the PSRAM port during vertical blanking for collision checks and trail updates. Movement uses Q10.6 fixed-point coordinates with a quarter-wave lookup for 64 directions, and two SNES-style controllers share the Gamepad Pmod serial interface. It requires the VGA, QSPI PSRAM and Gamepad Pmods plus a monitor, and its larger test suite compares more than forty game traces against an independent Python framebuffer model.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ja_achtung_1x2.review_notes: Removed 'memory' tag because the design uses external PSRAM rather than implementing a memory block.

ttsky26c/tt_um_jjy_spi_watchdog.summary: This design is a SPI-configurable watchdog timer intended to supervise an external microcontroller. The host sets a timeout over SPI and periodically kicks the watchdog either by SPI write or by a rising edge on a dedicated pin; if kicks stop, the watchdog first raises an IRQ warning and then pulls an active-low reset line low. It supports eight timeouts from 5.24 ms to 5.37 s with an optional prescaler, a window mode that flags kicks arriving too early, a lock bit that freezes configuration, and fault flags that survive the reset pulse so the cause can be read back. The design is notable for its two-stage response, giving the host a grace period to cancel a reset, and for its window mode that catches firmware stuck in a loop kicking too fast.

ttsky26c/tt_um_jonahsaunders_slsvga.summary: This project generates a real-time VGA animation of NASA's Space Launch System orbiting a crescent moon against a star-filled background. A compact Minsky circle oscillator updates the rocket's position once per video frame, while simple counters animate the flickering engine flames. The design outputs VGA signals through the Tiny VGA pinout and is written in Verilog. It is intended to be viewed on a VGA-compatible monitor or capture device.
ttsky26c/tt_um_jonahsaunders_slsvga.review_notes: Removed game/gamepad tags not supported by the source and added graphics/art/demoscene/oscillator tags.

ttsky26c/tt_um_joonatanalanampa_cordic.summary: This project implements a standalone bit-serial CORDIC sine generator in a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a bit-serial CORDIC engine with fixed-point output and a DDS phase accumulator to generate a sine wave on uo[7] and a phase-locked square wave on uo[6]. The design is verified with exhaustive angle tests, FFT analysis, and formal control-path proofs, not with a cocotb testbench. It outputs an analog sine via an RC low-pass filter or the Tiny Tapeout Audio Pmod, along with a heartbeat LED and a level bar.
ttsky26c/tt_um_joonatanalanampa_cordic.review_notes: Tags were replaced to match the CORDIC sine generator described in the source, removing unsupported accelerator/register-file/FSM/cocotb and adding CORDIC and related tags.

ttsky26c/tt_um_joram200.summary: This project implements the Kalman filter measurement-update step as a fixed-function hardware accelerator in a 1x1 Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a register interface with write data, address, byte select, write enable, reset, and start signals, and provides 8-bit read data. The design targets the sky130 HD standard-cell library and requires no external hardware. It is implemented in SystemVerilog.
ttsky26c/tt_um_joram200.review_notes: Tags and summary were about a perceptron neural network, but the source is a Kalman filter accelerator.

ttsky26c/tt_um_kashif_fp4_sparse_tpu.summary: This project implements a mini TPU that computes C = A x W with INT8 activations and 1:2 structurally sparse E2M1 weights. It uses one time-multiplexed processing element and avoids a hardware multiplier by replacing products with conditional adds, shifts, and negates. The design is driven over SPI and is verified with a cocotb testbench against an independent golden model. It is intended for machine learning inference.
ttsky26c/tt_um_kashif_fp4_sparse_tpu.review_notes: Replaced unsupported perceptron, esoteric, and bit-serial tags with tpu, spi, mac-unit, cocotb, and edge-ai.

ttsky26c/tt_um_kenchangh_mnist.summary: This project is a self-contained MNIST handwritten digit classifier using a ternary-weight multi-layer perceptron. All neural network weights are hardwired on-chip as Verilog constants, requiring no RAM or ROM. The design processes a 64-pixel bit-serial input and outputs the predicted digit on a seven-segment display. It achieves 80.3% test accuracy on MNIST images.
ttsky26c/tt_um_kenchangh_mnist.review_notes: Corrected tags and summary to match the MNIST digit recognition design.

ttsky26c/tt_um_kianv_rv32_regfile.summary: KianV uLinux RISC-V regfile edition is a 32-bit RISC-V IMA processor capable of booting Linux, featuring a 32x32 register file macro. It includes external SPI flash and PSRAM interfaces, a UART, and a SPI peripheral. The system runs at 30 MHz and requires a QSPI Pmod for external memory. Silicon tests showed partial functionality: it could not boot Linux due to an impedance mismatch when integrating the register file, though the register file itself works.
ttsky26c/tt_um_kianv_rv32_regfile.review_notes: Removed memory tag because memory is external; added silicon-tested, qspi, and pmod based on silicon reports and external hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_krisjdev_artwork.summary: This project is a silicon artwork featuring Hatsune Miku and Juno Teo Minh, implemented in Verilog. The documentation is essentially a template with no functional description, testing instructions, or external hardware details. It appears to be a decorative design rather than a functional circuit. As a result, its purpose and operation cannot be determined from the provided information.

ttsky26c/tt_um_krisjdev_manchester_baby.summary: This Verilog design is a modern implementation of the Manchester Baby, the first stored-program computer, with an 8-bit data path and control signals for the PTP interface. It exposes data in and out, stop lamp, RAM read/write, and debug controls, and can be driven from a microcontroller such as the official devkit or a Raspberry Pi Pico. A serial mode reduces the number of required GPIO pins. The design is notable as a historical reimplementation intended for education and demonstration.

ttsky26c/tt_um_kul_chromechain.summary: This project implements a ternary bit-serial MNIST handwritten digit classifier in a 4x2 tile Tiny Tapeout design. It uses a ternary-weight neural network with a distribution-free conformal early exit that stops classification when the answer is decided. The design supports loading config bytes and pixel data over an 8-bit bus, with control pins on the bidirectional lines. It is implemented in SystemVerilog and targets embedded AI inference applications.
ttsky26c/tt_um_kul_chromechain.review_notes: Replaced tags with those supported by the source: the design is a digital ternary neural-network classifier, not a temperature sensor.

ttsky26c/tt_um_kul_conway.summary: This project implements an interactive Conway's Game of Life on Tiny Tapeout with VGA output. It supports toggleable bounded and toroidal modes and cursor-based cell editing using 11 buttons. The simulation runs on a 25.175 MHz clock and outputs VGA graphics via the Tiny VGA Pmod. It is implemented in SystemVerilog and allows users to draw cells and control simulation speed and reset.
ttsky26c/tt_um_kul_conway.review_notes: Replaced incorrect temperature-sensor tags with tags matching the interactive VGA Game of Life implementation described in the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr01_analogicus.summary: This project is a temperature sensor design that uses an analog oscillator to produce a frequency dependent on temperature. It can be read either by measuring the OSC_TEMP frequency or by asserting REQUEST and reading the 8-bit TEMP value when DONE goes high. No external hardware is required, though a logic analyzer can be used to measure the oscillation frequency. It is suitable for temperature measurement applications.
ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr01_analogicus.review_notes: Removed unsupported education/sensor-interface tags; added instrumentation for the measurement purpose.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr02_analogicus.summary: This project is a temperature sensor design from Group 2. It is an analog design with a power-up input and an oscillator temperature output. The documentation is very thin and does not describe the internal circuit or measurement method. No silicon test results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr02_analogicus.review_notes: Removed unsupported oscillator, sensor-interface and education tags; kept only temperature-sensor and analog.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr03_analogicus.summary: This analog block contains a temperature sensor from a group of student designs. The pin list shows only a power-up input and a temperature-dependent oscillator output, and there is no documentation beyond the one-line description. A user would power the block and measure the output frequency, but without a data sheet or schematic the behaviour cannot be verified. The documentation is essentially absent, so the functionality is inferred from the title and pin names.
ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr03_analogicus.review_notes: Removed sensor-interface because the design itself is the temperature-sensing block rather than an interface to an external sensor.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr04_analogicus.summary: This analog block is a temperature sensor built by a student group. The pins provide start and power-up controls, an eight-bit parallel temperature output, and a temperature-dependent oscillator output. No documentation is provided beyond the title and pin names, so the exact encoding and accuracy of the eight-bit value are unknown. The design would be used by powering it up, starting a conversion, and reading the digital temperature word, but the lack of documentation makes its capabilities difficult to assess.
ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_gr04_analogicus.review_notes: Removed adc and sensor-interface as unsupported; added insufficient-doc.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lelo_temp_wulffern.summary: The design is an analog temperature-to-frequency sensor that uses a bandgap circuit to produce a PTAT current and CTAT voltage, which a relaxation oscillator converts to a frequency. It is used by powering the analog core and measuring the frequency on the output pin with a counter or logic analyzer; sweeping the ambient temperature allows calibration. No external hardware is needed beyond a frequency measurement tool, and the design was created to meet a specified temperature-sensor brief. Notable details include a non-linear frequency-versus-temperature curve that requires compensation and silicon measurements are not reported in the documentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_lfglabs_lsc1u.summary: The LSC-1 Micro is a SystemVerilog arithmetic kernel implementing XOR, GF(2^128) multiplication, and SET operations over a byte-wide ready/valid interface. It accepts an opcode followed by a fixed-size payload and returns a 16-byte response, with support for request and response stalls and a fault indication for unsupported opcodes. The core requires a 25 MHz clock, active-low reset, and chip enable, and is intended to be driven by a host controller or microcontroller; no external memory or packet framing is included. The design is a reduced sub-core of the larger LSC-1 and does not include BLAKE3 or other full-system features, and testing is performed by host-side arithmetic comparison.
ttsky26c/tt_um_lfglabs_lsc1u.review_notes: Removed crypto and pipeline tags not supported by the source; added sequential-logic.

ttsky26c/tt_um_libormiller_SIMON_V2.summary: This design is a hardware accelerator for the Simon block cipher in its 32/64 configuration, with an SPI slave interface that allows a master to load a key and data block, select encryption or decryption, and read the result. It also includes a variable-frequency ring oscillator and an analog multiplexer for measurement, with an analog output pin intended for oscilloscope monitoring. Testing can be done via an RP2350B microcontroller using SPI and GPIO control, and an oscilloscope with low-capacitance probes is required for the analog output. The design is a second version that adds the oscillator and measurement capability, though detailed silicon results are not included.

ttsky26c/tt_um_manasvibhat_bloom_filter.summary: The design implements a Bloom filter for probabilistic set membership testing using a 64-bit array and two XOR-fold hash functions on 8-bit inputs. It supports insert and query operations through a simple strobe interface, with a VALID signal indicating completion and a RESULT output for queries; debug outputs expose the computed hash indices. It requires no external hardware beyond the standard Tiny Tapeout demo board, and the documentation explains the operation sequence and timing. The design guarantees no false negatives and may produce false positives, as expected for a Bloom filter.
ttsky26c/tt_um_manasvibhat_bloom_filter.review_notes: Removed sram tag: the implementation is a 64-bit register-array Bloom filter, not an SRAM block.

ttsky26c/tt_um_mariavictoriaalm_qubit_si.summary: This project is a digital simulation of two qubits and an entangled pair, imitating quantum behaviour with registers, comparators, and three maximal-length LFSRs for probabilistic collapse. It is controlled by four input switches for initial states, Hadamard gate application, and measurement, with four LED outputs displaying the results. The design was prototyped in Wokwi and uses a 100 Hz clock, making it suitable for educational demonstrations. It does not perform real quantum computation and the randomness is a simplified stand-in based on LFSRs.

ttsky26c/tt_um_mattvenn_r2r_dac_3v3.summary: This analog block implements an 8-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter with a 3.3 V output achieved through level-shifting drivers. It can be driven externally via the digital input pins or by an internal digital sine waveform generator, with control pins for loading and an external data input. An oscilloscope is required to measure the analog output voltage on the dedicated analog pin. The design is straightforward and no detailed performance specifications are provided.

ttsky26c/tt_um_mini_nn.summary: This design is a neural network inference engine with four signed 4-bit MAC lanes that compute four dot products per job with 20-bit accumulation. It uses an acknowledged byte interface to receive commands and data from a host and to stream back twelve result bytes, with support for optional biases. The host is responsible for activation functions, requantization, and multilayer scheduling, as the core returns raw signed sums; a standalone ReLU block exists but is not connected. The design targets a 50 MHz clock pending SKY130 timing verification and requires a host with memory for images and weights, plus a Tiny Tapeout demo board or compatible host.

ttsky26c/tt_um_mlkem_coefficient_integri.summary: This Verilog design implements a streaming ML-KEM ciphertext codec and Fujisaki-Okamoto integrity checker supporting all three standard parameter sets (512, 768, 1024). It has two phases: decompression of bit-packed coefficients and auxiliary-reference verification where a recompressed coefficient is compared against the ciphertext, accumulating a sticky mismatch flag. The design is controlled via start, phase, and parameter bits, and communicates over the standard Tiny Tapeout pins with no external hardware required. Notable features include a divider-free bit-serial design, a parameter mismatch fault indication, and a cocotb test suite that exercises all parameter sets and tamper injection.

ttsky26c/tt_um_moein_maleki_arm16.summary: This design implements a 16-bit five-stage ARM pipeline with forwarding and hazard detection, executing a subset of the 32-bit ARM instruction encoding. It streams its program from a QSPI flash Pmod and uses PSRAM for data, while an internal demo ROM provides a standalone counting demo. Output is rendered as four large hexadecimal digits on a TinyVGA Pmod, with a second view showing the fetch address. The design is notable for being the first ARM core on Tiny Tapeout and includes a switch to disable forwarding for comparison, but the UART from the original specification was dropped for area.

ttsky26c/tt_um_morse_converter.summary: This design converts ASCII characters to ITU Morse code, streaming the elements on a key line and generating a PWM sidetone for the TT Audio Pmod. It also displays status bits on the 7-segment display, with options for speed selection, tone selection, and auto-repeat. The chip handles all Morse timing and provides a handshake protocol so a host can stream text without dropping characters. It is tested with a cocotb testbench and can be driven from a microcontroller using the ttboard SDK.
ttsky26c/tt_um_morse_converter.review_notes: Removed synchronizer; its two-flop load synchronizer is incidental, and added buzzer because the documentation mentions a piezo buzzer output option.

ttsky26c/tt_um_multi_precision_mult.summary: This design is a variable-precision multiplier that supports 2-bit, 4-bit, and 8-bit multiplication modes, selected via mode pins. It accepts an 8-bit data input and produces an 8-bit product output. The design is intended to be tested with an automated Cocotb testbench, and no external hardware is required. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pinout and a brief description.
ttsky26c/tt_um_multi_precision_mult.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu tag and added insufficient-doc for very thin documentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_namramazhar_popcnt_shiftr.summary: This design implements a 17-bit population counter using a Wallace-tree structure. It can be loaded with 16 bits in parallel and one serial input bit, and outputs a 5-bit count of the number of set bits. The design is documented only by its title and pin names, with no detailed explanation of operation or testing. It is likely intended for applications requiring efficient bit counting.
ttsky26c/tt_um_namramazhar_popcnt_shiftr.review_notes: Summary sentence about intended applications is speculative and not supported by the source; corrected.

ttsky26c/tt_um_neuropong.summary: This design implements a Pong game where a player can compete against an AI opponent or a second player, displayed on a VGA screen via the Tiny VGA Pmod. The AI uses a neural network whose weights are stored in a shift register, allowing retraining after fabrication by clocking in new weights. The game includes paddle control, ball physics with angle variation based on hit position, and score rendering. It requires external buttons for paddle movement and game reset, and a toggle switch for player mode selection.

ttsky26c/tt_um_nikita_face_detect.summary: This design performs streaming pixel-based face detection by classifying skin tone and counting dark pixels in eye, nose, and mouth zones. Pixels are input serially one channel at a time, along with channel select, pixel valid, frame done, and zone metadata. At the end of a frame, it evaluates conditions and outputs detection flags. Testing requires a MATLAB preprocessing script to convert images into a pixel stream, and the design is intended to be driven by a microcontroller or cocotb testbench.
ttsky26c/tt_um_nikita_face_detect.review_notes: Added image-processing and cocotb, both directly supported by the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_nkanderson_lut_snn.summary: This design implements a reconfigurable look-up-table spiking neural network that classifies the orientation of a line in a 3x3 binary grid as vertical or horizontal. It uses latency ordering without membrane potentials or time stepping, and the weights can be rewritten at runtime via a shift register interface. The design achieves 100% accuracy on clean patterns and 80.99% under 10% flip noise, with a fixed 2-cycle latency. It is tested exhaustively with a cocotb suite that covers all 512 possible inputs.

ttsky26c/tt_um_noahzperez29_riscv_core.summary: This design is a single-cycle RISC-V processor core implementing a subset of the RV32I base integer instruction set. It exposes the internal 32-bit program counter through a byte-select multiplexer on the output pins, allowing external observation of execution. The core is tested by cycling through byte selects to reconstruct the program counter and verifying that it advances correctly. Known limitations include incomplete support for non-addi I-type instructions and blt-style branches.

ttsky26c/tt_um_nobleg30_uart_vga_scrolle.summary: This design receives text messages over UART and scrolls them across a 640x480 VGA display. It provides inputs for scroll speed, pause control, and text/background color selection. The design is intended to be used with a Tiny VGA Pmod and a UART source. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of the title, description, and pin names, with no detailed explanation of operation or testing.
ttsky26c/tt_um_nobleg30_uart_vga_scrolle.review_notes: Removed redundant display tag and added verilog tag based on stated language.

ttsky26c/tt_um_np523_pong.summary: This design is a Pong game with retro visuals and an AI opponent, forked from an earlier version. It supports both two-player and AI modes, selectable via a DIP switch, and uses a VGA display and Pmod game controllers for input. The game includes serve and paddle controls for each player. Testing involves pressing the select button to serve and flipping the DIP switch to change modes.

ttsky26c/tt_um_obookstay_puf.summary: This design implements a 16-bit arbiter physical unclonable function that maps a challenge to a response, aiming to reduce linearity within a small area. A 16-bit challenge is driven on the input pins, and each response is emitted as four hexadecimal characters over a 115200 8N1 UART transmitter. A new measurement starts when the challenge bus changes, or the same challenge can be re-measured by pulsing reset. It requires an external 3.3 V host such as an RP2040 or FPGA to drive the challenge inputs and read the UART output, and the documentation is otherwise complete.

ttsky26c/tt_um_obstacle_avoider.summary: This chip implements a three-state finite state machine for obstacle avoidance, reading two sensor inputs and driving three mutually exclusive motor outputs. It transitions between FORWARD, TURNING and STOPPED states based on whether an obstacle is in range or dangerously close, with state held in a 2-bit register updated on each clock edge. Testing is done by applying a clock and toggling the two sensor inputs while monitoring which of the three output pins is high. It is described as a beginner project and needs no external hardware beyond the clock and input stimulus.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ogggggish_ota_ldo.summary: This tile is a fully analog capless low-dropout regulator implemented in SKY130A with 16 FETs and 6 passives. A two-stage Miller-compensated OTA drives a super-source-follower buffer that controls a 2000 um / 0.15 um PMOS pass device, regulating the output to 1.5 V from the 1.8 V analog supply. An on-chip poly divider senses the output and compares it against an external 0.9 V reference, while a single external 10 uA bias current is mirrored on-chip. Driving ui_in[0] high enables an on-chip switched load that steps the load to roughly 2.8 mA for observing transient response.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ogggggish_ota_ldo.review_notes: Tags were entirely wrong (ring oscillator/clock tags) for an analog LDO; replaced with LDO, opamp, voltage-reference, analog and transistor-level tags.

ttsky26c/tt_um_olaf8.summary: OLAF-8 is a fully digital fuzzy inference engine with an eight-rule bounded rule memory and online rule admission and replacement. It accepts two 4-bit inputs, computes LOW/MID/HIGH membership degrees, evaluates the stored rules with MIN firing strength, accumulates a weighted output and defuzzifies it with an iterative divider. When the maximum firing strength falls below a threshold, the least-utility rule is replaced by one derived from the current input, allowing adaptation without an external processor. It is a research demonstrator that needs no external hardware and uses the standard Tiny Tapeout clock, reset and pin interface.

ttsky26c/tt_um_orca.summary: ORCA is a self-optimizing and self-healing evolvable logic engine built around a 4x4 feed-forward CGP fabric of 4-bit LUT cells defined by a 132-bit genome. An on-chip (1+1) evolution strategy with a xorshift32 PRNG mutates the genome and scores circuits against a 16-row target truth table, with an optional annealing mode and a settle-time sensor that measures per-die speed. It can run host-free, evolving parity plus AND-OR at reset and lighting LEDs as fitness converges, while a bit-banged serial interface exposes control registers for targets, genome access, fault injection and annealing. A host-free HEAL demo injects stuck-at faults and shows evolution routing around dead cells, and no external hardware is required beyond optional scope probes and LEDs.
ttsky26c/tt_um_orca.review_notes: Removed error-correction (no ECC logic); the rest of the tags and summary are supported by the source.
