ttsky26c/tt_um_oscillating_bones.summary: This is a ring oscillator built from a chain of 21 SkullFET inverters running from the analog supply, with a buffer feeding both a level-shifted digital divider chain and an analog pad tap. The digital outputs provide the oscillator signal and divide-by-2, 4 and 8 versions, while the analog pin is a small-signal tap rather than a full-swing square wave. Silicon measurements on ttsky25b show the ring running at about 178-180 MHz, so only the divide-by-8 output at roughly 22 MHz is reliably observable through the GPIOs. Testing requires a scope or logic analyzer on the divide-by-8 output, and the analog tap is only a qualitative oscillation indicator.

ttsky26c/tt_um_osian_beam_controller.summary: This Verilog controller generates selectable 8-bit digital control patterns for a programmable 4x4 metasurface array used in beam steering. Two input bits select one of four beam-control modes, each producing a different pattern on the eight outputs. It is intended as a demonstration of the digital control principles used when configuring programmable antenna and metasurface elements. Physical testing needs two switches on the mode inputs and eight current-limited LEDs on the outputs, while simulation uses a cocotb testbench that checks all four mode selections.

ttsky26c/tt_um_poket_animal.summary: Poket Animal is a tamagotchi-style virtual pet that lives on a 7-segment display, tracking hunger, joy, sickness and death with distinct display moods and animations. Two debounced buttons feed and pet the creature, while status pins report alive, heartbeat, cause of death, sickness, hunger level and wiggle, and a two-bit speed selector sets the metabolic tick rate from about 1.9 hours down to simulation speed. Overfeeding causes indigestion and eventually death, starvation kills after two ticks, and death is sticky until reset. It needs a common-cathode 7-segment display with decimal point, two push buttons and optionally an LED for the heartbeat, and the cocotb testbench exercises the full lifecycle in turbo mode.

ttsky26c/tt_um_porkfreezer_rrio_opamp.summary: This tile contains four instances of a 1.8 V rail-to-rail input and output operational amplifier whose inputs are shared and whose outputs are multiplexed onto a single analog pin. An instance is selected with two digital select pins and enabled with a separate enable pin. The documentation notes that compensation is not very good, so the amplifier may not be unity-gain stable in practice, and it is optimized for roughly 10 pF of load capacitance. Testing requires external analog signal sources and a load on the selected output, and the documentation is otherwise brief.
ttsky26c/tt_um_porkfreezer_rrio_opamp.review_notes: Removed multiplexer; the design is an analog opamp with a simple output mux, not a multiplexer circuit.

ttsky26c/tt_um_poundbrad_reciprocal_coun.summary: This design is a two-channel reciprocal frequency counter that measures two asynchronous digital oscillator signals against the 7.2 MHz system clock. Each channel synchronizes its input, counts reference-clock cycles over a programmed number of input cycles, and stores the result in a COUNT register with a measurement counter, all configured through an SPI register interface. Channels are armed by writing a non-zero GATE_CYCLES value and include timeout and overflow detection with sticky status bits. The cocotb testbench covers reset, SPI readback, single and simultaneous channel operation, disabling, timeout and overflow behavior, and the documentation recommends exercising the SPI path on an FPGA before final submission.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pqc_ntt_bfly.summary: This design implements a bit-serial Montgomery NTT butterfly unit that supports the moduli of all three NIST post-quantum cryptography standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and FN-DSA) from a single shared datapath. It computes one Cooley-Tukey butterfly per transaction, with the scheme selected via two input pins and data loaded and unloaded serially over the 8-bit input and output ports. The design is controlled entirely through the Tiny Tapeout pins, requiring no external hardware beyond a host microcontroller such as a Raspberry Pi Pico. Notable features include the ability to switch schemes between transactions without a reset and the use of Montgomery domain twiddle factors, as detailed in the provided test instructions and golden model.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pranavUl_ascon_aead128.summary: This project is a bit-serial implementation of the Ascon permutation (NIST SP 800-232) with a streaming column-XOR interface, enabling full Ascon-AEAD128 authenticated encryption when driven by a host. The 320-bit state is processed one 5-bit column per cycle through a shared S-box, with rounds taking 64 cycles per substitution and diffusion lap. The host must be cycle-synchronous with the design clock and supplies columns for each lap, while the chip performs all state processing; no on-chip data buffers are included to save area. The design is verified with known-answer tests and a large KAT sweep, and it requires no external hardware beyond a host microcontroller.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pratibha_munnangi_qkt_mac.summary: This chip is a 1x4 INT4 signed dot-product MAC with an INT32 accumulator, designed as a scaled-down demonstrator of a transformer QK^T attention kernel. It features a 3-stage pipeline with four parallel multipliers, an adder tree, and an accumulator, and it uses a stateless streaming byte interface with commands for loading Q and K, resetting the accumulator, and reading the result. The design closes timing at 100 MHz on sky130 with no DRC, LVS, or antenna violations, and it is intended to be driven by a microcontroller or the demoboard's RP2040. A full cocotb testbench with directed and randomized regression is provided.

ttsky26c/tt_um_preethi8a_adaptive_lfsr_p.summary: This design implements a compact 16-bit Galois LFSR-based pseudo-random number generator with deterministic self-seeding, automatic polynomial switching, repetition detection, and cooldown control. It uses three internally selectable polynomials and generates an 8-bit output from the lower bits of the LFSR state. The PRNG is enabled via an input pin and seeded externally through 7 bits, with an 8-bit repetition monitor that triggers polynomial switching and reseeding when consecutive outputs repeat. The design is verified with a cocotb testbench covering reset, seeding, LFSR operation, and adaptive behavior.
ttsky26c/tt_um_preethi8a_adaptive_lfsr_p.review_notes: Removed pattern-generator; the design is a PRNG, not a digital test pattern generator.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pthomas_sigma_delta.summary: This project is a first-order continuous-time sigma-delta modulator ADC implemented in analog circuitry, featuring an active-RC integrator, a StrongARM comparator, and a return-to-zero resistive feedback DAC. It produces a 50 MHz bitstream that is decimated off-chip for either a fast path (~1 MHz bandwidth, ≥6 ENOB) or a precision path (~100 kHz, 10+ ENOB). The design is a work in progress toward the shuttle deadline, with the OTA macro verified and the remaining blocks to be integrated. Testing requires a low-jitter 50 MHz clock source and an FPGA or logic analyzer to capture the bitstream.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pump_out.summary: This chip is a 60 Hz RMS pump-out controller ASIC that automatically turns on a pump and uses a current transformer to measure the RMS current, detecting when a tank is empty or a timeout occurs. It includes LEDs for status indication and a button for manual start, and it interfaces with an external ADC and relay. The design was extensively tested using RTL simulation, gate-level simulation, and FPGA prototyping, and a development board with emulation headers was created for chip testing. The project includes a datasheet, block diagrams, and a detailed test methodology involving multiple FPGAs for emulation and monitoring.

ttsky26c/tt_um_pwm_spice.summary: This project is an educational example that implements a PWM module in Verilog, intended to demonstrate the power of Verilog and chip design. The design is simple and can be tested by plugging it in and observing the outputs, optionally with an oscilloscope. It requires external hardware such as an LED array, button, and pin for full interaction. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and basic testing instructions.
ttsky26c/tt_um_pwm_spice.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed.

ttsky26c/tt_um_quick_bus.summary: This is a test chip for a PLL/CDR/QuickBus interface, with 8 data inputs and outputs, and control pins for mode selection. The documentation is extremely sparse, providing only a one-line description and a note that a scope is needed to look at output signals. There is no explanation of functionality, usage, or testing procedures, making it difficult to determine the design's purpose beyond its title. The project appears to be a hardware test vehicle for high-speed serial communication experiments.
ttsky26c/tt_um_quick_bus.review_notes: Removed overly broad 'communication' tag and added 'pll' and 'insufficient-doc' to match the title and sparse documentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rangfuu_alu.summary: This design is a 4-bit ALU that displays its result on a hexadecimal 7-segment display, supporting operations such as addition, subtraction, logic, shifts, and equality. It is a combinational circuit with no clock, and it provides both the segment outputs and a binary result with a zero flag on the bidirectional pins. The design is intended for use with the Tiny Tapeout demo board and includes a Python demo script for testing all input combinations. Notable aspects include physical-design experiments and the integration of a 7-segment decoder.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rangfuu_alu.review_notes: Removed calculator and education; the project is an ALU demo with a hex display and a physical-design experiment, not a keypad calculator or explicitly educational design.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rcyaon_droop.summary: This design is an all-digital supply droop detector that uses a ring oscillator as a VDD sensor and includes an on-tile switching aggressor to create controlled di/dt events. It can measure the ring oscillator period or frequency to observe supply sag, with a self-test mode that replaces the ring with a known clock for calibration. The design is intended for characterization of power integrity and requires no external hardware beyond a bench supply and oscilloscope or logic analyzer. An optional FPGA port is provided for streaming samples over UART.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.summary: This design implements hardware logic to convert Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is tested via a Python test suite covering a comprehensive set of cases, and it is intended for use in any device that processes Unicode text. The documentation is thorough, describing the error signals and test methodology.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_hardware_utf8.review_notes: Removed error-correction because the design only detects and signals errors, it does not correct them.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.summary: This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_intercal_alu.review_notes: Removed register-file tag; the two 32-bit registers are not a register file.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_universal_deco.summary: This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.summary: This design displays a large collection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to select the flag by index or step through them. It is used by connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and using the input pins to change the displayed flag. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. Silicon testing confirmed that flag switching works, though the index-based selection via uio was not tested.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rebeccargb_vga_pride.review_notes: Removed generic display tag; added pmod, video, and silicon-tested tags supported by documentation and silicon status.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rmranjitkarNULL_pong_top.summary: This design implements a two-player Pong game rendered on a VGA display. It accepts button inputs for each player's paddle movement and select, and outputs VGA sync and color signals along with a sound output. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the internal implementation or testing procedure in detail. External hardware likely includes a VGA monitor and buttons, but this is not explicitly stated.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rmranjitkarNULL_pong_top.review_notes: Added incomplete and insufficient-doc because the documentation is unedited template placeholder text.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rom_vga_screensaver.summary: This design displays a bouncing 64x64 Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen, with options to tile or double the logo size. It can be controlled with a gamepad to start/pause and change direction. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally a Gamepad PMOD. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected, including tile, double, and gamepad modes.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rowles_fedmodel.summary: The Fed Model is a hardware implementation of a Federal Reserve rate-cycle risk model that counts rate cuts and signals when to exit the market. It uses event strobes for rate cuts, hikes, and months, and outputs the investment decision along with internal state. The design supports two model variants (F1 and F2) selectable at runtime, with configurable cut threshold. It is tested via a cocotb suite against a Python reference model and requires no external hardware beyond strobe drivers.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rowles_fedmodel.review_notes: Added timer and industrial tags supported by the model's timing and intended use.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rowles_regime.summary: This chip classifies an 8-bit input stream into a binary regime using a shift-only exponential moving average compared against a programmable threshold with hysteresis. It includes a persistence counter to require N consecutive qualifying samples before changing the output. The design is configurable via strobe pins for threshold, hysteresis, and persistence, and exposes the running average on outputs. It is tested with a cocotb testbench against a Python reference model and requires no external hardware.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rowles_regime.review_notes: Removed machine-learning and dsp tags not supported by the source; cocotb already present in proposed tags but listed here for clarity.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rsa_simple.summary: This project implements a textbook RSA encryption core that computes message^5 mod 221 using a pipelined square-and-multiply modular exponentiation algorithm. It uses an 8-bit datapath and a shift-and-add multiplier to fit in a 1x1 tile, taking up to 512 clock cycles per encryption. The design is for educational purposes only and is not secure. It requires no external hardware beyond input and output pins.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rsa_simple.review_notes: Removed pipeline because the source does not evidence pipelining; added education for the explicit educational/demonstration purpose.

ttsky26c/tt_um_rtfce.summary: RTFCE is a multi-context temporal latency monitor that measures time between configurable start and end events and classifies each measurement as PASS, EARLY, or TIMEOUT. It supports three independent contexts sharing a single classification datapath via selectable fixed-priority or round-robin arbitration. The design includes a near-miss diagnostic and is fully configurable via a bidirectional bus. It is tested with a cocotb regression and requires no external hardware.
ttsky26c/tt_um_rtfce.review_notes: Added timer, comparator, and reconfigurable tags supported by the latency-monitor description.

ttsky26c/tt_um_saltworks_ndf_c32.summary: This project is a bit-serial neural dataflow fabric with MAC cells on a self-routing banyan switch, accompanied by a 32-bit RV32I-subset core. The MAC cells are generated from a Lean model proved correct and then formally verified against their arithmetic specification. The design includes a 14-cycle frame protocol and supports edge input/output for streaming data. It is notable for its formal verification approach, though the sequencer and glue logic are not part of the proofs. No external hardware is required.
ttsky26c/tt_um_saltworks_ndf_c32.review_notes: Removed communication tag; added accelerator and soc to reflect the integrated neural fabric plus processor.

ttsky26c/tt_um_semiqa_diff_opamp.summary: This is a fully-differential Class-AB folded-cascode operational amplifier implemented in SKY130A. It achieves 100.3 dB open-loop gain, 9.34 MHz GBW, and 0.71 mW power consumption, with an on-chip bias generator requiring only two external bias voltages. The amplifier is tested in a closed-loop configuration with external resistors and a differential signal source. Notable limitations include non-rail-to-rail output and reduced phase margin at low temperatures.

ttsky26c/tt_um_serdes_ephotonics.summary: This design implements a UCIe-style SERDES with an 8b/10b encoder/decoder, PRBS BIST, and a 3x-oversampling CDR. It includes a custom analog TX driver and RX slicer for full analog loopback, as well as a digital loopback mode. The link self-trains and can recover from disconnection. It requires a 66.5 MHz clock and minimal external hardware for analog loopback (a resistor and jumper wire).
ttsky26c/tt_um_serdes_ephotonics.review_notes: Removed verilog tag (language is Analog) and added mixed-signal; no silicon test reports so silicon-tested is not added.

ttsky26c/tt_um_silicon_art_vga_screensav.summary: This design displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo with an animated color gradient on a 640x480 VGA screen, with the 128x128 monochrome bitmap stored in a custom NOR ROM macro. The ROM's transistor pattern doubles as silicon art, making the logo visible in the diffusion layer of the fabricated chip. Inputs allow tiling the logo, switching to a solid color, and optionally controlling bouncing with a Gamepad Pmod. It requires a Tiny VGA Pmod and an optional Gamepad Pmod.

ttsky26c/tt_um_silicon_edge_ns_sar_adc.summary: This is an 8-bit differential SAR ADC designed as the core for a future noise-shaping SAR ADC. It uses a capacitive DAC and dynamic comparator, with a digital controller that provides timing for sampling and successive approximation. The fabricated version implements only the fundamental SAR conversion, with noise-shaping and DEM reserved for future work. It requires external reference voltages, a bias current, and a 96 kHz clock.

ttsky26c/tt_um_siliconsonics.summary: This digital sonar processor drives a 40 kHz ultrasonic transducer and demodulates echoes from two PDM microphones using square-wave I/Q correlators. It computes echo distance and bearing via CORDIC atan2 and a lookup table, reporting results on parallel pins and a 115200 baud UART. It supports single-shot and automatic measurements, single-microphone operation, and UART-tunable thresholds. External hardware includes a custom PCB with microphones and a transducer.
ttsky26c/tt_um_siliconsonics.review_notes: Added instrumentation and multi-tile tags supported by the measurement application and 2x2 tile size.

ttsky26c/tt_um_sirajmuhammad_bpsk_mod.summary: This design is a transmit-only BPSK baseband modulator that generates a PRBS-7 data stream, maps bits to +/-1 symbols, and shapes them with a polyphase root-raised-cosine filter. The output is an 8-bit signed sample bus. The PRBS-7 generator uses a 127-bit period that is short enough to verify by eye in a waveform. The design is intended for communication applications.

ttsky26c/tt_um_sishi888_tinymind.summary: TinyMind SoC is a processor-controlled inference accelerator that classifies eight binary feature inputs into three classes using a custom CPU, program ROM, and a clocked TinyMind core with confidence logic. Results are shown on a seven-segment display, with a decimal point indicating a close prediction, and a CPU run-enable input on uio[0]. The documentation does not report silicon results. No external hardware is required for RTL or gate-level simulation, though a physical demonstration needs feature switches, a run-enable input, clock, reset, and a seven-segment display.
ttsky26c/tt_um_sishi888_tinymind.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag and the invented 'header filter' sentence; added rom and microcontroller tags supported by the description.

ttsky26c/tt_um_sky26c.summary: This design implements a discrete-time first-order kinetic synapse driving a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron. It is a spiking neural network model with neuromorphic characteristics, using fixed-point arithmetic and saturating stages. The design has no external hardware and includes a test suite covering impulse response, steady state, rest condition, and firing behavior. No silicon test reports are provided.
ttsky26c/tt_um_sky26c.review_notes: Removed unsupported analog, biomedical, perceptron, and ADC tags; summary corrected to match the documented LIF neuron/synapse model.

ttsky26c/tt_um_sky_tpu_3x3.summary: Sky TPU 3x3 is an int4 band-engine TPU built around a 3x3 systolic array of pipelined 4-bit MACs with dual weight planes and an 8-deep accumulator bank. It includes a requantize plus ReLU readout path and an autonomous SPI-RAM DMA engine, and can chain layers on-chip for multi-layer neural network inference. Commands and data are driven over an 8-bit beat bus on ui[7:0], with results emitted as count-deterministic output frames on uo and uio[7:4]. The design is verified in simulation with cocotb against a Python golden model, and no silicon test results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_sky_tpu_3x3.review_notes: Replaced hallucinated audio/i2s/pwm/dac/comparator/analog tags with the TPU, systolic-array, MAC, ML, SPI, DMA and verification tags supported by the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_smunigan_ipv4_filter.summary: This project streams in a 20-byte IPv4 header one byte per clock cycle and decides whether to allow or drop the packet. It checks the header for errors, verifies the checksum, and identifies the protocol as TCP, UDP, or ICMP. After the final byte it outputs its decision based on whether the header is valid, has a valid checksum, and does not match the configurable blocked protocol, which defaults to ICMP. A full testbench is provided in test/test.py, and no silicon test results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_smunigan_ipv4_filter.review_notes: Removed tags describing a RISC-V CPU that does not exist; added communication, crc, fsm and verilog matching the IPv4 header filter.

ttsky26c/tt_um_snn_lif_neuron.summary: This design is a compact spiking neural network heart-beat classifier for Tiny Tapeout. It accepts 12-bit ADC samples on the input pins and uses a heartbeat segmenter, delta encoder, a five-neuron parallel SNN matrix, and a multi-class voter to classify beats into AAMI-style classes. An alarm output asserts after three consecutive anomaly classifications, and a diagnostic-valid output pulses when a class result is available. The documentation describes a cocotb test suite including an MIT-BIH stream excerpt, but no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_snn_lif_neuron.review_notes: Tags were entirely wrong (music/audio) and the summary invented a BPM tempo detector; replaced with SNN/biomedical tags and a source-supported summary.

ttsky26c/tt_um_spdif_to_i2s_kilpelaj.summary: This project is an S/PDIF (AES3 consumer) receiver that converts an incoming digital-audio stream into an I2S master output. It recovers timing from the incoming biphase-mark-coded stream using only the free-running Tiny Tapeout clock, with no external audio clock or PLL. The design also includes an analog comparator intended for off-chip mute-delay hysteresis, and a 1-bit PWM mono audio output. A self-checking testbench with a behavioural S/PDIF encoder and I2S decoder is provided, but no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_spdif_to_i2s_kilpelaj.review_notes: Proposed tags and summary described an unrelated ML accelerator; replaced with the actual S/PDIF-to-I2S audio receiver tags and summary.

ttsky26c/tt_um_spi_reg_bank.summary: This project is an 8-bit modified RISC-V-inspired processor with four registers, four instructions in instruction memory, and one data-memory register, using a single 8-bit instruction encoding. It exposes an SPI interface on uio[3:0], debug program-counter bits, a CPU-done signal, and the data-memory byte on uo[7:0]. The documentation describes the instruction encoding and ALU operations but does not provide a test procedure or silicon results. It originated as a club's first tapeout project, and no external hardware is listed.

ttsky26c/tt_um_synapticrw_lif_neuron.summary: This design implements a single leaky integrate and fire neuron in Verilog, with an 8-bit membrane potential that accumulates a settable weight on each SPIKE_IN rising edge, leaks at a selectable rate, and fires when it reaches a settable threshold. SPIKE_IN is synchronized with a two-flop synchronizer and edge detector, and after firing the neuron enters a four-cycle refractory period while SPIKE_OUT stays high. The top nibble of the membrane potential is shown in hex on the 7-segment display, and the full 8 bits are available on uio[7:0]. Weight, leak, and threshold are set with the demo board's DIP switches, and no external hardware is required.
ttsky26c/tt_um_synapticrw_lif_neuron.review_notes: Removed unsupported analog, biomedical, perceptron, and adc tags; added synchronizer, edge-detector, dip-switch, and 7-segment tags backed by the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_taiwoopesade_tempo_detect.summary: This design detects the tempo (BPM) of a live audio stream entirely in hardware using onset detection and a bit-serial divider. It receives 8-bit unsigned audio amplitude samples with a sample_valid strobe and outputs a latched BPM estimate, beat pulse, tempo-locked, confidence, and overflow flags. The onset detector uses a shift-based IIR envelope and refractory window, and the tempo estimator averages the last four intervals. The BPM divider computes bpm = 6000 / interval_samples using a 13-cycle bit-serial restoring divider, with no CPU or multiplier.
ttsky26c/tt_um_taiwoopesade_tempo_detect.review_notes: Replaced unsupported neuromorphic/analog/biomedical tags with audio, instrumentation, and bit-serial tags supported by the detailed documentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_tamagotchi.summary: TamaGotThis implements a Tamagotchi-style virtual pet that renders a cat to a VGA screen and allows interaction via a gamepad. The cat's battery decreases over time unless the player uses the gamepad to make it eat, sleep, or play; if the battery empties, the cat loses a life, and after nine lives the system reboots. The gamepad buttons control the cat's actions, and the VGA output displays the cat's state. The design is notable for combining game logic with VGA graphics and gamepad input.

ttsky26c/tt_um_terihear_tinytearout.summary: This design implements a bit-serial fixed-point multiplier with an ALU and DSP capabilities. It processes data one bit at a time, trading throughput for reduced hardware complexity. The multiplier is intended for digital signal processing applications. The design is notable for its bit-serial architecture and fixed-point arithmetic.

ttsky26c/tt_um_teuscher_eml_fabric.summary: This is an analog computing tile that implements a chain of two EML cells, each computing exp(u) minus ln(v) in current mode using translinear NPN loops. The chain is configured through a 29-bit scan chain and biased from an on-chip PTAT core with a trimmed reference resistor. The design is built at the transistor level and includes a test cell, with only the final output observable through the analog pins. Testing requires a source-measure unit and attention to the slow PTAT start-up at cold corners.
ttsky26c/tt_um_teuscher_eml_fabric.review_notes: Corrected voltage-reference and full-custom tags; added mixed-signal, current-mirror and characterization based on the analog current-mode and test-cell content.

ttsky26c/tt_um_tilesos_dual_adc.summary: This design implements an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) with a sigma-delta modulator and a voltage-controlled oscillator (VCO). It is intended for frequency counting applications and is verified on an FPGA platform. The design is notable for its mixed-signal approach. It uses two analog pads and a 1.8 V supply.
ttsky26c/tt_um_tilesos_dual_adc.review_notes: Removed unsupported fpga and frequency-counter tags; added adc, analog, vco and sigma-delta tags.

ttsky26c/tt_um_tnt_mosbius.summary: This is an analog, reconfigurable design built at the transistor level with full-custom layout. It is intended for educational purposes, demonstrating analog circuit design. The design likely includes programmable analog blocks. The documentation is sparse, but the tags indicate a focus on reconfigurable analog circuits.

ttsky26c/tt_um_toby43479_iox.summary: This design is an I2C-controlled IO expander that provides eight general-purpose input pins and eight output pins, each with PWM capability. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no details on how the device works, how to test it, or what external hardware is needed. The design interfaces with a microcontroller via I2C, as indicated by the scl and sda pins. It is notable for its PWM output capability.
ttsky26c/tt_um_toby43479_iox.review_notes: Added insufficient-doc; changed 'likely' to a statement supported by the scl/sda pins.

ttsky26c/tt_um_tomvdsch_tiny32_soc.summary: This design is a system-on-chip (SoC) that includes a RISC-V processor, UART, GPIO, timer, QSPI, and memory. It is intended for general-purpose computing and interfacing. The design is notable for integrating multiple subsystems on a single chip. The documentation is sparse, but the tags indicate a full SoC implementation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_tpcannon7_fir.summary: This design is an SPI-programmable 12-bit 36-tap FIR filter implemented in Verilog. It uses a standard SPI Pmod pinout with CS_N, MOSI, MISO, and SCLK, and has a FIR_MODE input. The design spans a 2x2 Tiny Tapeout tile and requires external SPI hardware for programming. The documentation is very thin, providing only the title and pinout.
ttsky26c/tt_um_tpcannon7_fir.review_notes: Tags and summary were about a VGA game, but the source is an SPI-programmable FIR filter.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ttsky26c_oguz.summary: This design implements a VGA scene with flash palette, mirrored dual-PSRAM state, and two independent gamepads. It uses QSPI flash and PSRAM for memory and gamepad inputs for control. The design outputs video via VGA. The documentation is very thin, providing no explanation of how it works or how to test it.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ttsky26c_oguz.review_notes: Removed incorrect tags and added tags based on the VGA, QSPI, and gamepad interfaces.

ttsky26c/tt_um_ucl_display.summary: This project is titled 'Flashing... lights' and its one-line description says it flashes 'U C L 2 0 2 7' on a 7-segment display. It is implemented in Verilog. The documentation is essentially empty, providing no explanation of how it works, how to test it, or what external hardware is required. No further details about its operation are available from the source.
ttsky26c/tt_um_ucl_display.review_notes: Replaced speculative display/counter tags with 7-segment and verilog tags supported by the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_undip_ann_q610.summary: This design implements a small feedforward artificial neural network accelerator with a 4-5-1 topology, using fixed-point arithmetic for activations and weights. It is controlled via an SPI-like interface that separates weight loading from inference, allowing repeated calculations without resending weights. The chip includes four bring-up modes—normal, heartbeat, loopback, and self-test—selectable by pins, to aid post-fabrication verification without external hardware. Notable for its compact, time-multiplexed datapath and built-in self-test, it requires an SPI-capable host for real inference tasks.
ttsky26c/tt_um_undip_ann_q610.review_notes: Removed unsupported silicon-tested tag; added cocotb based on documented testbench.

ttsky26c/tt_um_urish_rings.summary: This project generates a mesmerizing VGA display of hypnotic concentric rings that expand or contract from the center of the screen. It is designed as a demoscene-style visual effect for the Tiny Tapeout platform. The design takes speed and direction inputs and outputs RGB222 VGA signals with VSync and HSync. Testing requires connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, then applying power and releasing reset.
ttsky26c/tt_um_urish_rings.review_notes: Removed unsupported accelerator/alu/pipeline tags and corrected the summary, which described hardware not present in the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_urish_sic1.summary: This is an 8-bit single instruction computer that implements the SUBLEQ instruction, which subtracts and branches if less than or equal to zero. It has 8 input pins for data, 8 output pins for data, and control pins for run, halted, set_pc, load_data, and out_strobe. The design is a hardware implementation of a minimalist computer architecture, likely intended for educational purposes. No specific external hardware or test setup is described in the documentation.

ttsky26c/tt_um_urish_simon.summary: This is a Simon Says memory game where the player repeats an ever-growing sequence of colors shown on four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone, and the current level is shown on a two-digit seven-segment display. It uses four buttons, four LEDs, an optional speaker and a multiplexed seven-segment display, and can be tested with a dedicated Simon Says Pmod or with discrete components. A Wokwi simulation with wiring diagram is provided. Silicon testing confirmed it works as expected with the Pmod when the design is reset after selection.
ttsky26c/tt_um_urish_simon.review_notes: Removed unsupported education tag; added pmod and silicon-tested from the source.

ttsky26c/tt_um_usfq_adc_procmon.summary: This mixed-signal chip integrates an 8-bit tracking analog-to-digital converter and an on-chip process variation monitor. The ADC uses analog pins for a reference voltage and input signal, while the process monitor outputs ring oscillator frequencies to assess fabrication variations. It is designed for analog and variation-sensing applications, with digital outputs for the ADC count and oscillator signals. The design is notable for combining these functions in a single Tiny Tapeout tile, but detailed usage and test procedures are not provided.
ttsky26c/tt_um_usfq_adc_procmon.review_notes: Removed dac: the VDAC pin is part of the tracking ADC loop, not a documented standalone DAC.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vaishnavipatil5_configura.summary: This design implements an 8-entry, 8-bit content-addressable memory (CAM) that supports exact matching, masked pattern matching, and priority-based resolution. It can be configured via control pins to write data, load masks, and search, returning the address of the highest-priority match within one clock cycle. The CAM is intended for compact pattern-matching and lookup tasks, such as network routing or data filtering. The project includes thorough documentation and is verified with Cocotb and gate-level tests.
ttsky26c/tt_um_vaishnavipatil5_configura.review_notes: Removed tags not supported by the CAM functionality; added cocotb and lookup-table.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vedam_dual_port_ram.summary: This design is an 8-bit, 16-word dual-port RAM with arbitration and write-collision detection, fitting in a single Tiny Tapeout tile. It uses a shared multiplexed address/data bus and control signals to select ports and perform reads or writes, with outputs indicating collision and grant status. The RAM can be accessed independently from two ports, and simultaneous writes to the same address are detected. Verified with Cocotb tests, it requires no external hardware for operation on the demo board.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vedic_mult.summary: This project implements a 4-bit Vedic multiplier that multiplies two 4-bit numbers. The design is purely combinational, with inputs and outputs directly mapped to the chip pins. There is no documentation beyond the title and pin names, so the exact implementation details and testing procedures are unclear. It appears to be a simple demonstration design.
ttsky26c/tt_um_vedic_mult.review_notes: Removed unsupported alu and education tags; added insufficient-doc because documentation is only placeholder text.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vga_ca.summary: This design displays a cellular automaton on a VGA screen, outputting RGB and sync signals compatible with the Tiny VGA PMOD. The project title indicates the core function, but no details on the automaton rules, operation, or testing are provided. It requires a VGA monitor and the Tiny VGA PMOD for output. The documentation is essentially empty, leaving the implementation and usage unclear.
ttsky26c/tt_um_vga_ca.review_notes: Tags and summary are supported; no changes needed.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vga_clock.summary: This project implements a VGA display controller that shows the time on a VGA screen. It uses a PMOD interface for external connections and is implemented in Verilog. The design targets the Tiny Tapeout platform and has a working silicon test report. The time is adjusted with the inputs and the VGA PMOD type is selected with input[3].
ttsky26c/tt_um_vga_clock.review_notes: Removed unsupported clock-generator/timer/rtc tags, added silicon-tested, and corrected the summary to match the VGA clock behavior and silicon status.

ttsky26c/tt_um_vital_ap.summary: VITAL-AP is an adaptive 8-bit pixel register designed for low-power image and video processing, deciding whether to update or hold its value based on pixel value, transition magnitude, temporal behavior, edge activity, and motion activity. It aims to reduce switching activity and dynamic power by suppressing unnecessary updates, with controls for sensitivity, prediction enable, force update, and various awareness modes. The design can be tested with provided Verilog and Cocotb testbenches covering static, small, and large transitions, sequences, and force-update. It is a research-oriented project, but no silicon results are reported.
ttsky26c/tt_um_vital_ap.review_notes: Removed register-file and edge-detector (not supported) and added low-power, image-processing, cocotb.

ttsky26c/tt_um_voltage_amplifier_neuron.summary: This analog design implements an integrate-and-fire neuron based on the van Schaik 2001 model, with a buffered membrane voltage output and multiple inputs. It is an analog circuit intended for neuromorphic computing applications. The project documentation is minimal, providing only the title, one-line description, and pin names, with no details on operation or testing. External hardware and usage instructions are not specified.

ttsky26c/tt_um_wecallemjazzyfact_bgr_ldo.summary: This analog IP integrates a Banba current-mode bandgap reference (1.2V) and a folded-cascode low-dropout regulator (1.8V output) in Sky130. No external hardware or clock is required, and the documentation is clear and sufficient.

ttsky26c/tt_um_wokwi_473800139156677633.summary: This project implements a tiny Snake game on a 7-segment LED display, combined with an 8-state finite state machine (PRISM). The game speed is controlled by the 8-bit ui_in input, with larger values meaning slower speed. It requires only the 7-segment display on the demo board and a 10 kHz clock. The design is a simple Wokwi example that demonstrates two different designs in one, but changing from slow to fast speed may cause a delay due to the simple equality-based speed comparison.

ttsky26c/tt_um_wokwi_474471160110403585.summary: This project implements a Cylon-style LED scanner using an 8-bit shift register. A direction flip-flop controls whether the lit bit moves left or right, and turn-around detection reverses the direction at the ends. On reset, the first LED is lit and the direction is cleared. The outputs drive eight LEDs directly.

ttsky26c/tt_um_x4ntha_nova.summary: This is a 16-bit Data General Nova 1200 CPU implemented with a 4-bit nibble-serial datapath, capable of executing programs stored in external QSPI Flash and using PSRAM for data storage. It includes a UART for serial communication at 19,200 baud and drives diagnostic blinkenlights on the 7-segment display. The design requires the official Tiny Tapeout QSPI PMOD for Flash and PSRAM, and programs are written in Nova assembly and flashed via a provided Python script. Notable features include full programmability and interactive terminal I/O, though it relies on external hardware for memory and communication.

ttsky26c/tt_um_yjeum11.summary: This project implements a DTMF (Touch-Tone) decoder that identifies telephone keypad tones using the Goertzel algorithm to perform a discrete Fourier transform. It accepts 8-bit audio samples at 44.1 kHz via a ready-valid handshake and outputs the detected row and column indices after processing 1024 samples. The design requires an external audio source and a clock of 50 MHz, and it uses a bit-serial multiplier that may introduce latency between samples. It is a specialized DSP application for decoding standard DTMF signals.

ttsky26c/tt_um_z2a_rgb_mixer.summary: The RGB Mixer demo takes inputs from three digital encoders, debounces them, and produces three PWM outputs whose duty cycles correspond to the encoder values. It is intended to be tested by twisting each encoder and observing the brightness of LEDs connected to the PWM outputs. For debugging, setting the debug port to 0, 1, or 2 outputs the internal encoder value on the bidirectional pins. The design requires three external digital encoders and was reported working by the author, who checked all three channels.
